abstract: We derive sharp relative-entropy asymptotics for increasing propagation of chaos in the Curie--Weiss model at zero external field. For every fixed inverse temperature $0<β<1$, the relative entropy of a $k$-spin marginal with respect to the symmetric product measure is $$ \frac{β^2}{4(1-β)^2}\frac{k(k-1)}{N^2}+o\left(\frac{k^2}{N^2}\right),\qquad k=o(N). $$ At the critical inverse temperature $β=1$, the rate changes to $α_{\mathrm c}^2 k(k-1)/(4N)+o(k^2/N)$ in the regime $k=o(\sqrt N)$, where $α_{\mathrm c}$ is the second moment of the limiting quartic law of the rescaled magnetization. We also obtain asymptotics for sequences $β_N\uparrow1$ that interpolate between these two regimes. Crucially, the proof reveals that the pair correlations determine the leading correction to the likelihood ratio, providing precise control of both the chi-square divergence and relative entropy.
label: arXiv:2611.17911v1

summary.background:
- Curie–Weiss model: a simple model of magnetism where N spins all interact equally with the average spin.
- Inverse temperature β: a parameter controlling interaction strength; larger β means spins align more strongly. β=1 is the critical point where a phase change begins.
- Propagation of chaos: the statement that k particles in a large interacting system behave nearly independently as the system grows.
- Marginal: the joint distribution of just k of the N spins, ignoring the rest.
- Relative entropy (KL divergence) and chi-square divergence: measures of how different one probability distribution is from another.
- Likelihood ratio: the ratio of the true joint density to the product of independent densities; its correction term carries the dependence.
- Asymptotics / o(·) notation: exact leading-order behaviour as N grows, with the error term small relative to it.
- Quartic law: the limiting distribution of the rescaled magnetization at β=1, and α_c is its second moment.
summary.one_liner: Sharp asymptotics for the relative entropy and chi-square divergence of k-spin marginals in the Curie–Weiss model, showing how fast propagation of chaos occurs for subsystems below, at, and near the critical inverse temperature β=1.
summary.plain: The paper studies a model of many interacting magnets (spins) that each feel the average of all the others. It asks how close a small group of k spins, taken from a large system of N spins, looks to being fully independent of each other, measured by relative entropy (a standard way of scoring how far one probability distribution is from another). The authors give precise formulas for how this distance shrinks as N grows, with separate answers for high, critical, and in-between interaction strengths.
summary.why: The result pins down the exact rate at which the independence of a few particles emerges in a mean-field system, including a change of rate at the critical temperature. The text says the proof works through pair correlations controlling the leading correction to the likelihood ratio, which may be useful for other mean-field or particle-system questions, though the text does not spell out wider applications.

title: The speed of convergence for propagation of chaos in the mean-field Ising model

abstract: In this note, we prove local central limit theorems and expansions in the central limit theorem for inhomogeneous Markov chains satisfying a one-step lower ellipticity condition. As for the local limit theorem, in the general inhomogeneous case, compared with \cite{DS}, we are able to prove results without two-sided ellipticity, although only in the one-step case. Compared with \cite{PeligradLLT1,PeligradLLT2}, we are able to prove local limit theorems without a lower $ψ$-mixing condition. Concerning Edgeworth expansions, compared with \cite{DHPTRF1}, we are able to get results without two-sided ellipticity (under some sequential Diophantine conditions). Our conditions are then verified for Markov chains in a random dynamical environment with a one-sided Doeblin condition under very mild assumptions. For Markov chains in a random environment, we also consider the more general case of $φ$-mixing chains and then, under some mild periodicity assumptions on the environment, we prove local central limit theorems and first-order Edgeworth expansions (without any ellipticity assumptions), matching the results for deterministic homogeneous chains. When the chain is driven by a topologically mixing subshift of finite type, we obtain high-order expansions for $φ$-mixing chains under some Diophantine conditions of a deterministic system generated by a periodic point. We then apply our results to bounded additive functionals of posterior states in disordered quantum trajectories and establish local central limit theorems and first-order Edgeworth expansions.
label: arXiv:2611.20233v1

summary.background:
- Markov chain: a random process where the next state depends only on the current state.
- Inhomogeneous: the transition rules change with time (or with a random environment).
- Central limit theorem: sums of random quantities look approximately normal (bell-shaped) when scaled.
- Local limit theorem: a finer version giving approximate probabilities for individual values, not just ranges.
- Edgeworth expansion: correction terms added to the normal approximation to improve accuracy.
- Ellipticity / Doeblin / mixing conditions: technical assumptions saying the chain forgets its past and does not get stuck in restricted moves.
- Diophantine condition: a number-theoretic condition on how well quantities can be approximated by fractions, used to control periodic behavior.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves local limit theorems and Edgeworth expansions for sums of inhomogeneous Markov chains under a one-step lower ellipticity condition, including random-environment and quantum-trajectory settings.
summary.plain: The paper studies sums of values taken along a chain of random steps, where the rules for each step can change over time. Classical limit results say such sums settle into a bell-shaped pattern; this work gives finer statements about how likely each exact value is, and corrections to the bell shape. The authors state that their conditions hold in several settings, including chains driven by random environments and a model of quantum trajectories.
summary.why: The text claims weaker conditions than several earlier results (no two-sided ellipticity, no lower psi-mixing in places), which matters for applying these tools to more models. The connection to quantum trajectories is stated only briefly, so its practical relevance is not clear from the text alone.

title: Local Limit Theorems and Edgeworth Expansions for some classes of inhomogeneous Markov chains

abstract: This paper is a continuation of our previous work on global regularity theory for the sphere-valued fractional harmonic maps which was initialized by several authors such as Millot-Pegon-Schikorra and Millot-Sire. By adapting the powerful quantitative stratification approach developed by Naber-Valtorta on harmonic mappings, we establish a corresponding stratification theory for fractional harmonic maps, from which an optimal first order global regularity theory and the rectifiable structure of singular sets follow.
label: arXiv:2611.19817v1

summary.background:
- Harmonic map: a map between spaces that minimises a Dirichlet-type energy, a geometric analogue of a smooth, stretch-minimising deformation.
- Fractional harmonic map: the same idea with a nonlocal energy, so each point's behaviour depends on distant points too.
- Sphere-valued: the map's outputs always lie on a sphere, a common constraint in geometry and physics.
- Regularity: whether solutions are smooth or only smooth away from a small singular set.
- Quantitative stratification: sorting singular points by how much the map looks like a lower-dimensional symmetric object at each scale.
- Rectifiable set: a set that is, up to small error, made of pieces of smooth surfaces, so it has a well-defined size and shape.
- First-order regularity: control of the map's first derivatives (its rate of change).
summary.one_liner: The paper extends quantitative stratification (a Naber-Valtorta technique) to sphere-valued fractional harmonic maps, yielding optimal first-order global regularity and rectifiable structure of the singular sets.
summary.plain: The paper studies "maps" that assign a point on a sphere to each point of a space, chosen to minimise a fractional energy, a version of the usual smoothness-favouring energy with a long-range twist. Such maps can develop singularities, meaning places where they stop being smooth. The authors adapt a powerful technique for classifying how singular a map can be, and use it to show how regular these maps are globally and how the singular set is structured.
summary.why: Regularity results say when solutions of these equations stay smooth, which is the core question for this kind of geometric variational problem. The text presents this as a continuation of the authors' earlier work and does not claim wider consequences, so its reach beyond this model setting is unclear from the text alone.

title: Optimal first order global regularity for fractional harmonic maps into spheres

abstract: The solution to a finite-dimensional Hamilton-Jacobi equation is classically known to admit a variational representation in two situations: when the nonlinearity is convex or concave, by the Hopf-Lax formula; and when the initial condition is convex or concave, by the Hopf formula. We identify a third situation: the space variable is split into two groups of coordinates, the nonlinearity is the scalar product of the two corresponding partial gradients, and the initial condition is the sum of a convex function of the first group of coordinates and of an arbitrary Lipschitz function of the second group. This structure is precisely that of the Hamilton-Jacobi equations describing the limit free energy of perceptron models. We illustrate this point by identifying the limit free energy of a class of perceptron models that can be rewritten as bipartite spin glasses, with Ising spins in one layer and bounded soft spins in the other. We also discuss how to extend the approach to several other classes of models, including general Ising and spherical perceptrons, possibly with labelled patterns.
label: arXiv:2611.20870v1

summary.background:
- Hamilton-Jacobi equation: a first-order PDE whose solution can often be found by optimizing over paths (a variational formula).
- Classical cases: Hopf-Lax formula (convex or concave nonlinearity) and Hopf formula (convex or concave initial condition).
- Lipschitz function: a function whose steepness is bounded.
- Perceptron: a simple one-layer neural network model; "free energy" here is a statistical-physics quantity describing its typical behaviour in the large-size limit.
- Spin glass: a disordered magnetic system with random interactions, used as a model for complex systems.
- Ising spin: a variable taking values ±1; soft spin: a continuous variable in a bounded range.
summary.one_liner: The paper identifies a third class of finite-dimensional Hamilton-Jacobi equations (split variables, scalar-product nonlinearity, convex-plus-Lipschitz initial data) that admits a variational representation, and applies it to limit free energies of perceptron and bipartite spin-glass models.
summary.plain: The paper studies a type of equation that describes how a quantity changes over time or space, and asks when its solution can be written as an optimization ("best choice") formula. It finds a new family of cases where this works, beyond the two classical ones. The authors show the family matches the equations that give the limiting free energy of certain neural-network-like "perceptron" models.
summary.why: Perceptron models are simple versions of neural networks studied in statistical physics and learning theory, so a closed-form variational solution for their limiting behaviour is useful for theory. The text does not claim wider impact, and its extensions to other models are described only as possibilities.

title: On Hamilton-Jacobi equations and perceptron models

abstract: Based on the recently developed random Brouwer fixed point theorem and the theory of stable compactness, we establish a random Knaster--Kuratowski--Mazurkiewicz (KKM) mapping principle in Hausdorff topological $L^0$-modules. As consequences of this principle, we obtain several results on fixed points, minimax problems, variational inequalities, and conditional games. These results solve a large class of noncompact problems in random functional analysis and its applications.
label: arXiv:2611.18408v1

summary.background:
- Fixed point theorem: a result guaranteeing that a map from a set to itself has at least one point it leaves unchanged; Brouwer's theorem is the classic example.
- KKM principle: a combinatorial covering lemma (Knaster–Kuratowski–Mazurkiewicz) that underpins many fixed-point and minimax results.
- Minimax problem: finding a value that is simultaneously the best worst-case outcome for one player and the worst best-case for another.
- Variational inequality: a condition describing an equilibrium or optimum in optimization and economics.
- Compactness: a property of sets that roughly means they are closed and bounded in a finite-type sense; "noncompact" problems lack it, which is why standard theorems fail.
- L^0-modules: spaces of random variables, used to model randomness within functional analysis.
- Stable compactness: a technical notion from the paper's framework, not explained in the text.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves a random version of the KKM mapping principle in Hausdorff topological L^0-modules, using the random Brouwer fixed point theorem and stable compactness, and derives fixed-point, minimax, variational inequality and conditional game results from it.
summary.plain: This paper is about extending a classic mathematical tool, the KKM principle (a covering-type result that guarantees certain points exist), to settings where the rules change randomly from one outcome to another. The authors build this version and use it to derive several existence results for fixed points, minimax problems, variational inequalities and conditional games. The text presents these as ways to handle problems that lack the usual compactness assumptions.
summary.why: Many economic, optimization and game-theory models involve randomness and infinite-dimensional spaces, where standard existence theorems often do not apply. The paper claims to cover a large class of such noncompact problems, though the abstract alone does not show how broad or practical that coverage is.

title: The random KKM mapping principle and its applications

abstract: We investigate the Fourier algebra of a certain class of groupoids, called the HLS groupoids, within Paterson's continuous framework for locally compact groupoids. We develop the basic harmonic analysis of HLS groupoids by obtaining concrete descriptions of their topology, representations, and Fourier algebra. We then study the restriction maps from the Fourier algebra $A(\mathcal{G})$ of an HLS groupoid $\mathcal{G}$ to the Fourier algebras of its isotropy subgroups, and construct explicit norm-preserving lifts for these restriction maps. As applications, we describe the norm of every element of $A(\mathcal{G})$ in terms of the norms of its restrictions to the isotropy subgroups. We prove an analogue of Leptin's theorem characterizing when $A(\mathcal{G})$ has a bounded approximate identity. We also show that the Gelfand spectrum of $A(\mathcal{G})$ is homeomorphic to $\mathcal{G}$. Finally, using abstract arguments that, unlike our methods for HLS groupoids, do not yield explicit constructions, we show that norm-preserving lifts exist and that the Gelfand spectrum of the Fourier algebra is homeomorphic to the groupoid for every étale groupoid. This generalizes Eymard's theorem and answers a question of Paterson for étale groupoids.
label: arXiv:2611.21572v1

summary.background:
- Groupoid: a generalization of a group where composition is only defined for some pairs of elements.
- Locally compact / étale groupoid: groupoids with a topology that is locally well-behaved; étale means the structure is locally like a discrete space.
- Fourier algebra: an algebra of functions on a group or groupoid, generalizing the classical Fourier transform setting.
- Isotropy subgroup: the subgroup of elements that start and end at the same point.
- Eymard's theorem: a classical result identifying the spectrum of the Fourier algebra of a locally compact group with the group itself.
- Leptin's theorem: a classical result characterizing when the Fourier algebra has a bounded approximate identity (a near-unit with controlled size).
- Gelfand spectrum: the set of nonzero multiplicative functionals on a commutative algebra, which can be used to recover the underlying space.
summary.one_liner: The paper studies Fourier algebras of HLS groupoids within Paterson's framework, constructing norm-preserving lifts of restriction maps to isotropy subgroups, proving a Leptin-type bounded approximate identity criterion, and extending Eymard's theorem on the Gelfand spectrum to all étale groupoids.
summary.plain: The paper looks at a algebra of functions attached to a "groupoid," a mathematical structure that generalizes groups by allowing some pairs of elements to be unable to combine. For a special class of these structures (HLS groupoids), the authors describe the algebra concretely, show how its norms relate to simpler pieces called isotropy subgroups, and show its underlying space can be recovered from it. They also use more abstract arguments to extend some of these results to all étale groupoids, answering a question posed by Paterson.
summary.why: Fourier algebras link abstract group-like structures to analysis, and this work extends classical results such as Eymard's and Leptin's theorems to broader settings. The text does not say what applications beyond pure harmonic analysis it may have, so its wider reach is uncertain from this abstract alone.

title: Fourier Algebras of HLS Groupoids: Lifts, Amenability, and Spectrum

abstract: We prove that the differential of a non-constant conformal curve between Euclidean spaces has full rank outside a discrete set. In particular, conformal curves are real-analytic outside a discrete set. We provide examples of entire associative and coassociative conformal curves with a non-empty singular set. We show that every non-constant Special Lagrangian conformal curve is a real-analytic conformal immersion. We also prove that a non-constant conformal curve has discrete fibers.
label: arXiv:2611.21505v1

summary.background:
- Conformal map: a map that preserves angles locally (here, in the sense defined in the source paper, between Euclidean spaces).
- Differential / full rank: the best linear approximation of the map at a point; full rank means it does not collapse any direction.
- Singular set: the points where the differential fails to have full rank.
- Discrete set: a set whose points are isolated from one another, with no clustering.
- Real-analytic: locally expressible by convergent power series; very smooth.
- Fibers: the sets of inputs that map to the same output.
- Associative, coassociative and Special Lagrangian: special classes of submanifolds from geometric analysis, which the examples concern.
summary.one_liner: The paper shows that the differential of a non-constant conformal curve between Euclidean spaces has full rank outside a discrete set, with consequences for real-analyticity, fibers, and examples of associative, coassociative and Special Lagrangian conformal curves.
summary.plain: The paper studies "conformal curves," maps between spaces of any dimension that preserve angles in a particular sense. It asks where such a map stops being well behaved (where it squashes space down instead of locally stretching it without collapse). The authors find that these bad points are isolated, forming a discrete set, rather than spread over large regions.
summary.why: Knowing that the troublesome points are isolated tells us conformal curves are, outside those points, as smooth and regular as the analysis allows. The text does not say how far the results reach beyond the examples it lists, so broader significance is uncertain.

title: Singular sets of conformal curves are discrete

abstract: In this paper, we introduce and study a generalized notion of multidimensional mixed Bohr radii for holomorphic functions defined on the unit ball of the finite-dimensional Minkowski sequence space with values in complex Banach spaces. We first prove that the multidimensional mixed Bohr radius is positive for every non-null bounded linear operator whose norm is sufficiently small relative to the scaling parameter. We then determine the exact asymptotic behavior of the multidimensional mixed Bohr radius for infinite-dimensional Banach spaces of finite cotype and we obtain analogous bounds for spaces without finite cotype. Finally, for concave Banach lattices and summing operators, we prove lower bounds that involve a logarithmic factor. These results connect classical scalar Bohr phenomena with operator-valued and Banach space valued settings, and highlight how the geometry of the spaces and the mapping properties of the operator influence coefficient estimates and their dependence on dimension. Several examples illustrate the consistency of our results with the classical Bohr radius and the sharp Defant--Frerick asymptotics.
label: arXiv:2611.19268v1

summary.background:
- Holomorphic function: a complex-differentiable function, which can be written as a power series.
- Bohr radius: the largest radius r such that a bounded holomorphic function's power series, evaluated inside that radius, stays bounded by the same bound; the classical result is about one-variable functions on the unit disc.
- Banach space: a complete normed vector space; functions here take values in such spaces, not just in numbers.
- Unit ball and Minkowski sequence space: the set of points of size at most one in a finite-dimensional space with a specified norm; the sequence space is the setting for the multidimensional version.
- Bounded linear operator and norm: a structure-preserving map between spaces and a measure of its maximum stretching.
- Cotype: a geometric measure of how "spread out" a Banach space is; finite cotype is a restriction on the space's geometry.
- Banach lattice, concave Banach lattice, summing operator: ordered Banach spaces and a class of operators with good summation properties, used to state the lower bounds.
- Asymptotic behavior: how a quantity behaves as the dimension grows large.
summary.one_liner: The paper defines multidimensional mixed Bohr radii for holomorphic functions on the unit ball of a finite-dimensional Minkowski sequence space with Banach-space values, and studies their positivity, asymptotics under cotype assumptions, and lower bounds for concave Banach lattices and summing operators.
summary.plain: The paper studies a generalized version of the Bohr radius, a classical quantity that measures how far a complex-valued function's power series can be bounded in size while its coefficients stay controlled. Here the functions take values in more general spaces of vectors or operators, and the domain is a higher-dimensional ball. The text reports results on when this radius is positive, how it behaves for large dimensions in spaces of finite cotype (a geometric property of the space), and some lower bounds for concave Banach lattices and summing operators.
summary.why: Bohr radii link complex analysis to coefficient estimates and to the geometry of the underlying space, so the paper's results on how the radius depends on dimension and space geometry may be of interest to specialists in the area. The abstract says the results are consistent with the classical Bohr radius and with sharp Defant–Frerick asymptotics, but I have not checked how these compare with other work in the field.

title: Multidimensional mixed Bohr radii for Banach space valued holomorphic functions

abstract: We establish a characterisation of the standard implementation for actions of locally compact quantum groups on von Neumann algebras, extending results of Daws-Skalski-Viselter and Haagerup. As a consequence, we prove that taking the standard implementation respects morphisms of quantum groups. We also prove that several natural conditions expressing relative $ρ$-invariance for n.s.f. weights are equivalent.
label: arXiv:2611.21776v1

summary.background:
- Von Neumann algebras: algebras of bounded operators on a Hilbert space, the mathematical setting for quantum measurements.
- Locally compact quantum groups: a noncommutative generalisation of locally compact groups, where symmetry is described by algebra rather than by points.
- Actions of quantum groups: ways a quantum group can "act" on a von Neumann algebra, analogous to a group acting on a space.
- Standard implementation: a canonical representation of an action on a Hilbert space, used to make the action concrete.
- Weights (n.s.f. weights): generalised, possibly infinite, ways of assigning sizes to positive elements of an algebra; "relative ρ-invariance" means the weight transforms in a controlled way under the action.
- Morphisms: structure-preserving maps between quantum groups.
summary.one_liner: The paper characterises the standard implementation of locally compact quantum group actions on von Neumann algebras, extending results of Daws-Skalski-Viselter and Haagerup, shows it respects quantum group morphisms, and proves equivalence of several conditions for relative ρ-invariance of n.s.f. weights.
summary.plain: This is a research paper in pure mathematics about "quantum symmetries": ways that abstract quantum versions of groups can act on collections of operators, which generalise the algebra of ordinary measurements. The authors give a new description of a canonical way to turn such an action into a standard form, and show that this canonical form behaves well when you map one quantum group to another. They also show that several different-looking conditions describing when a certain kind of weight (a generalised way of measuring size) is preserved in a relative sense are in fact equivalent.
summary.why: The text states the results as extensions of earlier work by Daws, Skalski and Viselter and by Haagerup, so it is a technical step within an established line of research. Its relevance beyond operator algebra specialists is not discussed in the text, so wider impact is unclear from this abstract alone.

title: Actions of quantum groups: the standard implementation and relatively invariant weights

abstract: In this paper, we study Fourier and convolution inequalities on locally compact quantum groups in the presence of the scaling group. For $1\le p\le 2$, we investigate a family of scaling Fourier transforms and the associated norms $H_{p,θ}(\mathbb G)$, and we show that $H_{p,θ}(\mathbb G)<1$ for the real quantum $az+b$ group and $0<θ<1$, $1<p<2$. We also investigate scaling convolution for locally compact quantum groups and, by extending the ordinary convolution, obtain the corresponding scaling Young inequality in four different regions. In Young Region~II, under $1<p,s<2$ and $2\leq r<\infty$, we construct sequences proving norm one at every effective vertex and prove strict inequality at every other effective point.
label: arXiv:2611.19855v1

summary.background:
- Group: a set with a consistent way of combining elements, such as rotations or shifts; a locally compact group is one where one can do calculus and integration.
- Fourier transform: rewrites a function in terms of frequencies; norms of this transform measure how it changes sizes between function spaces.
- Convolution: a way of blending two functions into a third; Young's inequality bounds the size of this blend.
- Quantum group: a non-commutative generalisation of a group, where the order of operations matters, studied within operator algebras.
- Scaling group: a family of symmetries that stretches or shrinks the structure, here used to define the parameterised transforms.
- Norm and strict inequality: a size measure; "norm one" means the bound is attained, while "strict" means it is never attained at other points.
- The "az+b" group: the group of affine maps x ↦ ax+b, a standard non-commutative example.
summary.one_liner: The paper extends scaling Fourier and Young-type convolution inequalities from classical groups to locally compact quantum groups, using the scaling group, and analyses norms for the real quantum az+b group.
summary.plain: This paper is about a family of inequalities that limit how large a transformed signal can be compared with the original, set in a generalized, non-commutative version of symmetry groups. The authors study a parameterised family of Fourier-type transforms and the norms that measure them, and they show one such norm is below 1 for a specific example (the real quantum "az+b" group) under certain parameter ranges. They also build a scaling version of convolution, a way of combining two functions, and derive a corresponding Young-type inequality in four regions of parameters.
summary.why: Sharp constants and extremal sequences in Fourier and Young inequalities are classical tools in analysis, and extending them to quantum groups is a natural step in that programme. The text does not indicate applications beyond this theory, so its wider significance is unclear from the excerpt alone.

title: Scaling Fourier Inequalities for Locally Compact Quantum Groups

abstract: We give new relations in the kernel of the foam evaluation. As a consequence we obtain categorifications of all the Kelulé relations introduced by Morrison. Along the way, we discover an equivalent set of relations for which we provide categorifications as well.
label: arXiv:2611.20184v1

summary.background:
- Representation theory and algebra: relations are equations that a structure must satisfy.
- Categorification: replacing a number-level identity with a richer structure (such as a category) whose "shadow" recovers the original identity.
- Foam evaluation: a way of assigning values to decorated surfaces ("foams") used in knot homology, with a kernel of relations that evaluate to zero.
- Kekulé relations: algebraic relations introduced by Morrison; the abstract gives no further detail on them.
- The abstract is brief, so full definitions and proofs are not visible here.
summary.one_liner: The paper finds new relations in the kernel of the foam evaluation and uses them to categorify all the Kekulé relations introduced by Morrison, plus an equivalent family of relations that also receives categorifications.
summary.plain: This is a research-level paper in algebra about a family of algebraic rules (called Kekulé relations) that were proposed by Morrison. The authors show how to lift these rules from simple numerical identities to richer structures built from geometric "foams," which is the sense of "categorification." They also find an equivalent set of rules and give categorifications for those as well.
summary.why: Categorification tends to link algebraic invariants to deeper structures, and foam evaluations are part of that framework, so the work is of interest to specialists in knot and link homology. The short abstract does not show what the categorifications are used for beyond this, so any wider connection is unclear from the text alone.

title: Two categorifications of the Kekulé relations

abstract: We prove the conjecture of Kang, Lawrie, and Song that Zhu's $C_2$-algebra of a simply-laced boundary admissible affine vertex algebra is isomorphic to the Jacobian ring of an invariant potential obtained by lifting a polynomial twisted period from a Cartan subalgebra via the Chevalley isomorphism. We further identify the $C_2$-algebras of the corresponding Drinfeld-Sokolov reductions with the Jacobian rings of the restrictions of this potential to Slodowy slices. We also extend the Jacobian presentation to non-simply-laced principal boundary admissible affine vertex algebras, where the restriction of the potential to the Cartan subalgebra satisfies a Dunkl-singularity equation with root-length-dependent multiplicities.
label: arXiv:2611.20659v1

summary.background:
- Affine vertex algebra: an infinite-dimensional algebraic structure from conformal field theory, built from a Lie algebra and a level (a number parameter).
- Admissible level: a special, non-generic value of that parameter where the representation theory is well-behaved.
- Zhu's C_2-algebra: a commutative, finite-dimensional quotient of a vertex algebra that captures its leading structure.
- Jacobian ring: the quotient of polynomials by the partial derivatives of a potential function; it measures how degenerate the function's critical points are.
- Chevalley isomorphism: a standard identification between invariant polynomials on a Lie algebra and on its Cartan subalgebra (a maximal commutative subalgebra).
- Drinfeld-Sokolov reduction and Slodowy slices: a procedure that reduces a symmetry algebra to a smaller one, and a transverse slice to a nilpotent orbit used to model that reduction.
- Simply-laced vs non-simply-laced: whether a Lie algebra's root system has all roots of equal length; Dunkl equations are a generalization of ordinary differential equations suited to unequal root lengths.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves a conjecture of Kang, Lawrie and Song that the C_2-algebra (Zhu's finite-dimensional quotient) of simply-laced boundary admissible affine vertex algebras is a Jacobian ring of an invariant potential built from a polynomial twisted period, and extends the description to non-simply-laced principal cases.
summary.plain: This paper is about a precise algebraic dictionary between two kinds of mathematical objects that arise in the study of symmetries of quantum field theories. The authors show that a certain finite-dimensional algebra attached to a family of such symmetry structures matches exactly the algebra of a polynomial "potential" function, which was conjectured earlier by Kang, Lawrie and Song. They also check that the same matching holds for related reduction constructions, and they extend the result to a class of cases where the underlying root structure is not simply-laced.
summary.why: Matching a conjectured identity to a proof is useful for specialists because it ties vertex algebra theory to singularity theory via Jacobian rings and Slodowy slices. The text does not discuss wider applications, so any further connections should be treated as speculative.

title: Polynomial twisted periods and affine vertex algebras

abstract: Zywina recently showed that infinitely many elliptic curves over $\mathbb{Q}$ have rank $2$, settling a long-standing open question. We explore the analytic version of this problem, showing that every elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$ has infinitely many quadratic twists with analytic rank either $2$ or $4$, subject to GRH. We also obtain, under the same assumption, infinitely many congruent number curves with odd analytic rank between $3$ and $17$.
label: arXiv:2611.21447v1

summary.background:
- Elliptic curve: a smooth cubic curve; its rational points form a group with a finite-rank part.
- Rank: the number of independent rational points of infinite order.
- Analytic rank: the order of vanishing at a central point of an L-function, a function encoding arithmetic data of the curve; it is conjecturally equal to the rank.
- Quadratic twist: a related curve obtained by a standard rescaling using a square-free integer.
- Congruent number curve: a curve whose rank determines whether a given integer is a congruent number (area of a right triangle with rational sides).
- GRH (Generalized Riemann Hypothesis): an unproven conjecture about the locations of zeros of L-functions; results assuming it are conditional.
- Zywina's result: unconditional proof that infinitely many elliptic curves over Q have rank 2.
summary.one_liner: Under the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, the paper shows every elliptic curve over Q has infinitely many quadratic twists with analytic rank 2 or 4, and infinitely many congruent number curves with odd analytic rank from 3 to 17, extending Zywina's recent result on rank 2 curves to the analytic setting.
summary.plain: The paper concerns elliptic curves, which are smooth curves defined by cubic equations and studied for their rational solutions. Each curve has a number, its rank, counting how many independent rational solutions it has, and an "analytic rank" that is a related quantity computed from a special function attached to the curve. The authors show, assuming a widely believed but unproven conjecture (GRH), that infinitely many curves in a standard family have analytic rank 2 or 4, and that infinitely many congruent number curves have odd analytic rank between 3 and 17.
summary.why: Whether elliptic curves of a given rank exist in infinite supply is a classical question in number theory, and the analytic version is easier to test with computable quantities. The result is conditional on GRH, so it is a partial step rather than a settled answer; its wider connections are to the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, which links analytic rank to the rank itself.

title: On elliptic curves with prescribed analytic rank at least $2$

abstract: For a positive integer $n\ge 2$, we look at the number of solutions of the Diophantine equation $$ n(x_1+\cdots+x_n)=x_1\cdots x_n. $$ Denoting by $f(n)$ this number we show that $\liminf_{n\to\infty} \log f(n)/\log n=0$.
label: arXiv:2611.20783v1

summary.background:
- Diophantine equation: a polynomial equation whose solutions are required to be whole numbers.
- Positive integer: a whole number 1, 2, 3, and so on.
- Liminf (limit inferior): the smallest value a quantity approaches infinitely often as n grows; here it says the ratio is close to 0 for infinitely many n.
- Logarithm: a function that turns multiplicative growth into additive growth; log f(n)/log n compares the size of f(n) on a log scale.
- Erdős problems: a collection of open questions posed by the mathematician Paul Erdős.
summary.one_liner: The paper studies f(n), the number of solutions of the Diophantine equation n(x_1+...+x_n) = x_1...x_n, and shows that liminf of log f(n)/log n equals 0.
summary.plain: The paper looks at a equation about whole numbers: multiply n by the sum of n unknown whole numbers, and set that equal to their product. For each n, it counts how many solutions exist, and asks how that count grows as n gets large. The author shows that along some sequence of n, the count grows so slowly that its logarithm is negligible compared with log n.
summary.why: This is a question about the Erdős problem on the equation, and the result is a precise statement about how solution counts behave for large n. The text does not say how it connects to wider work, and the abstract alone does not show whether the methods are new.

title: On Erdős' last equation

abstract: We consider the period map on families of parabolic Higgs bundle moduli spaces with varying parabolic weights $α$ and Higgs field eigenvalues $σ$. We assemble the moduli spaces into a smooth family $π:\mathscr M\toΛ_0$ where $Λ_0$ encodes the admissible pairs $(α,σ)$, and define parallel transport for homology along paths in $Λ_0$. By generalizing a classical theorem of Duistermaat and Heckman, we prove that the period map is affine linear in $(α,σ)$, with slope governed by the curvature class of a principal torus bundle over $\mathscr M$. For the four-dimensional moduli spaces of types $E_6,E_7,E_8$, we compute these classes to get explicit formulas for the period maps.
label: arXiv:2611.21990v2

summary.background:
- Moduli space: a space whose points are classified objects (here, bundles on a curve with extra structure).
- Higgs bundle: a vector bundle paired with a matrix-valued field; these spaces carry a hyperkähler (special kind of curved, symplectic) geometry.
- Parabolic structure and weights: extra data at marked points on a curve that act like adjustable numerical settings.
- Period map: assigns to each space the integrals of its geometric structure over chosen loops (homology classes); parallel transport tracks these as parameters move.
- Duistermaat–Heckman theorem: a classical result that certain integrals over symplectic spaces vary piecewise polynomially; the paper generalizes it to this setting.
- Curvature class and principal torus bundle: the topological data that sets the slope of the straight-line change.
- Exceptional types E6, E7, E8: the three largest exceptional symmetry-type root systems from Lie theory.
summary.one_liner: The paper studies how periods (integrals over homology cycles) of hyperkähler structures vary across families of parabolic Higgs bundle moduli spaces indexed by parabolic weights and Higgs field eigenvalues, proving the period map is affine linear and computing explicit formulas for the four-dimensional E6, E7 and E8 cases.
summary.plain: This is about a family of geometric spaces, each built from a curve together with extra data such as weights and a "Higgs field" (a twisting object attached to the space). The authors let those control numbers vary, track how the spaces change as the numbers move, and ask how certain measurements of the spaces, called periods, change along the way. They prove that these periods change in a simple straight-line way as the control numbers change, and for four-dimensional spaces of three exceptional types they compute the exact formulas.
summary.why: Hyperkähler spaces of this kind arise in the study of symmetry and duality in mathematical physics, and periods are a standard way to encode their geometry, so a clean formula is useful for comparing them. The text does not say how far the results extend beyond the stated cases, so the wider significance is uncertain from this abstract alone.

title: Hyperkähler Periods in Families of Parabolic Higgs Bundle Moduli Spaces

abstract: We determine the moduli space of complex projective canonical threefolds of volume $1/420$. It consists of an irreducible rational component of dimension $33$ and two isolated points, represented by the explicitly constructed rigid threefolds Vega and Altair.
label: arXiv:2611.18357v1

summary.background:
- Algebraic geometry studies shapes defined by polynomial equations, here over complex numbers.
- A threefold is a shape with three complex dimensions (six real dimensions).
- "Canonical" refers to a mild class of singularities (pointed spots) allowed on the shape, which is standard in the minimal model program for classifying such shapes.
- "Volume" here is an algebro-geometric invariant (the self-intersection of the canonical class), not an ordinary measured volume.
- A moduli space is a parameter space whose points correspond to isomorphism classes of such shapes.
- "Rational" means the component is parametrized by rational functions in a loose sense, i.e. it is geometrically simple; "rigid" means the shape admits no continuous deformations.
summary.one_liner: The paper classifies the moduli space (the family of all possible shapes) of complex projective canonical threefolds whose volume equals the minimal value 1/420, finding an irreducible rational component of dimension 33 plus two isolated rigid examples, Vega and Altair.
summary.plain: The paper studies a specific class of higher-dimensional geometric shapes, called canonical threefolds, that have the smallest possible "volume" of 1/420. It determines the full family of such shapes: one connected family that can be varied continuously, plus two special shapes that cannot be deformed at all. The two isolated shapes are named Vega and Altair and are constructed explicitly.
summary.why: Finding the smallest possible volume for these objects and listing every example that reaches it is a precise, concrete result in the classification of higher-dimensional shapes. The text does not say what wider applications it has, so any further connections are unclear from this summary alone.

title: The Moduli of Canonical Threefolds of Minimum Volume

abstract: The Extended Persistent Homology Transform (XPHT) describes a shape through the extended persistence diagrams of its directional height functions. We present an algorithm for computing a finite directional sample of the three-dimensional XPHT from a triangulated boundary. Our main construction determines essential first-homology pairings by combining an ordered tree-cotree decomposition with evaluation-dual cocycles. The decomposition supplies a homology basis compatible with the height filtration, while the cocycles are used to determine the essential birth-death pairs. Degree-zero persistence and duality determine the remaining boundary diagrams. Under the boundary-reduction hypotheses and with critical-point sign labels, these diagrams yield the extended persistence of the solid. The resulting procedure uses graph constructions and linear algebra over F2 on boundary meshes extracted from three-dimensional binary images.
label: arXiv:2611.20413v1

summary.background:
- Homology: a way of counting holes and voids of different dimensions in a shape (first homology here roughly means loops and tunnels).
- Persistent homology: tracks when holes appear (birth) and disappear (death) as a shape is filtered by a height function, recorded as a diagram of birth-death pairs.
- Extended persistence: a variant that also keeps track of features that are not paired in the usual way, using sign labels on critical points.
- Persistent homology transform: the collection of such diagrams over many directions, giving a shape signature.
- Triangulated boundary: the surface of a solid represented as a mesh of triangles.
- Tree-cotree decomposition: a way to split a surface's graph structure into a spanning tree and a dual spanning tree, used to find a basis of loops.
- Cocycle and F2: linear-algebra objects used to detect loops; F2 arithmetic means working with 0 and 1 where addition is mod 2.
summary.one_liner: The paper gives an algorithm for computing a finite directional sample of the three-dimensional Extended Persistent Homology Transform from a triangulated boundary mesh, using tree-cotree decomposition, evaluation-dual cocycles, and F2 linear algebra.
summary.plain: The paper describes a computer method for summarizing the shape of a solid object, such as one built from a 3D binary image, by looking at how its features appear as you sweep a height function across it from many directions. The method works from the object's surface mesh and combines graph constructions with arithmetic over the two-element field (0 and 1). Under stated assumptions about the surface, the result is a set of diagrams that describe the solid's extended persistence.
summary.why: Shape summaries that are stable and computable are useful for comparing and classifying 3D objects, such as biological structures or scanned materials. The text does not report experiments, timings, or comparisons, so its practical value is not shown here; it is best read as an algorithmic construction with stated hypotheses.

title: An Implementation of the 3-Dimensional Extended Persistent Homology Transform

abstract: One of the best known invariants of multi-parameter persistent homology is the rank invariant, which is subsumed by the generalized rank invariant (GRI), obtained by naturally extending its domain. Möbius inversion of the GRI not only provides a compact encoding of this invariant but is also useful for clarifying its relationship with other invariants of multi-parameter persistent homology. However, Möbius inversion of the GRI has been defined only under suitable finiteness conditions on its domain and support. This work studies the extent to which Möbius inversion can be extended beyond these finiteness conditions. Namely, we formalize the notion of Möbius invertibility, which captures when Möbius inversion exists beyond these finiteness conditions, and investigate when the GRI is Möbius invertible. A central result we establish is that Möbius invertibility of the GRI is guaranteed for finitely presentable $d$-parameter persistence modules when $d\leq 2$, but may fail when $d>2$. Establishing this failure also corrects an error in the existing literature. In response to this higher-dimensional obstruction, we show that for finitely presentable $d$-parameter persistence modules, restricting the GRI to intervals subordinate to the finite grid supporting a minimal free presentation preserves its Möbius inversion whenever the latter exists over all intervals. Since computing the GRI over all intervals in $\mathbb{R}^d$ is infeasible in practice, this result provides a principled justification for restricting the GRI to those intervals.
label: arXiv:2611.20463v1

summary.background:
- Persistent homology: a method that tracks holes and connected pieces of data across a range of scales.
- Multi-parameter persistence: the same idea when data is indexed by two or more scale parameters at once, which makes the mathematics much harder than the one-parameter case.
- Rank invariant: a numerical summary counting how many features persist between pairs of parameter values.
- Generalized rank invariant (GRI): an extension of the rank invariant defined over more general intervals.
- Möbius inversion: a systematic way of recovering a compact description from a function on an ordered set, analogous to undoing a cumulative sum.
- Finitely presentable module: a persistence module described by finitely many generators and relations, which can be stored on a finite grid.
- Minimal free presentation: the most economical finite description of such a module.
- Intervals: sub-regions of the parameter space over which the summary is evaluated.
summary.one_liner: This paper formalizes "Möbius invertibility" of the generalized rank invariant in multi-parameter persistent homology, proves it holds for finitely presentable modules when d ≤ 2, shows it can fail for d > 2 (correcting a prior error), and justifies restricting to intervals subordinate to a minimal free presentation's finite grid.
summary.plain: This is a mathematical paper about a tool used to summarize the shape of data that is measured along several settings at once, such as two or more scale parameters. The authors ask when a standard compact encoding of that summary, obtained by a reversal technique called Möbius inversion, still works when the usual finiteness assumptions do not hold. They find it always works in one or two parameters, can fail with three or more, and show that a practical restriction to a finite set of regions loses nothing whenever the full version works.
summary.why: The result matters for people who want to compute multi-parameter topological summaries in practice, since it gives a principled reason to compute only over a finite collection of intervals. It also corrects an error in the existing literature; the text does not indicate further applications beyond this theory.

title: Möbius Invertibility of Rank Invariants

abstract: We show that Morse representations can be algebraically described by spectral systems, a notion introduced by B. Matschke for poset-filtered chain complexes. This provides an algebraic alternative to connection matrices and yields algebraic invariants via R-modules over an arbitrary ring R. This approach applies in particular to Conley index theory for semi-flows. We discuss the theory of spectral systems and, as an application to dynamical systems, explain the relation to R. Franzosa's theory of connection matrices. In this context we introduce the concept of a spectral net. In contrast to traditional spectral sequences, spectral nets over a lattice display a rich network of (higher) differentials. In the application to dynamical systems these differentials provide information about connecting orbits.
label: arXiv:2611.24966v1

summary.background:
- Dynamical system / semi-flow: a rule describing how states evolve over time, possibly only forward in time.
- Orbit: the path a state traces under the evolution rule; connecting orbits link one equilibrium-like set to another.
- Conley index theory: a topological method for classifying the invariant sets of a dynamical system.
- Morse representation: a way of organising a system's invariant pieces into an ordered sequence, used to build topological invariants.
- Chain complex and differentials: algebraic objects made of linked groups, where a "differential" is a map relating consecutive pieces; higher differentials relate pieces further apart.
- Poset / lattice: a set with a partial order (some items come before others), used here to index the pieces.
- Ring and R-module: basic algebraic structures; an R-module generalises vector spaces to coefficients from a ring R.
- Connection matrix: a matrix recording how pieces of a system are linked, due to Franzosa.
summary.one_liner: The paper recasts Morse representations in Conley index theory as algebraic spectral systems (after Matschke) over an arbitrary ring, relates them to Franzosa's connection matrices, and introduces spectral nets whose higher differentials are said to encode connecting orbits.
summary.plain: The paper studies how the long-term behaviour of a system that changes over time, such as a flow, can be broken into simpler pieces that are ordered like steps. It offers an algebraic bookkeeping tool, called a spectral system, as an alternative to an older matrix-based method. The authors also introduce a new structure, a spectral net, which they say records how orbits (paths the system can follow) connect different pieces.
summary.why: Connection matrices are the established way to capture how pieces of a dynamical system link together, so an algebraic alternative that yields invariants over any ring could be useful to people working in this area. The text does not show any computed results or applications beyond the stated framework, so its practical impact is uncertain.

title: Lattice-ordered Spectral Systems for Morse Representations

abstract: Super-linearization is, roughly speaking, embedding an $n$-dimensional nonlinear dynamical system into an $(n + m)$-dimensional linear system. We introduce and address, in this paper, the inverse problem: given a linear system $\dot x= M x$, what type of dynamical systems can be super-linearized to it? We focus on the special case where the dimension reduction is one (i.e., $m = 1$) and the leading $n$-by-$n$ principal submatrix of $M$ is diagonalizable, and provide a solution to the problem.
label: arXiv:2611.20486v1

summary.background:
- Dynamical system: a rule describing how a set of quantities changes over time.
- Linear system x' = Mx: each rate of change is a weighted sum of the quantities, with weights given by a matrix M; these are well understood.
- Nonlinear system: rates of change depend on the quantities in more complicated ways (e.g. products or powers).
- Super-linearization: embedding an n-dimensional nonlinear system into a larger (n+m)-dimensional linear system, so the nonlinear one is a projection of a linear one.
- Principal submatrix: the block of M formed by its top-left n rows and columns.
- Diagonalizable: a matrix can be rewritten, after a change of coordinates, so that it only has numbers along its diagonal and zeros elsewhere.
- Inverse problem: starting from the answer (the linear system) and asking which questions (nonlinear systems) produce it.
summary.one_liner: The paper studies the inverse problem for super-linearization: given a linear system x' = Mx, it characterizes which nonlinear n-dimensional systems can be embedded into it with one extra variable (m = 1), under the assumption that the leading n-by-n principal submatrix of M is diagonalizable.
summary.plain: The paper looks at a way of turning a nonlinear system of changing quantities into a linear one by adding extra quantities to track it. Here the question is reversed: starting from a simple linear system, which nonlinear systems could be hidden inside it? The authors work out a solution for the case where only one extra quantity is added and a key block of the linear system's matrix can be simplified into a diagonal form.
summary.why: Linearizing nonlinear dynamics is a long-standing goal, since linear systems are much easier to analyze and solve. The inverse framing tells us exactly which nonlinear systems can be handled this way, which may be useful for modeling and analysis, though the text itself does not show specific applications.

title: Inverse Problem for Super-linearization with Single Observable and Diagonalizable Principal Submatrix

abstract: The worst-case stabilization time of a self-stabilizing algorithm usually says little about its typical behavior beyond the order of magnitude. This paper revisits the classical self-stabilizing $Delta+1$ coloring algorithm with vertices activated at random, one at a time (the random central daemon). Considering the number of color changes as a random variable, we study its mean, variance and, on several families of graphs, its exact distribution. The analysis rests on a reduction: a vertex changes color, at most once, exactly when it is not a local maximum of a uniformly random labeling of the vertices, maxima being taken among the neighbors that share its initial color (the monochrome initial configuration is the slowest case). What can be predicted depends on what is known of the graph. The degree distribution (the view at distance one) gives the mean. The variance needs the view at distance two, in particular the triangles, and the full law needs the whole graph. We give closed-form results, from monochrome and from uniformly random initial configurations, on paths, cycles, random trees, Erdős-R{é}nyi graphs and bipartite random graphs. From a monochrome start, the mean stays within a factor two of the worst case, whereas the variance ranges from zero (disjoint cliques) to order $n^2$ (the star on $n$ vertices)..
label: arXiv:2611.17989v1

summary.background:
- Graph: nodes (vertices) joined by edges; a coloring gives each node a color so that neighbors differ.
- Self-stabilizing algorithm: starts from any configuration, possibly corrupted, and converges to a correct state on its own.
- Random central daemon: a scheduler that activates one node at a time, chosen at random.
- Mean and variance: the average and the spread of a random count.
- Local maximum: a node whose label beats all its neighbors' labels.
- Degree (neighbors at distance one), distance-two view, triangles (three mutually adjacent nodes).
- Closed-form result: an exact formula rather than an estimate.
summary.one_liner: The paper computes the exact mean, variance and, on several graph families, the full distribution of the number of color changes made by the classical self-stabilizing Delta+1 coloring algorithm under a random central daemon, and relates these quantities to local graph structure (degrees, distance-two view, triangles).
summary.plain: The paper studies a simple procedure in which a network of nodes repeatedly fixes colors so that no two neighbors share one. Nodes are picked at random one at a time, and the authors ask how many times colors change on average, how much that number varies, and what its full spread looks like. Their main tool is a reduction: a node changes color at most once, exactly when it is not the largest in a random ordering among its neighbors that started with the same color.
summary.why: Worst-case bounds often say little about typical running time, so exact averages and variances for a well-known algorithm are a useful complement. The text indicates the mean from a monochrome start stays within a factor of two of the worst case, while the variance ranges widely, but I have not checked the derivations, and the text does not spell out wider applications.

title: The Exact Stabilization Time of Self-Stabilizing Coloring: Mean, Variance, and Distribution

abstract: What is the chance that a random shuffling of a deck of cards leaves no card in its original place? More precisely, what is the chance that a random permutation has no fixed points? A permutation with no fixed points is known as a derangement. Questions about derangements, like the ones above, go back centuries, but there are also several unsolved problems in this very active area of permutation group theory. Based on a minicourse given at "Groups and Algebras in Bicocca for Young Algebraists" in June 2026, this survey provides a general introduction to permutation group theory, with a specific focus on derangements. The survey features modern methods for studying permutation groups, recent developments and open problems concerning derangements and connections between this topic and other areas, such as combinatorics, graph theory, number theory, representation theory and topology.
label: arXiv:2611.21894v1

summary.background:
- A permutation is a rearrangement of a set of objects, such as shuffling a deck of cards.
- A fixed point is an object that stays in its original position under the rearrangement.
- A derangement is a permutation with no fixed points.
- Permutation group theory studies the collections of rearrangements that are closed under combining them, and their structure.
- The classic question: the probability that a random permutation is a derangement, which is roughly 1/e (about 37%) for large decks. This value is standard background and is not stated in the text.
summary.one_liner: A survey of permutation group theory focused on derangements (permutations with no fixed points), covering modern methods, recent results, open problems, and links to combinatorics, graph theory, number theory, representation theory and topology.
summary.plain: The paper asks a classic question: if you shuffle a deck of cards at random, what is the chance that no card ends up in its original position? Such shuffles are called derangements, and the paper is a survey, written from a short lecture course, that introduces the area and reviews recent progress and open problems. The text given is only the abstract-style overview, so it does not show specific new results.
summary.why: Derangements are a simple-to-state problem with a long history, and the survey is aimed at young researchers entering the field. It is said to connect to graph theory, number theory, representation theory and topology, but the text does not show how far those connections go.

title: Permutation groups, derangements and connections

abstract: Explicit finite element methods for transient solid dynamics commonly use lumped mass matrices to avoid solving systems of equations for nodal accelerations at each time step. However, diagonal mass matrices may inadequately represent inertia, particularly for higher-order elements and coarse or distorted meshes. This has limited the use of higher-order elements in explicit dynamic analyses. This paper presents a systematic method for directly evaluating the inverse of non-diagonal element-level mass matrices for solid isoparametric elements of arbitrary interpolation order. The method applies to mixed mass matrices defined as linear combinations of lumped and consistent mass matrices, with a weighting parameter controlling the transition between diagonal, consistent, and intermediate formulations. It therefore provides a framework for incorporating non-diagonal mass formulations, including those for quadratic elements, into explicit finite element algorithms. The approach is demonstrated by deriving an explicit inverse formula for the mixed mass matrix of the eight-node hexahedral element. This formula enables efficient element-level inversion without solving a global system. The proposed method can improve inertial representation in transient dynamic analyses while retaining the computational advantages of explicit time integration and is suitable for element-by-element implementations.
label: arXiv:2611.21820v1

summary.background:
- Finite element method: splitting a solid object into small connected pieces (elements) and solving equations for each piece.
- Mass matrix: a table describing how the element's mass is spread across its corner points (nodes); it sets how the element resists acceleration.
- Lumped mass: a simplified version that puts all mass on the nodes, giving a diagonal table that is trivial to invert.
- Consistent mass: a fuller version that spreads mass between nodes, which needs a system of equations to solve.
- Explicit time integration: a stepping scheme that advances the simulation without solving a large global system at each step, valued for speed.
- Isoparametric and higher-order elements: elements with curved edges or extra mid-side nodes, giving more accurate shapes and fields.
- Element-by-element: a computing approach that works on one element at a time rather than assembling a global matrix.
summary.one_liner: The paper derives a systematic, closed-form way to invert element-level mixed (lumped plus consistent) mass matrices for isoparametric solid elements of arbitrary order, with an explicit inverse given for the eight-node hexahedral element, for use in explicit transient dynamics.
summary.plain: Engineers simulating fast-moving solids, such as impacts or crashes, often use a simplified way of representing mass that makes each time step cheap to compute. This paper looks at when that simplification is too crude, especially for more detailed element shapes and poor-quality meshes. It presents a method for computing the exact inverse of a blended mass description directly at the level of each element, and works this out explicitly for a common eight-corner brick-shaped element.
summary.why: The text suggests that better inertia modelling could widen the use of higher-order elements in explicit simulations while keeping their speed. The text does not report test results or timings, so how much accuracy or speed is gained is not shown here.

title: Direct Element-Level Mass Matrix Inversion

abstract: In this paper, we propose a maximum principle preserving continuous finite element method for scalar conservation laws augmented with a fractional diffusion operator of order $s\in (0,1)$. Conservation laws with fractional diffusion operators arise in a variety of physical models involving anomalous transport and nonlocal regularization, including geophysical flows, plasma physics, and nonlinear acoustics. The fractional Laplacian is approximated using a sinc-quadrature representation, yielding a resolvent-based formulation compatible with continuous finite elements and explicit strong stability preserving Runge--Kutta time integration. A first-order monotone scheme is constructed using graph viscosity and is shown to satisfy a discrete maximum principle under an explicit CFL condition. A high-order extension is obtained via entropy-consistent corrections and convex limiting, achieving second-order accuracy while preserving the maximum principle, and hence positivity, as well as mass conservation in the periodic setting. Numerical experiments, including applications to the Surface Quasi-Geostrophic equation, confirm the second-order accuracy and the robustness of the proposed method on unstructured meshes.
label: arXiv:2611.20833v1

summary.background:
- Scalar conservation law: an equation saying a quantity is moved around by a flow without being created or destroyed.
- Fractional Laplacian (order s between 0 and 1): a long-range diffusion operator, a spreading process where distant points interact, unlike ordinary local diffusion.
- Finite element method: approximating a solution by simple pieces over a mesh of the domain.
- Maximum principle: the numerical solution stays between its smallest and largest starting values.
- Sinc quadrature: a numerical technique for approximating an integral-based operator by a sum of simpler terms.
- Graph viscosity and convex limiting: artificial damping added to suppress spurious oscillations while keeping accuracy where the solution is smooth.
- Strong stability preserving Runge–Kutta: a class of time-stepping schemes designed not to create new extremes.
- CFL condition: a limit on time-step size relative to mesh size needed for stability.
summary.one_liner: A continuous finite element method for scalar conservation laws with a fractional diffusion term of order s in (0,1), using sinc-quadrature resolvents, graph viscosity, and convex limiting to preserve the maximum principle and reach second-order accuracy.
summary.plain: The paper concerns computer simulation of equations describing how a quantity such as concentration or temperature is carried by a flow and also spreads out in a long-range way, rather than only locally. The authors build a numerical method that keeps the computed values within their physically allowed range (for example, staying nonnegative) and conserves the total amount. They report a first-order version that provably has this property under a time-step limit, and a higher-order version that keeps the property while being second-order accurate in tests.
summary.why: Keeping simulated values physically plausible while using higher-order accuracy is a standard concern in numerical modelling of transport. The text says the method is tested on the Surface Quasi-Geostrophic equation, a model used in geophysical fluid dynamics, and on unstructured meshes; wider impact beyond these tests is not shown in the text.

title: Maximum principle preserving approximation of scalar conservation equations with a fractional Laplacian

abstract: We introduce the notion of exact properness, a strong form of properness for uncountable models, and prove iteration theorems and the consistency of forcing axioms for this class. We discuss examples of posets in the class and give some applications of the forcing axioms.
label: arXiv:2611.21390v1

summary.background:
- Set theory: the foundation of mathematics built on sets, with the axioms of ZFC as the usual standard.
- Forcing: a technique for extending a model of set theory by adding new sets, used to show that statements are independent of the axioms.
- Properness: a property of forcing notions that ensures countable structures are preserved, allowing iterated constructions.
- Uncountable models: models whose underlying collection is larger than the natural numbers, where properness alone may not suffice.
- Forcing axioms: strong consistency principles (such as Martin's Axiom or Proper Forcing Axiom) asserting that certain forcing extensions already contain the needed objects.
- Iteration theorem: a result saying that a sequence of such forcings, taken in stages, still has the desired property.
summary.one_liner: Introduces "exact properness," a strengthened form of properness for forcing over uncountable models of set theory, proves iteration theorems, and shows consistency of forcing axioms for this class.
summary.plain: This paper is about a technical tool in set theory, the branch of mathematics that studies infinity and what can and cannot be proved about it. Set theorists build new mathematical universes by "forcing," a method for adding objects to a model while controlling what changes. The author introduces a stricter version of a known safety condition, called exact properness, and shows that the approach works when applied repeatedly and that certain general principles, called forcing axioms, can be consistently assumed for this class.
summary.why: Forcing axioms are central tools for settling questions that the standard axioms of set theory leave open, so a new class of well-behaved forcings that supports them may matter to specialists. The text is short and gives only the abstract, so I cannot judge how far the results reach beyond what is stated.

title: Exactly Proper Forcing

abstract: We answer a question of Goldberg about cover exacting cardinals. Concretely, we show that if $κ$ is $ω_1$-strongly compact, then no cardinal $λ>κ$ is $γ$-cover exacting for some cardinal $γ$.
label: arXiv:2611.20299v1

summary.background:
- Cardinals: infinite "sizes" of sets; large cardinals are very big ones whose existence cannot be proved from the standard axioms of set theory.
- Strongly compact cardinal: a large cardinal with a strong covering property for families of sets; ω_1-strongly compact is a weaker, countably-complete version of this.
- Cover exacting (γ-cover exacting): a property of a cardinal λ relative to a cardinal γ, defined in the literature the paper cites; the excerpt does not define it.
- Open question of Goldberg: the paper responds to a question in Goldberg's earlier work, which the excerpt does not describe.
- Background in forcing or inner-model theory is helpful but not needed for the headline claim.
summary.one_liner: The paper answers a question of Goldberg by showing that, if κ is ω_1-strongly compact, no cardinal λ > κ is γ-cover exacting for any cardinal γ.
summary.plain: This is a set-theory paper about very large infinite numbers called cardinals, which are used to measure how strong the basic axioms of mathematics can be. The author answers an open question posed by Goldberg about a particular large-cardinal property called "cover exacting." The result shows that a certain kind of large cardinal (an ω_1-strongly compact one) rules out any larger cardinal having that property.
summary.why: It settles a specific open question raised by another researcher, which narrows down which large-cardinal properties can coexist. The text itself does not say how far the result reaches beyond this question, so its wider significance is unclear from the excerpt alone.

title: On cover exacting cardinals

abstract: In this work we first revisit the Hooke-Newton duality and its generalisation to arbitrary power laws in classical and quantum mechanics. We then consider Wigner-Yang quantum mechanics on the real line, which is a deformation of standard Heisenberg-Schrödinger quantum mechanics closely related to Dunkl's differential-difference operator formalism. We consider the corresponding eigenvalue problem for the harmonic potential and a Coulomb-like potential. We observe that the Hooke-Newton duality is also applicable to these deformed quantum systems allowing us to solve the eigenvalue problem of one by mapping it onto the other system. This approach is then generalised to arbitrary power-law potentials in Wigner-Yang quantum mechanics. Whereas in standard quantum mechanics the classical re-scaling of angular momenta has to be applied to Langer-modified quantum angular momenta, Wigner-Yang quantum mechanics requires a rescaling of deformation parameters similar to the Langer-type modification but involving the reflection operator. The energy coupling-constant exchange, however, remains the same in all three cases, classical mechanics, quantum mechanics and Wigner-Yang quantum mechanics.
label: arXiv:2611.19246v1

summary.background:
- Potential: an energy landscape that sets the force on a particle; a power-law potential scales as distance raised to some power (harmonic is the square, Coulomb-like is an inverse distance).
- Eigenvalue problem: finding the allowed energy levels and states of a quantum system, which is the core task of quantum mechanics.
- Hooke-Newton duality: a known correspondence that swaps the roles of the power in the potential and the energy, linking different systems.
- Heisenberg-Schrödinger quantum mechanics: the standard formulation of quantum mechanics that the paper modifies.
- Wigner-Yang quantum mechanics: a deformed version on the real line, related to Dunkl's operators, which add a reflection (sign-flip) term to ordinary derivatives.
- Langer modification: a standard adjustment to angular momentum terms in radial equations, which the paper compares with its deformed case.
summary.one_liner: The paper extends the Hooke-Newton power-law duality, which maps eigenvalue problems between power-law potentials in classical and standard quantum mechanics, to the deformed Wigner-Yang quantum mechanics built on Dunkl's differential-difference operators, including harmonic and Coulomb-like potentials.
summary.plain: The paper studies a mathematical correspondence between two families of physical systems, each governed by a force law that follows a power of distance. It revisits a known trick that maps the solution of one such system onto another with a different power, then applies that trick to a modified version of quantum mechanics called Wigner-Yang quantum mechanics. The authors report that the trick still works there, so one hard problem can be solved by converting it into an easier one.
summary.why: The duality lets known solutions for one potential be reused for another, which is useful for solving quantum eigenvalue problems. The text does not say how far the approach reaches beyond the cases studied, so its broader significance is uncertain from this abstract alone.

title: On the Power-Law Duality in Wigner-Yang Quantum Mechanics

abstract: We consider 3-dimensional topological gauge theories with nilpotent gauge groups, both finite, that is Dijkgraaf-Witten theories, and continuous, that is Chern-Simons theories. Abelian topological quantum field theories are exactly those which do not detect the Borromean rings, and nilpotent gauge groups provide the natural next steps beyond the abelian case. We show that the untwisted Dijkgraaf-Witten theory with gauge group $G$ detects Brunnian links with up to $n+1$ components, but no Brunnian links with more components, if and only if $G$ is $n$-step nilpotent. Moreover, the expectation values of such links are determined by their Milnor invariants. We also study the properties of Chern-Simons theories with nilpotent Lie groups and draw parallels with those of the Dijkgraaf-Witten theories. Finally, we conjecture, using the Lazard correspondence, a relation between expectation values of line operators in the two types of theories, and test it in examples.
label: arXiv:2611.18237v1

summary.background:
- Topological quantum field theory: physical models whose predictions depend only on global shape (such as how loops are linked), not on distances or local geometry.
- Link: a collection of closed loops tangled in 3D space; a Brunnian link is one where removing any single loop frees the rest.
- Gauge group: the symmetry group that labels how a field is twisted as it moves along a loop; a finite gauge group gives a Dijkgraaf-Witten theory, a continuous (Lie) group gives Chern-Simons theory.
- Abelian vs nilpotent groups: abelian groups have fully commuting elements; nilpotent groups are a controlled step beyond this, measured by the number of steps n.
- Milnor invariants: numerical measures of how link components wind around each other.
- Lazard correspondence: a dictionary between certain finite nilpotent groups and certain nilpotent Lie algebras, used to compare the two theories.
- Line operator expectation value: the average value a physical model assigns to a loop-shaped observable.
summary.one_liner: The paper shows that 3D untwisted Dijkgraaf-Witten theories with a finite gauge group G detect Brunnian links up to a given number of components exactly when G is n-step nilpotent, relates their link expectation values to Milnor invariants, and conjectures (via the Lazard correspondence) a link between line-operator expectation values in finite and continuous nilpotent Chern-Simons theories.
