- EPTCS: Electronic Proceedings in Theoretical Computer Science, an open series that publishes workshop papers collected into volumes.
- Workshop proceedings: a bundle of papers presented at a small specialist meeting, usually published after it.
- Co-location: holding two conferences at the same place and time so attendees can attend both.
summary.one_liner: This EPTCS proceedings volume collects the papers from the Eighth International Workshop on Formal Methods for Autonomous Systems (FMAS 2026), held in Southampton in November 2026 alongside ICFEM.
summary.plain: This is the front matter for a published collection of papers from a specialist workshop on using mathematically rigorous checking methods to verify self-operating systems such as robots and autonomous vehicles. The text only gives the event details: the dates, the co-located conference, and the venue. It does not describe the individual papers or any findings.
summary.why: It signals an ongoing research community working on proving that autonomous systems behave safely, which matters as such systems spread. The text itself gives no specific results, so its direct importance is hard to judge from this excerpt alone.

title: Proceedings Eighth International Workshop on Formal Methods for Autonomous Systems

abstract: The metatheory of programming languages suffers from a lack of reuse. Researchers develop individual calculi and prove standard properties, but very few results are truly reused across papers. The problem is worse in proof assistants, where developments routinely duplicate code from prior work or rebuild it from scratch. Category theory provides the most promising path toward reusable programming language semantics. Universal properties capture the type connectives---products, functions, sums---together with their $β$/$η$ laws. Free categorical structures identify syntactic calculi. \emph{Displayed} categories provide a uniform language for specifying logical relations, and general theorems about fibrations allow their structure to be assembled compositionally. In this work we develop a library of formalized category theory in the Cubical Agda proof assistant directly applicable to programming language metatheory. We develop theories of universal properties and free categorical structures, apply them to define denotational semantics and logical relations for simply typed calculi, and identify encodings of the categorical constructions that make typechecking them tractable. From the same categorical components, we construct several familiar results via a logical relations construction---canonicity,parametricity,conservativity---and provide a proof of coherence for monoidal categories.
label: arXiv:2611.21826v1

summary.background:
- Programming language semantics: the mathematical meaning of programs and types.
- Logical relations: a proof technique that relates programs across types to establish properties such as canonicity (closed terms of base type reduce to values) and parametricity (polymorphic functions behave uniformly).
- Category theory: structures of objects and arrows; universal properties describe constructions like products and function types by a unique-mediating-map condition.
- Displayed categories and fibrations: a way to layer extra structure (such as relations) over a base category.
- Proof assistants and Cubical Agda: software where proofs are checked by computer; Cubical Agda supports equality ideas from homotopy type theory.
- Monoidal category coherence: the guarantee that different ways of rebracketing tensor products give equivalent results.
summary.one_liner: A library of formalized category theory in Cubical Agda, built on universal properties, free categorical structures, and displayed categories, used to derive denotational semantics and logical relations for simply typed calculi and to recover canonicity, parametricity, conservativity, and monoidal coherence.
summary.plain: Researchers who design programming languages often redo the same proofs for each new language, and proof-assistant code is frequently copied or rewritten. This paper builds a reusable library, inside a computer proof assistant called Cubical Agda, that expresses the basic ideas of programming language meaning using category theory, a general mathematical language of structures and mappings. From these shared parts the authors rebuild several known results, such as canonicity, parametricity, and conservativity, and also prove a coherence result for monoidal categories.
summary.why: Reusing proofs across languages and proof assistants could save a lot of duplicated effort, which is the motivation the text gives. The text does not measure how much reuse it achieves in practice, so its practical impact is still to be seen.

title: Logical Relations on Display

abstract: There has been extensive debate on how to summarize performance results, especially within the computer architecture community. This article presents a systematic approach to choosing the correct mean, aiming to answer this question for all computer scientists once and for all.
label: arXiv:2611.20618v1

summary.background:
- A "mean" is a single number that summarizes a set of values; common types include the arithmetic mean (ordinary average), geometric mean (multiplies values and takes a root, suited to ratios), and harmonic mean (suited to rates).
- A "benchmark" is a standard test program used to measure how fast a computer runs typical work.
- Performance summaries across many benchmarks often combine speedup ratios, and the choice of mean can change which system appears better.
- The article is a short position-style piece; only its introduction is available here.
summary.one_liner: A short article proposing a systematic way to pick the right mean (such as arithmetic, geometric, or harmonic) for summarizing computer performance results.
summary.plain: Computer researchers often disagree about how to boil many benchmark timings or speed measurements into a single average. This paper, based only on its opening summary, sets out a systematic method for choosing which kind of average to use, with the stated aim of settling the question. The text provided is only the abstract-level introduction, so the specific method and its results are not described here.
summary.why: Choosing the wrong average can make one computer system look faster than another when the comparison is actually misleading, so the question affects how performance claims are judged. The text does not show how widely the proposed approach has been adopted or tested, so its practical impact is uncertain.

title: One Mean Can't Rule Them All

abstract: Distributed systems deployed across the edge-cloud continuum are adapted continuously: scaled, re-routed, given more or less capacity. Each adaptation rests on an expectation of how the system will respond, yet operators cannot tell from the telemetry they already collect whether that response is predictable. We define top-level operational equilibrium (TLOE), a notion of equilibrium for a running system, stated relative to the controls its operator declares. TLOE has three conditions: stationarity with time-scale separation, sufficiency of a top-level aggregate for the controls, and time-reversibility of that aggregate. We prove that an aggregate satisfying the last two exists if and only if the minimal sufficient statistic of the controls is time-reversible, so the coarsest admissible aggregate is derived rather than chosen. Under the first two conditions, the response to a small control change follows from passive telemetry through the steady-state fluctuation-response identity, with a conjugate observable fixed by the type of control: the total work in progress for a change of load, the occupancy of a stage for a change of its capacity. For chains of exponential single-server stages with Poisson input, TLOE holds exactly for load control at every stable throughput, but never for a control on the capacity of the first or last stage. On reference models, a per-stage conjugate overestimates the early response about threefold, blocking between stages breaks both conditions weakly, and a hysteretic autoscaler leaves no admissible aggregate at any reaction time computed. We specify a test for each condition, show that a static sufficiency test with an estimated top-level conjugate has no power, and quantify on simulated telemetry the window lengths the prediction and the reversibility test need. The evidence is on reference models; real telemetry is left to future work.
label: arXiv:2611.20780v1

summary.background:
- Distributed system: many servers or services working together, often across edge devices and cloud data centres.
- Telemetry: the measurements a system already logs, such as queue lengths and throughput.
- Equilibrium / stationarity: statistical behaviour that does not drift over time.
- Time-reversibility: the statistics look the same when the time sequence is run backwards.
- Sufficient statistic: a summary that keeps all the information needed about a quantity.
- Fluctuation-response identity: a physics-style result relating how a system's random ups and downs predict how it reacts to a small push.
- Queueing terms: a stage is a server with a waiting line; throughput is how much work finishes per unit time; work in progress is the total items inside the system.
- Hysteretic autoscaler: a scaling rule that changes behaviour depending on recent history, so it does not respond the same way twice.
summary.one_liner: The paper defines top-level operational equilibrium (TLOE) for running distributed systems, with stationarity, sufficiency and time-reversibility conditions, and uses a fluctuation-response identity to predict small responses to control changes from passive telemetry, tested only on reference models.
summary.plain: Cloud and edge systems are constantly rescaled and rerouted, and each change assumes the system will respond in a predictable way. The paper asks when that response can be read from the telemetry operators already collect, and gives a set of conditions under which it can. On simple reference models, the authors report that the prediction works for load changes in one class of queueing chain, fails for capacity changes at the first or last stage, and needs specific window lengths of data.
summary.why: Operators adjust systems without a reliable way to know whether the system's reaction is predictable, so a telemetry-based test would be useful if it holds up. The results are only on reference models and simulated data, and real telemetry is explicitly left to future work, so practical value is not yet shown.

title: Top-Level Operational Equilibrium: When is the response of a distributed system predictable from its own telemetry?

abstract: Systems for modular, declarative and compositional specification for data visualizations, otherwise known as visualization grammars, often claim Wilkinson's Grammar of Graphics as motivation, inspiration or foundation. However, despite the shared intellectual lineage, visualization grammars can vary greatly in design scope and focus. In particular, systems that strongly adhere to domain-specific notions of correctness must trade-off expressivity for validity. This trade-off between semantics and graphical flexibility is currently under-articulated, leading to difficulty integrating various GoG-inspired visualization contributions, especially between InfoVis and Statistical Graphics. We propose three new types of visualization contributions to support such integration: Semantic Validity Theories, Semantic Visualization Systems and Graphical Arrangement Systems. The first two prioritize the adherence of data visualizations to correctness conditions, such as statistical or mathematical transformations and data semantics, whilst the third largely leave validity concerns to the user. We illustrate these new contribution types using examples from two recent grammar of graphics inspired papers, and show how they supported more nuanced notions of expressivity and usability in evaluation and design of visualization systems.
label: arXiv:2611.21073v1

summary.background:
- Grammar of Graphics: Leland Wilkinson's idea that a chart can be built from separate parts (data, transformations, marks, coordinates), much like a sentence is built from grammar rules.
- Visualization grammar: a software system that lets users specify charts declaratively, by describing what they want rather than drawing each element.
- Statistical graphics vs. information visualization (InfoVis): two research communities; the first emphasizes statistical correctness, the second often emphasizes expressive design.
- Semantic validity: whether a chart's transformations and encodings are correct for the data's meaning and the statistics involved.
- Expressivity vs. validity: the more freely a user can arrange graphics, the more easily a meaningless chart can be produced.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes three contribution types (Semantic Validity Theories, Semantic Visualization Systems, and Graphical Arrangement Systems) to clarify the trade-off between enforcing statistical or data correctness and allowing graphical flexibility in Grammar of Graphics-inspired visualization tools.
summary.plain: Software tools for making charts often describe a picture in layers and parts, following a framework called the Grammar of Graphics. This paper argues that these tools differ a lot: some strictly check that a chart makes statistical sense, while others give the user free rein over how things look. The authors propose three categories to label such work so that researchers from data-visualization and statistics communities can compare and combine their efforts more easily.
summary.why: Charting software is used widely in science and business, and the choice between strict checking and creative freedom affects what users can do and how mistakes are caught. The text is a conceptual framing; it does not report measured outcomes, so its practical impact is uncertain and would depend on how the categories are adopted by the field.

title: Semantic Validity vs. Graphical Arrangement in Visualization Grammars

abstract: Line is a foundational building block in visual design for traditional media and computer graphics. Controlled variation in line quality can be used to define form, create abstractions, distinguish categories, control affect, and more. Yet, when it comes to computer graphics visualizations of science, particularly those built upon 3D computer graphics, too often a line is just a line. This portfolio presents a series of visual design studies and lessons learned that explore the diverse character of line that might be useful for 3D visualizations. The imagery begins to show how more sophisticated use of this powerful visual building block could increase the clarity of data visualizations while also bringing a human, handcrafted aesthetic that reinforces the people and impacts behind scientific climate data.
label: arXiv:2611.20190v1

summary.background:
- Visualization: turning data into images so patterns can be seen.
- 3D computer graphics: software that renders objects and scenes in three dimensions.
- Line quality: variations in a line's thickness, texture, edge, or style, which artists use to suggest form and mood.
- Portfolio paper: a collection of design examples with reflections, rather than a controlled experiment.
- Human-computer interaction: the field that studies how people design and use computer systems and images.
summary.one_liner: A portfolio of visual design studies that explores how varying the character of lines (quality, weight, and style) in 3D scientific visualizations, especially climate data, can improve clarity and add a handcrafted feel.
summary.plain: Computer pictures of science, such as 3D charts of climate data, often draw every line the same plain way, so the lines carry little meaning beyond showing a path or edge. This portfolio presents a set of design experiments and lessons learned showing how varying the look of lines, much as artists do by hand, can make such images clearer and more human. The text describes the designs and lessons but does not report measured results from user testing.
summary.why: Scientific visualizations are used to communicate issues like climate change, so clearer and more engaging pictures could matter for public understanding. The text does not show whether these designs actually improve comprehension, so its practical impact remains to be tested.

title: A Line is Not Just a Line: Visualizing Harmonious Complex Line Sets

abstract: We introduce a new framework for the study and evaluation of the fundamental limits of channel coding, emphasizing genuinely nonasymptotic results. The {\em channel coding sample complexity} $n^*({\cal W},ε)$ of a channel ${\cal W}$ is defined as the smallest blocklength at which it is possible to transmit information through that channel with error probability below $ε$ and at a rate at least as high as that given by an appropriate constraint also in terms of $ε$. This formulation follows analogous developments in statistics, computer science and, more recently, in lossless source coding. For any discrete memoryless channel we derive nonasymptotic bounds on the sample complexity, with explicit constants. These bounds show that the sample complexity is characterized not by the usual channel capacity, but by the channel's Augustin--Csiszár capacity of order $1/2$, which coincides with the cutoff rate as well as with the channel's Sibson capacity of order $1/2$. The proof is partly based on a new channel-coding one-shot converse in terms of hypothesis testing. We also examine extensions of the sample complexity framework to general target rates. Moreover, we derive corresponding results for the sample complexity of the additive white Gaussian noise channel with a quadratic power constraint. Their proof relies on new, explicit upper bounds on the best achievable error probability, which may be of independent interest.
label: arXiv:2611.21395v1

summary.background:
- Channel coding: encoding messages with redundancy so they can be recovered after noise corrupts them.
- Blocklength: the number of symbols in one coded message.
- Error probability: the chance the receiver decodes the wrong message.
- Channel capacity: the highest rate achievable with vanishing error for very long blocks (the asymptotic limit).
- Rényi-type capacities of order α: generalized information measures, parameterized by α; order 1/2 is the case discussed here.
- Cutoff rate: an older coding-theory benchmark for practical decoding effort.
- Hypothesis testing: deciding between two possible distributions from data; used here as a tool for proving limits.
- AWGN channel: a channel adding Gaussian noise, with a limit on transmit power.
summary.one_liner: Introduces a nonasymptotic "sample complexity" framework for channel coding, showing that for discrete memoryless channels the minimal blocklength is governed by the Augustin–Csiszár (equivalently cutoff rate and Sibson) capacity of order 1/2 rather than ordinary capacity, with a one-shot hypothesis-testing converse and explicit AWGN results.
summary.plain: This paper asks how long a message must be, in terms of the number of symbols sent, before a noisy communication channel can carry information reliably at a target rate and error level. Instead of the usual question of the best rate for very long messages, it studies the smallest workable block length directly, with explicit constants. The authors find that this length is set by a different quantity than the familiar channel capacity, namely a related measure of order 1/2 (the cutoff rate).
summary.why: The result shifts attention from asymptotic capacity to concrete finite-length behavior, which matters for practical codes with limited delay. The link to the cutoff rate, an older quantity from coding theory, is the notable connection, though the text alone does not show how practical this is for specific systems.

title: The Sample Complexity of Channel Coding

abstract: A unified framework is proposed that characterizes supervised deep classification as the decoding of error-correcting codes in the Shannon sense. Cross-entropy optimization is shown to align softmax classifiers with maximum-likelihood decoding, where logits map to Hamming distances to class-specific codewords. This correspondence explains the emergence of standard divergence objectives (e.g., Kullback-Leibler, Jeffreys, Bregman) and provides a geometric basis for the stability of decision boundaries. Furthermore, the geometries of Neural Collapse and LeJEPA are identified as optimal constellations for decoding under isotropic noise. Unlike classical Error-Correcting Output Codes, deep networks are shown to learn effective codebooks in the feature space implicitly. This insight is leveraged to derive novel criteria for lossless quantization, improved knowledge distillation, and architectural regularization based on code redundancy. Finally, this perspective is extended to self-supervised encoders, offering a cohesive explanation for the geometry of latent representations in modern neural models.
label: arXiv:2611.18239v2

summary.background:
- Error-correcting codes: a way to add structured redundancy to a message so a receiver can recover it despite noise.
- Codeword: the fixed pattern assigned to each message or class.
- Hamming distance: the number of positions in which two patterns differ.
- Maximum-likelihood decoding: picking the codeword most likely to have produced what was received.
- Softmax and cross-entropy: the standard output scoring and training loss for classifiers.
- Neural Collapse: a late-training phenomenon where class representations form a symmetric, evenly spaced arrangement.
- Knowledge distillation: training a smaller network to copy a larger one's outputs.
- Self-supervised learning: training representations without labels.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes viewing supervised deep classifiers as Shannon-style error-correcting code decoders, claiming cross-entropy training aligns softmax outputs with maximum-likelihood decoding over class codewords, and extends this to Neural Collapse, LeJEPA and self-supervised encoders.
summary.plain: Neural networks that sort inputs into categories, such as recognizing images, are trained with a standard scoring rule. This paper argues that the same job can be seen as the problem of decoding a message sent through a noisy channel, where each category has a fixed codeword. From that view, the authors say the standard training rule, the shape of the learned representations, and some practical tools such as compression and distillation can be explained together.
summary.why: If the analogy holds, it could link deep learning training and representation geometry to a well-established body of coding theory, which may suggest new criteria for compression and regularization. The text itself gives only a high-level abstract, so how far the claims are supported by proofs or experiments cannot be judged from it; the authors' stated results should be checked in the full paper.

title: Neural Classifiers as Error-Correcting Codes

abstract: Inspired by exponential Maxwell models, we propose a new black hole solution in square root nonlinear electrodynamics. Using the analogy between black hole mechanics and thermodynamics, we investigate the corresponding stability, the P-v criticality and the phase transitions. As a result, we find that the obtained black hole exhibits Van der Waals behaviors without additional corrections which typically appear in universal ratio computations.
label: arXiv:2611.20162v1

summary.background:
- Black holes can be assigned a temperature, entropy and pressure, using analogies with ordinary thermodynamics.
- Anti-de Sitter (AdS) space is a curved spacetime with negative cosmological constant, often used as a testing ground for these analogies.
- Nonlinear electrodynamics is a modified version of Maxwell's theory of electric and magnetic fields in which the field energy does not simply add up linearly; here the modification has a square-root form.
- P-v criticality: plotting pressure against specific volume, some black holes show a critical point like a liquid-gas transition, with a Van der Waals-type curve.
- Stability and phase transitions describe whether the system stays put or switches between distinct states as conditions change.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes a new charged black hole in anti-de Sitter space, sourced by a square-root nonlinear electrodynamics inspired by exponential Maxwell models, and studies its thermodynamic stability, P-v criticality and phase transitions.
summary.plain: This paper looks at a theoretical model of a black hole, the dense object whose gravity is so strong that light cannot escape. The authors change the rule for how the electric field behaves, using a square-root form inspired by a family of "exponential" versions of Maxwell's electromagnetism. They then treat the black hole like a thermal system with temperature and pressure and check whether it is stable and whether it undergoes phase changes.
summary.why: The authors report that this black hole shows Van der Waals-like behaviour, the same kind of liquid-gas pattern seen in ordinary real gases, without extra correction terms that such comparisons often need. This is a theoretical result, and the text does not say how it bears on observations or other systems, so its wider significance is unclear.

title: On Thermodynamics of AdS Black Holes in Square-Root Nonlinear Electrodynamics

abstract: Newtonian gravity, in the light of the Equivalence Principle, is best understood as a localization of Galilean inertial structure --- or at least, of the part of Galilean inertial structure that defines rectilinear acceleration. I consider what kind of theory can be constructed if we also localize rotational inertia and spatial and temporal scales. The resultant theory, given weak assumptions, is unique up to a constant with the dimensions of velocity and an overall sign. For an appropriate choice of these, it coincides with the first post-Newtonian approximation to general relativity, so that this construction gives a method to bootstrap from Newtonian gravity to general relativity without explicitly presupposing special relativity.
label: arXiv:2611.20210v1

summary.background:
- Galilean inertial structure: the rules of motion in Newtonian physics, where straight-line uniform motion defines "inertial" frames.
- Equivalence Principle: the observation that gravity affects all bodies the same way, which lets gravity be treated as a feature of geometry or a local field.
- Localization (gauging) of a symmetry: making a symmetry transformation depend on position and time, which forces a new field to appear to compensate.
- Rotational and conformal (scale) symmetries: rotations of space and changes of length and time units; here they are made local.
- Post-Newtonian approximation: a series of small corrections to Newton's gravity, valid for weak fields and slow speeds, used to test general relativity.
- Special relativity: Einstein's theory of space and time without gravity, which the paper aims to avoid presupposing.
summary.one_liner: The paper argues that localizing rotational inertia and spatial and temporal scaling, on top of the Galilean structure underlying Newtonian gravity, yields a essentially unique theory that matches the first post-Newtonian approximation to general relativity for a suitable choice of a velocity constant and sign.
summary.plain: The paper asks what kind of gravity theory you get if you start from Newton's picture and additionally make rotations and changes of spatial and temporal scale "local", meaning they can vary from place to place, as Einstein did for straight-line motion. The author reports that, under weak assumptions, this construction gives one theory up to a single constant with units of speed and an overall sign. With the right choice of that constant, the theory agrees with the first post-Newtonian (small-correction) approximation to general relativity, offering a route from Newtonian gravity to Einstein's theory without assuming special relativity at the outset.
summary.why: It is a conceptual route to general relativity that does not start from special relativity, which may clarify why gravity has the structure it does. The text does not show how far the approach extends beyond the first post-Newtonian order, so its wider significance is uncertain.

title: A Gravitomagnetic Bootstrap: from Newtonian gravity to general relativity via localizing rotational and conformal symmetries

abstract: For dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) in open chains it has been noted that the boundary can change the bulk: in time windows bounded by DQPTs, exponentially localized edge modes of the Loschmidt matrix produce a finite change in the intensive return rate. These modes have been attributed to topological properties of the initial and final Hamiltonians. Here we show that it is not the topology of the Hamiltonians but rather that of the non-Hermitian Loschmidt matrix which protects these edge modes. In particular, we show that topological edge modes can exist in class A, where both Hamiltonians are topologically trivial. For classes A, BDI, and AIII we show that these modes are protected by $\mathbb{Z}$ indices of a Toeplitz operator and that K-splitting theorems provide a precise bulk-boundary correspondence. In class D, they are protected instead by a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ index that records whether the quench has flipped the fermion parity at the edge. The bulk invariant for class D can be formulated either as a ratio of the Loschmidt amplitudes for periodic and anti-periodic boundary conditions or as a winding number that counts phase vortices in momentum and time. We discuss examples and provide numerical data for all four topological classes.
label: arXiv:2611.19328v1

summary.background:
- Quantum quench: suddenly changing a system's Hamiltonian (its energy rulebook) and watching it evolve.
- Loschmidt amplitude: the overlap between the evolving state and its starting state; its decay rate measures how quickly the system "forgets" its start.
- Dynamical quantum phase transition (DQPT): non-analytic kinks in the return rate at certain times, analogous to phase transitions but in time.
- Open chain: a finite one-dimensional chain with ends, where edge modes can localize near the boundary.
- Non-Hermitian matrix: a matrix not equal to its own conjugate transpose; it can have complex eigenvalues and is used here for the Loschmidt matrix.
- Topological classes (A, BDI, AIII, D): the Altland-Zirnbauer tenfold classification of symmetry types; the Z and Z2 labels are integer and parity-type topological invariants.
- Toeplitz operator and K-theory: mathematical tools for counting edge states and index invariants.
- Winding number: a count of how many times a phase rotates around a loop, here in momentum and time.
summary.one_liner: The paper shows that edge modes of the non-Hermitian Loschmidt matrix in open-chain dynamical quantum phase transitions are protected by Z and Z2 topological indices (classes A, BDI, AIII, D), with K-splitting theorems giving the bulk-boundary correspondence.
summary.plain: When a quantum system is suddenly switched from one setup to another, its behavior over time can show sharp transitions. In open chains, edge effects at the ends can shift the overall rate at which the system's state "returns" to its starting point. The paper argues that the responsible edge modes are protected by the topology of the non-Hermitian Loschmidt matrix itself, not by the topology of the starting and ending Hamiltonians, and it says these modes can appear even when both Hamiltonians are topologically trivial.
summary.why: It revises the earlier explanation of why boundaries affect bulk behavior in these quench transitions, by moving the source of protection to a different mathematical object. The text does not establish links to applications beyond the theory, and the claims rest on the authors' analysis and numerical data for all four classes.

title: When the Boundary Changes the Bulk: Topological Edge Modes in Dynamical Quantum Phase Transitions

abstract: A language model is a complex system whose behavior is determined jointly by the Transformer and the corpus, yet how the representation geometry in the Transformer relates to the actual behavior of language models remains open. We analyze how the representation geometry changes along the forward propagation of actual language models and characterize the representation geometry of a document at a given layer by two collective coordinates, document distinguishability and document dimension. On the phase diagram spanned by these collective coordinates, inference is represented as a flow along depth. We find that, for untrained models, depending on their initialization scale, most of the 156 inference flows move toward the collapse and noise regions of the phase diagram. By contrast, the inference flows of 8 trained models from 5 architecture families all enter and reside in the central region of the phase diagram. Describing the evolution of the flows with a discrete Langevin equation, we find that the difference between the inference flows of untrained runs and those of trained models reduces to whether the effective force on the flows in this region is of saddle or stable-node type. On Pythia-1.4B, we interpret the training process as a phase transition. These results give a unified gateway to the relation between representation geometry and language-model behavior.
label: arXiv:2611.19848v1

summary.background:
- Language models are neural networks built from stacked layers (a "Transformer"); each layer produces an internal representation of the input text.
- "Representation geometry" refers to the arrangement of these internal vectors in high-dimensional space, such as how spread out or distinguishable they are.
- "Initialization scale" is the size of the random starting weights before training.
- A "phase diagram" is a map showing which regimes a system falls into under different conditions, borrowed from physics.
- A "phase transition" is a sudden qualitative change in a system's behavior, like water freezing.
- A Langevin equation describes motion under a deterministic push plus random noise; "saddle" and "stable node" are types of fixed points describing how trajectories settle or pass by.
- Pythia is a family of openly released language models of different sizes.
summary.one_liner: The paper maps how a language model's internal representation geometry evolves across layers, using two collective coordinates (document distinguishability and document dimension) on a phase diagram, and compares untrained and trained models via a discrete Langevin-style dynamical description.
summary.plain: The paper asks how the hidden internal geometry of a language model, the shape its representations take as text passes through successive layers, relates to how the model actually behaves. The authors summarize each document at each layer with two numbers and plot the path of each document through a "phase diagram," which is a map of regions with different qualitative behavior. They report that untrained models mostly drift toward collapsed or noisy regions, while trained models stay in a central region.
summary.why: It offers a geometric, physics-style way to compare trained and untrained language models, which could help explain why training changes behavior. The text reports only a limited set of models (156 untrained runs, 8 trained models from 5 architecture families, and one case study on Pythia-1.4B), so how far the framing generalizes beyond these is unclear from the text alone.

title: A phase diagram for training and inference in language models

abstract: A fundamental property of a Fermi liquid (FL) is that the volume enclosed by the Fermi surface is determined by $ρ$, the total density of electrons. In a fractionalized Fermi liquid (FL*), the volume enclosed by the Fermi surface is determined by the same expression after $ρ$ has been shifted by a quantized amount, most commonly to $ρ-1$ (we assume spin rotation invariance, for simplicity). The FL* shift is related to the quantized symmetry fractionalization data of a quantum spin liquid, whose fractionalized spinon excitations are present alongside the Fermi surface quasiparticles. In this review article, we establish the FL* Fermi volume by generalizing the original Luttinger proof for FL to parton gauge theories of the quantum spin liquid and FL*. We also discuss Oshikawa's flux insertion arguments for FL, and their extension to FL*, including a discussion of gapless spin liquids.
label: arXiv:2611.21720v1

summary.background:
- Fermi surface: the boundary in momentum space separating occupied from empty electron states; its enclosed volume can be measured in some experiments.
- Fermi liquid: the standard model of metals, where electrons behave like weakly interacting particles.
- Luttinger's theorem: the classic result that the Fermi-surface volume equals the electron density in a Fermi liquid.
- Quantum spin liquid: a magnetic material whose spins do not freeze into order even at very low temperature, with fractional excitations called spinons.
- Parton gauge theory: a method of writing electrons or spins as combinations of simpler particles tied together by an emergent gauge field.
- Flux insertion (Oshikawa's argument): a thought experiment threading magnetic flux through a ring of material to constrain allowed states.
summary.one_liner: A review that extends Luttinger's proof of the Fermi-surface volume in ordinary Fermi liquids to fractionalized Fermi liquids (FL*) described by parton gauge theories, and discusses Oshikawa's flux-insertion arguments including gapless spin liquids.
summary.plain: The paper is about how many electrons' worth of states are enclosed by the boundary (Fermi surface) between filled and empty electron energies in a metal-like quantum material. In an ordinary metal the enclosed volume is fixed by the electron density alone. In a more exotic state, where electrons split into pieces called spinons, the same rule holds but with the density shifted by a fixed whole number, and the review works out why using a generalized version of an old proof.
summary.why: This sets out a precise counting rule that tells experimentalists and theorists what Fermi-surface size to expect in exotic quantum spin liquids, which can help test whether such a state is present. The text does not indicate specific experimental results or claims beyond the theory itself.

title: Constraints on the volume enclosed by Fermi surfaces

abstract: Recently, an extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model with three atoms per unit cell has been experimentally realized in perovskite exciton-polariton micropillars. A distinctive feature of this system is that the second and third bands undergo a topological transition through a band crossing at the wave vector $k=0$, associated with a negative coupling. In this work, we analytically determine the phase diagram of the model as a function of the on-site energy splitting and the ratio of intercell to intracell hopping amplitudes. We identify seven regions in this lane, with four distinct topological phases, characterized by different Zak phases of the three bands. Our results provide a useful theoretical framework for interpreting existing experiments and serve as a guide for future experimental investigations of this system.
label: arXiv:2611.18456v1

summary.background:
- Topological phase: a property of a system's band structure that stays the same under smooth changes, often linked to edge states at boundaries.
- Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model: a simple one-dimensional chain of sites with alternating hopping strengths, a standard textbook example of topology.
- Unit cell: the repeating group of sites; here each contains three atoms (sites).
- Bands and wave vector k: energy levels of waves in a periodic lattice, labeled by momentum k; the k=0 point is the centre of the Brillouin zone.
- Zak phase: a number computed from a band's wavefunctions over the Brillouin zone that signals its topology in one dimension.
- Exciton-polariton: a hybrid of light and matter excitations in a semiconductor microcavity.
- Phase diagram: a map showing which topological phase occurs for each combination of parameters.
summary.one_liner: An analytic phase diagram for an extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain with three atoms per unit cell and negative coupling, mapping seven regions with four topological phases via Zak phases of the three bands.
summary.plain: The paper studies a model of waves hopping along a chain of repeating units, a simplified description of a structure recently built from light-matter particles (exciton-polaritons) in perovskite micropillars. The authors work out, by calculation, how the system's topological character changes as two parameters are varied: the energy offset between sites and the ratio of hopping strengths between and within units. They report seven regions in this parameter plane, falling into four distinct topological phases.
summary.why: The text notes that the second and third bands swap topological character through a band crossing tied to a negative coupling, a feature specific to this experimental system. The phase diagram is meant to help interpret existing experiments and guide future ones, though the text does not report experimental comparisons itself.

title: Topological phase diagram of an extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model with negative coupling

abstract: We derive new constraints on the interaction cross section between dark matter and neutrinos ($σ_{νχ}$) that improve upon existing limits. We adopt a mechanism where neutrinos emitted from core-collapse supernovae transfer their energy to the dark matter halo via elastic scattering, transitioning a centrally cusped profile to a flat-cored profile. We apply this mechanism to Low Surface Brightness Galaxies (LSBGs), which are characterized by their relatively large sizes, low stellar densities, and measurements of dark matter cores. We improve upon previous methods so that each dark matter particle is counted at most once, which weakens existing limits, e.g., from the Fornax dSph by a factor of $\sim 50$. Applying our new method to LSBGs, we derive an upper limit of $σ_{νχ}< 8.5 \times 10^{-25}\,\rm cm^2$ for a dark matter mass of $m_χ=1\,\rm GeV$ at a typical supernova neutrino energy of $E_ν=15\,\rm MeV$. This constraint is approximately three orders of magnitude stronger than the Fornax limit derived with the same method and slightly stronger than the bound from the dark matter diffused supernova neutrino background (DMDSNB).
label: arXiv:2611.17922v1

summary.background:
- Dark matter: unseen matter inferred from its gravity on stars and gas; its particle nature is unknown.
- Neutrinos: nearly massless, weakly interacting particles produced in huge numbers in supernovae.
- Elastic scattering: a collision where particles bounce off each other without changing identity; the cross section measures how likely such collisions are.
- Cusp vs. core: dark matter density in simulations often peaks sharply at the centre (cusp); observations sometimes show a flatter centre (core).
- Low surface brightness galaxies (LSBGs): large, dim, diffuse galaxies with low star density, where dark matter is dominant and cores are measured.
- Fornax dSph: the Fornax dwarf spheroidal galaxy, a previously used test system.
- DMDSNB: the dark matter diffuse supernova neutrino background, another way to constrain the same interaction.
- Units: cm² is an area; 10⁻²⁵ cm² is a very small effective target size, and GeV/MeV are energy units.
summary.one_liner: The paper sets new upper limits on the elastic scattering cross section between dark matter and neutrinos, using supernova neutrinos heating the cores of low surface brightness galaxies and correcting a double-counting flaw in earlier versions of the method.
summary.plain: Dark matter is an invisible substance that makes up most of the matter in galaxies, and it is not yet known how strongly it interacts with neutrinos, tiny nearly massless particles. The authors look at neutrinos from exploding stars (supernovae) that could push energy into a galaxy's dark matter and smooth out its dense central peak into a flatter core. Using faint, spread-out galaxies whose dark matter cores are measured, they find that the interaction must be weaker than a stated bound.
summary.why: Limits on how often dark matter and neutrinos collide narrow down what dark matter can be, and this work claims to tighten existing bounds. The main claimed gain is that each dark matter particle is counted only once, which the authors say weakens earlier Fornax-based limits by about a factor of 50; the result is a model-dependent bound at one mass and one neutrino energy, so its robustness depends on the assumptions behind it.

title: Improved Bounds on the Dark Matter-Neutrino Cross Section using LSBGs

abstract: The nature of dark matter remains one of the major open questions in particle physics and cosmology. Direct detection experiments aim to identify dark matter particles through their interactions with ordinary matter, but despite substantial improvements in experimental sensitivity, no conclusive detection has been achieved. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of the present status and future prospects of direct particle detection, focusing on searches for dark matter particles from the Galactic halo. We introduce the theoretical framework for interpreting experimental results, including nuclear and electron scattering, collective excitations, particle absorption, and time- and direction-dependent signatures. We review the detection technologies employed in these searches, highlighting their operating principles, advantages, and limitations, as well as the calibration techniques and background mitigation strategies required to achieve high sensitivity. Particular emphasis is placed on experimental results reported since 2020, covering nuclear and electron recoil searches, annual modulation measurements, and directional detection. We also discuss experiments under construction and proposed future detectors, ranging from large-scale noble-liquid experiments to low-threshold technologies targeting sub-GeV dark matter. Finally, we examine the challenges that will shape the next generation of experiments, including the need for increasingly low energy thresholds, improved background understanding and discrimination, and the growing importance of neutrino-induced backgrounds. The diversity and complementarity of detector technologies will remain essential for exploring the dark matter parameter space and establishing the nature of any potential signal.
label: arXiv:2611.21052v1

summary.background:
- Dark matter: invisible matter inferred from its gravitational effects on galaxies and the wider universe; its particle identity is unknown.
- Direct detection: looking for rare collisions of dark matter particles with atoms in a sensitive detector deep underground, where cosmic rays are shielded.
- Nuclear recoil: a dark matter particle knocks an atomic nucleus; electron recoil: it knocks an electron.
- Energy threshold: the smallest energy deposit a detector can register; lower thresholds let it search for lighter dark matter.
- Annual modulation: the expected yearly rise and fall in event rate as Earth's motion through the halo changes with the seasons.
- Directional detection: trying to measure the direction of recoils to pick out the wind of dark matter from the galaxy.
- Background: other signals (radioactivity, cosmic rays, neutrinos) that can mimic a dark matter event.
- Noble liquid: liquids such as xenon or argon used as detection media.
summary.one_liner: A review of direct dark matter detection covering the theory of halo-particle scattering (nuclear, electron, collective excitations, absorption, time and direction signatures), detector technologies, results since 2020, and planned low-threshold and noble-liquid experiments.
summary.plain: Dark matter is thought to make up much of the universe's mass, but no one has yet detected it directly in a lab. This review surveys the experiments that try to catch dark matter particles from our galaxy's halo bumping into ordinary matter in detectors. It summarises the theory behind these searches, the detector technologies used, recent results since 2020, and the next generation of experiments.
summary.why: The text notes that, despite much better sensitivity, no conclusive detection has been made, so a clear map of the current status and remaining challenges is useful for planning. It also flags neutrino-induced background as a growing problem for future searches; the text does not say how far these efforts will go.

title: Hunting dark matter: the present and future of direct particle detection

abstract: Numerical relativity simulations of binary neutron star mergers and core-collapse supernovae indicate that the neutron star matter can be driven far from equilibrium due to large amplitude density oscillations, with frequency in the kHz range. Urca processes in neutron star matter try to restore the system towards equilibrium providing strong bulk viscous damping of these density oscillations. Standard bulk viscosity calculations typically assume small amplitude density oscillations, such that the deviation from chemical equilibrium $μ_Δ$ is less than the temperature $T$. In this work we compute the complete amplitude dependent bulk viscosity, taking into account, for the first time, thermal blurring effects and collisional broadening of in-medium nucleons. Our results show that the non-linear effects in bulk viscosity start to become important when the oscillation amplitude is about $10$ percent of the background density. In this regime the bulk viscosity can increase by three to five orders of magnitude. These results have important consequences for simulations of binary neutron star mergers as well as their multi-messenger observations.
label: arXiv:2611.18146v1

summary.background:
- Neutron stars: extremely dense remnants of collapsed stars, made mostly of neutrons.
- Binary neutron star merger: two such stars spiralling together and colliding; a source of gravitational waves and multi-messenger (gravitational plus light and particle) signals.
- Bulk viscosity: a measure of how much a fluid resists volume changes; it turns the energy of compression into heat, damping oscillations.
- Urca processes: reactions where neutrons, protons, electrons and neutrinos convert into one another, pushing matter back toward chemical equilibrium.
- Chemical equilibrium deviation (μΔ) versus temperature (T): the paper compares how far the matter is pushed from balance with its thermal energy scale.
- Thermal blurring and collisional broadening: effects that smear out the sharp energy levels of nucleons due to heat and particle collisions.
- Numerical relativity: computer simulations of strong-gravity events such as mergers.
summary.one_liner: The paper computes the full amplitude-dependent bulk viscosity of neutron star matter from Urca reactions, including thermal blurring and collisional broadening of nucleons, for large density oscillations relevant to binary neutron star mergers.
summary.plain: When two neutron stars collide and merge, the dense matter inside them is shaken by large, fast squeezes and stretches. This paper asks how strongly that matter resists being squeezed, a property called bulk viscosity, when the shaking is large rather than small. The authors find that the damping from particle reactions grows substantially once the squeezing reaches about 10 percent of the background density.
summary.why: Simulations of mergers and their gravitational-wave and light signals depend on how fast such oscillations are damped, so a much larger viscosity in the large-amplitude regime could change those predictions. The text reports the size of the effect but does not show its consequences for specific simulations or observations, so those links remain to be tested.

title: Suprathermal bulk viscosity in binary neutron star mergers

abstract: We improve the Langevin model to incorporate both perturbative and non-perturbative interactions between heavy quarks and the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. The transport coefficient of heavy quarks is evaluated by a potential scattering model in which both the short-range Yukawa interaction and the long-range string interaction are included. The updated model provides the correct thermal equilibrium limit of the heavy quark system with the medium background, and improves the accuracy in describing the nuclear modification factor and elliptic flow coefficient of $D$ mesons observed at RHIC and the LHC. Nuclear modification of different chemical components of charm hadrons, including $D^0$, $D_s^+$, $Λ_c^+$, $Ξ_c^0$, and $Ω_c^0$, is investigated. Their spectrum ratios are found sensitive to not only the hadronization mechanism of charm quarks but also the medium-modified charm quark spectrum in heavy-ion collisions, offering additional constraints on the heavy quark dynamics inside a color-deconfined nuclear medium.
label: arXiv:2611.21161v1

summary.background:
- Quark-gluon plasma (QGP): a state of matter at extremely high temperature in which quarks and gluons are not bound into protons or neutrons.
- Heavy-ion collisions (RHIC, LHC): experiments that smash heavy nuclei together to create QGP briefly.
- Heavy quarks (charm): quarks much heavier than the light ones; they are produced early and carry information about the medium.
- Langevin model: a simulation approach that tracks particles being randomly kicked and dragged, like a grain of pollen in water.
- Transport coefficient: a number describing how strongly the medium slows and randomly kicks a particle.
- Nuclear modification factor: ratio of particle yields in heavy-ion collisions to those in simple proton collisions; values below one mean suppression.
- Elliptic flow: a measure of how particles are preferentially emitted in a particular direction, reflecting collective motion.
- D mesons and charm baryons (Lambda_c, Xi_c, Omega_c): particles formed when charm quarks combine with lighter quarks (hadronization).
- Yukawa interaction: a short-range force form; the string interaction is a long-range confining-type force.
summary.one_liner: An improved Langevin transport model adds both short-range (Yukawa) and long-range string interactions to heavy-quark scattering in quark-gluon plasma, and uses it to fit D-meson suppression and flow and to predict how charm-hadron species ratios depend on hadronization and the medium.
summary.plain: Heavy-ion collisions at RHIC and the LHC briefly create a very hot soup of free quarks and gluons, called quark-gluon plasma. Heavy charm quarks pass through this soup and get slowed and pushed around, and the paper refines a computer model of that motion. The authors report that the updated model better matches measured D-meson suppression and flow, and that ratios among different charm-containing particles are sensitive to both how charm quarks combine into particles and how the soup altered them.
summary.why: Charm quarks serve as probes of the properties of quark-gluon plasma, so a model that fits both suppression and flow data is useful for interpreting those measurements. The text only describes a model improvement and comparisons with data; it does not give the size of the improvement, so the strength of the claim is not clear from this summary alone.

title: Suppression, flow, and chemical components of heavy flavor hadrons in relativistic heavy-ion collisions within an improved Langevin framework

abstract: Spectroscopy is a versatile tool that drives scientific discovery and underpins modern technologies. Quantum sensing offers promising opportunities to advance spectroscopy through enhanced sensitivity and spectral and spatial resolution. However, existing approaches largely focus on improving general measurement capabilities, often overlooking the structure of specific sensing tasks and leaving potential performance gains untapped. Here, we develop an algorithmic approach to quantum sensing tailored to various spectroscopic tasks, providing new avenues for improvement. Specifically, we consider general time-varying signals supported on a known set of $N$ candidate frequencies, a setting we call discrete-frequency spectroscopy. We formulate three types of practically motivated sensing tasks---Detection, Search, and Learning---that require progressively more spectral information. For all tasks, we design optimal quantum sensing algorithms achieving a $\sqrt{N}$ speedup over conventional frequency-scanning approaches. Optimal Detection and Search need only a single-qubit sensor under $π$-pulse control, whereas optimal Learning provably requires coherent processing with a quantum computer. End-to-end numerical simulations incorporating various experimental imperfections predict up to two-orders-of-magnitude speedup in Detection. As an example, we analyze the feasibility of our Detection and Search algorithms for real-world molecular screening based on state-of-the-art nitrogen-vacancy centers. We also show how quantum-computing-enhanced Learning enables wireless communication in a weak-signal regime where conventional methods fail. Our results establish a practical route toward realizing quantum advantages via designing task-specific sensing algorithms.
label: arXiv:2611.21560v2

summary.background:
- Spectroscopy: identifying materials or signals by their characteristic frequencies.
- Quantum sensor: a tiny quantum system (here a single qubit, a basic quantum bit) whose state changes when it interacts with an external signal.
- Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center: a defect in diamond that is used as a quantum sensor.
- π-pulse control: a timed sequence of microwave pulses that flips the sensor's state to steer its response.
- Speedup of √N: the number of measurements needed grows with the square root of the number of candidate frequencies, rather than linearly as in scanning.
- Discrete-frequency spectroscopy: the setting where the signal's frequencies are restricted to a known list.
summary.one_liner: The paper designs task-specific quantum sensing algorithms for detecting, searching, and learning time-varying signals whose frequencies come from a known set of N candidates, claiming a √N speedup over frequency scanning.
summary.plain: The paper looks at spectroscopy, the practice of identifying substances or signals by the frequencies they contain. It assumes the possible frequencies are already known from a list of N candidates, and asks how quantum sensors can answer three kinds of questions faster: is a signal present, which frequency is it, and what is its full structure. The authors report algorithms that they say achieve a speedup of about the square root of N over checking frequencies one at a time.
summary.why: Spectroscopy is used across science and industry, so a faster way to sense frequencies could matter if the gains hold in practice. The text reports simulations with experimental imperfections and a feasibility analysis for nitrogen-vacancy diamond sensors, but these are the authors' own predictions and have not been tested in a lab here.

title: Optimal Quantum Sensing Algorithms for Discrete-Frequency Spectroscopy

abstract: We introduce and study a Krotov-inspired discrete adjoint optimization scheme for quantum machine learning and focus on a hybrid online-to-batch schedule. The method transfers the forward/costate/local-update logic of continuous-time optimal control to parameterized quantum circuits by replacing time locality with gate-index locality. For a broad class of fixed-generator variational gates and terminal-state losses, we show that the batch Krotov direction coincides with the exact gradient of the empirical loss. Under standard smoothness assumptions, this yields monotonic descent and convergence of the batch method, and convergence of the tail of the hybrid method after a finite switch to the batch phase. Empirically, we benchmark hybrid Krotov against the tuned PennyLane optimizer suite and L-BFGS-B on a four-bit parity classifier and on the Pérez-Salinas data re-uploading classifier for the crown problem. Across matched hyperparameter sweeps with three seeds per configuration, hybrid Krotov dominates every tuned first-order baseline and matches the strongest structured PennyLane methods on parity, while approaching the accuracy of L-BFGS-B on Pérez-Salinas at first-order per-iteration cost.
label: arXiv:2611.18082v1

summary.background:
- Parameterized quantum circuit: a sequence of quantum gates whose angles are tunable parameters, used like a neural network in quantum machine learning.
- Gradient descent: repeatedly adjusting parameters in the direction that lowers a loss (error) measure.
- Optimal control and Krotov's method: a technique from physics and engineering for steering a system over time, using forward and backward (adjoint) passes to compute updates.
- Adjoint/costate: a backward-running auxiliary quantity that gives the sensitivity of the final loss to earlier steps.
- Batch vs. online updates: batch uses the whole training set per update; online uses examples one at a time; a hybrid switches between them.
- Baselines: L-BFGS-B is a quasi-Newton optimizer that uses more curvature information than first-order methods; PennyLane is a software library whose built-in optimizers were tuned here.
- Convergence and smoothness: mathematical conditions under which an iterative method is guaranteed to settle toward a minimum.
summary.one_liner: The paper adapts the Krotov optimal-control update, with a discrete adjoint (backward-propagated sensitivity) and an online-to-batch schedule, to train parameterized quantum circuits, and reports convergence results and benchmarks on two small classifiers.
summary.plain: Training a quantum circuit means tuning its adjustable dials so it gives correct answers, and this is usually done with standard gradient-based methods. This paper borrows a technique from control engineering, Krotov's method, which updates settings by sweeping forward and backward through the circuit, and adapts it to step through the circuit's gates rather than through time. The authors report that, for a broad class of circuits and losses, their batch version gives the exact gradient of the training loss, and they compare it against other optimizers on two small test problems.
summary.why: Faster or more reliable training of small quantum circuits is a practical bottleneck for quantum machine learning, so a method that needs only first-order cost per iteration could matter if the claims hold. The text itself reports only two small benchmarks with three seeds per configuration, so its broader significance is unclear from this summary alone.

title: Hybrid Krotov gradient descent Optimization for Quantum Machine Learning

abstract: Quantum sensors such as atomic clocks, atom interferometers, and atomic magnetometers can be used as sensitive probes of physics beyond the Standard Model. Space offers microgravity, long baselines, low environmental noise, access to varying gravitational potentials, and unique opportunities involving the Sun, Moon, planets, and asteroids. These proceedings of the Aspen Center for Physics workshop on "Fundamental physics in space with quantum sensors," held February 22-27, 2026, summarize the scientific case, current capabilities, and space mission concepts for investigating dark matter, testing general relativity, and detecting gravitational waves in frequency bands inaccessible from the ground.
label: arXiv:2611.21997v1

summary.background:
- Quantum sensors: devices that use the behavior of individual atoms to measure time, acceleration, or magnetic fields very precisely.
- Atomic clock: a timekeeper based on the fixed oscillation frequency of atoms; extremely sensitive to tiny changes in gravity.
- Atom interferometer: splits a cloud of atoms along two paths and recombines them to measure gravity or acceleration from the pattern they form.
- Standard Model: the current best theory of particles and forces; dark matter and gravitational waves in some bands lie partly outside what it fully explains or what can be seen directly.
- General relativity: Einstein's theory of gravity as curved spacetime.
- Gravitational waves: ripples in spacetime from massive accelerating objects; low-frequency ones are hard to detect from Earth because of ground noise.
- Microgravity: the near-weightlessness found in orbit, which lets atoms be observed for longer.
- Proceedings: a collection of written papers from a scientific meeting.
summary.one_liner: Workshop proceedings surveying the scientific case, current capabilities, and mission concepts for using space-based quantum sensors (atomic clocks, atom interferometers, atomic magnetometers) to search for dark matter, test general relativity, and detect gravitational waves in bands hard to reach from the ground.
summary.plain: This is a set of proceedings from a 2026 physics workshop on using ultra-precise atomic instruments in space. The authors argue that space offers a quieter, weightless environment with long distances and varying gravity, which could help detect faint signals from unknown physics. The text is a summary of the case for these experiments and the mission ideas, not a report of new measurements.
summary.why: It maps out where space-based quantum sensing might probe dark matter, general relativity, and gravitational waves that ground experiments cannot reach. Whether these mission concepts become real depends on future funding and technical progress, which the summary does not assess.

title: Fundamental physics with quantum sensors in space

abstract: Laser processing has emerged as a transformative technology in the energy sector, enabling precise, efficient, and scalable solutions for energy generation, storage, and sustainability. This chapter explores the diverse applications of laser technology in energy applications. It begins with an overview of laser-driven inertial confinement fusion for energy production, highlighting key experimental facilities and crucial laser parameters. The role of lasers in solar energy harvesting is examined, including photovoltaic cell optimization, concentrated solar power, and laser-assisted recycling of solar modules. The chapter further reviews recent developments into laser-based techniques for enhancing electrochemical performance through surface texturing at various scales. Advancements in lithium-ion battery technology are also discussed, focusing on next-generation materials, battery manufacturing processes, and the impact of laser techniques on performance, safety, and scalability. The chapter concludes with insights into future prospects for laser applications in sustainable energy solutions.
label: arXiv:2611.21024v1

summary.background:
- Laser: a beam of concentrated light; power and pulse length determine what it can do to a material.
- Inertial confinement fusion: fusion reactions triggered by squeezing a tiny fuel pellet with intense laser pulses so it heats and compresses for a very brief moment.
- Photovoltaic (solar) cell: a device that converts sunlight into electricity; laser processing can shape its surfaces or contacts.
- Concentrated solar power: uses mirrors to focus sunlight to produce heat, often for generating electricity.
- Surface texturing: deliberately creating tiny patterns or roughness on a material's surface to change how it interacts with liquids, light or electric charge.
- Lithium-ion battery: a rechargeable battery whose electrodes store and release lithium ions; manufacturing steps such as cutting or joining electrodes can use lasers.
- Electrochemical performance: how well a material stores or transfers charge in a battery or similar device.
summary.one_liner: A book chapter surveying laser applications across energy topics: laser-driven inertial confinement fusion, laser roles in solar cells and concentrated solar power, laser-based surface texturing for electrochemical performance, and laser techniques in lithium-ion battery materials and manufacturing.
summary.plain: This is an overview chapter, not a report of a single experiment. It describes how lasers are used in several energy areas: creating fusion energy by compressing fuel with intense light, improving and recycling solar panels, roughening or patterning surfaces to help electrodes work better, and making and improving lithium-ion batteries. The text summarizes these topics and ends with a look at future possibilities.
summary.why: Laser processing is a common tool in manufacturing, and energy technologies such as fusion, solar power and batteries all depend on it to varying degrees, so a survey can help readers see how these areas connect. The provided text is only the abstract-level summary, so it does not show specific new results or how strong the evidence is for each claim.

title: Laser Processing for Energy Applications

abstract: We apply a geometric formulation of Newtonian dynamics to inviscid compressible geophysical flow, with gravity and the effects of rotating or moving coordinates incorporated in the metric tensor. This construction relies on the introduction of an auxiliary fifth coordinate, which allows mass and momentum transport, internal energy, and pressure work to be combined into a single mass--momentum tensor. The covariant divergence of this tensor leads to the continuity equation for mass density, the three momentum equations, and the thermodynamic equation, with the system closed by an equation of state. A time-independent metric also yields conservation of total energy. We recover familiar forms of the equations and illustrate the construction in rotating spherical and terrain-following coordinates. The thin-shell and spherical-geopotential approximations, with constant effective gravity, simplify the metric while retaining vertical gravity and the traditional Coriolis terms. Emphasis is placed on the connection between the geometric structure of the formulation and the equations commonly used in atmospheric dynamics.
label: arXiv:2611.19685v1

summary.background:
- Geophysical flow: motion of air or water on a rotating, gravitating planet.
- Inviscid and compressible: ignores friction and allows the fluid's density to change with pressure.
- Metric tensor: a mathematical rule for measuring distances and angles in a chosen coordinate system; here it carries gravity and rotation.
- Coriolis terms: apparent forces from the Earth's rotation that deflect moving air.
- Covariant divergence: a coordinate-independent way of taking the net outflow of a quantity.
- Thin-shell and geopotential approximations: simplifications that treat the atmosphere as a thin layer with constant effective gravity.
- Equation of state: relation linking pressure, density and temperature.
summary.one_liner: The paper rewrites the equations of inviscid compressible geophysical flow in a five-dimensional geometric framework, with gravity and rotating or moving coordinates built into the metric, and shows how the thin-shell and spherical-geopotential approximations simplify it while keeping vertical gravity and Coriolis terms.
summary.plain: This paper is about how to write down the equations that describe air and water movement on a rotating planet, such as the flow of the atmosphere. The author uses an added, artificial fifth coordinate so that mass, momentum, internal energy and pressure work can be packed into one mathematical object. The text reports that the familiar equations of atmospheric dynamics come out of this construction, and it illustrates the approach in rotating spherical and terrain-following coordinates.
summary.why: The main value is in the structure: it shows how standard atmospheric equations are linked by a single geometric framework, which may help in organizing or checking model equations. The text does not report new numerical results or forecasts, so its practical impact is not shown here.

title: A Five-Dimensional Geometric Formulation of Geophysical Fluid Dynamics

abstract: The threshold at which density-limiting plasma instabilities occur in tokamak fusion reactors is not well understood. Here, we present the first large-scale empirical evidence of a common collisionality threshold present across multiple devices and confinement regimes. Machine-learning-guided analysis of a diverse experimental database identifies a scaling in edge effective collisionality ($ν_*$) that bears resemblance to the widely utilized Greenwald limit but yields a substantially lower false positive rate. This threshold decreases with dimensionless pressure ($β$), consistent with theoretical expectations for enhanced transport from electromagnetic effects on resistive ballooning mode turbulence. These results suggest that future burning plasma devices such as ITER and ARC could potentially achieve higher density, and thus fusion power, than previously expected.
label: arXiv:2611.21899v1

summary.background:
- Tokamak: a donut-shaped magnetic device that confines fusion-grade plasma.
- Plasma density limit: the maximum density before instabilities cause the plasma to lose heat and confinement.
- Greenwald limit: an existing, widely used empirical density ceiling based mainly on average density and plasma current.
- Collisionality: how often charged particles bump into each other; at the plasma edge it is an effective measure of how 'sticky' the plasma is to flow and turbulence.
- Beta: the ratio of plasma pressure to magnetic pressure; higher beta means more pressure relative to the field.
- Resistive ballooning modes: a type of turbulent instability at the plasma edge that drives heat and particles outward.
- False positive rate: the fraction of cases the rule flags as unstable that are actually stable.
- Machine learning here is used to guide the analysis of the database, not as a black box replacing physics.
summary.one_liner: An empirical, machine-learning-assisted study across several tokamak devices finds that the onset of density-limiting instabilities tracks an edge effective collisionality threshold that falls with plasma beta, and that this threshold yields fewer false positives than the Greenwald limit.
summary.plain: Tokamaks are donut-shaped reactors that hold very hot plasma in magnetic fields, and there is a ceiling on how dense that plasma can be before it becomes unstable and loses confinement. This paper looks for a common rule for where that ceiling sits, using a large database from many experiments. The authors report a threshold based on how often particles collide at the plasma edge, and say it works better than the familiar Greenwald limit at sorting stable from unstable cases.
summary.why: Plasma density limits set how much fusion power a reactor can make, so a more accurate rule could matter for planning devices such as ITER and ARC. The text suggests these devices might reach higher densities than expected, but this is a claim from the authors and has not been independently tested here.

title: Collisionality scaling of the tokamak density limit

abstract: We propose a finite-element method to determine the dynamics of a fluid interacting with a membrane---a fluid layer equipped with a Helfrich elastic free energy [W. Helfrich, Z. Naturforschung C, 28, 693, (1973)]. Our analysis is based on a partitioned approach, where the state of the fluid, of the membrane, and of the mesh, are solved for at staggered steps. We show the predicting capabilities of the method by considering a macroscopic example of an elastomer membrane, which bulges as it interacts with air injected through a channel. We demonstrate that our method allows for describing large membrane deformations which are not accessible by perturbative methods. We discuss the limitations of our method, by characterizing its added-mass instability. Finally, we show how our analysis allows for understanding the physical mechanism of bulge formation, which is due to a combination of elastic stresses and membrane boundary conditions.
label: arXiv:2611.18808v1

summary.background:
- Fluid-structure interaction: computing how a moving fluid and a deforming solid affect each other.
- Finite-element method: splitting a shape into small pieces (a mesh) and solving equations on them numerically.
- Helfrich free energy: a standard model of the bending energy of thin membranes, originally developed for lipid bilayers.
- Partitioned approach: solving the fluid and the solid in separate alternating steps rather than all at once.
- Added-mass instability: a numerical problem where the simulation becomes unstable when the fluid's inertia is strongly tied to a light structure.
- Perturbative methods: approximations that assume deformations are small.
summary.one_liner: A partitioned finite-element scheme couples a fluid to a Helfrich-elastic membrane, validated on air-driven bulging of an elastomer sheet and analyzed for added-mass instability.
summary.plain: This paper studies what happens when a fluid pushes on a thin flexible sheet, such as air blown against a stretchy membrane that bulges outward. The authors built a computer method that tracks the fluid, the membrane, and the shape of the mesh used for calculation, solving each in turn. They tested it on a large-scale elastomer membrane inflated by injected air and used it to explain why the bulge forms.
summary.why: The method handles large membrane deformations that simpler small-deformation (perturbative) approaches cannot, and the authors also report a stability limit of their scheme, which matters for anyone building similar simulations. The text does not establish links to specific biological systems, so any connection to cell or tissue mechanics would be speculative.

title: Interaction between fluids and Helfrich membranes

abstract: While analytical theories of transcriptional feedback loops have been well established, exact stochastic analyses of post-transcriptional feedback loops remain relatively scarce and are notoriously challenging. Here, we develop an exact theory of post-transcriptional gene autoregulation, in which reversible protein-mRNA binding modulates both translation and mRNA stability. We derive the state-dependent protein burst-size distribution, the steady-state protein number distribution in terms of confluent Heun functions, and an exact criterion for sub-Poissonian fluctuations. By comparing transcriptional and post-transcriptional networks, we reveal a reversal in their relative advantages in noise suppression and rhythm transmission: negative feedback favors post-transcriptional regulation, whereas positive feedback favors transcriptional regulation. Our results reveal how the regulatory pattern fundamentally shapes gene expression fluctuations and dynamic responses.
label: arXiv:2611.18062v1

summary.one_liner: The paper derives an exact stochastic solution for a gene whose protein product autoregulates itself post-transcriptionally by reversibly binding its own mRNA, affecting both translation and mRNA stability, and compares this with transcriptional feedback.
summary.plain:
Cells control how much protein they make, and the amount fluctuates randomly from moment to moment.
