This paper studies a control loop in which a protein sticks to its own messenger RNA, the molecule that carries the blueprint for making it, and thereby changes both how fast the protein is made and how long the messenger survives. The authors work out the exact mathematical description of these random fluctuations rather than relying on approximations.</plain>
<parameter name="why">Post-transcriptional feedback has been much harder to analyse exactly than transcriptional feedback, so an exact result is a useful reference point. The reported contrast, that negative feedback suits post-transcriptional control for suppressing noise while positive feedback suits transcriptional control, could inform how cells balance steady expression against fast responses; the text does not show how directly this applies to specific biological systems.</plain>
<parameter name="background">Gene expression: DNA is transcribed into messenger RNA (mRNA), which is translated into protein. Transcriptional regulation acts on mRNA production; post-transcriptional regulation acts after that, on translation or mRNA decay. Feedback: a protein that influences its own production, either negatively (dampening it) or positively (boosting it). Stochastic noise: random fluctuations in molecule counts, which are significant when numbers are small. Poissonian vs sub-Poissonian: a Poisson distribution has variance equal to its mean; sub-Poissonian means less variable than that baseline, i.e. more regular. Burst size: the number of proteins produced from one mRNA molecule before it degrades. Confluent Heun functions: a family of special mathematical functions used here to write the exact solution.</background>
<parameter name="difficulty">research-level

title: Exact stochastic theory of post-transcriptional gene autoregulation mediated by RNA-binding proteins

abstract: Machine learning weather models now rival operational global forecasts but still start from analyses produced by separate, expensive data assimilation (DA) systems, which for global models are typically updated every six hours. Observation-to-observation models avoid this dependence, but most omit the recursive filtering cycle that lets DA systems carry a background state through sparse, irregular observations. We introduce WeatherDreamer, a world model that learns this cycle end-to-end from 18 global observing systems, without reanalysis. It infers a latent state from observations, carries it forward hour by hour with learned dynamics, corrects it each hour with new observations, and can predict what any of its observing systems would measure at any location. At held-out stations, its ensembles beat NOAA's Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) for temperature, dew point and wind out to 12 h and are better calibrated than GEFS and the ECMWF ensemble. Precipitation, cloud-top height and solar irradiance, never inputs at inference, are inferred with skill matching or exceeding operational products at short leads. Against the first guess of NOAA's Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) DA system, WeatherDreamer's short-range departures are within 10% of GSI's at surface stations and within 25% for moisture-sensitive microwave channels, but up to five times larger for temperature-sounding channels. Never given observation errors, its learned update assumes errors close to known instrument and retrieval errors of microwave sounders and scatterometer winds. WeatherDreamer also separates viewing geometry from atmospheric state, recovering 83-96% of observed limb darkening and producing seamless nadir-view imagery. Producing an hourly global analysis in about 1.5 minutes on one GPU, WeatherDreamer shows that assimilation and forecasting can be learned together directly from observations.
label: arXiv:2611.18393v1

summary.background:
- Weather forecasting starts from an "analysis": an estimate of the current atmosphere built by data assimilation (DA).
- DA systems typically run in cycles (here, every six hours for global models) and carry a background state forward, correcting it with new observations.
- Ensembles are sets of forecasts from slightly different starting points; calibration means the spread of the ensemble matches how often it is actually wrong.
- Reanalysis is a historical, retrospectively corrected record of the atmosphere, often used as training targets; this model is said to avoid it.
- Microwave sounders and scatterometer winds are satellite instruments measuring atmospheric temperature profiles and surface winds, respectively.
- Limb darkening is the way a planet's brightness varies toward its edge as seen from orbit, depending on viewing angle.
- GSI, GEFS and ECMWF are, respectively, NOAA's DA system, NOAA's forecast ensemble and the European Centre's ensemble forecast.
summary.one_liner: WeatherDreamer is a learned world model that jointly performs data assimilation (fusing sparse observations into an evolving atmospheric state) and multi-hour forecasting end-to-end from 18 global observing systems, without reanalysis targets.
summary.plain: Weather forecasts today start from a "best guess" of the current atmosphere, which is built by a separate, costly system that blends satellite, balloon, and ground readings. This paper presents WeatherDreamer, a machine-learning model that learns to do that blending and the forecasting together, directly from raw observations. The authors report that it beats NOAA's GEFS forecast ensemble for temperature, dew point, and wind out to 12 hours at held-out stations, and that it produces an hourly global analysis in about 1.5 minutes on one GPU.
summary.why: It challenges the standard split between data assimilation and forecasting, which could make weather analysis much cheaper if the approach holds up. The text reports some mixed results, though: temperature-sounding channels depart from the reference system by up to five times more, so the claim is promising rather than settled.

title: WeatherDreamer: Learning a World Model from Multimodal Earth Observations

abstract: The state space of a dynamical system can, under suitable conditions, be reconstructed from a single observational time-series through delay-coordinate embedding. However, reconstructing the spatiotemporal evolution of nonlinear water waves from highly sparse measurements remains a considerable challenge. Here, by combining deep learning, compressed sensing, and the self-similarity properties of unidirectional nonlinear water wave evolution equation, we show that the evolving surface elevation of a highly nonlinear wave field can be reconstructed from observations collected at a {\it single} measurement location. We subsequently use these reconstructions to forecast rogue waves associated with self-focusing soliton dynamics from point observations obtained in controlled water wave tank experiments, demonstrating excellent agreement with measurements of the fully evolved wave field. Our results show that extreme wave events can be forecast from remarkably sparse observations and provide a framework that may be extended to other nonlinear dispersive systems governed by the interplay of dispersion and nonlinearity.
label: arXiv:2611.21068v1

summary.background:
- Delay-coordinate embedding: rebuilding a system's full state from one measured time series by using time-shifted copies of that series.
- Compressed sensing: recovering a complete signal from far fewer measurements than usually needed, by exploiting structure in the signal.
- Deep learning: neural networks trained on data to learn mappings, here used in the reconstruction step.
- Rogue wave: an unusually large wave arising from nonlinear effects, where many waves reinforce each other.
- Self-focusing soliton: a localized wave packet that can concentrate energy as it travels, governed by the interplay of nonlinearity and dispersion.
- Unidirectional nonlinear water-wave equation: a simplified model of waves moving in one direction, used to describe such dynamics.
- Wave tank experiment: a laboratory basin where waves are generated and measured under controlled conditions.
summary.one_liner: Combines deep learning, compressed sensing, and the self-similarity of the unidirectional nonlinear water-wave equation to reconstruct a highly nonlinear wave field from a single point measurement and forecast rogue waves, validated in water-tank experiments.
summary.plain: The paper looks at how to predict freak ocean-style "rogue" waves, which can form when waves interact and focus their energy. Instead of measuring a wave across a wide area, the authors use readings from just one fixed point, such as a single wave gauge. They use these sparse readings to rebuild how the whole wave surface evolves over space and time, and then forecast the rogue wave. They report that the forecasts agree well with measurements of the fully developed wave in water-tank experiments.
summary.why: Extreme waves threaten ships and offshore structures, and most sensing gives only sparse data, so a method that works from a single point could matter for monitoring. The text supports the claim only for controlled tank experiments on one class of wave dynamics; its wider use in real seas or other dispersive systems is suggested by the authors but not shown here.

title: Reconstruction and Forecast of Extreme Waves from a Single Observation

abstract: Primordial black holes (PBHs) may constitute a fraction of dark matter, but distinguishing them from black holes of stellar origin remains a major challenge. We propose a new method based on the three-dimensional localization of Galactic Binary Black Holes (BBHs) by the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA). While stellar-origin BBHs are expected to be associated with the stellar distribution of the Milky Way, PBHs may trace its more extended dark matter halo. We introduce a spatial overlap ratio that compares the gravitational-wave localization of each binary with the normalized stellar and dark matter density profiles. Using a Fisher-matrix forecast and 1000 Monte Carlo realizations of a 10-year LISA mission, we find that detecting three BBHs with an overlap ratio ln B < 0 occurs in approximately 99% of simulations where BBHs trace dark matter, but in fewer than 0.1% of simulations where they follow the stellar distribution, even when including a stellar halo containing 3% of the Galactic stellar mass. These results suggest that the localization of only a few Galactic BBHs could provide strong evidence for a primordial population, offering an independent test of their possible contribution to dark matter.
label: arXiv:2611.21337v1

summary.background:
- Primordial black holes: black holes formed in the very early universe, not from collapsed stars.
- Dark matter: unseen matter that makes up most of the mass of galaxies, inferred from its gravity.
- Binary black holes: two black holes orbiting each other; their merging or inspiral emits gravitational waves, ripples in spacetime.
- LISA: a planned space-based gravitational-wave observatory (a set of three spacecraft) expected to launch in the 2030s.
- Fisher-matrix forecast: a standard statistical shortcut for estimating how precisely an instrument could measure parameters, without running full data analysis.
- Monte Carlo realizations: many randomly generated mock datasets used to estimate how often an outcome occurs.
- Overlap ratio (ln B): a log-odds style score comparing how well each binary's sky location matches the stellar versus dark-matter density; negative values favour the dark-matter picture here.
summary.one_liner: A Fisher-matrix forecast for a 10-year LISA mission proposes using the 3D sky localization of Galactic binary black holes, compared against stellar versus dark-matter density profiles via an overlap ratio, to tell primordial black holes from stellar-origin ones.
summary.plain: Black holes that formed in the early universe, called primordial black holes, might make up some of the invisible dark matter in our galaxy. Black holes made from dying stars should instead sit mostly where the galaxy's visible stars are. This paper proposes telling the two apart by pinning down where pairs of black holes orbiting each other in the Milky Way are located, using a future space gravitational-wave detector called LISA. The authors simulated 1000 mock 10-year missions and found that a few well-located pairs would usually separate the two scenarios.
summary.why: If it works, this gives a way to test whether primordial black holes contribute to dark matter that does not depend on seeing them directly. The result depends on modelling choices and simulated data rather than real detections, so it is a forecast, not an observed finding.

title: On the origin of Milky Way binary black holes with LISA

abstract: The dispersion measure (DM) of fast radio bursts (FRB) provides a noisy measure of the free-electron column density to the burst. With next-generation FRB surveys the number of bursts will drastically increase and measurements of the baryon distribution will be possible on the Mpc scales most relevant to Stage IV weak lensing surveys. Comparing the DM auto-spectrum, DM-shear cross-spectrum and the kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect, we argue that the cross-correlation of FRB catalogs with galaxy surveys offers many advantages. Hybrid Effective Field Theory (HEFT), often used in large-scale structure cosmology, is capable of modeling the clustering of electrons jointly with galaxies and matter to small scales. Using HEFT with the Padé model of baryonic feedback, we forecast that next-generation FRB surveys (combined with galaxy samples) will be able to constrain feedback at a level informative for Stage IV weak lensing surveys. In particular we should not be limited by modeling the manner in which galaxies trace the matter field. Rather constraints of the higher-order electron biases and the electron-galaxy cross-stochasticity provide the dominant limitation, and are an obvious target for improvement in order to reach percent-level constraints. The same measurements also provide a valuable means of constraining feedback in hydrodynamic simulations of galaxy formation in a way that is not tied to the modeling of particular galaxy samples.
label: arXiv:2611.18512v1

summary.background:
- Fast radio bursts (FRBs): millisecond radio flashes from far away; their dispersion measure (DM) is the total amount of free electrons along the line of sight.
- Baryons: ordinary matter (gas, stars); feedback is energy from stars and black holes that blows gas out of galaxies, changing its distribution.
- Weak lensing: measuring tiny distortions of background galaxy shapes caused by intervening mass; Stage IV surveys are the next generation of such projects.
- Power spectrum / cross-spectrum: statistics that show how strongly fluctuations cluster at different physical scales, and how two maps correlate.
- Hybrid Effective Field Theory (HEFT): a computational approach for modeling how galaxies and matter cluster, extended here to electrons.
- Padé model: a parameterized functional form used to describe the feedback effect.
- Kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect: a distortion of the cosmic microwave background caused by hot gas moving along the line of sight, another gas probe the paper compares against.
- Bias and stochasticity: how well a tracer (galaxies, electrons) follows the underlying matter, including random scatter.
summary.one_liner: Forecasts how well cross-correlating future fast radio burst dispersion-measure catalogs with galaxy surveys, modeled with Hybrid Effective Field Theory and a Padé feedback model, could constrain baryonic feedback relevant to Stage IV weak lensing.
summary.plain: Fast radio bursts are brief flashes of radio waves from distant sources, and the way their signals are delayed as they pass through gas reveals how much ionized matter lies along the path. The paper asks whether many such bursts, combined with galaxy maps, can show how gas is pushed around by galaxy formation (called baryonic feedback). The authors report that this cross-correlation looks more promising than other options they compare, and that the main limits would come from how electrons and galaxies relate to each other, not from how galaxies trace matter.
summary.why: Baryonic feedback is a major uncertainty for weak lensing surveys that map dark matter through galaxy shape distortions, so an independent probe could help calibrate it. The text is a forecast rather than a measurement, so the actual usefulness depends on future FRB surveys delivering the expected data.

title: Probing baryonic feedback using fast radio bursts and galaxy surveys

abstract: Multi-messenger and multi-wavelength observations of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) can provide otherwise inaccessible knowledge about physics Beyond the Standard Model (BSM), and may even lead to its discovery. Realizing this potential hinges on two parallel efforts: advancing our understanding of AGN and of the dark matter around them, and identifying the BSM signatures that are at once promising and robust against the gaps in that understanding. These fields have attracted growing interest in recent years, also motivated by the IceCube association of neutrinos to individual AGN, yet we have only begun to explore their cross-fertilization. This white paper offers a new perspective on this interdisciplinary endeavor. It concisely reviews the state of the art in each field and at their interface, and identifies the key open questions that must be addressed to strengthen our prospects for learning about BSM physics with AGN.
label: arXiv:2611.21736v1

summary.background:
- AGN: a galaxy's central supermassive black hole actively pulling in matter, often outshining its host galaxy.
- Beyond the Standard Model (BSM): physics not captured by the current best theory of particles and forces, for example dark matter or new particles.
- Multi-messenger astronomy: combining different kinds of cosmic signals, such as light, neutrinos and gravitational waves.
- IceCube: a neutrino detector buried in Antarctic ice, which reported associating some neutrinos with individual AGN.
- Dark matter: unseen matter inferred from its gravitational effects, thought to surround galaxies and their black holes.
- White paper: a position or overview document summarising the state of a field, rather than presenting new results.
summary.one_liner: A white paper reviewing how multi-messenger and multi-wavelength observations of active galactic nuclei (AGN) could probe physics beyond the Standard Model, through the AGN themselves, the dark matter around them, and their interface, and listing open questions.
summary.plain: This paper looks at supermassive black holes at the centres of galaxies that are feeding on gas, known as active galactic nuclei. The authors argue that watching these objects with several kinds of signals, such as light across wavelengths and particles like neutrinos, could reveal new physics that current theory does not cover. The text is a short review of the current state of research in this area, and it lists the main unanswered questions that need work before such discoveries become realistic.
summary.why: Interest has grown since IceCube linked neutrinos to individual AGN, which suggests these objects may act as natural particle-physics laboratories. The text does not report new measurements, so its value lies in organising a young, interdisciplinary field and its open questions.

title: Active Galactic Nuclei as Beyond the Standard Model Laboratories: a White Paper

abstract: Gravitational waves (GWs) from a stellar-mass binary black hole (BBH) orbiting a supermassive black hole (SMBH) can experience repeated gravitational lensing as the BBH passes behind the SMBH. Our previous studies of orbit-induced GW modulation motivate this investigation of repeated lensing in evolving hierarchical triple systems. We investigate how eccentricity, inclination, and relativistic precession of the outer orbit affect successive lensing events and parameter inference. The outer orbit follows post-Newtonian dynamics, and the inspiral waveform includes moving-source effects and de Sitter precession. An event-local point-mass lensing model tracks the changing source--lens alignment and GW frequency. For a one-year LISA observation, we examine lensing-event identification, Fisher-matrix estimates of parameter uncertainties, and waveform residuals when lensing is omitted. Our results show that outer-orbit evolution changes the timing and amplification of successive lensing events and can bring initially unfavorable configurations into the lensing region. A fixed circular, nonprecessing approximation misses all lensing events for a substantial fraction of the selected lensed systems. The median fractional reductions in uncertainty are largest for the outer-orbit inclination and SMBH spin. For some systems above the adopted detection threshold, lensing-induced waveform differences persist after local adjustments to the parameters of the unlensed model. Repeated lensing can thus provide complementary constraints on SMBH properties and outer-orbit geometry in LISA observations of hierarchical BBHs.
label: arXiv:2611.20416v1

summary.background:
- Gravitational waves: ripples in spacetime produced by accelerating massive objects, detected as tiny signals in instruments.
- Black hole binary: two black holes orbiting each other; here a stellar-mass pair orbits a supermassive black hole, forming a hierarchical triple.
- Gravitational lensing: a massive object bends and focuses waves passing near it, which can amplify the signal; here the big black hole acts as the lens.
- LISA: a planned space-based gravitational-wave detector.
- Eccentricity and inclination: how elongated an orbit is and how tilted its plane is.
- Post-Newtonian dynamics: approximate corrections to Newtonian gravity used to model orbits near strong gravity.
- Fisher matrix: a standard statistical estimate of how precisely model parameters can be measured from a signal, not an actual measurement.
summary.one_liner: A simulation study of how repeated gravitational lensing of gravitational waves from a stellar-mass binary black hole orbiting a spinning supermassive black hole, on an eccentric and precessing outer orbit, could be identified and used to constrain parameters for LISA.
summary.plain: The paper looks at gravitational waves from a pair of black holes that orbit a much larger black hole at the centre of a galaxy. As the pair travels behind the big black hole, its signal can be bent and brightened, and this can happen more than once as the outer orbit changes shape and direction. The authors model this for a one-year observation by the planned LISA space detector and report how the timing and strength of these repeated lensing events depend on the outer orbit.
summary.why: Repeated lensing could give extra information about the big black hole's spin and the tilt of the outer orbit, which would be hard to get otherwise. The text reports these effects within a modelling framework, not observed data, so their real-world size depends on assumptions the summary does not fully spell out.

title: Repeated Gravitational-Wave Lensing from Binary Black Holes on Eccentric and Precessing Orbits around Spinning Supermassive Black Holes

abstract: We present a multi-wavelength case study of the star T28 in the Chamaeleon I star-forming region and investigate the dust evolution of its highly Ca-depleted protoplanetary disk. We combine new observations from the MIKE spectrograph on the Magellan Clay Telescope with archival IRS spectrum and photometry. We constrain the optical extinction using the hydrogen column density of the region, and apply ROTFIT to obtain stellar parameters. We estimate the mass accretion rate by fitting the excess flux above the photosphere with an accretion shock model. We model the line profiles of Ca II K and H$α$ with magnetospheric accretion models to infer Ca/H abundance, while the infrared excess is modeled with irradiated accretion disk models to get disk properties. We find that T28 is a high accretor with significant Ca depletion in its accretion flows. We find that the disk is best fit with a pre-transitional model with a disk mass of 0.12 $M_{\odot}$, where two optically thick disks are separated by a gap filled with optically thin dust extending to 16 au. This gap would not be resolved in the existing observations. T28 follows the trend of increasing depletion with increasing mass accretion rate. This trend can potentially be explained by preferential and early giant planet formation in massive disks, as suggested by recent planet formation simulations, leading to enhanced capture of refractory material in the massive disks of high accretors and thus depletion in the material reaching the star.
label: arXiv:2611.21786v1

summary.background:
- T28 is a young star (a protostar still forming) in the Chamaeleon I star-forming cloud.
- Protoplanetary disk: a rotating disk of gas and dust around a young star, where planets form.
- Mass accretion rate: how fast the star pulls in gas from its disk.
- Calcium depletion: calcium is less abundant in the infalling gas than in the star's expected composition, likely because dust grains containing it were removed.
- Refractory material: rock-forming elements that condense at high temperatures and stick to dust.
- Pre-transitional disk: a disk with a gap separating an inner and outer ring of dust, often read as a sign of forming planets.
- Spectrograph and infrared excess: instruments that split light into colors; extra infrared light reveals warm dust around the star.
- Au (astronomical unit): the Earth–Sun distance.
summary.one_liner: A multi-wavelength study of the young star T28 in Chamaeleon I combines new MIKE optical spectra with archival infrared data to link its calcium depletion in accretion flows to its dust disk structure, which is modeled as a pre-transitional disk with a gap extending to 16 au.
summary.plain: This paper looks at a young star called T28 that is still pulling gas from a surrounding disk where planets may form. The authors found that the gas falling onto the star is unusually poor in calcium, and that the dust disk seems to have a gap that current telescope images would not resolve. They suggest this calcium shortage may be tied to how fast the star is feeding and to early giant planet formation, though the link is a proposal rather than a demonstrated result.
summary.why: Calcium depletion in accreting gas is a possible chemical fingerprint of planets locking up rocky material before it reaches the star, so the proposed link between accretion rate, disk mass, and early giant planet growth is worth watching. The authors present this as a possible explanation for a trend seen in their sample, and the single-object nature of the case study means it is a suggestive rather than settled connection.

title: Connecting Calcium Depletion and Dust Evolution in the Rapid Accretor T28

abstract: We present a homogeneous characterization of outer disk dust and gas properties for 51 protoplanetary disks from the JWST/MIRI Cycle 1 programs, combining new ALMA observations with archival data. Visibility fitting with frank recovers more and higher-contrast substructures in the mm continuum than image-plane analysis, placing the innermost features of several disks at 4-5 au and leaving only three disks featureless at the current resolution. CO gas disk sizes span $\sim$60-1000 au and correlate strongly with mm continuum sizes, with $R_{\rm CO}/R_{\rm mm}$ ranging from 1.4 to 9.7 (median 2.95). We then connect these outer disk properties to JWST/MIRI inner disk water diagnostics. We find no global correlation between the cold-to-hot water flux ratio ($F_{\rm cold}/F_{\rm hot}$), a proposed proxy of cold water enrichment by pebble transport, and any single outer disk parameter, including $R_{\rm mm}$, $R_{\rm CO}/R_{\rm mm}$, and innermost substructure location. Three compact ($R_{\rm mm}<30$ au), structureless disks with $R_{\rm CO}/R_{\rm mm}>4$ show both elevated $F_{\rm cold}/F_{\rm hot}$ and cold water emission near the snowline temperature, consistent with unimpeded inward drift of icy pebbles. For structured disks, the water properties instead vary widely at fixed gap location, reflecting the sensitivity of the inner disk water content to multiple factors, including gap leakiness, grain size, and thermal history. Linking outer disk dust evolution to inner disk water content thus requires carefully selected samples with detailed constraints on these additional parameters.
label: arXiv:2611.20617v1

summary.background:
- Protoplanetary disk: a rotating disk of gas and dust around a young star, where planets form.
- Snowline: the distance from the star beyond which water freezes into ice.
- Pebble drift: larger dust grains lose orbital energy and spiral inward, carrying ice with them.
- ALMA: a radio telescope array that measures millimetre-wavelength dust emission and gas (CO) emission.
- JWST/MIRI: the James Webb Space Telescope's mid-infrared instrument, used here to detect water vapour in the inner disk.
- Visibility fitting (frank): a way of modelling radio interferometer data directly to find ring and gap features.
- Astronomical unit (au): the Earth–Sun distance.
- Gap leakiness, grain size and thermal history: other factors the authors say also control inner-disk water.
summary.one_liner: A homogeneous survey of outer-disk dust and gas sizes and substructures for 51 protoplanetary disks, linked to JWST/MIRI inner-disk water diagnostics, finds no global correlation between cold-to-hot water flux ratio and single outer-disk parameters, but compact structureless disks show signs of unimpeded pebble drift.
summary.plain: This study looks at young planet-forming disks of gas and dust around stars and asks whether the outer part of each disk controls how much water reaches the inner, rocky-planet zone. The authors combined new radio observations (ALMA) with archived data for 51 disks, and matched them to infrared measurements of water from the JWST telescope. They found no simple overall link, but three small, smooth disks with very extended gas show the pattern expected if icy pebbles drift freely inward.
summary.why: Water delivered by drifting pebbles is one proposed route for putting water into forming planets, so tying it to measurable disk structure matters for planet-formation models. The text only supports a tentative link: it reports a few compact disks with a pattern consistent with pebble drift, and states that structured disks vary widely, so a clean rule is not established.

title: Complex Interplay between Outer Disk Dynamics and Inner Water Reservoir

abstract: Context: Cosmic rays escaping from their accelerators produce gamma-ray emission through interactions with ambient gas. While the scenario of an impulsive injection of cosmic rays has been extensively studied, that of a continuous injection in time has received comparatively less attention. The latter scenario is particularly relevant for stellar clusters, which may contribute to a non-negligible fraction of Galactic cosmic rays. Aims: We intend to characterize the excesses of cosmic rays around their accelerators and to assess the detectability of the gamma-ray emission resulting from the interactions of cosmic rays in nearby molecular clouds. We focus in particular on star clusters and seek to apply these considerations to the case of W43. Methods: We derive analytical estimates for the cosmic ray excess around sources as a function of source properties and transport parameters. We also evaluate under which conditions the predicted gamma-ray emission from illuminated molecular clouds can be detected by current and future instruments. We then apply these results to explain the gamma-ray emission from the the W43 region. Results: We find that producing detectable gamma-ray emission from molecular clouds illuminated by cosmic rays escaping from star clusters generally requires either suppressed diffusion relative to the Galactic value or anisotropic diffusion, with the latter scenario requiring a smaller global energetic. We applied this approach to the case of W43 and by fitting its gamma-ray emission we were able to constrain the underlying CR transport parameters.
label: arXiv:2611.21317v1

summary.background:
- Cosmic rays: fast charged particles, mostly protons, moving through the galaxy.
- Gamma rays: the highest-energy form of light; here produced when cosmic rays hit gas.
- Molecular clouds: cold, dense gas clouds where stars form; they act as targets.
- Diffusion: the random, scattering-driven spreading of charged particles through magnetic fields; the "Galactic value" is the typical rate across the galaxy.
- Anisotropic diffusion: spreading that is faster in some directions than others.
- Impulsive vs. continuous injection: a single burst of particles versus a steady release over time.
- Stellar cluster W43: a dense region of young massive stars in the Milky Way that emits gamma rays.
summary.one_liner: Analytical estimates of how continuously injected cosmic rays from star clusters build up around their sources and produce gamma rays in nearby molecular clouds, applied to the W43 region.
summary.plain: High-energy particles called cosmic rays are thought to leak out of their sources and crash into nearby clouds of gas, which then glow in gamma rays. This paper looks at the case where a group of young stars keeps releasing such particles over a long time, rather than in one burst, and asks when the resulting glow would be bright enough to detect. The authors apply this to the W43 star-forming region and use its gamma-ray emission to estimate how cosmic rays move through the surrounding medium.
summary.why: Star clusters may supply a non-negligible share of Galactic cosmic rays, so a way to test them through gamma rays from gas clouds is of interest. The text reports that detectable emission generally needs either suppressed diffusion or anisotropic diffusion, which constrains transport models; the broader significance beyond W43 is not established in the text.

title: Non-thermal emission from molecular clouds illuminated by continuous cosmic-ray accelerators: application to the stellar cluster W43

abstract: We present a search for optical bursts from the repeating fast radio burst FRB 20200120E, which is located in a globular cluster of M81 and is the closest known extragalactic FRB. We observed FRB 20200120E simultaneously with the high-speed, quintuple-beam optical camera HiPERCAM on the 10.4-m Gran Telescopio Canarias and the Effelsberg 100-m Radio Telescope. We detected one radio burst of fluence $\mathcal{F}_{\rm R} = 0.14\pm0.01$ Jy ms during our observations, but found no evidence for corresponding optical bursts in the 11.98 ms frames. We find 5$σ$ upper limits on the optical burst fluence of $\mathcal{F}_{\rm O} < 1.8\times10^{-3}$ Jy ms (combined $u_s g_s r_s i_s z_s$-bands) and the optical burst energy of $E_{\rm O} < 5.4\times10^{36}$ erg ($r_s$-band), corrected for interstellar extinction. We compare our upper limit on the optical-to-radio fluence ratio $\mathcal{F}_{\rm O}/\mathcal{F}_{\rm R} < 0.013$ to various emission models involving inverse-Compton scattering in the magnetosphere or nebula of a highly-magnetised neutron~star.
label: arXiv:2611.21861v1

summary.background:
- Fast radio burst (FRB): a very brief, very bright radio pulse from outside our galaxy, lasting milliseconds; the source is thought to be a highly magnetised neutron star (magnetar).
- Repeating FRB: one that has emitted more than one burst.
- Globular cluster: a dense, old ball of stars orbiting a galaxy.
- M81: a large spiral galaxy about 12 million light-years away.
- Fluence: the total energy received per unit area from a burst; here given in Jy ms (a radio flux unit times time).
- Optical burst and upper limit: a flash of visible light; an upper limit means the instrument would have seen anything brighter, and nothing was seen.
- Inverse-Compton scattering: a process where fast electrons boost low-energy light to higher energy; proposed as a way to make optical flashes.
- Interstellar extinction: dimming of light by dust between us and the source, corrected for here.
summary.one_liner: A simultaneous radio and high-speed optical monitoring campaign of the repeating FRB 20200120E in an M81 globular cluster finds no optical counterpart burst, yielding upper limits that constrain inverse-Compton emission models for magnetar-powered bursts.
summary.plain: Fast radio bursts are millisecond flashes of radio waves from distant space, and this one repeats and sits in a star cluster in the nearby galaxy M81. The team watched it at the same time with a radio telescope in Germany and a very fast optical camera on a large Spanish telescope, looking for a matching flash of visible light. They saw one radio burst but no matching optical flash, so they could only set upper limits on how bright any optical flash could have been.
summary.why: Finding out whether these bursts also flash in visible light would help show what produces them, and this source is the closest known extragalactic FRB, so it is a useful test case. The text reports only limits, not a detection, and it does not say how strongly these limits rule out particular models beyond the comparison it describes.

title: A search for optical bursts from the repeating fast radio burst in the M81 globular cluster, FRB 20200120E

abstract: We derive a conservation based dynamical stability frontier for interacting binary stars that distinguishes stationary mass transfer from the restoration of a perturbed contact state. We apply the formalism to conservative white dwarf binaries with direct impact accretion, coupling Roche overflow, stream angular momentum, gravitational radiation, and both stellar spin reservoirs. From the contact equations, we obtain the required orbital return torque, and an exact Jacobian identity yields the restoring gradient and an oscillatory stability boundary in the computed white dwarf domain. A dimensionally normalized quadrupolar tide reveals separate equilibrium fold and oscillatory thresholds, including coexisting stable and unstable stationary branches. Finite donor synchronization introduces an additional oscillatory stability frontier. The model recovers the classical Roche and gravitational radiation limits, while the calculated orbital period derivatives are consistent with published binary timing measurements within their combined observational and model uncertainties. These results specify the torque amplitude, restoring stiffness, and synchronization rate needed for local stability, providing quantitative targets for stellar tidal calculations and the interpretation of interacting binaries in the millihertz gravitational wave band.
label: arXiv:2611.19026v1

summary.background:
- Binary star: two stars orbiting a common centre of mass.
- Roche overflow: when a star swells enough to spill gas onto its companion, through the gravitational boundary (Roche lobe) around each star.
- Accretion: gas falling onto a star.
- White dwarf: a small, dense stellar remnant about the size of Earth.
- Angular momentum and spin: the rotational "spin" of an object and the orbital motion both carry angular momentum, which must be conserved overall.
- Stability (dynamical): whether a small disturbance dies away (stable) or grows (unstable).
- Fold and oscillatory thresholds: a fold is where a steady state stops existing or changes character; an oscillatory threshold is where small disturbances start to swing back and forth.
- Gravitational waves: ripples in spacetime emitted by orbiting masses; the millihertz band is a range of wave frequencies targeted by planned space detectors.
- Orbital period derivative: how fast the orbital period is lengthening or shortening, measured by timing observations.
summary.one_liner: The paper derives a conservation-based stability boundary for interacting binary stars, applies it to conservative white dwarf binaries with direct impact accretion, and examines equilibrium fold, oscillatory, and synchronization-induced thresholds.
summary.plain: The paper asks when a pair of stars orbiting each other, where one feeds gas onto the other, will settle into a steady exchange of mass or will drift away from that state. The authors work through this for pairs of white dwarfs, the dense leftover cores of small stars, using conservation of mass, angular momentum and energy. They report the conditions under which a steady state is stable and where the system can instead start to oscillate.
summary.why: Interacting white dwarf pairs are candidate sources of millihertz gravitational waves, so stability limits bear on how such systems evolve and what detectors might see. The abstract says the calculated orbital period changes are consistent with published timing measurements within stated uncertainties, but the text provides no further detail on that comparison, so its strength is hard to judge from this summary alone.

title: The Stability Frontier of Interacting Binary Stars

abstract: Solar wind charge exchange (SWCX) emission is often a major component of the soft X-ray background, but it also provides a remote diagnostic of the composition and ionization state of solar wind plasma. We present an analysis of a SWCX event observed with XRISM/Xtend during 2024 August 9-13. The event occurred during intense solar activity with multiple flares, including an X1.3-class solar flare, and associated coronal mass ejections (CMEs). We found a clear enhancement in the 0.3-3.0 keV count rate that occurred nearly simultaneously with an increase in the solar wind proton flux measured by ACE. We fitted the spectrum during the enhancement period with a set of Gaussian emission lines. In addition to the commonly detected C, N, and O lines, we detected Ne, Mg, Si, and Fe lines at $>15σ$ significance. We extracted two characteristic periods within the enhanced interval based on the CME arrival timeline. The O$_{\rm VIII}$/Si$_{\rm XIII}$ line ratio changed significantly between the two periods, suggesting contributions from multiple CME components. We then applied the AtomDB charge exchange model with a multi-temperature setup. The estimated ionization temperatures for Ne, Mg, Si, and Fe increased with the peak soft X-ray flux of the associated solar flares. This trend suggests that coronal heating becomes more efficient for more intense flares. Meanwhile, the ionization temperatures were lower than typical flare electron temperatures, implying that CME plasma may have been released into interplanetary space under non-equilibrium ionization conditions. We also found an indication of an inverse-FIP pattern, with reduced relative abundances of Si and S. These results demonstrate that XRISM/Xtend can diagnose the coronal plasma through SWCX emission, including heavy ions such as Ne, Mg, and Si, which are difficult to measure with current in-situ instruments (e.g., ACE satellite).
label: arXiv:2611.20934v1

summary.background:
- Solar wind: a continuous stream of charged particles flowing outward from the Sun.
- Coronal mass ejection (CME): a large burst of magnetised gas thrown from the Sun's outer atmosphere, sometimes after a solar flare.
- Solar wind charge exchange (SWCX): when highly charged ions in the solar wind capture electrons from neutral gas, they emit X-rays; this is a known part of the faint X-ray background seen near Earth.
- Emission lines: sharp bright X-ray wavelengths that act like fingerprints identifying specific elements and their ionization states.
- Ionization temperature: an effective temperature describing how stripped of electrons the ions are, which hints at the conditions where the gas was heated.
- Abundance and inverse-FIP pattern: how much of each element is present relative to others; the first ionization potential (FIP) effect is a known pattern in which low-FIP elements are enhanced in the corona, and an inverse pattern is the opposite.
- XRISM: a Japanese-led X-ray space observatory; Xtend is its wide-field X-ray imaging instrument.
- ACE: a NASA spacecraft at a point between Earth and the Sun that measures solar wind in situ.
- AtomDB: a public atomic database used to model X-ray emission from plasmas.
summary.one_liner: Using the XRISM/Xtend X-ray imager, the authors analyse a solar wind charge exchange (SWCX) X-ray enhancement during multiple coronal mass ejections in August 2024, fitting emission lines from C, N, O, Ne, Mg, Si and Fe and modelling ionization temperatures and abundances with AtomDB.
summary.plain: The Sun regularly throws out clouds of charged gas, called coronal mass ejections, and when this gas collides with neutral atoms near Earth it glows in X-rays. This paper looks at one such glow observed over five days in August 2024, when several solar flares and clouds hit at once. By splitting the X-ray light into its characteristic colours (spectral lines), the authors identified the elements present and estimated how hot the gas was when it left the Sun.
summary.why: The Sun's charged gas is hard to measure directly with spacecraft for some heavy elements, so reading it from X-ray glow could give a complementary view of the Sun's corona and of how solar eruptions differ in strength. The text reports that the ionization temperatures rose with flare intensity and were lower than typical flare temperatures, but the link to coronal heating and the composition patterns are suggestive interpretations from a single event that would need further checks.

title: XRISM/Xtend detection of solar wind charge exchange induced by multiple coronal mass ejections in 2024 August

abstract: Brownian chain molecular dynamics (BCMD) [M. Shiga, J. Comput. Chem. 43, 1864 (2022)] was introduced as a practical path-integral-based approach to approximate quantum vibrational dynamics in molecular and condensed-phase systems. Its equations of motion combine Newtonian dynamics of the centroid variables with overdamped Brownian dynamics of the non-centroid path variables. Here, we introduce a path-resolved quasi-density-operator (path-QDO) representation by extending the QDO construction underlying centroid molecular dynamics to the full discretized imaginary-time path. For two position-diagonal observables, this representation gives an exact expression for the Kubo-transformed correlation function in the fine-discretization limit, without requiring either observable to be linear. BCMD can be viewed as a phenomenological, time-homogeneous Markov approximation to the exact reduced propagation in these path variables, although its generator is not derived from the path-QDO formulation. We also formulate and validate a multiple-time-step algorithm that allows pseudo-Hamiltonian errors in the deterministic propagation to be controlled by separating the Brownian refresh interval from the inner integration time step. We test the path-QDO representation on one-dimensional models and present BCMD infrared spectra of q-TIP4P/F ice, ambient water, and hot water, comparing them with published results from other approximate quantum-dynamics methods.
label: arXiv:2611.19645v1

summary.background:
- Path-integral methods: they represent a quantum particle as a closed chain of beads in imaginary time, capturing zero-point motion and quantum spreading.
- Centroid variables: the average position of the chain; the rest of the chain describes its spread.
- Kubo-transformed correlation function: a standard quantum-statistical quantity from which spectra are computed.
- Infrared spectrum: the pattern of light frequencies a molecule absorbs, reflecting its vibrations.
- Brownian (overdamped) dynamics: random, friction-dominated motion, as in pollen grains jittering in water.
- Markov approximation: assumes the next step depends only on the current state, not on history.
- Multiple-time-step algorithm: uses small internal steps for fast motion and a longer interval for the random updates, to control numerical error.
summary.one_liner: This paper formulates Brownian chain molecular dynamics (BCMD), a path-integral-based approximation for quantum vibrational dynamics, via a new path-resolved quasi-density-operator representation, and validates a multiple-time-step integration scheme with tests on 1D models and infrared spectra of ice and water.
summary.plain: Quantum effects such as nuclei being "smeared out" matter for how molecules vibrate, but exact quantum calculations are very expensive. This paper refines a practical simulation method (BCMD) that mixes ordinary Newton-style motion for the average position of each atom's quantum "smear" with random, Brownian-style jiggling of the rest. The authors give a new mathematical framework for it, test it on simple one-dimensional models, and compute infrared spectra for ice and water.
summary.why: The work tries to make a quantum-aware simulation of vibrations in liquids and solids cheaper and more controllable, which matters for predicting infrared spectra. The text does not show how far the approach extends beyond the tested models and water/ice systems, so its wider impact is uncertain.

title: Formulation of Brownian chain molecular dynamics and the path-resolved quasi-density operator

abstract: Oxirane (ethylene oxide, \ce{C2H4O}) is a prototypical system for investigating photoinduced bond cleavage and ring-opening dynamics. Previous time-dependent density functional theory studies identified the initial HOMO $\rightarrow$ LUMO (\ce{S1}) excitation as nonreactive and attributed ring opening to higher-energy excitations. Subsequent constrained density functional theory simulations, however, reported ring opening following an \ce{S2} $\rightarrow$ \ce{S1} transition. Here, we investigate photochemistry of oxirane using time-dependent $GW$ molecular dynamics (TD$GW$-MD), a many-body approach based on extended quasiparticle theory [\textit{J. Chem. Phys.} \textbf{160}, 184102 (2024)]. Our simulations reveal ring opening initiated by asymmetric \ce{C-O} bond cleavage following direct HOMO $\rightarrow$ LUMO (\ce{S1}) excitation. Following the selected surface hop, separate conditional trajectories on the broken-symmetry open-shell singlet and triplet potential energy surfaces lead to distinct products. The singlet trajectory yields acetaldehyde via intramolecular hydrogen transfer, while the triplet trajectory produces formaldehyde and methylene via \ce{C-C} bond fragmentation. These products are consistent with those identified in previous photolysis experiments. Our results demonstrate that direct excitation to the lowest singlet excited state can initiate ring opening within the present TD$GW$-MD framework. They further reveal distinct subsequent reaction pathways under the selected spin conditions. This study highlights the potential of TD$GW$-MD for elucidating photoinduced reaction mechanisms from a many-body perspective.
label: arXiv:2611.20723v1

summary.background:
- Oxirane (ethylene oxide) is a small ring molecule made of two carbons, one oxygen and four hydrogens.
- "Photolysis" means breaking molecules apart with light; "ring opening" means the ring of atoms splits into a chain.
- Electronic excited states are higher-energy arrangements of a molecule's electrons, reached when it absorbs light. S1 is the lowest singlet excited state, and HOMO→LUMO is the main electron jump that produces it.
- Singlet and triplet refer to electron spin arrangements; they can lead to different reaction paths.
- Potential energy surface: a map of how a molecule's energy changes with its atom positions; reactions follow paths across it.
- Density functional theory (DFT) and GW are approximate quantum-chemistry methods; GW is a many-body approach designed to treat electron interactions more explicitly.
- Molecular dynamics: simulating how atoms move over time, here with trajectories that branch after a "surface hop" between energy maps.
summary.one_liner: A many-body time-dependent GW molecular dynamics study that finds direct excitation to the first singlet state of oxirane can trigger ring opening, with singlet and triplet follow-up trajectories giving different products.
summary.plain: Light can break chemical bonds, and this paper looks at a small three-atom ring molecule, oxirane, which opens up when struck by ultraviolet light. Earlier computer studies disagreed on whether the lowest-energy light-absorbing state could open the ring, so the authors used a newer many-body simulation method to re-examine it. They report that direct excitation to that lowest state does start the ring opening, and that the molecule then splits into different products depending on its spin state.
summary.why: The disagreement between earlier methods makes the question of which excited state drives the bond breaking worth settling, and the reported products match earlier photolysis experiments. The work is mainly a test of whether this simulation approach can handle photochemistry, so its broader significance depends on further tests on other molecules.

title: Oxirane Ring-Opening Dynamics Mediated By The First Singlet Excitation Using Time-Dependent \textit{GW} Molecular Dynamics

abstract: Crystal structure prediction (CSP) determines periodic atomic or molecular arrangements from chemical composition and physical conditions. Over three decades, CSP has evolved from chemical construction and global energy optimization to hybrid approaches combining symmetry, learned potentials, adaptive search, and deep generative models. This survey reviews method, software, review, and benchmark records from 1996 to October 2026, covering inorganic and molecular crystals, including formula-conditioned diffusion, flow, and autoregressive models that preserve composition. We classify methods by candidate construction and exploration: template and discrete construction, random search, evolutionary search, swarm and differential evolution, energy-landscape exploration, adaptive machine-learning-guided search, and learned generation. We distinguish representation, relaxation, ranking, and physical qualification. Benchmarks reveal no universally dominant approach. In a 46-target leaderboard snapshot, the best-performing template method achieves higher top-1 recovery than leading generative models, but paired tests show no statistically significant differences from several generative competitors. We also audit predictions for 68 experimentally examined materials, including 52 with structures confirmed by diffraction or microscopy. Predictions for 23 of the 68 preceded experiment, mostly through first-principles global search. Within the reviewed evidence, we find no independently confirmed discovery in which a deep generative model predicted the structure before experiment. We conclude with the principal limitations of current CSP algorithms and priorities for future research.
label: arXiv:2611.17670v1

summary.background:
- Crystal: a solid whose atoms repeat in a regular 3D pattern.
- Crystal structure prediction: computing the likely repeating pattern from chemical composition alone.
- Energy landscape: the map of how stable each possible arrangement is; the most stable one is usually the one seen in nature.
- First-principles calculation: physics-based quantum calculations, with no fitting to experimental data.
- Deep generative model: a machine-learning model (such as diffusion or flow models) that proposes new candidate structures.
- Benchmark / leaderboard: a shared set of test targets used to compare methods, here reported as top-1 recovery (whether the correct structure is ranked first).
- Diffraction or microscopy: experimental techniques used to confirm a crystal's atomic arrangement.
summary.one_liner: A survey of 30 years of crystal structure prediction (CSP) methods, software, and benchmarks, classifying search and learning approaches and auditing predictions against experimentally confirmed materials.
summary.plain: This paper reviews three decades of work on predicting how atoms or molecules will arrange themselves into a crystal, given only the chemical recipe and conditions like pressure. The authors sort the many computer methods into families, such as trial-and-error searches, evolutionary searches, and newer machine-learning generators. They report that no single approach clearly wins on benchmarks, and that most of the 68 audited materials with predicted structures were predicted before experiments, mostly by first-principles search rather than deep generative models.
summary.why: Predicting crystal structures before synthesis could help guide the search for new materials for batteries, electronics, or pharmaceuticals, so the field's track record matters to those who fund and use it. The text's most specific finding is that, within the reviewed evidence, no confirmed discovery was made by a deep generative model ahead of experiment, which tempers claims about AI-driven materials discovery.

title: Crystal Structure Prediction from Search to Learning: A 30-Year Expedition

abstract: One of the defining characteristics of most energy materials, used as e.g.~battery electrodes, photovoltaics, or photocatalysts, is their ability conduct charges such as electrons and holes. The exact mechanism of this conductivity depends on the material, but is often dominated by the existence of mobile small polarons, i.e.~electrons or holes strongly localised through the polarisation of their environment. Computationally, small polarons can be treated with reasonably accuracy through the use of self-interaction corrected or hybrid density functional theory (DFT) together with local geometry optimisation. Similar approaches can be employed to determine the energy barriers to movement of the polarons through hopping. Unfortunately, realistic energy materials tend have very large numbers of symmetry inequivalent polaronic configurations and correspondingly large numbers of hopping barriers, making them hard to tackle explicitly. In this work we therefore extend the computational reach of DFT calculations with machine-learned (ML) surrogate models, which then feed into a kinetic model to quantitatively estimate the conductivity of a battery anode material (Li$_4$Ti$_5$O$_12$ or LTO) at realistic, defected conditions. We calculate the conductivity at room temperature to be 6.7 $\times$ 10$^{-3}$ S/cm which lies well in the experimental range. To this end, we only needed a total of 154 polaron barrier calculations, out of 3649 symmetry inequivalent ones, achieving an over 20-fold increase of computational efficiency. Overall, our work demonstrates how DFT-trained ML surrogates can be used to quantitatively and efficiently sample the dynamics of small polarons in energy materials.
label: arXiv:2611.18041v1

summary.background:
- Conductivity: how easily electric charge moves through a material, measured in siemens per cm (S/cm).
- Small polaron: an electron or hole that is trapped by distorting the atoms around it, so it moves by hopping between sites.
- Density functional theory (DFT): a quantum-mechanical computational method for estimating material energies and structures; hybrid and self-interaction corrected variants are more accurate for trapped charges.
- Energy barrier: the energy needed for a polaron to hop from one site to the next; it sets how fast hopping happens.
- Machine-learning surrogate: a fast statistical model trained on expensive calculations to predict their results for new cases.
- Kinetic model: equations that combine hopping rates into an overall transport property.
- Li4Ti5O12 (LTO): a lithium-ion battery anode material.
summary.one_liner: The paper uses machine-learning surrogate models trained on density functional theory (DFT) calculations to sample small-polaron hopping barriers in the battery anode material Li4Ti5O12 (LTO), feeding them into a kinetic model to estimate room-temperature conductivity.
summary.plain: Many battery and solar materials conduct electricity because electrons or holes get trapped in a local distortion of the surrounding atoms, forming a "small polaron" that hops from site to site. Simulating every possible trapped state and hop is too expensive, so the authors trained a machine-learning model on a smaller set of quantum calculations to predict the rest. They used the results in a kinetic model to estimate how well lithium titanate (LTO), a battery anode material, conducts at room temperature.
summary.why: Estimating charge transport in realistic, defective materials from first principles is hard, and this work reports a predicted conductivity that the authors say falls within the experimental range, using 154 explicit calculations out of 3649 inequivalent barriers. The approach may be useful for other energy materials, but the text does not show how well it generalises beyond LTO.

title: A Machine-learning-aided Workflow for Sampling Small Polaron Dynamics in Energy Materials

abstract: Active matter consists of energy-consuming units that generate motion, making it a powerful platform for exploring nonequilibrium physics and engineering adaptive materials. Robotic active matter brings this physics into programmable, macroscopic agents with controllable actuation, sensing, and response, but its scalability is limited by onboard power, communication, and control complexity. Field-driven active matter addresses these limitations by shifting part of the control burden from individual agents to external or environmental fields, such as magnetic, electric, acoustic, optical, and fluidic fields, which can power, guide, and couple many agents simultaneously. Beyond applications in targeted navigation, adaptive collaboration, and flexible transport, field-driven robotic active matter offers a controllable testbed for nonequilibrium phenomena that are difficult to isolate in molecular or colloidal active matter, including tunable interactions, programmable phase transitions, solid-fluid switching, hyperuniform order, and reconfigurable collective motion. Here, we present field-driven active matter as a bridge between active matter physics and functional material engineering, organized through a unified field-to-information-to-physics-to-function framework that links field-mediated interactions, information processing, and memory to collective transport, reconfiguration, and mechanical performance. By distributing control between agents and fields, field-driven active matter offers a pathway toward intelligent materials capable of sensing, adaptation, computation, reconfiguration, and performing complex tasks, while expanding both the scientific scope of nonequilibrium physics and the practical capabilities of engineered matter.
label: arXiv:2611.19806v1

summary.background:
- Active matter: many units that consume energy to move, so the group behaves differently from a system at rest.
- Nonequilibrium physics: the study of systems that are continuously driven by energy input, rather than settled into equilibrium.
- Colloids: tiny particles suspended in a fluid, often used as model systems.
- Hyperuniform order: a structured arrangement that is uniform at large scales while looking irregular at small scales.
- Solid-fluid switching: a group that can change between jammed, solid-like and flowing, liquid-like behavior.
- Field-driven control: using external magnetic, electric, acoustic, optical or fluid forces to power and steer many units at once.
summary.one_liner: A review-style perspective arguing that field-driven robotic active matter, where external magnetic, electric, acoustic, optical or fluidic fields power and couple many agents, can serve as a testbed for nonequilibrium physics and a route to functional adaptive materials, organized around a field-to-information-to-physics-to-function framework.
summary.plain: This paper looks at groups of small machines that move on their own, where much of the steering and power comes from outside fields such as magnetic or sound waves instead of from each machine's own battery and processor. The authors propose that this setup lets researchers study how many moving parts organize themselves, and could lead to materials that sense, adapt and carry out tasks. The text is a framing and overview; it does not report a specific new experiment or measured result.
summary.why: Moving control from each agent to shared external fields is a proposed way to make large groups of machines easier to scale, and the physics of such groups may be easier to control than in tiny molecular or colloidal systems. The excerpt gives only the framing, so its practical impact is not demonstrated here.

title: Field-Driven Active Matter Physics and Material Applications

abstract: Interparticle adhesion plays a critical role in the flow behavior of cohesive granular materials, yet quantitative characterization at the particle scale remains challenging. Here, we present a cantilever-based method that combines a glass-beam cantilever for force measurements with a novel catapult mode for energy measurements, enabling the determination of both quasi-static detachment force and kinetic detachment energy. Applied to three different cohesive materials: polymer-coated silica particles, wet granular media, and cross-linked poly(2-ethylhexyl acrylate) (PEHA) microparticles, this method reveals a fundamental decoupling between force and energy, suggesting that both quantities are equally critical for characterizing grain properties.
label: arXiv:2611.18021v1

summary.background:
- Cohesive granular material: a powder or grain pile whose particles stick together, such as damp sand or fine powders.
- Adhesion force: the pull needed to separate two touching particles.
- Detachment energy: the work needed to pull them apart, which can differ from the peak force if the process is dynamic (kinetic) rather than slow (quasi-static).
- Cantilever: a thin beam fixed at one end; its bending reveals how much force is applied.
- Polymer-coated particles, wet granular media (grains with a liquid film between them), and cross-linked polymer microparticles (networks of linked polymer chains) are the three test systems.
summary.one_liner: A cantilever-based technique measures both the quasi-static pull-off force and the kinetic detachment energy between adhesive particles in cohesive granular materials, applied to polymer-coated silica, wet granular media, and cross-linked PEHA microparticles.
summary.plain: This paper is about how strongly tiny grains stick to each other, which controls how powder-like materials flow or clump. The authors built a measuring setup using a thin glass beam that bends as particles are pulled off, and a "catapult" mode that captures the energy released during detachment. They tested it on three sticky materials and report that force and energy can differ from one another, so both matter for describing the grains.
summary.why: Interparticle adhesion is hard to measure at the scale of single particles, yet it governs how cohesive powders flow, so a method that captures both force and energy may give a fuller picture. The text does not indicate specific applications, and the abstract gives no quantitative results, so the practical reach is unclear from this text alone.

title: A Cantilever-Based Method for Probing Adhesion Force and Kinetic Detachment Energy in Cohesive Granular Materials

abstract: Generative models play a rapidly growing role in the design and simulation of molecules. The most widely used applications of generative models are in large language models (LLMs), owing to the natural flexibility of language for specifying and answering queries. However, generalist LLMs do not effectively handle large sets of 3D coordinates, whereas specialist generative models of 3D molecules cannot reach the controllability afforded by language. To bridge these capabilities, we propose Nahual, a decoder-only autoregressive diffusion model for any sequence of text and 3D molecules. To enable expressive autoregression on continuous coordinates, we propose next-token diffusion, whereby a causal transformer denoises each token while attending to the clean tokens before it, without increasing context size. We train Nahual on a curated set of twelve 3D chemistry tasks ranging from microsolvation to molecular conformer search to adsorption on metal surfaces, with associated evaluation metrics and baselines. The result is a single set of end-to-end-trained weights that simultaneously performs all tasks and surpasses state-of-the-art models specialized for crystal structure prediction and property-conditional molecule generation. Our results demonstrate the viability of scaling generalist decoder-only models for native multimodal understanding and generation across language and chemistry. Code is available at https://github.com/the-matter-lab/nahual.
label: arXiv:2611.19072v1

summary.background:
- Generative model: a model that produces new examples (text, images, molecules) after learning from data.
- Autoregressive: generating output one piece at a time, each piece conditioned on the earlier ones, as large language models do.
- Diffusion model: a model that creates data by starting from noise and gradually removing it; here it is applied to each token.
- Decoder-only transformer: the architecture behind most chatbots, which predicts the next item in a sequence.
- Token: a unit of input, such as a word or here a text piece or an atom's 3D position.
- Crystal structure prediction: working out how atoms arrange themselves in a solid crystal.
- Conformer search: finding plausible 3D shapes a flexible molecule can adopt.
- Microsolvation and adsorption on metal surfaces: small numbers of solvent molecules clustering around a solute, and molecules sticking to a metal surface.
summary.one_liner: Nahual is a decoder-only autoregressive diffusion model that jointly handles text and 3D molecular coordinates, using a next-token diffusion scheme to generate continuous atomic positions, and is trained on twelve chemistry tasks.
summary.plain: Chemists design and simulate molecules in 3D, and language models are good at taking flexible text instructions but handle lists of 3D atom positions poorly. This paper proposes Nahual, a single model that reads and writes both text and 3D molecular structures in one sequence. The authors train it on twelve chemistry tasks and report that one set of weights performs all of them.
summary.why: The paper claims one trained model can match or beat specialist models on crystal structure prediction and property-conditioned molecule generation, which would be useful if it holds up under independent testing. It is also a test of whether general-purpose sequence models can extend to scientific data beyond text. The abstract gives only summary claims, so the size of the gains and the robustness of the comparisons cannot be judged from this text alone.

title: Nahual: A Sequence Model for Language and Atoms

abstract: Ion transport in solids has conventionally been understood from equilibrium diffusion, yet ions in batteries are driven by electric fields. Does field-driven ion transport follow equilibrium behavior? We examined this question in bulk Li2O and at its grain boundaries (GBs) using electric-field molecular dynamics combining a machine learning interatomic potential with a Bader charge prediction model. Although Li diffusion in cubic Li2O is isotropic at zero field, an electric field renders it orientation dependent because Li hops along a limited set of crystallographic pathways that the field biases unequally. At GBs, this anisotropy becomes a qualitative difference: a GB that strongly traps Li vacancies but exhibits a strong field response releases them under a field, whereas a weakly responsive GB retains them despite weaker vacancy trapping. These results show that field-driven GB transport is governed not by static thermodynamics alone but by the angle between the electric field and the diffusion pathways of the constituent grains.
label: arXiv:2611.17679v1

summary.background:
- Ion diffusion: random hopping of ions through a solid, usually studied with no electric field.
- Electric-field molecular dynamics: computer simulation of atoms moving under an applied field.
- Machine learning interatomic potential: a fast, learned stand-in for quantum calculations of the forces between atoms.
- Bader charge: a way of assigning partial electrical charge to atoms from electron density.
- Vacancy: a missing ion in a crystal lattice; these gaps carry ion transport.
- Grain boundary: the interface where two differently oriented crystal grains meet; often acts as a trap for defects.
- Li2O: lithium oxide, a simple lithium compound relevant to battery interphases.
summary.one_liner: Using machine-learning-potential molecular dynamics with a Bader charge model, the paper shows that an applied electric field makes Li diffusion in cubic Li2O orientation-dependent and changes how Li vacancies move through grain boundaries, depending on the angle between the field and the grains' diffusion pathways.
summary.plain: Batteries work because electric fields push ions through solid materials, but most models of how ions move in solids assume no field. This paper asks whether ions moving under a field behave the same way as in a field-free solid, using simulations of lithium oxide (Li2O), a material found in battery interfaces. The authors found that a field makes lithium movement depend on direction, and at grain boundaries (the seams between crystal grains) a boundary that holds onto lithium gaps can release them under a field, while a less responsive boundary keeps them.
summary.why: It suggests that grain-boundary behavior in battery materials may depend on the field direction relative to the crystal grains, not only on static energetics, which could matter for how such materials are designed. The text is limited to simulations of one material, so how far these results carry to real batteries is unclear.

title: Electric Fields Turn Vacancy-trapping Grain Boundaries into Li-Ion Pathways in Li2O

abstract: Dynamic assembly of actin filaments drives cell protrusion and other aspects of cell motility. Reconstitution of actin assembly from purified components is a powerful approach for understanding the molecular mechanisms that underlie these processes. Purified preparations of actin, actin-binding proteins, and regulators of actin-binding proteins enable a broad spectrum of reconstitution experiments. Much of this actin filament assembly occurs at the plasma membrane, with exquisite temporal and spatial regulation. We developed a biomimetic reconstitution system using purified lipids or glutathione on the surface of functionalized beads as models for actin assembly at the plasma membrane. The system incorporates two critical pathways for regulation of actin assembly: nucleation of actin polymerization by Arp2/3 complex and activation of heterodimeric actin capping protein (CP). Arp2/3 complex and CP are both essentially inactive in the basal resting state of the cytoplasm. The system incorporates membrane-bound activators for Arp2/3 complex, such as WASP and WAVE family proteins, and for CP, such as CARMILs and other CPI-motif proteins. Membrane-bound components are coupled to beads either through lipids, which allow lateral mobility, or through glutathione groups attached to the bead surface via flexible linkers. Fluorescence microscopy of labeled components, combined with quantitative image analysis, is used to assess the combined effects of the regulators and thereby test molecular mechanisms for regulation of actin assembly. Here, we describe protocols for preparing functionalized beads, coupling regulators to the bead surface, performing actin assembly reactions, and imaging and quantifying the resulting actin networks.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.11.765950 v1

summary.background:
- Actin: a protein that forms long filaments, the main scaffolding that pushes cell edges forward.
- Arp2/3 complex: a protein assembly that starts new actin branches from existing filaments.
- Capping protein (CP): a protein that caps the ends of filaments and stops them growing; regulators can switch it off.
- WASP/WAVE and CARMIL proteins: membrane-bound regulators that activate Arp2/3 and capping protein at the right place and time.
- Reconstitution: rebuilding a biological process from purified parts outside the cell to see what each part does.
- Biomimetic: designed to imitate a natural structure, here a cell membrane, using simple materials.
- Functionalized beads: beads with chemical groups attached so that proteins can be anchored to them.
summary.one_liner: This methods paper describes a bead-based biomimetic system, with lipid- or glutathione-coated surfaces, for reconstituting Arp2/3-driven actin nucleation and capping protein regulation, along with protocols for imaging and quantifying the resulting actin networks.
summary.plain: Cells move partly by building networks of protein fibers (actin) at their outer membrane, and this work describes a way to rebuild that process in a test tube. The researchers coat small beads with fat-like lipids or a chemical tag, attach the proteins that switch actin growth on and off, and then watch and measure the fiber networks that form under a microscope. The text presents this as a set of step-by-step protocols rather than reporting new findings.
summary.why: A controlled, purified version of the cell's membrane machinery lets researchers test how specific regulators change actin assembly, without the full complexity of a living cell. The text does not report specific results, so its usefulness depends on how well the protocols work for other labs, which it does not show.

title: Actin Assembly on Biomimetic Lipid-coated and Functionalized Bead Surfaces

abstract: Surveillance of functional centers in the mature 60S ribosomal subunit by SBDS licenses its translational debut. Timely release of eIF6 from 60S by SBDS is essential to permit 40S joining. Biallelic mutations in SBDS associated with Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (SDS), an inherited ribosomopathy, impair dissociation of eIF6 from 60S. How SBDS variants that bind to 60S structurally perturb the maturation and surveillance of 60S is yet to be deciphered. Here, we report high-resolution cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of human SBDS and pathogenic variants in complex with human 60S. The structures reveal that disease mutations disrupt key interactions of SBDS with the functional centers of the 60S subunit destabilizing critical bases and protein interactions across the P-site, peptidyl transferase center, polypeptide exit tunnel and GTPase-associated center. These mutations remodel the N-terminal contacts with 60S, altering critical interactions with uL16 (RPL10) distant from the mutation site. Mutations in domains II and III trigger conformational changes that propagate across the entirety of SBDS and remodel distant ribosomal regions, revealing an elegant mechanism of pathogenic allostery. The profound effects of SBDS mutations on both the surveillance and mature conformation of the 60S subunit provide a structural framework for understanding the molecular pathology of SDS.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.11.766026 v1

summary.background:
- Ribosomes build proteins; the large subunit (60S in humans) is assembled and checked in stages.
- SBDS is a protein that helps remove the factor eIF6 from the 60S subunit so that the small subunit (40S) can join and translation can start.
