We develop two modeling frameworks that incorporate empirical age-stratified contact matrices: a deterministic framework for deriving the final size relation and a stochastic framework based on a Continuous-time Markov chain epidemic model, for which a multi-type branching-process approximation is used to characterize early-stage outbreak risk. The framework is illustrated using empirical social contact data from Guangzhou, Foshan, and Zhuhai, China, under two disease-motivated scenarios representing COVID-19 and hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD). The illustrative analyses indicate that the relationship between cumulative infection burden and early-stage outbreak risk depends on both epidemiological characteristics and population contact patterns. In particular, age groups with the highest final attack rates do not necessarily have the highest probability of triggering a major outbreak. These findings highlight the complementary nature of the two measures and the value of considering both when assessing age-specific epidemic risks in practice.
label: arXiv:2611.19854v1

summary.background:
- Attack rate: the fraction of a group that ends up infected over the whole outbreak.
- Final size relation: a mathematical equation that predicts the eventual total infected from transmission parameters and contact patterns.
- Contact matrix: a table of how often people in one age group mix with people in each other age group, estimated from surveys.
- Continuous-time Markov chain: a random model of step-by-step changes (infections, recoveries) occurring at random times.
- Branching process: a model of early growth where each case produces a random number of new cases; it is used to estimate the chance an outbreak takes off.
- Major outbreak: an epidemic that grows to infect a large share of the population rather than fizzling out.
- HFMD: hand, foot and mouth disease, a common childhood viral illness.
summary.one_liner: Compares age-specific final attack rates with the early-stage probability of a major outbreak in age-structured populations, using empirical contact matrices from Guangzhou, Foshan and Zhuhai (China) with COVID-19 and HFMD scenarios, via a final-size relation and a multi-type branching-process approximation of a continuous-time Markov chain model.
summary.plain: When an infection enters a community, two questions matter: how many people in each age group will eventually be infected, and how likely the infection is to take off into a large outbreak in the first place. This paper uses real survey data on who has contact with whom by age in three Chinese cities to study both questions for two diseases, COVID-19 and hand, foot and mouth disease. The authors report that the age groups with the largest eventual share infected are not always the ones most likely to set off a major outbreak, so the two measures give different information.
summary.why: Public health planners often look at only one of these measures, so the finding that they can disagree suggests that age-targeted control decisions may need both. The text does not show how directly the results would translate into policy, so this should be read as a modelling insight rather than a settled recommendation.

title: Indication of demographic and epidemiological data on early-stage risks and long-term epidemic burden

abstract: BackgroundThe American Heart Association defined Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic (CKM) syndrome in 2023. Census-tract studies often examined one condition without spatial modeling. It is unclear where combined Stage 1-2 burden concentrates and how it relates to aging, environment, and socioeconomic conditions. MethodsWe built a CKM burden index for 70,336 tracts from five CDC PLACES crude prevalences (obesity, diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, chronic kidney disease) and compared it with NHANES 2017-2020. In 69,530 contiguous-U.S. tracts, we fit Bayesian spatial (BYM2) models with demographic, socioeconomic, and environmental predictors and aging x environment interactions, plus descriptive machine learning. The primary model excluded behavioral measures sharing the outcomes BRFSS source; a second added them. Credible intervals (CrIs) are conditional on PLACES estimates. ResultsAgreement with NHANES was modest. Burden clustered spatially (Morans I = 0.657) and highest in the South. Behavioral measures had the largest machine-learning importance (52.6%), partly from shared sourcing. Each percentage-point increase in adults [≥]65 years was associated with 0.112 units higher burden (95% CrI 0.111-0.113) outside low-income, low-access (LILA) tracts. LILA tracts had 0.10-0.14 units higher burden from the 25th aging percentile but not consistently in the youngest decile. Aging and socioeconomic associations held across sensitivity analyses. The primary models residual Southern excess approached zero after adding behavioral measures, which may reflect shared measurement, real differences in these behaviors, or both. ConclusionsCKM burden is spatially clustered and highest in the South. LILA tracts had modestly higher burden above the youngest tracts. These cross-sectional estimates support area-level surveillance and needs assessment. Clinical PerspectiveO_ST_ABSWhat Is New?C_ST_ABSO_LIAcross 69,530 US census tracts, a combined cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic burden index built from CDC PLACES was clustered in space and highest across the South. C_LIO_LIEach 1-percentage-point higher share of adults aged [≥]65 years was associated with 0.112 units higher burden (crude prevalence, not age-standardized). C_LI What Are the Clinical Implications?O_LITract-level burden maps can help health systems and public health agencies direct cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic screening and prevention to high-burden areas, including the South, as area-level needs assessment rather than individual risk prediction. C_LI
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.12.26367979 v1

summary.background:
- Census tract: a small neighborhood-sized area, roughly 1,200 to 8,000 people, used for U.S. statistics.
- CDC PLACES: a CDC project that estimates local health measures for tracts from survey data, rather than measuring people directly.
- Crude prevalence: the raw share of adults with a condition, not adjusted for age structure.
- Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome: a 2023 American Heart Association framework linking heart disease, kidney disease, and obesity/diabetes/metabolic problems.
- NHANES: a national health examination survey used here as a benchmark for comparison.
- Bayesian spatial model (BYM2): a statistical model that accounts for neighboring areas being similar, and borrows strength across them.
- Moran's I: a measure of spatial clustering; values near 1 indicate strong clustering, with 0.657 reported here.
- Credible interval: the Bayesian counterpart of a confidence interval.
- LILA tract: a low-income, low-access area, where many residents live far from a supermarket.
- Machine learning importance: a score showing how much a predictor contributes to a descriptive model.
summary.one_liner: A Bayesian spatial analysis of a composite cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) burden index built from CDC PLACES tract-level crude prevalences across 69,530 contiguous U.S. census tracts, examining clustering, aging and neighborhood correlates, and sensitivity to behavioral measures.
summary.plain: This paper maps how a combined load of heart, kidney and metabolic conditions (obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol and chronic kidney disease) is spread across small neighborhood areas in the United States. The authors built a single burden score for each census tract from public survey estimates and checked it against a national health survey. They found the burden clusters geographically, is highest in the South, and rises with the share of older adults, with some differences in low-income, low-access areas.
summary.why: Area-level maps like this can help health agencies decide where to focus screening and prevention. The results are cross-sectional and rely on modeled survey estimates, so they point to where needs may be rather than predicting risk for any individual.

title: Aging, Structural, and Neighborhood-Environmental Correlates of Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Risk Factor Burden Across U.S. Census Tracts

abstract: BackgroundHypertension is a major modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease, yet the relative contributions of proteomic (ProtS), metabolomic (MetS), and polygenic risk scores (PRS) to incident hypertension risk remain incompletely characterized. MethodsWe developed ProtS and MetS for systolic (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP), and hypertension using Elastic Net regression in the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA). We incorporated these scores with previously developed BP PRSs into 5 incremental XGBoost models, with external validation in the Jackson Heart Study (JHS). We further applied transfer learning to adapt the MESA-derived models to JHS. Elastic Net selected proteins were prioritized using Mendelian randomization, colocalization, and functional analyses. ResultsIn MESA, model discrimination improved with the addition of omics scores, with the combined model achieving an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.72 compared with 0.63 for the clinical baseline model. In JHS, ProtS showed the highest AUC of 0.68 and the smallest cross-cohort performance decline, compared to MetS and PRS. Incorporating measured SBP and DBP substantially improved discrimination, with the PRS+BP model achieving an AUC of 0.80 in MESA and the baseline+BP model achieving an AUC of 0.74 in JHS. Among JHS participants with normal baseline BP, ProtS provided the strongest discrimination among models without measured BP (AUC = 0.62), while PRS+BP model achieved an AUC of 0.69. Leaf-weight refreshing consistently improved calibration in JHS while preserving discrimination. Mendelian randomization identified 77 proteins associated with BP traits or hypertension, involved in vascular, inflammatory, renal, and natriuretic pathways. ConclusionsProtS demonstrated superior predictive performance and cross-cohort transferability among the omics modalities evaluated, while measured BP remained the strongest predictors of incident hypertension. Proteomic and genetic information may provide complementary biological signals for identifying individuals at elevated hypertension risk, particularly before clinically elevated BP is detectable.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.26368055 v1

summary.background:
- Hypertension: persistently high blood pressure; systolic (SBP) is the pressure during heartbeats, diastolic (DBP) between beats.
- Proteomic / metabolomic scores: summaries of measured blood proteins or metabolites that estimate a person's risk.
- Polygenic risk score (PRS): a summary of many small inherited genetic variants linked to a trait.
- Elastic Net: a regularized regression method that selects a limited set of predictors.
- XGBoost: a machine-learning method that combines many decision trees.
- AUC: area under the ROC curve; 0.5 is chance and 1.0 is perfect discrimination.
- Transfer learning: adapting a model trained on one population to another.
- Mendelian randomization: using genetic variants as natural experiments to probe whether a biomarker plausibly causes a trait.
- Calibration: how well predicted risks match observed risks.
summary.one_liner: Elastic Net proteomic, metabolomic, and polygenic scores for blood pressure and hypertension were combined in XGBoost models, trained in MESA, externally validated and transfer-learned in the Jackson Heart Study, with Mendelian randomization used to prioritize proteins.
summary.plain:
This study asks whether blood proteins, small-molecule metabolites, and inherited genetic risk scores can help predict who will develop high blood pressure before it is clearly detectable. The researchers built these scores in one large cohort (MESA), tested them in a second cohort (Jackson Heart Study), and found that protein-based scores performed best and transferred most reliably between the two groups. Measured blood pressure remained the strongest predictor overall.</plain>
<parameter name="why">Hypertension is a major modifiable driver of heart disease, so better early risk tools matter, and the protein-based signal may point to biological pathways worth studying. The text reports only modest discrimination without measured blood pressure (AUC about 0.62 to 0.69), so any clinical use is unproven.

title: Multi-omics models for hypertension prediction using blood pressure PRS and omics scores

abstract: BackgroundPseudomonas aeruginosa infections in bronchiectasis airways result in poorer lung function, advanced lung lobe involvement, worsened life quality, and higher hospitalisation rates. Despite high prevalence, little is known about P. aeruginosa population genomics, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) rates, persistence, and transmission dynamics in Australians with bronchiectasis. MethodsP. aeruginosa (n=137) isolated between 2009 and 2025 from 59 Australians with bronchiectasis underwent antimicrobial susceptibility testing against 11 antipseudomonal drugs, whole-genome sequencing, comparative genomics, and in silico AMR determinant identification. Data were integrated with 4,575 publicly available bronchiectasis-derived P. aeruginosa genomes to determine global phylogenomic and AMR determinant patterns. ResultsHigh AMR rates were identified in the Australian isolates, with 75.9% resistant to at least one antimicrobial, 19.7% multidrug-resistant, and 9.5% extremely drug-resistant. AMR rates were highest (64.2%) for ciprofloxacin and cefepime (44.5%), and lowest for piperacillin/tazobactam (8.8%) and colistin (0.7%). Phylogenomics uncovered several instances of within-host evolution, hypermutation, persistence, and multi-lineage infections. Of the fifty-seven identified multilocus sequence types (STs), seven (12.3%) were novel, five were high-risk international clones (ST274 [6.6%], ST395 [0.7%], ST244 [0.7%], ST277 [0.7%], ST298 [0.7%]) and three were common global clones (ST253 [5.1%], ST155 [3.6%], ST260 [0.7%]). No high-risk AMR-conferring mobile genetic elements were seen, although numerous chromosomal AMR determinants were identified. AMR determinant prevalence was consistent with the global dataset, with no evidence of geographic clustering. ConclusionsOur study provides critical insights into P. aeruginosa diversity in Australians with bronchiectasis. High AMR rates and chronic colonisation highlight the need to improve diagnostics, antimicrobial stewardship measures, and infection control practices in this neglected clinical cohort.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.26367559 v1

summary.background:
- Bronchiectasis: a long-term lung disease in which damaged airways become widened and clogged with mucus, making chronic infection likely.
- Pseudomonas aeruginosa: a common, hard-to-kill bacterium that often colonises damaged lungs.
- Antimicrobial resistance (AMR): when bacteria survive drugs meant to kill them; multidrug-resistant means resistant to several drug classes, and extremely drug-resistant means resistant to nearly all available options.
- Whole-genome sequencing: reading the complete DNA of a bacterium to trace relationships between strains.
- Sequence type (ST): a standard label for a bacterial lineage based on a few housekeeping genes; "high-risk international clones" are lineages widely linked to resistance and spread.
- Within-host evolution and persistence: the bacterium changing and staying in one patient over years.
- Mobile genetic elements: pieces of DNA that can move between bacteria and carry resistance genes; the authors found none of the high-risk type here.
summary.one_liner: Genomic and antimicrobial susceptibility study of 137 Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates from 59 Australians with bronchiectasis, compared against 4,575 public bronchiectasis-derived genomes.
summary.plain: People with bronchiectasis, a chronic lung condition where the airways are widened and scarred, often carry a bacterium called Pseudomonas aeruginosa that is hard to treat. This study collected bacterial samples from 59 Australian patients over 2009 to 2025, tested how well they resisted common antibiotics, and read their full genetic code. The authors then compared these bacteria with thousands of publicly available genomes from other bronchiectasis patients.
summary.why: The reported resistance levels are high, with about three-quarters of isolates resistant to at least one drug, which matters for treatment choices in a group the authors describe as neglected. The findings are limited to one country's small clinical sample, so they describe Australian patients rather than establishing wider trends.

title: Pseudomonas aeruginosa in bronchiectasis: unmasking population diversity and antimicrobial resistance in the Australian context

abstract: BackgroundGenomic surveillance of respiratory viruses typically relies on sequences from individuals seeking health care, and whether these sequences represent the viruses circulating in the community is not well-characterized. We aimed to compare the diversity, proportion, and dynamics of influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and SARS-CoV-2 between clinical and community samples. MethodsIn this retrospective comparative genomic analysis, we used whole-genome sequences from community-based surveillance studies in the Seattle area, and clinical sequences from the Washington State Department of Health. We compared clade proportions and dynamics, sequence-cluster diversity, non-synonymous mutations, and Ct values between clinical and community samples. FindingsWe analyzed 538 RSV sequences collected between 2019 and 2021 (278 community, 260 clinical), 1506 influenza sequences (260 community, 1246 clinical) between 2019 and 2020, and 8660 SARS-CoV-2 sequences (5923 community, 2737 clinical) from 2020 to 2022. Clade proportions did not differ between clinical and community samples for RSV or influenza, but differed for SARS-CoV-2: clades 21J (Delta) and 21K (Omicron BA.1) were more frequent in community samples and clade 22B (Omicron BA.5) in clinical samples. SARS-CoV-2 clinical sequence clusters were more diverse than community clusters, whereas RSV and influenza showed no significant difference. Several spike mutations associated with monoclonal antibody resistance were more prevalent in community samples for SARS-CoV-2. Ct values were lower in clinical samples for multiple SARS-CoV-2, RSV, and influenza clades. InterpretationSeasonal respiratory viruses had similar dynamics and diversity in clinical and community samples, whereas pandemic SARS-CoV-2 differed between settings. Genomic surveillance programs should combine clinical and community sampling, particularly during pandemics in order to better capture viral diversity. FundingThis analysis was funded by the Washington State Department of Health Northwest Pathogen Genomics Center of Excellence (WA DOH contract number HED29377-1, federal grant number NU50CK000630 to University of Washington). The underlying studies were funded by Gates Ventures. RESEARCH IN CONTEXTO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSGenomic surveillance of respiratory viruses expanded substantially during the COVID-19 pandemic and has since been extended to respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and influenza, but most sequences come from people who sought medical care. We searched PubMed for studies published in English up to September 2026 using combinations of terms "genomic surveillance", "community surveillance", "respiratory syncytial virus", "influenza", "SARS-CoV-2", "whole genome sequencing", and included studies that sequenced respiratory viruses from defined clinical or community populations. Previous work has sampled hospitalized patients, sequenced random positive specimens, or sequenced wastewater, and has shown that such data can track variant emergence, clade replacement, and nosocomial transmission. However, few studies compared clinical and community sampling for the same virus in the same population and period, so it remains unclear whether clinically derived sequences represent the viruses circulating in the community. Added value of this studyTo our knowledge, this is the first study to compare viral diversity between clinical and community sampling for three respiratory viruses in the same region and overlapping time periods. Using more than 10,000 whole genomes from community-based surveillance studies and state clinical surveillance in Washington State, we found that clade proportions and dynamics were similar between sources for RSV and influenza, but differed for SARS-CoV-2. At finer genetic resolution, clinical SARS-CoV-2 sequences formed more diverse clusters than community sequences, and several spike mutations associated with monoclonal antibody resistance were more prevalent in community samples. Implications of all the available evidenceFor seasonal respiratory viruses, sampling people who seek care appears to capture much of the diversity circulating in the community, which may allow surveillance programs with limited resources to rely on clinical specimens. In contrast with seasonal circulation in a population with some pre-existing immunity, during pandemic-level transmission, when very large numbers of people in a largely susceptible population are infected over a short period, clinical and community samples are not interchangeable, and programs that sequence only clinical specimens risk missing variants circulating in the community, including mutations relevant to antiviral and monoclonal antibody resistance. These differences may partly reflect the much larger number of SARS-CoV-2 genomes available, as well as heterogeneous mixing and co-circulation of multiple variants during the pandemic. Surveillance programs should therefore combine clinical and community sampling, and future studies should test whether these patterns hold in other regions, seasons, and pathogens.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.11.26367863 v1

summary.background:
- Genomic surveillance: sequencing viral genomes from samples to see which lineages (clades) are circulating and how they change.
- Clade: a group of closely related viral lineages, named by convention (e.g., 21J = Delta, 22B = Omicron BA.5).
- Clinical vs community samples: clinical samples come from people seeking care; community samples come from people enrolled in studies regardless of symptoms.
- Non-synonymous mutation: a genetic change that alters the protein built from it; spike-protein changes can affect antibody binding.
- Monoclonal antibody: a lab-made antibody treatment; resistance means a variant evades it.
- Ct value: PCR cycle threshold; lower values generally mean more virus in the sample.
- RSV: respiratory syncytial virus, a common cause of winter respiratory illness, especially in young children and older adults.
summary.one_liner: A retrospective comparison of whole-genome sequences of SARS-CoV-2, RSV and influenza from clinical (health-care-seeking) and community-based surveillance samples in Washington State, examining clade proportions, cluster diversity, spike mutations and viral load (Ct values).
summary.plain: Public health teams track how viruses change by sequencing their genetic code, but most of these samples come from people who went to a clinic. This study asks whether those clinic samples reflect what is actually spreading in the wider community, using data from Seattle-area community studies and Washington State clinical records. For RSV and influenza, the two sources looked similar; for COVID-19 during the pandemic, they differed in which variants were common and in the mutations seen.
summary.why: Genome sequencing guides decisions about vaccines, treatments and monoclonal antibodies, so knowing whether clinic-based samples miss important variants matters for surveillance budgets. The authors suggest that during pandemic-level spread, clinic-only sampling may miss variants, though the difference may partly reflect the much larger number of SARS-CoV-2 sequences and the effects of many co-circulating variants; the study is from one region and the authors call for testing elsewhere.

title: Genomic diversity of respiratory pathogens in clinical versus community surveillance: a comparative analysis of SARS-CoV-2, RSV, and influenza viruses in Washington State

abstract: In Germany, statutory health insurance covers the rental or purchase of breast pumps when a medical indication is present for the mother or infant, and a physician has issued a prescription. However, parents must pay out of pocket for commercially available breast pumps for returning to work or personal circumstances. High indirect costs for continuation of breastfeeding and direct costs for breast pumps and related equipment may pose substantial barriers to breastfeeding families, an issue relevant for health equity. To our knowledge, no studies have assessed the direct financial costs associated with the purchase of commercially available breast pumps. In this cross-sectional study, we examined digital marketplaces in Germany for commercial electric breast pumps between March 2025 and May 2026, across major online platforms. Our objective was to explore pump features that predict price. We identified 282 commercial electric pump models from 108 brands. Basic information was unavailable for half of surveyed breast pump brands. The median price for surveyed commercial electric pumps was {euro}72.70 (IQR: {euro}82.70), with costs ranging widely from {euro}19.99 to {euro}659.57. Prices varied by marketplace, manufacturer location, accessories, pump system type, power source, battery capacity, flange sizes, availability of instruction manuals, and "single user" claims; predicting significantly higher costs. Half of pumps surveyed offered only one flange size, signaling additional expenses for mothers needing alternative sizes. These findings highlight important considerations for maternal health and consumer safety. Health technology assessments and a review of current health policy on reimbursement for commercial electric breast pumps is needed. Key messagesO_LITo our knowledge, there have been no published empirical studies on direct costs for commercial electric breast pumps C_LIO_LIBasic information was unavailable for half of the surveyed breast pump brands on digital marketplaces in Germany C_LIO_LIThe median cost for a commercial electric breast pump in our survey was {euro}72,70 (IQR: {euro}82,70), with a very wide price range ({euro}19,99 - {euro}659,57) C_LIO_LIPrices varied significantly by marketplace, manufacturer location, accessories, pump system type, power source, battery capacity, number of flange sizes, availability of instruction manuals, and "single user" claims, which all positively correlated with prices. C_LIO_LIThere is a sparsity of flange sizes sold outside of the mid-range (24 mm), signaling ancillary costs for flanges with appropriate fit C_LIO_LIHealth technology assessments for commercial electric breast pumps and a review of health policy related to breast pump reimbursement in Germany are warranted C_LI
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.26367926 v1

summary.background:
- Breast pumps: devices that extract milk from the breast; electric ones run on power from mains or batteries.
- Statutory health insurance: Germany's public insurance; it covers pumps only with a medical indication and prescription.
- Flange: the funnel-shaped part that fits over the nipple and areola; sizes vary, and a poor fit can reduce comfort and milk output.
- Cross-sectional study: a snapshot of many items at one point in time, which can show associations but not cause and effect.
- Interquartile range (IQR): the spread of the middle half of prices; the median is the middle value.
- Health technology assessment: a systematic review of whether a medical device is safe, effective and worth paying for.
summary.one_liner: A cross-sectional survey of 282 commercial electric breast pump models from 108 brands sold on German online marketplaces (March 2025 to May 2026) that examines which pump features are associated with higher prices.
summary.plain: Breast pumps are covered by German health insurance only when a doctor prescribes one for a medical reason, so many parents returning to work must buy one themselves. The authors looked at pumps sold on major German online shopping sites and recorded their prices and features. They found a wide price range, from about 20 to about 660 euros, with a median near 73 euros.
summary.why: Out-of-pocket costs for breast pumps may be a barrier to continuing breastfeeding, which links to health equity and consumer safety. The paper is a descriptive price survey, so it shows associations rather than causes, and its findings are most relevant to German policy on reimbursement.

title: Determinants of prices of commercial electric breast pumps sold in Germany: a cross-sectional analysis

abstract: BackgroundMental health problems among young people impose a burden extending beyond healthcare, including impaired health-related quality of life and high societal costs from disrupted education, lost productivity, and informal care. Youth-friendly interventions may reduce this burden by providing early support and preventing escalation. However, their broader societal economic impact remains insufficiently explored. Evaluations incorporating consequences beyond healthcare and longer time horizons can better capture their societal value. MethodsThis protocol outlines harmonised trial-based and model-based economic evaluations of YEAH, SELFIE, and MOST, three mental health interventions for young people aged 12-25. Each intervention will be compared separately against care as usual over 12 months, with longer-term costs and outcomes projected at 2, 3, 5, and 10 years. Multicountry participant data will be pooled, using a prespecified reference country for base-case costing and methodological guidance. A harmonised, context-specific Resource Use Measurement instrument was developed to capture healthcare and broader societal resource use consistently across participating countries and to support evaluation of the economic impact of youth mental health interventions from a multicountry perspective. Uncertainty will be assessed through sensitivity and scenario analyses. DiscussionThe proposed harmonised methodological framework will support consistent estimation of the short- and long-term cost-effectiveness of three youth-friendly mental health interventions. It will enable comparison of intervention-specific results generated using different trial designs and support consistent estimation of costs and outcomes across the three interventions. The context-specific Resource Use Measurement instrument will further support consistent measurement of healthcare utilisation, productivity losses, and informal care across the economic evaluations. ConclusionBy integrating trial-based evidence with long-term modelling and standardised measurement of resource use, this study aims to generate robust, policy-relevant evidence to inform health technology assessment and decision-making for youth mental health interventions. The context-specific Resource Use Measurement instrument is also intended to support future economic evaluations of mental health interventions conducted across multiple countries.
authors: van Mastrigt, G. A. P. G.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.12.26367972 v1

summary.background:
- Cost-effectiveness analysis compares the costs of an intervention with the health gains it produces, often expressed per unit of quality-adjusted life.
- Trial-based evaluation uses costs and outcomes collected alongside a randomised or controlled trial; model-based evaluation uses mathematical projections to estimate longer-term effects.
- "Care as usual" is the standard support people would receive without the new intervention.
- Societal perspective counts costs to the whole of society, not just the health budget, including lost productivity and unpaid care by family members.
- A resource use measurement instrument is a questionnaire used to record the services and time people use.
- A reference country is a chosen country whose prices and methods are used as the base case so that pooled multicountry results are consistent.
- Health technology assessment is the process bodies use to decide whether to fund a health intervention.
summary.one_liner: A study protocol describing harmonised trial-based and model-based economic evaluations of three youth mental health interventions (YEAH, SELFIE, MOST) against care as usual, with a shared multicountry resource-use measurement instrument.
summary.plain: This is a plan for measuring whether three programmes designed to help young people with mental health problems are good value for money, looking at costs well beyond the healthcare system, such as missed school, lost work, and unpaid family care. The researchers describe how they will follow participants for 12 months and then project costs and outcomes out to 10 years, using data pooled across several countries. The text is a protocol, so it reports no results.
summary.why: Youth mental health costs society well beyond clinics, so an evaluation that counts education, productivity and informal care over longer periods may better show what early support is worth. The shared measurement tool could also help future multicountry studies compare results on a like-for-like basis.

title: A multicountry trial-based and model-based economic evaluation of youth mental health interventions: a protocol for assessing the short- and long-term societal impacts of YOUTHreach interventions

abstract: Models trained on rich multimodal data may depend on modalities unavailable at deployment. In generalized distillation, a teacher trained on such privileged data guides a student using only deployable features. We ask whether students inherit clinically meaningful properties beyond predictions in brain-age modeling, where brain-age gaps index deviations from normative aging and brain health. In simulations, distillation recovered a gap-severity association which an age-trained baseline missed. In UK Biobank analyses of depression, anxiety, and alcohol use disorder, students using structural MRI, functional MRI or biosocial data produced gaps closer to their teachers than matched baselines in 10 of 12 comparisons. Where teachers most exceeded baselines (anxiety in biosocial, alcohol use in functional MRI students), gap-severity associations rose toward their teachers. Our findings characterize conditions for successful distillation, i.e. clinical signal the teacher holds, the baseline misses and deployable features contain, and demonstrate their relevance in a real-life psychiatry application.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.26368025 v1

summary.background:
- Generalized distillation: training a simple "student" model to imitate a stronger "teacher" that was trained on extra information (privileged data) the student will not have at use time.
- Brain-age gap: estimated brain age minus actual age; larger positive gaps are often read as signs of accelerated brain aging, though interpretation is debated.
- Normative modeling: building a reference of typical values (here, typical brain age for a given age) and measuring how far an individual deviates.
- Structural MRI (brain anatomy) and functional MRI (brain activity patterns) are the imaging inputs; biosocial data means non-imaging factors such as health and lifestyle measures.
- UK Biobank: a large UK research database of volunteers with health, imaging and lifestyle data.
- Gap-severity association: how strongly brain-age gaps track symptom severity or disorder severity.
summary.one_liner: Evaluates whether generalized distillation, where a student model trained on deployable features learns from a teacher trained on richer privileged data, yields brain-age gaps that match the teacher's clinically meaningful associations in depression, anxiety and alcohol use disorder using UK Biobank data.
summary.plain: Some medical prediction tools are trained on detailed scans and test results that are not available in everyday clinics. This paper asks whether a simpler model, using only what a clinic can actually collect, can learn from a model trained on the richer data and still reflect the same clinically useful patterns. It reports simulations and UK Biobank analyses in which these simpler "student" models usually produced brain-age gaps closer to their "teacher" models than comparable baselines did.
summary.why: Brain-age gaps, the difference between a scan-based age estimate and a person's real age, are studied as a marker of brain health in psychiatry, so a way to get such markers from cheaper inputs could matter in practice. The text reports success in 10 of 12 comparisons and notes that gains were largest where the teacher most beat the baseline, but it does not show that these markers improve diagnosis or treatment, so its clinical value remains to be tested.

title: Privilege Is Not Enough: Evaluating Generalized Distillation for Normative Brain Age Modeling in Depression, Anxiety and Alcohol Use Disorder

abstract: PSEN1 variants are the most common cause of familial early-onset Alzheimers disease (EOAD), but it is debated whether they act through a loss- or gain-of-function. Following a recent report of a duo with EOAD carrying a predicted loss-of-function (LoF) stop-gain variant (p.K109*) in PSEN1, we sought to determine whether PSEN1 LoF variants, as a class, cause EOAD. We identified 45 carriers of PSEN1 LoF variants predicted to trigger nonsense-mediated decay in the Alzheimers Disease Sequencing Project, UK Biobank, and BioVU databases. None of these carriers had a recorded diagnosis of early-onset dementia, and 17 were older than 65 years at last follow-up with no dementia or AD reported. Re-analysis of the reported AD-associated variant p.K109* revealed a cryptic splice site predicted to produce an in-frame deletion of 5 amino acids (p.K109_L113del). These results suggest that PSEN1 variants must produce an altered PSEN1 protein product to cause EOAD, while true null LoF PSEN1 alleles do not cause EOAD.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.26367865 v1

summary.background:
- Alzheimer's disease: a brain disease causing progressive memory loss; "early-onset" means starting before about age 65.
- PSEN1: a gene that makes presenilin-1, a protein involved in cutting other proteins in brain cells; variants in it are the most common known cause of early-onset familial Alzheimer's.
- Loss-of-function vs gain-of-function: a loss-of-function variant reduces or removes a gene's activity; a gain-of-function variant makes the protein act abnormally or more strongly.
- Stop-gain (nonsense) variant: a DNA change that inserts an early "stop" signal, producing a truncated protein.
- Nonsense-mediated decay: a cell quality-control process that destroys messages carrying early stop signals, so little protein is made.
- Splicing: the process that cuts out non-coding parts of a gene's message and joins the rest; a faulty splice site can remove pieces of the protein.
- In-frame deletion: removal of a whole number of amino acid building blocks, keeping the rest of the reading frame intact.
summary.one_liner: Genetic carriers of predicted loss-of-function PSEN1 variants (nonsense-mediated decay) showed no early-onset dementia, and re-analysis of the p.K109* variant suggests it instead disrupts splicing to create an in-frame deletion.
summary.plain: Some inherited mutations in a gene called PSEN1 strongly raise the risk of developing Alzheimer's disease before age 65, but scientists have debated whether they work by breaking the gene's protein or by making it do something harmful. The authors looked at 45 people across three large databases who carry mutations that should switch the gene off entirely, and found none had early-onset dementia. They also found that a previously reported mutation likely changes how the gene's message is cut and pieced together, rather than simply stopping it.
summary.why: The result bears on whether drugs that reduce PSEN1 activity could be safe, since it suggests that fully switching off the gene does not cause early-onset Alzheimer's. It is a focused genetic study, so its conclusions depend on how accurately the databases record diagnoses and on the small number of carriers.

title: PSEN1 loss-of-function variants do not cause early-onset Alzheimer's disease

abstract: ObjectiveOsteosarcoma is a rare primary bone cancer of adolescents and young adults without significant improvement in treatments or outcomes in several decades. Resection is standard of care for recurrent disease. Patients with lung only osteosarcoma recurrence following surgical resection (LOOR-FSR) may present the most meaningful opportunity for impactful intervention but alternative trial endpoints to objective response are needed. Here we update benchmarks for LOOR-FSR with contemporary clinical trial data. Patients/MethodsThis study included patients with pathologically confirmed LOOR-FSR enrolled on three Childrens Oncology Group phase 2 single arm trials. Benchmark endpoints assessed in this patient population were event-free survival (EFS) and overall survival (OS). In addition, we evaluated the impact of demographics and baseline clinical factors on outcome. ResultsNinety-nine patients met criteria for inclusion in this analysis. Median EFS and OS were 4.8 (95% CI: 3.5, 6.3) and 26.2 (23.3, 56.8) months respectively. Twelve-month EFS was 22% (15-31%) and ranged from 14% to 29% across the 3 trials, a difference that did not achieve statistical significance. The risk of EFS event was higher for those whose first recurrence occurred within two years of diagnosis (p=0.009). Other demographic and clinical factors did not statistically impact risk of event though estimated EFS for males was lower than for females. ConclusionDespite almost doubling the number of patients in this historical control cohort, wide variance in outcomes led to confidence intervals unchanged from previously published work. Until the most significant factors contributing to variability of outcomes in this patient population are quantified, single arm trials of new approaches will only be able to identify large effect sizes. Smaller effect sizes will require randomization.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.26368045 v1

summary.background:
- Osteosarcoma: a rare cancer of bone, mostly affecting adolescents and young adults.
- Recurrence: the cancer returning after initial treatment; here, returning only in the lungs and after surgical removal.
- Phase 2 trial: an early-stage study testing whether a treatment works, often with a single group rather than a comparison group.
- Single-arm trial: all patients get the same treatment, so results are compared with historical data rather than a concurrent control group.
- Event-free survival (EFS): time until cancer returns, progresses, or the patient dies.
- Overall survival (OS): time until death from any cause.
- Median: the midpoint of the time-to-event data; 95% confidence interval (CI): the range within which the true value likely falls.
- Randomization: assigning patients to treatment groups by chance, which allows fairer comparisons of effect size.
summary.one_liner: A pooled analysis of 99 patients from three Children's Oncology Group phase 2 single-arm trials updates survival benchmarks (event-free and overall survival) for osteosarcoma that returns only to the lungs after surgical removal, and examines which baseline factors affect outcome.
summary.plain: Osteosarcoma is a rare bone cancer that can come back in the lungs after surgery. This paper pools data from 99 patients in three clinical trials to set updated benchmarks for how long these patients live and how long they stay free of further events. The main finding is that outcomes vary widely, so the estimates remain about as uncertain as in earlier published work, and only the timing of the first recurrence (within two years of diagnosis) was clearly linked to a higher risk of an event.
summary.why: Lung-only recurrence after surgery is a group where new treatments might have the most impact, so reliable benchmarks matter for judging future trials. The authors argue that single-arm trials can only detect large effects in this setting and that smaller effects would need randomized comparisons; this is their reasoning from the data, not a settled consensus.

title: Updated outcome of patients with lung only osteosarcoma recurrence following surgical resection enrolled in phase 2 clinical trials: A report from the Children's Oncology Group

abstract: BackgroundAccurate characterization of the tumor microenvironment (TME) is crucial for inferring tumor biology, subsequent tumor behavior, and predicting therapeutic response. Current characterization methods are inadequate in capturing the complexity of immune signaling networks, hindering robust clinical decision making. To address this, we have developed FlahyRecovery - an artificial intelligence (AI) and gene expression based immune profiling biomarker, implemented via a supervised classification machine learning model, that integrates response prediction and prognostic insights to personalize treatment design, particularly immunotherapy. MethodsGene expression data of 7424 tumor specimens across 14 cancers was annotated specimen wise into three immune subtypes: Elevated Immunity (Hot) with high cytotoxic T-cell infiltration, Suppressed Immunity (Cold) marked by immune exclusion and stromal dominance, and Moderate Immunity (Intermediate) exhibiting mixed features. Following annotation validation, an AI model was trained and tested on the annotated data to classify new tumor specimens into the three immune subtypes - Elevated Immunity (Hot), Suppressed Immunity (Cold) and Moderate Immunity (Intermediate) based on the expression of a panel of 1275 genes involved in immune cell signaling and immune signal transduction. ResultsIn a multi-tumor validation cohort (N=1337), the subtyping model showed a sensitivity of 79%, a specificity of 89%, and a one-vs-rest AUC of 0.93. Elevated Immunity tumors correlated with prolonged survival and immunotherapy response, while Suppressed Immunity tumors correlated with treatment resistance and need for combination therapy. ConclusionArtificial intelligence can be effectively used to process tumor biology digitized via next-generation sequencing, to accurately mark the TME from an immunological perspective. Its clinical utility mechanisms andying patients who can benefit from immunotherapies, identifying treatment resistance mechanisms, and informing combination treatment regimes.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.12.26367994 v1

summary.background:
- Tumor microenvironment: the mix of immune cells, blood vessels, and supporting tissue surrounding a tumor.
- "Hot" vs "cold" tumors: informal labels for tumors with many versus few immune cells inside them. Cold tumors often resist immunotherapy.
- Immunotherapy: treatments that boost the body's own immune system to attack cancer.
- Gene expression: a measure of how actively each gene is being used in a tissue sample, usually obtained by sequencing.
- Supervised machine learning: a model trained on examples with known labels, then used to label new cases.
- Sensitivity and specificity: the share of true cases the model catches, and the share of non-cases it correctly rules out.
- AUC (area under curve): a 0 to 1 score of how well a model separates classes; 0.5 is chance, 1 is perfect.
- Validation cohort: a separate group of patients used to test the model after it was built.
summary.one_liner: A machine-learning classifier built on a 1,275-gene immune-signaling panel sorts tumor gene-expression profiles into Hot, Cold, or Intermediate immune subtypes, with reported links to survival and immunotherapy response in a multi-cancer validation cohort.
summary.plain: Tumors contain immune cells that can either attack cancer or be shut out of it, and doctors want to know which situation a patient's tumor is in before choosing treatment. This paper describes a computer model that reads the activity levels of about 1,275 immune-related genes in a tumor sample and sorts the tumor into one of three immune groups: "hot" (immune cells active), "cold" (immune cells kept out), or "intermediate." In a validation set of 1,337 tumors, the authors report the model agreed with the labels reasonably well and that "hot" tumors tended to have longer survival and better response to immunotherapy.
summary.why: Sorting tumors by immune activity could help decide who might benefit from immunotherapy and who may need combination treatment, which is a practical clinical question. However, the text is a short abstract and gives little detail on how the labels were assigned, how the model was tested, or how it would perform on independent patient groups, so its clinical value is not yet established.

title: FlahyRecovery is an AI & gene expression based immune profiling biomarker for decision support in precision oncology

abstract: Agentic healthcare platforms that combine large language models with physician oversight are growing quickly, but little is known about who uses them. We characterized 3,223 enrollees of Lotus AI, a free, physician-supervised agentic platform, who completed onboarding, messaged the agent, and had a linked health record between February and July 2026, and compared them with national benchmarks. Median age was 51 years and 62% were male. Chronic condition prevalence exceeded 2024 National Health Interview Survey estimates in every age band by 4 to 7 percentage points; 18% had a functional or symptom-defined disorder; among the 30% with four or more ambulatory visits in the prior year, care was spread across nearly five providers, with 44% meeting a threshold for high fragmentation. Users with functional disorders generated 1.8 times as many physician escalations and 2.6 times as many laboratory orders as other users, but no more prescriptions. This profile differs from the younger, predominantly female populations reported for direct-to-consumer telemedicine. It moves chronic disease management, functional disorder pathways, and care coordination from aspirations to design requirements, and we argue that deployed AI care platforms should characterize their populations against national benchmarks early.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.12.26367291 v1

summary.background:
- Agentic AI platform: software where a large language model (a text-generating AI) carries out multi-step tasks for a user, here with physicians reviewing its work.
- Physician escalation: the AI passing a case to a human doctor.
- Laboratory orders: requests for blood or other lab tests.
- Functional or symptom-defined disorders: conditions diagnosed mainly by symptoms, such as irritable bowel syndrome or chronic fatigue, without a clear structural cause.
- Care fragmentation: when a patient's outpatient care is spread across many different providers, here measured with a threshold for "high" fragmentation.
- National Health Interview Survey (NHIS): a large annual US government survey used as the comparison benchmark.
- Percentage points: the absolute difference between two percentages.
- Direct-to-consumer telemedicine: online medical services that patients access directly, without a referral.
summary.one_liner: A descriptive study of 3,223 enrollees in Lotus AI, a free, physician-supervised agentic healthcare platform, comparing their chronic disease burden, care fragmentation, and functional-disorder utilization against national survey benchmarks.
summary.plain: This paper looks at who signs up for an AI health assistant that works alongside doctors. The authors examined 3,223 people who joined the free Lotus AI platform between February and July 2026 and compared them with national health survey figures. The users were middle-aged (median age 51), mostly male, and had more chronic conditions than national averages in each age group.
summary.why: Most published data on digital health users comes from younger, mostly female telemedicine patients, so a different user profile matters for how such tools should be designed. The paper argues that AI care platforms should check their users against national benchmarks early; its practical impact depends on how far these findings generalize beyond this one platform, which the text does not establish.

title: Enrollees and Early Lessons from an Agentic Healthcare Platform with Physicians in the Loop

abstract: ObjectiveTo develop and internally validate a calibrated discharge model of 30-day within-system readmission in Medicare-insured adults, and to quantify how a future-information leak and outcome artifacts distorted performance, timing, and subgroup conclusions. Materials and MethodsRetrospective study of 236,906 Medicare-insured MIMIC-IV v3.1 admissions (87,750 patients; prevalence 21.4%). Predictors were audited for discharge-time availability; history features were tested for future information and recomputed from raw timestamps. A consensus gradient-boosted (XGBoost) model was selected inside patient-grouped folds; CIs used patient-cluster bootstrap. ResultsA feature documented as a prior 180-day length-of-stay trend used each patients whole record, including later admissions; removing it and two derived terms lowered test area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) from 0.774 to 0.706. The corrected procedure reached an out-of-fold AUROC of 0.7057 (95% CI 0.7016 to 0.7102; primary); the 44-feature model scored 0.7056 on the historically exposed test partition (calibration slope 0.99), above reconstructed LACE and HOSPITAL (both P<.001). A day-1 discrimination peak largely reflected 2,368 probable administrative continuations within 1 hour of discharge; merging these into the preceding stay gave test AUROC 0.698 (0.702 after refitting). The White minus Black AUROC difference was 0.003 (95% CI -0.018 to 0.024); specificity was lower for Black patients (0.61 vs 0.69). DiscussionDocumentation audits and patient-grouped validation missed a leak that inflated discrimination and created spurious subgroup and calendar-period differences; simple empirical checks found it. ConclusionEmpirical leakage checks should accompany availability audits. The corrected model is calibrated, moderately discriminating, and needs external validation before clinical use.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.26368026 v1

summary.background:
- Readmission: a patient returning to hospital soon after discharge; here, within 30 days.
- Medicare: US government health insurance mainly for people aged 65 and over, plus some younger people with disabilities.
- MIMIC-IV: a public, de-identified database of hospital records from an intensive care center in Boston.
- Data leakage: when a model is trained on information that would not be available at the time of prediction, making it look more accurate than it will be in practice.
- AUROC (area under the ROC curve): a 0–1 score for how well a model ranks higher-risk patients above lower-risk ones; 0.5 is chance, 1.0 is perfect.
- Calibration: whether predicted risks match actual observed rates.
- XGBoost: a widely used machine-learning method that builds many decision trees.
- LACE and HOSPITAL: two established, simple readmission risk scores used as comparisons.
- Patient-grouped validation: testing so that the same patient never appears in both training and test data.
- Bootstrap confidence intervals: a resampling method to estimate the uncertainty of a result.
summary.one_liner: A retrospective study of 236,906 Medicare-insured MIMIC-IV admissions that finds a future-information leak inflated a 30-day readmission model's discrimination, and reports a corrected, calibrated XGBoost model with AUROC about 0.706 (internal validation only).
summary.plain: The paper looks at a model that predicts whether a patient will return to the same hospital system within 30 days of going home. The authors found that one history-based input quietly used records from later visits, which made the model look better than it really was. After removing that leak and related problems, the corrected model still predicts somewhat better than chance (AUROC about 0.71), and its predicted risks match observed rates, but it has only been tested internally.
summary.why: Readmission models are used to decide who gets follow-up care, so a hidden leak that makes them look more accurate could mislead hospitals and create false conclusions about groups of patients. The paper's main lesson is that simple empirical checks can catch leaks that documentation audits miss; the authors themselves say external validation is needed before any clinical use.

title: Future-Information Leakage in 30-Day Readmission Prediction: An Empirical Audit and a Calibrated Electronic Health Record Model in Medicare-Insured Adults

abstract: Identifying time preference shocks is challenging: shocks large enough to shift survey-elicited stated impatience also tighten financial resources, confounding the interpretation of stated time preference. Jointly examining stated and revealed preferences resolves this identification problem: impatience shocks and reductions in financial resources generate opposite consumption responses, even though both raise stated impatience. Applying our identification framework to the 2009 L'Aquila earthquake, we combine panel data with spatially granular seismic and damage data in a difference-in-differences design that compares undamaged households that experienced the earthquake with a spatial control group at similar distances from the epicenter. Treated households report greater impatience and increase nondurable consumption by 11 percent relative to controls. Effects are consistent with a psychological stress channel, concentrated among the most vulnerable to stress, and persist as households deplete their liquid wealth buffer over time.
label: arXiv:2611.19662v1

summary.background:
- Time preference: how strongly people prefer rewards now over later; higher impatience means a stronger preference for the present.
- Stated preference: what people say in a survey about their patience or choices.
- Revealed preference: what people actually do, here measured through consumption spending.
- Difference-in-differences: comparing the change over time in a treated group against the change in a control group, to isolate an event's effect.
- Liquid wealth: money that is quickly available, such as savings or cash, used as a buffer against shocks.
- Non-durable consumption: spending on goods used up quickly, such as food and services.
- Psychological stress channel: the idea that trauma itself changes behavior, apart from any loss of money.
summary.one_liner: The paper uses joint stated and revealed preference evidence, in a difference-in-differences design around the 2009 L'Aquila earthquake, to separate true time preference shocks from the confounding effect of tighter financial resources.
summary.plain: The paper asks whether a disaster makes people more impatient for rewards now, or simply poorer. It looks at households hit by the 2009 L'Aquila earthquake in Italy and compares undamaged households that felt the quake with similarly distant households that did not. Treated households reported being more impatient and increased their spending on non-durable goods (things like food and everyday items) by about 11 percent relative to controls.
summary.why: Time preference, or how much people discount future rewards, is a core input to economic models of saving and policy, and survey answers about it are hard to interpret when shocks also change income or wealth. The authors' argument that comparing stated answers with actual spending can separate these effects is a useful methodological point, though the text alone does not show how well it generalizes beyond this one event.

title: Identifying Time Preference Shocks: Stated and Revealed Preferences after an Italian Earthquake

abstract: We compare three estimators in a two-sample summary-data instrumental variables (IV) model: inverse-variance weighting (IVW), debiased inverse-variance weighting (dIVW), and the profile score (PS) estimator. The framework assumes independent samples and instrument-specific summary estimates, with two-sample Mendelian randomisation as a leading application. We compare existing fixed- and many-weak-instrument results and the sufficient conditions for the three estimators. Under the variance scaling used in the profile-score literature, the principal collective-strength conditions for PS and dIVW are equivalent, although their additional restrictions on instrument concentration and growth differ. We then compare their asymptotic variance formulae for fixed and diverging numbers of instruments. For fixed $L$, IVW and dIVW have the same first-order asymptotic variance. Under a common variance-ratio condition, the PS variance formula exceeds the IVW variance by a positive term of order $n^{-2}$, compared with the order-$n^{-1}$ leading variance. For diverging $L$, we establish variance orders across instrument-strength regimes and the exact ordering $\mathsf{V}_{\mathtt{IVW}} < V_{\mathtt{PS}} \leq \mathsf{V}_{\mathtt{dIVW}}$ under the same variance-ratio condition. Absolute variance gaps vanish when $\sqrt{L}κ\to\infty$, whereas relative equivalence holds if and only if $κ\to\infty$. These comparisons concern asymptotic variance formulae rather than finite-sample efficiency or mean squared error.
label: arXiv:2611.19690v1

summary.background:
- Instrumental variables (IV): a way to estimate a cause's effect using a factor that influences the outcome only through that cause.
- Weak instruments: instruments that are only loosely related to the cause, which makes standard estimates unreliable or biased.
- Two-sample design: the instrument-exposure and instrument-outcome associations come from two independent samples.
- Summary data: only per-instrument estimates and standard errors are used, not individual-level records.
- Inverse-variance weighting (IVW): a precision-weighted average of per-instrument ratio estimates; the debiased version corrects a bias from weak instruments.
- Profile score (PS) estimator: a likelihood-based alternative.
- Asymptotic variance: the approximate spread of an estimator in large samples; the paper contrasts fixed numbers of instruments with numbers that grow with sample size.
summary.one_liner: The paper compares the asymptotic variance formulas of three two-sample summary-data IV estimators (IVW, debiased IVW, and the profile score estimator) for fixed and diverging numbers of instruments, under weak instruments.
summary.plain: The paper looks at three statistical recipes for estimating a cause-and-effect strength when the data come from two separate studies and each genetic or other instrument is weak. It compares how precise each recipe is in large samples, using theoretical formulas rather than simulations or real data. The main finding is that the three recipes are close in precision, with differences that shrink as the instruments get stronger, and the paper states these are comparisons of formulas, not of finite-sample performance.
summary.why: Two-sample Mendelian randomisation is a widely used way to estimate causal effects from published summary statistics, so clarifying how the standard estimators compare when instruments are weak bears on applied practice. The text does not say how these results will be used in practice, and it does not establish finite-sample performance.

title: Comparing Two-Sample IV Estimators under Weak Instruments

abstract: The questions of voting rights, group membership, and the boundaries of acceptable discourse all involve a recursive, self-stability issue, wherein the voters, group members, and acceptable commentators are often the ultimate arbiters of their own rules for inclusion and exclusion. In order to understand how ideological or issue diversity may impact the stability of such inclusion and exclusion, we introduce franchise elections, where voting members of a group vote to change the electorate. In particular, when agents are positioned inside an ideological or issue space, a social choice function that aggregates agent viewpoints induces a preference for agents over group composition, where agents prefer groups that improve the social choice function outcome for them. We demonstrate that when ideological space is two-dimensional, these franchise elections can generate complex behavior and that this complexity exists for any social choice function. Using the Yolk social choice function from voting theory, we illustrate that franchise elections can predict that agents attempting to introduce a new ideological axis perpendicular to an existing left-right spectrum risk disenfranchisement unless they ally with either side of the spectrum, and that franchise elections can cycle with any period.
label: arXiv:2611.18468v1

summary.background:
- Spatial voting: voters and candidates are placed as points in an ideological space, often a left-right line or a two-dimensional plane.
- Social choice function: a rule that turns individual preferences into a collective outcome, such as a majority or median rule.
- Yolk: a voting-theory concept, roughly the smallest circle that intersects every majority-winning line through the ideal points; it is used as a way to summarize where majority-based outcomes are likely to fall.
- Cycling: a situation where majority votes can go in a loop, with no stable winner.
- Disenfranchisement: losing the right to vote or to be counted as a member.
- Recursive stability: a system where the rules for membership are set by the members themselves, so changing rules can change who decides.
summary.one_liner: The paper introduces "franchise elections," in which group members vote on who counts as a member, and shows in two-dimensional ideological space that these votes can produce complex dynamics, including cycles, under any social choice function and, for the Yolk rule, that new issue axes can lead to disenfranchisement.
summary.plain: The paper studies a self-referential problem: the people who already have voting rights are the ones who decide who gets them. It models this as a series of votes in which members choose which group composition they want, based on how each choice would shift the outcome for them when views are spread across two issue dimensions. The authors report that these votes can behave in complicated ways, and that under the Yolk voting rule, people who try to add a new issue axis at right angles to an existing left-right divide risk losing their vote unless they side with one end of the existing spectrum.
summary.why: Questions about who may vote, who belongs to a group, and what speech is acceptable all involve groups deciding their own boundaries, so a formal model of that loop may be useful for thinking about such disputes. The text does not show how well the model matches real political or organizational behavior, so its practical relevance is uncertain.

title: Disenfranchisement in Spatial Voting Games

abstract: AI agents learn what principals want from what principals choose. We offer a criterion for when a principal's decisions, at every belief an AI might hold, are all the AI needs. For acting, they are. Cautious actions, such as deferring to a person, typically divide the principal's actions into blocks, and for choosing costless evidence, decisions are enough exactly when the same evidence is best in every block. Otherwise, the AI acts as its principal would yet can gather the wrong evidence, and greater capability can turn that error into incorrect actions. Choices between two mistakes reveal what decisions miss.
label: arXiv:2611.19417v1

summary.background:
- Revealed preferences: an economic idea that a person's wants can be inferred from the choices they make.
- AI alignment: the effort to make AI systems act in line with what people actually want.
- Principal: the person or party an AI acts on behalf of.
- Belief: the AI's current estimate of what the principal wants, which it updates as it learns.
- Blocks: groups of the principal's possible actions that the AI treats as similar, such as all actions that amount to deferring.
- Costless evidence: information the AI can gather without any cost, so the question is only which information to gather.
summary.one_liner: The paper gives a criterion for when observing a principal's decisions, across every belief an AI might hold, is enough to act for them, and shows that for choosing costless evidence the same test requires the same evidence to be best in every block of actions.
summary.plain: The question is how an AI system can learn what its user or overseer wants just by watching what that person chooses. The paper sets out a test for when those observed choices are enough for the AI to act correctly. When they are not, the AI can act as its principal would but still gather the wrong information, and a more capable AI can turn that mistake into wrong actions.
summary.why: The AI alignment problem of inferring human goals from behaviour is central to safety work, and this paper frames it with economic revealed-preference reasoning. The text is only an abstract, so its wider relevance to real AI systems is not something I can judge from it.

title: Are Revealed Preferences All You Need for AI Alignment?

abstract: The survey compares two research traditions within the mathematical theory of designing the rules of interaction (mechanisms) for purposeful participants: mechanism design, together with contract theory and implementation theory, and the theory of active systems created by V.N. Burkov and developed into the theory of control in organizations (TCO) by D.A. Novikov's school; the main results of Yu.B. Germeier's school and of the domestic schools adjacent to active systems theory (AST) are covered as well. The problem statements and principal results of 2006-2026 are presented: for mechanism design (MD) - robust and dynamic mechanism design, multidimensional screening, information design, simplicity of mechanisms and credibility of the designer, market design, algorithmic and learning-based design, mechanisms for AI agents, and robust, relational, dynamic and algorithmic contracts; for AST and TCO - a general typology of control, strategy-proof and incentive-compatible planning mechanisms, decomposition of the agents' game, systems with distributed control and coalitional interaction, reflexive games and informational control, control of staff and structure, dynamic active systems, and project management. A correspondence between the classical results is established (the fair play principle and the revelation principle, the serial resource allocation mechanism and the uniform rule, active expertise mechanisms and generalized median schemes, quasi-compensatory incentive schemes and contracts under observable actions), and priorities are delineated by uniform rules; the areas where the two traditions diverge are identified, as are the dimensions of the problem (staff, structure, institutions, awareness, agents' beliefs) covered only by TCO.
label: arXiv:2611.21803v1

summary.background:
- Mechanism design: building rules (auctions, contracts, voting, planning procedures) so that people who pursue their own interests still produce a desired outcome.
- Revelation principle: a standard result saying that one can restrict attention to rules where participants simply report their private information honestly.
- Incentive compatibility: a rule is designed so that telling the truth is in each participant's own interest.
- Contract theory: how a principal pays an agent when effort or information is hidden or hard to observe.
- Implementation theory: whether a designer can get a desired outcome as the equilibrium of some game.
- Active systems theory: a framework, developed from work by V.N. Burkov, that studies control of organizations where participants have their own goals and information.
- Robust and dynamic design: rules that still work when assumptions are wrong or when interaction unfolds over time.
summary.one_liner: A survey that compares mechanism design, contract theory and implementation theory with the Russian-origin theory of active systems and its successor, the theory of control in organizations, covering results from 2006 to 2026 and mapping where the two traditions agree and diverge.
summary.plain: This is a review paper about how to design the rules of a game or organization so that self-interested people act in a way that serves the designer's goals. It sets two research traditions side by side: the widely known Western mechanism design field and a separate Russian-led line of work called active systems theory. The authors say they match up classic results from both and point out topics that only the second tradition covers, such as staff, organizational structure and participants' beliefs.
summary.why: It is useful as a map for researchers who know only one of these two bodies of work, and it may help link ideas on incentives, contracts and AI agents across the two. The text itself gives no outside evidence of impact, so its practical importance is unclear from the abstract alone.

title: Mechanism Design and Active Systems Theory: 60 Years of Parallel Development

abstract: We study the fair division of indivisible chores among agents with additive disutilities, focusing on the central fairness notion of envy-freeness up to any chore (EFX), and its multiplicative approximations. Although the existence of constant-factor approximations to EFX are known, computing such an allocation in polynomial time remained open. We resolve this question by giving an algorithm that, for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, computes a $(3+\varepsilon)$-EFX allocation in time polynomial in the input length and $1/\varepsilon$. Our result relies on two algorithmic contributions. First, we give a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) for earning-restricted (ER) equilibria with equal earning requirements and arbitrary feasible chore earning limits. We develop a new nonconvex program with chore payouts and money-flow variables, and prove that every local maximum yields an exact ER equilibrium. We then give a mirror-ascent algorithm for this program and prove that it converges to an approximate ER equilibrium in polynomial time. Second, we give a new procedure that converts the approximate equilibrium into a $(3+\varepsilon)$-EFX-friendly allocation, a suitable starting point for the chore-swap framework of Garg and Murhekar (2026). The procedure uses a flexible price threshold to choose swap chores and their recipients together, overcoming a factor-four bottleneck in the earlier approaches while accommodating approximate earnings. We expect these ideas to be useful more broadly in fair division, including for goods and other fairness notions.
label: arXiv:2611.21387v1

summary.background:
- Fair division: splitting items among agents so each feels their share is fair; "chores" are items people want to avoid, so agents have disutility (cost) rather than value.
- Additive disutilities: each agent's total cost is the sum of the costs of the chores they receive.
- EFX (envy-freeness up to any item): no agent prefers another's bundle after removing any single chore from it. A multiplicative approximation relaxes this by a constant factor.
- Polynomial time: the running time grows at most like a fixed power of the input size, which is the usual meaning of "efficient" in algorithms.
- FPTAS: a method that gets arbitrarily close to an optimal answer with running time polynomial in both input size and 1/ε.
- Equilibrium with earning limits: a market-style balance where agents earn payouts for chores and money flows are constrained; the paper uses such equilibria as a starting point.
- Mirror ascent: an iterative optimization method for maximizing a function over a constrained set.
- Local maximum of a nonconvex program: a point better than all nearby points, which may not be the global best; the paper proves such points are exact equilibria.
summary.one_liner: The paper gives the first polynomial-time algorithm that computes a (3+ε)-approximate EFX allocation of indivisible chores to agents with additive disutilities, via an FPTAS for earning-restricted equilibria and a new conversion procedure feeding into the Garg–Murhekar chore-swap framework.
summary.plain: The paper studies how to divide a set of indivisible tasks ("chores") among several people so that nobody feels treated unfairly. Earlier work showed that roughly fair divisions always exist, but no efficient method was known to find one. The authors give a procedure that finds a division that is fair up to a factor of 3 plus a small tunable slack, in running time that grows polynomially with the problem size and with how small the slack is.
summary.why: Fair division of chores is a core question in algorithmic economics, and turning an existence result into an efficient algorithm is a standard and meaningful step. The authors also suggest their techniques may carry over to goods and other fairness notions, though the text does not show that.

title: A Polynomial-Time Algorithm for Constant-Factor EFX Allocations of Chores

abstract: We propose a calibration method for local stochastic volatility models that determines the leverage factor by a fixed-point iteration. Each iteration simulates the model with the current leverage factor and approximates the conditional expectation of the stochastic variance given the spot by a single regression in time and state, with a quasi-likelihood loss for positive responses. The resulting leverage factor is a smooth function of time and spot with relatively few parameters, which can in addition be refined directly against option quotes. We recalibrate the leverage factor to S&P 500 index options on the day of an interest rate announcement, keeping the parameters of a two-factor Bergomi model calibrated four weeks earlier. After five iterations, leverage factors with 63 and 143 coefficients reproduce the implied volatility surface fitted to the quotes within a few basis points over the quoted strikes, the smaller one except in the left wing, and further iterations change them little. A few regularized Gauss-Newton steps against the quotes then bring 87% and 95% of the liquid quotes inside their bid-ask intervals.
label: arXiv:2611.18214v1

summary.background:
- Option: a contract whose payoff depends on a future asset price; its quoted price implies a volatility.
- Implied volatility surface: implied volatilities across strikes and maturities, the usual way option prices are compared.
- Stochastic volatility: a model in which volatility itself moves randomly over time.
- Local volatility / leverage factor: a model where the volatility depends on the current price and time, scaled by a factor that the paper solves for.
- Calibration: adjusting model parameters so model prices match market quotes.
- Fixed-point iteration: repeating a computation, feeding each output back as the next input, until the result stabilises.
- Regression and quasi-likelihood: standard statistical tools for estimating an average relationship from simulated data.
