summary.why: Having one explicit coordinate system that covers nearly everything makes it easier to do calculations such as integration and optimization on these spaces. The text itself does not say much about wider applications, so any link beyond these calculations is uncertain.

title: Almost-Global Coordinates on Matrix Manifolds

abstract: We refine the classical pro-homotopy type of the end of a manifold by recording the boundaries of a compact exhaustion together with the bordisms between them. We show that this assignment, the bordism-end, is functorial in embeddings, and independent of the choice of exhaustion. Its target is the free sequential colimit completion of the bordism $\infty$-category. Along the way of defining the bordism-end, we show that the category of all smooth $d$-dimensional manifolds and embeddings is formally obtained from the analogous category of compact manifolds. Through the formalism of the bordism-end, it follows that a manifold is diffeomorphic to the interior of a compact manifold if and only if its bordism-end is representable. Moreover, this formalism yields a fibre sequence relating the classifying spaces of the compactly supported diffeomorphism group of a manifold and its full diffeomorphism group, and a space of bordism-ends. Finally, we set up the pro-end functorially in embeddings, with target the cospan $\infty$-category of pro-spaces, and show that it factors through the bordism-end.
label: arXiv:2611.23166v1

summary.background:
- Manifold: a space that locally looks like ordinary Euclidean space, e.g. a sphere or torus.
- Compact exhaustion: writing a manifold as an increasing union of compact (closed and bounded) pieces.
- End of a manifold: the behaviour of the space near infinity, captured up to homotopy.
- Pro-homotopy type: a way of recording a system of spaces indexed by these pieces, rather than a single space.
- Bordism: a higher-dimensional region whose boundary is a given manifold; bordisms can be composed like morphisms in a category.
- ∞-category: a category with higher-dimensional morphisms, used to organise bordisms and spaces coherently.
- Diffeomorphism group: the group of smooth, invertible, structure-preserving maps of a manifold to itself.
- Fibre sequence: a standard homotopy-theory pattern relating a total space, a base and a fibre.
summary.one_liner: The paper refines the pro-homotopy type of a manifold's end by recording the boundaries of a compact exhaustion and the bordisms between them, obtaining a functorial, exhaustion-independent invariant valued in the free sequential colimit completion of the bordism ∞-category.
summary.plain: A manifold is a smooth curved space, such as a surface or a higher-dimensional analogue. Its "end" describes how the space looks when you go out toward infinity, which is what remains after you cut away larger and larger compact pieces. This paper refines that picture by also keeping track of the boundary surfaces of those pieces and of the higher-dimensional "bordisms" (shapes that connect one boundary to another).
summary.why: The text claims a clean criterion: a manifold is the interior of a compact manifold exactly when this new invariant is representable. It also links the diffeomorphism groups (the symmetries of a space) to a fibre sequence involving a space of these ends, which may be of interest to researchers in geometric topology and homotopy theory. The abstract does not show how widely these tools will be applied beyond the results stated.

title: A bordism perspective on ends of manifolds

abstract: We establish a Hurewicz-type inequality relating mean dimension and conditional metric mean dimension. For every equivariant continuous map between dynamical systems, the mean dimension of the domain is bounded above by the sum of the mean dimension of the target and the conditional metric mean dimension of the map. In particular, any equivariant continuous map that decreases mean dimension must have infinite topological conditional entropy. The key ingredient is a new waist inequality, which we believe is of independent geometric interest beyond its application to dynamical systems. Compared with Gromov's original waist inequality, a distinctive feature of this inequality is that it applies to finite simplicial complexes of arbitrary topology, subject only to dimensional restrictions.
label: arXiv:2611.22390v1

summary.background:
- Dynamical system: a space together with a map that describes how points move in discrete time steps.
- Equivariant map: a map between two such systems that commutes with the motion, so it respects the dynamics.
- Mean dimension: a measure of how many independent "degrees of freedom" a moving system needs per unit of time, averaged over long runs; it can be infinite or fractional.
- Metric mean dimension and conditional entropy: finer ways of measuring complexity or information loss in a map, tied to how small scales are resolved.
- Hurewicz-type theorem: a classical kind of result relating the dimension of a space to the dimension of its images under maps.
- Waist inequality (Gromov): a geometric result saying any map from a high-dimensional sphere onto a lower-dimensional one must have some fiber that is large in a measurable sense.
- Finite simplicial complex: a space built by gluing triangles, edges and vertices together, used as a discrete model of shapes.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves a Hurewicz-type inequality bounding the mean dimension of a domain by the mean dimension of a target plus the conditional metric mean dimension of an equivariant map, using a new waist inequality for finite simplicial complexes of arbitrary topology.
summary.plain: This paper studies how "complexity" of a moving system, measured by mean dimension, behaves when one system is mapped onto another in a way that respects the motion. It shows that the complexity of the starting system is at most the complexity of the target plus a measure of how much the map can squeeze things. A key geometric tool, a new "waist inequality," is proved and is said to apply to shapes of almost any topology, not only to the standard spheres in Gromov's original result.
summary.why: The text gives a concrete consequence: any such map that lowers mean dimension must have infinite topological conditional entropy. The authors also say the waist inequality is of interest in its own right, but the text does not say what further applications it has.

title: Waist inequality and a Hurewicz-type theorem for mean dimension

abstract: Let $F$ be a holomorphic endomorphism of $\mathbb{P}^k(\mathbb C)$ of algebraic degree $d\ge2$, with $k\ge1$. We prove that every ergodic $F$-invariant probability measure $μ$ of entropy strictly greater than $(k-1)\log d$ admits compact sets of $μ$-measure arbitrarily close to one on which the restrictions of $μ$ have Hölder continuous super-potentials. Consequently, $μ$ gives zero mass to every Borel pluripolar set.
label: arXiv:2611.23490v1

summary.background:
- Holomorphic endomorphism of complex projective space P^k(C): a map given by complex-polynomial-type formulas on a space of dimension k, applied repeatedly.
- Algebraic degree d: roughly how many times the map stretches things; d at least 2 makes the dynamics nontrivial.
- Invariant probability measure: a way of assigning weights to sets that the map leaves unchanged; ergodic means it cannot be split into smaller invariant pieces.
- Entropy of a measure: a number measuring how quickly orbits become unpredictable under the map.
- Super-potential: a smooth-ish auxiliary function built from the measure, used to describe its regularity.
- Hölder continuity: a quantitative smoothness condition, a step below differentiability.
- Pluripolar set: a very thin set in complex analysis, akin to a measure-zero set of special type.
summary.one_liner: For holomorphic endomorphisms of complex projective space of degree at least two, ergodic invariant measures with entropy above (k-1) log d are shown to have compact sets of nearly full measure on which their super-potentials are Hölder continuous, implying the measure charges no pluripolar Borel set.
summary.plain: This paper studies how a repeated complex-number map acts on a space and how its long-run "averaged" behaviour, a probability measure, is distributed. The authors show that when the measure is sufficiently "spread out" (its entropy, a measure of how unpredictably the map mixes points, exceeds a threshold), the measure is concentrated on compact pieces where a certain smoothness property holds. As a consequence, the measure assigns zero weight to a special class of very small "pluripolar" sets.
summary.why: The result gives a concrete regularity condition that high-entropy measures must satisfy, which matters for understanding the fine structure of these dynamical systems. The text does not say more about wider applications, so the broader significance is best treated as unclear from this abstract alone.

title: Large entropy implies Hölder regularity on large sets

abstract: We initiate the study of Ramsey theory for edge ideals. The edge ideal I_G is generated by the monomials x_ux_v for all edges uv of G. A central invariant measuring structure in algebraic geometry and commutative algebra are the betti number beta_{i,j}(S/I) for some ideal I in a ring S. We prove the Ramsey Theorem for Edge Ideals: For any betti number indices i,j, and any number of colors m, there is a graph F such that for every m-coloring of the edges of F, there is a color l such that beta_{i,j}(S/I_{F_l}) >0, where F_l is the subgraph of F whose edges are in color l. Moreover, the number of vertices of F is at most jm^2.
label: arXiv:2611.23485v2

summary.background:
- Graph: a set of vertices joined by edges.
- Edge ideal: for a graph G, the ideal generated by the monomial x_u x_v for each edge uv; it encodes the graph as a polynomial object.
- Betti number beta_{i,j}: a count of minimal generators/relations at each step i and degree j in the algebraic resolution of an ideal; it measures how complicated the ideal is.
- Ramsey theory: results saying that sufficiently large structures must contain a well-ordered substructure whatever colouring is used.
- m-colouring: assigning one of m colours to each edge; F_l is the subgraph of edges of colour l.
summary.one_liner: The paper initiates Ramsey theory for edge ideals of graphs, proving that for any Betti number index pair (i,j) and any number of colors m, there is a graph F with at most jm^2 vertices such that every m-coloring of its edges leaves some color class whose edge ideal has a nonzero Betti number beta_{i,j}.
summary.plain: The paper asks a Ramsey-style question: if you take a large enough network (graph) and colour its connections with a few colours, must some colour still carry a certain algebraic signature? Ramsey theory says that enough structure forces some order no matter how you colour, and here the "signature" is a Betti number, a count of certain building blocks in the algebraic description of a graph. The authors prove that such a graph always exists, and they give a bound on how many vertices it needs.
summary.why: It links two areas, extremal combinatorics and commutative algebra, by showing a Ramsey-type guarantee for an algebraic invariant. The text gives only the main theorem and a vertex bound, so its wider reach and the sharpness of the bound are not shown here.

title: Ramsey Theory for Edge Ideals

abstract: We study growth models for random graphs where the growth is established by vertex or edge creations and where there is no dependence between vertices and edges. Creations are logged by time stamps such that the history of the resulting graph can be reconstructed. We investigate two prototypical models, an undirected and a directed one, called undirected independent growth model (UIG-model) and directed independent growth model (DIG-model). The generating functions for the number of histories have radius of convergence equal to zero. In the UIG-model, we express the asymptotic number of histories as a sum that is amenable to the discrete Laplace method. We derive the asymptotic number of histories, study the number of vertices of a random history, and prove a central limit theorem. In the DIG-model we use a rescaled Borel transform to get an entire function. Then we show that this function is Hayman admissible, which enables us to derive the asymptotic number of histories in this model. The counting sequence is closely related to the framework of generalized Legendre-Stirling numbers. To determine the number of vertices in a random history, we prove that the bivariate generating function is e-admissible and infer that again a normal limit law holds. Finally, we discuss a correspondence to set partitions with even block sizes and present an algorithm based on Boltzmann samplers that generates such graphs uniformly at random.
label: arXiv:2611.22535v1

summary.one_liner: The paper counts histories of two random graph growth models (undirected and directed, with vertex and edge creations logged by time stamps), derives asymptotics via discrete Laplace method and Hayman admissibility, and proves normal limit laws for the number of vertices.
summary.plain:
The paper studies how random networks can grow over time, where each new vertex or edge is recorded with a time stamp so the full growth history can be replayed. It asks how many such histories exist when the graph gets large, and what a typical history looks like. The authors find formulas and approximations for these counts in two model variants, and show that the number of vertices in a random history follows a bell-shaped (normal) distribution.</plain>
<parameter name="why">Counting histories links random graph growth to classical combinatorial sequences such as generalized Legendre-Stirling numbers and to set partitions with even block sizes. The text does not indicate applications beyond this combinatorial setting, so its wider significance is unclear from the abstract alone.</why>
<parameter name="background">- A random graph: a network of vertices (nodes) joined by edges, grown by a random process.
- A history: a record of the order in which vertices and edges were added, via time stamps.
- Generating function: a formal power series whose coefficients count objects of each size; its radius of convergence describes how fast those counts grow.
- Asymptotic enumeration: finding a simple formula that approximates a count as size goes to infinity.
- Laplace method: a standard way to estimate sums and integrals dominated by a peak.
- Hayman admissibility: a technical condition under which coefficients of a power series can be estimated accurately.
- Central limit theorem / normal limit law: the statement that a suitably centred and scaled random quantity looks bell-shaped for large sizes.
- Set partition: splitting a set into non-overlapping groups; "even block sizes" means every group has an even number of elements.
- Boltzmann sampler: a randomized algorithm that generates structures of a given class uniformly at random.</background>
<parameter name="difficulty">research-level

title: Asymptotic enumeration of histories and limit laws in two random graph evolution models

abstract: Nonlinear nudging augments the classical linear nudging (continuous data as- similation) term with a nonlinear feedback that strengthens as the observed error decreases, and yields super-exponential convergence to the true state. In this paper, we study nonlinear nudging for the 3-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with the finite element method, which allows complex geometries and physical boundary conditions. We propose an implicit-explicit (IMEX) finite element scheme with inf-sup stable elements, prove its unconditional long-time stability, and show for the spatially semi-discrete scheme that the error reaches a prescribed tolerance in finite time. Our analysis also suggests that the non- linear nudging term requires the mesh resolution to be fine enough (${χ= O(H^{-1})}$, where $χ$ is the nonlinear nudging intensity and ${H}$ is the observation mesh size). Further, our error estimates suggest that a larger nonlinear exponent $γ$ requires finer observational resolution, which is confirmed by numerical tests. Numerical experiments, including two-dimensional forced viscous flow in a periodic box, flow past a cylinder, and flow over a flat plate, show that nonlinear nudging synchronizes with the true solution considerably faster than linear nudging. We also show that observations in a subregion suffice to synchronize the whole flow
label: arXiv:2611.23036v1

summary.background:
- Navier-Stokes equations: the standard equations describing how viscous fluids such as air and water move.
- Data assimilation / nudging: adding a term to a simulation that pushes it toward real measurements, so the model tracks the actual system.
- Linear vs nonlinear nudging: linear nudging corrects in proportion to the error; the nonlinear version uses a stronger, nonlinear correction as the error gets smaller.
- Finite element method: a way of splitting a domain into small pieces (a mesh) to approximate solutions of differential equations, well suited to irregular shapes.
- Mesh size: the spacing of the grid; finer meshes give more accurate results but cost more computation.
- Implicit-explicit (IMEX) scheme: a time-stepping method that treats some terms implicitly for stability and others explicitly for speed.
- Inf-sup stability: a mathematical condition on the pairing of velocity and pressure approximations that prevents spurious numerical results.
- Super-exponential convergence: error shrinking faster than any simple exponential decay.
summary.one_liner: The paper analyzes an implicit-explicit finite element scheme for nonlinear nudging (data assimilation with a feedback term that grows stronger as the error shrinks) applied to the 3D incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, proving long-time stability and finite-time error convergence for the spatially semi-discrete scheme, with a mesh-resolution condition χ = O(H^{-1}) and numerical tests in 2D.
summary.plain: The paper studies how to pull a computer simulation of fluid flow (such as air or water moving around an object) onto the real flow, using sparse measurements taken from the actual flow. The authors use a correction term whose strength increases as the mismatch shrinks, which they report makes the simulation lock onto the true flow faster than the standard correction. The text reports that the method is proven stable and accurate under conditions on mesh size, and that tests on three 2D flows show faster synchronization, including when measurements cover only part of the region.
summary.why: Fluid flow prediction from partial, noisy observations matters for weather, ocean, and engineering modeling, and this work gives a finite element method (a standard tool for complex shapes and boundaries) with stated proofs for the nonlinear version. Its practical relevance beyond these test cases is not established by the text alone.

title: Finite element nonlinear nudging for the Navier-Stokes equations

abstract: We develop a singular-layer enhanced Finite Volume Neural Network (sl-FVNN) methodology for solving singularly perturbed boundary value problems. The proposed framework combines flux-conserving finite volume residuals with analytically derived boundary layer correctors, enabling stable and efficient approximation of sharp boundary variations induced by small perturbation parameters. Numerical experiments over a broad range of small perturbation parameters ($10^{-4}$ to $10^{-12}$), demonstrate that the sl-FVNN yields uniformly accurate predicted solutions and significantly improved convergence behavior compared to conventional FVNN methods. Further comparisons with sl-PINNs from (Gie, Hong, Jung, Appl. Anal. 2024) show that our sl-FVNNs attain comparable accuracy for reaction--diffusion and Burgers equations, while achieving significantly improved convergence for convection-dominated nonlinear problems. These results highlight the effectiveness of incorporating asymptotic layer structures into finite volume based neural networks, offering a practical and scalable framework for multiscale PDE learning in stiff regimes.
label: arXiv:2611.22066v1

summary.background:
- Boundary value problem: an equation solved on a region with values fixed at its edges.
- Singular perturbation: a small parameter multiplies the highest-order derivative, so the solution changes abruptly in a thin boundary layer.
- Boundary-layer corrector: an added term that captures the rapid change near the edge.
- Finite volume method: a numerical method that enforces conservation by balancing fluxes across the faces of small cells.
- Physics-informed neural network (PINN): a neural network trained to satisfy the governing equation and boundary conditions.
- Convection-dominated / Burgers-type problems: transport-heavy equations where shocks or steep fronts can form.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes sl-FVNN, a finite volume neural network augmented with analytically derived boundary-layer correctors, to solve singularly perturbed boundary value problems and compares it with singular-layer PINNs on reaction-diffusion and Burgers-type equations.
summary.plain: The paper looks at equations where a tiny parameter makes the solution change very sharply in a thin strip near the edge of the domain. The authors build a neural-network solver that enforces conservation of quantities over small cells, and adds known mathematical correction terms for those thin edge regions. Their tests cover very small parameter values, from 10^-4 down to 10^-12, and they report more uniform accuracy and better convergence than a conventional version of the method.
summary.why: Sharp, thin-layer behavior is hard for standard solvers, including neural ones, so a method that handles it stably is of practical interest for multiscale modeling. The text claims comparable accuracy to an existing physics-informed approach on some problems and better convergence on convection-dominated nonlinear ones; the evidence is limited to the abstract, so these claims are not independently checked here.

title: Finite volume neural networks for singularly perturbed boundary value problems

abstract: Classically, a set is computable from an oracle if both the set and its complement are computably enumerable (c.e.) relative to that oracle. We construct a countable nonstandard model of true arithmetic with sets A and X such that both A and its complement are c.e. relative to X, yet A is not pointwise Turing reducible to X. The Turing functionals used here are single-valued at every oracle. For regular oracles, we prove that the classical equivalence holds over ISigma_1. Two further phenomena, each known from earlier work, are realized with the same oracle X that witnesses our main separation. Strong and pointwise Turing reducibility differ for this X, and some Delta_1^X set is not X-c.e.
label: arXiv:2611.22871v1

summary.background:
- Computable set: one where a procedure can decide membership for any input.
- Computably enumerable (c.e.): one whose members can be listed by a procedure, though non-members may never be confirmed.
- Oracle: extra information handed to a procedure for free; "relative to X" means computing with X as the oracle.
- Turing reducibility: A is Turing reducible to X if X-powered procedures can decide A.
- Pointwise vs. strong reducibility: two variants of the reduction notion that can differ.
- Nonstandard model of arithmetic: a model of the arithmetic truths that contains extra, non-standard numbers; true arithmetic is the set of all sentences true in the standard integers.
- ISigma_1: a fragment of induction axioms restricted to simple formulas, used to say how much arithmetic is assumed.
- Delta_1 set: one that is both c.e. and co-c.e. (so decidable in the simple sense).
summary.one_liner: In nonstandard models of true arithmetic, the classical equivalence between computability and "both the set and its complement are c.e. relative to an oracle" is shown to fail for general (nonregular) oracles, with the regular case still holding over ISigma_1.
summary.plain: This paper works in logic about what can be computed from a given body of information (an "oracle"). The authors build a countable nonstandard model of arithmetic in which a set A and its complement can both be listed by a procedure using oracle X, yet A cannot be obtained from X by a standard step-by-step reduction. The result is a counterexample, and the authors also prove that the usual equivalence does hold for regular oracles.
summary.why: It shows that a classical equivalence in computability theory depends on the kind of oracle used, which clarifies the boundaries of a basic principle. The text does not say what further applications it may have, so its wider connections are unclear from the given material.

title: Relative computability and definability for nonregular oracles

abstract: We present a construction of the Euclidean two-dimensional $φ^4$ quantum field theory model on $\mathbb R\times S$ using parabolic stochastic quantization and discuss the Osterwalder-Schrader axioms. Motivated by one-loop string scattering amplitudes, we first construct finite-volume measures on a family of tori with varying geometry. To construct an infinite-volume measure on the cylinder, we establish uniform renormalization and stochastic estimates as the complex structure varies, including the degenerating regime in which the torus approaches an infinite cylinder.
label: arXiv:2611.23032v1

summary.background:
- Quantum field theory: a framework where particles and forces are described by random-like fields spread over space and time.
- φ^4 model: a standard toy model with a quartic self-interaction; in two dimensions it is one of the best-understood interacting models.
- Euclidean theory: the same theory written with imaginary time, which turns quantum problems into probability problems.
- Stochastic quantization: a way of constructing the measure by evolving the field under a random noise-driven equation until it settles into equilibrium.
- Renormalization: removing infinities that appear in these models by subtracting carefully chosen terms.
- Torus and cylinder: a torus is a surface shaped like a donut; a cylinder is what a torus becomes when one loop is made infinitely long.
- Osterwalder-Schrader axioms: conditions that ensure a Euclidean theory can be converted back into a physical quantum theory.
- Complex structure: a parameter describing the shape of a torus.
summary.one_liner: Constructs the Euclidean two-dimensional φ^4 quantum field theory on the infinite cylinder R×S via parabolic stochastic quantization, building finite-volume measures on tori and taking a limit where the torus degenerates into a cylinder, with uniform renormalization and stochastic estimates across varying complex structure.
summary.plain: This paper is about building a mathematically rigorous version of a simple quantum field theory, the two-dimensional φ^4 model, on an infinitely long cylinder. The authors approach it by first defining the theory on a family of donut-shaped surfaces (tori) with varying shape, then letting these surfaces stretch into an infinite cylinder. The text says they also check that the resulting theory satisfies the Osterwalder-Schrader axioms, which are the standard consistency conditions that connect Euclidean (imaginary-time) theories to ordinary quantum theories.
summary.why: The work is motivated by one-loop scattering amplitudes in string theory, which involve integrating over tori of varying shape, so the construction may be a step toward making such string calculations rigorous. The text does not show how far this connection goes, so the link to string theory should be treated as a motivation rather than an established result.

title: On the $φ^4_2$ theory on $\mathbb R\times S$

abstract: A system of ordinary differential equations (ODE) $\ddot{y}_k=\sum_{l=1}^n M_{kl}\exp y_l,~k=1,...,n$, where $M$ is an $n\times n$ nonsingular symmetric matrix, is discussed in detail. A two-parameter family of exact solutions is found and proved to be unstable for general $n$. A result of Adler and Moerbeke is shown to apply to our systems; it states that the only completely integrable cases of this system are equivalent to the Toda lattice with included non-nearest neighbour interactions. A few interesting applications are shown for some special $n$'s.
label: arXiv:2611.23515v1

summary.background:
- Ordinary differential equation (ODE): an equation giving how quantities change in time, here second derivatives set by exponentials of the variables.
- Symmetric matrix: a square grid of numbers that equals its own transpose; M sets how the equations are coupled.
- Nonsingular: the matrix can be inverted (no degenerate coupling).
- Exact solution: a closed-form formula that solves the equations exactly.
- Unstable solution: a solution that drifts away when slightly disturbed.
- Completely integrable: enough conserved quantities exist that the system can be solved in principle by exact methods.
- Toda lattice: a classic model of particles on a line with exponential interactions, known to be integrable.
- Nearest-neighbour interaction: coupling only between adjacent particles; the paper concerns extra longer-range couplings.
summary.one_liner: A study of a family of nonlinear ODE systems with exponential terms governed by a symmetric matrix M, showing a two-parameter exact solution family that is unstable for general n and that the only completely integrable cases are equivalent to Toda-lattice-type systems with extra non-nearest-neighbour couplings.
summary.plain: The paper looks at a set of coupled equations describing how several quantities change over time, where each rate of change depends on exponentials of the others, with the pattern of coupling set by a grid of numbers (a matrix). The authors find an exact family of solutions with two free settings, but show these solutions are unstable when the number of quantities is general. They also use a known result to argue that the only cases that can be solved fully are close relatives of the Toda lattice, a classic model of particles in a chain.
summary.why: Systems of this kind, related to the Toda lattice, appear in integrable systems theory, and classifying which cases are fully solvable is a central question there. The text does not indicate specific applications beyond a few special cases it mentions, so its wider significance is unclear from this summary alone.

title: A multipurpose system of ordinary differential equations with exponential nonlinearity

abstract: We study optimal control of an evolution equation in which a scalar control multiplies a bounded operator acting on the state, with free dynamics given by a $C_0$-semigroup. The cost combines tracking terms, a quadratic control cost and an $L^1$ term promoting sparsity in time. We prove existence, derive optimality conditions, and show that optimal controls are thresholded functions of a switching function whose derivative is governed by the commutator of the drift and control operators. Consequently, commuting problems with a terminal cost admit no temporally sparse controls. The $L^1$ term also matters for uniqueness: two distinct controls satisfying the optimality conditions differ on a set of measure bounded from below, contained in the union of their supports, which yields, for the first time, uniqueness for every horizon in stable problems steered to zero. Second-order sufficient conditions and experiments on a bilinear heat equation complete the study.
label: arXiv:2611.23098v1

summary.background:
- Optimal control: choosing an input over time to minimize a cost that trades off tracking a target against control effort.
- Evolution equation / C_0-semigroup: a partial differential equation viewed as a system that moves a state forward in time in an infinite-dimensional space (e.g., a temperature profile).
- Bilinear control: the control multiplies the state, so its effect depends on the current state.
- L1 penalty: a cost proportional to the total size of the control, which tends to make the control exactly zero on long stretches (sparsity in time).
- Switching function and thresholding: a derived signal whose sign or size determines when the optimal control is zero or active.
- Commutator: a measure of how much the order of two operations matters; zero for commuting operations.
- Second-order sufficient conditions: tests using curvature information that confirm a candidate solution is a genuine local minimum.
summary.one_liner: Existence, first- and second-order optimality conditions, and a uniqueness result for L1-sparse (in time) optimal controls of infinite-dimensional bilinear evolution equations, with a bilinear heat equation as the numerical test case.
summary.plain: The paper studies how to steer a system that evolves over time, such as a heat distribution, by switching a single control strength up and down, while using as few switching moments as possible. The authors prove that an optimal control exists and characterize it: it takes the form of a thresholded "switching function," whose behavior is tied to a commutator of the system's operators. They also show that the sparsity-promoting penalty helps guarantee uniqueness of the optimal control, and test the results on a bilinear heat equation.
summary.why: Sparse control, which aims to act only at a few times, is useful when each action is costly, and the paper gives a structural result (no temporally sparse controls for commuting problems with terminal cost) and a uniqueness statement that the text presents as new for stable problems steered to zero. The text does not indicate specific applications beyond the heat-equation experiments, so broader impact is uncertain.

title: Sparse optimal control for a class of infinite-dimensional bilinear systems: optimality conditions and uniqueness

abstract: In this paper, we study a class of constrained convex finite-sum optimization problems. In many practical applications, all or some of the constraints are hard constraints that represent imperative requirements. Consequently, any desirable approximate solution must (nearly) satisfy these constraints. Motivated by this, we focus on computing an $ε$-$surely\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ ($ε$-SFSO) solution, in which the constraint violation is deterministically bounded by $ε$, and the expected optimality gap is at most $ε$. While a recently proposed stochastic variance-reduced first-order penalty method can compute an $ε$-SFSO solution, there remains a significant gap between its first-order oracle complexity for computing an $ε$-SFSO solution and that for computing an $ε$-$expected\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ solution, where both the expected constraint violation and the expected optimality gap are bounded by $ε$. To narrow this gap, we propose an inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient (SVRG) method that significantly improves the previously best-known first-order oracle complexity for computing an $ε$-SFSO solution. Furthermore, when the objective consists of a single function, the proposed method reduces to a novel deterministic first-order method for solving standard convex conic optimization. It achieves a significantly lower gradient evaluation complexity with respect to the objective function compared to existing methods, and can outperform them when computing constraint gradients and projections onto the associated cone is cheaper than evaluating the objective gradient. Preliminary numerical results are presented to illustrate the performance of the proposed method.
label: arXiv:2611.23221v1

summary.background:
- Convex optimization: minimizing a bowl-shaped (convex) function, where local search finds the global best.
- Finite-sum objective: the function is an average of many smaller functions, as in machine learning training on a dataset.
- Stochastic gradient methods: algorithms that take steps using gradients estimated from random samples of the terms.
- Variance reduction (SVRG): a technique that corrects noisy sampled gradients so the steps become more accurate over time.
- Penalty method: a way to handle constraints by adding a cost for violating them.
- First-order oracle complexity: the number of gradient (slope) evaluations needed to reach a target accuracy.
- Conic optimization: problems with constraints that require a solution to lie inside a cone-shaped set.
summary.one_liner: An inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient method is proposed for constrained convex finite-sum problems, targeting ε-surely feasible stochastic optimal solutions (constraint violation deterministically bounded by ε, expected optimality gap at most ε) with lower first-order oracle complexity than a prior penalty-based method.
summary.plain: This paper looks at optimization problems where many objective terms are averaged together and some rules must be strictly obeyed, such as limits in engineering design. The authors aim for an answer that always stays within those rules to a tolerance ε, while being near-optimal in expectation. They propose a new method based on variance-reduced gradient steps that needs fewer gradient evaluations than a recent comparable approach, according to the stated complexity bounds.
summary.why: Requiring that constraints hold for every returned answer, not just on average, matters in settings where violations are costly. The paper also states that, for a single objective, the method becomes a deterministic first-order method for convex conic problems that can be cheaper when constraint gradients and cone projections are cheap; the text gives only preliminary numerical results, so practical impact is not yet established.

title: An inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient method for constrained convex finite-sum optimization

abstract: We study mean estimation under federated differential privacy (FDP) constraints and batch contamination, considering both Gaussian and heavy-tailed distributions. In the homogeneous setting, where sample sizes and privacy budgets are constant across servers, we show that the costs of privacy and contamination disentangle. Under a bounded $v$th moment condition, with $v \in (1, \infty)$, the cost of batch contamination is of order $(\varepsilon/n)^{2-2/v}\vee \varepsilon^2/n$, where $\varepsilon$ is the contamination level and $n$ is the per-batch sample size. This reveals a phase transition at $\varepsilon\asymp n^{1-v/2}$, for $v > 2$, which is the first of its kind in the literature. We develop a two-stage procedure that achieves the minimax rate up to poly-logarithmic factors. A key component is a private smoothed voting procedure tailored to the FDP setting that provides optimal sensitivity control. For heterogeneous batch sample sizes and privacy budgets, we introduce a batch partitioning framework that groups batches with comparable per-batch sample sizes and privacy budgets. Surprisingly, the minimax rate is determined, up to poly-logarithmic factors, by the most informative group of batches. Consequently, in some regimes, it is minimax optimal to use only an arbitrarily small proportion of the data set. Heterogeneity also introduces interactions between the costs of privacy and contamination, in contrast to their disentanglement in the homogeneous setting. For unknown contamination level, we propose an adaptive, near-minimax optimal Lepski-type extension for the heterogeneous Gaussian setting, designed specifically to prevent privacy leakage by ensuring no repeated use of data points.
label: arXiv:2611.23551v1

summary.background:
- Differential privacy: a guarantee that an output reveals little about any single person's record, usually achieved by adding carefully calibrated noise.
- Federated learning: data stays on separate servers or devices; only summaries or privatised results are shared.
- Batch contamination: a fraction of the batches (groups of samples held by one server) may be corrupted or unrepresentative.
- Mean estimation under heavy tails: the data may have a finite v-th moment only, so extreme values can occur more often than in a bell curve.
- Minimax rate: the best worst-case error any method can achieve; "up to poly-logarithmic factors" means accurate apart from log-sized terms.
- Lepski-type method: a data-driven way to choose tuning parameters without knowing the unknown contamination level.
summary.one_liner: The paper gives minimax rates for private mean estimation across federated batches where some batches may be adversarially contaminated, covering homogeneous and heterogeneous batch sizes and privacy budgets, and an adaptive Lepski-type extension for unknown contamination in the Gaussian case.
summary.plain: The paper studies how to estimate an average value from data split across several servers, when each server must protect individual privacy and some of the servers' data may be corrupted. The authors find that, when all servers look alike, the error caused by privacy and the error caused by corruption can be separated, and they identify a threshold where the corruption cost changes behavior. They also propose a two-stage method that reaches the best achievable rate up to logarithmic factors.
summary.why: The result of a phase transition in the cost of batch contamination is presented as the first of its kind in the literature, which makes it of interest to researchers in robust and private statistics. Its practical reach beyond this theoretical setting is not addressed in the text.

title: Federated Differential Privacy with Batch Contamination

abstract: We consider the nonparametric estimation of the conditional hazard, cumulative hazard and survival functions of a time-to-event variable from streaming data subject to censoring, truncation, or a cure fraction. A time-to-event model is a map from the distribution of the latent variables to that of the observed ones. For a large class of models this map has an explicit inverse, and the conditional hazard is the ratio of the density of the exactly observed durations to an at-risk function. Both are estimated by one-pass learners, in which each observation contributes once and is never revised, such as recursive kernel, series and histogram estimators. Our main result is an asymptotic confidence band sequence for the conditional hazard at a fixed covariate value, uniform in time and in the sample size, which allows monitoring after a burn-in, and stopping at a data-dependent time. The band can shrink at the optimal uniform rate up to a logarithmic factor. Bands for the cumulative hazard and the survival function follow. In simulations, a fixed-sample band inspected repeatedly fails in about half of the streams, while the miscoverage of the recommended bands stays below, or close to, the nominal level.
label: arXiv:2611.22477v1

summary.background:
- Hazard function: the instantaneous risk of the event at a given time, given survival up to then.
- Survival function: the probability of still being event-free at a given time; the cumulative hazard is the running total of risk.
- Censoring and truncation: some event times are only partly observed (cut off, or only recorded if they fall in a window).
- Cure fraction: a share of subjects who will never experience the event.
- Nonparametric estimation: estimating the curve without assuming a fixed formula for it.
- Confidence band: a range around an estimated curve that should contain the true curve with a stated probability.
- Anytime-valid (sequential) inference: intervals that stay valid when checked repeatedly and at data-dependent stopping times.
- Uniform rate with logarithmic factor: the band width shrinks at the best possible speed, up to a slowly growing log term.
summary.one_liner: The paper builds asymptotic confidence band sequences, uniform in time and sample size, for the nonparametric conditional hazard, cumulative hazard and survival functions of time-to-event data observed as a stream under censoring, truncation or a cure fraction, using one-pass recursive estimators.
summary.plain: The paper is about estimating how likely an event (such as failure, relapse or death) is to happen next, given that it has not happened yet, when the data arrive continuously and some cases are incomplete, for example because they were cut off early or some subjects will never have the event. The authors use estimators that process each observation once and never revisit it, and they produce bands that can be checked at any time and stopped at a data-dependent moment. In simulations, a standard fixed-sample band checked repeatedly failed in about half of the streams, while the recommended bands kept errors near or below the intended level.
summary.why: Many monitoring settings, such as clinical trials, reliability tests or online services, look at data repeatedly and stop when a result looks clear, which inflates false alarms for ordinary intervals. The paper's sequential bands are meant to remain valid under that kind of peeking, and the text reports simulations supporting this, though it does not show real-world applications here.

title: Anytime-valid inference for conditional hazard and survival functions with streaming data

abstract: We develop a framework for small area causal inference (SACI). Unlike the traditional doubly robust (DR) estimation approach, the new framework is based on the empirical best prediction (EBP) method. EBP takes into consideration not only the bias but also the variance factor, which is often a more dominant component in the mean squared prediction error (MSPE). Under a linear mixed model for SACI, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator of the model parameters. More relevant to our main objective, we establish asymptotic optimality of the EBP in terms of minimizing the MSPE of the area-specific causal-effect (ASCE) predictor. Moreover, in view of the traditional interest in causal inference, we establish asymptotic normality of the EBP of the ASCE , which is used to construct prediction intervals for the ASCEs. We carry out extensive simulation studies to investigate finite-sample performance of the proposed EBP and its comparison with the traditional DR and other existing methods. Our simulation results show that the proposed EBP method has significant advantage over the comparing methods in terms of MSPE and coverage probability and length of the resulting prediction interval. A real-data example from agricultural-animal genetics is discussed.
label: arXiv:2611.22339v1

summary.background:
- Causal inference: estimating what would have happened to the same units with and without a treatment.
- Small area estimation: producing reliable estimates for subgroups (regions, farms, clinics) that have few observations.
- Doubly robust (DR) estimation: a standard causal method that stays valid if either of two underlying models is correctly specified; it is mainly judged by bias.
- Linear mixed model: a regression model with fixed effects plus random effects that let each area borrow strength from the others.
- Empirical best prediction (EBP): predicting an area's value using estimated model parameters, chosen to minimise expected squared prediction error.
- Mean squared prediction error (MSPE): the average squared gap between prediction and truth; lower is better.
- Asymptotic results (consistency, normality, optimality): statements about how estimators behave as sample size grows large, not guarantees for small samples.
- Prediction interval and coverage: a range meant to contain the true value, and the share of cases where it actually does.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes an empirical best prediction (EBP) framework for estimating area-specific causal effects in small areas, using a linear mixed model, with theory on estimator consistency, asymptotic normality, MSPE optimality, and prediction intervals, compared against doubly robust estimation in simulations and a real agricultural-genetics example.
summary.plain: The paper looks at how to estimate the effect of a treatment or intervention separately for small geographic or group areas, where there are only a few observations per area. The authors propose a method, called empirical best prediction, that balances bias against the noise in small samples rather than focusing mainly on bias as the traditional doubly robust approach does. In their simulations it gave more accurate predictions and prediction intervals with better coverage than the comparison methods, and they also apply it to a farm-animal genetics dataset.
summary.why: Estimating causal effects for small subgroups is hard because each subgroup has little data, so noise often dominates error. The paper's claim that variance, not just bias, drives most of the error is a reasonable point for small-area work, but the advantage is shown only in the authors' simulations and one real example, so its broader practical reach is not yet established.

title: Small Area Causal Inference

abstract: We study general distributional change point analysis for high-dimensional time series under nonstationary temporal dependence and limited computational resources. To mitigate noise accumulation from irrelevant coordinates and reduce the computational cost, we propose a sparse random projection procedure based on characteristic functions. We quantify the computational complexity of the random projections and show that the required number of projections grows polynomially with the ambient dimension. To accommodate nonstationary temporal dependence, a Gaussian multiplier bootstrap based on contrasts of local empirical characteristic functions is developed. We establish asymptotic false detection control and simultaneous guarantees for estimating the number and locations of multiple change points, with a near-parametric uniform localization rate up to logarithmic factors. A key technical innovation is a Gaussian approximation for high-dimensional multi-scale sparse time series, which is of independent interest. Simulation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed procedure in detecting and localizing distributional changes under various temporal dependence structures. An application to neural recordings further illustrates the practical utility of the proposed method in detecting diverse distributional changes in neural activity.
label: arXiv:2611.22422v1

summary.one_liner: A method for detecting and locating distributional change points in high-dimensional, nonstationary time series, using sparse random projections of characteristic functions and a Gaussian multiplier bootstrap for inference.
summary.plain: The paper addresses a common problem: spotting the moments when the overall pattern of a long, many-variable data stream shifts, such as when the way neurons fire changes. The authors propose a procedure that compresses the many variables into a small number of random summaries, which keeps computation cheap and limits noise from irrelevant variables. They report theoretical guarantees on false alarms and on how precisely change times are located, and show simulations and an application to neural recordings.
summary.why:
Many real data streams have dozens or hundreds of variables and dependence that changes over time, which breaks many standard change detection tools. The paper's main claims are theoretical guarantees under these conditions, plus a Gaussian approximation result for high-dimensional sparse time series that the authors say is of independent interest. The text alone does not show how it compares with existing methods in practice, so its practical reach is uncertain.</research-level>
<parameter name="background">- Change point: a time at which the statistical behavior of a data sequence changes.
- Distribution: the full pattern of how likely each value is, which is broader than just the average.
- Characteristic function: a mathematical fingerprint of a distribution, used here to compare distributions via a set of numbers.
- High-dimensional: many variables measured at once, so the number of variables may be large relative to the sample.
- Random projection: multiplying data by random weights to compress many variables into fewer summaries.
- Nonstationary dependence: the way observations relate to their neighbors in time changes over time.
- Gaussian multiplier bootstrap: a resampling technique that uses random normal weights to approximate the distribution of a test statistic, giving thresholds for false alarms.
- Asymptotic: describes behavior as the amount of data grows large.

title: Distributional change point analysis: high dimensionality, nonstationary dependence, and computational constraints

abstract: To access a report, click on the corresponding image below.
label: Artificial intelligence – MIT Technology Review

summary.background:
- A "research report" is usually a document from a company, lab, or analyst group summarizing findings or market trends.
- Clicking an image to open a report is a common web layout, but the image itself carries no text here.
- Without the report titles or summaries, no claims, figures, or conclusions can be reported.
summary.one_liner: A listing page titled "Research Reports" that links to AI industry reports through clickable images, with no descriptive text about their contents.
summary.plain: This is a navigation page rather than an article. It says that you open a report by clicking an image, but it gives no titles, authors, dates, or summaries of the reports it points to. The text is too thin to say what any report found.
summary.why: Its value depends entirely on the reports behind the images, which are not included here, so its importance cannot be judged from this page alone. It may be worth a look if you want to find the underlying reports directly.

title: Research Reports

abstract: Explore the new Sales plugin and 30+ new and expanded partner plugins in ChatGPT to research prospects, prepare pitches, update your CRM, and move deals forward.
label: OpenAI News

summary.background:
- ChatGPT: an AI chatbot from OpenAI that generates text in response to prompts.
- Plugin: an add-on that lets the chatbot connect to outside apps or data sources.
- CRM (customer relationship management): software that stores records of customers, contacts, and sales deals.
- Partner plugins: add-ons built by other companies that integrate their own products with ChatGPT.
- Sales pipeline: the stages a potential customer passes through before buying.
summary.one_liner: OpenAI announces a Sales plugin and more than 30 new or expanded partner plugins that let ChatGPT help sales teams research prospects, prepare pitches, update CRM records, and advance deals.
summary.plain: This is a short product announcement from OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT. It describes a new add-on, called a "plugin," that lets the chatbot work with sales tools. The text says salespeople can use it to look up potential customers, draft presentations, and keep their customer-tracking software up to date. The article is a brief overview and gives no detailed results or measurements.
summary.why: It shows AI chatbots being connected directly to business software, such as customer-relationship (CRM) systems, rather than only answering general questions. Whether this saves real time for sales teams is not shown in the text, so the practical impact is unclear.

title: Introducing ChatGPT for Sales

abstract: OpenAI and the Government of Chile are partnering to support responsible AI adoption, build public-sector skills and help local startups develop AI applications.
label: OpenAI News

summary.background:
- OpenAI is a US artificial intelligence company that makes ChatGPT and related tools.
- "Responsible AI adoption" generally means using AI in ways that are safe, fair, and well governed, though the text does not define it.
- "Public-sector skills" means training people who work in government.
- Startups are new small companies; "AI applications" are software products built on AI models.
- The source is a brief company announcement, so its claims are the partners' own and have not been independently checked.
summary.one_liner: OpenAI and the government of Chile announce a partnership to promote responsible adoption of AI, build public-sector skills, and help local startups build AI applications.
summary.plain: OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, and the Chilean government say they will work together on using artificial intelligence more widely. The stated goals are to use AI responsibly, to train government workers in these tools, and to help small local companies build AI-based products. The text is a short announcement and gives no details on how this will be carried out.
summary.why: This is a company-government agreement, so it may show how AI firms are seeking public-sector partnerships in individual countries. The announcement alone does not say what the effects will be, and it is unclear how much funding or what concrete programs are involved.

title: Introducing OpenAI for Chile

abstract: Overparameterized learners can fit noisy training labels perfectly and still predict well, which neither classical complexity measures nor information-theoretic generalization bounds explain. We develop an information-theoretic framework that separates two things an interpolating learner does with its sample: storage, the information the trained model retains about its training labels, and expression, the information about the sample that reaches its predictions at fresh inputs. We first characterize the ideal model: for a loss l, the least complex l-sufficient representation is the Bayes act, whose entropy is the minimal sufficient complexity; this generalizes, and corrects, an earlier "lossless maximal compression" view of boosting. We then show that every interpolator stores exactly nH(Y|X) bits of label noise, so storage, and bounds built on it (including CMI bounds), cannot tell interpolators apart. Expression can: excess risk is bounded above and below by the expressed information V, the entropy over training samples of the prediction at an input, plus a modal-bias term, exactly so for binary labels. Benign overfitting is therefore vanishing expression, a picture that covers nearest-neighbour rules, averaging, minimum-norm least squares and double descent, and that links V to classical bias-variance decompositions and to model disagreement. Finally, V gives a model-selection criterion that needs no held-out labels. Among overparameterized learners on 15 noisy datasets, V estimated from two disjoint halves has 60% less regret than holdout validation at the same cost and matches 5-fold cross-validation at a quarter of its cost; at matched cost it also beats selection by conditional mutual information. We characterize when it fails and give remedies. Code: https://github.com/nnikolaou/GLMC
label: arXiv:2611.23630v1

summary.background:
- Overfitting: a model fits training data too closely, including noise in the labels.
- Interpolator: a model that gets every training example exactly right.
- Benign overfitting: such a model still predicts new cases well.
- Information theory and entropy: entropy measures how much uncertainty or information a variable carries, in bits.
- Conditional mutual information (CMI): a standard information-theoretic measure of how much a model's output depends on one training example, used in generalization bounds.
- Bias-variance decomposition: splits prediction error into error from systematic assumptions and error from sensitivity to the training sample.
- Holdout validation and k-fold cross-validation: standard ways to estimate performance by reserving labelled data for testing.
- Regret (in model selection): how much worse the chosen model is than the best model in the candidate set.
summary.one_liner: The paper splits what an interpolating learner does with its training sample into storage (label information kept by the model) and expression (sample information reaching predictions at new inputs), and uses the expressed information V both to explain benign overfitting and as a label-free model-selection criterion.
summary.plain: Some machine learning models memorize noisy training labels perfectly and still predict well on new cases, which older theories struggle to explain. The paper separates what such a model stores about its training labels from what it actually passes on to its predictions, and argues that only the second part matters for how well it generalizes. The authors also propose a way to choose between models without setting aside labelled data for testing.
summary.why: It offers a new explanation for benign overfitting and a selection method that needs no held-out labels, which could matter for settings where labels are scarce. The reported gains (60% less regret than holdout validation at the same cost, comparable to 5-fold cross-validation at a quarter of the cost, on 15 noisy datasets) come from the authors' experiments; I have not verified them, and the approach is limited to cases where the authors say it fails under certain conditions.

title: What Interpolators Store and What They Express: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Benign Overfitting and Label-Free Model Selection

abstract: Conformal prediction provides distribution-free uncertainty quantification, but in sequential deployment, standard coverage guarantees can still allow substantial fluctuations in the number of miscoverages over time. We study an online setting in which prediction sets are produced one round at a time and the cumulative number of miscoverages must stay within a prescribed budget throughout deployment.Such a hard coverage guarantee can be enforced by enlarging prediction sets, but how much additional prediction-set size is fundamentally necessary remains unclear. We characterize this unavoidable efficiency cost over $T$ prediction rounds. Remarkably, the cost persists even with i.i.d.\ data, a known score distribution, and perfect knowledge of the population-optimal prediction set. Under suitable regularity conditions relating coverage and prediction-set size, we determine the minimum cumulative excess prediction-set size required by any online method satisfying the hard coverage constraint. This minimum cost is $Θ(\log T)$ for expected cost at a fixed time known in advance, $Θ(T^{1/3})$ for the largest expected cost over all fixed times up to $T$, and $Θ(\sqrt{T})$ for the expected worst realized cost when the evaluation time is chosen in hindsight. We further show that these rates can be attained using past scores, without knowing the score distribution. Thus, even perfect statistical knowledge does not make sequential reliability free.
label: arXiv:2611.22646v1

summary.background:
- Prediction set: instead of one guess, a method outputs a set of plausible outcomes; bigger sets are more likely to contain the truth but are less informative.
- Miscoverage: an event where the true outcome falls outside the predicted set.
- Coverage guarantee: a promise about how often the true outcome lands inside the set, typically on average.
- Online setting: predictions are made one round at a time, with data arriving sequentially.
- Hard (cumulative) budget: the total number of misses must stay under a limit at all times, not just on average.
- Big-O / Theta notation: Theta(f(T)) means the cost grows at the same rate as f(T) up to constant factors.
- Regularity conditions: mathematical assumptions the authors need for the exact rates to hold; the text says these are required but does not list them.
summary.one_liner: The paper characterizes the unavoidable extra prediction-set size needed by online conformal prediction methods that must keep cumulative miscoverages within a hard budget over T rounds, showing the cost holds even with i.i.d. data and known score distribution.
summary.plain: The paper looks at a forecasting-with-safety-margin problem: a system makes a set of possible answers each round and must keep the number of times the true answer is missed under a fixed budget over the whole run. The authors show that enforcing this strict budget forces the sets to grow by a minimum amount, and they pin down how that minimum scales with the number of rounds. The extra cost depends on which kind of time horizon is being judged, growing like log T, T^(1/3), or the square root of T in different cases.
summary.why: Conformal prediction is widely used to attach reliability guarantees to predictions, so knowing the exact price of a strict, cumulative guarantee is useful for deployment decisions. The result is theoretical, and the text does not say how it would translate to specific practical systems.

title: The Price of Hard Coverage Constraints in Online Conformal Prediction

abstract: This study developed and evaluated a computer vision model for automated ethological behavior classification of broiler chickens in climate-controlled poultry houses. Using publicly available videos preprocessed and manually annotated into three classes (sitting, standing, and feeding), the YOLOv11 model was trained and deployed on an Android application via TFLite conversion. Exploratory analysis ensured dataset consistency and visual quality, while evaluation showed class-dependent performance: higher robustness for static postures (sitting, AP=0.531; precision=100%) and lower accuracy for dynamic behaviors (feeding, AP=0.292; recall=0.20). Tests with unseen images demonstrated significant improvements, achieving accuracies of 98.04% for sitting, 83.33% for standing, and 67.65% for feeding. The model showed effective generalization in real farm environments, supporting its potential for continuous behavioral monitoring, early welfare assessments, and decision-making in precision poultry farming. These findings establish a technical foundation for future mobile-based applications at commercial scale, reinforcing the role of computer vision in automated animal welfare evaluation.
label: arXiv:2611.23007v1

summary.background:
- Object detection models (such as YOLO) find and label objects in images or video frames.
- AP (average precision) and precision/recall are standard scores: precision is how often a detection is correct, recall is how many true cases are found.
- Annotation means humans labeling example images so the model can learn from them.
- TFLite is a format that lets trained models run on phones.
- Ethology is the scientific study of animal behavior; broiler chickens are meat-production birds.
- Precision farming uses sensors and data to manage livestock and crops more finely.
summary.one_liner: A YOLOv11 object-detection model was trained on annotated public videos to classify broiler chicken postures (sitting, standing, feeding) and deployed in an Android app via TFLite conversion, with per-class accuracy reported on unseen images.
summary.plain: Farmers need to know how chickens are behaving, since changes in posture or eating can signal welfare problems, but watching thousands of birds by eye is impractical. This paper describes training a computer vision model to recognize three behaviors from videos (sitting, standing, and feeding) and running it on a phone. The model did well on sitting, moderately on standing, and worst on feeding, which is the most movement-based behavior.
summary.why: Automated, low-cost monitoring of animal behavior could support earlier welfare checks on farms, which is the stated motivation. The text is limited, though: it reports per-class scores and small-sample accuracies but gives little detail on dataset size, test conditions, or how well results would hold on commercial farms, so the practical value is still unproven.

title: Tracking Ethological Behaviors of Broiler Chickens Through Computer Vision (YoloV11) Using an Android Mobile Device

abstract: We show that an appropriate visual harness can substantially improve the performance of general vision-language models (VLMs) across diverse medical imaging tasks. We introduce VERA, a medical visual harness that equips general VLMs with interactive visual tools and systematic diagnostic evidence management. With VERA, general VLMs interactively explore medical images and progressively acquire diagnostic evidence, which is preserved in a lossless memory for subsequent retrieval and use. After submitting an initial answer, the VLM receives an assessment of potential omissions and the reliability of identified findings. This assessment guides further image inspection and measurement, followed by answer revision in an iterative agentic loop until sufficient evidence is obtained. Across 11 tasks and four imaging modalities, VERA improves performance on all tasks with Qwen3.8-27B, with notable gains in spleen measurement (63.3% to 98.3%), renal search (57.5% to 71.2%), and pulmonary nodule detection (0.0% to 28.2%). High-capability API-based VLMs achieve even higher performance with VERA. For example, GPT-6.1 Sol improves pulmonary nodule detection from 10.8% to 69.2% with VERA, demonstrating the complementary benefits of stronger model capabilities and an effective medical visual harness. Our results highlight the potential of visual harnesses as a new paradigm for scaling general VLMs to medical imaging tasks.
label: arXiv:2611.22815v2

summary.background:
- Vision-language model (VLM): an AI system that takes images and text as input and answers in text.
- Agentic loop: the model repeatedly acts (for example, inspects an image), checks results, and revises its answer.
- Harness: the software scaffolding around a model that supplies tools, memory, and feedback, without changing the model's weights.
- Lossless memory: a store that keeps all gathered findings intact for later use.
- Medical imaging modalities: the types of scans, such as CT or X-ray; the paper covers four.
- Benchmarks are reported as percentage accuracy; the text does not describe the datasets in detail.
summary.one_liner: VERA is a medical "visual harness" that wraps general vision-language models in interactive image tools and an evidence memory, and reports gains across 11 medical imaging tasks.
summary.plain: General AI models that read both pictures and text often struggle with medical scans. This paper proposes a wrapper, called VERA, that lets such a model zoom in, take measurements, and keep notes on what it has found. It then reviews its own answer and goes back to look again until it has enough evidence.
summary.why: The paper reports large gains on some tasks, such as detecting pulmonary nodules (small spots in the lung), for both an open model and a commercial API model. It suggests that the surrounding tooling around a model may matter as much as the model itself, though the text gives no independent validation or clinical testing.

title: Visual Harness Scales General VLMs to Medical Images

abstract: Large language models increasingly produce AI slop in generated code: verbose, redundant, non-idiomatic implementations that pass functional checks but bloat codebases. The problem compounds on SDKs released after the model's training cutoff, where the model has neither idiomatic priors nor compositional understanding. We present Option-GRPO, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that adapts a code LLM to an unseen SDK from its source code alone, without human-written usage examples or test cases, and that explicitly optimizes for both functional correctness and code elegance. Our key insight is that SDK source code contains compositional structure that defines a hierarchy of reusable code patterns (code options) which simultaneously serve as the building blocks of a curriculum and the action space for efficient policy optimization. We show that code options induce a valid semi-Markov decision process, give conditional bounds under which shorter option description length implies more concise and, in expectation, more API-efficient programs, and analyze under stated assumptions how the option hierarchy improves credit assignment by a factor of $\sqrt{T/K}$. Using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with execution-based rewards at each curriculum level, Option-GRPO discovers SDK idioms, composes them into patterns, and assembles patterns into complete programs. Experiments on 12 unseen SDKs with a 32B-parameter base model demonstrate 61.4% pass@1, outperforming flat GRPO by 8.7 points, ExploraCoder by 11.2 points, and ReCode by 6.3 points. Option-GRPO produces solutions that use 34.7% fewer API calls and are 27% shorter than flat-GRPO outputs while maintaining higher correctness, directly attacking the slop problem.
label: arXiv:2611.23633v1

summary.background:
- Large language model (LLM): a neural network trained on text, including code, that generates new text or code.
- Reinforcement learning (RL): training by trial and error, where the model gets a reward signal for good outcomes.
- GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization): an RL method that scores several sampled answers against each other to decide which to reinforce.
- Pass@1: the fraction of tasks solved correctly on the first attempt.
- SDK (software development kit): a set of libraries and functions a programmer uses to build software for a platform.
- API call: a single request to a library function; fewer calls usually means more efficient code.
- Semi-Markov decision process: a decision model where actions can last multiple steps, used here for multi-step code-building options.
- Curriculum: training ordered from simpler to harder tasks.
summary.one_liner: Option-GRPO applies hierarchical reinforcement learning, using reusable code patterns extracted from SDK source code as options and a curriculum, to adapt a 32B code LLM to unseen SDKs while rewarding both functional correctness and concise, idiomatic code.
summary.plain: AI coding models often write code that works but is bloated, repetitive, and unidiomatic, and this gets worse for software libraries released after the model was trained. This paper proposes a training method that teaches a model a new library using only its source code, without hand-written examples or tests, by breaking the library into reusable building blocks and training step by step. The authors report that on 12 unseen libraries their method solved 61.4% of tasks on the first try and produced programs with about 35% fewer API calls than a standard baseline.
summary.why: Verbose, redundant generated code is a practical cost for software teams, so cutting it while keeping correctness is a relevant goal. The results are self-reported on the authors' own benchmark, and the theoretical claims rest on stated assumptions, so the gains should be checked by independent evaluation before weighing them heavily.

title: Option-GRPO: Hierarchical RL Against AI Slop in Code Generation for Unseen SDKs

abstract: Model-based offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) enables sample-efficient adaptation by leveraging offline pre-training for online fine-tuning. However, the distribution shifts between offline and online stages often hinder fine-tuning performance. Many existing methods encode the optimism-pessimism trade-off through a single-objective formulation. Selecting its trade-off coefficient through online fine-tuning can require costly bi-level optimization. We identify the balance established during offline training as a key challenge: in our motivating experiments, optimistic policies adapt better to novel tasks, whereas pessimistic policies perform better on the same online tasks. To address this challenge, we propose a bi-objective formulation that captures this trade-off, yielding a Pareto policy pool during offline training. This policy pool enables adaptive selection during online fine-tuning across diverse online tasks. To generate the pool, we introduce Multi-Objective Soft Actor-critIC (MOSAIC), which solves bi-objective problems and constructs diverse Pareto policies. After offline training, a contextual bandit algorithm hierarchically selects the most suitable policy for fine-tuning at each online interaction step. Empirically, our pipeline, Hierarchical Pareto Policy Pool (HiP3), achieves the strongest aggregate performance across both same and novel online tasks and maintains its advantage under stronger distribution shifts. Comprehensive ablations further clarify the roles of the policy pool, MOSAIC-based pool construction, and the online selection mechanism.
label: arXiv:2611.22172v1

summary.background:
- Reinforcement learning (RL): an agent learns by trying actions and receiving rewards.
- Offline RL: learning only from a fixed dataset collected earlier, with no new interaction.
- Online fine-tuning: continuing to improve the learned policy through live interaction.
- Model-based RL: the agent learns a model of how the environment behaves and plans with it.
- Optimism vs. pessimism: optimism favors uncertain actions that might pay off; pessimism avoids them. Both are used to handle uncertainty from limited data.
- Pareto front: a set of solutions where improving one objective requires worsening another.
- Soft actor-critic: a common RL algorithm that rewards both task success and action randomness.
- Contextual bandit: a simple method for choosing among options based on observed context and feedback.
summary.one_liner: A model-based offline-to-online RL method that trains a Pareto pool of optimistic-to-pessimistic policies offline (via a multi-objective soft actor-critic, MOSAIC) and uses a hierarchical contextual bandit to pick among them during online fine-tuning (HiP3).
summary.plain: Robots and game-playing agents are often first trained on a fixed batch of past data and then keep learning while acting in the real setting. This paper addresses the problem that the switch from the old data to new experience can make learning worse. Instead of committing to one cautious-or-bold setting during the first stage, the authors train a set of policies spanning that trade-off and let the agent choose among them as it goes.
summary.why: The core idea is that the best level of caution depends on the new task, so deferring that choice to online fine-tuning may avoid costly tuning. The text reports the strongest aggregate performance across same and novel online tasks, but gives no further detail here, so the size and generality of the gain should be checked in the full paper. It may be of interest to people working on sample-efficient adaptation of learned controllers.

title: Towards Optimism-Pessimism Trade-off in Model-based Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Language models increasingly exhibit behaviors that are difficult to detect in transcripts, such as reward hacking, deception, and sycophancy. Asking the assistant follow-up questions about its actions is unreliable, since models are generally not trained to report their own misbehavior. As a result, approaches to oversight typically involve querying external models. These face limitations: external transcript monitoring operates only on visible model outputs, and activation decoders lack full context and are prone to confabulation. We introduce introspective oversight, which trains a new role in the model to answer arbitrary questions about the assistant, rewarding answers that are verified against the assistant's actual behavior. We implement this by adding a separate, third-person observer role that answers these queries, which we can train solely for accuracy and separately from the assistant.
