summary.one_liner: A study of the 2D Ising model on square and triangular lattices that defines a spin-odd Euler-characteristic observable from the cell complexes of positive and negative spin domains, relates it to standard Ising quantities, disproves a conjectured lower bound, and uses finite-size scaling to locate the ferromagnetic transition.
summary.plain: This paper looks at a simple magnet model (the Ising model, where tiny spins point up or down on a grid) and asks whether a purely geometric "shape count" of the up-spin and down-spin regions can signal when the magnet loses its ordering as it heats up. The authors build such a count, the Euler characteristic, from the difference between the two kinds of regions, and simulate the model on a computer to test it. They report that this count behaves like an order parameter near the transition and gives estimates of the transition temperature that approach the known value on both grid types.
summary.why: The work tests whether topology, which ignores exact measurements and looks only at connectivity and holes, can locate a phase transition as well as conventional measures. The authors suggest it may help in systems where no standard order parameter can be written down, but the text does not show this beyond the Ising model, and the critical-exponent estimate on the square lattice is reported as sensitive to the fitting range.

title: Topological signatures of criticality: the Ising case

abstract: Many systems are controlled by intermittent control variables that take on a random value for a random time interval. In the presence of such noise at update steps, the main equation for the controlled variables has a memory kernel whose coefficients are the cumulants, also known as $G$-cumulants, of the noise, which are fully ordered in time. In the case of Poisson switching, these correspond to the Boolean cumulants of the jump distribution, and the kernel can be summed exactly. We derive an exact decomposition of these coefficients for any waiting-time distribution with independent amplitudes and durations, which separates the jump statistics from the renewal statistics. In the case of waiting times that follow a power-law distribution with a finite mean, it is highly probable that a long time interval will be covered by a single period, and we have shown that, as a result, the coefficients for long delays intersect in all orders, from Boolean cumulants to the usual moments of the jump law. The long-lag kernel thus becomes a superposition of frozen deterministic flux kernels, weighted by the expression $ξ^2p(ξ)$, and from this the corresponding main equation in closed form follows. For $2<μ<3$, where the noise correlation time is infinite, the second-order closure retains a finite error even in the presence of slow dynamics, whereas the main equation of the frozen flows in this limit yields an exact stationary mean value. The telegraphic process is the only case of noise with renewal steps for which second-order conclusions are exact. An exactly solvable model with additive and correlated multiplicative noise confirms these predictions.
label: arXiv:2611.23092v1

summary.background:
- Memory kernel: a term in an equation describing how the system's past influences its present.
- Cumulants and moments: statistical summaries of a random quantity; G-cumulants are a specific ordered version used here.
- Boolean cumulants: a particular cumulant type that arises for Poisson (memoryless) switching.
- Renewal process: a sequence of events where waiting times between them are independent and identically distributed.
- Power-law distribution: waiting times with a heavy tail, so very long intervals are not rare; a finite mean means the average waiting time is finite.
- Closure: an approximation that truncates an infinite hierarchy of terms, here at second order.
- Telegraphic process: a signal that switches between two values.
summary.one_liner: The paper derives an exact decomposition of the memory kernel (G-cumulant coefficients) for a controlled variable driven by intermittent random forcing with general renewal waiting times, and studies closure approximations for power-law waiting times with finite mean.
summary.plain: The paper studies systems that are pushed by a signal that changes value only at random moments, holding each value for a random stretch of time. It writes down the exact way past pushes continue to influence the system's future, and shows how this memory simplifies when the waiting times between changes follow a power-law distribution. The authors also give a closed-form approximate equation for the system and test it on a solvable model.
summary.why: Intermittent, switching forcing appears in many physical and control settings, so a clean way to handle its memory could be useful there. The text does not show how widely the results apply beyond the model studied, so the broader significance is uncertain.

title: Memory kernel and closure for systems driven by intermittent forcing with power-law waiting times

abstract: Nonlinear transport provides an efficient probe of the electronic structure and symmetry of quantum materials. As a prominent example, the intrinsic nonlinear Hall effect has attracted considerable attention in recent years because it is independent of impurity scattering and directly reflects the quantum geometry of Bloch electrons. Here we establish a simple textbook-style perturbation theory for the intrinsic nonlinear conductivity. Based on the well-defined Bloch-state velocity, our formulation perturbatively determines the field-corrected velocity and distribution function, from which the conductivity follows directly. We further compare our approach with wavepacket-based theories and discuss their consistency.
label: arXiv:2611.22229v1

summary.background:
- Hall effect: a sideways current or voltage produced by a field, classically from a magnetic field; the "nonlinear" version here arises without one, from the crystal's electronic structure.
- Nonlinear response: the output is not proportional to the input; a second-order term scales with the field squared.
- Bloch electrons: electrons in a periodic crystal, described by states labeled by momentum.
- Quantum geometry: properties of electron states, such as Berry curvature, that depend on how states change with momentum.
- Perturbation theory: solving a problem by expanding in powers of a small quantity (here the applied field) and solving order by order.
- Distribution function: the statistical occupancy of electron states in momentum space.
- Wavepacket theory: an alternative approach that treats electrons as localized packets of states.
summary.one_liner: The paper derives the intrinsic second-order nonlinear Hall conductivity from a textbook-style perturbation expansion of the Bloch-state velocity and distribution function, and checks it against wavepacket-based theories.
summary.plain: The paper is about how electrons in a crystal carry current in a sideways (Hall) direction when the applied electric field is strong enough that the response is no longer simply proportional to the field. Instead of relying on more specialized wavepacket methods, the authors use a standard step-by-step (perturbation) calculation to work out this response. They report that the approach gives a well-defined result and that it is consistent with the existing wavepacket-based theories.
summary.why: The effect is described as independent of impurity scattering and tied to the quantum geometry of electron states, so it may serve as a probe of crystal symmetry and electronic structure. The text does not report new measured values, so its practical reach beyond clarifying the theory is unclear.

title: Intrinsic second-order nonlinear Hall effect from perturbation theory

abstract: Layered ferromagnets with strongly correlated electrons provide a platform for exploring the interplay among magnetism, spin-orbit coupling, and nontrivial band topology. $\mathrm{Ni}_{1/4}\mathrm{TaSe}_2$ is a correlated van der Waals ferromagnet with a transition temperature of 58 K that lies close in composition to a superconducting phase that emerges upon Ni depletion. Here, we combine spin- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, circular-dichroism measurements, and density functional theory calculations to investigate its spin-resolved electronic structure. We observe spin-polarized states crossing the Fermi level and signatures of broken time-reversal symmetry in the ferromagnetic state. Spin-resolved circular-dichroism measurements further reveal a helicity-dependent spin response consistent with a finite spin Berry curvature and suggestive of local topological character. Together, these results establish an experimental connection between ferromagnetism, spin-polarized electronic states, and topological signatures in $\mathrm{Ni}_{1/4}\mathrm{TaSe}_2$, providing a foundation for investigating how these properties may relate to the emergence of superconductivity upon Ni depletion.
label: arXiv:2611.24468v1

summary.background:
- Van der Waals material: a crystal built from layers that are weakly bonded to each other, so thin flakes can be peeled off.
- Ferromagnet: a material whose atomic magnetic moments align in one direction, below a transition temperature (here 58 K).
- Photoemission: shining light on a surface to eject electrons; measuring their energy and direction reveals the electronic band structure.
- Spin-resolved: also recording which way each ejected electron's spin points.
- Circular dichroism: a difference in response to left- versus right-handed (circularly polarized) light.
- Berry curvature and topology: mathematical properties of how electron states twist through momentum space; nonzero values are linked to topological effects.
- Time-reversal symmetry: the symmetry broken when a material becomes magnetic; its breaking is one signature the paper looks for.
- Density functional theory: a standard computer method for estimating electronic structure from first principles.
summary.one_liner: Spin- and angle-resolved photoemission, circular-dichroism measurements and density functional theory are used to map the spin-polarized electronic structure of the van der Waals ferromagnet Ni1/4TaSe2, reporting signs of broken time-reversal symmetry and a helicity-dependent spin response suggestive of local topological character.
summary.plain: This paper studies a layered magnetic material, Ni1/4TaSe2, which becomes ferromagnetic below about 58 K and sits close in composition to a superconducting version of the material. The authors used light shining on the surface to knock electrons out and measured their spin and momentum, and they compared the results with computer calculations. They report spin-polarized electrons near the energy level that controls electrical behavior, plus a response to light polarization that they interpret as a sign of topological character.
summary.why: The work links magnetism, electron spin and possible topology in one material, which the text suggests may bear on why superconductivity appears when nickel is depleted. That connection is stated as a motivation for future work; the text does not show it, so its relevance to superconductivity remains unconfirmed.

title: Hidden topological signatures in a van der Waals ferromagnet revealed by spin-resolved circular-dichroic photoemission

abstract: Dark matter may consist of multiple components with distinct particle-physics origins. We investigate a scenario in which a universal axion couples to both visible and twin QCD, with twin baryons providing a possible dominant dark-matter component. The presence of a second strongly interacting sector can substantially enhance the axion mass while preserving its role in resolving the strong-CP problem, provided the physical vacuum angles are appropriately aligned. For a representative uniformly rescaled twin spectrum with a confinement scale five times that of ordinary QCD, the axion mass is enhanced by approximately a factor of 25. Using lattice-informed QCD results and a two-temperature description of the early universe, we investigate the cosmological evolution and relative abundances of the dark-sector components. In a representative conditional numerical benchmark, axions account for a small percentage of the observed dark matter, while twin baryons could constitute the remainder for a suitable primordial baryon asymmetry. We also examine the implications for additional relativistic species, strong-CP alignment, and the interactions of stable twin matter. Our results provide a quantitative framework for exploring mixed axion--twin-baryon dark matter and identify the particle-physics and cosmological conditions necessary for a viable realization, including constraints from the thermal history and formation of cosmic structure.
label: arXiv:2611.23015v1

summary.background:
- Dark matter: unseen matter that makes up most of the mass of galaxies, inferred from gravity.
- QCD (quantum chromodynamics): the theory of the strong force that binds quarks into protons and neutrons.
- Strong-CP problem: QCD allows a symmetry-breaking term that experiments have not seen; an axion is a hypothetical particle that would explain why it is effectively zero.
- Axion mass: the axion's mass is set by QCD; a larger mass changes how much axion dark matter is produced.
- Twin sector: a hypothetical hidden copy of the Standard Model's strong force with its own particles and confinement scale.
- Baryons: heavy particles like protons and neutrons, made of three quarks.
- Lattice QCD: a computer method for solving strong-force physics numerically; "lattice-informed" means its results are used as inputs.
- Two-temperature description: modelling the visible and hidden sectors as having different temperatures in the early universe.
- Baryon asymmetry: the small excess of matter over antimatter produced early on.
summary.one_liner: A theoretical study proposing a single axion coupled to both ordinary QCD and a mirror "twin" QCD sector, where the enhanced axion mass and twin baryons form a mixed dark-matter scenario, with lattice-informed estimates and a two-temperature early-universe treatment.
summary.plain: The paper asks whether dark matter could be made of two things at once: a light particle called the axion and a heavier kind of matter built from a hidden "twin" version of the strong force that holds atomic nuclei together. The authors show that adding this hidden sector can raise the axion's mass, for example by about a factor of 25 in one illustrative case, while still solving the strong-CP problem, a puzzle about why a certain symmetry is not violated in nuclear physics. They then estimate how much of the dark matter each component could supply under chosen assumptions.
summary.why: It offers a quantitative framework for mixed dark-matter models and spells out conditions the scenario must meet, including limits from the early-universe thermal history and from structure formation. The results are conditional on chosen benchmark values, so they should be read as a proposal to be tested rather than an established finding.

title: A Universal Axion in a Twin-QCD Sector

abstract: We introduce interstellar optical line emission as a new probe of axion dark matter. Axion decays to photons or electrons can excite or ionize neutral hydrogen, producing H$α$ emission at a fixed atomic wavelength rather than at an energy set by the axion mass. Developing the formalism and applying it to the Leo T galaxy with Very Large Telescope data, we derive strong constraints for eV--GeV scale axions, covering new regions of parameter space for both axion-photon and axion-electron couplings. These results establish optical line measurements as a new discovery channel for axion dark matter, probe poorly constrained parameter space below hydrogen's ionization threshold, and constrain axion explanations of JWST's high-redshift supermassive-black-hole observations.
label: arXiv:2611.23385v1

summary.background:
- Dark matter: invisible matter inferred from its gravitational effects; its composition is unknown.
- Axion: a hypothetical light particle proposed to solve a problem in particle physics and as a dark matter candidate.
- Axion coupling: how strongly an axion interacts with photons (light) or electrons; the paper constrains these couplings.
- Decay: an unstable particle transforming into other particles; here axions decaying to photons or electrons.
- Ionization threshold: the minimum energy needed to strip an electron from an atom; the paper covers axion masses below this for hydrogen.
- H-alpha: a specific red optical emission line of hydrogen, at a fixed wavelength.
- Leo T: a small, faint dwarf galaxy, rich in dark matter relative to its light.
- Constraint/limit: an upper bound on a parameter, from showing that a signal was not seen.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes using optical hydrogen-alpha emission from the interstellar medium, produced when axion dark matter decays to photons or electrons, as a new probe of axions in the eV-to-GeV mass range, and applies it to Very Large Telescope data from the Leo T galaxy.
summary.plain: Axions are hypothetical very light particles that some physicists think could make up dark matter, the unseen material that holds galaxies together. This paper suggests looking for them through faint light from hydrogen gas in a nearby dwarf galaxy, Leo T: if axions decay, they can knock hydrogen atoms into emitting a specific red glow. Using telescope data from that galaxy, the authors report limits on axion properties that the text describes as strong and covering regions not previously explored.
summary.why: Searches for axion dark matter usually look for signals at energies set by the axion mass, so a channel that emits at a fixed atomic wavelength is a different approach and could cover parameter ranges that are poorly constrained now. The abstract also links the limits to explanations of JWST observations of early supermassive black holes, though the strength of that connection is not something the abstract itself establishes.

title: Leading Axion Sensitivity with Interstellar Medium Optical Line Emission

abstract: Isospin and the symmetry energy are linked within the symmetry term of the liquid-drop mass formula and within the corresponding term of the equation of state of asymmetric nuclear matter. The Pauli exclusion principle leads to a leading quadratic dependence of the kinetic part of the symmetry term of the nuclear binding-energy formula on the neutron-proton asymmetry (N-Z)/A. Charge symmetry ensures the same leading quadratic dependence for the potential part. Charge invariance further generalizes this dependence, to lowest order, from T$_3^2$ to T(T+1). The strength of the symmetry term, in contrast, is determined by the symmetry energy. At sub-saturation densities the symmetry energy can be constrained by nuclear-structure observables, such as neutron skin thicknesses, isovector collective modes and the related electric dipole polarizability, and excitation energies of isobaric analog states. It can also be constrained by reaction observables, such as charge exchange and elastic scattering cross sections, isoscaling and isospin diffusion. At supra-saturation densities, by contrast, the only means of studying asymmetric nuclear matter under laboratory conditions are relativistic heavy-ion collisions. These studies use differential observables such as neutron/proton flows and light isobar or $π^{-}/π^{+}$ ratios. Complementary information can be obtained from neutron star observations including gravitational waves. The latest measurements and analyses of the stiffness of the symmetry energy will be presented, together with the recent NA61/SHINE observation of an unexpectedly large isospin-symmetry violation in kaon production. Attention will also be paid to the challenges of measuring charged and neutral products of relativistic heavy-ion collisions in the context of the recent ASY-EOS II experiment at GSI and to the new detectors used in the setup.
label: arXiv:2611.23355v1

summary.background:
- Atomic nuclei are made of protons and neutrons; isospin is a label for this neutron-proton balance, and (N-Z)/A measures the asymmetry.
- The liquid-drop model treats a nucleus like a drop of liquid, with terms for volume, surface, charge and an asymmetry (symmetry) term.
- The symmetry energy is the extra energy cost per unit of neutron-proton imbalance in nuclear matter; its "stiffness" describes how fast that cost rises with imbalance.
- Sub-saturation density means matter less dense than ordinary atomic nuclei; supra-saturation means denser.
- Heavy-ion collisions at high energy briefly create dense, hot matter in the lab; neutron stars provide the natural astrophysical counterpart.
- Kaons and pions are short-lived particles produced in such collisions; their production ratios serve as probes.
summary.one_liner: A review-style overview of how isospin (the neutron-proton balance in nuclei) and the symmetry energy (the cost of making nuclear matter neutron-rich) are constrained by nuclear-structure, reaction, heavy-ion and neutron-star observations, with a mention of recent NA61/SHINE and ASY-EOS II results.
summary.plain: This is an overview of how physicists work out how the balance between neutrons and protons affects the energy of atomic nuclei and of very dense nuclear matter. It covers the theory behind this balance, the ways it is measured in ordinary nuclei and in high-energy collisions of heavy ions, and the link to neutron stars. The abstract also mentions a recent experiment that saw an unexpectedly large violation of isospin symmetry in kaon production, and new detectors used in the ASY-EOS II experiment. The text is an abstract only, so it does not give the actual measured values or the details of those results.
summary.why: The symmetry energy controls how neutron-rich matter behaves, which matters for understanding heavy nuclei and the interiors of neutron stars. The abstract's note of an unexpectedly large isospin-symmetry violation in kaon production suggests a point of current interest, but the text does not show how much it changes the picture.

title: Isospin effects and symmetry energy in nuclear reactions

abstract: We perform a quantitative study of dilepton production and elliptic flow in In+In collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=17.3$ GeV and isobar collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=200$ GeV, concentrating on the low and intermediate invariant mass regions. The medium evolution is simulated event-by-event with the multistage iEBE-MUSIC framework, and the electromagnetic emission combines for the first time quark-gluon plasma (QGP) emission calculated at next-to-leading order (NLO) in the strong coupling with in-medium radiation calculated with hadronic many-body theory. Freeze-out and surviving primordial $ρ$ decays are also included. The calculations are compared with the high-precision dimuon spectra measured by the NA60 Collaboration, and with STAR preliminary measurements of dielectron spectra and elliptic flow. We obtain effective temperatures extracted from the transverse-mass spectra, and we calculate the elliptic flow of the different dilepton sources. Our results suggest that dilepton measurements in the low-mass and high $p_T$ region can provide insight into higher-order corrections to the QGP emission rate.
label: arXiv:2611.23506v1

summary.background:
- Heavy-ion collisions: smashing large nuclei together to create quark-gluon plasma (QGP), a very hot state of matter where quarks and gluons are not locked into protons and neutrons.
- Dileptons: pairs of oppositely charged electrons or muons; their invariant mass indicates the energy released in the emission.
- Elliptic flow: a measure of how particles are preferentially pushed out in one direction relative to the collision plane, reflecting pressure in the expanding matter.
- Next-to-leading order (NLO): a more precise level of perturbative calculation in the strength of the strong force.
- Hadronic many-body theory: describes emission from the later, cooler stage of matter made of hadrons (particles like pions and rho mesons).
- Effective temperature: a temperature inferred from the spread of particle momenta in the transverse direction.
- Experiments named: NA60 (dimuon data at SPS energies) and STAR (dielectron data at RHIC, preliminary).
summary.one_liner: A theory-plus-data study computing dilepton (lepton-pair) yield and elliptic flow in In+In and isobar heavy-ion collisions, combining next-to-leading-order quark-gluon plasma emission with hadronic many-body radiation and comparing against NA60 dimuon and STAR dielectron data.
summary.plain: This paper looks at pairs of electrons or muons produced when heavy atomic nuclei are smashed together at high speed, which briefly create a very hot soup of quarks and gluons. The authors built a computer simulation of how that hot matter evolves, predicted how many lepton pairs of different masses come out and how they spread out in direction, and compared the results with existing measurements. The text suggests that the low-mass, high-momentum part of the spectrum may be sensitive to finer corrections in how the hot matter emits these pairs.
summary.why: Lepton pairs pass through the hot matter without being strongly disturbed, so they offer a comparatively clean window into its temperature and emission behaviour. The authors say the low-mass, high transverse-momentum region may reveal higher-order corrections to the emission rate, but the text does not establish how decisive this would be.

title: The production of lepton pairs in heavy-ion collisions at SPS and RHIC energies

abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence and quantum technologies have driven the emergence of quantum machine learning, yet imperfections in near-term quantum devices remain a major obstacle for achieving practical quantum advantage. In the absence of fault-tolerant machines, ensemble learning, which combines multiple imperfect quantum devices, may unlock new quantum computing applications. Here, we introduce two ensemble-learning algorithms, namely Bagging and AdaBoost, for enhancing the accuracy of nonlinear regression problems. While Bagging trains variational quantum regressors independently, AdaBoost employs a sequential training strategy and achieves significantly better prediction accuracy. By incorporating systematic feature selection into our ensemble learning algorithms, we enhance their predictive power for highly nonlinear functions. We further improve prediction accuracy through a feature-to-qubit mapping strategy based on repeated feature encoding. The performance of our ensemble-based algorithms improves with both the number of regressors in the ensemble and the size of each regressor. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using four benchmarking functions with varying degrees of nonlinearity by relying on a feature pool limited to first- and second-order polynomial terms.
label: arXiv:2611.22389v1

summary.background:
- Machine learning regression: fitting a model that predicts a numerical output from inputs, such as estimating a curve.
- Variational quantum circuit: a quantum circuit with adjustable settings, trained by a classical optimizer, that is used here as a predictor.
- Ensemble learning: combining several models to make one prediction; Bagging trains models independently on resampled data, while AdaBoost trains them in sequence and upweights cases earlier models got wrong.
- Feature selection: choosing which input quantities to feed the model.
- Feature encoding: converting classical input numbers into the rotations applied to quantum bits (qubits); repeating encoding can let a small circuit represent more complex functions.
- Nonlinear function: a relationship where output does not change in proportion to input, so simple straight-line fits fail.
- Noisy near-term devices: current quantum hardware that is error-prone and lacks full error correction.
summary.one_liner: The paper adapts classical ensemble methods (Bagging and AdaBoost) to variational quantum regressors, adds feature selection and repeated feature encoding, and reports improved accuracy on four nonlinear benchmark functions using only first- and second-order polynomial features.
summary.plain: The paper looks at how to get more reliable predictions from today's noisy quantum computers, which are too imperfect to do much alone. The authors combine several small quantum models into a group, using two well-known team-based strategies from classical machine learning: one trains the models independently, the other trains them one after another so each corrects the last. They test this on four mathematical functions of varying complexity.
summary.why: Reducing the impact of device imperfections is a central practical question for near-term quantum computing, so an ensemble approach is worth watching. The text reports that the sequential AdaBoost strategy predicts more accurately than the independent Bagging strategy, but the evidence shown is limited to four benchmark functions, so its relevance to real-world problems is unclear.

title: Nonlinear function regression using quantum ensemble learning

abstract: Classical sampling of quantum error correction (QEC) circuits supports fault-tolerant protocol evaluation, but estimating rare logical failures requires many independent shots. Frame-active-state simulators isolate non-stabilizer information in a dense active-state vector, yet dense-state processing remains exponential in the active width. This paper presents MASQ, an exact measurement-adaptive sampler for near-Clifford QEC circuits based on selective materialization of non-Clifford rotations. At each measurement boundary, MASQ materializes only rotations in a measurement-relevant closure capturing direct and indirect non-commuting dependencies, deferring the rest to limit active-state expansion. Stabilizer-assisted elimination further removes rotations certified to be invisible to all future measurements. A circuit-dependent schedule is computed once and shared across shots, while adaptive caching of conditional Born probabilities and batched execution reduce repeated sampling work while preserving the measurement-record distribution. Across 19 QEC benchmarks, MASQ reduces peak active width by up to 40 active virtual qubits and achieves up to 8,098-fold CPU throughput speedup over Clifft on multi-round circuits.
label: arXiv:2611.22232v2

summary.background:
- Quantum error correction (QEC): encoding information across many physical qubits so errors can be detected and fixed.
- Clifford circuits: a restricted class of quantum operations that can be simulated efficiently on classical computers; "near-Clifford" means mostly such operations plus a few harder non-Clifford rotations.
- Active width: the number of qubits that must be tracked at once in a simulation; cost grows exponentially with it.
- Shot: one complete run of a circuit with random outcomes; rare failures need many shots.
- Measurement record: the sequence of classical outcomes from measurements, which the sampler must reproduce with the correct probabilities.
- Clifft: an existing simulator for this kind of circuit, used here as the baseline.
summary.one_liner: MASQ is an exact sampler for near-Clifford quantum error correction circuits that materializes only the non-Clifford rotations relevant to each measurement, using a shared circuit-dependent schedule, stabilizer-assisted elimination, and caching to shrink active width and speed up shot sampling.
summary.plain: Quantum error correction circuits are simulated on ordinary computers to check how well a planned protocol protects fragile quantum information, but catching rare failures means running huge numbers of simulated trials. This paper presents MASQ, a simulation method that only does the expensive bookkeeping for the parts of a circuit that affect the next measurement, and postpones the rest. The authors report that it cuts the peak number of active virtual qubits by up to 40 across 19 benchmark circuits and runs up to 8,098 times faster on CPU than the existing tool Clifft on multi-round circuits.
summary.why: Faster exact sampling of error-correction circuits would make it cheaper to estimate rare logical failure rates when designing fault-tolerant protocols. The text reports benchmark speedups only; it does not say how these gains carry over to hardware or to larger code sizes.

title: MASQ: Measurement-Adaptive Sampling for Near-Clifford Quantum Error Correction Circuits

abstract: Organic nonlinear optical (NLO) crystals offer efficient nonlinear frequency conversion for broadband THz spectroscopy. Unfortunately, only a subset of NLO crystals is compatible with the telecom (~1.5 $μ$m) pump wavelength region, where convenient MHz-rate femtosecond fiber lasers are available. Here, we present ultra-broadband (1-30 THz) THz generation and detection using a benzoindolium iodide (MBI, C$_{24}$H$_{24}$NOI) crystal illuminated by a 1.5 $μ$m MHz-rate fiber laser. At 200 mW of average pump power, the crystal delivers ~1 $μ$W of THz radiation as quasi-discrete peaks covering the whole emission region with a prominent peak at 11.8 THz. High-dynamic range (>40 dB) time-domain spectroscopy is demonstrated within minutes of integration.
label: arXiv:2611.22729v1

summary.background:
- Terahertz (THz) radiation: electromagnetic waves between microwave and infrared frequencies (1 THz is about 1 trillion cycles per second); used to study molecular vibrations and material properties.
- Optical rectification: a nonlinear optical effect in which a strong laser pulse in a crystal generates a THz pulse at low frequencies.
- Pockels effect: a change in a crystal's refractive index under an electric field; used here to detect THz pulses by how they alter a probe laser's polarization.
- Time-domain spectroscopy: measuring the THz electric field pulse over time, then computing its frequency spectrum.
- Telecom wavelength (~1.5 μm): the infrared band used in fiber-optic communications, where cheap, reliable lasers exist.
- MHz-rate femtosecond fiber laser: a laser emitting ultrashort pulses millions of times per second.
- Dynamic range (dB): the ratio between the strongest and weakest signals a measurement can distinguish; 40 dB is a factor of 10,000.
summary.one_liner: The paper reports terahertz (THz) generation and electro-optic detection in the organic nonlinear crystal MBI pumped by a 1.5 μm MHz-rate femtosecond fiber laser, yielding quasi-discrete emission spanning 1–30 THz with a prominent peak at 11.8 THz.
summary.plain: Terahertz light sits between microwaves and infrared light, and it is useful for probing materials by how they absorb it. This paper describes making and detecting this kind of light with a special organic crystal (MBI) driven by a telecom-wavelength laser, the same wavelength family used in fiber-optic internet equipment. The authors report that the crystal emits roughly 1 microwatt of THz light across a very wide range, and that a measurement with more than 40 dB of dynamic range can be done within minutes.
summary.why: Most strong THz sources need bulkier, more expensive lasers, so a crystal that works with inexpensive, high-repetition-rate fiber lasers could make THz spectroscopy more accessible. The text does not compare this against other sources or give application results, so the practical significance beyond the reported measurements is uncertain.

title: Optical rectification and Pockels effect in the organic nonlinear crystal MBI for quasi-discrete THz time-domain spectroscopy

abstract: Higher-order topological states are studied in a woodpile photonic crystal (PhC) having a large complete photonic bandgap. According to theoretical predictions, we fabricate a three-dimensional all-dielectric PhC with a millimeter-scale lattice period. The structure consists of two distinct lattice types that coincide through a structural displacement, where their interface intersection gives rise to hinge states. Microwave transmission measurements reveal transmission peaks and spatial localization at the intersection, demonstrating the hinge states. Furthermore, we confirm the absence of hinge states at a specific intersection. As theoretically predicted, hinge states emerge at intersections where the localized boundary polarizations are topologically different, whereas they are absent at intersections where the boundary polarizations are equivalent.
label: arXiv:2611.22196v1

summary.background:
- Photonic crystal: a periodic structure whose repeating pattern blocks waves in certain frequency ranges, the way a crystal affects electrons.
- Photonic bandgap: a range of frequencies that cannot propagate through the structure in any direction.
- Topological insulator: a material that is an insulator in its bulk but supports protected edge or surface waves at its boundaries.
- Higher-order topology: a generalization in which protected states appear at lower-dimensional features, here hinges (edges where two surfaces meet), not just surfaces.
- Woodpile structure: a stack of crossing rods or layers forming a 3D lattice.
- Microwaves: electromagnetic waves with wavelengths of about a millimeter to a centimeter, which is why the lattice can be built at millimeter scale.
- Boundary polarization: a label describing how the material's charge-like response is arranged at a boundary; matching or mismatching labels determine whether a hinge state exists.
summary.one_liner: The paper reports experimental observation of higher-order topological hinge states, localized at intersections of two interfaces, in a millimeter-scale all-dielectric woodpile photonic crystal at microwave frequencies, and shows their absence at intersections where boundary polarizations are equivalent.
summary.plain: Researchers built a three-dimensional structure out of a non-metallic material that blocks microwaves in a full range of directions, somewhat like a crystal that blocks light. Where two special boundaries of this structure meet along an edge, the team found that microwaves can travel along that edge and stay trapped there. They also found that at other meeting points, where the boundaries are equivalent, no such edge-trapped wave appears, as the theory predicted.
summary.why: The work tests a theoretical prediction about a newer class of topological states, in which waves are confined to edges (hinges) rather than surfaces. It is worth attention as an experimental check of higher-order topology in three dimensions, though the text does not indicate specific applications.

title: Microwave hinge states in an all-dielectric woodpile photonic crystal insulator

abstract: Nonlinear modelling has improved significantly in dealing with physics issues encountered in magnetically confined toroidal pinches, such as the Reversed Field Pinch and Tokamak configurations. Here, recent results relevant to the understanding of helical self-organization processes are presented: formation of internal transport barriers, temporary loss of operational point, relaxation-reconnection events, excitation of Alfvèn waves, and a possible fundamental mechanism for ion heating in plasmas. Starting from physics processes in Reversed Field Pinch plasmas, several similarities with Tokamaks are presented. In addition, data analysis tools, machine learning autoencoding techniques, are here trained for the first time on a RFP data analysis case.
label: arXiv:2611.22435v1

summary.background:
- Plasma: a gas so hot its atoms have lost electrons; it conducts electricity and responds to magnetic fields.
- Toroidal pinch: a plasma shaped like a donut and squeezed by its own and external magnetic fields.
- Tokamak and Reversed Field Pinch (RFP): two magnetic donut designs for fusion; in an RFP the field lines near the edge reverse direction.
- Helical self-organization: plasma spontaneously settling into twisted, spiral-like structures.
- Internal transport barrier: a thin region inside the plasma where heat or particles leak out much more slowly.
- Magnetic reconnection: field lines break and reconnect, releasing stored energy in a burst.
- Alfvén waves: magnetic waves travelling along field lines in a plasma.
- Autoencoder: a neural network that learns a compressed representation of data, often used to find patterns.
summary.one_liner: A review-style overview of nonlinear modelling of helical self-organization in toroidal magnetic-confinement plasmas (Reversed Field Pinch and Tokamak), covering transport barriers, relaxation-reconnection events, Alfvén waves, a proposed ion-heating mechanism, and first use of autoencoder machine learning on RFP data.
summary.plain: This paper is about hot, electrically charged gas (plasma) held in a donut-shaped magnetic cage, the kind of device studied for fusion energy. The authors summarize recent computer-model results on how these plasmas organize themselves into twisted, helical patterns and suddenly rearrange, including a possible explanation for why ions get heated. They also report trying a machine-learning method, called an autoencoder, on data from one of these devices for the first time.
summary.why: Understanding how confined plasmas lose or hold heat is a central obstacle to practical fusion power, so the mechanisms described may matter for both Reversed Field Pinch and Tokamak designs. The text does not show how far these results have been confirmed experimentally, so their practical impact is uncertain.

title: Modeling of basic physics issues in toroidal pinches and tools for performance control

abstract: The drag-reducing properties of streamwise-elongated surface corrugations, commonly referred to as riblets, have been extensively studied through experiments, simulations, and reduced-order modeling. Notably, the linearized Navier-Stokes framework introduced by Ran, Zare, and Jovanovic (J. Fluid Mech., vol. 906, 2021) employs volume penalization to model riblet-induced boundary conditions and predict drag reduction. These approaches typically quantify drag reduction as a function of a single geometric parameter, such as spanwise spacing or groove cross-sectional area, evaluated over fixed riblet shapes. As a result, identifying optimal riblet geometries across a broader design space often necessitates exhaustive parametric studies. To address this problem, we propose an optimization framework for the systematic design of optimal riblet shapes. Accordingly, we reformulate the volume penalization term in the linearized dynamics as a structured state-feedback operator. Targeting maximal suppression of turbulence, we pose a composite optimization problem that minimizes the steady-state variance of velocity fluctuations and riblet-induced dynamical augmentations while maintaining a constant bulk-flux. For a fixed spanwise wavelength (riblet spacing), this framework yields optimal wall-normal profiles that achieve maximal turbulence attenuation.
label: arXiv:2611.22249v1

summary.background:
- Riblets: small streamwise-aligned surface grooves that can reduce skin-friction drag.
- Turbulence in channel flow: chaotic fluid motion between two walls; its velocity fluctuations are a measure of its intensity.
- Linearized Navier-Stokes: a simplified, linear version of the fluid equations used to analyze small disturbances.
- Volume penalization: a mathematical trick that represents a solid or patterned boundary inside a fluid domain by adding a strong damping term.
- State-feedback operator: a control-theory term for a rule that adjusts the system based on its current state.
- H2 norm: a measure of how much steady random disturbances are amplified, here used as the optimization objective.
- Spanwise wavelength: the spacing between neighboring riblets, measured across the flow direction.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes an H2-optimal design framework that treats riblet wall-normal profiles as a structured state-feedback operator within a linearized Navier-Stokes model, optimizing for minimal steady-state velocity variance at a fixed spanwise spacing.
summary.plain: Riblets are tiny ridges and grooves cut into a surface, aligned with the flow, that can reduce drag from air or water rubbing against it. Past studies mostly tested a few fixed shapes and tuned one measurement, such as spacing, which makes it slow to search for the best shape. This paper describes a computer-based method that instead searches for the best wall-normal shape of the riblets, aiming to calm turbulence near the surface for a given spacing.
summary.why: Finding riblet shapes by a systematic optimization rather than exhaustive trial-and-error could make the design search more efficient. The text does not report specific results or performance gains, so its practical impact is unclear from this description alone.

title: $H_2$-optimal riblet profiles for turbulence suppression in channel flows

abstract: The homochiral proteins in living organisms are rather stable, but they tend to lose their secondary conformations and homochiral order over time. This instability is found in all living organisms, from bacteria to humans. The aging of living organisms, with the destruction of their vital homochiral order, raises the questions about the emergence of homochirality and how the homochiral order in the building molecules was ensured in prebiotic times before life evolved. Based on thermodynamic arguments, we propose that the homochiral order was achieved by a ``Frank-synthesis'' of homochiral peptides from racemic amino acids and in a capillary environment in the vents in the Earth's crust, perhaps at crystalline chiral surfaces, and that the peptides are stable over long times in such an environment. The $hypothesis$ can be confirmed by experimental analysis of the stability of the secondary structures in proteins as a function of water activity and in a capillary environment.
label: arXiv:2611.22311v1

summary.background:
- Chirality: a molecule is chiral if it cannot be superimposed on its mirror image, like left and right hands.
- Homochirality: living organisms use only one handedness of amino acids (proteins) and sugars.
- Racemic: an equal mix of left- and right-handed forms, as expected from non-biological chemistry.
- Peptides and proteins: chains of amino acids; secondary structure refers to local folding patterns such as helices.
- Frank synthesis: a named idea, after Frank's 1953 proposal, that an autocatalytic process could amplify one handedness from a mixture; here the text uses the term for a proposed route.
- Water activity: a measure of how much water is available in a system, affecting molecular stability.
- Capillary environment: narrow pores or cracks where water is held and surfaces strongly influence chemistry.
summary.one_liner: A theoretical proposal that homochiral peptides (chains of single-handed amino acids) could have formed from racemic amino acids in capillary environments in Earth's crust, with stability tested only as a hypothesis.
summary.plain: Living proteins are built from amino acids that all have the same "handedness," and this order slowly decays over time. The paper asks how that handedness first arose before life, and proposes that short chains of one-handed peptides could have formed and persisted in tiny water-filled cracks in rocks deep in the Earth's crust.
summary.why: The origin of biological handedness is a long-standing open question in origin-of-life research, so a mechanism tied to specific geological settings is of interest. The text is a short hypothesis based on thermodynamic arguments; it presents no experimental data, so its support is currently limited.

title: Stability of Homochiral Peptides in Capillary Environments: Implications for the Origin of Biological Homochirality

abstract: Molecular size alters spatial distributions, reaction equilibria, and transport in crowded mixtures, but resolving individual particle encounters can make large stochastic simulations computationally costly. We developed a lattice-based framework for simulating reaction-drift-diffusion systems with volume exclusion captured as a free energy functional in each voxel. Changes in this free energy, together with external one-body potentials, modify diffusion and reaction propensities. Our framework accommodates mixtures of particle sizes without resolving each particle's position within a voxel. We implemented our framework in an operator splitting scheme and compared our predictions with off-lattice interacting-particle simulations. Inclusion of the local free energy functional improved spatial occupancies and shifts in reaction equilibria relative to point-particle simulations. With separate approximations for larger spheres and polymers, we simulated crowding-induced slowing and spatial segregation. We then modeled motor proteins' traffic jams on a structured track representing a microtubule. Our results demonstrate how local composition can inform stochastic reaction and transport rates without resolving individual encounters.
label: arXiv:2611.22902v1

summary.background:
- Reaction-diffusion simulation: tracking molecules that move randomly (diffuse), drift, and react, often on a grid of small cells (voxels).
- Stochastic simulation: randomness is modeled explicitly, which matters when only a few molecules are present.
- Volume exclusion: two objects cannot occupy the same space, so crowded larger particles limit where smaller ones can go.
- Free energy: a measure of how favorable a configuration is; here it is used to penalize crowded voxels and alter move and reaction rates.
- Point-particle versus finite-size models: point models treat molecules as having no size; this work accounts for size.
- Operator splitting: a numerical technique that handles diffusion, drift and reaction in separate steps.
- Motor proteins and microtubules: molecular walkers that move along filament tracks inside cells; "traffic jams" occur when they crowd each other.
summary.one_liner: A lattice-based stochastic reaction-drift-diffusion framework that encodes volume exclusion among mixed-size particles as a local free-energy functional per voxel, validated against off-lattice interacting-particle simulations and applied to crowding, segregation, and motor-protein traffic on a microtubule-like track.
summary.plain: Molecules inside cells are packed so tightly that their size changes where they sit, how fast they move, and how often they react. Simulating every molecule's exact position is very expensive, so this paper builds a faster grid-based method that accounts for crowding through a free-energy term in each grid cell, without tracking each particle's position. The authors compare it with more detailed particle simulations and report that it better captures how particles are distributed and where reactions settle, as well as crowding-driven slowdown and motor-protein traffic jams.
summary.why: Crowding is known to affect biochemical reactions and transport inside cells, so a cheaper way to include it in large stochastic simulations could be useful for modeling cell biology. The text does not show how broadly the method performs beyond the cases it tests, so its wider usefulness remains to be seen.

title: A free-energy approach for stochastic reaction-drift-diffusion lattice simulations of crowded biological systems

abstract: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a critical component of the climate system. Climate models have long predicted a slowing of the AMOC due to anthropogenic forcing, with a risk of passing tipping points in the future. The question of whether the AMOC is already weakening is still somewhat controversial. Continuous monitoring is only available for the past two decades, a period too short to tease apart contributions of natural variability and climate change. Reconstructions of AMOC strength going back further in time have different limitations which are debated in the literature. Here we compile and discuss this heterogeneous body of evidence, focusing on latitudes south of 45°N where northward and southward flow are separated vertically. We conclude that the balance of multiple lines of evidence strongly supports a past and ongoing AMOC slowing in response to global warming, although some uncertainty remains regarding its magnitude and timing.
label: arXiv:2611.23429v1

summary.background:
- AMOC: a network of Atlantic ocean currents that moves warm surface water northward and cold deep water southward.
- Monitoring: direct measurements exist only for about the last two decades, which is too short to separate natural swings from long-term climate change.
- Reconstructions: indirect estimates of past circulation strength, built from proxies such as ocean properties recorded in sediments or other archives. Each has debated limitations.
- Tipping point: a threshold beyond which a system changes abruptly and may not easily recover.
- 45°N: the review focuses on latitudes south of this line, where northward and southward flows separate vertically, which makes measurement easier to interpret.
summary.one_liner: A review that compiles heterogeneous observational and reconstructed evidence, focused on latitudes south of 45°N, to assess whether the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation is already slowing under global warming.
summary.plain: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a large system of ocean currents that carries warm water north and cold water south, and it helps shape climate. This paper asks whether that system is already weakening because of human-caused warming, or whether that is still uncertain. The authors gather many different kinds of evidence, mainly from the subtropics, and conclude that together they point strongly to a slowdown, though how large and how soon remains unclear.
summary.why: Climate models have long predicted an AMOC slowdown, and a weakened circulation could have large effects on regional climate and carry a risk of tipping points. The text does not discuss specific impacts, so the wider consequences are not established by this summary alone.

title: The balance of evidence indicates a slowing AMOC

abstract: The Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP) events have been recorded for decades. However, the nature of these events remains unknown. We advocate an idea that the dark matter (DM) in form of the axion quark nuggets (AQN) made of standard model quarks (or {\it antiquarks}) and gluons could {\it simultaneously} explain many observed puzzling features which always accompany the UAP events, such as high velocity, enormous acceleration, absence of any remaining materials in affected area, etc. This long list of mysterious features also includes the absence of any sound which normally accompanies any supersonic motion. The AQN framework answers this last puzzle as well, which represents the title of the present work. The AQN dark matter model was invented long ago without any intension to apply the model to UAP events. Rather, it was invented with a single motivation to explain the observed similarity $Ω_{\rm DM}\sim Ω_{\rm visible}$ between visible and DM components, which represents a very generic feature of this framework, not sensitive to any parameters of the construction. In this work we use the same framework with the same set of parameters to study the observed UAP events. Essentially we argue that a specific class of UAP represents the close cousin of other mysteries known for decades (even centuries), such as sky-quakes, Ball Lightnings, and Mysterious Transient events. In other words, the UAPs represent different manifestations of exactly the same objects, the AQNs propagating in atmosphere. The fuel powering all these mysterious energetic events is one and the same: it is the antiquark core of the AQNs. We also present some suggestions on type of instruments required to study this specific (and well defined) type of the UAP events.
label: arXiv:2611.23373v1

summary.background:
- UAP: unidentified anomalous phenomena, reported aerial objects with no confirmed identity.
- Sonic boom: the pressure shock wave made when an object moves faster than the speed of sound.
- Dark matter: invisible matter inferred from its gravitational effects; it makes up most of the matter in the universe.
- Axion quark nugget (AQN): a hypothetical dense lump of quarks (the building blocks of protons and neutrons) and antiquarks, proposed as a dark matter form.
- Quark and antiquark: matter and antimatter forms of the same particle family; the antiquark core is said to supply the energy.
- The paper's central claim that the omega ratio of dark matter to visible matter is roughly equal is a known motivation for the model, not a result of this paper.
summary.one_liner: A speculative paper proposing that a specific class of UAP events are axion quark nugget (AQN) dark matter objects moving through the atmosphere, and that this framework explains the absence of sonic booms during supersonic UAP motion.
summary.plain: This paper tries to explain unidentified aerial phenomena (UAP, the more formal name for "UFO" sightings) by suggesting they are dark matter particles of a hypothetical type, called axion quark nuggets, passing through the air. The authors say the same model explains why these objects make no sonic boom even when moving faster than sound. The text offers this as an argument rather than a tested result.

title: Why supersonic UAP events are not accompanied by acoustic booms?

abstract: Over the past decade, cosmological observations have started to challenge the $Λ$CDM model. If these tensions persist, they immediately raise one fundamental question: what new physics could be responsible for them? More specifically, do these deviations arise from a modification of gravity, from an evolving or clustering dark energy component, or from dark matter properties beyond the cold dark matter paradigm? In this paper we show that, with current methods, any observed deviation can always be attributed to more than one sector, preventing us from determining if the tension is due to gravity, dark energy or dark matter. The main reason is that current tests rely on unobservable quantities. These quantities are then either related to observables by assuming the validity of specific equations, or compared with theoretical predictions computed within a given class of theories. Both approaches inevitably break the model independence of the tests, leading to degeneracies between gravity, dark energy, and dark matter. To overcome this limitation, we construct a set of three tests that rely only on observable quantities and that, when combined, can distinguish between the three sectors. We show that the $0i$ Einstein equation -- which is never tested in standard analyses -- adds crucial information to that provided by the gravitational slip equation and the Euler equation.
label: arXiv:2611.22498v1

summary.background:
- ΛCDM: the standard "concordance" model of cosmology, with dark energy (a constant-like term), cold dark matter, and general relativity.
- Cosmological tension: measurements from different methods or epochs that disagree with ΛCDM predictions.
- Modified gravity: changing Einstein's general relativity on cosmic scales.
- Dark energy and dark matter: the unseen components that drive cosmic expansion and clump around galaxies.
- Degeneracy: when different underlying causes produce the same observed effect, so they cannot be told apart.
- Gravitational slip: a comparison of two gravitational potentials; a nonzero value signals departure from general relativity.
- Euler equation: an equation describing how matter flows under gravity, used to track how matter moves.
- Einstein equations: the field equations of general relativity linking spacetime curvature to energy and matter; the "0i" component is one of their parts (mixing time and space directions) that is usually not used in tests.
summary.one_liner: The paper argues that current cosmological tests cannot separate modified gravity, dark energy, and dark matter explanations of deviations from ΛCDM, and proposes three tests built only on observables, including the 0i Einstein equation, to break these degeneracies.
summary.plain: Astronomers have found some measurements that do not quite fit the standard model of the universe. This paper asks whether the mismatch comes from gravity itself, from dark energy, or from dark matter, and argues that today's tests cannot tell these apart because they rely on quantities that cannot be directly observed. The authors propose three tests that use only directly observable quantities, and they say that combining them, including a rarely tested equation (the 0i Einstein equation), can distinguish the three possibilities.
summary.why: If the cosmic tensions are real, knowing which part of physics needs changing matters a great deal, so a way to separate these explanations is useful. The text describes the proposal and its motivation but does not show results from applying the tests to data, so its practical payoff is not yet demonstrated.

title: Using the 0i Einstein equation to break dark-sector degeneracies

abstract: The unresolved gamma-ray background (UGRB) provides a promising avenue for probing the cosmological annihilation of weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) dark matter through its cross-correlation with large-scale structure (LSS). While most previous studies have assumed a velocity-independent (s-wave) annihilation cross section, many well-motivated particle physics models predict annihilation rates that depend on the relative velocity of dark matter particles. In this work, we develop a generalized halo-model framework to investigate the cosmological signatures of velocity-dependent WIMP annihilation. Parameterizing the velocity-weighted annihilation cross section as $σv_{\rm rel}\propto v_{\rm rel}^{n}$, we consider four representative cases corresponding to Sommerfeld-like (n=-1), s-wave (n=0), p-wave (n=2), and d-wave (n=4) annihilation. We show that velocity dependence modifies not only the overall annihilation emission but also the halo population dominating the signal, leading to distinct effective halo biases, redshift distributions, and angular clustering properties. As a result, different annihilation mechanisms leave characteristic signatures in the UGRB-LSS cross-correlation that cannot be captured by the overall gamma-ray intensity alone. As an illustration of the formalism, we perform a statistical forecast for the cross-correlation between the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) UGRB and the Two Micron All Sky Survey Redshift Survey (2MRS) galaxy catalog and derive the projected sensitivities to the velocity-independent annihilation coefficient for these four annihilation scenarios. Our results demonstrate that cosmological cross-correlations provide a powerful and complementary probe of velocity-dependent dark matter annihilation, offering a new avenue for constraining the particle physics of dark matter through its imprints on large-scale structure.
label: arXiv:2611.22387v1

summary.background:
- WIMPs (weakly interacting massive particles): a leading hypothetical dark matter candidate that could annihilate into gamma rays.
- Annihilation cross section: a measure of how likely two dark matter particles are to destroy each other; here it is written as a power law in relative velocity, with the exponent n setting the dependence.
- s-wave (n=0): rate independent of speed; p-wave and d-wave: rate rising with speed; Sommerfeld-like (n=-1): rate enhanced at low speed.
- Unresolved gamma-ray background (UGRB): the diffuse gamma-ray glow from sources too faint to be individually resolved, such as measured by Fermi LAT.
- Cross-correlation: a statistic measuring how similar two sky maps are at matching positions, here gamma rays versus galaxies.
- Halo model: a framework that describes dark matter as clumps (halos) and computes clustering from how those halos are distributed.
- Large-scale structure: the cosmic web of galaxies and dark matter on very large scales.
summary.one_liner: A generalized halo-model forecast of how velocity-dependent WIMP dark matter annihilation (power-law in relative velocity, n = -1, 0, 2, 4) would imprint on the cross-correlation between the unresolved gamma-ray background and the 2MRS galaxy catalog.
summary.plain: Dark matter may be made of particles that sometimes destroy each other, releasing gamma rays, and how fast they collide may change how much they do so. This paper studies how such collisions, if they depend on speed, would show up in the faint gamma-ray glow from the whole sky when it is compared with the map of where galaxies sit. The authors model four cases and forecast how well a combined gamma-ray and galaxy survey comparison could constrain the annihilation rate.
summary.why: Most earlier searches assumed the annihilation rate does not depend on speed, so this work asks whether different particle physics models leave distinguishable fingerprints in large-scale structure. It is a forecast built from the text alone; the text does not report any actual measured detection, so its practical reach depends on how well the assumptions hold.

title: Probing Velocity-Dependent WIMP Dark Matter Annihilation in Large-Scale Structure

abstract: We study the local regulation of star formation efficiency (SFE) in star-forming regions of nearby galaxies using spatially resolved data from the Mapping Nearby Galaxies at Apache Point Observatory (MaNGA) and the ALMA-MaNGA QUEnching and STar formation (ALMaQUEST) surveys. We define the local SFE as $Σ_{\rm SFE} \equiv Σ_{\rm SFR}/Σ_{\rm H_2}$, where $Σ_{\rm SFR}$ is the star formation rate surface density derived from dust-corrected $\rm Hα$ emission, and $Σ_{\rm H_2}$ is the molecular hydrogen surface density derived from CO measurements. Combining these data with dynamical properties from the MaNGA DynPop project, we use random forest regression to identify the dominant factors of $Σ_{\rm SFE}$. Galactic shear, quantified by the Oort parameter $A_{\rm Oort}$, emerges as the dynamical property most strongly associated with lower SFE on average, exceeding the predictive power of mass surface density (either total or stellar), Toomre stability, and mid-plane pressure. However, these quantities provide only modest predictive power and primarily trace the radial variation of SFE. After removing the shear-related radial trends, only weak correlations remain between SFE and other local galactic properties, implying that the remaining azimuthal variations are likely governed by cloud-scale processes below our resolution limit. Furthermore, the relationship between SFE and shear varies among galaxies and weakens in gas-rich regions, suggesting that gas density may modulate the impact of shear. This behavior is consistent with competition between shear-induced cloud stabilization and shear-driven cloud-cloud collisions. Overall, galactic shear appears to regulate the large-scale radial distribution of SFE, while cloud-scale interstellar medium physics may drive the remaining variation.
label: arXiv:2611.22300v1

summary.background:
- Star formation efficiency (SFE): the fraction of molecular gas converted into stars per unit time, here measured per area.
- H-alpha emission: red light from hydrogen gas ionized by young hot stars, used as a star formation tracer (after correcting for dust).
- Molecular hydrogen traced via CO: carbon monoxide emission is the standard proxy for the H2 gas that forms stars.
- MaNGA: an optical survey that maps the light and motions of nearby galaxies spatially; DynPop is its dynamical modeling project.
- ALMaQUEST: a survey pairing MaNGA galaxies with ALMA radio observations of their molecular gas.
- Oort parameter A_Oort: a measure of differential rotation/shear in a galactic disk.
- Toomre stability: a parameter describing whether a rotating gas disk resists collapse into clumps.
- Mid-plane pressure: the pressure of gas at the disk's central plane, which affects cloud formation.
- Random forest regression: a machine-learning method that ranks which input variables best predict an outcome.
- Resolution limit: the smallest scale the data can resolve; cloud-scale processes lie below it.
summary.one_liner: Using MaNGA and ALMaQUEST data, the authors combine dynamical measurements with random forest regression to show that galactic shear (the Oort parameter A_Oort) is the dynamical property most associated with lower local star formation efficiency, mainly through its effect on radial trends, with gas density appearing to modulate that link.
summary.plain: Stars form from cold molecular gas, and this paper asks which conditions in a galaxy decide how efficiently that gas turns into stars, across small patches of nearby galaxies. The authors measured star formation from H-alpha light and molecular gas from carbon monoxide, then used a machine-learning method to rank which galaxy properties best predict the efficiency. Among the properties tested, the stretching force of galactic rotation (shear) was most associated with lower efficiency, though the predictions were only modest overall.
summary.why: It offers a measured link between large-scale galactic rotation and how well gas forms stars, which matters for models of star formation over galaxy lifetimes. The text does not show how far the result generalizes beyond the sampled galaxies, so its wider significance is uncertain.

title: The Role of Galactic Shear in Regulating Local Star Formation Efficiency: A Combined MaNGA DynPop and ALMaQUEST Study

abstract: Galaxy formation models necessitate that actively growing supermassive black holes, or quasars, strongly impact their environments. Theory suggests that quasar winds produce very hot gas bubbles that extend through the host galaxy and into the circumgalactic medium. Because this gas component is so hot and diffuse, the only way to measure its total energy is through the thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ) effect. Here we report the discovery of a dual quasar system at z=2.37 which is embedded in a bubble of hot gas as detected (at 6 $σ$) by a tSZ flux decrement at millimeter wavelengths. The total thermal energy of the hot gas is 9.7 x 10$^{60}$ erg. This energy exceeds the amount expected from all of the hot gas in a 10$^{13}$ M$_\odot$ dark matter halo by a factor of 3.6, and constitutes at least 0.6% of the quasar's lifetime energy output. We also find evidence for hot gas on larger (100-600 kpc) scales that may also originate in quasar outflows. This considerable excess energy is more than sufficient to shut off star formation and heat the intergalactic medium, implying a significant impact from quasar-driven winds on their surroundings. Such feedback plausibly explains the steep decline of the bright end of the luminosity function of galaxies across the observable Universe, and thus provides evidence to further support leading galaxy evolution theory.
label: arXiv:2611.23487v1

summary.background:
- Quasar: a supermassive black hole at a galaxy's center that is actively swallowing gas and shining very brightly.
- Feedback: energy from a black hole's winds or radiation that heats or blows away gas, which can stop a galaxy from forming new stars.
- Circumgalactic medium: diffuse gas surrounding a galaxy, out to its halo.
- Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ) effect: hot electrons in gas slightly shift the cosmic microwave background light passing through them; the size of this shift measures the gas's total thermal energy.
- Redshift z=2.37: light is stretched by cosmic expansion; this corresponds to the universe at roughly 2.8 billion years old.
- Sigma (σ): a measure of statistical confidence; 6 sigma is a strong detection.
- Luminosity function: the count of galaxies at each brightness; its bright-end decline is a key test for galaxy formation models.
- Gyr, erg, kpc, solar mass: billion years, unit of energy, thousand parsecs, and mass of the Sun.
summary.one_liner: Reports a dual quasar at z=2.37 embedded in a hot gas bubble detected at 6 sigma via a thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich flux decrement, with a total thermal energy of 9.7e60 erg, plus hints of hot gas on 100-600 kpc scales.
summary.plain: Astronomers studied a pair of very bright, rapidly feeding black holes (quasars) seen as they were about 2.8 billion years after the Big Bang. They detected a large, hot, thin cloud of gas around them by how it slightly dims millimeter-wavelength light passing through it. They estimate the gas holds more heat energy than ordinary models of a halo of this mass would predict.
summary.why: If the result holds, it suggests quasar winds can heat and push gas far beyond their host galaxies, which is one proposed reason large galaxies are rarer than simple models predict. The text itself frames this as supporting evidence for feedback theory rather than a settled proof, and the link to the galaxy luminosity function is an interpretation the authors offer.

title: Excess intergalactic heating around a dual quasar system 2.8 Gyr after the Big Bang

abstract: We present the Grain Residence-Time Method (GRTM), a computationally efficient particle-tracking approach for studying dust evolution and trapping in protoplanetary disks. By reconstructing steady-state dust distributions from particle residence times, this method provides a way to obtain radial dust surface density profiles without directly evolving the dust as a fluid. We compare the GRTM with dust profiles computed via standard methods using the $\texttt{FARGO3D}$ code, which models the dust as a pressureless fluid, and find very good agreement over a wide range of parameter space. Finally, we investigate how dust gap formation depends on the planet-to-star mass ratio ($q$) and Stokes number ($\mathrm{St}$), through a parameter study, establishing an empirical criterion for dust gap opening. In doing so, we have discovered a new regime of gap opening for small grains with $St \lesssim 10^{-2}$ and for planet mass well below Jupiter's, which is likely very relevant for gaps seen in ALMA images.
label: arXiv:2611.22913v1

summary.background:
- Protoplanetary disk: a rotating disk of gas and dust around a young star, where planets form.
- Dust gap: a ring-shaped region with little dust, often carved by a forming planet's gravity.
- ALMA: a radio telescope array that images these disks in detail.
- Stokes number (St): a measure of how strongly a dust grain is coupled to the gas; small St means small grains that move with the gas.
- Planet-to-star mass ratio (q): planet mass divided by star mass, a dimensionless size measure.
- Particle tracking vs. fluid modelling: following individual grains versus treating dust as a continuous fluid.
- FARGO3D: a widely used fluid simulation code for disks, used here as the reference.
- Residence time: how long a dust particle spends in a given region.
summary.one_liner: The paper introduces the Grain Residence-Time Method, a particle-tracking shortcut that reconstructs steady-state radial dust profiles in protoplanetary disks, validates it against FARGO3D fluid simulations, and proposes an empirical criterion for dust gap opening as a function of planet-to-star mass ratio and Stokes number.
summary.plain: The paper is about how dust is distributed in the disks of gas and dust around young stars, where planets form. The authors built a faster computer method that tracks individual dust particles and works out how long they stay at each distance from the star, and then uses that to estimate the dust density profile without simulating the dust as a fluid. They report that it agrees very well with standard fluid simulations over a wide range of settings, and they use it to study when a forming planet carves a gap in the dust.
summary.why: Gaps in dust seen in ALMA images are often linked to planets, so a cheaper way to model them and a simple rule for when they open could help interpret observations. The abstract claims a new gap-opening regime for small grains and low planet masses, which may matter for those images, but the text given does not show how strongly this is supported beyond the authors' own parameter study.

title: A novel method for dust evolution in protoplanetary disks and a new criterion for gap opening

abstract: External photoevaporation is increasingly recognised as an important influence on protoplanetary disk evolution. However, there are no established molecular line diagnostics that can reliably distinguish external irradiation from variations in intrinsic stellar and disk properties. We use a large grid of thermochemical models to predict the fluxes of 48 transitions from eight species observable with ALMA, spanning a wide range of system properties and external FUV fields of 100 to 100,000 G0. At fixed stellar and disk properties, all transitions generally brighten with increasing FUV field strength. HCO+ and CO fluxes increase monotonically in virtually all disks, whereas lower-excitation lines, particularly those of C2H and N2H+, respond weakly and non-monotonically. However, variations in stellar mass and disk size introduce substantial degeneracies, limiting the usefulness of individual line fluxes as tracers of external irradiation. We therefore assess all pairwise line flux ratios, which can significantly reduce these degeneracies, evaluating their correlation with the external field, the magnitude of their change across the FUV range, and predicted ALMA detectability. We identify 135 promising ratios, including several combining strong FUV sensitivity and high detectability with efficient single-tuning ALMA observations. The strongest diagnostics either contrast high- and low-excitation lines of the same or co-spatial species (e.g. CO J=8-7/J=1-0), probing different regions of the photoevaporative wind, or pair an FUV-sensitive wind tracer with comparatively insensitive emission arising closer to the disk (e.g. HCO+ J=3-2/C2H N=3-2). Our results provide a framework for identifying externally photoevaporating systems from spatially unresolved emission and constraining their incident FUV field strengths.
label: arXiv:2611.22952v1

summary.background:
- Protoplanetary disks: rotating disks of gas and dust around young stars, where planets may form.
- Photoevaporation: heating and blowing away disk gas by ultraviolet or X-ray light.
- External photoevaporation: the stripping is driven by UV light from nearby massive stars, not by the host star.
- FUV field (G0): far-ultraviolet light strength, measured relative to the average interstellar background (G0 = 1).
- Molecular line emission: molecules such as CO, HCO+ and C2H emit radio light at specific frequencies when they change energy level; these are the "transitions" studied.
- ALMA: a millimetre/submillimetre radio telescope array in Chile.
- Thermochemical models: simulations that combine heating, cooling and chemistry to predict what molecules emit.
- Flux ratio: dividing one line's brightness by another's, which can cancel out shared effects such as stellar mass.
summary.one_liner: Using a large grid of thermochemical disk models, this paper predicts millimetre-wavelength ALMA line fluxes under external FUV fields of 100 to 100,000 G0 and identifies 135 line-flux ratios that could help diagnose external photoevaporation in spatially unresolved protoplanetary disks.
summary.plain: Young stars are often surrounded by disks of gas and dust that can be stripped away by ultraviolet light from nearby massive stars, a process called external photoevaporation.
