This paper uses computer models to predict how the radio signals from 48 molecular transitions in these disks would change with the strength of that outside light. It finds that single line brightnesses are confused by differences in the star and disk themselves, so the authors instead propose comparing pairs of lines, of which they identify 135 that look promising.
summary.why: Knowing whether a disk is being eroded by its neighbours matters for how quickly planets can form there, and this gives observers a concrete set of line ratios to test with ALMA. The text is based on modelling only, so how well these ratios work on real observed disks remains to be shown.

title: Observational diagnostics of external photoevaporation at millimetre wavelengths

abstract: Active galactic nucleus (AGN) variability is widely recognized as a promising avenue for constraining black hole mass, yet its practical application remains limited. Although the correlation between black hole mass and variability timescale has been extensively investigated, finite observational baselines often lead to systematic underestimation of the timescale, thereby hindering reliable mass estimation for individual sources. To address this limitation, we develop the Black hole ADaptive Multi-relation Mass Estimation based on Timing analysis (BADMET), an extendable framework that provides black hole mass estimates by assimilating multiple mass-related parameters that include variability properties. We show that incorporating the variability timescale improves mass recovery in the simulated sample and enhances agreement with the reference masses in the observed sample, achieving uncertainties of $\lesssim 0.5$ dex even with a single X-ray observation.
label: arXiv:2611.22771v1

summary.background:
- Active galactic nucleus (AGN): a galaxy whose central supermassive black hole is actively feeding and emitting strongly.
- Black hole mass: usually inferred indirectly, since it cannot be weighed directly.
- Variability: changes in brightness over time; the timescale of these changes is linked to black hole size and therefore mass.
- Finite observational baseline: the total time span over which a source is observed; short spans can miss slow changes and bias timescales low.
- Dex: a logarithmic unit; an uncertainty of 0.5 dex means a factor of about 3 either way.
- X-ray observation: a single telescope pointing used to measure high-energy emission from the source.
summary.one_liner: BADMET is a multi-relation framework that estimates supermassive black hole masses in AGN by combining several mass-related parameters, including X-ray variability timescales, to correct for timescale underestimation from short observation baselines.
summary.plain: This paper is about estimating how massive the black hole at the center of an active galaxy is, using how its brightness flickers over time. The authors note that a known link between flicker speed and black hole mass tends to underestimate the timescale when observations cover only a short period. They built a flexible method, called BADMET, that combines several mass-related measurements, and report that adding the flicker timescale improves estimates in simulated and observed samples.
summary.why: Measuring black hole masses for individual galaxies is difficult, and a method that works from a single X-ray observation could make such estimates more practical. The text reports uncertainties of about 0.5 dex (a factor of roughly three), but it does not say how this compares with other methods, so its wider significance is unclear from the summary alone.

title: Black hole ADaptive Multi-relation Mass Estimation based on Timing Analysis (BADMET)

abstract: In this work, we investigate a rotating regular black hole described by the Fan-Wang solution, which arises from nonlinear electrodynamics coupled to gravity. We examine the motion of neutral test particles along circular equatorial orbits and derive the corresponding orbital parameters, including the angular velocity, specific angular momentum, and specific energy. By perturbing these orbits in the radial and vertical directions, we calculate the associated fundamental epicyclic frequencies. We then employ the relativistic precession model to interpret the observed quasiperiodic oscillations (QPOs) in terms of these frequencies. We numerically determine the radii of the innermost stable circular orbits and perform Markov chain Monte Carlo simulations to constrain the spacetime parameters. Using observational and theoretical estimates of the black hole mass and spin parameter from the literature, together with theoretically motivated priors on the Fan-Wang parameter, we obtain the best-fit parameter values. The inferred black hole mass, spin parameter, and QPO emission radii are consistent with the corresponding estimates reported in the literature. Furthermore, the dimensionless Fan-Wang parameter satisfies $l/M < 8/27 \approx 0.296$, in agreement with its theoretical upper bound.
label: arXiv:2611.22423v1

summary.background:
- Black hole spin: how fast a black hole rotates; it affects where stable orbits lie.
- Circular orbits and innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO): the closest orbit a particle can keep without spiralling in.
- Epicyclic frequencies: the rates at which a slightly disturbed orbiting particle wobbles radially and vertically.
- Quasiperiodic oscillations (QPOs): nearly regular brightness flickers in X-rays from accreting black holes.
- Relativistic precession model: a framework linking observed QPO frequencies to orbital frequencies near the black hole.
- Regular black hole: a black hole model without a central singularity, here arising from nonlinear electrodynamics (a modified theory of electromagnetic fields coupled to gravity).
- Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC): a statistical method for estimating parameter values and their uncertainties by random sampling.
- Dimensionless parameter l/M: the extra model parameter divided by the black hole mass, so it has no units.
summary.one_liner: The paper tests a rotating regular black hole (the Fan-Wang solution from nonlinear electrodynamics coupled to gravity) against quasiperiodic oscillation frequencies using the relativistic precession model and MCMC fitting, obtaining a bound l/M < 8/27 on its dimensionless parameter.
summary.plain: The paper asks whether a particular modified model of a spinning black hole can explain the rhythmic flickering in X-ray light coming from black hole systems. The authors calculate how small particles would orbit such a black hole, derive the wobble frequencies of those orbits, and compare them with observed flicker rates. Using statistical fitting, they find the model's extra parameter must be below about 0.296 (in units of the black hole's mass), which they say matches the theoretical limit.
summary.why: Observed flicker frequencies offer an indirect way to test whether black holes follow general relativity or a modified theory, so this is a concrete test of a specific alternative model. The text does not show how strongly the result favours this model over the standard black hole, so its significance should be treated as modest and specialist-facing.

title: QPO constraints on the rotating Fan-Wang spacetime

abstract: The observed ratio of Wolf-Rayet (WR) star subtypes (e.g., WC/WN) in M31 is significantly higher than the predictions of standard stellar evolution models, yet this key diagnostic discrepancy remains unresolved. This is partly due to incomplete census and the challenge of resolving individual stars in compact clusters with ground-based telescopes. In this work, we report a young cluster with WR features with the (R.A., Dec) = (00:43:39.36, +41:10:08.7), discovered with LAMOST spectra. We use the high spatial resolution of the HST imaging data to resolve the cluster members, leading to the identification of four WR star candidates, four OB stars, and one yellow supergiant. Based on the current known WR sample in M31 observed in the HST F275W filter, about one-third of WRs are contaminated by other sources within a 1. "1 $\times$ 1. "1 aperture, while this fraction can reach up to two-thirds for the LAMOST fiber size of 3. "3. Applying the approach demonstrated in this work to a larger sample of crowded regions in M31 will yield a more complete census and allow for the measurement of a definitive WC/WN ratio, corrected for contamination. Whether this refined ratio increases or decreases the current tension with models remains to be seen, but it will provide the essential observational constraint needed to advance our understanding.
label: arXiv:2611.22375v1

summary.background:
- Massive stars: very heavy, hot stars that live short lives and often end as supernovae.
- Wolf-Rayet (WR) stars: a late, evolved phase of massive stars that has lost its outer layers; WC and WN are two subtypes distinguished by their chemical signatures in the spectrum.
- OB stars: hot, blue, young massive stars; yellow supergiants are a cooler, later evolutionary stage.
- M31 (Andromeda): our nearest large neighbouring galaxy, a common target for studying stellar populations from outside the Milky Way.
- LAMOST: a Chinese wide-field spectroscopic survey telescope; its fibre aperture (3.3 arcseconds here) collects light from a wide patch, so nearby stars blend together.
- HST (Hubble Space Telescope): its sharper imaging resolves stars that ground telescopes see as one blob. F275W is an ultraviolet filter.
- Contamination: light from unrelated nearby stars that leaks into a measurement and makes a star look different than it is.
summary.one_liner: Using HST imaging to resolve individual stars in a young, LAMOST-discovered cluster in M31 that shows Wolf-Rayet features, and quantifying how much crowding contaminates Wolf-Rayet photometry at HST and LAMOST scales.
summary.plain: The paper looks at a tight group of young stars in the Andromeda galaxy that shows the spectral signature of Wolf-Rayet stars, which are very hot, stripped-down massive stars. Ground-based telescopes blur such crowded groups together, so the authors used sharper space-telescope images to pick out the individual stars. They identified four Wolf-Rayet candidates, four hot OB-type stars and one yellow supergiant in the cluster.
summary.why: The observed ratio of two Wolf-Rayet subtypes (WC/WN) in Andromeda is higher than standard stellar evolution models predict, and the authors argue that contamination from neighbouring stars in crowded regions may be part of the reason the census is incomplete. The text says the approach could eventually give a contamination-corrected WC/WN ratio, but it does not say whether that will resolve the tension with models.

title: Resolving Individual Massive Stars in an M31 Star Cluster Exhibiting Wolf-Rayet Features

abstract: Decameter-hectometric (DH) type-III bursts, produced by energetic electron beams escaping into interplanetary (IP) space, are often associated with strong soft X-ray (SXR) flares, coronal mass ejections (CMEs), and solar energetic particle events (SEPEs). With future DH missions being planned, these intense bursts could provide reliable exospace weather event diagnostics, given the lack of direct stellar IP particle and CME probes. We present a catalog of DH type-III bursts associated with 538 out of 734 $\geq$C5-class flares observed by Wind and STEREO spacecraft during 2006-2025. Independent of the SXR flare strength, the occurrence and Sun-as-a-star emission properties of DH type-III bursts distinguish confined flares, CMEs with and without strong IP shocks, and SEPEs. We find that logistic-regression models combining SXR and type-III properties provide more accurate and well-calibrated CME/SEPE occurrence probabilities than a model based only on SXR parameters. Further, a space weather event probability-estimation model based on physically meaningful, scale-free parameters derived from SXR and type-III properties outperforms an SXR parameter-only model. This result presents a way to define solar-calibrated exospace weather prediction models extendable to stellar flares with a range of energy scales but similar underlying physics. We also present a catalog of 26 shock-associated type-III (S-type-III) bursts that appear to start from cotemporal DH type-II bursts and are generally associated with fast halo CMEs and major SEPEs. Our catalogs and the scale-free model form a benchmark for exospace weather studies.
label: arXiv:2611.22606v1

summary.background:
- Type-III radio bursts: brief radio emission made by fast electron beams travelling outward from the Sun through interplanetary space.
- Decameter-hectometric (DH): the wavelength/frequency range, roughly tens to hundreds of metres in wavelength, where these bursts are seen from spacecraft.
- Soft X-ray (SXR) flares: sudden brightenings of the Sun in X-rays; C5-class is a moderate flare strength on the standard scale.
- Coronal mass ejections (CMEs): large clouds of magnetised plasma thrown out from the Sun.
- Solar energetic particle events (SEPEs): bursts of high-energy protons and electrons reaching near-Earth space.
- Shock-associated (S-type) bursts: type-III bursts that coincide with a DH type-II burst, a signature of a shock wave moving outward.
- Logistic regression: a standard statistical method that gives the probability of a yes/no outcome from several inputs.
- Sun-as-a-star: treating the Sun as if it were a distant star, observing only its integrated signal.
summary.one_liner: A catalog of 538 Sun-as-a-star decameter-hectometric type-III radio bursts linked to C5+ flares (2006–2025), plus logistic-regression and scale-free models that use these bursts with soft X-ray flare data to estimate the odds of coronal mass ejections and solar energetic particle events, and a catalog of 26 shock-associated type-III bursts.
summary.plain: Solar flares can throw out fast electron beams, which make radio bursts that travel out through space. This paper builds a large list of such radio bursts from 2006 to 2025 and asks whether they help forecast which flares will be followed by dangerous eruptions of material or high-energy particles. The authors report that combining the radio information with the X-ray strength of the flare gives more accurate and better-calibrated predictions than using X-ray data alone.
summary.why: The idea is that the same radio signatures could one day help assess space weather around other stars, where we cannot directly measure particles or eruptions. This link to stellar flares is a proposal in the text rather than something tested here, so it should be read as a possibility.

title: A comprehensive Sun-as-a-star catalog of interplanetary type-III bursts: Statistics and a framework for stellar exospace weather applications

abstract: We show that, given a sufficiently regular time-dependent density, there exists a unique potential such that the Schrödinger equation with this external potential has the prescribed one-particle density. We treat densities that are twice differentiable in time and of finite Sobolev regularity in space; the resulting potentials are continuous in time and of finite Sobolev regularity in space. Our method of proof is to rewrite the problem as a nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a loss of derivatives, which we in turn handle with a completion-of-the-square argument. This is a refinement of our recent work [Lauritsen, Lewin, and Oldenburg, arXiv:2609.08984], which handled this loss of derivatives using the Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem and treated analytic-in-space densities and potentials.
label: arXiv:2611.22942v1

summary.background:
- Schrödinger equation: the equation describing how a quantum system's wave function evolves in time.
- One-particle density: the probability distribution of where electrons are in space, a smooth "cloud" function.
- External potential: the outside force field (for example from atomic nuclei or a laser) acting on the electrons.
- Time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT): a method that uses the electron density instead of the full wave function to describe dynamics.
- Inverse problem: starting from the observed output (the density) and asking which input (the potential) produced it.
- Torus: a periodic space, like a box whose opposite edges are joined, used to simplify the mathematics.
- Sobolev regularity: a measure of how smooth a function is, counting how many derivatives are well behaved.
- Loss of derivatives: a difficulty where an equation seems to need more smoothness than it gives back, making direct solution hard.
- Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem: a classical result guaranteeing solutions for certain equations with analytic (very smooth, power-series-like) data; used in the earlier work.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves, on a torus, that a sufficiently regular time-dependent one-particle density determines a unique external potential whose Schrödinger evolution produces that density, extending earlier analytic-regularity results via a completion-of-the-square argument for a nonlinear Schrödinger equation with loss of derivatives.
summary.plain: Quantum chemists often ask a reverse question: if you know how the electron cloud of a molecule changes over time, can you work out the force field that caused it? This paper proves that, for densities that are smooth enough in time and space, such a force field (the potential) exists and is unique. The authors reach this by turning the question into a tricky nonlinear equation and handling its difficulty with a mathematical trick.
summary.why: This is the basis for time-dependent density functional theory, a widely used tool for simulating how molecules respond to light, and the reverse "inverse" problem underlies many practical methods. The text is a refinement of the authors' earlier work, so it strengthens a known foundation rather than opening a new application; its direct practical impact is not stated in the text.

title: Sobolev theory for the inverse problem of time-dependent density functional theory on the torus

abstract: We provide a unified modeling framework for thermalization and non-equilibrium spectroscopy in overdamped polar environments. This framework extends dynamical density functional theory to describe the coupled quantum-classical evolution of a molecular electronic subsystem and an overdamped polar solvent represented by a reaction-field coordinate. The nonadiabatic dynamics is formulated in terms of an operator-valued distribution obeying a quantum-classical Ehrenfest--Smoluchowski equation which exhibits nonlinear classical diffusion and non-increasing free energy, thereby retaining detailed balance. In contrast, a quantum-classical Liouville--Smoluchowski model with quantum-classical linear diffusion develops unstable long-time behavior and fails to reach a stationary thermal state. The method is applied to a two-level model of a polar dye in three different solvents: chloroform, dichloromethane, and dimethyl sulfoxide, each differing in polarity and dielectric relaxation time. Absorption and time-resolved emission spectra are obtained from dipole-dipole correlation functions, capturing the solvent-induced spectral broadening, the dynamic Stokes shift, and the time evolution of the emission bandwidth. The calculated solvent spectral response agrees well with the experimental relaxation trends of the three solvents.
label: arXiv:2611.22786v1

summary.background:
- Solvation dynamics: how a liquid's molecules reorient around a newly changed solute over time.
- Stokes shift: the gap between where a molecule absorbs and where it emits light; it grows as the solvent reorganizes.
- Overdamped solvent: a liquid whose motion is heavily damped by friction, so it relaxes slowly and smoothly rather than oscillating.
- Reaction-field coordinate: a single simplified variable summarizing the electric field the solvent exerts on the molecule.
- Density functional theory (here, dynamical): a way of tracking the probability distribution of a system's configurations over time instead of every particle.
- Ehrenfest-type mixed quantum-classical dynamics: the quantum part of the molecule is treated exactly while the solvent is treated as classical particles.
- Free energy and detailed balance: a system at equilibrium should settle down without net energy-dissipating drift; the method is designed to respect this.
- Dipole-dipole correlation functions: time-based measurements of how the molecule's electric dipole fluctuates, from which spectra are computed.
summary.one_liner: The paper extends dynamical density functional theory to a quantum-classical framework (Ehrenfest–Smoluchowski equation) for a molecule's electronic states coupled to an overdamped polar solvent described by a reaction-field coordinate, and applies it to solvation dynamics and spectra of a polar dye.
summary.plain: The paper models what happens when a light-absorbing molecule's electronic state changes while the surrounding liquid rearranges around it, a process that shows up as shifts and broadening in absorption and emission spectra. The authors build a combined quantum and classical description of the molecule and the solvent, and they compare two versions of it. The version they favor keeps the total free energy from increasing and settles into a proper thermal equilibrium, while the alternative drifts into unstable long-time behavior.
summary.why: Solvent-driven spectral shifts matter for understanding dyes, photochemistry and light-driven reactions in liquids, so a method that reproduces these trends could be useful. The text reports good agreement with experimental trends for three solvents, but only in the abstract; how general the method is beyond this two-level dye model is not shown here.

title: Quantum-classical dynamical density functional theory for solvation dynamics

abstract: Crystal Structure Prediction (CSP) is an important step in accelerating the generation and discovery of new materials. In recent years, diffusion-based CSP methods have made significant progress. However, existing models still suffer from generation bias when facing diverse materials spaces, while systematic approaches for tracing the sources of such performance variations remain limited. To address this issue, we propose LAS (Layered Analysis Strategy), a mechanism analysis framework that identifies crystal complexity and elemental composition imbalance as two key factors affecting generation difficulty and further reveals their relationships with model generation performance. Building on these findings, we further propose DSADiff (Data Structure-Aware Diffusion), a data structure-aware diffusion model that transforms the key factors identified by LAS into a unified generation difficulty representation and uses it to jointly drive feature modeling and training strategy optimization. This enables the model to adapt its representation and generation capability to samples with different data structures and difficulty levels, thereby mitigating learning bias across samples. Experiments on three CSP benchmark datasets, including Carbon-24, demonstrate that DSADiff consistently improves both Match Rate and RMSE, with a maximum Match Rate improvement of 9%, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods and achieving new state-of-the-art performance. This work deepens the understanding of diffusion-based CSP models from the perspective of generation bias and provides a new direction for designing less biased generative models for complex materials spaces.
label: arXiv:2611.22050v1

summary.background:
- Crystal structure prediction: working out the 3D arrangement of atoms in a crystal from its chemical makeup.
- Diffusion model: a generative AI method that learns to turn random noise into structured data by reversing a gradual noising process.
- Match Rate: the fraction of generated structures that match a known reference structure.
- RMSE (root-mean-square error): a measure of how far predicted atom positions are from the true ones; lower is better.
- Generation bias: systematic unevenness in how well a model performs across different data types.
- Benchmark datasets: standard test collections, such as Carbon-24, used to compare methods.
summary.one_liner: DSADiff is a diffusion model for crystal structure prediction that uses a layered analysis (LAS) to identify crystal complexity and elemental imbalance as sources of generation bias, then feeds these factors into a unified difficulty representation that guides both feature modeling and training.
summary.plain: Predicting how atoms arrange themselves in a crystal is a key step in finding new materials, and AI models that do this often work well on some kinds of materials but poorly on others. This paper looks for the reasons behind that uneven performance and finds two likely causes: how structurally complex a crystal is, and how unevenly its chemical elements are represented in the training data. The authors then build a model that takes these two factors into account so it learns more evenly across different kinds of samples.
summary.why: Reducing bias in generative models could matter for materials discovery, where models that fail on certain material types give misleading results. The text reports that the approach improves Match Rate and RMSE on three benchmarks, with a maximum Match Rate gain of 9% and claims of new state-of-the-art results; the broader significance beyond these benchmarks is not established in the text.

title: DSADiff: Data Structure-Aware Diffusion for Crystal Structure Prediction via Mitigating Complexity- and Imbalance-Induced Biases

abstract: A materials discovery campaign often begins with almost no measurements of the property it is searching for, and the models that rank candidates or screen the output of a generator then have to be built from those first few labels. Following recent work on weight-space programming, in which a language model writes the weights of a small network directly as text, we show that a general-purpose model, given the task in words, the names of the inputs and a network of 16 hidden units with every weight set to zero, can provide this starting point by filling in all of the weights from what it has learned about materials. With no labels, the networks of the strongest model rank experimental alloys at Spearman co-efficient = 0.64 to 0.79, where the best of five simple descriptors reaches 0.47 to 0.62. They rank the bulk modulus of crystals added during generative discovery loops at 0.95, where the inverse volume per atom reaches 0.89, and 35 phase-equilibrium targets computed with Thermo-Calc at a mean of 0.67, close to the 0.70 of an extrapolation from calculated binary and ternary data. As the prior mean of a Gaussian process they raise the ranking at five labels from 0.35 to 0.69 on alloys and from 0.15 to 0.95 on crystals, and they lower the regret of Bayesian optimization significantly on 4 of 5 experimental tasks and on 13 to 16 of 33 computed targets, depending on how multiple tests are corrected, without raising it significantly on any. The same networks also serve as the mean of a Bayesian neural network and as a screen for the samples of two crystal generators, where they do as well as standard models trained on 400 labeled structures. The gain is confined to the first tens of labels and to targets that no rule or sub-system extrapolation already ranks.
label: arXiv:2611.22013v1

summary.background:
- Spearman correlation: a score from -1 to 1 for how well a ranking matches the true order; higher is better.
- Weights: the adjustable numbers inside a neural network that set how it turns inputs into predictions.
- Hidden units: the intermediate computing nodes of a small network between inputs and outputs.
- Gaussian process: a statistical model that gives predictions with uncertainty and can use a prior mean as its starting guess.
- Bayesian optimization: a strategy for choosing which experiment to run next, aiming to find a good result in few tries; "regret" measures how far the chosen results fall short of the best possible.
- Bayesian neural network: a neural network that expresses uncertainty about its outputs.
- Phase-equilibrium targets: properties describing which phases of an alloy are stable at given conditions, here computed with Thermo-Calc software.
- Generative discovery loops: cycles where a model proposes new crystal structures, which are then evaluated and fed back.
- Weight-space programming: the idea, from prior work, of having a language model write network weights directly as text.
summary.one_liner: A general-purpose language model writes all the weights of a small neural network as text, using only a task description and input names, and the resulting networks serve as zero-label priors for ranking materials, Gaussian-process and Bayesian-optimization surrogates, and screening generated crystals.
summary.plain: Materials scientists often start a search with almost no measured data, so their predictive models have little to learn from. This paper asks a language model to write out the numbers (weights) of a small network from its general knowledge of materials, given only a plain-words task description and the input names. The reported result is that these written-out networks rank candidate materials reasonably well before any labels are collected, and they help as a starting point once a few labels are added.
summary.why: Early-stage materials searches are expensive and data-poor, so a useful zero-label starting model could cut wasted experiments. The paper reports gains mainly in the first few tens of labels and only for targets that simple rules or sub-system extrapolation do not already capture, so its value is narrower than the headline numbers alone suggest.

title: Weight-Space Programming for Materials Science

abstract: Unequal splay and bend elastic constants endow planar nematic liquid crystals with a director-dependent anisotropic geometry. Here, we show that this geometry is quasiconformal: the magnitude of the associated Beltrami coefficient is fixed by the elastic constants, while its phase depends on the director relative to a compatible rotating frame introducing an SO(2) spin connection. We construct explicit maps for a hybrid-aligned film and isolated defect textures, generalizing the conformal construction of isotropic defects. These results provide a new insight into the classical Dzyaloshinskii defect solutions, which are shown to define an auxiliary reference cone on which the defect texture is quasiconformally distorted before being projected conformally into physical space. Numerical simulations of constrained +2 defects reveal core morphologies consistent with the quasiconformal geometry. Our results suggest that quasiconformal maps provide a broader geometric language for anisotropy in liquid crystals and other materials.
label: arXiv:2611.22978v1

summary.background:
- Nematic liquid crystal: a fluid whose rod-like molecules tend to align along a common direction, called the director.
- Elastic constants (splay, bend): stiffness values for twisting the director pattern in different ways; unequal values make the material respond differently in different directions.
- Defect: a point where the director pattern is singular; a +2 defect is a winding of the pattern by two full turns around a point.
- Conformal map: a mapping that preserves angles locally, so small shapes are only scaled and rotated.
- Quasiconformal map: a generalization that allows bounded angular distortion; the Beltrami coefficient measures how strongly a map departs from conformal.
- SO(2) spin connection: a rule for how a local reference frame rotates from place to place, used to keep track of orientation.
- Dzyaloshinskii solution: a classical analytic solution describing a defect in a nematic.
summary.one_liner: The paper shows that planar nematic liquid crystals with unequal splay and bend elastic constants have an anisotropic geometry that is quasiconformal, with the Beltrami coefficient's magnitude fixed by the elastic constants and its phase set by the director relative to a rotating reference frame (an SO(2) spin connection), and builds explicit maps for hybrid-aligned films and defects.
summary.plain: Liquid crystals are fluids whose molecules point along a preferred direction, and the pattern of those directions can contain localized flaws called defects. This paper asks how unequal stiffness for bending versus splaying the pattern changes the underlying geometry. The authors find that this geometry can be described by quasiconformal maps, which are mappings that stretch shapes by a bounded, controlled amount, and they construct such maps for a hybrid-aligned film and for isolated defects.
summary.why: It offers a geometric language for elastic anisotropy that extends the familiar conformal (angle-preserving) treatment of isotropic defects, and it gives a new reading of the classical Dzyaloshinskii defect solutions. The text also reports simulations of constrained +2 defects whose core shapes match the predicted geometry; the broader claim that this language applies to other materials is suggested rather than demonstrated in the text.

title: Quasiconformal geometry and elastic anisotropy in liquid crystals

abstract: While polymer adsorption is theoretically well established on flat surfaces --- and somewhat understood on rough surfaces --- the common and practically relevant case of nearly flat stepped surfaces remains poorly studied. Here, we address this gap via extensive simulations of flexible polymer chains grafted at the step edge of vicinal surfaces. For wide terraces, the polymer-step interaction yields a stable step-attached (SA) phase, alongside the desorbed and terrace-adsorbed (TA) phases, all of them separated by continuous transition lines that meet at a multicritical point previously unanticipated in polymer thermodynamics. This scenario is observed for terrace widths $\mathcal{W} \gtrsim 3 R_g^{(2D)}$, being $R_g^{(2D)}$ the radius of gyration of TA polymers. Simpler phase diagrams, absent this multicriticality, are found for $\mathcal{W} \lesssim 3 R_g^{(2D)}$, where a simple crossover exists between the SA and TA phases. The presence of kinks at the steps does not alter these behaviors. Besides their theoretical relevance, these findings unveil an interesting route to produce polymer nanowires and control polymer conformation via step attachment-detachment on designed stepped surfaces.
label: arXiv:2611.22966v1

summary.background:
- Polymer: a long chain of repeated molecular units, here modeled as a flexible chain.
- Adsorption: a molecule sticking to a surface; "desorbed" means not stuck.
- Vicinal surface: a nearly flat surface with regularly spaced atomic-scale steps.
- Terrace: a flat strip between two steps; terrace width is the distance between them.
- Radius of gyration (Rg): a typical size of a coiled chain; the paper compares terrace width to the size of a chain lying flat.
- Phase diagram: a map showing which state a system is in under different conditions.
- Multicritical point: a special condition where several phase boundaries meet at once.
- Simulation: computer modeling used here instead of lab experiments.
summary.one_liner: Extensive simulations of flexible polymers grafted at step edges of vicinal (nearly flat, stepped) surfaces map out desorbed, terrace-adsorbed and step-attached phases, with a multicritical point for wide terraces and simpler phase diagrams for narrow ones.
summary.plain: This paper studies how long chain-like molecules (polymers) stick to a surface that is almost flat but has tiny steps, like a staircase with very shallow risers. The authors used computer simulations to see where the chains stay loose, lie flat on the terrace, or attach to the step edge. They report that for wide terraces these three states meet at a single special point, and for narrow terraces the picture is simpler.
summary.why: Most polymer adsorption theory assumes perfectly flat or strongly rough surfaces, while nearly flat stepped surfaces are common in practice. The text suggests the results could point to ways of making polymer nanowires and controlling chain shape by attaching and detaching chains at steps, but this is a proposal from the abstract and has not been tested in the text provided.

title: Polymer adsorption on vicinal surfaces

abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) reach an accuracy close to quantum mechanical reference calculations at a small fraction of the cost. Efficiency is the purpose of MLIPs, yet strategies for efficient MLIPs have not been reviewed systematically. This review takes efficiency as its guideline. To compare MLIPs on a common footing, we represent them in a complete basis expansion, the Atomic Cluster Expansion (ACE) and its graph generalization (GRACE). The expansion is canonical, built from products of single-particle functions. Classical interatomic potentials, such as the embedded-atom method, and many modern MLIPs, including equivariant transformers, can be represented within this expansion. Much of the apparent diversity of MLIP architectures therefore reflects how non-linearity, layer coupling and optimization are handled rather than which interactions the models can represent. We show how the cost of an MLIP becomes linear in system size and, at fixed rank of the tensor decomposition, in model complexity, and we discuss the role of machine learning, which provides non-linear parameterizations and optimization. Because efficiency is meaningful only at a given accuracy, we also compare accuracy and cost. On the Matbench Discovery leaderboard, models with three to five layers approach the accuracy of deeper models, and one basis, truncated along the Pareto front of error and speed, spans more than two orders of magnitude in cost. Ultimately, training data determine the quality of any MLIP.
label: arXiv:2611.22444v1

summary.background:
- Interatomic potential: a formula giving the energy of a group of atoms from their positions; used to run molecular simulations.
- Quantum mechanical reference calculations: expensive first-principles computations (e.g., density functional theory) that MLIPs are trained to imitate.
- Basis expansion: writing a complicated function as a weighted sum of simpler building blocks.
- Equivariant model: one whose predictions rotate consistently with the molecule's orientation.
- Embedded-atom method: a classical, hand-designed interatomic potential.
- Matbench Discovery: a public leaderboard that ranks models for predicting material stability.
- Pareto front: the set of options where you cannot improve accuracy without increasing cost, or vice versa.
summary.one_liner: A review that uses the Atomic Cluster Expansion (ACE) and its graph generalization (GRACE) as a common framework to compare the computational efficiency and accuracy of machine learning interatomic potentials, including Matbench Discovery results.
summary.plain: Machine learning interatomic potentials are fast stand-ins for quantum calculations of how atoms push and pull on each other, and this review asks which design choices make them efficient. The authors put many different models into one shared mathematical form so they can be compared on equal terms. They report that much of the variety among these models comes from how they handle non-linearity, layers, and optimization rather than from the physical interactions they can capture.
summary.why: Simulating materials at useful scales depends on how cheaply these potentials can be run, so a systematic comparison of cost against accuracy could guide which models researchers choose. The text is a review and does not show that its framing will change practice; its specific benchmark claims are limited to what the abstract states.

title: Efficient Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials

abstract: In this research, we employed a deep reinforcement learning (RL)-based molecule design platform to generate a diverse set of compounds targeting the neuraminidase (NA) of influenza A and B viruses. A total of 60291 compounds were generated, of which 86.5% displayed superior physicochemical properties compared to oseltamivir. After narrowing down the selection through computational filters, nine compounds with non-sialic acid-like structures were selected for in vitro experiments. We identified two compounds, DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 that effectively inhibited the NAs of both influenza A and B viruses (IAV and IBV), including H275Y mutant strains at low micromolar concentrations. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed a similar pattern of interaction with amino acid residues as oseltamivir. In cell-based assays, DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 inhibited IAV and IBV in a dose-dependent manner with EC50 values ranging from 0.29 uM to 2.31 uM. Furthermore, animal experiments showed that both DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 exerted antiviral activity in mice, conferring 65% and 85% protection from IAV (H1N1 pdm09), and 65% and 100% protection from IBV (Yamagata lineage), respectively. Thus, these findings demonstrate the potential of RL to generate compounds with promising antiviral properties.
label: arXiv:2611.22230v1

summary.background:
- Influenza has types A and B; neuraminidase is a viral enzyme that helps new virus particles leave infected cells. Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) is an existing drug that targets it.
- Reinforcement learning is a machine learning approach where a system improves by receiving rewards for good outputs, here for generating molecules with desirable properties.
- In vitro means in test tubes or lab dishes; in vivo means in living animals.
- EC50 is the concentration needed to reduce viral activity by half; lower means more potent. Micromolar means millionths of a mole per liter.
- H275Y is a mutation that makes some flu strains resistant to oseltamivir.
- Molecular dynamics simulations are computer models of how molecules move and bind to a target.
- The text gives no details on the AI model's architecture, the mouse study design, or comparison statistics.
summary.one_liner: A deep reinforcement learning molecule-design platform generated candidate compounds against influenza neuraminidase, and two non-sialic-acid compounds were tested in vitro, in cells, and in mice.
summary.plain: Researchers used an AI system that learns by trial and reward to invent new small molecules that might stop influenza viruses. Out of tens of thousands of generated molecules, nine were picked for lab tests, and two of them blocked the flu enzyme neuraminidase in both influenza A and B, including a drug-resistant variant. In mice, these two compounds protected a substantial share of animals from infection (65% to 100%, depending on compound and virus).
summary.why: It is an early test of whether AI-generated molecules can reach real antiviral activity in living animals, which matters for faster drug discovery. The text reports only a small number of compounds and mouse experiments, so it is too early to judge whether these compounds would work as medicines.

title: Discovery of new antiviral agents through artificial intelligence: in vitro and in vivo results

abstract: Plant ATP-binding cassette transporter C1 (ABCC1) mediates the vacuolar sequestration of heavy metal-phytochelatin (PC) complexes for cytosolic detoxification, yet the structural mechanisms of substrate recognition and metal coordination remain uncharacterized. Here, we report functional assays and single-particle cryo-EM structures of maize ABCC1 (ZmABCC1) in its apo state and bound to an PC2-As(III) complex. Functional assays demonstrate that ZmABCC1 ATPase activity is sequentially increased by glutathione, PC2, and PC3 in the presence of , supporting that longer PC chain lengths increase transport efficiency. The substrate-bound structure reveals the mode of substrate binding of the heavy metal complex, with the As(III) atom coordinated in a trigonal pyramidal geometry by three sulfur atoms from two PC2 ligands. Arg1200 plays a key role through nonpolar interaction with As(III) through its aliphatic side chain and an electrostatic interaction with the carboxyl group of PC2. These results define the molecular basis of PC-mediated heavy metal transport by plant ABCC1 which could be utilized to inform efforts to engineer crop stress resilience.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.767027 v1

summary.background:
- ABC transporters: membrane proteins that use energy from ATP to move molecules across cell membranes.
- Vacuole: a storage compartment inside plant cells where waste and toxins can be sequestered.
- Phytochelatins (PCs): short peptides that bind heavy metals; PC2 and PC3 are versions with two and three units.
- Arsenic(III): a toxic form of arsenic that binds strongly to sulfur atoms.
- ATPase activity: the rate at which a protein breaks down ATP to power transport; used here as a readout of function.
- Cryo-EM: an electron microscopy method that images frozen molecules to reconstruct their three-dimensional atomic structure.
- Apo state: the protein without any bound substrate.
- Note: the abstract text is missing the co-factor after "in the presence of", so the exact assay conditions cannot be stated.
summary.one_liner: Cryo-EM structures of maize ABCC1, a plant vacuolar transporter, in apo form and bound to a PC2-As(III) complex, with ATPase assays showing how phytochelatin chain length affects transport.
summary.plain: Plants can trap toxic heavy metals such as arsenic by binding them to small peptides called phytochelatins and then pumping the complexes into a storage compartment inside the cell. This paper uses a very high-resolution imaging method to look at the maize pump protein, ABCC1, both empty and holding an arsenic-peptide complex. The authors show where the arsenic sits and which protein residues help hold it.
summary.why: Knowing exactly how this pump grabs arsenic could help plant scientists think about engineering crops that tolerate contaminated soil, though the text itself does not test any crop. The work is a structural study, so its practical value is still speculative.

title: Cryo-EM structure of plant ABCC1 reveals mode of arsenic transport

abstract: Protein design campaigns are often run as multi-stage pipelines with a generative backbone model, an inverse-folding model, and a structure predictor chained together in that order. The stages differ by one to two orders of magnitude in cost per candidate, and the allocation of sampling effort across them is fixed before a campaign begins. Such a filter cascade can only discard candidates. It cannot redirect sampling toward the regions of design space a model stack can reach, and for targets whose constraints are far from the generative model's training distribution it may return no solution at any practical sample count. We present IMPRESS (Integrated Machine-learning for PRotein Structures at Scale), a framework in which design pipelines are stateful objects that halt, continue, resample, or branch at runtime from their own accumulated results. Adaptive decisions are evaluated asynchronously with respect to execution, so a campaign refines itself without global synchronization. We apply IMPRESS to three problems: backbone generation on discontinuous enzyme active-site motifs, de novo small molecule binder design, and PDZ binder redesign. Adaptive parameterization solves active-site motifs carried on three or more discontinuous residue islands that a fixed cascade does not solve, shifts the realized task mix toward inexpensive sequence exploration, and produces sequence ensembles that explore broadly but stay near their inputs. All comparisons reported here are between in silico metrics. We expect that adaptive parameterization will matter most for targets furthest from the training distributions of the underlying models, and that the same primitives will accommodate experimental measurement as a steering signal.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.766417 v1

summary.background:
- Protein design: inventing amino-acid sequences and 3D shapes that fold and perform a chosen function.
- Backbone: the main chain of a protein's 3D structure, generated first by a generative model.
- Inverse folding: predicting a sequence that would fold into a given backbone shape.
- Structure predictor: a model that estimates the 3D shape a sequence will fold into.
- Active-site motif: the few residues in an enzyme that do the chemistry; "discontinuous" means they are far apart in the sequence.
- Binder: a molecule or protein that attaches to a target; PDZ domains are a common protein-binding module.
- In silico: done by computer simulation or prediction, not in a physical experiment.
- HPC workflow: software that runs many compute-heavy jobs across a high-performance computing cluster, here asynchronously.
summary.one_liner: IMPRESS is a runtime framework in which chained AI protein-design pipelines (backbone generation, inverse folding, structure prediction) adaptively halt, resample, or branch based on their own results, evaluated asynchronously, and is tested on enzyme active-site motifs, small-molecule binder design, and PDZ binder redesign using in silico metrics.
summary.plain: Designing new proteins with AI usually runs a fixed chain of models, where each stage filters candidates and the effort split between stages is set in advance. This paper describes IMPRESS, a system where each design pipeline can change its own course while it runs, such as trying more of the cheap steps or branching into new searches. The authors report that this helped on some hard enzyme-site problems that the fixed chain could not solve, though all their comparisons are computer-based predictions rather than lab experiments.
summary.why: Fixed pipelines can only discard candidates and may find nothing for targets far from what the AI models were trained on, so a way to redirect effort at runtime addresses a real limitation. The claims rest on in silico metrics only, and the authors themselves expect the benefit to matter most for distant targets, which they have not shown experimentally.

title: IMPRESS: AI-coupled HPC workflows for protein design

abstract: Intestinal organoid research in drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADME-T) has focused predominantly on small intestinal enteroids, leaving colonic drug handling comparatively unexplored. Here, we established and characterized adult colonic stem cell-based three-dimensional (3D) organoid (colonoid) models as physiologically relevant New Approach Methodologies (NAMs). Donor-matched mucosal tissue, isolated primary epithelial cells, and 3D colonoids were characterized using global and targeted proteomics, fixed and live-cell microscopy, functional ADME-T assays and targeted lipidomics. This complementary analysis identified isolated primary epithelial cells as a more representative native epithelial reference than excised mucosal tissue. Suspended differentiated apical- and basal-out colonoid configurations more closely matched this reference across the assessed characteristics. Together, these two configurations provided access to both apical and basolateral epithelial surfaces, enabling functional studies of key drug transporters (P-gp, BCRP) and metabolizing enzymes (CYP3A4, UGT1A, SULT1A) in a native-like setting. Measurement of intracellular bioavailability (Fic), reflecting drug availability to intracellular targets, revealed lipophilicity-dependent microvillar absorption mechanisms. Hydrophilic compounds exploited the enlarged membrane surface provided by microvilli, whereas highly permeable lipophilic compounds seemingly entered only at the microvillus tips. Compared with HEK293 cells, an established reference model for Fic measurements, colonoids combined native-like epithelial geometry with higher phospholipid content and generally stronger intracellular drug binding, highlighting the importance of both architecture and cellular composition for studying colonic drug disposition. These colonoid models provide a physiologically relevant platform for investigating colonic ADME-T and reveal how microvillar architecture shapes intracellular drug bioavailability.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.766943 v1

summary.background:
- Organoids: small 3D clusters of cells grown in a dish from stem cells that mimic parts of an organ.
- Colonoid: an organoid grown from colon tissue.
- ADME-T: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity, the body's handling of a drug.
- Transporters (P-gp, BCRP) pump drugs in or out of cells; enzymes (CYP3A4, UGT1A, SULT1A) chemically modify drugs.
- Apical vs basal-out: whether the cells' inner-facing or outer-facing surface is exposed to the liquid around them.
- Microvilli: tiny projections on intestinal cells that greatly enlarge the absorbing surface.
- Proteomics and lipidomics: measuring the sets of proteins and fats in cells.
- HEK293: a standard, simpler human cell line used as a reference.
- Fic: intracellular bioavailability, the fraction of a drug that is free to reach targets inside cells.
summary.one_liner: Establishes adult colonic stem-cell-derived 3D organoids (colonoids) as a more native-like model for studying how drugs are absorbed, metabolised and transported in the large intestine, and links microvillar surface architecture to intracellular drug availability.
summary.plain: Drug researchers have mostly studied how medicines pass through the small intestine using lab-grown mini-organs, and the large intestine (colon) has received much less attention. This paper grows colon mini-organs from adult stem cells and compares them with real colon tissue and with cells taken directly from it. The authors report that the cells taken from tissue were a better reference than the tissue itself, and that certain mini-organ setups matched that reference most closely.
summary.why: Colon drug handling matters for oral medicines and for predicting how drugs behave in the body, and better lab models could make such predictions more reliable. The finding that the shape of the cell surface (microvilli, the tiny finger-like projections) affects how drugs enter cells may be relevant to drug design, though the text alone does not show how far this extends to patients.

title: Native-like 3D colonoids reveal mechanisms of colonic drug disposition

abstract: Published pharmacological knowledge is distributed across heterogeneous scientific literature, databases, and computational models, making systematic reuse, comparison, and reproducibility difficult. We present Pharmacolibrary v26.11, a source-traceable resource that connects pharmacokinetic (PK), pharmacodynamic (PD), and pharmacogenomic (PGx) knowledge with executable models, simulations, and interactive visualizations. A multi-agent workflow combines LLM-assisted literature retrieval and extraction with deterministic validation, ontology mapping, provenance tracking, automated model generation, and rule-based review. The system transforms published evidence and extracted parameters into executable models across Modelica, FMI, SBML, MATLAB, and CellML and provides browser-based simulations for research and education. Preliminary evaluation indicates that decomposing literature extraction into multiple stages improves parameter recovery compared with single-pass extraction and that locally deployed open-weight models can provide performance that is at least comparable with frontier commercial LLMs. Pharmacolibrary provides a foundation for scalable, auditable curation of pharmacological knowledge and for connecting published evidence to reusable computational models across research, simulation, and education.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.766960 v1

summary.background:
- Pharmacokinetics (PK): what the body does to a drug, such as absorption, distribution and clearance.
- Pharmacodynamics (PD): what the drug does to the body, such as its effect on a target.
- Pharmacogenomics (PGx): how a person's genes change their response to drugs.
- Executable model: a mathematical model written in software code that can be run to simulate outcomes.
- Standard formats (Modelica, FMI, SBML, CellML, MATLAB): shared file types that let models be exchanged between tools.
- Large language model (LLM): an AI system that reads and generates text; here used to extract numbers from papers.
- Open-weight model: an AI model whose trained parameters are publicly released, so it can be run locally.
- Provenance tracking: recording where each piece of data came from.
summary.one_liner: Pharmacolibrary v26.11 is a source-traceable resource that uses a multi-agent LLM-plus-validation workflow to turn published pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic and pharmacogenomic evidence into executable models in several standard modelling formats.
summary.plain: Knowledge about how drugs move through and act on the body is scattered across journal papers, databases and existing computer models, which makes it hard to reuse or check. This paper describes a system that uses AI language models to pull drug parameters out of the published literature, checks them with fixed rules, records where each value came from, and turns them into runnable simulation models with browser-based demos. The authors report only preliminary tests, which suggested that splitting extraction into several steps worked better than a single pass, and that locally run open-source models performed at least comparably to leading commercial AI models.
summary.why: Automated, auditable curation of drug data could make pharmacological models easier to reuse, compare and reproduce across research, simulation and teaching. The evaluation is described only as preliminary, so the reliability of the extracted parameters at scale is not yet established by the text.

title: Pharmacolibrary: Interoperable executable models for PK, PD and PGx derived from published evidence

abstract: The ability for a subset of cells to establish a heterogeneous cell population with multi-lineage competency is crucial for the self-renewal capacity of tissues and organs. Restoration of heterogeneous gene expression patterns has been observed in pluripotent and multi-potent stem cells, and the heterogeneity restoration can influence the potential of differentiation into multiple cell types. Similarly, cancer cells can acquire the capacity to establish non-genetic heterogeneity that plays a role in cancer progression and resistance to therapeutics. Specific models of gene regulatory networks have been proposed to explain heterogeneity restoration. However, due to the lack of systematic analysis, it is unclear which network topologies are more efficient for this multicellular function, and what intrinsic and extrinsic factors can determine the optimal choice of network topology. In this work, we use mathematical models describing gene expression of single cells and their underlying population dynamics to examine the influence of network topology on the recovery of multimodal expression patterns originating from a homogeneous population. We found that feedback loops are a key factor contributing to heterogeneity restoration. Negative and positive feedback loops support the existence of heterogeneity restoration, but only positive feedback can accelerate the process with low cost of single-cell-level variations of expression. Furthermore, networks with mixed feedback were the most robust ones for heterogeneity restoration with respect to changes in both kinetic rate constants and noise levels. Using experimentally validated network databases, we showed that genes involved in feedback loops are enriched with functions related to cell fate decisions, and we identified examples of realistic gene regulatory networks cell fate dynamics. Our results suggest multiple potential evolutionary paths towards gene circuits governing heterogeneity restoration and key factors contributing to the dynamics of this process. We expect that this systematic study will enable future discoveries of new gene regulatory networks governing progenitor and cancer cell dynamics as well as therapeutic strategies targeting heterogeneity-enabling circuits.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.767011 v1

summary.background:
- Gene regulatory network: a set of genes whose activity switches one another on or off, like a wiring diagram.
- Feedback loop: a gene's output loops back to affect its own activity. Positive feedback tends to reinforce a state; negative feedback tends to hold it steady or oscillate.
- Heterogeneity: cells in one population differ from each other in gene activity, even when genetically identical.
- Multimodal expression: when measured across many cells, gene activity clusters into several distinct groups or peaks.
- Stochastic noise: random fluctuations in gene activity inside individual cells.
- Self-renewal: a population's ability to maintain itself while still producing varied cell types.
summary.one_liner: A systematic mathematical study of how gene regulatory network topology, especially feedback loops, can restore a multimodal (heterogeneous) gene expression pattern in a population that started out homogeneous, with implications for stem and cancer cell dynamics.
summary.plain: Cells in a tissue or a tumor often end up with a mix of different gene activity states, even when they began as identical copies. This paper uses computer models of gene activity in single cells and of how populations of cells grow and change to ask which wiring patterns of genes can rebuild that mix from a uniform starting group. The authors report that feedback loops are a key ingredient, and that networks with both positive and negative feedback were the most robust to changes in rates and noise.
summary.why: Keeping a mix of cell types is part of how stem cells maintain tissues and how tumors resist treatment, so knowing which gene circuit designs can rebuild that mix may point to new targets. The text is a modeling study and does not test these predictions experimentally, so its relevance to real cells is still an open question.

title: Gene network topologies for heterogeneity restoration during self-renewal

abstract: Missense variants in the KCNQ family of voltage-gated potassium channel genes are associated with a broad spectrum of neurological and cardiac disorders for which computational tools capable of differentiating benign and pathogenic variants are essential. Here, we present, to our knowledge, the first application of quantum machine learning (QML) to missense pathogenicity prediction. We employ a hybrid quantum framework combining data re-uploading quantum neural networks with quantum support vector machines and applied it to pathogenicity classification across the full KCNQ gene family. Systematic exploration of circuit architectures revealed that optimal hyperparameter choices enable the proposed quantum model to achieve predictive performance superior to or comparable to state-of-the-art classical machine learning approaches, reaching AUC-ROC values of approximately 0.94 across the full dataset. Although no clear quantum advantage is observed at present, these results demonstrate that quantum feature representations can effectively capture biologically relevant patterns in variant data and establish QML as a viable framework for future applications in computational genomics and precision medicine.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.767028 v1

summary.background:
- Missense variant: a single-letter change in DNA that swaps one amino acid for another in a protein; it may be harmless or disease-causing.
- KCNQ genes: a family of genes that build voltage-gated potassium channels, which help control electrical signaling in nerves and heart muscle.
- Pathogenicity prediction: using computer models trained on labeled examples to estimate whether a variant causes disease.
- Machine learning classifier: a model that learns from labeled data to sort new cases into categories.
- Quantum machine learning: using quantum circuits as part of a learning model; current hardware is small and noisy, so these are often simulated or hybrid with classical computing.
- AUC-ROC: a score from 0 to 1 summarizing how well a classifier ranks positive cases above negative ones; higher is better, 0.5 is chance.
- Quantum advantage: a clear, demonstrated benefit of a quantum method over the best classical ones; the paper says this was not observed.
summary.one_liner: A hybrid quantum machine learning model (data re-uploading quantum neural networks combined with quantum support vector machines) is applied to classifying missense variants as benign or pathogenic across the KCNQ potassium channel gene family, reporting AUC-ROC around 0.94 but no clear quantum advantage over classical methods.
summary.plain: The paper asks whether quantum computing methods can help tell harmless genetic typos from harmful ones in a family of genes that code for potassium channels, which are involved in brain and heart disorders. The authors tested a hybrid quantum-classical model and tuned its circuit design, reporting performance around 0.94 on a common accuracy score that they describe as comparable to or better than standard classical methods. They also state plainly that no clear quantum advantage was observed.
summary.why: Accurate prediction of which variants in these genes are harmful matters for diagnosing neurological and cardiac disease, so the tools are of practical interest. The work is a early exploratory test of quantum machine learning on this task; its value lies mainly in showing the approach is workable, not in a demonstrated improvement over existing tools.

title: Quantum Machine Learning for Missense Variant Pathogenicity Prediction in the KCNQ Gene Family

abstract: Humans often seek information without direct external reward. Theories distinguish two major dimensions of this intrinsic motivation: wanting, the desire to resolve an information gap, and liking, the enjoyment of the information itself. However, how these motivational dimensions shape self-guided information-seeking behavior, neural activity, and memory formation in realworld contexts remains underexplored. To address this gap, we developed a naturalistic fMRI paradigm in which participants freely browsed the internet, subsequently recalled their browsing experiences, and retrospectively reported their moment-to-moment wanting and liking. We found that both dimensions predicted more stable browsing trajectories but engaged partially dissociable neural systems: wanting recruited regions supporting goal-directed cognition, whereas liking engaged affective regions. Wanting and liking also interacted to predict memory, with wanting predicting recall primarily when liking was low. Compared with active browsing, passive viewing of the same web content reduced wanting and liking and diminished their dissociation, yet both continued to predict memory and intersubject neural similarity in the default mode network. These findings show that naturally fluctuating wanting and liking guide how we seek and remember information through overlapping yet distinct neurocognitive mechanisms.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.12.765917 v1

summary.background:
- fMRI: a brain scanner that tracks blood flow as a proxy for neural activity, so it shows which regions are active, not direct signals.
- Intrinsic motivation: doing something for its own sake, not for an external reward.
- Wanting vs. liking: two proposed dimensions of motivation, the drive to close an information gap versus the pleasure of the content itself.
- Intersubject neural similarity: how similar brain activity is across different people watching the same material; a sign of shared processing.
- Default mode network: a set of brain regions often active during internal thought and not focused on an external task.
- Retrospective ratings: participants reported their feelings after the fact, which can be affected by memory.
summary.one_liner: An fMRI study of free internet browsing that separates self-reported "wanting" (wanting to resolve an information gap) from "liking" (enjoying the information), and links each to browsing stability, brain activity, and later recall, compared with passive viewing of the same content.
summary.plain: People often look things up or read online without any outside reward, simply because they are curious. This study put volunteers in a brain scanner while they browsed the internet freely, then asked them to recall what they had looked at and rate, moment by moment, how much they wanted the information and how much they enjoyed it. The authors report that both ratings tracked steadier browsing and different brain systems, and that wanting helped memory mainly when enjoyment was low.
summary.why: It moves the study of curiosity from simple lab tasks toward self-directed behaviour in a realistic setting, which may matter for understanding learning and attention online. The text does not show how far the findings generalise beyond this sample and setup, so their broader significance is still uncertain.

title: Neurocognitive signatures of intrinsic motivation in naturalistic information seeking and memory

abstract: Adaptive behavior requires learning where relevant information can likely be found, but also where distraction is likely to occur. For such learning to be useful in everyday life, it must generalize across changing viewpoints as observers move through the environment. Recent work suggests a striking asymmetry in this regard: whereas target-location learning can be grounded in world-centered coordinates, distractor-location learning appears tied to the observer's current viewpoint. One possibility is that allocentric distractor-location learning requires stronger contextual support than allocentric target-location learning. Alternatively, distractor suppression may be fundamentally constrained by viewer-centered spatial coding. To distinguish between these possibilities, participants performed an additional-singleton search task displayed on a tabletop and continuously changed their standing position around the table, while the high-probability distractor location remained fixed in the external environment. Unlike previous studies using this paradigm, contextual anchors were embedded directly within the search display, allowing distractor locations to be encoded relative to a stable task-relevant allocentric structure. In a second experiment, participants were additionally explicitly informed about the distractor-location regularity. Despite task-relevant contextual structure and explicit knowledge, distractor-location learning failed to emerge in world-centered coordinates. Together with previous findings showing robust egocentric distractor-location learning using the same set-up, these findings strengthen the view that learned distractor suppression relies primarily on viewer-centered spatial coding, potentially reflecting a process linked to viewpoint-specific action selection.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.767044 v1

summary.background:
- Additional-singleton search task: finding a target among items where one item is a salient, task-irrelevant distractor.
- Statistical learning of distractor locations: attention can become biased away from a spot where distractors often appear, without awareness.
- Egocentric (viewer-centered) coding: locations described relative to the observer's current position or view.
- Allocentric (world-centered) coding: locations described relative to the external environment, independent of the observer's view.
- Prior work found target locations can be learned in world-centered coordinates, but distractor locations seem tied to the viewpoint.
- Contextual anchors: stable landmarks that help define a spatial layout.
- Explicit knowledge: the participant is told about the regularity, as opposed to learning it implicitly.
summary.one_liner: Across two experiments in a tabletop additional-singleton search task where observers moved around the table, learned suppression of a high-probability distractor failed to follow the fixed external location even with embedded contextual anchors and explicit instruction, supporting viewer-centered spatial coding for distractor learning.
summary.plain: The study asks whether people can learn where a distracting item is likely to appear in a way that stays correct as they walk around a table. Participants searched a display on a table while changing their standing position, and the distractor stayed in a fixed spot in the room. The authors report that people did not learn the distractor's room-based location, even when landmarks were built into the display and participants were told about the pattern.
summary.why: It suggests that ignoring distractions may be tied to the viewpoint a person is currently in, which is a useful constraint for theories of attention and spatial memory. The text does not show how far these findings extend beyond this set-up, so the broader implications remain uncertain.

title: No allocentric distractor-location learning following self-movement even with contextual anchors and explicit knowledge

abstract: Motivated by issues of the maintenance of genetic variation in a highly endangered species, we continue earlier studies into the population genetics ancestry and descent of genome segments. In this paper, we focus on the survival and descent of genome in a population pedigree of a diploid dioecious species. We consider a population potentially being maintained from a small founder base, taking the canonical example a random-mating population of 100 males and 100 females. We show how previous methods to examine the ancestry of a single genome in such a population can also be used to account the survival genetic lengths and number of descendant copies of founder genome segments, and explore the variance of these measures. We show the variance of the population distribution over realizations within a pedigree is scarcely smaller then the variance over pedigrees: variation is in meiosis rather than in pedigree. While all founders continue to lose genome over time, the very first generations are critical to determining the amount of surviving genome. Dependence among founders is slight, except for between the two genomes of a founder: however when monogamy is enforced this high dependence extends to founder mates. We briefly consider extensions of population size (both smaller and larger), of mating structure, and of variance in offspring number, including variance in male reproductive success.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.14.766719 v1

summary.background:
- Diploid: organisms carry two copies of each chromosome, one from each parent.
- Dioecious: species with separate males and females.
- Founders: the original individuals whose genomes enter a population.
- Pedigree: a family tree showing who descends from whom.
- Meiosis: cell division that makes eggs and sperm, shuffling and splitting parental DNA.
- Identity by descent: sharing a segment because both copies trace back to one ancestor.
- Variance: how much a quantity fluctuates across repeated outcomes.
summary.one_liner: A population-genetics study of how much of each founder's genome survives, and how many descendant copies it leaves, in a pedigree of a diploid dioecious population started from a small founder group, with variance and dependence among founders analysed.
summary.plain: This paper asks what happens to the DNA that a small group of founding animals passes into a population over many generations: how much of their genome segments survive, and how many copies end up in living descendants. The authors use a model of a random-mating population, such as 100 males and 100 females, and build on earlier methods for tracing the ancestry of a single genome. They report that the amount of surviving genome varies about as much from meiosis (the random shuffling when eggs and sperm form) as it does between different pedigrees, and that the first few generations matter most.
summary.why: The work is motivated by keeping genetic variation in a highly endangered species, where a small founder group may be all that remains, so it bears on how much diversity a managed population can hold. The text does not describe any applied conservation outcome, so its practical reach beyond the modelling is uncertain.

title: Genome survival and descent in population pedigrees

abstract: Across dog breeds, the inverse correlation between body size and lifespan is well documented, but its genetic basis remains poorly understood, in part because size and lifespan are confounded at the breed level. Here, we assembled the Cani-DNA discovery cohort of 540 dogs from 27 breeds, with 20 dogs per breed, genotyped by low-pass whole-genome sequencing and imputation. We performed genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of breed-average body weight, breed-median lifespan and individual age at death, and tested the age-at-death loci for replication in the GRLS replication cohort of 3,024 Golden Retrievers. The GWAS of breed-average body weight recovered established body-size loci, confirming that the cohort could detect known associations. Of the 69 breed-weight loci, 30 were shared with breed-median lifespan, and at all of them the allele increasing body weight was associated with shorter lifespan. At the individual level, age at death, with breed-average body weight as a covariate, identified loci distinct from all breed-level loci. Three of them, the CDH4, TSHZ3 and TSC22D2 loci, replicated in the GRLS replication cohort. In humans, CDH4 and TSHZ3 have been implicated in longevity, and the region orthologous to the TSC22D2 locus has been associated with markers of biological ageing. Together, these results identify genetic variation associated with the lifespan of individual dogs beyond breed body size, and support the dog as a model in which genetic leads on ageing can be identified.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.766459 v1

summary.background:
- Genome-wide association study (GWAS): a scan of DNA across many individuals to find small genetic variants that statistically track with a trait.
- Breed-level versus individual-level analysis: breed averages (weight, median lifespan) describe whole groups, while age at death describes each dog; the two can be confounded.
- Low-pass sequencing and imputation: a cheap, partial genome read that is filled in statistically using reference data.
- Replication cohort: a separate group used to check whether findings hold up.
- Orthologous region: the stretch of DNA in another species that corresponds to the same gene region.
- Loci: specific locations in the genome where variants are found.
summary.one_liner: A genome-wide association study in 540 dogs from 27 breeds, with replication in 3,024 Golden Retrievers, separates genetic lifespan signals from breed body size and flags three candidate loci (CDH4, TSHZ3, TSC22D2) linked to individual lifespan.
summary.plain: Bigger dog breeds tend to die younger, but it has been unclear which genes cause this, partly because size and lifespan move together across breeds. The authors sampled 20 dogs from each of 27 breeds, scanned their genomes for DNA variants linked to body weight and age at death, and then checked promising hits in a much larger group of Golden Retrievers. They report three genetic regions linked to how long individual dogs live, beyond what body size alone explains.
