summary.why: Dogs have large, well-recorded differences in size and lifespan, so they offer a useful route to finding genetic leads on ageing. Two of the three candidate genes, CDH4 and TSHZ3, have been linked to longevity in humans, and the third region has been associated with markers of biological ageing; these connections are suggestive, and the text does not show that the dog genes act the same way in people.

title: Deciphering the genetic bases of canine longevity

abstract: Endogenous single-strand DNA breaks (SSBs) that arise during active DNA demethylation, regulate neurodevelopmental gene expression. Thymine (TDG) and alkyladenine (AAG) DNA glycosylases recognize oxidized methylcytosines. While TDG is required for excision, role of AAG in active demethylation and neurodevelopment remains unknown. Using mouse neurospheres, hippocampus, and human induced neurons (iNs), we show that AAG is needed for neurogenesis. Loss of AAG contributes to delayed neurodevelopmental and premature synaptic gene expression, evident from single-cell RNA sequencing of differentiating iNs. Synaptic gene expression is co-regulated by both AAG and TDG, with loss of single glycosylase inducing an opposing effect, implying competition. Single-molecule and biochemical assays directly demonstrate this competition, with AAG inhibiting TDG on 5fC. Without AAG, TDG has higher affinity, resulting in reduced global 5fC and increased SSB intermediates. In summary, AAG substrate competition plays an important role in fine tuning active demethylation, thereby regulating gene expression and DNA breaks during neurogenesis.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.766739 v1

summary.background:
- DNA methylation: a chemical tag on DNA (mainly on cytosine) that usually silences genes.
- Active demethylation: removing these tags through oxidized forms (such as 5fC) and repair enzymes, not just by passive dilution.
- DNA glycosylases (TDG, AAG): enzymes that cut out damaged or modified bases as the first step of repair.
- Single-strand break (SSB): a nick in one strand of the DNA backbone, which can be an intermediate of demethylation.
- Neurospheres and induced neurons (iNs): lab-grown clusters of neural cells and neurons made from other cells, used as models of brain development.
- Single-cell RNA sequencing: measuring which genes are active in individual cells.
summary.one_liner: Mouse and human neuronal models show that the glycosylase AAG competes with TDG for oxidized methylcytosine substrates (notably 5fC), and this competition tunes active DNA demethylation, single-strand break formation, and neurodevelopmental gene expression.
summary.plain: Cells sometimes remove chemical tags from their DNA to switch genes on or off, and this process briefly leaves small cuts in the DNA strand. This paper asks whether a second repair enzyme, AAG, takes part in that process during brain cell development, alongside the enzyme TDG. The authors found that losing AAG disturbed the timing of neuron-related gene activity in developing mouse and human neurons, and that AAG and TDG compete for the same DNA targets.
summary.why: It suggests that the balance between two DNA-repair enzymes, rather than one enzyme alone, can set how finely genes are timed during neurodevelopment. The text does not link these findings to any disease, so any clinical relevance is unclear from this work alone.

title: Alkyladenine DNA glycosylase regulates TDG-mediated demethylation and neuronal gene expression by competitive substrate binding

abstract: Functional characterization of cis-regulatory elements (CREs) is essential for understanding developmental gene regulation and interpreting human noncoding variation. However, conventional transgenesis assays are limited by integration copy number variability and genomic position effects, while species-specific developmental differences constrain the study of human regulatory sequences in classical model organisms, demanding assays based on human-specific contexts. Here, we developed RepoV, a transgenesis vector enabling single-copy integration of enhancer reporter constructs in the genome of human iPS cells through PhiC31-mediated recombination. Transgenic iPSCs were subsequently used to assess candidate neurodevelopmental enhancers in neural organoids. RepoV recapitulated the expected activity of previously characterized regulatory elements and enabled the evaluation of candidate sequences associated with the neurodevelopmental genes POU3F2 and FOXG1. Notably, two FOXG1 enhancers displayed different activities in zebrafish larvae and human neural organoids. The organoid results were more consistent with endogenous the FOXG1 expression and the pathological phenotypes associated with disease-related regulatory variants identified in patients. Together, these findings establish RepoV transgenesis combined with human organoid cultures as a valuable platform for the functional evaluation of human developmental regulatory sequences.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.766570 v1

summary.background:
- Enhancer: a DNA segment that controls when and where a nearby gene is turned on.
- Cis-regulatory element (CRE): a DNA sequence that regulates genes on the same chromosome; enhancers are one type.
- Transgenesis: inserting an extra piece of engineered DNA into an organism or cell to study it.
- Reporter construct: a DNA piece that makes a visible signal (such as a fluorescent protein) when the enhancer under test is active.
- Copy number and position effects: random insertions can differ in how many copies they add and where they land, which can distort results.
- PhiC31 recombinase: an enzyme that inserts DNA at a defined site in the genome, allowing controlled single-copy insertion.
- iPS cells: adult cells reprogrammed into stem cells that can become many cell types.
- Organoid: a small 3D tissue culture grown from stem cells, here modeling parts of the developing brain.
- FOXG1 and POU3F2: transcription factor genes important in brain development.
summary.one_liner: The paper introduces RepoV, a PhiC31-mediated transgenesis vector that places single-copy enhancer reporters into human iPS cells, which are then used to test candidate neurodevelopmental enhancers (including POU3F2 and FOXG1 elements) in neural organoids.
summary.plain: Genes are switched on and off by short stretches of DNA called enhancers, and many disease-linked changes in human DNA sit in these regions. This paper describes a way to test such stretches in human stem cells that are grown into small brain-like tissue clumps (organoids), rather than only in mice or zebrafish. The authors report that the method reproduced the activity of enhancers already known to work, and that two FOXG1 enhancers behaved differently in zebrafish than in human organoids, with the organoid results matching the gene's real expression pattern and patient-linked findings.
summary.why: Many human genetic variants found in patients fall outside genes, and it is hard to tell whether they matter. A human-cell test that controls for how many copies of a construct are inserted and where it lands could make such tests more reliable. The text does not report the size of the study or statistical strength, so its general usefulness remains to be seen in wider testing.

title: ORGANOID- BASED ASSESSMENT OF ENHANCER ACTIVITY VIA RECOMBINATION-MEDIATED TRANGENESIS

abstract: Rabies remains a major public-health challenge, with pre-exposure vaccination strategies constrained by the need for multiple doses and repeated healthcare visits. Here we describe YF-RabG, a live-attenuated rabies vaccine candidate based on the yellow fever 17D (YF17D) vaccine backbone that stably expresses the rabies virus glycoprotein (RabG). YF-RabG exhibited an attenuated phenotype and favourable safety profile compared with parental YF17D across several preclinical models, including neonatal and immunocompromised mice. A single immunization induced robust humoral and cell-mediated immune responses in non-human primates. Rabies virus-neutralizing antibody titres readily exceeded the widely accepted correlate of protection in mice, hamsters and non-human primates by several orders. Accordingly, vaccination conferred protection against lethal rabies challenge in a range of stringent mouse models, maintained seroprotective antibody levels for at least one year, and increased following a boost using a licensed rabies vaccine. Furthermore, the YF17D vector was readily adapted to accommodate glycoproteins from distant lyssaviruses, generating protective vaccine candidates against Mokola, Lagos bat and Lleida bat lyssaviruses. Collectively, these findings identify YF-RabG as a promising single-dose rabies vaccine candidate and highlight the versatility of the YF17D platform for lyssavirus vaccine development.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.766779 v1

summary.background:
- Rabies is a viral disease that is almost always fatal once symptoms start; vaccination after exposure or before it is the main protection.
- Live-attenuated vaccine: a weakened but still replicating virus that triggers a strong immune response without causing disease.
- YF17D: a long-used, weakened yellow fever vaccine virus, here used as a carrier ("vector") for a rabies gene.
- Glycoprotein (RabG): the rabies virus surface protein that the immune system targets.
- Neutralizing antibodies: immune proteins that block a virus from infecting cells; their level is used as a benchmark ("correlate") of protection.
- Lyssaviruses: a genus of viruses related to rabies, including Mokola and Lagos bat viruses.
- Non-human primates, mice and hamsters: animal models used before human testing.
summary.one_liner: Preclinical study of YF-RabG, a live-attenuated yellow fever 17D vaccine vector expressing the rabies glycoprotein, reporting neutralizing antibody responses, protection in mouse challenge models, durability to one year, and adaptation to other lyssaviruses.
summary.plain: Rabies is a deadly virus, and the usual preventive shots need several doses and repeated clinic visits. This study tests a possible single-dose rabies vaccine built on a weakened yellow fever virus that carries a rabies surface protein. In animal experiments, one dose produced strong immune responses, and the authors report that it protected mice against lethal rabies and kept protective antibody levels for at least a year.
summary.why: A single-dose rabies vaccine would be useful where repeated visits are hard, and the paper also suggests the same platform could be adapted to related lyssaviruses. Whether this holds in people is not shown here; the work is in animals and would need clinical trials.

title: Seroprotection and improved polyfunctional immunity conferred by a YF17D-vectored rabies vaccine

abstract: The cellular composition and spatial organization of immune responses within tuberculosis (TB) granulomas have been increasingly characterized, yet how these spatially organized immune cell populations coordinate local adaptive immunity remains largely unknown. Here, we integrated single-cell multi-omics, spatial transcriptomics, and immune receptor profiling to construct a comprehensive spatial atlas of human TB granulomas. We identified two concentric adaptive immune niches surrounding the central necrotic core. The outer niche comprised granuloma-associated tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) that supported TFH-B cell interactions and exhibited functional germinal center-like features associated with antigen-driven B-cell maturation toward FCRL5 antibody-producing cells. The inner niche contained antigen-experienced and Mtb-reactive effector memory CD8 T cells (TEM), which were recruited from distal lung regions by LGALS9high chemokine-expressing macrophages and activated to undergo local clonal expansion. In lgals9l1 deficient zebrafish, macrophage depletion was accompanied by marked reductions in T- and B-cell enrichment within granulomas and increased bacterial loads, supporting a role for LGALS9high macrophages in coordinating local adaptive immunity against TB infection. Finally, AI-based prediction of spatial gene expression from clinical hematoxylin and eosin-stained specimens revealed that inferred TLS abundance increased with TB disease severity. These findings identify spatially interconnected adaptive immune niches that organize protective immune responses within human TB granulomas, therefore providing a foundation for understanding granuloma adaptive immunity and developing host-directed therapies and vaccines for TB (https://tbomics.smart-nbc.org.cn/).
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.766905 v1

summary.background:
- Granuloma: a organized ball of immune cells that forms around TB bacteria; its centre can become dead tissue (necrotic core).
- Tertiary lymphoid structure (TLS): a lymph-node-like cluster that forms in inflamed tissue, where B cells and helper T cells interact.
- Germinal center-like features: signs of B cells maturing and improving their antibodies, here linked to FCRL5-expressing antibody-producing cells.
- CD8 T cells: killer T cells; effector memory (TEM) cells are experienced cells ready to act quickly.
- Single-cell multi-omics and spatial transcriptomics: methods that measure genes in individual cells and record where in the tissue they sit.
- LGALS9: a signalling protein (galectin-9) that macrophages produce here in high amounts.
- Zebrafish: a small fish model used to study mycobacterial infection, with an lgals9 gene variant used to test the macrophage role.
- H&E staining: the standard coloured stain on pathology slides; AI here predicts gene activity from these images.
summary.one_liner: Single-cell multi-omics, spatial transcriptomics and immune receptor profiling of human tuberculosis granulomas identify two concentric adaptive immune niches (a tertiary lymphoid outer layer and a CD8 effector-memory T cell inner layer) organized by LGALS9-high macrophages, with supporting zebrafish experiments and an AI-based link to disease severity.
summary.plain: Tuberculosis forms small clusters of immune tissue called granulomas that wall off the infection. This paper maps how immune cells are arranged inside human granulomas and finds two rings around a dead central core: an outer ring that looks like a mini lymph node where B cells mature, and an inner ring of memory T cells that appear to be drawn in and expanded locally by a particular type of macrophage. Experiments in zebrafish suggest these macrophages help bring in T and B cells and limit bacterial growth.
summary.why: Granulomas are where the body fights TB, so knowing how immune cells are arranged there may help guide host-directed treatments and vaccines. The finding that predicted lymph-node-like structures rise with disease severity, inferred from routine tissue slides, could in principle be useful for clinical assessment, but the text does not show that this has been tested as a diagnostic.

title: Spatially-Organized Adaptive Immune Niches in Granulomas Dictate Local Defense and Correlate with Disease Severity in Tuberculosis Patients

abstract: Despite the clinical success of cancer immunotherapy, many patients fail to respond or develop resistance, highlighting the need to understand how interactions between tumor and immune cells influence treatment outcomes. Three-dimensional in vitro models allow these interactions to be studied under controlled conditions. However, Matrigel and other biologically derived scaffolds can vary in composition, offer limited independent control over matrix properties, and require cell-recovery procedures that complicate downstream analysis. Here, we present a co-culture model of melanoma spheroids and primary CD8+ T cells based on a defined, thermoreversible synthetic polyisocyanopeptide (PIC) hydrogel. PIC supported T cell viability and migration, with mean motility parameters similar to those in Matrigel and lower variability between experiments. Fluorescence imaging revealed CD8+ T cell infiltration and increased melanoma-cell apoptosis during co-culture. Cooling enabled recovery of nearly all embedded cells in less than 3 min without chemical or enzymatic matrix digestion. Metabolic profiling of recovered T cells identified time-dependent changes in intracellular lactate, amino acids, and tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediates, alongside changes in extracellular metabolite availability. Flow cytometry distinguished T cell populations with different effector profiles, with higher expression of effector markers in the fraction associated with melanoma spheroids. By combining a defined synthetic matrix with in situ imaging and rapid recovery for ex situ analysis, this model connects the spatial dynamics of tumor-immune interactions with metabolic and immune phenotypes, providing a basis for studies of immune-cell function and responses to immunotherapy.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.766807 v1

summary.background:
- Immunotherapy: treatments that boost the patient's own immune system to attack cancer.
- CD8+ T cells: immune cells that can directly kill cancer cells.
- Spheroids: small 3D clusters of cells grown in the lab that mimic parts of a tumour.
- Hydrogel: a water-rich gel that holds cells in a scaffold, similar to a soft, jelly-like environment.
- Matrigel: a common gel extracted from animal tumour material; its composition varies between batches.
- Thermoreversible: the gel turns liquid or solid with temperature changes, so cooling can release the embedded cells.
- Metabolic profiling: measuring small molecules such as lactate and amino acids to see how cells are fuelling themselves.
- Flow cytometry: a method that counts and characterises individual cells by their surface and internal markers.
summary.one_liner: A defined, thermoreversible synthetic polyisocyanopeptide hydrogel is used as a 3D co-culture system for melanoma spheroids and primary CD8+ T cells, enabling in situ imaging and rapid cold-based cell recovery for metabolic and flow cytometry analysis.
summary.plain: Immunotherapy works for many cancer patients but not all, so scientists want lab models where tumour cells and immune cells can be studied together in three dimensions. This paper describes a lab gel made from a defined synthetic material, rather than a biologically derived mix like Matrigel, in which skin-cancer clusters and immune T cells are grown together. The authors report that the T cells survived and moved through the gel, that tumour cells showed more cell death during co-culture, and that cooling the gel released nearly all the cells in under 3 minutes for further testing.
summary.why: Reproducible, chemically defined culture systems could make it easier to compare how immune cells behave and what they do to tumours, which is relevant to understanding treatment response. The text is a summary of a study design and early measurements; its wider relevance to patient outcomes or clinical use is not shown here.

title: A thermoreversible hydrogel model for in situ and ex situ analysis of tumor-immune interactions

abstract: Reactive astrocytes have emerged as important components of the brain metastasis niche, yet a state-resolved framework for metastasis-associated astrocyte biology is still lacking. Here, we integrate single-cell and spatial transcriptomics across syngeneic breast, lung and melanoma models of brain metastases to define a state-resolved astrocyte landscape. We identify recurrent tumor-associated astrocyte states shared across tumor origins, map their spatial distribution, and find that a subset, which we term AST-BrM, becomes selectively reprogrammed at the tumor-microenvironment interface, supporting niche-coupled organization rather than a diffuse brain-wide reactive response. AST-BrM defines distinct metastasis-associated astrocyte states at the peritumoral interface, distinguishes them from homeostatic-like astrocytes beyond generic inflammatory activation, and resolves into two therapeutically actionable programs: an AP-1-high axis and a STAT3+/HOPX+-associated axis. Genetic and pharmacologicall perturbations establish functional relevance, and an AP-1/c-FOS-driven signature is associated with clinical outcome. Together, these findings define conserved, spatially organized and actionable astrocyte programs that drive brain metastasis progression.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.766881 v1

summary.background:
- Astrocytes are star-shaped support cells of the brain; "reactive" astrocytes change state in response to injury or disease.
- A "niche" is the local surrounding environment that a tumor depends on.
- Single-cell transcriptomics measures which genes are active in each cell; spatial transcriptomics also records where in the tissue each cell sits.
- Syngeneic models are mice with immune systems matched to the tumor cells, used to study cancer in a living animal.
- AP-1, STAT3 and HOPX are gene regulators or markers; AP-1 and c-FOS are involved in stress and inflammatory signaling.
- "Peritumoral interface" means the boundary zone around a tumor.
- Preprint-style claims on mouse models do not automatically carry over to human patients.
summary.one_liner: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics in syngeneic breast, lung and melanoma mouse models of brain metastasis identify recurrent, spatially organized astrocyte states, including an AST-BrM subset with AP-1-high and STAT3+/HOPX+-associated programs that were tested by genetic and pharmacological perturbation.
summary.plain: When cancer spreads to the brain, the nearby support cells called astrocytes change their behavior. This study mapped those changes in mice with breast, lung, or skin (melanoma) tumors that had spread to the brain, looking at individual cells and their locations in tissue. The authors report that a subset of these astrocytes changes specifically at the edge of the tumor, and that similar changes appear regardless of where the cancer started.
summary.why: Brain metastases are hard to treat, and the tissue around a tumor can help it grow. If the astrocyte programs described here hold up, they could point to new targets that act on the tumor's surroundings rather than the cancer cells alone. The text reports perturbation experiments and a link to clinical outcome, but the strength of these links cannot be judged from the abstract alone.

title: Recurrent astrocyte transcriptional states with spatial and functional specialization are induced by brain metastases independently of their primary tumor origin

abstract: Subaerial biofilms (SABs) colonizing exposed stone surfaces provide natural systems for investigating microbial community assembly under challenging environmental conditions. Although bacterial diversity on stone has been widely described, whether taxonomic variation reflects broader phylogenetic and ecological differences remains unclear. Here, we characterized SAB communities inhabiting two geographically separated historic urban marble monuments, Federal Hall National Memorial (New York) and the Lincoln Memorial (Washington, DC), using SSU rRNA amplicon sequencing. Additional samples from the Merchants' Exchange Building (Philadelphia) were also examined. Bacterial communities exhibited pronounced taxonomic turnover but substantially greater phylogenetic similarity, indicating that community variation primarily reflected replacement among closely related bacterial lineages rather than turnover among distantly related clades. Despite this taxonomic turnover, core assemblage analyses identified conserved bacterial lineages shared across monuments, several of which were also detected in the independent Philadelphia samples. Consistent with these patterns, inferred ecological composition remained remarkably similar among monuments, with chlorophyll-containing bacteria dominating all communities. Together, these findings demonstrate that these monuments harbor distinct bacterial assemblages while maintaining a conserved phylogenetic and inferred ecological framework, suggesting that environmental filtering and local ecological processes may contribute to SAB community assembly across spatial scales.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.766465 v1

summary.background:
- Subaerial biofilm: a thin layer of microbes (mostly bacteria) growing on surfaces exposed to air and weather.
- Taxonomic turnover: the replacement of one set of species by another across places or samples.
- Phylogenetic similarity: how closely related the organisms are on the evolutionary family tree, regardless of exact species.
- SSU rRNA amplicon sequencing: a method that reads a standard gene region to identify which bacteria are present and roughly how they are related.
- Core assemblage: a set of lineages found consistently across sites.
- Inferred ecological composition: functional roles estimated from the identities of the organisms, not measured directly here.
- Chlorophyll-containing bacteria: photosynthetic bacteria that use light for energy.
- Environmental filtering: the idea that local conditions select which organisms can survive.
summary.one_liner: Amplicon sequencing of subaerial biofilm bacteria on marble monuments in New York, Washington DC and Philadelphia finds strong taxonomic turnover among sites but conserved phylogenetic structure and inferred ecological composition, with a shared core of lineages.
summary.plain: Thin films of microbes grow on the outside of stone buildings and statues exposed to weather. This study looked at the bacteria living on marble at two historic monuments in different cities, Federal Hall in New York and the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, DC, and also sampled a third building in Philadelphia. The bacterial species differed from site to site, but the types of bacteria were closely related and played similar inferred roles.
summary.why: It asks whether differences in which microbes live in a community reflect deeper evolutionary or ecological differences, a question relevant to how microbial communities assemble in harsh environments. The text does not establish how these findings bear on stone conservation or other systems, so broader implications remain unclear.

title: Taxonomic turnover with phylogenetic conservation in subaerial biofilm (SAB) communities of marble monuments

abstract: One of the earliest described cases of putative homoploid hybrid speciation was 35 years ago for the Australian cotton species, Gossypium bickii. This inference was based on discordance between chloroplast- and nuclear-based phylogenetic reconstructions, a type of incongruence that has become a relatively common observation in plants. Here we reevaluate evidence bearing on the evolutionary history of G. bickii in the context of an expanded sampling of all but one of the 17 described Australian cotton species, using whole-genome resequencing data based on 18,784 single-copy nuclear genes and entire plastome sequences. Genome-wide phylogenomic analyses resolved three well-defined sections (Sturtia, Hibiscoidea and Grandicalyx) and recapitulate the previously reported discordance between nuclear and plastid phylogenies. Although plastome inferences mirror phylogenetic discordance inferred earlier for G. bickii and G. cunninghamii, genome-wide nuclear data did not reveal compelling signals of interspecific introgression, perhaps because of population genetic nuclear swamping by a quantitatively larger paternal population and by subsequent genomic divergence. All analyses, including genome-wide phylogenetics and dating estimation, support a narrative in which there was early and rapid diversification of the three Australian sections, accompanied by early intersectional reticulation of plastomes without residual evidence in the nuclear genome.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.12.765769 v1

summary.background:
- Homoploid hybrid speciation: a new species forms from a cross between two species without a change in chromosome number.
- Plastome / chloroplast genome: the small genome inside plant energy-producing organelles, usually inherited from the mother only in cotton-type plants.
- Nuclear genome: the main genome in the cell nucleus, inherited from both parents.
- Phylogenetics: reconstructing evolutionary family trees from DNA sequences.
- Discordance / incongruence: when trees from different genomes give different branching patterns.
- Introgression: the transfer of genes between species through repeated crossing.
- Nuclear swamping: a rare hybrid lineage's organelle DNA can be overwhelmed by nuclear DNA from the more numerous parent population.
- Sections: taxonomic groupings below genus level.
summary.one_liner: A genome-wide reanalysis of Australian Gossypium (cotton) species, using ~18,800 nuclear genes and whole plastomes, re-tests an early homoploid hybrid speciation claim for G. bickii and finds plastid-nuclear discordance without clear nuclear signs of introgression.
summary.plain: Scientists revisited a 35-year-old claim that one Australian wild cotton species, G. bickii, formed when two other species crossed and kept the same chromosome number. They sampled nearly all of the 17 Australian cotton species and compared thousands of nuclear genes with the chloroplast (plastid) genome. The chloroplast family tree conflicts with the nuclear one, but the nuclear genes showed no strong sign of mixing between species.
summary.why: It matters because plant family trees built from different genomes often disagree, and hybridization is one common explanation; this paper tests that explanation with much more data than the original study. The authors suggest the plastid mismatch may reflect old, early hybridization whose nuclear traces were later diluted, but the text does not establish this beyond their analyses.

title: Revisiting homoploid hybrid speciation in Australian cotton (Gossypium) species

abstract: Phosphate (Pi) limitation is a major constraint on plant productivity and is aggravated by heat stress. In nature, soil buffers air temperature, creating a vertical thermal gradient that shields roots from extreme heat; thus, heat and Pi starvation, although often co-occurring, are perceived mainly by different organs, shoots and roots respectively. How plants integrate these organ-specific stresses into a coordinated response remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated how Arabidopsis responds to combined Pi deficiency and elevated temperature, using a root-zone temperature gradient and an integrated analysis of ion accumulation, phytohormone levels and transcriptomic profiles in roots and shoots. The combined stress elicited a distinct response that cannot be explained by the addition of individual stress effects. Jasmonate levels changed in an organ-specific manner, with JA-Ile accumulating in roots and JA declining in shoots, and mutants with reduced (jar1-1) or constitutive (jazQ) JA signaling showed altered transcriptional, growth and leaf-temperature responses. These results identify jasmonic acid (JA) as a modulator of the balance between acclimation and growth under combined nutritional and thermal limitation, advancing our understanding of how plants cope with the multi-stress scenarios driven by climate change.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.766386 v1

summary.background:
- Phosphate (Pi) is an essential nutrient plants take up from soil; shortage limits growth.
- Heat stress means temperatures above what a plant normally tolerates, which can damage growth and cooling.
- Root-zone temperature gradient: an experimental setup in which roots and shoots are kept at different temperatures, mimicking soil buffering air temperature.
- Phytohormones are signaling chemicals (here jasmonates) that coordinate growth and stress responses.
- JA and JA-Ile are two forms of jasmonate; jar1-1 and jazQ are Arabidopsis mutants with reduced or constitutive jasmonate signaling.
- Multi-omics means measuring many molecule types at once (ions, hormones, transcripts).
- Transcriptomics: measuring which genes are switched on or off.
summary.one_liner: In Arabidopsis, combined phosphate starvation and heat applied through a root-zone temperature gradient produced a distinct response, with jasmonate hormone levels shifting in opposite directions in roots and shoots and jasmonate-signaling mutants showing altered transcription, growth and leaf temperature.
summary.plain: Plants often face low phosphate in the soil while the weather is hot, and the two stresses hit different parts of the plant: the heat reaches the leaves, while the soil keeps the roots cooler. This study grew the plant model Arabidopsis with its roots and shoots at different temperatures and measured minerals, plant hormones and gene activity in each organ. The authors report that the combined stress caused a response that was not just the sum of the two stresses alone, and that the plant hormone jasmonate changed in opposite directions in roots and shoots.
summary.why: Crops in a warming climate may face low soil phosphate and heat together, so understanding how organs coordinate these signals could inform future breeding or management. The text only shows effects in one model plant under controlled conditions, so how far it carries over to field crops is not established here.

title: Integrated multi-omics reveals organ-specific jasmonate signaling in Arabidopsis under combined heat and phosphate starvation

abstract: Efficient photosynthesis is crucial to agricultural productivity and can be constrained by the plant carbon-nitrogen balance, offering an opportunity for genetic improvement. Furthermore, soil N availability limits grain yields, and crops require substantial N fertilizer to be productive. In C4 plants, carbon-concentrating mechanisms respond to decreased soil nitrogen and share molecular intermediates with N metabolism. Maize, one of the most widely grown crops globally, uses a combination of two C4 photosynthetic pathways. Most carbon fixation occurs through the NADP-malic enzyme (NADP-ME) pathway, yet some fixation is also thought to occur via phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK). However, genetic evidence for the contribution of PEPCK is lacking. Here, we used a transposon-based mutagenesis approach to study the function of the C4 isoform of PEPCK1 in maize. The C4 pathway intermediate aspartate accumulated to high concentrations in the leaves of the pepck1-2::Ds knock-down mutant, providing genetic support for the PEPCK secondary pathway as a complement to the dominant NADP-ME shuttle in maize. Field experiments over multiple seasons in either N-limiting or N-sufficient soils demonstrated the pepck1::Ds mutants produced higher vegetative and grain biomass without changes in leaf photosynthetic rates or parameters. This study confirms that PEPCK1 catalyzes the decarboxylation of carbon shuttled as aspartate, as an alternative route to decarboxylation by NADP-ME in a nominally NADP-ME subtype C4 species maize, providing clear genetic support for two-pathway operation. Further, the greater resilience and N-responsiveness of mutant plants are valuable traits for sustainable and subsistence farming in the future.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.766785 v1

summary.background:
- Photosynthesis: plants fix carbon dioxide into sugars; many crops, including maize, use the "C4" pathway, which first concentrates CO2 in special cells to boost efficiency.
- Maize mainly uses the NADP-malic enzyme (NADP-ME) route to release the concentrated CO2; PEPCK is a second enzyme thought to play a smaller role.
- Aspartate is an amino acid-like intermediate that can carry carbon between cell compartments in this pathway.
- Transposon mutagenesis: using mobile DNA elements to disrupt a gene so its function can be studied; "knock-down" means the gene's activity is reduced, not removed entirely.
- Nitrogen (N) is a key nutrient that often limits crop yield; the study compares plants grown with limited and sufficient soil nitrogen.
summary.one_liner: Transposon knockout mutants of the C4 isoform PEPCK1 in maize show that aspartate-shuttled carbon can be decarboxylated via PEPCK as a secondary route alongside NADP-ME, with field-grown mutants producing more biomass and grain under varying nitrogen levels.
summary.plain: Maize is one of the world's most important food crops, and it captures carbon from the air using a multi-step chemical route. This paper asks whether a second, minor route, run by an enzyme called PEPCK, really helps, by knocking out the gene for one version of that enzyme. The mutant plants built up a related chemical (aspartate) in their leaves, and in field trials over several seasons they grew more leaf and grain material, whether the soil was short of nitrogen or not.
summary.why: It gives genetic evidence, rather than only indirect evidence, that maize uses two carbon-concentrating routes instead of one, which matters for understanding how a major crop photosynthesizes. The yield result is interesting for low-fertilizer farming, but the text does not show how large or consistent the gain is, or whether it would transfer to other crops.

title: Plant growth, biomass, and nitrogen utilization are impacted by mutations in C4 PEPCK1 in maize

abstract: Engineering bacterial two-component systems (TCSs) to sense new molecules would enable programmable whole-cell biosensors, but retargeting membrane-bound sensor histidine kinases is challenging because ligand recognition and signal transduction are tightly coupled. Here, we reprogram the thiosulfate-responsive TCS from Shewanella halifaxensis (ThsSR) to detect perchlorate, for which no naturally occurring TCS sensor has been reported. Using a dual growth selection, we simultaneously selected for perchlorate-dependent signaling and against native thiosulfate responsiveness. This strategy first converted wild-type ThsS into a perchlorate-responsive generalist and then produced specialized variants with improved sensitivity, greatly reduced thiosulfate response, and discrimination against related oxyanions. We next applied the physicsinformed reinforcement learning design method protCAD to functional intermediates identified by directed evolution. protCAD-selected substitutions further enhanced sensitivity or signaling output in specialized sensors, even in backgrounds that were refractory to additional random mutagenesis and gene shuffling. As a final demonstration, we used the engineered TCS sensor in a whole cell biosensor to detect perchlorate in unsterile environmental samples. Together, these results define a productive division of labor between experiment and computation: directed evolution discovers signaling-competent, specificity-altered sequence space, while computation explores that evolved space more completely to refine performance. This evolution-computational strategy provides a framework for reprogramming TCS biosensors toward non-native analytes.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.766565 v1

summary.background:
- Two-component system (TCS): a bacterial signalling circuit with a membrane sensor (histidine kinase) that detects a molecule and passes the signal to a response protein that switches genes on or off.
- Whole-cell biosensor: a living bacterium engineered so that a gene output, often light or colour, reports the presence of a target chemical.
- Directed evolution: repeated rounds of random mutation and selection in the lab to find variants with a desired trait.
- Computational protein design: software that proposes specific amino acid changes to a protein, here protCAD, which uses physics-informed reinforcement learning.
- Perchlorate: a persistent oxyanion (a negatively charged oxygen-containing ion) found as a contaminant, related to thiosulfate and similar ions.
- Ligand: the small molecule a sensor binds to.
summary.one_liner: The authors reprogram the membrane-bound sensor kinase of a thiosulfate-responsive bacterial two-component system (ThsSR from Shewanella halifaxensis) to respond to perchlorate, combining directed evolution with the protCAD computational design method, and use the result in a whole-cell biosensor.
summary.plain: Bacteria often sense chemicals using a two-part switch: a sensor protein on the cell membrane and a partner that turns on genes in response. This paper takes a bacterial sensor that normally detects thiosulfate and evolves it to detect perchlorate, a pollutant for which no natural bacterial sensor was known. The researchers combined lab evolution, which selects for better variants, with a computer design method, and then tested the resulting engineered cells on unsterile environmental samples.
summary.why: Engineered bacteria that detect specific pollutants could offer cheap, programmable field monitoring, so the approach matters for environmental sensing. The text reports the method and a proof-of-use test, but does not give detection limits or field performance details here, so the practical reach is not yet clear.

title: Reprogramming a thiosulfate bacterial two-component system into a perchlorate biosensor

abstract: Cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) activity underpins cell cycle progression through dynamic and temporally ordered phosphorylation events. While transcriptional regulation has been extensively exploited in synthetic biology, the rational engineering of post-translational signaling circuits remains underdeveloped. Here, we introduce modular CDK-responsive phospho-degron tags derived from the Far1 regulatory region and demonstrate their ability to confer tunable, cell cycle-dependent control over protein stability in budding yeast. By systematically modifying cyclin docking motifs and Cks1 priming sites, we generate degron variants with distinct degradation kinetics and phosphorylation thresholds. These modules enable predictable modulation of transcription factor abundance and downstream gene expression. We further combine CDK-responsive degrons with phosphorylation-controlled localization modules for multi-layered regulation of sequential nuclear import and degradation. We encode multiple kinase activity thresholds within a single protein, demonstrating how complex phosphorylation logic can be compactly implemented. Finally, we show that degron performance is strongly influenced by culture conditions, particularly cell density and associated changes in CDK activity. Together, our results establish CDK-driven phospho-degrons as versatile building blocks for engineering dynamic protein regulation and provide a foundation for constructing synthetic post-translational signaling circuits.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.766399 v1

summary.background:
- Protein degradation: cells tag unwanted proteins so they are broken down; engineering this changes how long a protein lasts.
- Phosphorylation: adding a phosphate group to a protein, often acting as an on/off switch.
- CDK (cyclin-dependent kinase): an enzyme whose activity rises and falls through the cell cycle, driving division steps.
- Degron: a short sequence that marks a protein for destruction.
- Budding yeast: a single-celled fungus widely used as a model organism in cell biology.
- Transcription factor: a protein that switches genes on or off; its abundance sets how strongly those genes are expressed.
- Synthetic biology: designing biological parts and circuits with predictable behavior.
summary.one_liner: The paper introduces modular, CDK-responsive phospho-degron tags derived from the Far1 regulatory region that give tunable, cell-cycle-dependent control of protein stability in budding yeast, and shows they can be combined with localization modules and tuned by culture density.
summary.plain: Cells control their own division with a chemical "on/off" signal: an enzyme called CDK adds phosphate tags to proteins at specific times. This paper builds short, reusable tags based on a piece of the yeast protein Far1 that cause a protein to be destroyed when that signal is active. The authors report that changing parts of the tag gives different destruction speeds and thresholds, which lets them adjust how much of a regulator protein, and the genes it controls, a cell has.
summary.why: Most synthetic biology tools control gene switching at the DNA level, so a set of parts that controls protein stability after translation, tied to a natural cell-cycle signal, could offer a second, faster layer of control. The text does not show how well these tags would work outside yeast or in more complex systems, so their broader usefulness remains to be tested.

title: CDK phospho-degron tags for dynamic protein regulation

abstract: Fluctuations in gene expression affect the timing precision of downstream events triggered when a gene product reaches a critical threshold. The first-passage time (FPT) to this threshold characterizes the timing of such events. In conventional single-step birth--death models, reaction waiting times are exponentially distributed and hence memoryless. In this setting, FPT noise exhibits a U-shaped dependence on the threshold, attaining its minimum near one-half of the steady-state mean. However, mRNA production and degradation often involve multiple sequential steps, leading to hypoexponential distributions of mRNA production times and mRNA lifetimes. Here, we investigate how molecular memory arising from multistep mRNA production and degradation affects FPT statistics in bursty gene expression. We calculate FPT statistics in the small-noise limit. Both multistep mechanisms reduce FPT noise, but through distinct mechanisms. Multistep burst arrival reduces mRNA copy-number fluctuations, thereby suppressing timing noise. Multistep degradation instead reshapes transient accumulation dynamics, reducing relative timing noise even when steady-state mRNA noise increases. The threshold that minimizes FPT noise remains close to one-half of the steady-state mean, except for multistep burst arrival with constant burst sizes, for which it shifts to lower values. Stochastic simulations support the analytical predictions within their regimes of validity and show that these qualitative conclusions persist beyond the small-noise approximation.
label: arXiv:2611.22554v1

summary.background:
- Gene expression: a gene is copied into mRNA, which is then translated into protein.
- Bursty expression: mRNA is often produced in short clusters ("bursts") rather than steadily.
- First-passage time (FPT): the waiting time until a quantity first reaches a set threshold.
- Noise: the relative spread or variability of a quantity; here, the variability of the crossing time.
- Birth-death model: a simple model where molecules are created and destroyed in single random steps, so waiting times are exponential and have no memory of the past.
- Multistep (hypoexponential) waiting times: a sum of several sequential exponential steps, which gives the process a kind of memory.
- Small-noise limit: an approximation valid when fluctuations are small relative to the mean.
summary.one_liner: Analytical small-noise first-passage-time statistics for bursty gene expression with multistep (hypoexponential) mRNA production and degradation, showing how this molecular memory changes timing noise relative to memoryless birth-death models.
summary.plain: The paper asks how reliably a cell can time an event, such as a protein reaching a level that switches something on, when the molecules involved are made and destroyed in several steps rather than one. Using mathematical calculations in the small-noise limit and computer simulations, the authors find that these multistep processes reduce timing noise, but for two different reasons. One reason is that multistep production of mRNA bursts smooths out fluctuations in how many mRNA copies exist; the other is that multistep degradation changes how the molecule level builds up over time.
summary.why: Cell-level timing precision matters for processes that depend on a threshold being crossed, so showing that "memory" in molecular steps can make timing more precise is a useful conceptual point. The text does not indicate specific biological systems or experimental tests, so its connection to real measurements is something the reader would need to check in the full paper.

title: Molecular memory reduces timing noise in stochastic gene expression

abstract: People differ in how they judge faces, artworks, photographs and jokes. Previous work measured the size of these differences; we ask what shape they take. We wrote three candidate shapes as nested generative models (same-sign reweighting of shared dimensions, a linear transform that allows reversal, and stimulus-specific offsets) and compared how well they predict people unseen in training, using ten public datasets (about 20,000 raters). The models recovered a person's judgment space from 10-20 judgments and predicted judgments of unseen stimuli. For faces, reweighting was sufficient, and weights opposing the population were not statistically detected. For artworks, weights spread continuously along the shared abstract-figurative direction, and 28 percent of raters fell on the opposite side from the population. This tail was much smaller when a different rater sample judged the same artworks. Individual differences thus differ in shape as well as size, and the shape depends on domain and raters.
label: arXiv:2611.22440v1

summary.background:
- Generative model: a mathematical story of how data are produced, here how each person's ratings are generated from shared dimensions.
- Judgment space: a low-dimensional map in which each stimulus (face, artwork) sits at a position along shared axes, such as abstract versus figurative.
- Reweighting: each person gives the shared axes different importance, which can be negative, meaning they point opposite to the group.
- Nested models: simpler models are special cases of more flexible ones, so they can be compared directly.
- Held-out prediction: testing how well a model predicts people or items it was not trained on, which guards against overfitting.
- Rater sample: the group of people who made the judgments; results can depend on who they are.
summary.one_liner: The paper compares three nested generative models of how individuals' judgments deviate from a shared judgment space (same-sign reweighting, reversible linear transforms, and stimulus-specific offsets) and evaluates them by predicting unseen raters across ten public datasets of about 20,000 raters.
summary.plain:
People often disagree about whether a face, painting, photo, or joke is attractive or good. This paper asks not how big those disagreements are, but what form they take, and tests three candidate descriptions against public rating datasets. For faces, a simple reweighting of shared judgment dimensions was enough, while for artworks about 28 percent of raters leaned opposite to the group on the main abstract-versus-figurative direction, though that opposing group was much smaller when a different set of raters judged the same artworks.</plain>
<parameter name="why">Most work on individual differences in taste or judgment measures how large they are, so describing their shape is a different question that could inform how consensus and disagreement are modeled. The text does not show how far these findings generalize beyond the datasets studied, and the claim about shape depending on domain and raters rests on the paper's own comparisons.

title: The shape of individual differences in judgment: shared axes, personal weights, and when their spread crosses the consensus

abstract: Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis (MDR-TB) represents a global public health threat, with a rising prevalence, particularly among vulnerable populations. This cross-sectional study analyzed MDR-TB notifications in Brazil from 2001 to 2021, using data from DATASUS, and stratified by periods and risk groups (HIV-positive individuals, smokers, drug users, healthcare workers, incarcerated individuals, and people experiencing homelessness). Descriptive analyses and parametric statistical tests (ANOVA and Tukey, p<0.05) were applied. A significant increase in cases was observed across all groups, especially between 2017 and 2021, with growth ranging from 294% to 574% depending on the population. Factors such as treatment abandonment, coinfection, social vulnerability, and occupational exposure were key determinants for MDR-TB dissemination. The findings indicate that current public health policies are insufficient, highlighting the urgent need for targeted prevention strategies, therapeutic follow-up, and control measures for high-risk populations.
authors: Dailton Guedes de Oliveira Moraes, C.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.26368155 v1

summary.background:
- Tuberculosis (TB) is a bacterial infection, mainly of the lungs, spread through the air.
- Multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) does not respond to at least two of the first-line antibiotics, so treatment is longer and harder.
- DATASUS is Brazil's national public health information system, the source of the case counts.
- Notifications are cases reported to health authorities, which depend on testing and reporting practices.
- A cross-sectional study takes a snapshot of data at one point or across periods; it shows associations, not cause.
- ANOVA and Tukey tests are standard statistical methods for comparing averages across groups.
- Growth percentages describe change in reported counts and do not by themselves show a change in true rates.
summary.one_liner: A cross-sectional analysis of Brazilian DATASUS notifications (2001–2021) of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis across six high-risk groups, testing period differences with ANOVA and Tukey post-hoc tests.
summary.plain: This study looks at a hard-to-treat form of tuberculosis, a lung infection caused by bacteria that resist the standard drugs, in Brazil over 21 years. The researchers counted reported cases among groups considered especially vulnerable, such as people with HIV, smokers, drug users, health workers, people in prison, and people experiencing homelessness. They report that cases rose across all these groups, with the steepest growth between 2017 and 2021, by 294% to 574% depending on the group.
summary.why: Drug-resistant tuberculosis is harder and longer to treat, so rising case counts among high-risk groups matter for both patients and public health planning. The paper's authors link the rise to treatment abandonment, coinfection, social vulnerability and occupational exposure, but the text does not show how strongly each factor contributed.

title: Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis Rates Among High-Risk Populations in Brazil: An Analysis from 2001 to 2021

abstract: IntroductionThe introduction of pneumococcal conjugate vaccines resulted in a decline in invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD). Nevertheless, recent studies report a re-emergence of vaccine-included serotypes. AimTo describe the recent re-emergence of serotype 14 IPD among adults in Catalonia and to investigate the factors underlying its resurgence. MethodsWe analysed two collections of adult IPD isolates: a historical series from Hospital Universitari de Bellvitge (1996-2025) and a multicentre series from seven tertiary hospitals in Catalonia (2023-2025). Isolates were serotyped (Quellung) and genotyped by PFGE/MLST (1996-2022) or Illumina sequencing (2023-2025). Clinical data were retrospectively collected. ResultsThe historical series showed that, after peaking in 2009, serotype 14 frequency gradually declined, with only 0-4 cases reported annually between 2016 and 2020. However, the number of serotype 14 isolates increased again in 2025, reaching 11.0% of all isolates at HUB and 10.8% across Catalonia. Genomic data showed that this increase involved multiple previously circulating lineages (GPSC6, GPSC18, GPSC16 and GPSC39), with no dominant clone. Analysis of the capsular locus revealed substantial genetic diversity, with no association between capsular variants and either lineage or year of isolation. A substantial proportion of patients (56.3%) had multiple comorbidities and only 18.8% were appropriately vaccinated. DiscussionThe re-emergence of serotype 14 was not associated with a novel lineage or capsular variant. Instead, it may reflect a combination of post-pandemic transmission changes, higher-valency paediatric vaccines, and natural fluctuations in serotype circulation. These findings highlight the limits of herd protection and underscore the need to strengthen adult vaccination, particularly among at-risk populations.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.26367621 v1

summary.background:
- Pneumococcus (Streptococcus pneumoniae) is a bacterium that can cause pneumonia, blood infection and meningitis.
- Serotype: a variant of the bacterium defined by its outer sugar coat (capsule); vaccines target specific serotypes.
- Conjugate vaccines: vaccines that train immunity against these capsules; paediatric schedules in recent years use more serotypes ("higher valency").
- Herd protection: indirect protection of unvaccinated people when many others are vaccinated; the paper notes its limits here.
- Lineage / clone: a family of closely related bacteria; GPSC is a naming system for pneumococcal lineages.
- Genotyping methods: PFGE and MLST (older fingerprinting and gene-typing), and whole-genome sequencing by Illumina (newer, more detailed).
- Quellung: a classic microscope-based serotyping test.
summary.one_liner: A retrospective genomic and clinical study of adult invasive pneumococcal disease in Catalonia (1996-2025) reports a 2023-2025 resurgence of vaccine-type serotype 14, driven by several previously circulating lineages rather than one new clone or capsule variant.
summary.plain: Pneumococcal bacteria cause serious infections such as blood infections and pneumonia, and vaccines have cut these infections a lot. This paper looks at a type of these bacteria called serotype 14, which had become rare in adults in the Catalan region of Spain but has become more common again in 2025. The authors compared older bacterial samples with recent ones and looked at patients' health records.
summary.why: Vaccine-covered types coming back in adults is a concern for public health planning, and the paper suggests the rise may reflect general shifts in circulation rather than a new, more dangerous strain. The authors themselves say the causes are uncertain, so the explanations offered are possibilities, not established findings.

title: Old lineages, new threat: the re-emergence of pneumococcal serotype 14 in adults in Catalonia, Spain (2023-2025).

abstract: Urinary tract infections are commonly caused by bacteria whose antibiotic susceptibility varies between clinical settings.1 We studied urinary isolates from 95 patients with suspected infection at Lahore General Hospital, Pakistan, between July and December 2023. Urine culture showed significant bacterial growth in 63 specimens (66.3%). Escherichia coli accounted for 30 isolates, followed by 18 Klebsiella isolates, comprising 16 Klebsiella pneumoniae and two Klebsiella oxytoca. Klebsiella was recovered from 12 female and six male patients, and the largest number of Klebsiella isolates occurred in patients aged 21-30 years. The aggregate susceptibility results, recorded for 18 isolates per antibiotic, showed the highest susceptibility to imipenem and meropenem (17/18 each), followed by nitrofurantoin (16/18). Resistance to several cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones and aminoglycosides was frequent. These findings describe the bacterial distribution and reported susceptibility patterns in a small hospital sample. Larger studies with verified species-specific susceptibility data are needed before these findings can guide local treatment policy.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.26368163 v1

summary.background:
- Urinary tract infection (UTI): an infection of the urinary system, usually by bacteria that enter the bladder.
- Klebsiella: a group of bacteria, including the species K. pneumoniae and K. oxytoca, that can cause UTIs and other infections.
- Antibiotic susceptibility: whether a bacterial sample is killed or held back by a given antibiotic in lab testing; "susceptible" means it responds, "resistant" means it does not.
- Isolate: one bacterial sample grown from one patient's specimen.
- Carbapenems (imipenem, meropenem): strong, broad-spectrum antibiotics often kept for serious infections.
- Cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides: other antibiotic families mentioned as frequently ineffective here.
- Limitation: the paper reports results for 18 isolates per drug in aggregate, and notes species-level susceptibility was not verified.
summary.one_liner: A small single-hospital study from Lahore, Pakistan (95 urine samples, July–December 2023) reporting how often Klebsiella bacteria caused urinary infections and how susceptible those isolates were to common antibiotics.
summary.plain: Urinary tract infections are often caused by bacteria that respond differently to different antibiotics, so doctors need local data to choose treatment. The authors examined urine samples from 95 patients at one hospital in Lahore and found bacteria grew in 63 of them. Among these, 18 were Klebsiella, and the lab tests suggested that imipenem and meropenem worked against almost all of those 18 isolates.
summary.why: Rising antibiotic resistance is a worldwide concern, and local resistance patterns help show which drugs may still work. However, the sample is small, from a single hospital, and the authors themselves say the results are not yet reliable enough to guide local treatment policy.

title: Frequency and antibiotic susceptibility of urinary Klebsiella in Lahore

abstract: BackgroundThe traditional business model for sustaining United States (U.S.) community pharmacies has relied on income generated by product sales. A fee-for-service model could help alleviate insufficient profit by monetizing conventionally free pharmacy services if patients are willing to pay out-of-pocket. ObjectivesThis study evaluated public acceptability of out-of-pocket payment for community pharmacist-provided services, variation in payment acceptability across services, and assessed whether payment acceptability differed by respondent characteristics and trust constructs. MethodsThis study represents a cross-sectional online survey of U.S. adults conducted during spring 2026 using a non-probability sampling approach. Primary outcomes were binary stated payment-acceptability judgments for a variety of pharmacist and health services. The survey used a between-subjects randomized payment-framing design, where participants were assigned to either a stated-price condition or an any-payment condition. Secondary outcomes included trust designations and participant demographic characteristics. ResultsA total of 1069 respondents completed the survey. A $20 fee was viewed more favorably than a general "any amount of money" fee. In the $20 stated-price condition, agreement was highest for osteoporosis screening (75.8%) and travel-related vaccines (69.0%), and lowest for antibiotic use consultation (23.9%) and wound care (32.1%). Older respondents and Hispanic respondents were less likely to view payment as acceptable, whereas men and respondents with greater pharmacist trust were more likely to view payment as acceptable. ConclusionAlthough patients historically have received many community pharmacy services at no cost, this study demonstrates that the concept of self-payment ifor certain services is considered acceptable, especially for services not typically provided. Key pointsO_LIIn a quota-matched survey of 1,069 U.S. adults, this study evaluated public acceptability of direct out-of-pocket payment for 27 community pharmacist-provided clinical services. C_LIO_LIPublic acceptability of a $20 out-of-pocket payment varied substantially by service, ranging from 23.9% for antibiotic-use consultation to 75.8% for osteoporosis screening. Higher acceptability was observed for discrete or specialized services, including travel-related vaccines and pharmacogenomic result review. C_LIO_LIPayment acceptability was associated with respondent characteristics and trust in pharmacists. Older respondents and Hispanic respondents were less likely to view payment as acceptable, whereas men and respondents with greater pharmacist trust were more likely to view payment as acceptable. C_LI
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.26368139 v1

summary.background:
- Community pharmacy: a retail drugstore where pharmacists dispense medicines and provide health services.
- Fee-for-service: a model where each service is paid for separately, rather than through product sales.
- Out-of-pocket payment: money a patient pays directly, not through insurance.
- Non-probability sampling: participants are recruited, not randomly selected from the whole population, so results may not represent all U.S. adults exactly. The sample was quota-matched to population characteristics.
- Between-subjects randomized framing: different groups of respondents saw different versions of the fee question, so their answers can be compared fairly.
- Stated-price vs. any-payment condition: one group was told a specific $20 fee; the other was asked about paying "any amount."
- Trust constructs: survey measures of how much respondents trust pharmacists.
summary.one_liner: A 2026 non-probability online survey of 1,069 U.S. adults tests whether the public would accept out-of-pocket fees for 27 community pharmacist services, with a randomized comparison of a stated $20 price versus an unspecified "any amount" fee.
summary.plain: U.S. community pharmacies have traditionally earned most of their income from selling products, and many pharmacist services are free to patients. This study asked over a thousand American adults whether they would find it acceptable to pay out of pocket for various pharmacist services. Acceptance was higher for some services, such as osteoporosis screening, and much lower for others, such as antibiotic-use consultations.
summary.why: Pharmacies face thin profit margins, so whether patients will pay for services is a practical question for how these businesses might stay open. The findings are based on a non-probability online sample, so they show stated attitudes in one survey rather than measured willingness to pay in real life.

title: Public Acceptability of Self-Payment for Community Pharmacists' Services: A National Online Survey

abstract: Background and ObjectivesNormative modeling expresses an individuals brain measures as deviations from a large healthy reference and has been advanced as a route to precision imaging biomarkers in epilepsy, where structural abnormality is distributed rather than confined to the presumed focus. Whether this framework can inform clinical classification from clinically acquired T1-weighted and diffusion MRI is untested. We asked whether normative deviations discriminate between (1) epilepsy and functional seizures; (2) focal and generalized epilepsy; and (3) drug-resistant and drug-responsive epilepsy. MethodsWe retrospectively studied patients with epilepsy or functional seizures without comorbid epilepsy who underwent 3-Tesla epilepsy-protocol MRI at the University of Pennsylvania. Morphometric deviation scores (cortical thickness, subcortical volume) were derived from CentileBrain (n>37,000 healthy references). White matter fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity profiles were referenced to harmonized Human Connectome Project cohorts. Lobar composites, hemispheric asymmetry indices, and whole-tract means were compared with rank-sum tests; discrimination was summarized as area under the ROC curve (AUC) with bootstrap confidence intervals and Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Whole-brain deviation burden was examined as a secondary analysis. Minimum detectable effects were estimated by Monte Carlo simulation at 80% power (=0.05). ResultsWe included 273 patients with epilepsy (203 focal, 37 generalized, 33 unclassified; 97 drug-resistant, 176 drug-responsive) and 32 with functional seizures. In the primary analyses, no regional or tract-level normative measure distinguished epilepsy from functional seizures, focal from generalized epilepsy, or drug-resistant from drug-responsive epilepsy; AUCs did not exceed 0.62, with upper confidence limits up to 0.72. In the secondary analysis, whole-brain morphometric deviation burden was modestly higher in epilepsy than in functional seizures (AUC 0.66, 95% CI 0.57-0.74) but did not separate the within-epilepsy comparisons. The study could detect AUC [≥]0.65 for epilepsy versus functional seizures, [≥]0.64 for focal versus generalized, and [≥]0.60 for drug-resistant versus drug-responsive epilepsy. DiscussionUnivariate normative deviation summaries from clinical MRI do not currently distinguish these groups well enough to guide care. Whole-brain deviation burden, the only summary measure that differed after correction, was detectable at the group level but insufficient for individual-level classification. Progress may require network-targeted analysis of patient-specific deviations and multimodal integration.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.14.26368080 v1

summary.background:
- Epilepsy: recurrent seizures caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain. Functional seizures look similar but come from a different cause, not abnormal electrical discharges, so telling them apart matters.
- Focal vs generalized epilepsy: seizures starting in one area of the brain versus seizures involving both sides from the outset.
- Drug-resistant epilepsy: seizures that continue despite trials of appropriate medicines.
- T1-weighted MRI: a standard brain scan that measures brain structure, such as cortical thickness and the volume of deep brain structures.
- Diffusion MRI: a scan that tracks how water moves along white-matter fibres; fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity are summary measures of this.
- Normative modeling: comparing one person's measurements with a large reference group of healthy people, expressed as how many standard deviations away they fall.
- AUC (area under the ROC curve): a 0.5 score means chance and 1.0 means perfect separation. Values around 0.6 are weak.
- Multiple-comparison correction (Benjamini-Hochberg): an adjustment that reduces false positives when many tests are run.
summary.one_liner: A retrospective study of 273 patients with epilepsy and 32 with functional seizures tests whether normative brain-deviation scores from clinical T1 and diffusion MRI can separate epilepsy from functional seizures, focal from generalized epilepsy, and drug-resistant from drug-responsive epilepsy, finding little discrimination in the primary analyses.
summary.plain: Doctors sometimes must tell apart different kinds of seizure disorders from brain scans, but the scans often look normal or show abnormalities spread across the brain. This study asked whether comparing each patient's scan with a large group of healthy people could help sort patients into these groups. In the main analyses it did not: none of the regional or tract measures separated the groups well, and the best overall signal, a general measure of how far the whole brain deviated from healthy norms, only modestly separated epilepsy from functional seizures.
summary.why: The paper is a useful check on a promising idea: normative brain-comparison methods were proposed as a route to individual-level biomarkers in epilepsy, and this work reports that such measures, as applied to routine clinical scans, do not yet support individual classification. It may matter for how much weight future imaging tools are given in epilepsy care, though the authors' suggested next steps (network-level analysis and combining data types) are proposals, not tested results.

title: Normative Modeling of Structural and Diffusion MRI for Epilepsy Diagnosis and Classification

abstract: ObjectiveClear vision across viewing distances requires the eyes to achieve binocular alignment and hold it steady. Alignment can be established through smooth dysconjugate eye movement, vergence, alone or in conjunction with rapid saccades. The circuits governing movement strategy and subsequent gaze holding remain less understood. MethodsWe used subthalamic nucleus (STN) deep brain stimulation (DBS) to probe these components in 23 participants with Parkinsons disease (PD), comparing binocular eye movements with stimulation on and off and relating behavioral changes to modeled stimulation anatomy. ResultsCombined saccade-vergence responses predominated in both stimulation states, but individual strategy changes were associated with stimulation location. Greater field of Forel coverage was associated with reduced saccade-assisted divergence, and stimulation anatomy helped predict individual changes in this movement strategy. Greater right associative STN coverage correlated with shorter convergence latency. The clearest group effect emerged after movement ended; DBS reduced gaze-holding variance by 37.0% after convergence and 29.4% after divergence, an overall reduction of 33.3% (95% confidence interval, 13.7-49.3%; p{approx}0.008). Participants with improved gaze holding had numerically greater modeled exposure to Forel and cerebellothalamic pathways. ConclusionsThese findings suggest distinct contributions of associative STN to initiation, consistent with go/no-go control, and Forel pathways to movement strategy. Improved gaze holding raises the novel possibility that stimulation engaging Forel and cerebellar outflow pathways enhances vergence neural integration. SignificanceBinocular eye movements reveal how basal ganglia and cerebellar pathways establish movement strategy and sustain alignment, guiding targeted stimulation studies in PD.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.14.26368127 v1

summary.background:
- Vergence: the inward (convergence) or outward (divergence) turning of the eyes so both point at the same object at different distances.
- Saccade: a fast, jerky eye movement that shifts gaze from one point to another.
- Gaze holding: keeping the eyes steady on a target once they are aligned.
- Subthalamic nucleus (STN): a small brain region involved in starting and stopping movements; deep brain stimulation (DBS) delivers electrical pulses through an implanted electrode.
- Parkinson's disease: a movement disorder caused by loss of certain brain cells that control movement.
- White-matter pathways: bundles of nerve fibers connecting brain regions. The field of Forel and cerebellothalamic pathways are two such bundles discussed here.
- Modeled stimulation anatomy: estimates, from computer models, of which fiber bundles the electrical current reaches around each electrode.
- Go/no-go control: the brain's process of deciding whether to start or hold back an action.
summary.one_liner: In 23 people with Parkinson's disease, switching subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation on and off changed how the eyes converge and how steadily they hold alignment, with effects linked to modeled stimulation location in white-matter pathways.
summary.plain: People with Parkinson's disease often have implanted electrodes that stimulate a deep brain region, and this study asked how that stimulation affects the coordinated movement of both eyes. Researchers recorded eye movements with the stimulator on and off, then compared the results with computer models of where the current spread in the brain. Stimulation reduced how much the eyes wobbled after they had moved into alignment, and the size of this change was linked to stimulation reaching particular nerve-fiber bundles.
summary.why: Keeping both eyes aligned is a simple, measurable window into how the basal ganglia and cerebellum shape movement, which may help guide more targeted stimulation in Parkinson's. The links to specific pathways are based on modeling and correlations in a modest sample, so they are suggestive rather than settled.

title: White Matter Pathway-Specific Effects of Subthalamic Deep Brain Stimulation on Vergence Motor Strategy and Binocular Stability

abstract: Microbiome modulation can augment responses to immunotherapy in advanced cancer. Early studies of anti-PD-1 therapies in combination with fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) reported efficacy in immunotherapy-naive and -refractory settings. However, FMTs are variable in composition, difficult to scale, and risk the transfer of emerging pathogens. VE800 is a consortium of 11 strains of commensal bacteria derived from healthy donors and grown from clonal cell banks. VE800 increased anti-PD-1 efficacy in preclinical models of cancer. CONSORTiUM-IO was a first-in-human, open-label phase 1 study that evaluated safety and efficacy of VE800 with nivolumab in advanced PD-1-refractory melanoma, PD-1-naive gastric/gastroesophageal junction (G/GEJ) adenocarcinoma and PD-1-naive microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer (MSS CRC). VE800 plus nivolumab was well tolerated but offered no improvement over historic response rates. Exploratory analyses in patients with melanoma revealed that VE800 strain engraftment was associated with greater progression-free survival (PFS) and increased immune activation peripherally. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCEThe first-in-human study of the safety and efficacy of a defined bacterial consortium in combination with anti-PD-1 treatment in various solid tumors demonstrated the safety of the combination, albeit with low clinical efficacy. The results provide important knowledge and considerations about microbiome modulation in cancer, to help design future trials.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.26368051 v1

summary.one_liner: A first-in-human phase 1 trial testing VE800, a defined 11-strain commensal bacterial consortium, combined with nivolumab (anti-PD-1) in PD-1-refractory melanoma, PD-1-naive gastric/GEJ adenocarcinoma, and PD-1-naive MSS colorectal cancer, reporting good safety but no clear efficacy gain over historical rates.
summary.plain:
Researchers tested whether a standardized mix of 11 beneficial gut bacteria, given alongside an immunotherapy drug called nivolumab, could help patients with several hard-to-treat cancers. The combination was found to be well tolerated, but it did not do better than response rates seen in earlier studies. In patients with melanoma, those whose bodies picked up the added bacteria tended to have longer progression-free survival, meaning their disease stayed controlled for longer.</plain>
<parameter name="why">Gut bacteria are being studied as a way to make cancer immunotherapy work better, and this trial suggests a defined, lab-grown bacterial mix may be safer and more consistent than transplanted stool. The honest takeaway is that the main efficacy result was negative, and the link between bacterial engraftment and survival is only an exploratory finding from a small melanoma group.</why>
<parameter name="background">- Immunotherapy with anti-PD-1 drugs (such as nivolumab) works by releasing the brakes on the immune system so it can attack tumors.
- Gut microbiome: the community of bacteria living in the intestine, which can influence immune responses.
- Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT): transferring stool from a donor to a patient; it is variable and carries infection risk.
- VE800: a defined consortium of 11 commensal bacterial strains grown from clonal cell banks, so each batch is intended to be the same.
- Engraftment: whether the added bacterial strains take hold and persist in the patient's gut.
- Phase 1 trial: an early study focused mainly on safety and dosing, with efficacy results only preliminary.
- Progression-free survival (PFS): time until the cancer grows or the patient dies.
