- MSS colorectal cancer: microsatellite-stable tumors, which usually respond poorly to PD-1 drugs.</background>
<parameter name="difficulty">intermediate

title: CONSORTiUM-IO: A Phase 1 Study Evaluating VE800 Plus Nivolumab in Treatment of Select Refractory or Metastatic Cancers

abstract: BackgroundPsychological care is an important component of cancer care, addressing psychological distress and supporting patients as they cope with illness. Meditation-based approaches, including mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs), have been incorporated into supportive cancer care internationally. Clinical Meditation (Rinsho Meiso-ho), a meditation method developed in Japan, integrates traditional Buddhist meditation with a contemporary medical care perspective. However, its feasibility and psychological outcomes in patients with cancer have not been sufficiently studied. ObjectiveThis study aimed to evaluate the feasibility of a Clinical Meditation intervention and to explore psychological outcomes and participants experiences among patients with cancer who were receiving or scheduled to receive pharmacotherapy at the time of recruitment. MethodsThis single-arm pilot study used a convergent mixed-methods design to evaluate an 8-week program consisting of a 4-week structured phase (1 face-to-face session and 3 brief online group sessions, with prescribed home practice) and a 4-week self-directed phase (1 individual online session, with voluntary home practice). Feasibility was assessed descriptively using retention, attendance, practice frequency, and poststudy feedback. Anxiety, depression, insomnia, fatigue, spiritual well-being (SWB), and posttraumatic growth (PTG) were assessed at baseline, 4 weeks, and 8 weeks. Changes were examined using Friedman tests and exact Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, with adjustment for multiple comparisons. Free-text responses were analyzed thematically and integrated with questionnaire findings at the participant level. ResultsEleven patients were enrolled; 9 (81.8%) completed the 4-week assessment and 8 (72.7%) completed the 8-week assessment. Median practice frequency declined from 5-6 days per week during the structured first month to 3-4 days per week during the self-directed second month (P=.031). Quantitative analyses included 9 participants, of whom 8 completed all 3 assessments; qualitative analyses included 8 participants. SWB and PTG showed significant overall changes (adjusted P=.02 and P=.04, respectively). SWB was higher than baseline at 4 weeks (adjusted P=.012), but the difference was not significant at 8 weeks. PTG was higher than baseline at both 4 and 8 weeks (both adjusted P=.047). No significant changes were observed in anxiety, depression, insomnia, or fatigue. Five themes were identified, encompassing experiences such as relaxation, greater distance from rumination, and meditation as a source of support. Participants accounts generally aligned with increases in SWB and PTG scores, although perceived benefits did not always correspond to changes in all questionnaire measures. ConclusionsThis mixed-methods pilot study suggests that Clinical Meditation may be feasible and acceptable for patients with cancer, although sustaining meditation practice remains challenging. Exploratory increases in SWB and PTG warrant further investigation. Larger controlled studies, comparisons with established MBIs, and deeper qualitative research are needed to evaluate outcomes and clarify the distinctive features of Clinical Meditation.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.11.26367801 v1

summary.background:
- Psychological care (support for distress, anxiety, low mood) is a recognized part of cancer care.
- Mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) are structured programs teaching attention-focused meditation; they are widely studied in cancer.
- Clinical Meditation is a Japanese method that combines traditional Buddhist meditation with a medical-care perspective.
- Pilot study: a small preliminary test to check whether a program is feasible before a larger trial.
- Single-arm: all participants receive the intervention; there is no comparison group.
- Mixed-methods: combines questionnaire scores with participants' written comments, analyzed for common themes.
- Friedman and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests: statistical tests for comparing repeated measurements in the same people; "adjusted P" means values corrected for testing several outcomes.
- Posttraumatic growth: positive personal change reported after a serious illness or stressful event.
- Attrition: only 8 of 11 completed the final assessment, and analyses used even smaller subsets.
summary.one_liner: A single-arm, mixed-methods pilot of an 8-week Clinical Meditation (Rinsho Meiso-ho) program for patients receiving pharmacotherapy for cancer, reporting feasibility, practice adherence, exploratory changes in spiritual well-being and posttraumatic growth, and thematic participant accounts.
summary.plain: Cancer patients often experience worry, low mood, and emotional strain during treatment, and meditation programs are sometimes offered to help. This small study tested whether a Japanese-developed meditation method, Clinical Meditation, could be run and accepted by 11 patients undergoing drug treatment over eight weeks. Most participants stayed in the program and reported feeling more spiritual well-being and personal growth at the midpoint and end, while practice frequency dropped in the second month and no change was seen in anxiety, depression, sleep, or fatigue.
summary.why: Meditation-based programs are already part of supportive cancer care in many countries, so knowing whether a different method is workable and acceptable adds to that evidence base. The study is too small and has no control group, so its outcome findings are only exploratory and should not be read as proof of benefit.

title: Feasibility and Psychological Outcomes of a Clinical Meditation Intervention for Patients with Cancer: A Mixed-Methods Pilot Study

abstract: BackgroundRisk of pregnancy complications is reassessed at each antenatal visit, but whether earlier predictions add information beyond the most recent one is unclear. Classifying every prediction as low or high risk can leave uncertainty unexpressed. Whether reliability per visit holds across visits is also unclear. MethodsThis secondary analysis included 9,289 nulliparous women from the nuMoM2b cohort (eight US centres, 2010-13). Logistic regression models predicted gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, suspected fetal growth restriction and large for gestational age at 6-13, 16-21 and 22-29 weeks (Visits 1-3). Mondrian conformal prediction reported no (low risk), yes (high risk), or both (review). To test whether prediction history adds information beyond the Visit 3 prediction, we compared, among women classified as high risk at Visit 3, those first classified as high risk at Visit 2 or 3 (emerging high) with those classified as high risk at all three visits (persistent high), adjusting for Visit 3 predicted probability. FindingsThe adjusted proportion with the outcome was higher in the emerging-high than the persistent-high group, by 6.1 percentage points for large for gestational age (95% CI -0.4 to 12.2) and 3.8 percentage points for suspected fetal growth restriction (-0.9 to 8.1). Other outcomes showed adjusted differences close to zero. With conformal prediction calibrated to a 90% level at each visit, the reported answers included the actual outcome in 89.6-90.6% of women at each visit (coverage). Coverage decreased when each womans three visits were considered together (79.0-85.4%). InterpretationFor fetal growth outcomes, how a womans predicted risk evolved during pregnancy may add information beyond her Visit 3 prediction. For repeated clinical use, the target coverage level should reflect the acceptable risk of incorrect low- or high-risk classifications over a womans follow-up and the clinical decisions supported at each visit. FundingNone. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed from database inception to Oct 28, 2026, for English-language studies in humans, combining terms for gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, fetal growth restriction or small for gestational age, and large for gestational age with terms for prediction models and for longitudinal or repeated assessment, risk trajectories, conformal prediction, or predictive uncertainty. We also searched for conformal prediction applied to longitudinal clinical data. Most models predicted a single complication at a fixed gestational age. Longitudinal models updated risk using repeated measurements of blood pressure, biomarkers or fetal biometry, and some showed that changes in these measurements, including fetal growth velocity, improved prediction. We found no study that tested whether a womans earlier predictions add information beyond her most recent prediction. Individual-level uncertainty was rarely quantified in antenatal prediction, and we found no application of conformal prediction in antenatal care. Conformal methods have been used for repeated prediction in other clinical settings, but we found no evaluation of how often prediction sets include the actual outcome across a patients successive predictions.
authors: van der Hout-van der Jagt, M. B.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.26368140 v1

summary.background:
- Antenatal care: prenatal check-ups where risk is reassessed at several gestational-age windows (visits 1 to 3 here).
- Logistic regression: a standard statistical model that turns risk factors into a probability of an outcome.
- Conformal prediction: a method that wraps any model and returns a set of possible answers guaranteed to contain the truth at a chosen rate (here 90%); when the set holds both answers, the case is flagged for review.
- Mondrian conformal prediction: a variant that applies this guarantee separately within subgroups, here likely by outcome class.
- Coverage: the share of cases where the returned answer set includes the true outcome.
- nuMoM2b: a US cohort of nulliparous (first-time) pregnant women, 2010 to 2013.
- Fetal growth restriction and large for gestational age: abnormal fetal size relative to gestational age.
- Adjusted difference: a comparison between groups after statistically accounting for other factors; a confidence interval spanning zero means the result is not clearly different from no effect.
summary.one_liner: Secondary analysis of the nuMoM2b cohort testing whether a woman's trajectory of repeated logistic-regression risk predictions, and Mondrian conformal prediction sets with a "review" option, add information for five adverse pregnancy outcomes across three antenatal visits.
summary.plain: Doctors reassess a pregnant woman's risk of complications such as gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, and abnormal fetal growth at several prenatal visits. This study asks two things: whether a woman's earlier risk estimates tell us anything beyond her latest one, and whether a method that can answer "low risk", "high risk", or "needs review" stays reliable across repeated visits. The authors report that for fetal growth outcomes, women whose risk rose to high only recently showed somewhat higher outcome rates than those high-risk at every visit, though the confidence intervals include zero, and that reliability was close to target at each single visit but lower when all three visits were considered together.
summary.why: Most prenatal risk tools give one prediction at one point in time and force a yes or no answer, so this work looks at how risk changes over pregnancy and how much uncertainty is admitted. It may matter for designing repeated-use clinical tools, though the evidence is from one cohort with wide uncertainty, so its clinical value is not yet established.

title: Uncertainty-aware longitudinal prediction of multiple adverse pregnancy outcomes

abstract: ObjectiveTo compare the performance and cost of System One models (SOMs) with general-purpose large language models (LLMs) on biomedical tasks and evaluate confidence-based routing. Materials and MethodsWe evaluated three SOMs and three LLMs across seven datasets and eight endpoints covering question answering, error detection, structured extraction, and clinical-note assessment. Outcomes included task-specific performance, recorded inference cost and latency, and confidence calibration. Calibration data determined routing schemes and confidence thresholds to evaluate test predictions, with cost-matched random referral as a comparator. ResultsClaude Opus 5.5 had the highest primary performance on all eight endpoints. The strongest SOM, Jev, had competitive performance with the evaluated LLMs and cost less than 1% of Opus on most datasets. Three selected SOM-to-LLM routes reduced costs by 30.0%-71.7% relative to the receiving LLM, with modest reductions in performance. On one benchmark, SOM-to-SOM routing achieved 91.1% accuracy, compared with 82.3% and 82.2% for the individual models. DiscussionSOMs offered favorable performance-cost tradeoffs for most tasks. The magnitude of the advantages depended on task structure and prompting requirements. Confidence-based routing between SOMs and LLMs can leverage complementary model strengths and offers additional flexibility in performance-cost tradeoffs. The price advantages offered by SOMs can facilitate experimentation and development of workflows. This warrants further evaluation on closed datasets. ConclusionFor biomedical tasks with predefined choices, SOMs represent a competitive stand-alone or first-stage approach.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.26368126 v1

summary.one_liner: This paper benchmarks three "System One" models (SOMs) against three general-purpose large language models (LLMs) on seven biomedical datasets, comparing accuracy, inference cost, and confidence-based routing between the two model types.
summary.plain: Researchers asked whether smaller, cheaper AI models designed for fast, intuitive-style answers can handle medical and biomedical text tasks nearly as well as large general-purpose AI models. They tested both kinds on question answering, error detection, data extraction, and clinical-note assessment. The most capable large model scored highest on every task, while the strongest cheaper model was competitive and cost under 1% of that large model on most datasets.
summary.why:
The work points to a practical trade-off: cheaper models may be good enough for many predefined-choice biomedical tasks, and routing easy cases to them could cut costs. The text itself notes the findings still need evaluation on closed (held-out, non-public) datasets, so the advantages should be treated as preliminary.</why>
<parameter name="background">- Large language model (LLM): a general-purpose AI system trained on huge amounts of text, used here as the comparison baseline.
- "System One" model (SOM): the paper's term for a model class; the abstract does not define its design in detail, so it is unclear from the text how these models work internally.
- Inference cost and latency: the price and time to get an answer from a model.
- Confidence calibration: how well a model's stated confidence matches how often it is actually right.
- Confidence-based routing: sending a query to a cheap model first and passing it to a more powerful model only when confidence is low.
- Cost-matched random referral: a baseline that sends the same share of queries to the bigger model at random, to check whether routing by confidence actually helps.
- Endpoint: a specific task-and-dataset evaluation setting.
- Benchmark accuracy: the share of test items answered correctly.</why>
<parameter name="difficulty">intermediate

title: Evaluation of System One Models on Biomedical Texts

abstract: This paper studies the identification, estimation, and inference of long-term quantile treatment effects (LTQTEs) when short-term experimental data are supplemented with long-term observational data. Under a latent unconfoundedness framework, we establish identification of the LTQTE curve and derive the corresponding efficient influence functions. Building on these influence functions, we propose a semiparametrically efficient estimation procedure and develop a multiplier bootstrap method for uniform inference on the LTQTE curve, yielding valid simultaneous confidence bands over a continuum of quantile indices.
label: arXiv:2611.22984v1

summary.background:
- Treatment effect: the difference in outcomes caused by an intervention, compared with not receiving it.
- Quantile treatment effect: the effect at a given rank in the outcome distribution, such as the median or the 90th percentile, rather than the average.
- Experimental vs. observational data: randomized experiments assign treatment by chance; observational data record what happened without such assignment.
- Unconfoundedness: the assumption that, after accounting for observed characteristics, treatment is as good as random.
- Latent unconfoundedness: a version of this assumption that works through unobserved (latent) variables linking the short-term and long-term data.
- Efficient influence function: a tool that describes the most precise possible estimator for a quantity and underlies its variance.
- Multiplier bootstrap and simultaneous confidence bands: resampling methods that produce a band covering the whole curve of effects across quantiles with a stated probability.
summary.one_liner: The paper identifies, estimates, and performs uniform inference on long-term quantile treatment effects by combining short-term experimental data with long-term observational data under a latent unconfoundedness assumption, using efficient influence functions and a multiplier bootstrap for simultaneous confidence bands.
summary.plain: Researchers often want to know how a policy or treatment affects outcomes years later, but experiments that run long enough to measure those outcomes are rare. This paper asks how to estimate the effect on the whole distribution of long-term outcomes (not just the average) by pairing a short experiment with long-term observational records. The authors state an estimation method and a way to draw confidence bands across many quantile levels at once.
summary.why: Policy evaluation frequently needs long-run effects that short trials cannot observe directly, so methods that combine data sources could matter for fields such as labor economics and program evaluation. The text itself does not report empirical applications or comparisons, so the practical reach of the method is not shown here.

title: Long-Term Quantile Treatment Effects with Combined Experimental and Observational Data

abstract: This study examines how AI-based code reviewers reshape contribution behavior and maintenance dynamics in open-source software (OSS) communities. AI reviewers provide scalable, fast, and standardized evaluations. They reshape contributions as well as maintainers' workload. Leveraging the introduction of GitHub Copilot Reviewer on GitHub as a natural experiment in 2025, we investigate how AI review affects maintainers' workload and review efficiency as well as contribution behavior. We find that repository maintainers initially face a sharp increase in PR submissions and a higher review workload after the adoption of the AI reviewer. Over time, human contributions decline while the increase in bot-generated PRs is sustained. Interestingly, survival analysis reveals that AI reviewers increase review efficiency for human PR contributions, whereas bot PRs take longer to review and merge. Our findings suggest that while AI reviewers increase review efficiency, they aggravate the maintenance burden by encouraging more code contributions via humans and bots.
label: arXiv:2611.22793v1

summary.background:
- Open-source software: publicly shared code that anyone can view, use, or contribute to, often maintained by unpaid volunteers.
- Pull request (PR): a proposed code change submitted for review before it is merged into a project.
- Maintainer: a person who reviews, accepts, and looks after a project.
- Bot: an automated account that submits or handles changes without a human writing them.
- Natural experiment: a real-world event (here, a product launch) that changes conditions for some users but not others, letting researchers study its effects without running a controlled trial.
- Survival analysis: a statistical method for how long until an event happens, here how long until a PR is reviewed or merged; it is used here to compare review speed.
summary.one_liner: A natural-experiment study of how the 2025 rollout of GitHub Copilot Reviewer, an AI code-review tool, changed pull-request volume, maintainer review workload, and review speed in open-source projects.
summary.plain: Open-source software is built by volunteers and companies who submit proposed code changes, called pull requests, which project maintainers must check before accepting. This paper looks at what happened when GitHub added an AI tool, Copilot Reviewer, that automatically reviews these changes. The authors use the tool's 2025 introduction as a natural experiment to compare how projects changed afterward.
summary.why: Maintainer time is a real bottleneck for open-source work, and AI tools are being pushed as a fix, so evidence on whether they reduce or increase that load matters for software practice and for how we think about automation in volunteer communities. The text does not show the size of the effects or the statistical details, so the strength of the conclusions cannot be judged from it alone.

title: Does the AI Reviewer Alleviate or Aggravate the Maintenance Burden? Evidence from GitHub Copilot Reviewer

abstract: In the seminal Bertrand network game introduced by Babaioff et al. (2013), each seller posts a single price to captive buyers and to the markets it shares with neighboring sellers, where sellers cannot price discriminate across the markets. Although the existence of equilibria and polynomial-time algorithms to compute them in trees (Babaioff et al. (2013)) have been known, it has been a major open problem whether there exist efficient algorithms to compute them for general graphs. In this paper, we resolve this open question negatively by proving that computing any constant-error approximate Nash equilibrium in a Bertrand network is $\PPAD$-complete. This hardness holds even on sparse bipartite graphs of maximum degree five with constant integer market weights. Complementing our hardness result, we design an efficient polynomial-time approximation scheme (EPTAS) when both the maximum degree and the number of sellers with captive buyers are bounded. Beyond time complexity, since exact equilibria require randomizing prices over continuous intervals, another fundamental question left open by Babaioff et al. (2013) is whether an exact equilibrium can always be represented with a finite number of price intervals, \ie whether its structural complexity is finite. We resolve this question affirmatively by proving that every achievable equilibrium revenue profile can be realized by an equilibrium with structural complexity $O(2^n)$, which leads to an exact algorithm running in doubly exponential time. We further show that this bound is tight: there exist instances for which the unique equilibrium realizing target revenue profiles has structural complexity $Ω(2^n)$.
label: arXiv:2611.22216v1

summary.background:
- Bertrand competition: sellers compete by setting prices; here each seller posts one price for all its markets.
- Network game: sellers are nodes, and edges join sellers who share a market.
- Nash equilibrium: a set of strategies where no seller gains by changing its price alone; an approximate equilibrium allows a small slack.
- Mixed strategies: because exact equilibria require randomizing prices over continuous intervals, a seller's behavior is a probability distribution over prices.
- PPAD: a complexity class containing problems (like finding Nash equilibria) believed to be hard but not known to be NP-hard; PPAD-completeness is the usual evidence that a problem has no known efficient algorithm.
- EPTAS: an efficient approximation scheme whose running time is polynomial for each fixed accuracy, with the exponent fixed by parameters.
- Structural complexity: how many price intervals are needed to describe an equilibrium.
summary.one_liner: The paper shows that computing approximate Nash equilibria in Bertrand network pricing games on general graphs is PPAD-complete, and that exact equilibria always admit a finite (though possibly exponentially large) description of price intervals, with a matching lower bound.
summary.plain: The paper studies a model where sellers on a network each pick one price, and that price applies both to customers who only buy from them and to shared markets with neighboring sellers. It asks whether the stable pricing outcome (an equilibrium) can be found efficiently, and whether it can be described in a finite way. The authors report that finding an approximate equilibrium is computationally hard in general, and that exact equilibria can always be described with a finite number of price intervals, though that number can grow exponentially with the number of sellers.
summary.why: Earlier work had found equilibria and efficient algorithms only for tree-shaped networks, so this result marks where general efficient methods are unlikely to exist. It bears on the broader study of how computationally hard it is to find equilibria in games, which is a central topic in algorithmic game theory; the text does not discuss practical applications beyond this.

title: Settling the Time and Structural Complexity of Bertrand Networks

abstract: Research on reserve systems mainly considers static settings, formulating and studying choice rules for a given allocation problem. Dynamic settings are different in that the problem is not given. Over time, more positions become available, and each time the institution must build the current problem from its past. We distinguish the ledger, which stores information about earlier allocations, the account, which transforms these data into the current problem, and the choice rule, which selects an outcome for that problem. The same choice rule can implement very different policies under different accounts. If each new batch is assigned while holding earlier recipients and their categories fixed, then as batches shrink, over-and-above, the most generous reserve policy we study, can select nearly the same recipients as minimum guarantee, the most conservative one. Cumulative implementation uses a different account, which reconsiders the categories of earlier recipients, and prevents this compression. We characterize it by resource-release invariance. With arrivals or changes in priorities, the ordinary choice rule might reject an earlier recipient whose appointment has to be honored. We introduce and characterize retain, reassign, and boost (RRB) choice rules, under which every incumbent retains her appointment and can have her category changed. Combining RRB with individual-proposing deferred acceptance gives a strategy-proof mechanism under which each incumbent keeps her appointment or receives one she prefers. Applications include waiting lists in school and university admissions, public recruitment, and court-ordered corrections.
label: arXiv:2611.22116v1

summary.background:
- Reserve system: a rule that sets aside some places for members of particular categories (e.g., a minimum number for a group).
- Over-and-above vs. minimum guarantee: two reserve policies; the first is more generous in how it counts reserved seats, the second is more conservative.
- Deferred acceptance: a standard matching algorithm where applicants propose to institutions and institutions tentatively hold the best offers; it is strategy-proof, meaning truthful reporting is optimal.
- Strategy-proof: no participant gains by misreporting their preferences.
- Incumbent: someone already assigned a place in an earlier batch.
- Ledger / account / choice rule: the record of past allocations, the step that builds the current problem from it, and the step that selects outcomes.
- Resource-release invariance: the paper's property for cumulative implementation, roughly that freeing up resources is handled consistently; the excerpt does not define it precisely.
summary.one_liner: The paper studies reserve systems (affirmative-action-style category quotas) in dynamic settings where positions arrive in batches, separating the ledger, account, and choice rule, and proposes cumulative implementation and retain-reassign-boost (RRB) choice rules that keep incumbents' appointments while allowing their categories to change.
summary.plain: The paper is about how institutions that give reserved seats to groups, such as school places or public jobs, should handle seats that open up over time in batches rather than all at once. The authors separate three pieces: a record of past allocations, a rule that turns that record into the current problem, and the rule that picks the outcome. They show that with the simplest way of tracking past decisions, two reserve policies can end up choosing nearly the same people as batches shrink, and they propose a different accounting method that avoids this.
summary.why: Many real waiting lists and recruitment processes fill places in stages, so how past decisions are carried forward matters for fairness and for whether people already admitted keep their places. The text presents this as a conceptual and theoretical contribution; its practical impact and any empirical evidence are not described in the excerpt.

title: Reserve Systems in Dynamic Settings: Account Design and Inherited Rights

abstract: In many multi-agent systems, an agent's payoff depends on its own action and an aggregate of other agents' actions, rather than their individual decisions. This paper investigates decentralized equilibrium learning in Markov games (MGs) with such aggregative reward structures. However, existing decentralized learning algorithms for general MGs typically rely on bandit feedback, without exploiting the additional information available from aggregate observations. To exploit this information, we develop an aggregation-predictive stage-based V-learning algorithm with hybrid-feedback Exp3-IX. Using known local reward functions and observed aggregate quantities, each agent evaluates the immediate rewards of all candidate actions and predicts their immediate losses from historical aggregate feedback, while continuation values are learned from selected-action state transitions. The algorithm requires neither opponents' individual information nor knowledge of the transition kernel. We establish a high-probability regret bound that explicitly depends on aggregate prediction errors and retains the standard worst-case order. Under a regularity condition on adaptive stage lengths, the algorithm learns an $ε$-approximate coarse correlated equilibrium (CCE) within $\widetilde O(SA_{\max}T^5/ε^2)$ episodes and extends to correlated equilibrium (CE) learning. We further apply the algorithm to a renewable-rich microgrid with strategic prosumers and shared energy storage. Numerical results show smaller deviation gaps and lower gap-AUC than three learning baselines. Compared with representative demand-response rules, the learned policies exhibit weaker incentives for unilateral deviations while maintaining favorable user rewards, high renewable utilization, and relatively stable electricity prices.
label: arXiv:2611.22762v1

summary.background:
- Markov game: a repeated multi-player game where the situation (state) changes over time based on everyone's actions.
- Equilibrium (CCE / CE): a set of strategies where no player gains by unilaterally deviating; a coarse correlated equilibrium (CCE) and correlated equilibrium (CE) are two standard versions, with CE being the stronger notion.
- Regret: how much worse an agent does than the best fixed strategy in hindsight; low regret bounds mean learning converges efficiently.
- Bandit feedback: the learner only sees the reward of the action it chose, not of the alternatives.
- Aggregate feedback: observing a summary (like a total or average) of all players' actions.
- Exp3-IX: a known algorithm for learning under bandit feedback with an added bias-reduction step.
- Smart grid / prosumer: households that both consume and produce energy, often with storage and demand-response programs.
- Epsilon (ε): the small allowed gap from perfect equilibrium; the sample cost scales as 1/ε².
summary.one_liner: A decentralized V-learning method for Markov games with aggregative rewards, using hybrid bandit and aggregate-predictive feedback (Exp3-IX), with a regret bound, CCE/CE learning guarantees, and a smart-grid microgrid evaluation.
summary.plain: The paper studies how several self-interested decision-makers, such as households with solar panels sharing a battery, can each learn a stable way to act when their payoff depends mostly on the combined behaviour of everyone else. Standard learning methods usually only see the reward of the action they actually took. The authors design a method that also uses the group-level totals it can observe, which they report makes learning more informative, and they test it in a simulated microgrid.
summary.why: Many real systems, such as energy markets, traffic, and pricing, have payoffs that depend on aggregates, so using aggregate signals could matter there. The text reports theoretical guarantees and simulation comparisons against three baselines, but the evidence is limited to a single simulated microgrid setting, so its practical impact is not yet established.

title: Exploiting Aggregate Feedback for Decentralized Equilibrium Learning in Markov Games: A Smart Grid Application

abstract: Online platforms often struggle with inflated, uninformative user ratings. This issue can be mitigated by better design of the data collection mechanism, for example through changing the phrasing of user questions. Previous work optimizes a single rating scale to best distinguish the inherent qualities of items under binary feedback. In this paper, we demonstrate the power of utilizing different rating scales for different users. First, we show that a designer can always split a single rating scale into two to improve item rankings. Next, we formally characterize the optimal design of multiple scales as a series of 0-1 step functions whose threshold values are evenly spaced. Finally, we consider an adaptive model where subsequent rating scales can depend on the responses from previous users and items are ranked by their full sequence of responses, and show that adaptivity leads to exponentially greater distinguishing power. All in all, our theoretical results show that using multiple rating scales significantly improves item rankings on platforms.
label: arXiv:2611.23626v1

summary.background:
- Binary feedback: each user answers a yes/no style question (a rating scale reduced to two outcomes).
- Rating scale as a threshold: a question can be modeled as a step function that says "yes" when an item's underlying quality exceeds a cutoff.
- Ranking items: the goal is to order items by their true quality based on the aggregated responses.
- Multiple scales: different users see different cutoffs, so the pooled answers carry more information.
- Adaptive design: later users' questions can depend on how earlier users responded.
- Exponential gain: the improvement in distinguishing power grows exponentially, not just linearly, with the number of rounds or scales (as stated in the text).
summary.one_liner: The paper studies how platforms should design multiple binary rating scales (with thresholds spread evenly) for different users, showing that splitting one scale into two improves item rankings and that adaptively chosen scales can give exponentially better distinguishing power.
summary.plain: Online platforms like review sites often get ratings that are inflated and tell them little, partly because of how the question is worded. This paper asks whether giving different users different rating questions, each with a yes-or-no style answer, can help separate good items from mediocre ones. The authors prove that splitting one rating scale into two can always help rankings, and that using several scales, chosen adaptively based on earlier responses, can be far more informative.
summary.why: Better rating design affects which products, hotels or videos users see first, so the question matters for platforms and their users. The text is purely theoretical and gives no empirical tests on real platforms, so its practical impact is uncertain.

title: Two is better than one: optimizing binary rating scales for online platforms

abstract: Optimized Certainty Equivalents (OCEs) are an important class of risk measures for optimization and risk management that includes the Mean--Variance criterion, Expected Shortfall, the Entropic Risk Measure, and expectation. Despite their importance, economic axioms have not characterized OCEs. We propose a new axiom called Fair-Coin Compensation, which characterizes OCEs together with Strong Risk Aversion and Normalization. We interpret Fair-Coin Compensation through the fair assignment of two losses by a coin toss: transfers between two participants can remove the additional risk created by the random assignment. Adding further axioms yields sharper characterizations. Monotonicity yields standard OCEs; Positive Homogeneity, together with Prudence, yields Expected Shortfall; and Fair-Coin Independence yields the Entropic Risk Measure. We also axiomatize the Mean--Variance criterion using our novel axiom of Equal-Mean Randomization, which states that random assignment of two losses with the same expected value does not produce a risk measure above the average of their risk measures.
label: arXiv:2611.22119v1

summary.background:
- Risk measure: a rule that assigns a single number to an uncertain loss, indicating how risky it is.
- Certainty equivalent: the sure amount that a person would regard as equally good as an uncertain prospect.
- Axiom: a basic rule or property that a measure is assumed to satisfy; a characterization shows that the axioms pick out exactly one family.
- Examples named in the text: Mean-Variance (balances average loss and its spread), Expected Shortfall (average of the worst losses), Entropic Risk Measure (an exponential-weighted average of losses).
- Positive homogeneity: scaling losses by a factor scales the risk by the same factor.
- Monotonicity: a uniformly larger loss never gets a lower risk score.
summary.one_liner: The paper gives economic axioms (including a new Fair-Coin Compensation axiom) that characterize Optimized Certainty Equivalent risk measures, and shows which extra axioms single out Expected Shortfall, the Entropic Risk Measure, and Mean-Variance.
summary.plain: The paper asks how to justify a family of tools used to measure financial risk, called Optimized Certainty Equivalents, by listing simple rules of fair behavior that any such measure should follow. The authors add a new rule, Fair-Coin Compensation, based on a thought experiment where two people's losses are assigned by a coin toss and a transfer between them can cancel the extra risk the coin creates. Adding further rules narrows the family down to specific well-known measures.
summary.why: Economic axioms give a principled reason for choosing one risk measure over another, which matters for portfolio optimization and regulation. The text does not discuss applications or practical uptake, so its wider significance is uncertain.

title: An axiomatic foundation for optimized certainty equivalents

abstract: Call option prices, viewed as functions of strike and time-to-expiration, are totally positive of order 2 (TP2) if the ratio of the price of a higher-strike call to a lower-strike call increases with time-to-expiration. A corresponding property applies to put option prices. Prior work has developed conditions for these properties to hold for European options; here we establish these properties for American options. The key condition we require is that log returns on the underlying asset have a log-concave density. Gaussian densities provide an important special case. Within our framework, we show that total positivity properties hold more broadly for American than European options. Empirically, we find that violations of TP2 properties are infrequent, typically small, and reverse quickly. Trades that bet against violations achieve high hit rates. Violations are more frequent among European than American options, a pattern that is qualitatively consistent with our theoretical results.
label: arXiv:2611.23495v1

summary.one_liner: The paper proves that total positivity (TP2) monotonicity properties of call and put prices, previously known for European options, also hold for American options under a log-concave log-return density assumption, and tests these properties empirically.
summary.plain: Option prices are contracts whose value depends on a chosen price level (the strike) and how long until the contract expires. The paper asks whether a particular ordering pattern in these prices, called total positivity of order 2, holds for American-style options, which can be exercised at any time before expiry. The authors show it holds under a mild shape condition on the distribution of returns, and that it holds more broadly for American options than for European ones. They also report that violations in real market data are rare, small, and quickly corrected.
summary.why:
The result extends a known theoretical property from European to American options, which are the more common type traded in many markets, and it is supported by market data. The text does not say what practical trading or pricing consequences follow beyond the reported hit rates for bets against violations, so the broader importance is uncertain.</why>
<parameter name="background">- Call option: the right to buy an asset at a fixed strike price; put option: the right to sell at a strike.
- European option: exercisable only at expiry. American option: exercisable at any time up to expiry.
- Time-to-expiration: how many days or years remain before the contract ends.
- Log return: the logarithm of the ratio of an asset's price at two times; it measures percentage change.
- Log-concave density: a probability distribution whose log has a concave (bowl-down) shape; the Gaussian (bell curve) is a standard example.
- Total positivity of order 2 (TP2): a sign-consistency condition on a two-by-two grid of values. Here it means the ratio of a higher-strike to lower-strike option price rises as expiry gets further away.
- Arbitrage-free pricing: prices that do not allow riskless profit; violations of monotonic patterns can signal mispricing.
- Hit rate: the share of trades that profit when betting against a violation.</background>
<parameter name="difficulty">research-level

title: Total Positivity Properties of American Options

abstract: This study investigates the integration of sentiment analysis with machine learning models to forecast stock price movements using the Nvidia Corporation as a case study. Sentiment scores were derived from Nvidia-related financial news headlines using two sentiment analysis tools: FinBERT, a domain-specific tool, and TextBlob, a general-purpose tool. These scores were integrated into predictive frameworks based on bidirectional long short-term memory (Bi-LSTM) networks and multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) developed alongside historical stock price data. This study assesses the predictive performance over the entire observation period and across distinct market phases: bullish, stagnation, and strong bullish conditions. The findings indicate that sentiment features enhance predictive accuracy in specific contexts, particularly during stagnation phases, with TextBlob demonstrating superior performance to FinBERT in specific scenarios. In addition, Bi-LSTM models exhibit consistently superior performance in capturing temporal dependencies compared to MLPs. However, the impact of sentiment features diminished during strongly directional trends, such as those observed in strong bullish markets. The combination of FinBERT and TextBlob in the same dataset allows for a dual-perspective approach to sentiment analysis, thereby providing new insights into the dynamic relationship between market sentiment and stock price behavior. This research contributes to the existing literature on applying sentiment analysis to financial forecasting by advancing the integration of complementary sentiment tools and phase-specific evaluations.
label: arXiv:2611.23057v1

summary.background:
- Stock price forecasting: predicting future prices or price moves from past data and other signals.
- Sentiment analysis: software that scores text as positive, negative or neutral.
- FinBERT: a language model trained specifically on financial text.
- TextBlob: a general-purpose, simpler sentiment tool.
- MLP (multilayer perceptron): a basic type of neural network.
- Bi-LSTM (bidirectional long short-term memory): a neural network designed for sequences such as time series, reading data in both directions.
- Market phases: the study splits the period into bullish (rising), stagnation (flat) and strong bullish (sharply rising) conditions.
- The text gives only an abstract, so specific accuracy figures, data sizes and time spans are not available here.
summary.one_liner: The paper tests whether sentiment scores from Nvidia news headlines, produced by FinBERT and TextBlob, improve Bi-LSTM and MLP stock price forecasts across overall and market-phase periods.
summary.plain: Researchers tried to predict Nvidia's stock price movements using both past prices and the tone of financial news headlines about the company. They compared two kinds of prediction models and two tools that rate whether text sounds positive or negative. The reported findings are that the news tone helped mainly during flat (stagnant) market periods, and helped less during strong upward trends.
summary.why: It addresses a practical question in finance: whether news sentiment adds real predictive value beyond price history, and whether that value depends on market conditions. The text does not give enough detail to judge how large or reliable the gains are, so its significance should be considered tentative.

title: Integrating market sentiments for stock price prediction: A comparative study of Bi-LSTM and multilayer perceptions

abstract: Can we explain asset price movements even with hindsight? Reinterpreting Roll's (1988) AFA Presidential Address, "$R^2$," as a modern empirical exercise, we show that conventional macroeconomic, cash-flow, expectations, and flow variables explain less than 10% (often with negative $R^2$) of monthly U.S. equity return variation out of sample and lack daily observations. We use generative AI to extract reasons stated in Wall Street Journal market summaries while filtering out price-related language. These reasons explain around 30-40% of daily and monthly return variation out of sample. Their content spans interpretable themes, including corporate news, macroeconomic conditions, monetary policy, sentiment, and geopolitics.
label: arXiv:2611.22277v1

summary.background:
- Roll (1988) asked how much of stock return movement can be explained by public news and economic variables; his answer was "not much."
- R-squared (R²) is the share of variation in an outcome that a model accounts for; out-of-sample means tested on data not used to build the model.
- Negative R² means a model predicts worse than simply using the average return.
- Monthly and daily returns are the changes in stock prices over those periods.
- Generative AI here is used to read news summaries and label the reasons they give for market moves, while ignoring language that merely describes price changes.
- The Wall Street Journal market summaries are the text source.
summary.one_liner: Revisits Roll's 1988 finding that macro and firm variables explain little of monthly stock return variation, and tests whether reasons extracted from Wall Street Journal market summaries with generative AI explain more of realized daily and monthly returns out of sample.
summary.plain: Economists have long struggled to explain why stock prices move as they do, even after the fact. This paper revisits that question by checking how well standard economic indicators explain U.S. stock returns, then tests whether the reasons newspapers give for market moves, pulled out by an AI tool, do a better job. The authors report that the usual indicators explain under 10% of monthly return variation out of sample, while the AI-extracted reasons explain roughly 30-40% of daily and monthly variation.
summary.why: It bears on a long-standing puzzle in finance: why prices move so much more than fundamentals seem to justify. Using text explanations as a new source of data may be useful to researchers, though the summary only gives the abstract, so the robustness of the method is not yet clear.

title: Explaining Realized Returns: Roll's $R^2$ 40 Years Later

abstract: Currently, an increasing number of irregular signals are being defined within graph structures. This paper proposes a Least ln-cosh-based Adaptive Filtering for Graph Signal Processing (GSP LLAF) algorithm for offline/online graph signal estimation under various non-Gaussian noise conditions. Compared to the recently proposed Graph Adaptive Least Mean p-th Power (GSP LMP) algorithm, GSP LLAF eliminates the need for prior knowledge of the noise characteristics. Simultaneously, GSP LLAF addresses the limitation in estimation accuracy encountered by the Sign Algorithm for Graph Signal Processing (GSP Sign) and the Graph Signal Processing algorithm based on the Generalized Maximum Correntropy Criterion (GSP GMCC). Furthermore, the algorithm features low computational complexity and fast execution speed. To achieve a balance between convergence speed and estimation accuracy, a variable step-size variant, the Modified Variable Step-Size Least ln-cosh-based Adaptive Filtering Algorithm for Graph Signal Processing (GSP MVSS-LLAF), is proposed. In estimation experiments involving both static and time-varying graph signals, the proposed GSP LLAF and GSP MVSS-LLAF algorithms demonstrate fast, stable, and robust graph signal estimation performance under various non-Gaussian noise conditions, including Bernoulli-Gaussian (BG) modeled impulse noise, as well as alpha-stable, Cauchy, and Laplace distributions.
label: arXiv:2611.22559v1

summary.one_liner: Proposes a least ln-cosh adaptive filter, and a variable step-size variant, for estimating signals defined on graphs under non-Gaussian noise, compared against existing graph sign, GMCC and LMP algorithms.
summary.plain: Many measurements now live on networks rather than on a regular time line or grid, such as sensors linked to each other or users linked in a social network. This paper presents a new computational method that estimates the true values of such network-based signals while noise is messy and not the usual bell-curve kind, including sudden large spikes. The authors report that their method stays accurate and stable across several noise types in both fixed and changing signal tests.
summary.why:
Noise that is not well behaved is common in real sensor data, so a method that does not need advance knowledge of the noise type could be useful for network-based sensing. The text does not show real-world deployments, and its claims rest on the authors' own estimation experiments, so practical value is still unconfirmed.</why>
<parameter name="background">- Graph signal: data values attached to nodes of a network (e.g., sensors or users), where links show which nodes relate.
- Adaptive filtering: a method that updates its estimate step by step as new data arrives, offline or online.
- Non-Gaussian noise: noise that does not follow the familiar bell-shaped distribution; it can include rare, large outliers.
- Impulse noise (Bernoulli-Gaussian model): occasional large disturbances on top of normal noise.
- Alpha-stable, Cauchy, Laplace: named families of noise with heavier tails than the bell curve.
- Step size: how big each update correction is; larger steps converge faster but can be less accurate.
- Loss function: the rule measuring how wrong an estimate is; ln-cosh behaves like a squared error for small errors and like an absolute error for large ones, which limits the influence of outliers.</why>
<parameter name="difficulty">research-level

title: Least ln-cosh-based adaptive filtering algorithm for graph signal processing

abstract: Blind source separation (BSS) is increasingly needed in sensing architectures where mixtures are acquired by multiple remote devices but the inference itself is carried out centrally. In such systems, the sensors often cannot transmit their raw observations since the communication links are rate-limited, energy-limited, or both. The fusion center therefore must recover the latent sources from compressed versions of the mixtures. This setting raises questions that classical BSS models do not address directly: whether source identifiability survives compression, how separation accuracy changes under a specified compression model, and how the separation procedure should be modified to account for the statistical model induced by the compression stage. In this work, we develop a framework for distributed BSS from compressed mixtures that addresses these issues at three levels. First, we formalize identifiability under compression and establish a data-processing viewpoint showing that compression cannot introduce distinguishability that is absent before compression. Second, for mixtures of Gaussian sources with general covariance structures, we derive an idealized Gaussian rate-distortion-based Cramér-Rao lower bound benchmark for the interference-to-source ratio. Third, we develop practical compression-aware separation schemes based on subtractively dithered quantization together with debiasing at the fusion center for both fourth-order-cumulant-based and second-order-statistics-based methods. Simulation experiments demonstrate the resulting tradeoffs between communication rate and separation performance and the gains obtained by compression-aware separation in representative distributed sensing scenarios.
label: arXiv:2611.23024v1

summary.background:
- Blind source separation: recovering several unknown original signals from mixtures of them, without knowing the mixing process.
- Fusion center: a central node that combines data gathered from many sensors.
- Quantization: rounding measurements to a finite set of levels so they can be sent with fewer bits.
- Subtractive dithering: adding a known pseudo-random noise before quantizing and removing it afterward, so the rounding error behaves like independent noise.
- Debiasing: correcting the systematic bias that compression introduces into an estimate.
- Rate-distortion theory: the minimum number of bits needed to describe a signal to a given level of accuracy.
- Cramér-Rao lower bound: a theoretical floor on the error any unbiased estimator can achieve.
- Fourth-order cumulants and second-order statistics: summary statistics of signals (higher-order and covariance-based) that many separation methods exploit.
- Interference-to-source ratio: a measure of how much of one source leaks into the estimate of another; lower is better.
summary.one_liner: The paper develops a framework for blind source separation when sensors send compressed (rate-limited, quantized) versions of their mixtures to a central fusion center, covering identifiability under compression, a Gaussian rate-distortion-based Cramér-Rao benchmark for interference-to-source ratio, and compression-aware separation using subtractively dithered quantization with debiasing.
summary.plain: Several remote sensors each measure mixtures of hidden signals, but they can only send a compressed version of their data to a central computer, which must still separate out the original signals. The paper asks whether those signals can still be told apart after compression, how much accuracy is lost at a given data rate, and how the separation method should change to account for the compression. The authors report a theoretical benchmark and separation methods that are tested in simulations showing the trade-off between communication rate and separation quality.
summary.why: Sensor networks and edge devices often face tight bandwidth and energy limits, so deciding how to compress before central inference matters in practice. The paper ties together information-theoretic limits and practical quantization-based estimators, though the text only describes simulations, so how well the gains hold in real deployments is not established here.

title: Distributed Blind Source Separation from Compressed Mixtures

abstract: Neural vocoders have achieved remarkable progress in high-fidelity waveform generation in recent years, but most existing methods still rely on full-precision operators, leading to non-negligible storage and computational costs during inference. Binary neural networks (BNNs) provide an alternative direction by quantizing weights and activations to 1 bit. However, directly applying binarization to neural vocoders is rather challenging as it inherently incurs severe information loss. To this end, we propose BiVoC, a BNN-oriented time-frequency neural vocoder for high-fidelity waveform generation. Building on our previous full-precision RNDVoC framework, BiVoC adapts the inverse-problem formulation, range-null decomposition, and fineto-coarse non-uniform subband modeling to the 1-bit setting. Specifically, we develop a simple binarized convolutional unit to provide stable time-frequency feature modeling under binary representations. Furthermore, we analyze the quality-complexity sensitivity of different modules and propose a mixed-precision design to retain quality-sensitive components in full precision while binarizing computation-dominant parts. Extensive experiments are conducted on LibriTTS and multiple out-of-distribution benchmarks. Both objective and subjective results demonstrate that BiVoC substantially outperforms BNN variants obtained by directly binarizing existing vocoders, while achieving competitive performance against several mainstream full-precision vocoder baselines under much lower theoretical computational cost. These results demonstrate the promising potential of BNNs in the audio generation field. Codes and pre-trained weights are available at https://github.com/Andong-Li-speech/BiVoC.
label: arXiv:2611.22593v1

summary.background:
- Vocoder: the model that generates the audio waveform from an intermediate speech representation (such as a spectrogram).
- Full-precision network: a neural network whose weights and activations use ordinary floating-point numbers (many bits each).
- Binary neural network (BNN): a network that stores and processes values as 1 bit, greatly reducing memory and arithmetic cost, but losing information.
- Mixed-precision: keeping some parts of a network at higher precision while binarizing the rest.
- Time-frequency modeling: processing sound as a grid of frequency content over time.
- Inverse problem / range-null decomposition: a way of framing waveform reconstruction as recovering a signal from partial information, split into the parts the input determines and the parts it leaves open.
- LibriTTS: a public English speech dataset; out-of-distribution tests use data unlike the training set.
summary.one_liner: BiVoC is a binary neural network (1-bit weights and activations) time-frequency vocoder that adapts a prior full-precision framework (RNDVoC) and uses a mixed-precision design to keep quality-sensitive parts at full precision.
summary.plain: Neural vocoders are programs that turn compact speech representations into audio waveforms, but the best ones are large and costly to run. This paper tries to shrink them by storing and computing with just one bit per value, a technique called binarization, which is harder because it throws away a lot of information. The authors report that their model, BiVoC, does much better than simply binarizing existing vocoders and gets close to several standard full-precision ones at much lower theoretical computing cost.
summary.why: Making high-quality speech synthesis cheap enough for small devices is a practical goal, and the text suggests binary networks could be useful in audio generation more broadly. The text reports only objective and subjective listening results on LibriTTS and some out-of-distribution sets, and "lower cost" is a theoretical figure, not a measured speed or energy saving, so real-device benefit is not established.

title: High-Fidelity Binarized Neural Vocoder

abstract: Joint multi-talker ASR with speaker attribution and timestamps is particularly challenging when the speaker count is unknown and the output must follow a strict structure. We observe that Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)-only alignment of SpeechLLMs is brittle under dense overlaps, often leading to burst hallucinations and malformed speaker/timestamp tags. We propose a unified two-stage generative framework: (i) CoT-augmented SFT that infers the global speaker count before transcription, and (ii) GRPO-based constrained exploration guided by a Multi-dimensional Constraint-Aware Reward (MCAR) that directly optimizes permutation-invariant accuracy while enforcing counting, temporal, and structural constraints. On Libri3Mix and a Dynamic-Mix (2+3) set (speaker count unknown at test time), our model achieves 14.52%/9.24% cpWER and 1.95%/1.12% WDER, respectively, with GRPO yielding a 35%/54% relative cpWER reduction over SFT+CoT.
label: arXiv:2611.22627v1

summary.background:
- ASR (automatic speech recognition): software that turns speech into text.
- Diarization: working out who spoke when.
- Multi-talker / overlapping speech: several people talking at the same time.
- SpeechLLM: a large language model extended to take audio as input.
- SFT (supervised fine-tuning): training a model on example input-output pairs.
- Chain-of-thought (CoT): having the model write intermediate reasoning steps before its answer.
- GRPO (group relative policy optimization): a reinforcement-learning method that scores several sampled outputs against each other and favors the better ones.
- cpWER (concatenated minimum-permutation word error rate): a transcription error rate that allows speaker labels to be matched in any order; lower is better.
- WDER (word diarization error rate): the share of words assigned to the wrong speaker; lower is better.
- Reward: a score that tells the training process how good an output is.
summary.one_liner: A two-stage training approach for speech-language models that transcribes overlapping multi-speaker audio with speaker labels and timestamps, when the number of speakers is unknown, using chain-of-thought supervised fine-tuning followed by GRPO reinforcement learning with a constraint-aware reward.
summary.plain: The paper looks at the task of writing down what several people say at once in a recording, including who said what and when, without being told how many people are talking. The authors report that standard supervised training of a speech-language model is fragile when speech overlaps heavily, producing made-up text and broken speaker or timestamp tags. They add a step where the model first estimates the speaker count, then use a reinforcement-learning method that rewards correct output and penalizes malformed structure.
summary.why: Transcribing overlapping speakers with reliable labels is a hard problem for meeting transcription and similar tools, and the reported gains come from a specific training recipe. The text reports results on two test sets (Libri3Mix and a dynamic 2+3 speaker mix) but gives no comparison to other published systems, so how much it advances the field is unclear.

title: Beyond Mimicry: Constrained Exploration with GRPO for Joint Multi-Talker ASR and Diarization under Unknown Speaker Counts

abstract: Failure avoidance in complex robot-environment interactions is challenging because the underlying dynamics are difficult to model accurately, and available predictive models may not provide reliable derivatives. We present Sim2CBF, a failure-avoidance framework that solves the Control Barrier Function (CBF)-Safety Filter (SF) optimization problem using only forward-model evaluations, thereby avoiding differentiation of the predictive model. Specifically, we approximate the CBF constraint using finite differences and local linear interpolation over sampled control inputs while preserving failure-avoidance guarantees. The underlying CBF is implicit and constructed from backup-policy rollouts, enabling the use of expressive predictive models such as physics-based simulators and learned world models. Compared with purely sampling-based SFs, our formulation requires fewer control samples and yields less conservative behavior than direct nominal-backup blending. We evaluate Sim2CBF in simulation, hardware box-toppling, and vision-based control tasks, demonstrating its applicability to contact-rich and learned dynamics, as well as its adaptability to changes in the predictive model.
label: arXiv:2611.22954v1

summary.background:
- Control barrier function (CBF): a function whose sign marks safe versus unsafe states; keeping it nonnegative keeps the system safe.
- Safety filter: a layer that minimally modifies a nominal controller's command so it satisfies the safety condition.
- Backup policy: a fallback controller whose rollouts (predicted future trajectories) are used to define safety implicitly.
- Forward model: a simulator or predictor that maps current state and action to future states; no derivatives are needed.
- Finite differences: estimating how a quantity changes by evaluating it at nearby inputs.
- Sampling-based control: choosing among many candidate control inputs and checking each one.
summary.one_liner: Sim2CBF builds a control barrier function safety filter from backup-policy rollouts and solves its constraint using only forward evaluations of a predictive model, via finite differences and local linear interpolation over sampled controls.
summary.plain: Robots that interact with messy surroundings, such as pushing objects or tipping boxes, need a way to avoid failure even when their models of physics are imperfect. This paper proposes a safety layer that only needs to ask a simulator or learned world model "what happens if I do this?", without needing the model's mathematical derivatives. The authors report that it works in simulation, on a hardware box-toppling task, and in vision-based control, and that it needs fewer control samples than purely sampling-based filters and is less conservative than simply blending the nominal and backup controls.
summary.why: Safety filters are a common way to keep learned or hand-designed robot controllers from failing, and many of the most expressive models (physics simulators, learned world models) do not provide usable gradients. The approach may matter for robotics teams that want to add safety guarantees on top of such models, though the text alone does not show how it compares with other safety methods across wider settings.

title: Sim2CBF: From Forward Simulations to Implicit Control Barrier Function Safety Filtering without Model Derivatives

abstract: Data-driven predictive control (DDPC) predicts system responses from recorded trajectories, but nonlinear dynamics can limit the accuracy of fixed linear predictors. This paper studies geometric robust DDPC for trajectory tracking of a fully actuated manipulator using model-based feedback linearisation. A mechanical model maps virtual acceleration commands into joint torques, while recorded data capture residual dynamics arising from imperfect model parameters. The controller minimises worst-case prediction error over an open Grassmannian ball centred at the fitted trajectory subspace. Simulations on a planar 2R manipulator under gravity compare the proposed method with double-integrator model predictive control (MPC) and direct regularised data-enabled predictive control (DeePC). Results show improved tracking over double-integrator MPC despite increased torque effort, while performance relative to DeePC depends on the reference trajectory.
label: arXiv:2611.23215v1

summary.background:
- Model predictive control (MPC): choosing control inputs by repeatedly predicting future behaviour and optimising over a short horizon.
- Data-driven predictive control: making predictions directly from recorded input-output trajectories instead of a written system model.
- Feedback linearisation: using a nonlinear model to cancel out nonlinear terms so the system behaves approximately like a simple linear one.
- Fully actuated manipulator: a robot arm where each joint has its own motor, so every motion direction can be controlled.
- Robust control: designing for the worst case within a stated range of uncertainty.
- Grassmannian ball: a set of possible subspaces (here, ways the data's trajectory space can be tilted) lying within a set distance of a fitted one; used to describe the uncertainty.
- Double-integrator model: the simplest mechanical model, where acceleration is the input and position is its double integral.
- DeePC: a known data-driven predictive control method that uses regularisation to handle noise.
summary.one_liner: A geometric robust data-driven predictive controller, built on a feedback-linearised manipulator model, is tested in simulation against double-integrator MPC and regularised DeePC on a planar 2R arm under gravity.
summary.plain: This paper is about steering a robot arm so it follows a planned path, using past recordings of the arm's motion to predict how it will respond. A simple physics model first cancels most of the arm's nonlinear behaviour, and the recorded data are used to handle what the model misses. The authors test the method in computer simulation on a two-joint arm with gravity and report better tracking than a simpler prediction-based controller, though it uses more motor effort and does not clearly beat the other data-driven method in every case.
summary.why: Data-driven predictive control is an active area for systems where writing an accurate model is hard, and this work shows one way to combine a physical model with recorded data under worst-case uncertainty. The text reports only simulations on one small arm, so its wider value for real robots is unclear.

title: Feedback-Linearised Trajectory Tracking via Model-Informed Robust Geometric DDPC

abstract: Interacting particle systems with selection and mutation mechanisms arise in biological modeling, evolutionary optimization, and particle filtering methods. In this work we will consider the paradigmatic replicator-mutator PDE, which combines a diffusive component with a source term that depends on an external potential. We derive quantitative error estimates for the distance between the empirical measure of an unweighted particle system and the solution of the PDE. The proof uses a Wasserstein-1 distance with a bounded ground cost, which allows us to treat unbounded potentials on an unbounded state space. The key tools are the optimal coupling of newly resampled particles and, for the time-continuous limit, the use of a discrete-time killing resampling.
label: arXiv:2611.24472v1

summary.background:
- A PDE (partial differential equation) describes how a quantity, here a population density, changes smoothly over space and time.
- Replicator-mutator dynamics: a model where individuals grow or shrink according to fitness (selection) and occasionally change type (mutation, modeled as diffusion).
- Empirical measure: the distribution formed by placing a point mass at each particle's location.
- Wasserstein distance: a way to measure how far apart two probability distributions are, by the cost of moving mass from one to the other.
- Coupling: a way of pairing up particles from two systems so their distance can be bounded.
- Resampling: duplicating particles with high weight and discarding low-weight ones, here done so the particles end up unweighted.
summary.one_liner: The paper derives quantitative error bounds for how closely an unweighted interacting particle system with resampling tracks the solution of a replicator-mutator PDE, using a bounded-cost Wasserstein-1 distance to handle unbounded potentials on an unbounded state space.
summary.plain: This paper looks at a system of many randomly moving "particles" that are duplicated or removed depending on how well they fit an external landscape, and asks how well their overall distribution matches a smooth mathematical equation describing the same process. The authors measure the mismatch with a distance between probability distributions and prove explicit error estimates for it. The text indicates the approach works even when the landscape values are unbounded and the space is unbounded.
summary.why: Particle systems of this kind appear in evolutionary biology, optimization methods and particle filtering, so error bounds for their approximation of a continuous equation are useful for justifying such methods. The text does not discuss specific applications or compare results to prior work, so its wider significance is not established from the excerpt alone.

title: Convergence of replicator-mutator particle systems via bounded Wasserstein distance

abstract: We study parametric inference for interacting particle systems driven by independent fractional Brownian motions, based on discrete observations of all particles over a fixed time horizon. Our goal is to estimate an unknown drift parameter in the joint limit as the number of particles increases and the observation mesh vanishes. For $H>\frac 12$, we construct contrast based estimators by extending the discrete time least squares approach of Neuenkirch and Tindel to the interacting setting. For the rough regime $H\in(\frac 14,\frac 12)$, we introduce a modified contrast and use the stochastic sewing lemma to handle the first order approximations available from discrete observations. Our analysis combines the propagation of chaos for the associated fractional McKean Vlasov equation with estimates controlling the temporal discretization error. When the Hurst parameter and the diffusion coefficient are known, we establish strong consistency and asymptotic normality of the proposed estimators. The asymptotic results reveal an interplay between the number of particles and the temporal discretization: the convergence rate with respect to the observation mesh changes at $H=\frac 34$, while the asymptotic normality holds in both regimes considered. We further develop a joint estimation procedure for the drift parameter, the Hurst parameter, and the diffusion coefficient, extending quadratic-variation methods for fractional Brownian motion to the interacting particle framework. Numerical experiments illustrate the performance of the proposed estimators.
label: arXiv:2611.24287v1

summary.background:
- Fractional Brownian motion: a random path like Brownian motion, but with memory; the Hurst parameter H controls its roughness (H = 1/2 is ordinary Brownian motion).
- Interacting particle system / McKean-Vlasov equation: many particles whose motion depends on the average behaviour of the group; propagation of chaos means that as the group grows, particles behave increasingly independently, each like a single representative particle.
- Contrast estimator / least squares: a parameter estimate found by minimising a fit criterion built from the observed data.
- Consistency: the estimate converges to the true value as data grow. Asymptotic normality: the estimation error, rescaled, approaches a bell-shaped distribution.
- Stochastic sewing lemma: a tool for controlling sums of rough random increments.
- Quadratic variation: a sum of squared increments over a fine grid, used to estimate noise scale and roughness.
summary.one_liner: Parameter estimation for a system of interacting particles driven by fractional Brownian motions, using discrete observations of all particles, with consistency and asymptotic normality results for the drift parameter in the joint limit of many particles and vanishing observation mesh, including a rough regime H in (1/4, 1/2).
summary.plain: The paper studies how to estimate an unknown tuning value that governs how a large group of randomly moving particles drifts, when we can only watch their positions at discrete moments in time. The particles are pushed by correlated, rough random noise and also influence each other. The authors build estimators, prove they become accurate and behave like a normal distribution as the number of particles grows and the time gaps between observations shrink, and add a procedure that also estimates the noise's roughness and scale.
summary.why: Estimating parameters from coarse, noisy snapshots of many interacting systems is a basic problem in statistics applied to physics, biology and finance-style models. The text reports that the rate of convergence in the observation spacing changes at H = 3/4, which is a specific technical finding; its wider relevance beyond this model class is not shown in the text.

title: Parameter estimation for discretely observed rough fractional interacting particle systems

abstract: We introduce quadratic convexity for mean curvature flow in high codimension. It combines quantitative convexity in the mean curvature direction with control of the full second fundamental form. Strict Andrews-Baker quadratic pinching implies quadratic convexity, while the new inequality also admits curvature tensors beyond the critical quadratic ratio. For compact connected closed submanifolds of dimension $n\geq5$, we prove preservation of quadratic convexity and convergence in finite time to a round point. For compact connected submanifolds of dimension $n\geq4$ with spherical free boundary, we prove preservation and convergence to a round hemisphere in a uniquely determined $(n+1)$-plane. To our knowledge, this is the first such convergence theorem for spherical free boundary MCF in arbitrary codimension. The closed theorem requires additional quadratic pinching for $5\leq n\leq7$, and the free boundary theorem for $4\leq n\leq7$. For $n\geq8$, the necessary quadratic bound follows from quadratic convexity. We also establish preservation of ordinary quadratic pinching $|A|^2\leq c|H|^2$ under spherical free boundary flow for $n\ge2$ and $\frac{9}{8n}\leq c\leq\frac{4}{3n}$, including both endpoints.
label: arXiv:2611.24246v1

summary.background:
- Mean curvature flow: a family of shapes moving in the direction that reduces their area, with normal speed given by mean curvature.
- Codimension: how many extra dimensions a submanifold has beyond its own dimension; high codimension means the shape sits in a space with many extra directions.
- Second fundamental form: the object measuring how a surface bends in each direction; "pinching" means bounding it relative to the mean curvature.
- Round point: a point where the shape looks like a perfect sphere after rescaling, the typical end state of the flow.
- Free boundary: the submanifold has its edge lying on a fixed sphere and meets it at right angles; the limit is a round hemisphere.
