- Finite-time convergence: the shape reaches its limiting round form in a finite amount of time.
summary.one_liner: The paper introduces a "quadratic convexity" condition for mean curvature flow of high-codimension submanifolds and uses it to prove finite-time convergence to round points (closed case, n≥5 with extra pinching for 5≤n≤7) and to round hemispheres (spherical free boundary case, n≥4).
summary.plain: The paper studies how a curved, multi-dimensional shape evolves when it is allowed to shrink under its own curvature, a process called mean curvature flow. It defines a new convexity-type condition that controls the curvature in more directions than earlier criteria, and shows that shapes satisfying it stay that way and eventually become round. The authors state that, for shapes with a spherical free boundary, this is the first such convergence result in arbitrary codimension, and that some dimension ranges need an extra assumption.
summary.why: Convergence of shrinking shapes to round ones is a central question in geometric analysis, and the high-codimension setting is much harder than the hypersurface case. The paper's new inequality also covers some curvature tensors that the classical Andrews-Baker pinching condition does not, which may matter for future work on this flow; the text does not say more about applications.

title: Quadratic Convexity for Closed and Free Boundary High Codimension Mean Curvature Flow

abstract: We study the planar cubic--quintic nonlinear Schrödinger equation \[ i\partial_tu+Δu=-|u|^2u+|u|^4u, \qquad (t,x)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^2, \] with initial data $u_0\in H^1_x(\mathbb R^2)$. We prove scattering in both time directions when the mass of \(u_0\) equals the mass of the ground state for the focusing cubic equation. This resolves the nonradial threshold scattering problem posed by Murphy [\emph{Comm.\ Partial Differential Equations} \textbf{46} (2021), 2213--2234]. Together with the known subthreshold scattering theory and the existence of standing waves at every larger mass, this identifies the sharp mass range in which every $H^1$ solution scatters. The proof combines localized interaction Morawetz estimates with propagation estimates on moving halfspaces to control exterior kinetic energy.
label: arXiv:2611.23741v1

summary.background:
- Nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NLS): a model for waves whose behaviour depends on their own amplitude, used in optics, plasma and condensed matter.
- Cubic–quintic term: the equation has a nonlinear term of power 3 (|u|^2 u) with a focusing sign and a higher-order term of power 5 (|u|^4 u) that changes the long-run behaviour.
- Mass: the total squared size of the wave, conserved over time.
- Ground state / standing wave: a special stationary solution that holds its shape; the threshold is set by the mass of this shape.
- Scattering: the solution eventually behaves like a free wave, with its nonlinear self-interaction fading away over time.
- Nonradial: solutions are not assumed to be symmetric around a central point, which makes the analysis harder.
- H^1: the space of functions with finite energy and finite mass; the natural class of solutions.
- Morawetz estimates: integral inequalities that control how waves spread out, used as a key tool.
summary.one_liner: Proves scattering in both time directions for nonradial H^1 solutions of the planar cubic–quintic NLS at exactly the mass of the focusing cubic ground state, answering a question posed by Murphy (2021).
summary.plain: This paper studies a wave-like equation that describes how a light beam or wave packet spreads and interacts with itself in a two-dimensional medium. The question is whether solutions with a given amount of "mass" (total intensity) eventually disperse into free-flowing waves rather than staying bunched together. The authors show that at one specific threshold mass, every solution with no special symmetry disperses in both time directions.
summary.why: The text says this closes an open problem from Murphy's 2021 paper and, together with earlier results, pins down the exact mass range where every finite-energy solution scatters. This is a precise mathematical classification rather than a practical application; the text does not claim any physical or engineering consequences.

title: Nonradial threshold scattering for the planar cubic--quintic NLS

abstract: We study edge variation for the centered Hardy--Littlewood maximal operator on finite connected graphs. We determine the optimal uniform coefficient controlling the oscillation of the maximal function by the edge variation of the original function and derive two-sided estimates for the variational constant of an individual graph. These estimates involve point-mass tests, the diameter, and the number of edges. On star graphs, we determine the sharp constant for exponents greater than one and characterize all nonconstant real-valued extremizers for every exponent.
label: arXiv:2611.24180v1

summary.background:
- Graph: a set of points (vertices) joined by edges; "finite connected" means finitely many points, all reachable from each other.
- Maximal operator: for each point, take the largest average of the function over neighbourhoods centred there; this gives a new function.
- Edge variation: the total size of changes in a function's values across edges of the graph.
- Variational constant: a number bounding how much the maximal function's edge variation can exceed the original's.
- Star graph: one central point joined to several outer points.
- Exponent: a parameter p in the setting of function-size measures; results are stated for p greater than one.
- Extremizer: a function that makes the inequality as tight as possible.
summary.one_liner: The paper establishes sharp uniform and graph-specific bounds on the edge variation of the centered Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator on finite connected graphs, and determines the optimal constant on star graphs for exponents above one.
summary.plain: The paper studies a way of averaging values on a network of points connected by edges, called a finite graph. It asks how much the averaged values can jump along edges compared with the original values. The authors find the best possible general constant for this, estimate the constant for each individual graph, and work out the exact answer for star-shaped graphs.
summary.why: The text is limited to the abstract, so its wider significance is unclear. It concerns discrete versions of a classical tool from analysis, the maximal operator, which is used in areas such as harmonic analysis and partial differential equations; any connection to those applications is not described in the text.

title: Variational Estimates for the Hardy--Littlewood Maximal Operator on Finite Graphs

abstract: We study edge variation estimates for the centered fractional maximal operator on finite connected graphs. For $0<α<1$, we determine the optimal coefficient in the uniform estimate of the oscillation of the maximal function by the edge $p$-variation of the original function. We also obtain two-sided variation bounds involving the number of vertices and the diameter. On complete graphs, we prove that the sharp $(p,q)$ constant is $(1-n^{α-1})(n-1)^{1/q-1/p}$ for all $0<p\leq q\leq\infty$. On star graphs with $n\geq4$, we determine the sharp infinite-exponent constant and show that the sharp constant for $p=2$ equals $1-n^{α-1}$ if and only if $n^{α-1}\geq1/2$. Combining this with the known estimate for $p=1$, we also obtain sharp mixed estimates. Extremizers and counterexamples are given.
label: arXiv:2611.24189v1

summary.background:
- Graph: a set of vertices (nodes) joined by edges; "finite connected" means finitely many nodes, all reachable from one another.
- Maximal operator: replaces the value at a node with the largest (here, fractionally weighted) average over nearby nodes.
- Fractional exponent α with 0<α<1: weights decay with distance in a non-integer power, interpolating between local and global averaging.
- p-variation: a measure of how much a function changes along edges, using the p-th power of differences (p=∞ means the largest single jump).
- Sharp constant: the smallest coefficient that makes an inequality hold for all functions, shown with extremal examples.
- Complete graph: every pair of vertices is joined; star graph: one central vertex connected to all others.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves sharp edge-variation estimates for the centered fractional maximal operator on finite connected graphs, including exact constants on complete and star graphs.
summary.plain: The paper studies a way of averaging values over nearby points on a network of nodes and connecting lines, where a fractional exponent controls how quickly distant points lose influence. It asks how much this averaging can make a function's changes along the edges grow, measured in a "variation" sense. The authors find exact best-possible constants for the uniform oscillation estimate, and for complete graphs and star graphs they compute sharp constants and show when certain bounds hold.
summary.why: The text gives exact constants for specific graph families and shows when a sharp bound holds, which gives concrete benchmarks for this kind of inequality. Its connection to wider analysis or applications is not spelled out in the text, so any broader significance is unclear from this abstract alone.

title: Variational Estimates for the Fractional Maximal Operator on Finite Graphs

abstract: Suppose $G$ is a connected complex Lie group and $H$ is a closed complex subgroup. Then there exists a closed complex subgroup $J$ of $G$ containing $H$ such that the fibration $π:G/H \to G/J$ is the holomorphic reduction of $G/H$, i.e., $G/J$ is holomorphically separable and ${\mathcal O}(G/H) \cong π^*{\mathcal O}(G/J)$. In this paper we prove that if $G/H$ is pseudoconvex, i.e., if $G/H$ admits a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function, then $G/J$ is Stein and $J/H$ has no non-constant holomorphic functions.
label: arXiv:2611.24922v1

summary.background:
- Complex manifold: a space that locally looks like complex-number coordinates, with holomorphic (complex-differentiable) functions on it.
- Complex Lie group and homogeneous space G/H: a group of complex symmetries G acting transitively on the space, with H the stabiliser of a point.
- Pseudoconvex: a shape condition, here defined by the existence of a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function (a function that grows to infinity toward the edge and is "convex" in complex directions).
- Holomorphic reduction: the largest quotient of the space that still separates its holomorphic functions, so that it has the same holomorphic functions as the original.
- Stein space: a complex space that is holomorphically separable and has good cohomological properties; it is the complex analogue of an affine variety.
- Holomorphically separable: any two distinct points can be told apart by some holomorphic function.
summary.one_liner: For a pseudoconvex homogeneous complex manifold G/H (G a connected complex Lie group, H a closed complex subgroup), the paper shows that the holomorphic reduction G/J is Stein and that the fibre J/H carries no non-constant holomorphic functions.
summary.plain: The paper studies a certain kind of smooth space built from a symmetry group acting on a complex space, where the space is "pseudoconvex," a shape condition on how its boundary-like behaviour can be measured. It starts from a known result that such a space can be simplified by a canonical quotient, called the holomorphic reduction, which keeps all its complex-valued functions. The authors show that, under the pseudoconvexity assumption, this simplified quotient is a Stein space (a especially well-behaved type of complex space) and that the leftover piece has only constant complex functions.
summary.why: The result sharpens the general picture of how homogeneous complex spaces decompose, which is a structural question in complex geometry. The text itself does not describe applications beyond this classification-style statement, so its wider significance is unclear from the excerpt.

title: The Holomorphic Reduction of Pseudoconvex Homogeneous Manifolds

abstract: Diffusions with singular drifts appear naturally in the study of certain classes of interesting particle systems. Due to the singularities involved in the equations describing them, studying their dynamics is both interesting and challenging as they fall outside of the usual regularity assumptions on the vector fields in the literature. One needs to introduce and study them with different methods, with the use of symmetric polynomials being a particularly promising approach. In this expository work, we give an overview of some models and methods, and we further explore their interactions with the areas of Multiple Loewner chains (in particular, multiple Schramm-Loewner Evolutions), the new links with Random Matrices, and the novel area of Machine Learning for Singular Dynamics.
label: arXiv:2611.24610v1

summary.background:
- Stochastic differential equation: an equation describing motion with random noise, such as a particle jiggling while being pushed by a force (the "drift").
- Singular drift: a force that becomes infinitely strong or undefined at certain points, so the usual smoothness assumptions fail.
- Interacting particle system: many randomly moving objects whose motion depends on each other.
- Symmetric polynomials: polynomials unchanged when variables are swapped; used here as a tool to handle the equations.
- Loewner chain / Schramm-Loewner evolution: a family of growing random curves in the plane, used in modeling random shapes such as boundaries of random clusters.
- Random matrices: matrices with random entries, whose eigenvalues often form interacting particle systems.
summary.one_liner: An expository survey of stochastic differential equations with singular drifts, covering symmetric-polynomial methods and their links to multiple Schramm-Loewner evolutions, random matrices, and machine learning.
summary.plain: This is an overview paper about random motion of interacting particles whose governing equations blow up or behave badly at certain points, so standard mathematical tools do not directly apply. The author surveys several models and the methods used to study them, especially an approach based on symmetric polynomials. The text also points to connections with random curves, random matrices, and machine learning, though it is a survey rather than a report of new results.
summary.why: Particle systems with singular interactions show up in several areas of probability and mathematical physics, so a consolidated map of methods and links may help newcomers. The text does not state specific new theorems, so its value is mainly as an orientation guide, and I cannot judge from the abstract how complete the coverage is.

title: Recent developments in stochastic systems with singular dynamics -- a brief survey --

abstract: We prove that, for every inclusion $M\subset P$ of countably decomposable von Neumann algebras with a normal faithful conditional expectation, $M\subset c(P)$ has the weak Dixmier property, where $c(P)$ is the continuous core of $P$. By Haagerup's characterization, we have a completely new proof of Connes' bicentralizer conjecture, independent of the recent proof of Houdayer--Marrakchi. By Marrakchi's characterization, we also prove his relative bicentralizer conjecture. We also give a new solution to Kadison's problem after Popa and Marrakchi: further assuming that $M$ and $P$ have separable preduals and $M'\cap P=\mathcal Z(M)$, then there is a maximal abelian subalgebra of $M$ that is also maximal abelian in $P$. The proofs are based on a Poisson boundary theory for general von Neumann algebras, developed here as an extension of the theory of Das--Peterson for finite von Neumann algebras. Once this theory is established, the proofs for Connes' bicentralizer conjecture and Kadison's problem are short (around 7 pages each) and self-contained, relying only on results established by 1990. In both proofs, no separate treatment is needed for the type $\mathrm{III}_1$ case.
label: arXiv:2611.24787v1

summary.background:
- Von Neumann algebra: an algebra of bounded operators on a Hilbert space, closed under taking limits; a basic object of quantum mechanics and operator theory.
- Inclusion M ⊂ P: one such algebra sitting inside a larger one.
- Conditional expectation: a projection-like map from the larger algebra onto the smaller one that preserves its structure.
- Factor types (I, II, III): a classification of von Neumann algebras; type III_1 is a particularly subtle case.
- Continuous core: a construction that turns an algebra with a state-like weight into a new algebra with a canonical action.
- Weak Dixmier property: a property of an inclusion describing how the algebra's elements can be approximated by averages of unitaries, a tool for structure results.
- Maximal abelian subalgebra (MASA): a commutative subalgebra not contained in any larger commutative one.
- Poisson boundary: a measure-theoretic object associated with a random walk or group action, used here in a non-commutative setting.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves that continuous cores of inclusions of countably decomposable von Neumann algebras have the weak Dixmier property, which yields new proofs of Connes' bicentralizer conjecture and Marrakchi's relative version, and a new route to Kadison's problem on maximal abelian subalgebras, via a Poisson boundary theory for general von Neumann algebras.
summary.plain: This is research in the theory of operator algebras, which are infinite-dimensional analogues of matrix algebras used to describe quantum systems. The paper addresses two long-standing open questions in that area: Connes' bicentralizer conjecture and Kadison's problem about maximal abelian subalgebras. The authors build a general "Poisson boundary" framework, extending an existing theory for finite algebras, and use it to give new, shorter proofs of both results under the stated hypotheses.

title: A Poisson boundary solution to Connes' bicentralizer conjecture and Kadison's problem on MASA

abstract: We look at the Liouville property (triviality of harmonic functions) of topological groups G relative to a compact subgroup K. We show that Gelfand pairs have this property. Furthermore, we show that this property holds if and only if G admits a product decomposition G = K S for an amenable subgroup S. We identify the Poisson and Furstenberg boundaries of these groups. This applies in particular to reductive algebraic groups over local fields.
label: arXiv:2611.24299v1

summary.background:
- Group: a set with a consistent way of combining elements (e.g. rotations).
- Topological group: a group where nearby elements are well defined, so it can be studied continuously.
- Compact subgroup: a subgroup that is closed and bounded in a suitable sense, like a rotation group of a sphere.
- Amenable group: one that admits averaging rules, roughly "no paradoxical decomposition"; a standard notion in analysis.
- Harmonic function: a function equal to the average of its neighbours under a random step rule.
- Liouville property: every bounded harmonic function is constant.
- Poisson and Furstenberg boundaries: the spaces where random walks on the group settle down.
- Gelfand pair: a pair of groups where a certain averaging algebra is commutative.
- Reductive algebraic group over a local field: matrix-type groups over fields like the p-adic numbers or real numbers.
summary.one_liner: The paper studies the Liouville property (no non-constant bounded harmonic functions) for topological groups relative to a compact subgroup, shows Gelfand pairs have it, characterises it via a product decomposition G = KS with S amenable, and identifies Poisson and Furstenberg boundaries, with application to reductive algebraic groups over local fields.
summary.plain: The paper asks when a group that contains a compact piece behaves in a "rigid" way when you random-walk on it: specifically, whether every bounded function that stays balanced under averaging must be constant. The authors show this holds for Gelfand pairs, and that it holds exactly when the group can be written as a product of a compact subgroup and a amenable subgroup. They also identify the boundaries that random walks converge to, and note this covers reductive algebraic groups over local fields.
summary.why: Boundaries of groups describe where random walks end up, and they connect harmonic analysis, probability and geometry of groups. The text gives a clean if/only if criterion, but its wider significance beyond this setting is not stated in the text, so I cannot say more.

title: Boundaries of groups with compact-by-amenable decomposition

abstract: This paper studies vertex operator superalgebras strongly generated by their weight-1, weight-$\frac{3}{2}$ and weight-2 homogeneous subspaces. The presence of a nontrivial weight-1 subspace introduces derivative and quadratic current terms in weight-2. To address this, we use low-weight quasi-primary projections to identify two canonical commutative associative algebras, $\mathcal{A}$ and $A$, within the weight-2 subspace. We demonstrate that the algebraic structures of the generating subspaces are encoded by a quadruple that generalizes Lie--Rinehart algebras and their weak representations. This quadruple yields necessary and sufficient compatibility conditions for constructing an associated Lie superalgebra $\mathcal{L}(\mathfrak{g},A,U)$. Based on this, we construct a family of universal vertex operator superalgebras $V_{\mathcal{L}}(\ell,0)$ and establish a reconstruction theorem for their simple quotients under certain conditions. If $A$ is finite-dimensional, we prove that its orthogonal idempotent decomposition into local Artinian summands naturally induces a tensor product isomorphism of the corresponding vertex operator superalgebras. In addition, our general construction encompasses many vertex operator superalgebras, such as superconformal algebras and generalized $\mathrm{BMS}_3$ (super)algebras.
label: arXiv:2611.24139v1

summary.background:
- Vertex operator superalgebra: a graded algebraic structure with both even and odd (fermion-like) parts, used to describe two-dimensional conformal field theory.
- Weight: the grading by scaling dimension; weight-1, weight-3/2 and weight-2 pieces are the generators studied here.
- Strong generation: the whole structure is built from the given low-weight pieces.
- Quasi-primary: a vector annihilated by the lowest-order part of the symmetry action, used to project out unwanted terms.
- Lie superalgebra: a Lie algebra extended with odd elements.
- Lie–Rinehart algebra: a pairing of a Lie algebra acting on a commutative algebra by derivations.
- Commutative associative algebra, idempotent, Artinian: standard algebra notions; an idempotent decomposition splits the algebra into orthogonal pieces.
- Universal object and simple quotient: the largest structure with given generators, and its irreducible version.
summary.one_liner: The paper classifies and constructs vertex operator superalgebras strongly generated by weight-1, weight-3/2 and weight-2 subspaces, using two canonical commutative algebras inside the weight-2 part and a Lie–Rinehart-type quadruple that encodes compatibility conditions for an associated Lie superalgebra.
summary.plain: This paper is about a family of algebraic structures that behave like symmetry systems in physics: they are built from pieces graded by "weight" (a measure of how the pieces scale). The authors show how the rules among the building pieces can be packed into a single four-part object, and they use it to construct a family of these structures and describe their simple versions. They also state that when one of the key algebras is finite-dimensional, it splits into a tensor product of simpler pieces.
summary.why: The work offers a general framework that the authors say includes known examples such as superconformal algebras and generalized BMS_3 (super)algebras, which is why it may matter to people working on conformal field theory and related symmetry algebras. The text does not show wider applications, so its reach beyond this algebraic setting is uncertain.

title: Canonical weight-two algebras and strongly generated vertex operator superalgebras

abstract: We introduce the notion of semi-exact functors between abelian categories, which are characterised by either preserving or breaking exactness of sequences. We prove semi-exact functors are always exact with respect to a canonically determined exact structure. For a symmetric tensor category $\Cs$, we define a support theory by considering all $\Bbbk$-linear symmetric monoidal, semi-exact functors $\mathscr{C}\to\operatorname{Ver}_{p^\infty}$ up to equivalence, and conjecture that it agrees with the Balmer spectrum of the stable category when $\mathscr{C}$ is finite. We prove a weak form of this conjecture and other results for Tannakian categories and in characteristic 0. Critical to the positive characteristic case is a functor constructed by Coulembier and Flake who were interested in higher Frobenius functors. We show that their construction, which relies on the theory of abelian envelopes, gives a natural source for semi-exact functors, and at least in the Tannakian setting gives all $\Bbbk$-linear, symmetric monoidal, semi-exact functors.
label: arXiv:2611.24471v1

summary.background:
- Category: a collection of objects and maps between them, used to organise algebraic structures.
- Abelian category: a category that behaves like modules over a ring, with kernels and cokernels.
- Exact sequence: a chain of maps where the image of each map equals the kernel of the next; exact functors preserve these.
- Tensor (symmetric monoidal) category: a category with a compatible notion of multiplying objects together.
- Field k and characteristic p: the number system base; positive characteristic means arithmetic wraps around modulo p.
- Tannakian category: a tensor category that arises as representations of a group.
- Balmer spectrum: a topological space built from a tensor triangulated category, used to classify its ideals.
- Frobenius functor: a functor tied to raising elements to the p-th power in characteristic p.
summary.one_liner: The paper introduces semi-exact functors between abelian categories, shows they are exact for a canonical exact structure, and uses them to define a support theory for symmetric tensor categories that is conjectured to match the Balmer spectrum of the stable category when the category is finite.
summary.plain: This work is about the abstract algebra of "categories" (collections of mathematical objects and the structure-preserving maps between them). The authors study a class of maps called semi-exact functors, which either preserve or break exact sequences, a kind of chain of objects that is neatly balanced. They show such maps always behave well with respect to a suitably chosen notion of exactness, and they use them to build a way of assigning "support" to symmetric tensor categories.
summary.why: The support theory is meant to match an existing invariant, the Balmer spectrum, which organises the structure of tensor triangulated categories, so the work links two frameworks. The authors state the main matching is only conjectured and proved in a weak form and in special cases (Tannakian categories and characteristic 0), so its full scope is not yet settled.

title: Semi-exact functors and the conjecture of Coulembier and Flake

abstract: Given a quadratic number field $K$ we show that the $abc$ conjecture over $K$ implies that $\mathbb{Z}$ is Diophantine in $K$ and, hence, a negative answer to Hilbert's tenth problem over $K$. More generally, the same conclusions hold for an arbitrary number field $K$ provided that the $abc$ conjecture holds over $K$ and that there is an elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$ whose rank is positive and does not increase over $K$.
label: arXiv:2611.24748v1

summary.background:
- Diophantine equation: a polynomial equation whose solutions are sought in whole numbers (or numbers from a given field).
- Hilbert's tenth problem: whether there is a general algorithm to decide if any Diophantine equation has a solution; the answer is negative over the integers.
- Diophantine definability: a set is Diophantine in a field if it is the set of solutions to some polynomial equation system with extra unknowns.
- Number field: a finite extension of the rational numbers, such as the field obtained by adjoining the square root of 2.
- abc conjecture: an unproven statement relating the prime factors of three numbers a, b, c with a + b = c; it is widely studied but not proven.
- Elliptic curve and rank: a curve defined by a cubic equation; its rank is the size of its free family of rational points, a measure of how many independent solutions it has.
summary.one_liner: Conditional on the abc conjecture holding over a number field K, the paper shows that the integers Z are Diophantine in K (hence Hilbert's tenth problem has a negative answer over K), and gives a more general criterion involving an elliptic curve of positive rank that does not gain rank over K.
summary.plain: This paper is about Hilbert's tenth problem, which asks for a general method to decide whether a polynomial equation with integer unknowns has a solution. The author works over number fields, which are extensions of the ordinary rational numbers. The paper shows that if a well-known open conjecture called the abc conjecture holds, then the ordinary whole numbers can be described by polynomial equations in these fields, which rules out a general solving method there.
summary.why: Hilbert's tenth problem was settled negatively over the integers by Matiyasevich and others, and the open question is whether the same holds over larger number fields. This result links that question to the abc conjecture, a major unproven statement about how prime factors add up, so it shows how one open problem could resolve another. The result is conditional on abc, so it does not settle the question outright.

title: On Hilbert's tenth problem for number fields

abstract: Superspecial curves of genus two over a prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$, and the rational $(2,2)$-isogenies between their Jacobians, are the vertices and edges of the graph on which genus-two isogeny-based cryptography is built. Let $C$ be such a curve, with Jacobian $J$ and Frobenius endomorphism $π$. We show that $π^2 = p\,α_*$ for a unique automorphism $α$ of $C$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$ whose action on the Weierstrass points is the square of that of Frobenius. For $p \ge 7$ this gives the list of Frobenius types of the Weierstrass points: eight types, each with its Weil polynomial, a congruence condition on $p$, and its number 15, 3, 3, 7, 1, 1, 3 or 1 of $\mathbb{F}_p$-rational $(2,2)$-kernels; when all Weierstrass points are rational, the 2-Tate pairing on $J[2]$ is determined by $p \bmod 8$. We then prove closed formulas, in terms of class numbers of imaginary quadratic orders and of $ζ_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt p)}(-1)$, for the mass of the curves of each type and for the mass of the rational kernels whose quotient is a product of elliptic curves. For $π^2 = \pm p$ the total masses are due to Ibukiyama and to Xue and Yu; our proofs use the 2-adic Tate modules, the symmetry of the Richelot correspondence and Eichler's mass formula, and, for the other curves, modules over orders of a quartic CM field. The kernels are counted through gluings of supersingular elliptic curves. As a consequence, the proportion of rational kernels with decomposed quotient is of order $p^{-1/2}(1+L(1,χ))$, where $χ$ is the quadratic character of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-p})$. All formulas agree with an exact enumeration for the 37 primes $7 \le p \le 173$. Finally we describe the graph of $\mathbb{F}_p$-rational Richelot isogenies, which is far from connected in the range computed, and discuss what these results say about its use in isogeny-based cryptography.
label: arXiv:2611.23694v1

summary.background:
- Elliptic and genus-two curves: smooth algebraic curves; genus two means a curve with two "handles", and its Jacobian is a higher-dimensional group variety.
- Finite field F_p: arithmetic on integers modulo a prime p.
- Superspecial curve: a curve whose Jacobian is as highly symmetric as possible in characteristic p; these are the nodes of the graph.
- Frobenius endomorphism: the map raising coordinates to the p-th power; its action on Weierstrass points (the six branch points of a genus-two curve) determines a "Frobenius type".
- Weil polynomial: a polynomial encoding how many points a curve has over finite fields.
- (2,2)-isogeny / Richelot isogeny: a structured map between Jacobians whose kernel is a set of 2-torsion points; a "rational" kernel is one fixed by Frobenius.
- Class number and mass: counting invariants of imaginary quadratic fields; a mass is a weighted count of curves, with Eichler's mass formula used to compute it.
- Isogeny-based cryptography: schemes whose security relies on the difficulty of finding paths between such curves.
summary.one_liner: The paper classifies Frobenius types and rational (2,2)-kernels of superspecial genus-two curves over prime fields and proves class-number mass formulas for them, checked against enumeration for primes up to 173.
summary.plain: The paper studies a specific family of geometric curves over the integers modulo a prime, the kind used as building blocks in some proposed cryptosystems. It sorts these curves by how a basic symmetry (the Frobenius map) acts on their special points, and it counts the curves and the rational "kernels" (structures that link them to other curves) in each class. The counts are given by exact formulas involving class numbers, and they match a brute-force computation for all 37 primes from 7 to 173.
summary.why: The results give exact counts for the graph of connections that isogeny-based cryptography relies on, and the paper reports that this graph of rational Richelot isogenies is far from connected in the range computed, which bears on whether that graph can be used for cryptography. The text does not state any direct cryptographic consequence beyond this observation, so the practical impact is a matter for specialists to judge.

title: Superspecial curves of genus two over prime fields: Frobenius types and rational (2,2)-kernels

abstract: We tropicalize the Grassmannian and the flag variety of the algebraic group of type $G_2$. The two tropical varieties are strictly contained in the associated Dressians. Their points are trees in the $G_2$-forest and decorated trees in the $G_2$-orchard. These form hexagons in incidence geometry. We classify all toric degenerations and their Newton-Okounkov polytopes. Mukai theory leads us to tropical canonical curves of genus 10. This article serves as a blueprint for studies of reductive groups in tropical geometry.
label: arXiv:2611.24456v1

summary.background:
- Algebraic variety: the solution set of a system of polynomial equations.
- Tropical geometry: a piecewise-linear "shadow" of an algebraic variety, obtained by replacing multiplication with addition and taking minimums, so curved objects become polyhedral ones.
- Grassmannian and flag variety: standard spaces parametrizing subspaces and nested subspaces; here they are attached to the exceptional group G2.
- Dressian: a combinatorial space containing the tropical Grassmannian, whose points are tree-like objects.
- Toric degeneration and Newton-Okounkov polytope: tools for simplifying a variety into a toric (lattice-polytope) form that is easier to study.
- Mukai theory: a classical correspondence relating certain curves of genus 10 to the G2 setting.
- Reductive group: a class of symmetry groups (like G2) central to Lie theory.
summary.one_liner: The paper tropicalizes the Grassmannian and flag variety of the exceptional algebraic group G2, showing their tropical varieties sit strictly inside the associated Dressians and describing them via G2-forests and G2-orchards, with classification of toric degenerations and Newton-Okounkov polytopes.
summary.plain: This paper studies a piece of algebraic geometry: shapes that describe solutions to polynomial equations, here tied to G2, one of the exceptional symmetry groups. The authors replace these shapes with a simpler "tropical" version made of straight-line pieces and trees, which is easier to count and compare. The text reports that the tropical versions are strictly contained in larger known spaces (the Dressians), that their points are described as trees in a "G2-forest" and decorated trees in a "G2-orchard", and that the resulting structures form hexagons in incidence geometry.
summary.why: The work is a foundational example for applying tropical geometry to reductive groups beyond the more familiar type A case, and the authors call it a blueprint for such studies. The text also links it to Mukai theory and tropical canonical curves of genus 10, though the abstract does not explain those connections in detail, so their full significance is unclear from this text alone.

title: Tropical Geometry of $G_2$

abstract: An exceptional collection in the derived category of a smooth projective variety may fail to generate the whole category, and this failure cannot be detected by K-theory or by Hochschild homology. Kuznetsov's height detects it through Hochschild cohomology, that is, through natural transformations from the identity functor to its shifts. We replace the identity functor by an arbitrary endofunctor $F$ and define the height of a collection with coefficient $F$. It controls, in a range of degrees, the restriction of natural transformations $\mathrm{id}\to F$ to the orthogonal complement of the collection, and it is computed from the collection by a finite complex. For collections of line bundles on surfaces whose Hom divisors have nonnegative canonical degree, the tensor product with a skyscraper sheaf has height exactly two, and the projections of skyscraper sheaves form a two-dimensional family of point-like objects in the orthogonal complement. We apply these tools to Orlov's rationality conjecture. A smooth projective complex surface is rational if its derived category has a full exceptional collection in which all members except possibly one are line bundles, or one that consists of at most three completely orthogonal blocks of arbitrary objects; we also obtain rationality in several cases with four blocks or with a hereditary component. If $S\times\mathbb P^1$ has a full exceptional collection of the form $(M_i\boxtimes\mathcal O(a_i))$, then the $M_i$ with relative degrees of a fixed parity form a full exceptional collection on $S$; consequently $S$ is rational whenever $S\times\mathbb P^1$ has a full exceptional collection of line bundles. Finally, we show that the general case of the conjecture for surfaces is equivalent to the surjectivity and injectivity of two maps in Hochschild cohomology.
label: arXiv:2611.23707v1

summary.background:
- Smooth projective variety: a smooth geometric object (here a complex surface) cut out by polynomial equations in projective space.
- Derived category: an algebraic universe of complexes of sheaves attached to a variety; its objects can be thought of as generalized spaces.
- Exceptional collection: a sequence of objects with no maps between them in the wrong directions and with trivial self-maps; a full one generates the whole category.
- Line bundle: a basic twisted-function object on a variety, the algebraic analogue of a sheaf of rank one.
- Skyscraper sheaf: an object concentrated at a single point.
- Hochschild cohomology: an invariant measuring natural transformations from the identity functor to its shifts; Kuznetsov's height is defined through it.
- Endofunctor: a functor from a category to itself; the paper replaces the identity by an arbitrary one.
- Rational surface: a surface birational to the projective plane, i.e. essentially a plane in disguise.
- Orlov's rationality conjecture: the claim that a surface is rational exactly when its derived category has a suitable full exceptional collection.
summary.one_liner: The paper generalizes Kuznetsov's height of exceptional collections from the identity functor to an arbitrary endofunctor F, applies it to line bundles and skyscraper sheaves on surfaces, and uses it to study Orlov's rationality conjecture for smooth projective complex surfaces.
summary.plain: The paper studies whether a geometric object (a smooth surface) can be described by a complete set of standard building blocks in its "derived category," a bookkeeping universe of objects and maps. It introduces a generalized measure, called the height with coefficient F, of how far a set of building blocks fails to generate everything, and uses it to make partial progress on a conjecture of Orlov about when surfaces are rational. The text claims several special cases are settled, such as surfaces whose product with the projective line has a full collection of line bundles, and that the general case reduces to two maps being bijective.
summary.why: Rationality of surfaces is a classical question, and Orlov's conjecture links it to a purely algebraic description via exceptional collections, so partial results and an exact reformulation are useful to specialists. The text does not indicate wider consequences beyond this area, and I have not checked the proofs or how the new results compare with prior work.

title: Functorial height and Orlov's rationality conjecture

abstract: Persistence diagrams are widely used in topological data analysis to summarize topological and geometric structure in data. We study nonparametric regression where inputs are persistence diagrams and outputs are real-valued. Using kernel-based local averaging estimators defined directly over diagram space with Wasserstein distance, we establish consistency and derive bounds on the rate of convergence under suitable assumptions in the $L^2$-theory. We also present computational experiments that demonstrate strong performance of the proposed estimator, particularly in low data regimes.
label: arXiv:2611.25295v1

summary.background:
- Persistence diagram: a compact summary of the holes and loops in data across scales, drawn as a set of points.
- Wasserstein distance: a way to measure how far apart two sets of points are, by the minimum cost of moving one onto the other.
- Nonparametric regression: predicting an outcome from inputs without assuming a fixed formula, often by averaging nearby examples.
- Kernel estimator: a local average where closer inputs get more weight.
- Consistency and convergence rate: the estimator approaches the true answer as data grows, and the rate says how fast.
- L^2 theory: error is measured as the average squared difference between prediction and truth.
summary.one_liner: The paper studies kernel-based local averaging regression where the inputs are persistence diagrams, compared via Wasserstein distance, and proves consistency and convergence-rate bounds in the L^2 sense.
summary.plain: The paper looks at how to predict a single number from a shape summary of data, called a persistence diagram, which records the loops and holes that appear in a dataset at different scales. The authors build a prediction method that works directly on these diagrams, averaging outcomes from similar diagrams, and measure how similar two diagrams are with a distance called the Wasserstein distance. They prove the method gets closer to the right answer as data grows, and report experiments where it performs well, especially when data is scarce.
summary.why: Many scientific datasets are better described by their shape than by a fixed list of numbers, so a predictor that works directly on shape summaries could be useful in areas like materials science or biology. The text does not say how it compares with other methods beyond the claimed strong performance in low-data settings, so its practical reach is still unclear.

title: Kernel Regression using Persistence Diagrams

abstract: Sivek conjectured that, for every nontrivial knot $K\subset S^3$, the dimension of the next-to-top term of $\widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}(K)$ is at least that of the top term. We show that this inequality holds for knots with $U$-torsion order one in either the minus theory $\mathrm{HFK}^-$ or the unoriented theory $\mathrm{HFK}'$. Combined with Eftekhary's work, this implies that knots with rational unknotting number one satisfy the conjecture. In particular, the result applies to every nontrivial satellite knot whose pattern can be unknotted in the solid torus by a single rational tangle replacement.
label: arXiv:2611.24539v1

summary.background:
- Knot: a closed loop in 3D space, considered up to bending and stretching without cutting.
- Knot Floer homology (HFK): an algebraic invariant assigned to a knot, built from counting solutions to equations in a related space; it comes as a graded collection of vector spaces.
- "Top" and "next-to-top" terms: the pieces of this invariant at the two highest grading levels.
- U-torsion order: a measure of how many times the algebraic operator U must be applied before a class vanishes; order one is the simplest case.
- Unknotting number: the minimum number of crossing changes needed to turn a knot into the unknot; the rational version allows more general tangle replacements.
- Satellite knot: a knot formed by placing a pattern knot inside a solid torus around another knot.
- Conjecture (Sivek): the claimed inequality that the next-to-top term is at least as large as the top term for nontrivial knots.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves Sivek's conjectured inequality between the next-to-top and top terms of knot Floer homology for knots with U-torsion order one (in HFK^- or HFK'), and deduces it for knots with rational unknotting number one, including certain satellite knots.
summary.plain: The paper is about knots, which are closed loops tied in three-dimensional space, and a set of algebraic invariants called knot Floer homology that act as fingerprints for them. A conjecture by Sivek predicts a comparison between two of these fingerprint pieces for every nontrivial knot. The authors show the predicted comparison holds for a specific class of knots, namely those where a certain algebraic "torsion order" equals one, and for knots that can be undone by one rational tangle replacement.
summary.why: It gives partial but concrete support for a open conjecture about a well-studied invariant, and it extends the result to a family of satellite knots (knots built by embedding one knot inside a solid torus). The text does not indicate further consequences beyond this.

title: Torsion order and the next-to-top term of knot Floer homology

abstract: This paper develops a comprehensive theory of conditional limit theorems for open dynamical systems. We study the statistical properties of the dynamics within transient regimes by establishing a suite of limit theorems describing the behavior of trajectories under the condition that they remain outside a ``hole'', or region of no return. Under a spectral gap assumption for the associated open transfer operator, we first establish conditioning and Yaglom limits and identify the corresponding conditionally invariant and conditionally ergodic measures. We then establish conditional exponential decay of correlations and the Strong Law of Large Numbers for both deterministic and quenched random systems. We also obtain a conditional Central Limit Theorem, Large Deviation Principle, and Berry--Esseen theorem, with additional assumptions in the quenched random case. We also derive standard (non-conditional) limit theorems on the surviving set of points that never enter the hole.
label: arXiv:2611.23662v1

summary.background:
- Dynamical system: a rule that moves a point forward in time, step by step.
- Hole (open system): a region where trajectories are considered lost once they enter it.
- Transfer operator: a mathematical tool that tracks how the distribution of points evolves under the dynamics.
- Spectral gap: a property of that operator implying that the system forgets its starting distribution at a fast, exponential rate.
- Conditional limit theorem: a statistical law stated for trajectories conditioned on not having entered the hole.
- Limit theorems (LLN, CLT, LDP, Berry–Esseen): standard results describing averages, fluctuations and rare deviations over long times.
- Quenched random system: a random system where the randomness is fixed once and for all, and results must hold for almost every choice.
summary.one_liner: The paper builds a general set of conditional limit theorems (conditioning, Yaglom, decay of correlations, SLLN, CLT, LDP, Berry–Esseen) for open dynamical systems with a hole, under a spectral gap assumption on the open transfer operator, covering deterministic and quenched random cases.
summary.plain: The paper studies what happens to a system that moves step by step, when any trajectory that falls into a designated "hole" is lost and never returns. It asks how the behaviour of the orbits that survive, given that they have avoided the hole so far, can be described statistically. The authors prove a collection of such statistical laws and describe the long-run patterns they settle into.
summary.why: Open systems with holes model escape, leakage and transient behaviour, so results on the statistics of surviving trajectories may be relevant to those settings. The text does not indicate specific applications, so the broader practical reach is unclear from the abstract alone.

title: Conditional limit theorems in dynamical systems

abstract: This paper investigates the stability of stochastic systems through the lens of the Koopman operator framework. In particular, we establish the connection between the convergence properties of the Koopman semigroup and specific stability properties of the underlying stochastic system. Moreover, we demonstrate that specific Koopman eigenfunctions capture stochastic attractivity properties and we illustrate these results with two numerical examples. This work mirrors existing Koopman operator-based stability results for deterministic systems and extends them to the stochastic framework.
label: arXiv:2611.24040v1

summary.background:
- Stochastic differential equations: equations of motion with a random noise term, such as particles jittering in a fluid.
- Stability and attractivity: whether a system returns to or settles near a state, and whether it does so with probability one or in some other sense.
- Koopman operator: a linear operator acting on functions of the state; it describes how observables evolve under the dynamics.
- Koopman semigroup: the family of such operators indexed by time, for stochastic systems.
- Eigenfunctions: special functions that the operator only rescales over time; their decay rates reveal long-run behaviour.
- The deterministic version of these results already exists, and this paper extends it.
summary.one_liner: The paper links convergence of the Koopman semigroup to stability properties of stochastic differential equations, and shows that certain Koopman eigenfunctions capture stochastic attractivity, illustrated with two numerical examples.
summary.plain: The paper studies whether a system that is pushed around by random noise will settle toward a stable state over time. It uses the Koopman operator, a mathematical tool that tracks how measurements of a system evolve rather than the system's states themselves. The authors connect this tool's convergence behaviour to stability, and show that certain special functions tied to it capture when the noisy system tends to settle, with two numerical examples.
summary.why: Extending Koopman-based stability methods from deterministic to random systems could give a linear-algebra style route to analysing noisy dynamics. The text does not say how broadly the approach applies beyond the two examples, so its practical reach is unclear.

title: Stability analysis of stochastic differential equations with the Koopman operator

abstract: A $2$-quasi-bisection of a graph is a vertex $2$-coloring in which the color classes differ in size by at most two and every monochromatic component has at most two vertices. Esperet, Mazzuoccolo, and Tarsi in [J. Graph Theory, 86(2017), 149-158] conjectured that every cubic graph admits such a coloring. DeVos and Nurse proved the conjecture for cubic graphs whose edge sets can be partitioned into a tree and a circuit. This result is generalized in this paper for a larger family of cubic graphs. The conjecture is verified for cubic graphs whose edge set can be partitioned into two subsets $E(T)$ and $E(J)$, where $T$ is a tree of $G$ and $J$ is an even subgraph containing at most two odd circuit components.
label: arXiv:2611.23885v1

summary.background:
- Graph: a set of vertices (points) joined by edges (connections).
- Cubic graph: a graph where every vertex has exactly three edges.
- Vertex 2-coloring: assigning one of two colors to each vertex.
- Quasi-bisection: the two color classes differ in size by at most two, and every monochromatic component (a group of same-colored vertices linked by edges) has at most two vertices.
- Tree: a connected graph with no cycles.
- Even subgraph / circuit: a set of edges forming closed loops; a circuit is odd if it has an odd number of edges.
- The conjecture is by Esperet, Mazzuoccolo and Tarsi (2017); DeVos and Nurse proved the special case of tree-plus-circuit decompositions.
summary.one_liner: The paper extends DeVos and Nurse's proof of the Esperet–Mazzuoccolo–Tarsi conjecture that every cubic graph has a 2-quasi-bisection, verifying it for a larger family of cubic graphs whose edges split into a tree plus an even subgraph with at most two odd circuits.
summary.plain: The paper studies a way of coloring the points (vertices) of a network so that the two colors are almost equal in number and each same-colored cluster is tiny, with at most two points. A conjecture says every network of a certain common shape (each point connected to exactly three others) admits such a coloring. The authors prove this for a wider class of these networks than was previously known, namely those whose connections can be split into a tree and a simple loop-like structure with at most two odd loops.
summary.why: This is a partial result on a published conjecture, so it narrows the open question rather than settling it. It is of interest to researchers working on graph colorings and balanced partitions, and the cubic-graph setting is a common test case in that area.

title: Quasi-Bisections of Cubic Graphs with Tree and Circuit Decompositions

abstract: An additive square over $\mathbb{N}$ is two consecutive nonempty blocks of the same length and same sum. For example, 1423 is an additive square, since 14 and 23 both have length 2 and sum 5. Solving a problem that has been open for more than 50 years, we give an example of an infinite word over a 6-letter subset of N that avoids additive squares.
label: arXiv:2611.24441v1

summary.background:
- A "word" here is simply an ordered sequence of symbols (letters).
- The natural numbers are the counting numbers 0, 1, 2, and so on; the "alphabet" is the set of six numbers allowed.
- An "infinite word" is a sequence that goes on forever.
- A "square" in ordinary word combinatorics is a block repeated twice in a row; an "additive" square replaces equality of letters with equality of block lengths and block sums.
- "Avoiding" a pattern means the pattern never occurs anywhere in the sequence.
- The abstract gives only the statement and the example; the construction itself is not described in the provided text.
summary.one_liner: The paper gives an infinite word over a 6-letter subset of the natural numbers that contains no additive squares, settling a question open for over 50 years.
summary.plain: The paper is about sequences of whole numbers that avoid a particular kind of repeated pattern. An "additive square" is two neighbouring chunks of the sequence that have the same length and the same total, such as 14 and 23 (both length two, both summing to 5). The authors construct an infinite sequence using only six distinct numbers in which no such pattern ever appears.
summary.why: The question was reported as open for more than 50 years, so a construction resolving it is a notable result in combinatorics on words. The text does not say what broader applications or connections it may have, so beyond the field itself its significance is unclear.

title: An additive-square-free word over an alphabet of size 6

abstract: Residual-based methods, including physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), physics-informed Kolmogorov--Arnold networks, and some physics-informed neural operator architectures, approximate PDE solutions by minimizing a discrete least-squares loss formed from the PDE and boundary residuals over a prescribed trial class. This structure is shared by classical least-squares Kansa collocation, whose kernel trial spaces admit an established convergence theory. For neural trial classes, approximation power alone does not ensure that discrete residuals control the continuous solution error. For linear elliptic Dirichlet problems, we extend the kernel-based collocation framework to neural trial classes through elliptic regularity, discrete stability, and consistency. Elliptic regularity supplies the PDE estimate relating solution error to continuous residuals. Discrete stability identifies admissible trial subclasses in which continuous residuals are controlled by a computable discrete loss. This step also quantifies the required number of collocation points. Furthermore, the stability analysis naturally demands a scale-dependent, physics-balanced boundary weight. For the constrained problem, consistency requires accurate comparison functions within the same admissible subclass, a requirement not supplied by neural approximation estimates alone. Specializing to multilayer perceptrons with tanh activations (tanh-MLPs), we construct admissible comparison networks and establish convergence for the constrained residual minimization problem. We further obtain conditional convergence of unconstrained physics-balanced PINNs based on tanh-MLPs under joint network and sampling refinement.
label: arXiv:2611.24355v1

summary.background:
- PDE (partial differential equation): an equation relating a function to its rates of change in space, used to model physical systems such as heat or elasticity.
- Elliptic Dirichlet problem: a steady-state PDE with prescribed values on the boundary of the domain.
- Residual: how far a candidate solution is from satisfying the equation, evaluated at sample points.
- Least-squares loss: a training objective that sums squared residuals over points.
- Kansa collocation: a classical meshfree method that uses kernel functions and point-wise residuals, with an established convergence theory.
- Trial class: the family of functions (here neural networks) the approximate solution is searched within.
- Tanh-MLP: a multilayer perceptron, a standard feedforward neural network, using the tanh activation function.
- Stability and consistency: the two properties needed so that small discrete error implies small true error.
summary.one_liner: The paper extends the convergence theory of least-squares kernel collocation (Kansa) to neural trial classes for linear elliptic Dirichlet problems, establishing conditions under which tanh-MLP-based PINNs provably converge.
summary.plain: Neural-network methods such as PINNs solve equations describing physical systems by training a network to make the equation's residual small at sample points. This paper asks when that kind of training actually guarantees the network is close to the true solution, and it answers using tools from elliptic regularity (how smooth solutions of steady-state equations behave), discrete stability and consistency. It proves convergence for a constrained version using tanh networks, and gives a conditional result for the standard unconstrained PINN form under joint network and sampling refinement.
summary.why: Practitioners use PINNs widely but often without guarantees that a small training loss means a small solution error. The paper's framework may help clarify when such methods can be trusted, though the text alone does not show how well the conditions hold in practice.

title: Stable admissible neural classes and convergent physics-informed neural networks

abstract: In this paper, we develop and analyze a local discontinuous Galerkin (LDG) finite element method for the Boussinesq system of equations, and employ an upwind scheme to effectively manage the nonlinear convective terms, thereby ensuring stability and accuracy. Our analysis establishes new \emph{a priori} regularity estimates for the semidiscrete LDG approximations. We establish optimal \emph{a priori} error estimates for the velocity approximation in $\bL^2$--norm, the pressure approximation in $L^2$--norm and for temperature in $L^2$--norm for all $t>0$. Our proof relies on the standard elliptic and parabolic duality arguments and modified Stokes operators defined on appropriate broken Sobolev spaces. Under suitable smallness assumptions on the given data, we further establish error estimates that remain uniform in time. Furthermore, the backward Euler scheme is considered for a full discretization, and optimal fully discrete error estimates are derived. Finally, we carry out numerical experiments to substantiate our theoretical findings.
label: arXiv:2611.23901v1

summary.background:
- Boussinesq system: a set of partial differential equations coupling fluid velocity, pressure and temperature, used for buoyancy-driven flow.
- Finite element method: approximating a continuous problem by piecewise simple functions on a mesh.
- Discontinuous Galerkin (DG): a finite element variant that lets approximate functions jump between mesh cells, with "local" (LDG) referring to a specific way of handling derivatives.
- Upwind scheme: a stabilization that takes flow direction into account when computing transport terms.
- A priori error estimate: a bound on the approximation error derived before computing, in terms of mesh size and time step.
- Backward Euler: a simple implicit method for stepping forward in time.
- Uniform in time: the error bound stays controlled over arbitrarily long times, not just over a fixed interval.
summary.one_liner: The paper analyzes a local discontinuous Galerkin finite element scheme with upwind treatment of convective terms for the Boussinesq system, proving optimal a priori error estimates (including time-uniform bounds under smallness assumptions) for velocity, pressure and temperature, plus fully discrete backward Euler estimates.
summary.plain: The paper studies a numerical method for simulating the Boussinesq equations, a standard model of fluid flow where temperature differences drive motion, such as warm air rising in a room. The authors build a computational scheme that splits the domain into pieces and allows solutions to jump across their edges, then prove how close its approximate velocity, pressure and temperature stay to the true values. They also add a time-stepping version and report numerical experiments that the authors say support the theory.
summary.why: Mathematical guarantees on accuracy tell engineers and scientists how far to trust simulations of heat-driven flows, such as weather or industrial convection models. The text does not indicate how the results compare with existing methods beyond the stated analysis, so the practical reach is best judged by specialists.

title: On global error estimates of a local discontinuous Galerkin method of the Boussinesq system of equations

abstract: We define a wide class of tree forcings that we call $\textit{normed-tree forcings}$ and prove that they can preserve Ramsey ultrafilters. These include $\textit{fat-tree forcings}$ as particular cases. As an application, we prove the consistency with $\mathsf{ZFC}$ of $\mathfrak{d}=\mathfrak{u}=\aleph_1 < \mathsf{minLc}=\mathfrak{c}=\aleph_2$, where $\mathfrak{d}$ denotes the dominating number, $\mathfrak{u}$ the ultrafilter number, and $\mathsf{minLc}$ the minimum localization cardinal. This solves some open questions about pairs of classical cardinal characteristics, such as the consistency of both $\mathfrak{e}_{\mathsf{ubd}}$ and its dual strictly larger than $\mathfrak{u}$.
label: arXiv:2611.23713v1

summary.background:
- Cardinal characteristics: numerical invariants measuring the size of infinite collections, such as the dominating number d and the ultrafilter number u.
- ZFC: the standard axioms of set theory (Zermelo-Fraenkel with Choice); a consistency result shows a statement cannot be ruled out from these axioms.
- Forcing: a technique for extending a model of set theory by adding new sets, used to build models where chosen statements hold.
- Ultrafilter: a maximal family of subsets of the natural numbers that is closed under finite intersections and supersets; a Ramsey ultrafilter is a special, well-behaved kind.
- Preservation: showing a forcing extension keeps a given ultrafilter from being destroyed, which controls how cardinals relate.
- Aleph notation: aleph_1 and aleph_2 denote the first and second infinite cardinals.
summary.one_liner: The paper defines normed-tree forcings, a broad class of tree-shaped set-theoretic forcing notions (including fat-tree forcings), shows they can preserve Ramsey ultrafilters, and uses this to establish the ZFC consistency of d = u = aleph_1 < minLc = c = aleph_2.
summary.plain: This is a paper in set theory, the branch of mathematics that studies infinity and its different sizes. The authors study a family of ways of enlarging the universe of sets, built from tree-shaped structures, and show that these enlargements keep a special kind of large collection of sets (a Ramsey ultrafilter) intact. They use this to show that a certain arrangement of infinite sizes of several mathematical quantities is consistent with the standard axioms.
summary.why: The work settles open questions about how several classical cardinal characteristics relate to one another, in particular whether the ultrafilter number can be strictly smaller than certain localization and evasion-type cardinals. The text does not indicate further applications beyond these relations, so its wider significance is best judged by specialists.

title: Preserving Ramsey ultrafilters with tree forcings

abstract: This paper introduces a proof format and proof checker for certifying reachability computations of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) with polynomial vector fields. Establishing a proof checking framework for certifying ODE reachability is similar to the checking of UNSAT proofs for propositional satisfiability solving, but it is even more important due to the challenges inherent in dealing with ODEs, and even more challenging due to the numerical nature of ODE reachability algorithms. The proofs are expressed in differential dynamic logic (dL), and can be independently verified with symbolic theorem provers for dL (e.g. KeYmaeraX). Such proofs are naturally generated by reachability algorithms based on Taylor models, a popular technique to obtain rigorous bounds on approximations of ODEs. This paper proves the completeness of such proofs - if an approximation was correctly computed by some (possibly untrusted) reachability algorithm via Taylor models, then a corresponding proof in dL can be automatically generated and checked to be correct in dL's proof calculus. A dedicated proof checker is implemented in Lean4 for improved performance, which is capable of formally verifying benchmarks in the ARCH competition.
label: arXiv:2611.25303v1

summary.background:
- Ordinary differential equations (ODEs): equations describing how quantities change continuously over time.
- Reachability: determining which states a system can reach from a set of starting states.
- Taylor models: a way of representing a function as a polynomial plus a rigorously bounded error term, giving guaranteed bounds on numerical answers.
- Polynomial vector fields: rules of change where the rates are polynomial expressions in the variables.
- Differential dynamic logic (dL): a formal logic for stating and proving properties of hybrid systems, with KeYmaera X as its prover.
- Proof checking: independently re-verifying a proof produced by a solver, so the solver need not be trusted; the SAT/UNSAT proof analogy is the model here.
- Lean 4: a proof assistant and programming language used to implement the checker.
- ARCH competition: a community benchmark contest for verifying continuous and hybrid systems.
summary.one_liner: The paper introduces a proof format and a Lean 4 proof checker that certify Taylor-model reachability computations for ODEs with polynomial vector fields, expressed as proofs in differential dynamic logic (dL) and checkable in KeYmaera X, and proves that such proofs can be generated whenever a correct approximation exists.
summary.plain: Computer programs that predict where a system governed by continuous change (such as a moving machine or physical process) will end up often use numerical approximations that can be wrong without anyone noticing. This paper designs a way for such a program to output a formal proof of its answer, and a separate checker that verifies that proof. The authors show that if an approximation was computed correctly, a matching proof can always be generated and checked, and they report that the checker verifies benchmarks from the ARCH competition.
summary.why: Certifying results from untrusted numerical software matters for safety verification of cyber-physical systems, where a wrong prediction could hide a dangerous state. The approach is modeled on proof checking for SAT solvers, which is a useful precedent, though the text alone does not show how widely it will be adopted.

title: Proof Checking Continuous Reachability

abstract: We study quiver-invariant triality between 2d (0,2) supersymmetric gauge theories described by brane brick models associated with toric Calabi-Yau 4-folds. The dual theories share the same gauge groups, field content and E-terms but have distinct J-terms. We present an explicit pair of such brane brick models and identify the sequence of triality mutations relating them. This sequence returns the quiver to its original form while transforming the J- and E-terms. We explain the relation between quiver-invariant triality and the orbifold reduction of quiver-invariant brane tilings.
label: arXiv:2611.25017v1

summary.background:
- Quiver: a diagram whose nodes are gauge groups and arrows are matter fields, used to encode a gauge theory.
- Gauge theory: a physics theory whose interactions are fixed by symmetry groups; here it lives in 2 spacetime dimensions with (0,2) supersymmetry.
- Supersymmetry: a symmetry pairing particles of different spin; "(0,2)" describes how it acts in 2 dimensions.
- Calabi-Yau 4-fold: a higher-dimensional special geometric space from string theory; "toric" means it is built from polygon-like combinatorial data.
- Brane brick model: a 3D-tiling-style combinatorial object encoding a gauge theory from branes wrapped on such a space.
- E-terms and J-terms: the two kinds of superpotential constraints that define the interactions in these theories.
- Triality: a three-way symmetry-type relation among these theories, realized by a sequence of mutations (local rewiring operations).
- Orbifold reduction: a construction that relates a theory to a simpler one by quotienting a symmetry.
summary.one_liner:
The paper studies quiver-invariant triality, a set of mutations relating two 2d (0,2) gauge theories encoded by brane brick models on toric Calabi-Yau 4-folds that share gauge groups, fields and E-terms but differ in J-terms, and links it to orbifold reduction of quiver-invariant brane tilings.</one_liner>
<parameter name="plain">The paper is about a family of physics theories that can be drawn as diagrams (called quivers) and described by geometric objects called brane brick models. The authors give a concrete pair of such models that look the same in their diagram and particle content but differ in their interaction rules, and show a specific sequence of "triality" moves that turns one into the other while leaving the diagram unchanged.
summary.why: Dualities that keep the underlying diagram fixed while changing the hidden interaction rules help map out which physical theories are truly equivalent. The text says it also connects this idea to orbifold reduction of brane tilings, a related construction, but the abstract does not show how far that connection extends.

title: Quiver-Invariant Triality between Brane Brick Models

abstract: We construct a map of filtered spectra inducing a map from the Atiyah--Hirzebruch spectral sequence (AHSS) to the Baker--Lazarev Adams spectral sequence of a $\mathit{ko}$-module $M$. Using this and a theorem of Bruner--Rognes, we construct a hastened Adams spectral sequence (HASS) for the Postnikov truncations of $\mathit{ko}$ and the connective Adams summand. Then, motivated by questions in quantum field theory, topological phases of matter, and tensor category theory, we apply the HASS to supercohomology, the cohomology theory $I_{\mathbb{C}^\times}(τ_{\le 2}\mathit{ko})$, and observe that in examples of interest it is easier to calculate with than either the AHSS or the usual Adams spectral sequence. We include a User's Guide to the HASS and several worked examples, as well as hastened Adams charts for many commonly encountered $\mathcal{A}(1)$-modules.
label: arXiv:2611.24725v1

summary.background:
- Spectral sequence: a systematic bookkeeping device that computes complicated invariants in successive approximation layers.
- Atiyah–Hirzebruch and Adams spectral sequences: two standard such tools in stable homotopy theory, the branch of topology studying generalized cohomology theories.
- ko and the Adams summand: specific spectra (generalized homology objects) from topology, with connective ko being the usual real K-theory variant.
- Supercohomology: a cohomology theory used in physics to classify certain topological phases of matter, including fermionic ones.
- Modules over the Steenrod subalgebra A(1): algebraic objects that encode the input data for Adams-type computations.
summary.one_liner:
The paper builds a map from the Atiyah–Hirzebruch spectral sequence to the Baker–Lazarev Adams spectral sequence for a ko-module, uses it with a Bruner–Rognes theorem to define a "hastened" Adams spectral sequence for truncations of ko and the connective Adams summand, and applies it to supercohomology.</one_liner>
<parameter name="plain">This is a research paper in algebraic topology, a branch of mathematics that studies shapes using tools that compute "layered" invariants. The authors introduce a new computational method, the hastened Adams spectral sequence, for a particular family of invariants called supercohomology, which arise in physics. According to the text, in the examples of interest this method is easier to calculate with than two existing methods, and the paper includes a user's guide, worked examples, and charts.
summary.why: The text motivates the work by questions in quantum field theory, topological phases of matter, and tensor category theory, which is where supercohomology appears. The stated advantage is computational ease in examples, so its wider usefulness is something the abstract only suggests rather than establishes.

title: An Atiyah--Hirzebruch to Adams map and the hastened Adams spectral sequence for supercohomology

abstract: We study the almost sure convergence of the last-iterate optimization error of Stochastic (sub)Gradient Descent (SGD) for convex objectives. For smooth objectives, we establish convergence rates of order $k^{-1/3}$ when a stationary minimizer exists, and $k^{-1/4}$ otherwise, up to polylogarithmic factors, where $k$ denotes the iteration counter. We further show that the latter rate extends to nonsmooth convex objectives. All these rates are achieved by deterministic, anytime stepsize policies. Finally, we establish matching lower bounds showing that the exponents $-1/3$ and $-1/4$ are optimal, up to polylogarithmic factors, for the corresponding problem classes.
label: arXiv:2611.24151v1

summary.background:
- Gradient descent: repeatedly nudging a guess downhill along the slope of a function to find its minimum.
- Stochastic gradient descent (SGD): the same method using noisy slope estimates, typical in machine learning training.
- Convex function: a bowl-shaped function with one overall low region, which makes minimization well-behaved.
- Smooth vs. nonsmooth: smooth functions have no sharp corners or kinks; nonsmooth ones do.
- Last iterate: the final point the algorithm outputs, as opposed to an average over the run.
- Almost sure convergence: convergence that holds for essentially every random run, not just on average.
- Convergence rate and exponent: how fast the error shrinks as steps k grow; k^{-1/3} means error scales like one over the cube root of k.
- Polylogarithmic factors: extra slowly growing log terms ignored in the rate.
- Lower bound: a proof that no method can do better than a given rate on a problem class.
summary.one_liner: This paper proves almost sure last-iterate convergence rates for SGD on convex objectives, with rates of k^{-1/3} for smooth problems with a stationary minimizer and k^{-1/4} otherwise (up to polylog factors), extends the latter to nonsmooth convex problems, and gives matching lower bounds for the exponents.
summary.plain: The paper studies a standard method for finding the lowest point of a function when only noisy estimates of its slope are available, as in training many machine learning models. It asks how close the final point produced by the method gets to the best possible answer, and how that gap shrinks as the number of steps grows. The authors show the gap shrinks at specific speeds, about k to the power -1/3 for smooth problems and -1/4 in other cases (ignoring logarithmic factors), and they show these speeds cannot be improved in general.
summary.why: Results of this kind pin down how many steps a noisy optimizer needs, and the matching lower bounds indicate the rates are tight rather than just proven upper bounds. The text does not discuss specific applications, so its practical impact is unclear from the abstract alone.

title: Nearly Tight Almost Sure Convergence Rates for the Last iterate of SGD

abstract: We study a conditional mean-field type linear quadratic optimal control problem for regime-switching diffusions with indefinite weights. The dynamics and cost depend on conditional expectations of the state and control given the history of the Markov chain. Under standard definiteness conditions, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the optimal control and derive its feedback representation and optimal cost through two sets of coupled Riccati equations and a linear backward stochastic differential equation driven by the Markov chain. To treat the case of indefinite weights, we extend the equivalent cost functional approach to this setting using regime-dependent quadratic adjustments for the conditional mean of the state and its deviation from that mean.
