When the transformed weights in the equivalent cost functional satisfy standard definiteness conditions, this construction yields unique solvability of the original Hamiltonian system and a feedback representation of the unique optimal control. The proposed results also provide an effective method for establishing the solvability of fully coupled linear conditional mean-field forward-backward stochastic differential equations that do not satisfy certain existing monotonicity conditions. We further apply the results to conditional mean-variance portfolio selection with exogenous liability in an incomplete regime-switching market and derive the optimal investment strategy.
label: arXiv:2611.24454v1

summary.background:
- Optimal control: choosing a decision rule over time to minimize a cost.
- Linear-quadratic problem: linear dynamics and a cost that is quadratic (squared-error-like) in state and control.
- Regime-switching: the system's parameters change depending on a hidden Markov chain that jumps between discrete states.
- Mean-field type: the dynamics and cost depend on averages (expectations) of the state and control, here conditioned on the chain's history.
- Riccati equations: matrix equations that give the optimal feedback gain.
- Backward stochastic differential equations: equations solved backward in time from a terminal condition, used to describe optimal adjoint variables.
- Indefinite weights: cost weights that are not all positive or all negative, which breaks standard convexity arguments.
- Mean-variance portfolio: an investment problem balancing expected return against variance of wealth.
summary.one_liner: The paper solves a conditional mean-field type linear-quadratic optimal control problem for regime-switching diffusions with indefinite weights, using an equivalent-cost-functional transformation and coupled Riccati and backward SDE systems, and applies it to conditional mean-variance portfolio selection with exogenous liability.
summary.plain: The paper studies how to steer a randomly evolving system, whose dynamics switch between regimes according to a hidden Markov chain, so that a cost tied to averages of the state and control is minimized. Under standard conditions the authors show the best strategy exists, is unique, and can be written as a feedback rule. For cases where the cost weights are "indefinite" (not all of one sign), they use a change of cost function to reduce the problem to the standard case.
summary.why: The method is offered as a way to establish solvability of coupled forward-backward equations that fail certain monotonicity conditions, which the text presents as the main technical gain. The worked application to portfolio selection with a liability suggests relevance to finance and insurance, though the text does not report numerical examples or comparisons with other methods.

title: Conditional Mean-Field Type Linear Quadratic Optimal Control Problem for Regime-Switching Diffusions with Indefinite Coefficients

abstract: We study how the local geometry of a linear stochastic optimization problem determines its statistical difficulty, measured by expected decision regret. The optimal local rate is governed by how fast the support function of the feasible set grows away from its linearization at the true mean; depending on the instance, it can be $n^{-1/2}$, $n^{-1}$, $n^{-2}$, or a non-power rate, and sample average approximation (SAA) attains these rates in a Gaussian mean model. At smooth instances, SAA also attains the classical sharp local minimax constant. We then allow the data distribution to vary in a Kullback--Leibler (KL) ball of radius proportional to $1/n$ around a reference distribution $P$. The exact local minimax limit of this benchmark, which may depend on $P$, coincides with that of a Gaussian model whose local parameter set is the covariance ellipsoid of $P$. A simple coordinatewise truncated SAA rule, which does not use $P$, attains the minimax rate, and at smooth instances its constant matches the minimax constant as the neighborhood radius grows. Ordinary SAA, in contrast, can have strictly suboptimal worst-case expected regret when the local rate is fast relative to the tails of $P$, because rare tail events then dominate the expectation. The results delineate when SAA is sharply optimal, rate-optimal, or statistically suboptimal, and quantify the local price of distributional robustness.
label: arXiv:2611.25007v1

summary.background:
- Stochastic optimization: choosing a decision that performs well when some quantity is random, judged on average.
- Expected regret: the average extra loss compared with the best decision had the true distribution been known.
- Sample average approximation (SAA): replacing the unknown average with the average over observed data, then optimizing.
- Minimax rate: the best worst-case error any method can guarantee, as sample size n grows.
- Support function and linearization: a way of describing a convex set by its extent in each direction, and its local straight-line approximation.
- Kullback–Leibler (KL) ball: a set of probability distributions close to a reference distribution, measured by an information distance.
- Gaussian mean model: a simplified setting where the data are normal, used as a benchmark.
summary.one_liner: A local minimax analysis of linear stochastic optimization shows how the geometry of the feasible set sets the best achievable expected decision regret, when sample average approximation (SAA) is optimal, and how a truncated SAA rule and a KL-ball robustness model change the picture.
summary.plain: The paper asks how hard it is to make a good decision when you only have data about an uncertain quantity, and how much that difficulty depends on the shape of the set of allowed decisions. It finds that the achievable error rate can be n to the power of minus one half, minus one, minus two, or an unusual non-power rate, depending on that shape. It also shows that a simple averaging method is best in some cases, but can do worse when rare extreme data points dominate the average, and that a modified rule avoids this.
summary.why: The text gives a theoretical characterization rather than an application, so its practical reach is unclear from the text alone. It may matter for anyone choosing decisions from limited data under possible distribution shift, since it quantifies a cost of robustness, but the text does not show how it connects to specific applied problems.

title: Geometry, Local Minimax Risk, and the Limits of Sample Average Approximation in Linear Stochastic Optimization

abstract: Functional principal component analysis (FPCA) plays a central role as a dimension-reduction and representation tool in functional data analysis, but its minimax theory for diverging spectral indices under noisy discrete observation has remained open for over two decades. To fill this gap, we consider a sieve-based FPCA framework that pools discrete measurements across subjects and accommodates sampling frequencies ranging from sparse to dense under random designs. We begin by establishing new minimax rates for covariance estimation over general bivariate function classes beyond tensor-product low-complexity structures, thereby identifying the intrinsically two-dimensional optimal rate. Our central theoretical contribution is to establish minimax optimal rates for both individually labelled eigenfunctions with diverging indices and leading principal subspaces of increasing dimensions, under explicit growth and regularity conditions. To establish these results, we develop a general framework for sharp minimax analysis of FPCA under discrete observation, separating spectral approximation from stochastic perturbations and exploiting their distinct structures, thereby offering a new approach to a broad class of nonparametric spectral estimation problems. For both spectral targets, the optimal rates reveal two distinct statistical mechanisms, spectral identification and nonparametric reconstruction, whose interplay gives rise to either four or two sampling regimes. This yields, for the first time, a precise characterization of the impact of discrete sampling across the full range from sparse to dense designs. Finally, as a downstream application, we analyze FPCA-based functional linear regression and show that the FPCA-based estimator attains the minimax-optimal rates.
label: arXiv:2611.24228v1

summary.background:
- Functional data: each subject gives a whole curve (e.g., a growth trajectory), observed only at scattered time points with noise.
- Principal components: the main modes of variation in the data, here extended to functions; eigenfunctions are these modes and eigenvalues measure their importance.
- Minimax rate: the best worst-case error any estimator can achieve; matching it means the method is essentially optimal.
- Sparse vs. dense design: few vs. many observation points per curve, which changes how much information is available.
- Sieve method: approximating unknown functions by a growing family of simple basis functions.
- Functional linear regression: predicting a scalar outcome from a whole curve, here via its principal components.
summary.one_liner: This paper establishes minimax-optimal rates for sieve-based functional principal component analysis under noisy, discretely sampled random designs, covering eigenfunctions with diverging indices and growing principal subspaces, from sparse to dense sampling.
summary.plain: The paper studies how to find the main patterns in curves that are measured at a handful of points each, with noise, and how well that can be done at best. It proves the best achievable accuracy for estimating these patterns, including higher-order ones, across the full range from very sparse to very dense sampling. It also shows that the resulting method, applied to functional linear regression, reaches the same best-possible rates.
summary.why: The text says the minimax theory for this setting had been open for over two decades, so the rates fill a known gap in statistical theory. Its claimed link to a wider class of spectral estimation problems is stated by the authors, and the text does not show how far that reaches beyond FPCA.

title: Functional Principal Component Analysis: Minimax Optimality from Sparse to Dense Designs and Beyond

abstract: Causal inference seeks to learn how outcomes change under alternative interventions, but network interactions complicate this task. Under network interference, outcomes depend on both own treatment and neighbors' treatments, making causal effects functions of neighborhood exposure rather than single treatment contrasts. Existing methods primarily target prespecified causal contrasts or their estimation precision, leaving global response-function recovery largely unexplored. We study sequential experimentation under a limited experimental budget, with the goal of recovering the full exposure-dependent population-average response function. To this end, we propose FANCI (Fill-Distance-Guided Active Learning for Network-Interference Causal Inference). For function learning, treatment-specific Gaussian processes flexibly model nonlinear conditional response surfaces. For experimental design, we formulate global response-function recovery as a coverage problem and propose a fill-distance criterion that guides new experiments toward poorly covered regions. To account for network constraints on attainable exposure patterns, we develop full-network and target-screened strategies for selecting feasible network--assignment pairs. Theoretically, we derive uniform error bounds linking fill distance to response-function estimation and characterize the approximation loss from target screening. Simulations and an online-game experiment show that FANCI improves recovery of nonlinear exposure-dependent effects and reveals treatment patterns obscured when network interference is ignored.
label: arXiv:2611.24143v1

summary.background:
- Causal inference: estimating how outcomes would change under different interventions.
- Network interference (spillovers): one unit's outcome depends on others' treatments, so the treatment effect depends on the neighborhood exposure pattern.
- Response function: the curve or surface giving the average outcome for each exposure pattern.
- Active learning: choosing the next data points adaptively to learn a function efficiently under a limited budget.
- Gaussian processes: flexible statistical models for unknown nonlinear functions that also give uncertainty estimates.
- Fill distance: a measure of the largest gap between data points in a space; small fill distance means the space is well covered.
- Uniform error bounds: guarantees on estimation error holding across the whole domain, not only at selected points.
summary.one_liner: FANCI uses fill-distance-guided active learning with treatment-specific Gaussian processes to recover the full exposure-dependent population-average response function under network interference, with uniform error bounds and a target-screening approximation analysis.
summary.plain: When people in a network influence each other, one person's outcome depends on their own treatment and on their neighbors' treatments. This paper asks how to run a limited number of experiments so that the whole curve of outcomes across these neighborhood exposure patterns can be learned, rather than just one or two comparisons. The authors propose a method that chooses new experiments in regions where the data is sparse, and they report simulations and an online-game experiment where it recovers nonlinear effects better.
summary.why: Most causal methods focus on specific contrasts or on how precisely they are estimated, so learning the whole response shape under interference is a less-explored goal. The approach may be relevant to platform experiments, public health, and social-network interventions, though the text alone does not show how broadly it transfers.

title: Fill-Distance-Guided Active Learning for Causal Function Recovery under Network Interference

abstract: Non-Newtonian dam-break flows are a classical problem with numerous engineering applications. These flows are particularly important in alternative rheometry, where they are used to rapidly and affordably estimate rheological properties, such as in the slump test and Bostwick consistometer test. However, the lifting dynamics of the containing obstacle introduce inertial effects that can compromise the accurate estimation of these properties. These effects are influenced by the lifting velocity, the fluid's viscosity, and the initial geometry of the sample. This study aims to quantify the influence of lifting velocity and to provide physical insights into how inertial effects influence the flow. A global sensitivity analysis (GSA) framework adapted for functional outputs (e.g., time series) is employed, using data generated from high-fidelity simulations with ANSYS Fluent. The GSA produces sensitivity curves that track the evolving importance of each input parameter over time. Three distinct flow regimes are identified, namely mobilization, transition and viscous regimes, each governed by different dominant factors. The first two regimes are significantly affected by the lifting velocity, revealing the influence of inertial effects, whereas the viscous regime is dominated by fluid rheology and shows a increasing importance of the yield stress. These results are contextualized in terms of traditional rheometry tests.
label: arXiv:2611.24335v1

summary.background:
- Non-Newtonian fluid: a material whose resistance to flow changes with how it is pushed (e.g., paste, concrete, some foods), unlike water.
- Dam-break flow: what happens when a retaining barrier is removed and the fluid collapses and spreads.
- Rheometry: the measurement of how a material flows and deforms.
- Yield stress: the minimum push needed before the material starts to flow.
- Slump test / Bostwick consistometer: simple empirical tests that measure how far a sample spreads under its own weight.
- Global sensitivity analysis: a statistical way to rank how much each input variable contributes to output variation across its full range; here adapted to outputs that change over time.
- High-fidelity simulation: detailed computer modelling, here done with ANSYS Fluent software.
summary.one_liner: A global sensitivity analysis adapted for time-series outputs, applied to ANSYS Fluent simulations, that maps how lifting velocity, viscosity and initial sample geometry influence the time-evolving dynamics of non-Newtonian dam-break flows used in rheometry.
summary.plain: When a container holding a thick, paste-like material is lifted, the material spreads out, and how it spreads depends on how fast the container is lifted and on the material's properties. This paper uses computer simulations of that spreading and a statistical method to measure how much each input (mainly lifting speed) matters at different stages. It finds three phases, and the lifting speed matters most in the first two.
summary.why: Simple field tests such as the slump test and Bostwick consistometer test estimate a material's flow properties from how it spreads, so unwanted effects from lifting the container could bias those estimates. The paper's time-resolved sensitivity curves give a way to see when those effects matter, though the text itself does not report how far the findings transfer to real test equipment.

title: Global sensitivity analysis of transient regimes in non-Newtonian dam-break flows applied in rheometry

abstract: Diffusion models have transformed generative modeling through their ability to capture and generate samples from complex data distributions. This success has spurred substantial interest in using pretrained diffusion models as expressive priors for highly ill-posed inverse problems in imaging and sensing. Despite strong empirical performance, theoretical understanding of this approach remains limited: existing guarantees are often asymptotic or entail prohibitive computational costs in the worst case. In this paper, we address this gap by studying sparse recovery from a small number of linear measurements, a classical problem in compressed sensing. We show that, given an accurate diffusion model capturing a sparsity-promoting Bernoulli-Gaussian prior, a likelihood-guided annealed Langevin sampler provably recovers the sparse signal in polynomial time with near-optimal sample complexity for a broad family of random and deterministic sensing matrices. When the signal is indeed drawn from the postulated prior, we further establish total variation guarantees for posterior sampling after a final denoising step. These results lay a theoretical foundation for statistically and computationally efficient inverse solvers with diffusion priors.
label: arXiv:2611.24602v1

summary.background:
- Sparse signal: a vector where most entries are zero; compressed sensing recovers it from far fewer measurements than its length.
- Linear measurements: each observation is a weighted sum of the unknown signal's entries.
- Ill-posed inverse problem: many different signals could explain the same measurements, so a prior is needed to choose a plausible one.
- Prior: a probability distribution over signals encoding what they typically look like; here a Bernoulli-Gaussian model (each entry is zero with some probability, otherwise Gaussian).
- Diffusion model: a generative model that learns to turn noise into data by reversing a gradual noising process.
- Langevin sampling: an iterative method that moves toward high-probability regions with added random noise, used to draw samples from a distribution.
- Sample complexity: how many measurements are needed for recovery; "near-optimal" means close to the theoretical minimum.
- Total variation distance: a measure of how different two probability distributions are.
- Posterior sampling: drawing signals consistent with both the measurements and the prior.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves that a pretrained diffusion model used as a prior, combined with a likelihood-guided annealed Langevin sampler, can provably recover sparse signals from few linear measurements in polynomial time with near-optimal sample complexity, and gives total variation guarantees for posterior sampling when the signal follows the assumed prior.
summary.plain: The paper studies how to reconstruct a signal that is mostly zeros from a small number of indirect measurements, a classic problem in compressed sensing. It asks whether a generative model trained to produce such signals (a diffusion model) can be used as a guide for this reconstruction, with a theoretical guarantee rather than only empirical success. The authors show that, under stated assumptions, the method recovers the signal efficiently and with a near-minimal number of measurements.
summary.why: Diffusion models are widely used as priors for imaging and sensing problems, but their theoretical behavior has been poorly understood, and prior guarantees were often asymptotic or computationally costly. This work offers finite, polynomial-time guarantees for a clean model problem, which may help explain when such solvers can be trusted; the extent to which the results carry over to real images is not established by the text.

title: Diffusion Models are Provably Efficient Priors for Sparse Recovery

abstract: Conformal prediction gives finite-sample, distribution-free marginal coverage and has begun to be applied to gridded weather forecasts. Marginal coverage concerns the long-run fraction of covered points at a location, not how coverage behaves jointly across space and time on a given day. I benchmark eight interval-construction procedures (Gaussian, pooled and per-cell split conformal, per-season, adaptive conformal inference and rolling windows) for gridded 2 m temperature forecasts at eight lead times from 6 hours to 10 days, using ERA5 at 5.625 degree resolution, a deliberately modest convolutional forecaster and ECMWF's operational HRES, with calibration in 2017-2018 and testing in 2019-2021. Alongside coverage, width and interval score, I report dependence diagnostics: a spatial overdispersion index, quantiles of daily spatial coverage and miss persistence relative to a shuffled-days null. Per-cell methods reach near-nominal marginal coverage, yet the day-to-day variance of the fraction of cells covered is roughly 3 to 10 times what independent cells would give, and misses cluster in time; both effects grow with lead time for the CNN, also appear for HRES, and are shared by all methods. An oracle that divides each day's normalised errors by that day's mean removes 81 to 92 percent of the excess dispersion for the CNN and 93 to 98 percent for HRES, so days of large errors across much of the grid account for most of it. A day-scale predicted from seasonal terms and already-verified errors lowers the overdispersion index without widening intervals but improves interval score by at most 0.6 percent; on HRES from 12 hours to 3 days it has the lowest overdispersion index while ACI or season-conditional calibration has the best interval score, so no method is best on both. The study covers one variable, one coarse grid, a reanalysis target and two forecasters.
label: arXiv:2611.24329v1

summary.background:
- Forecast interval: a range around a predicted value meant to contain the outcome a chosen share of the time (e.g. 90%).
- Conformal prediction: a family of methods that builds such ranges from past errors, with guaranteed average coverage under exchangeability assumptions.
- Marginal coverage: the long-run fraction of cases covered at one location, averaged over time.
- Spatial and temporal dependence: nearby places and consecutive days tend to have correlated errors, which breaks the independence assumptions behind many standard statistics.
- Overdispersion: variance larger than what independent cases would produce; here, the day-to-day spread in the fraction of the map covered.
- ERA5 and HRES: a reanalysis dataset used as the "truth" and ECMWF's operational forecast model; a CNN is a small neural-network forecaster.
- Interval score: a single number rewarding narrow intervals that still cover the outcome, penalising misses.
summary.one_liner: A benchmark of eight conformal prediction interval methods for gridded 2 m temperature forecasts (CNN and ECMWF HRES, ERA5 target), showing that near-nominal marginal coverage hides strong day-to-day and temporal clustering of misses, which is largely driven by days with large errors across much of the grid.
summary.plain: Weather forecasts often come with a "plus or minus" range meant to contain the true temperature a set share of the time. This paper checks whether those ranges are right not just on average over many places, but also within a single day across the whole map and across consecutive days. The authors find that the average coverage looks fine, yet on some days many places are missed together, and misses bunch up in time; a simple daily-scale correction helps only slightly.
summary.why: Calibrated uncertainty matters for anyone who acts on forecast ranges, and the paper suggests that a method can pass a standard average-coverage check while still failing on joint, day-level behaviour. The study is limited to one variable, one coarse grid, a reanalysis target and two forecasters, so its findings should be read as a case study rather than a general verdict.

title: Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification for Weather Forecasting: Conformal Prediction Under Spatiotemporal Dependence

abstract: Agentic video understanding requires models to actively interact with video environments to gather evidence and form judgments. Evaluating this capability therefore requires assessing whether models can translate opportunities for interaction into better understanding. We introduce VideoACE, a benchmark for assessing video understanding under conditions that support sustained interaction. We focus on high-frame-rate action videos, where rapid, subtle changes make targeted observation especially valuable. The benchmark comprises 1,000 multiple-choice questions spanning six categories of fine-grained action understanding, accompanied by temporal evidence annotations and user hints screened for answer leakage. Its evaluation environment combines video inspection tools with a user simulator, allowing models to adjust temporal coverage, sampling density, and spatial detail, and to revisit evidence and revise their judgments under simulated user feedback. We evaluate single-pass observation, autonomous tool use, and tool use combined with user feedback to examine how effectively models exploit these opportunities. Evaluation of five models reveals distinct patterns in how they acquire evidence and respond to opportunities for further interaction. These findings establish VideoACE as a testbed for examining agentic video understanding beyond performance under a fixed observation setting.
label: arXiv:2611.24184v1

summary.background:
- Agentic video understanding: a model that can take actions, such as replaying or zooming into a video, instead of only reading it once.
- Frame rate: how many still images per second make up a video; high-frame-rate footage has fast, subtle motion.
- Benchmark: a standard test set used to compare models.
- Temporal evidence annotations: labels marking which moments in the video show the answer.
- User simulator: a scripted stand-in for a human who gives hints or feedback.
- Answer leakage: when a hint accidentally gives away the correct answer; the authors say their hints were screened for this.
summary.one_liner: VideoACE is a benchmark of 1,000 multiple-choice questions on fine-grained high-frame-rate action videos, designed to test whether video models improve when they can actively inspect clips, adjust sampling, and revise answers under simulated user feedback.
summary.plain: Most video AI systems are tested by watching a clip once and answering a question. This paper proposes a test where the model can instead go back, zoom in on particular moments, look at finer detail, and change its answer after hints from a simulated user. The authors tested five models under three setups (one pass, using tools on its own, and using tools with user feedback) to see how each one gathers evidence and whether it makes use of the extra chances to look again.
summary.why: It shifts video evaluation from a fixed one-time view toward measuring how well a model uses interaction, which matters as video AI is increasingly deployed in agent-like roles. The text reports patterns across five models but gives no summary of how large the differences were, so its practical weight is still for specialists to judge.

title: VideoACE: Benchmarking Agentic Video Understanding through High-Frame-Rate Actions

abstract: Proactive video understanding requires vision-language models (VLMs) to decide not only what to answer as a video unfolds, but also when newly arrived evidence warrants a response and when to remain silent. Although modern VLMs excel at offline long-video understanding, they struggle in proactive streaming settings, leading prior work to introduce task-specific reinforcement learning or auxiliary triggering modules. We find that explicit reporting rules and structured streaming context substantially improve a frozen VLM's proactive response performance. We exploit this observation to build SIMPLEPRO, a training-free baseline for proactive video understanding. At each decision step, the model combines recent high-resolution frames, bounded historical observations, and prior answer records to determine whether new information warrants a response and, when needed, generate a concise answer. The system then filters consecutive duplicate answers while retaining the raw outputs as context for subsequent decisions. Without any parameter updates or auxiliary triggers, SIMPLEPRO with a 4B backbone consistently outperforms specialized proactive systems across OVO-Bench, StreamingBench-PO, and ProactiveVideoQA. SIMPLEPRO shows overall performance gains as backbone size increases from 2B to 32B. We hope this simple yet effective method will serve as a strong baseline for proactive video understanding, and we will release our code and inference pipeline to support future research.
label: arXiv:2611.23954v1

summary.background:
- Vision-language model (VLM): an AI model that takes images or video frames plus text and produces text.
- Proactive video understanding: the model must choose when to speak during a live video, not only answer when asked.
- Streaming setting: video arrives frame by frame, so the model cannot see the future.
- Training-free / frozen model: the model's weights are not updated; only the prompting and context handling are designed.
- Benchmarks named: OVO-Bench, StreamingBench-PO, ProactiveVideoQA (evaluation suites for this task).
- Backbone size: the number of parameters in the underlying model (2B to 32B here).
- Duplicate filtering: repeated identical answers are suppressed while raw outputs remain as context.
summary.one_liner: SimplePro is a training-free baseline that prompts a frozen 4B vision-language model with explicit reporting rules, recent high-resolution frames, bounded history, and prior answers to decide when to respond in streaming video, reporting gains over specialized proactive systems on three benchmarks.
summary.plain: The paper looks at AI systems that watch a video as it unfolds and must decide on their own when to say something and when to stay quiet. The authors show that a general-purpose vision-language model, used without any retraining, can do this well if it is given clear rules about when to report and a structured memory of what it has already seen and said. They call the resulting method SimplePro and report that it beats more specialized systems on three test suites.
summary.why: Most proactive video systems rely on task-specific training or extra trigger modules, so a strong no-training baseline is useful for judging whether those added parts are needed. Its relevance beyond these benchmarks, such as to live assistants or monitoring tools, is not addressed in the text.

title: SimplePro: A Simple Baseline for Proactive Video Understanding

abstract: Frontier post-training follows a common recipe: train one expert per domain with reinforcement learning (RL), then consolidate the experts into one model via multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). Such consolidation is expensive: the student samples in every environment again, an expert scores every sampled token, and the student inherits the drift of the final experts. Yet we argue that the experts' RL runs have already produced what consolidation needs: rollouts with their sampling probabilities and rewards, in the order the experts learned from them. We propose multi-expert replay policy distillation (MRPD), which replays these training logs through the student in the experts' order. At each step, the policy gradient is recomputed on these scored trajectories, and the final experts' distributions are distilled at the logged prefixes. Following the experts' own trajectory reduces the training-inference mismatch and keeps the student within the clip range, so the replay is off-policy in origin but quasi-on-policy throughout consolidation. MRPD samples nothing and calls no environment or reward model: the trainer is the sole process, and consolidating the experts costs only about a seventh of the compute used to train them. On three long-horizon agentic domains (reasoning, search and SQL), MRPD yields the best student model, substantially outperforming online RL baselines, and surpassing MOPD from the same experts at a fraction of MOPD's cost. Our analysis on the same logs shows that the replayed trajectories carry most of the gain, and that both the policy gradient and the distillation term add to it. Most interestingly, the order of the logs matters more than their amount or rewards, suggesting that expert training logs are a curriculum, not a data mixture.
label: arXiv:2611.24059v1

summary.background:
- Reinforcement learning (RL): training by trying actions and receiving rewards for good outcomes.
- Expert model: a version trained for one specific domain.
- Distillation: training a student model to imitate the output probabilities of one or more teacher models.
- On-policy vs. off-policy: on-policy learns from the model's own current attempts; off-policy learns from attempts generated by some other process, such as logged earlier runs.
- Rollout: one complete attempt at a task, recorded with its actions, probabilities and reward.
- Policy gradient: the update rule that nudges a model toward actions that led to higher reward.
- Clip range: a limit on how far each update can change the model, for stability.
- Long-horizon agentic task: a multi-step task where the model acts over many turns, such as searching or writing SQL queries.
summary.one_liner: MRPD consolidates several RL-trained domain experts into one student by replaying the experts' logged training rollouts, in the order the experts saw them, instead of sampling new data with on-policy multi-teacher distillation (MOPD).
summary.plain: Training AI models today often means first training separate "expert" versions, each good at one task, and then merging them into a single model. The usual merging step is expensive because it generates fresh practice attempts and has teachers score them again. This paper proposes reusing the record of what the experts already did during their own training, replaying it in the same order to train one combined model.
summary.why: The paper reports that the replay approach matches or beats the standard merging method at a fraction of its cost, on three multi-step tasks (reasoning, search and SQL). It also claims the order of the training records matters more than their size or reward values, which, if it holds up, would suggest those logs are better treated as a learning sequence than as a data pile; the text alone does not show how general this is.

title: Replay, Don't Resample: Off-Policy Consolidation of Long-Horizon RL Experts

abstract: We study the stochastic multi-armed bandit problem in which the reward associated with each arm is the survival probability at a pre-specified time horizon, and the observed outcome is a right-censored time-to-event variable. Standard bandit algorithms face delayed and partial observations in this setting. Prior adaptations for the Kaplan--Meier (KM) estimator rely on Hoeffding-type bounds that ignore the inherent heteroscedasticity of continuous survival processes. To bridge this gap, we propose KM-UCB, a variance-adaptive policy that unites continuous-time survival analysis with discrete sequential decision-making. By leveraging martingale theory and continuous influence functions, we derive a fixed-cohort empirical Bernstein bound parameterized by Greenwood's variance formula. For realtime allocation, we retain the Greenwood index and use a survival bound from completed records to review the recommended arm. Under catch-up reporting, the policy has logarithmic expected regret with an arm-specific variance term in the exploration bound. We evaluate the original policy in a dual-layer delayed simulation and a retrospective replay of breast cancer trial data, and evaluate the correction in a separate paired simulation.
label: arXiv:2611.24988v1

summary.background:
- Multi-armed bandit: a setting where an algorithm repeatedly picks one of several options (arms) and learns their average payoff only from what it picks.
- Upper confidence bound (UCB): a rule that favours options whose payoff estimate could still be high given uncertainty.
- Right-censoring: the event of interest (e.g., death) has not been observed by the end of follow-up, so the record only says it happened after some time.
- Kaplan-Meier estimator: a standard method for estimating survival curves despite censored records.
- Greenwood's formula: a standard estimate of the variance (spread of uncertainty) of a Kaplan-Meier survival estimate.
- Empirical Bernstein bound: a confidence bound that uses the observed variance, so it can be tighter when outcomes are less variable.
- Regret: how much reward is lost compared with always picking the best option; logarithmic regret grows slowly with the number of rounds.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes KM-UCB, a variance-adaptive upper-confidence bandit policy for right-censored survival rewards, using a fixed-cohort empirical Bernstein bound built on Greenwood's variance formula and a Kaplan-Meier estimator, with a logarithmic regret claim under catch-up reporting.
summary.plain: The paper looks at choosing between several treatment options when the result for each is whether a patient survives to a set time, but some patients leave a study before that time, so their outcome is only partly known. The authors build a decision rule that adjusts how much it explores based on how uncertain each option's survival estimate is, and they test it in simulations and on replayed breast cancer trial data. The text describes both the method and its theoretical guarantee, and also mentions a separate paired-simulation check of a correction.
summary.why: Adaptive allocation of patients to treatments under censored outcomes is a practical problem in clinical trial design, so the work may matter there. How much it helps in real trials is not established by the text, which describes simulations and one retrospective replay.

title: Variance-Adaptive Upper Confidence Bounds for Multi-Armed Bandits with Kaplan--Meier Survival Estimation

abstract: Characteristics of Artificial Intelligence (AI) severely restrict human control. This creates new challenges for socio-technical systems design especially in safety-critical domains, where control over risks is essential along with the accountability for any harm caused. Drawing from human factors and AI governance literature, expert interviews and participant observation in a complex high-risk AI use case from the railways, we developed ALIGN, a scenario-based method that supports the governance of and stakeholder involvement in AI development and implementation in three ways: raising awareness for potential accountability-control misalignments in socio-technical systems and their negative consequences, offering a structured approach to assessing the alignment between accountability and control for stakeholders in a given use case, and supporting effective design decisions to mitigate AI risks. We describe the iterative development and evaluation of ALIGN and discuss how this method promotes AI governance by highlighting the relevance of control-accountability alignment throughout the AI life cycle.
label: arXiv:2611.24609v1

summary.background:
- AI safety and alignment: work on making AI systems behave as intended and be safely overseen by people.
- Human factors: the study of how people interact with complex systems, including how much control they really have.
- Socio-technical systems: setups where technology, people, organisations and rules all interact.
- Accountability vs. control: control is the ability to influence outcomes; accountability is being answerable for consequences. The paper argues these can come apart when AI is involved.
- AI governance: the rules, institutions and processes that guide how AI is developed and used.
- Scenario-based method: a way of testing a design by walking through concrete hypothetical situations.
- Expert interviews and participant observation: qualitative research methods used to gather information from people working in the field.
summary.one_liner: This paper presents ALIGN, a scenario-based method for assessing and negotiating how control and accountability are distributed among stakeholders in high-risk AI systems, developed and evaluated using a railway use case.
summary.plain: The paper looks at a practical problem: when AI systems are used in safety-critical settings, it becomes hard for people to keep meaningful control over risks, and it is often unclear who is answerable if harm happens. The authors built a structured method, called ALIGN, to help the people involved spot and fix mismatches between who controls a system and who is accountable for it. They developed it using expert interviews and observation of a railway AI use case, and describe how it was refined over several rounds.
summary.why: As AI is deployed in risky fields such as transport, the question of who can actually intervene and who bears responsibility matters for safety and for governance. The text does not report how well ALIGN works beyond its development and evaluation, so its practical impact is unclear from this summary alone.

title: Negotiating Control and Accountability among Stakeholders in High-Risk AI Use Cases: Development and Evaluation of the Method ALIGN

abstract: Automated red teaming is essential for identifying safety failures in large language models (LLMs), but its practical scalability depends on the resources required to discover those failures. Multi-agent systems can combine complementary capabilities, yet repeated planning, redundant exchanges, and ineffective information routing can make their coordination expensive. Moreover, a target model's response indicates the outcome of a test without identifying which collaboration decision should change. We present Learning to Coordinate (L2C), an LLM-guided framework that evolves an executable multi-agent workflow for each red-teaming case. L2C represents agent responsibilities, execution dependencies, and input bindings in a versioned graph, and associates each graph with records of the information actually delivered and produced. A controller trained through supervised fine-tuning integrates these records with target responses, evaluator verdicts, and remaining budget to retain the workflow, refine instructions, restructure collaboration, or lock further editing. This design connects feedback to explicit changes in subsequent execution while allowing a useful organization to continue without repeated controller intervention. The evaluation protocol covers HarmBench with three execution backbones and two target models, together with component ablations, dataset transfer, and evaluator checks. Across the six executor-target configurations, L2C improves ASR over EvoSynth by 1.4 to 4.5 percentage points while reducing mean online tokens by 35.6% to 37.3%. L2C connects adaptive collaboration to the resource requirements of automated security evaluation.
label: arXiv:2611.24221v1

summary.background:
- Red teaming: deliberately probing an AI system with adversarial inputs to find harmful outputs.
- Attack success rate (ASR): the share of test attempts that elicit a harmful response, as judged by an evaluator.
- Multi-agent system: several AI components, each with a role, that pass messages and work together.
- Tokens: units of text that models read and generate; more tokens generally means more cost and time.
- Workflow graph: a diagram of which agent does what, what depends on what, and what inputs each step receives.
- Supervised fine-tuning: training a model on labeled examples of desired decisions.
- HarmBench: a public benchmark of harmful behaviors used to test model safety.
- EvoSynth: a prior automated red-teaming system used here as the comparison baseline.
summary.one_liner: L2C is an LLM-guided framework that evolves a versioned, executable multi-agent workflow for each red-teaming case, with a supervised-fine-tuned controller that decides whether to keep, refine, restructure, or lock the workflow, reporting higher attack success than EvoSynth with roughly 35–37% fewer online tokens on HarmBench.
summary.plain: The paper looks at how to find safety failures in AI chatbots by "red teaming," where one AI tries to get another AI to misbehave. It proposes a way for several cooperating AI agents to adjust how they split up and pass information during each test, so they waste less effort. According to the authors, across six setups of executor and target models, the method succeeded slightly more often than a prior system (by 1.4 to 4.5 percentage points) while using about 36% fewer tokens, which are the chunks of text a model processes and bills for.
summary.why: Testing AI systems for safety costs compute, so a method that finds failures with less cost could make routine safety evaluation more practical. The text reports results on one benchmark (HarmBench) with specific models, and it does not show how well the approach holds up beyond these settings.

title: Learning to Coordinate: LLM-Guided Workflow Evolution for Token-Efficient Red Teaming

abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are effective tools for mechanistic interpretability by decomposing neural representations into sparse and interpretable features. However, a single sparse representation in traditional SAEs is responsible for both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability, which are not guaranteed to align. To separate these objectives, we propose DualSAE, a modular framework that augments standard SAEs with a plug-in Residual Branch. A standard SAE serves as the Sparse Branch, learning a sparse code that contains the dominant semantics of the input. The added Residual Branch models the non-semantic information omitted by the Sparse Branch. We ensure that the contributions of the two branches towards the overall reconstruction have minimal overlap through a decorrelation loss. We also adopt a two-stage training strategy that first stabilizes sparse representation learning before coupling with the Residual Branch. Across diverse encoder-SAE configurations on two vision datasets and two language corpora, DualSAE achieves mean relative improvements of approximately 29% in reconstruction fidelity and 34% in interpretability (measured by monosemanticity score). Moreover, with more interpretable representations, DualSAE yields consistent performance gains in the downstream applications of topic modeling, hypothesis generation, and LLM steering. Qualitative analysis further suggests that the Sparse Branch indeed preserves dominant semantic content, whereas the Residual Branch captures non-semantic information to improve reconstruction fidelity.
label: arXiv:2611.25165v1

summary.background:
- Neural network representation: the numerical internal signals a model uses for an input such as an image or sentence.
- Autoencoder: a model that compresses an input into a code and then tries to rebuild the original from that code.
- Sparse autoencoder (SAE): an autoencoder that forces only a few code entries to be active at once, so each entry tends to correspond to a distinct idea.
- Reconstruction fidelity: how closely the rebuilt signal matches the original.
- Monosemanticity: a score for whether a code feature corresponds to one clear concept rather than several mixed ones.
- Decorrelation loss: a training penalty that discourages two outputs from carrying the same information.
- Steering: nudging a model's behavior by adjusting its internal features.
summary.one_liner: DualSAE augments a standard sparse autoencoder with a plug-in Residual Branch, decorrelated from a Sparse Branch, so that interpretability and reconstruction fidelity are handled by separate components.
summary.plain: Researchers study how to break a neural network's internal signals into simple, human-readable pieces. A common tool does this with one set of pieces that must both explain the signal accurately and be easy to interpret, but those two goals may pull against each other. The paper proposes splitting the job into two parts: one part keeps the main meaning, and a second part captures the leftover details, with a penalty that keeps the two parts from overlapping.
summary.why: The paper reports gains in reconstruction accuracy (about 29%) and in a measure of interpretability called monosemanticity (about 34%) across vision and language tests, plus improvements in topic modeling, hypothesis generation, and steering a language model. These are the authors' own reported averages from the abstract, and the text does not show how robust they are beyond those experiments. It may matter for efforts to understand what large AI models represent internally.

title: Separating Interpretability and Reconstruction in Sparse Autoencoders

abstract: As large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed, monitoring their behavior becomes important for detecting unsafe or unintended actions. Activation probes offer an efficient approach, but existing methods face trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and computational overhead. Probes on raw activations lack interpretable inputs, whereas sparse autoencoder (SAE) probes use interpretable features but often rely on additive classifiers and large SAE encoders, limiting interpretability and increasing memory overhead. We introduce GateWatch, a compact, interpretable classifier that expresses its entire decision rule as an explicit Boolean logic over a small number of binarized SAE features. We explore three approaches to constructing these circuits under a specified gate budget. For efficient deployment, GateWatchServe computes only selected SAE features, enables streaming of their binary values across layers during inference, and evaluates multiple GateWatch classifiers in parallel using compact lookup tables. Across 24 tasks on Gemma-2-9B, GateWatch achieves 80.49% mean test accuracy using only 3.8 SAE features and 3.5 logic gates per probe on average, just 1.17 percentage points below full 16K-feature SAE probes, while matching or outperforming them on 10 tasks and reducing probe memory by 99.98%. Inside vLLM, 1,000 concurrent multi-layer, multi-token GateWatch classifiers retain 97-98% of baseline throughput and 99.8% of KV-cache capacity.
label: arXiv:2611.24619v1

summary.background:
- Activation probe: a small classifier trained on a model's internal numbers (activations) to detect a property, such as unsafe output.
- Sparse autoencoder (SAE): a tool that re-expresses internal activations as a larger set of sparse features, many of which can be interpreted by humans.
- Boolean logic / logic gates: rules built from AND, OR and NOT on yes/no inputs; here, SAE features are first turned into on/off values.
- Gate budget: a limit on how many logic gates a rule may use, keeping it small and interpretable.
- KV cache: memory a language model keeps for previously processed tokens; losing capacity to monitors reduces serving efficiency.
- vLLM: a widely used open-source system for serving language models efficiently.
summary.one_liner: GateWatch is a compact monitor for LLM activations that expresses its decision as Boolean logic over a few binarized sparse-autoencoder features, and is evaluated on 24 tasks with Gemma-2-9B and inside vLLM serving.
summary.plain: Large language models are increasingly used in agents, and developers want cheap ways to spot unsafe or unintended behavior while the model runs. This paper proposes GateWatch, a small classifier that makes its yes/no decision with simple AND/OR/NOT-style rules over a handful of readable internal features of the model. On 24 tasks with Gemma-2-9B, the authors report about 80.5% mean test accuracy using roughly 4 features and 3.5 logic gates per probe, about 1.2 points below probes that use all 16K features, while cutting probe memory by 99.98%.
summary.why: Monitoring that is both cheap and human-readable could matter for safety checks on deployed models, since the decision rule can be inspected rather than being a black box. The text reports serving results inside vLLM (97-98% of baseline throughput with 1,000 concurrent classifiers), but the evaluation is limited to one model family and the paper's own tasks, so how well it generalizes is not established here.

title: GateWatch: Low-Overhead LLM Monitoring with Boolean Circuits

abstract: Most existing approaches enhance mathematical reasoning in large language models (LLMs) as a monolithic capability, despite the fact that different mathematical problems require different reasoning skills. Recent work has explored a more fine-grained perspective by decomposing mathematical reasoning into atomic skills and developing specialized modules for individual capabilities. However, how to effectively utilize these atomic abilities remains underexplored. To address this challenge, we propose Atomic MathReasoner (AMR), an instance-level framework for composing atomic reasoning skills. AMR first trains a library of capability-specific LoRA experts and performs gradient-free optimization over held-out validation subsets to discover a diverse set of low-loss composition prototypes. It evaluates the preference of each prototype using the token-level negative log-likelihood of reference solutions, filters ambiguous assignments through a confidence margin, and distills the resulting pseudo-labels into a lightweight router. During inference, the router selects an appropriate composition prototype for each problem, enabling problem-specific utilization of atomic skills without costly online optimization. Experiments on the AtomicMath benchmark across general and mathematics-specialized LLMs demonstrate consistent improvements. On Qwen2.5-Math-Instruct-7B, AMR increases average field accuracy from 64.4% to 68.1% at Level 1 and from 59.3% to 63.7% at Level 2, while improving average logical reasoning performance from 39.4% to 46.8%. These results demonstrate that effectively composing specialized atomic skills provides a promising approach to strengthening mathematical reasoning in LLMs.
label: arXiv:2611.24846v1

summary.background:
- LLM: a large language model trained on text, here applied to math problems.
- Mathematical reasoning benchmark: a standard test set used to measure how accurately a model solves problems.
- LoRA (low-rank adaptation): a small add-on set of trainable weights that specializes a large model for a task without retraining all of it.
- Expert/router: in this setting, the LoRA add-ons are "experts" and a router decides which to activate or how to combine them.
- Negative log-likelihood: a measure of how surprised a model is by a reference answer; lower means the model finds it more likely.
- Pseudo-label: an automatically generated label used as training target when no human label exists.
- Gradient-free optimization: searching for good settings by trying candidates rather than using gradient-based training.
summary.one_liner: Atomic MathReasoner trains a set of skill-specific LoRA experts for LLMs and uses a lightweight router, distilled from pseudo-labels derived from reference-solution likelihoods, to pick a per-problem composition of those experts on the AtomicMath benchmark.
summary.plain: Large language models often handle math as one general ability, even though different problems need different kinds of reasoning. This paper splits math reasoning into smaller "atomic" skills, trains a separate small add-on module for each, and teaches a small router to choose which combination to use for each individual problem. On the AtomicMath benchmark, the authors report gains for a math-specialized 7B model, for example average field accuracy rising from 64.4% to 68.1% at Level 1.
summary.why: Routing each problem to a tailored mix of skills is a modular alternative to making one model do everything, and it avoids expensive per-problem optimization at inference time. The text reports consistent gains but only on one benchmark and a few model families, so how well it generalizes beyond these experiments is unclear from the text alone.

title: Atomic MathReasoner: Instance-Level Composition of Atomic Reasoning Skills for Mathematical LLMs

abstract: Isabelle Pool Server (IPS), a verification service with a pool of warm headless Isabelle sessions behind an HTTP API, with session leasing and reclamation, memory-aware admission control, and a time budget on every call. Its verification interface spans single-step execution, block-level proof checking and whole-theory builds, with checkpoints for cheap branching and backtracking, and a build from scratch as the final arbiter. The service runs as a single container with monitoring and is accessible via a Python client, two MCP servers and a raw HTTP API. In our measurements IPS is level with PIDE MCP, a PIDE frontend for agents, at one worker and ahead of it at eight, at its commit of October 2026 (the tool is now PIDE AI). Once its sessions are up it scales to 32 concurrent workers on one host at 24 times the single-worker rate, and under memory pressure it refuses new sessions rather than losing existing ones. IPS is free software and publicly available at https://github.com/Deep-LCF/Isabelle-Pool-Server
label: arXiv:2611.24788v1

summary.background:
- Isabelle: a proof assistant, software that checks formal mathematical proofs step by step.
- Headless session: a proof-checking process running without a graphical interface, which can be controlled by a program.
- Warm pool: sessions started in advance so requests do not pay the startup cost.
- HTTP API: a standard way for programs to send requests to a server over the web.
- Admission control: deciding whether to accept new work based on available memory.
- Checkpoint and backtracking: saving a proof state so one can try alternatives and return to it.
- MCP server: a connector that lets AI agents call external tools.
- Multi-agent proving: several AI programs attempting proofs at the same time.
summary.one_liner: The paper presents Isabelle Pool Server, an HTTP service that manages a pool of pre-started headless Isabelle proof sessions for step-wise, block-level and whole-theory verification, with admission control, time budgets, and checkpoints for branching and backtracking.
summary.plain: Isabelle is a computer system where mathematical proofs are written and checked by machine. This paper describes a server that keeps a pool of ready-to-use proof-checking sessions, so that programs (including AI agents) can ask it to check proof steps or whole proofs without waiting for a fresh start each time. The authors report that it handles many parallel requests on one machine and refuses new work rather than crashing existing sessions when memory runs low.
summary.why: Automated provers used to train or guide AI systems need to check many candidate proofs quickly, so shared infrastructure of this kind may matter for that work. The text itself gives only the authors' own measurements, and it does not show how it performs on real training or proving tasks beyond those tests.

title: Isabelle Pool Server: a pooled verification service for prover training and multi-agent proving

abstract: In contact-rich dexterous manipulation, occlusion by the fingers and interacting objects obscures local geometry, preventing visual observations from fully capturing contact locations. Visually similar scenes may also differ subtly in the relative positions of interacting objects, leading to different contact states. We propose 3DTouch, a tactile-geometric conditioning approach for vision-language-action (VLA) models. 3DTouch constructs a shared 3D visuo-tactile representation by expressing RGB-D scene points and dense five-finger tactile measurements in the robot-base frame, preserving each taxel's spatial location and force vector. Hand-object and object-object relations derived from hand landmarks and pose-aligned reconstructed surfaces explicitly describe the relative arrangement of interacting entities. Together, these representations condition the VLA action expert on spatially localized contact forces and relative surface geometry, providing explicit cues for contact adjustment and object alignment. We evaluate 3DTouch on five real-world contact-rich dexterous manipulation tasks using a UR7e robot arm equipped with an XHand dexterous hand. 3DTouch improves the average success rate by 42 percentage points over the corresponding VLA baseline and by 20 percentage points over the strongest evaluated alternative. Ablation studies reveal the complementary benefits of scene geometry and spatial tactile feedback, with further gains from shared spatial grounding and explicit geometric relations.
label: arXiv:2611.23961v1

summary.one_liner: 3DTouch conditions a vision-language-action robot policy on a shared 3D representation of RGB-D scene points and dense five-finger tactile readings, plus hand-object and object-object geometric relations, for contact-rich dexterous manipulation.
summary.plain: Robot hands often grasp things in ways the cameras cannot fully see, because the fingers and objects block the view. This paper proposes giving a robot's AI controller both 3D camera geometry and touch-sensor readings, placed in the same coordinate frame, so it knows where contact happens and how hard. The authors report testing this on five real-world hand tasks with a robot arm and a dexterous hand.
summary.why:
Combining touch and 3D geometry in one spatial representation is a plausible route to more reliable robot hand skills, since vision alone can miss contact details. The text reports a 42-point average success-rate gain over the base model and 20 points over the strongest alternative, but the summary provides no task details or variance, so the size of the benefit is hard to judge from this text alone.</ahem>
<parameter name="background">["VLA (vision-language-action) model: a large AI model that takes camera images and a language instruction and outputs robot motor actions.", "Dexterous hand: a multi-fingered robot hand, here a five-finger XHand, with many joints for fine manipulation.", "Tactile sensing (taxel): touch sensors made of many small pressure cells; each reports where and how strongly it is pressed.", "RGB-D: a camera that records color plus depth (distance) for each pixel, giving 3D points.", "Robot-base frame: a single fixed coordinate system centered on the robot arm's base, used to put all sensor data in one spatial reference.", "Ablation study: tests that remove one component at a time to see how much each part contributes."]

title: 3DTouch: A Tactile-aware VLA Model with 3D Geometric Relations for Dexterous Manipulation

abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can propose multi-step manipulation plans, but they have no grounded model of how a scene will change, and the pixel-level world models that could check those plans are slow and drift over long horizons. We present Verify2Act, a modular verification framework that separates semantic action proposal from latent physical verification. A VLM proposes candidate plans, a latent world model (V2A-WM) imagines each of them in the DINOv2 feature space, and a dual-head critic checks the imagined rollouts for temporal consistency and goal satisfaction before anything is executed. V2A-WM extends recent flow-matching world models with cross-attention action grounding and a causal temporal history window. We deploy the full system on a low-cost robot arm, training the world model and critic only on data generated in a digital twin. Across six language-conditioned tasks, Verify2Act reaches 83.3\% task success, compared with 61.7\% for a latent world model without our architectural changes, 53.3\% for the VLM alone, and 46.7\% for a pixel-diffusion world model. It verified every plan it executed and incurred no planning-induced failures: all of its failed episodes were caused by low-level grasp or placement slips. In simulation, Verify2Act obtains the highest five-task chain success on CALVIN among the compared baselines with 30$\times$ fewer reflective VLM calls than pixel-diffusion verification, and the highest success on cluttered nut assembly.
label: arXiv:2611.25243v1

summary.background:
- Vision-Language Model (VLM): a model that reads images and text and can propose step-by-step plans, but does not simulate physics.
- World model: a learned model that predicts how a scene will change after an action.
- Latent space / DINOv2 features: a compressed numerical description of images produced by a pretrained vision network, used instead of raw pixels.
- Flow matching: a training method for generative models that learns to transform noise into plausible predictions; here it predicts future scene features.
- Critic: a learned scorer that rates imagined rollouts on temporal consistency and goal satisfaction.
- Digital twin: a simulated copy of the real robot and workspace used to generate training data.
- CALVIN: a public benchmark of long-horizon, language-instructed robot tasks; "five-task chain success" means completing five tasks in a row.
- Pixel-diffusion world model: a slower predictive model that generates full images, used here as a comparison.
summary.one_liner: Verify2Act checks language-model-proposed robot manipulation plans by imagining their outcomes in a latent (feature-space) flow-matching world model, scored by a dual-head critic before execution.
summary.plain: Robots that take spoken or written instructions often use a language model to suggest a sequence of steps, but the language model has no real sense of how the scene will change. This paper adds a checking stage: each proposed plan is first "imagined" by a predictive model working on compact visual features rather than raw pixels, and a critic judges whether the imagined outcome is consistent and reaches the goal. Only plans that pass are run on a low-cost robot arm.
summary.why: The reported gains on a real arm (83.3% task success versus 53.3% for the language model alone) and the claim of fewer costly model calls suggest that checking plans in a compact imagined space is a practical route to more reliable robot planning. The results come from one lab's six-task setup and a simulation benchmark, so how far they generalize is not yet clear.

title: Verify2Act: Critic-Guided Latent World Models for Verifying Language-Conditioned Manipulation Plans

abstract: Local differential privacy (LDP) is vulnerable to output manipulation by malicious clients. Zero-knowledge proofs can enforce correct report computation, but clients may still selectively drop out after inspecting their outputs. Prior work combines zero-knowledge proofs with homomorphic encryption to hide reports from clients and prevent selective dropout, but incurs substantial computational cost. We instead develop a three-message lightweight verification framework for robust histogram estimation that uses proofs of plaintext evaluation to restrict output manipulation to selective dropout. Across the evaluated settings for PI-RAPPOR and Hadamard Response, mean per-client online latency remains below 500 milliseconds. We further establish tight error bounds showing that, for RAPPOR, PI-RAPPOR, and Hadamard Response, restricting malicious clients to selective dropout reduces attack-dependent error by a factor proportional to the square root of the domain size compared with output manipulation. Additionally, when client protocols cannot be modified, we propose server-side consistency checks for RAPPOR and Hadamard Response. These checks improve robustness without client-side cryptography and can be applied post-hoc to collected reports, offering an alternative under different deployment constraints. Experiments demonstrate that both verification and consistency checks substantially reduce attack error for certain mechanisms, with consistency checks yielding errors intermediate between those obtained with verification and those under unrestricted output manipulation.
label: arXiv:2611.24623v1

summary.background:
- Local differential privacy: each user randomizes their own data before it leaves their device, so the collector never sees raw values.
- Histogram estimation: counting how many users fall into each category, such as the frequency of each item.
- RAPPOR and Hadamard Response: two specific randomized-response schemes for reporting category counts under this privacy model.
- Zero-knowledge proofs: a way for a client to prove its report was computed correctly without revealing the underlying data.
- Homomorphic encryption: a method for computing on encrypted values; prior work using it is costly, which motivates this paper's lighter approach.
- Selective dropout: a participant ending their participation after seeing their output, which is the residual attack the paper studies.
- Server-side consistency checks: tests the collector runs on received reports, without changing what clients do.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes a lightweight three-message verification protocol using proofs of plaintext evaluation for robust locally differentially private histogram estimation (PI-RAPPOR, Hadamard Response), restricting malicious clients to selective dropout, and offers server-side consistency checks for RAPPOR and Hadamard Response as a client-unmodified alternative.
summary.plain: Privacy-preserving surveys let each person add noise to their answer before sending it, so a server can estimate overall counts without seeing anyone's true answer. The weakness is that a dishonest participant can send a falsified answer to skew the totals. This paper shows how to limit such cheating to just dropping out of the survey after seeing their own output, and reports that the checks run in under half a second per client in the settings tested.
summary.why: Estimates from privacy-preserving data collection are used in products and government statistics, so resistance to manipulation matters. The authors also give error bounds claiming that restricting attackers to dropping out reduces attack-dependent error by a factor on the order of the square root of the domain size; the text does not show how general that claim is beyond the mechanisms named.

title: Robust, Lightweight Locally Differentially Private Histogram Estimation and the Role of Dropout Attacks

abstract: Tabular in-context learning (TabICL) enables large language models (LLMs) to predict target records using a handful of labeled demonstrations in their prompts. However, these demonstrations often contain sensitive personal information. Differential privacy (DP) offers principled protection, but noise-based methods introduce substantial noise, distorting the feature-label relationships essential for accurate prediction, especially as data dimensionality grows. In this work, we study DP data synthesis for generating privacy-preserving TabICL demonstrations. We identify two limitations of directly applying general-purpose DP synthesis to entire datasets: modeling a global distribution can obscure local structure and minority patterns in heterogeneous data, while measuring broad attribute dependencies under a limited privacy budget can reduce the accuracy available for relationships most relevant to prediction. More broadly, global statistical fidelity may fail to preserve heterogeneous structures needed by downstream predictive and generative models. To address these challenges, we propose PriTabICL, a general framework compatible with existing DP synthesis algorithms. It partitions records into DP clusters and synthesizes each independently, using a fixed feature-target workload to prioritize prediction-relevant statistical relationships. At inference, each query is routed to a DP cluster, and demonstrations are sampled from its synthetic dataset without additional privacy loss for the original records. Experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods across heterogeneous datasets. In particular, one of our instantiations, PriTabICL-PrivSyn, improves over global PrivSyn in 8 out of 12 settings and outperforms existing private TabICL approaches in nearly all evaluated settings. Open-source code is available.
label: arXiv:2611.25073v1

summary.background:
- In-context learning: giving a language model a few labeled examples in its prompt, instead of retraining it.
- Tabular data: records organized in rows and columns, like a spreadsheet or database table.
- Differential privacy (DP): a mathematical guarantee that the output reveals little about any single person's record, achieved by adding carefully calibrated randomness and tracking a "privacy budget" that limits how much can be learned.
- DP data synthesis: generating a fake dataset that statistically resembles the real one while satisfying DP.
- Clustering: grouping similar records together.
- Workload: the set of feature-and-label relationships the method chooses to preserve accurately.
summary.one_liner: PriTabICL applies differentially private data synthesis, clustering records and using a fixed feature-target workload, to generate privacy-preserving demonstrations for tabular in-context learning with LLMs.
summary.plain: Large language models can make predictions on spreadsheet-style data by reading a few labeled examples placed in their prompt, but those examples may reveal private personal information. This paper proposes a way to create artificial example sets that keep the useful patterns for prediction while carrying formal privacy guarantees. The approach splits the data into groups, builds a separate synthetic set for each group, and sends each new query to the matching group.
summary.why: Privacy-safe prompting matters for anyone who wants to use LLMs on sensitive records such as health or financial tables without leaking individual entries. The paper reports that one variant beat a global synthesis method in 8 of 12 settings and beat existing private approaches in nearly all settings across four datasets; the text does not show how far these gains would carry to other data.

title: PriTabICL: Differentially Private Tabular In-Context Learning with Task-Aligned Cluster-Wise Synthesis

abstract: The impartial game Undirected Vertex Geography is known to be polynomial time solvable. The variant in which vertices are assigned heights with maximum value m that reduce by 1 whenever the token is moved from that vertex, denoted UIRm, is known to be polynomial time solvable when m=2 and PSPACE-complete when m=4. We solve the open question of the computational complexity of UIR3 by a reduction from Directed vertex geography, and show that the complexity holds when the underlying graph is planar and (a) has degree at most 3, (b) is bipartite with maximum degree 4, or (c) is bipartite with maximum degree 5 and only has heights of 1 and 3.
label: arXiv:2611.24709v1

summary.background:
- Impartial game: both players have the same moves available, and the player who cannot move loses.
- Vertex Geography: a game where a token moves along edges of a graph (dots and lines) to unvisited dots; the standard version is solvable in polynomial time.
- Heights: a modification where each dot has a number that counts down with each move from it, limiting how often it can be used.
- Polynomial time vs PSPACE-complete: "easy to solve efficiently" versus "believed to need a very large amount of memory or time as the game grows."
- Reduction: showing one problem is at least as hard as another by converting instances of the known hard problem into instances of the new one.
- Planar graph: a network that can be drawn on a flat surface with no crossing lines. Bipartite: dots can be split into two groups with lines only between groups. Maximum degree: the largest number of lines meeting at one dot.
summary.one_liner: The paper settles the complexity of the impartial game Undirected Vertex Geography with maximum height 3 (UIR3) by reducing from Directed Vertex Geography, showing it remains hard on planar graphs of maximum degree 3, on bipartite graphs of maximum degree 4, and on bipartite graphs of maximum degree 5 with heights restricted to 1 and 3.
summary.plain: This is a theory paper about a two-player game played on a network of dots connected by lines, where a token is moved along the lines one step at a time. Each dot carries a height number that drops by one each time the token leaves it, and the question is how hard it is to work out who wins. The authors show that the height-3 version is hard to solve in general, even when the network is drawn flat or has special structure, by translating a known hard game into this one.
summary.why: The result closes an open question the authors identify: the difficulty of the height-3 case was unknown, sitting between a case known to be easy (height 2) and one known to be hard (height 4). It is mainly of interest to researchers in game complexity and computational complexity theory; the text does not claim applications beyond that.

title: The computational complexity of Undirected Vertex Geography with maximum height 3

abstract: Minimum spanning tree interdiction asks for edge deletions within a budget that maximize the weight of a remaining minimum spanning tree. We give two deterministic $(2+ε)$-approximation algorithms for every fixed $ε>0$, improving the previous best factor of $4$. Both algorithms respect the original budget and run in $N^{O(1/ε)}$ time for $0<ε\le1$, where $N$ is the binary input size. The first algorithm uses two weight thresholds to choose initial deletions that force every remaining spanning tree to contain edges at or above these thresholds. It then uses the remaining budget to further increase the MST weight through Lagrangian rounding. The second algorithm achieves the same guarantee through a different decomposition: it enumerates vertex partitions and heavy trees connecting their parts, then approximates a bounded-weight interdiction problem within the parts.
