An objective-preserving reduction from Maximum Components shows that, assuming the Small Set Expansion Hypothesis and $\mathsf P\ne\mathsf{NP}$, no deterministic polynomial-time $(2-δ)$-approximation exists for any fixed $0<δ<1$, even on simple graphs with weights in $\{0,1\}$. Thus, our approximation guarantee is conditionally tight up to an arbitrarily small additive constant. Finally, the MST guarantee yields a $(4+ε)$-approximation for metric-TSP interdiction.
label: arXiv:2611.24526v1

summary.background:
- Graph: points (vertices) joined by weighted links (edges).
- Spanning tree: a set of links connecting all points with no loops; the minimum spanning tree (MST) is the one with the smallest total weight.
- Interdiction: an adversary deletes edges within a budget to hurt the network; here the goal is to maximize the MST weight after deletions.
- Approximation factor: an efficient algorithm guarantees a result within a stated multiple of the best possible value; (2+ε) means within about twice optimal, for any small ε>0.
- Hardness assumptions: the Small Set Expansion Hypothesis and P≠NP are unproven conjectures; the lower bound holds only if they are true.
- Metric TSP: the traveling salesman problem where distances satisfy the triangle inequality.
- Lagrangian rounding: a standard technique that replaces a budget constraint with a penalty term and then rounds the solution.
summary.one_liner: The paper gives two deterministic (2+ε)-approximation algorithms for minimum spanning tree interdiction (improving a previous factor of 4), shows a matching (2−δ) hardness under the Small Set Expansion Hypothesis and P≠NP, and derives a (4+ε)-approximation for metric TSP interdiction.
summary.plain: The problem asks how to remove a limited number of connections from a network so that the cheapest way to connect all points, the minimum spanning tree, becomes as expensive as possible. The authors present two computer procedures that get within a factor of about two of the best possible damage, improving on a previous factor of four. They also argue, under standard but unproven complexity assumptions, that no efficient procedure can do much better than two.
summary.why: It narrows a gap between known upper and lower bounds for a well-defined optimization problem, and the hardness result is said to be tight up to an arbitrarily small constant. The text does not say how it affects practical applications, and the TSP result is only a consequence of the spanning tree guarantee.

title: Two $(2+ε)$-Approximation Algorithms for Minimum Spanning Tree Interdiction

abstract: HyperLTL extends LTL with quantification over traces. AUtoHyper is the de facto explicit-state model checker for HyperLTL, complete for an arbitrary quantifier prefix: it eliminates quantifiers through products of the formula's omega-automaton with the systems, complementing on quantifier alternations. However, it suffers from state explosion, as it fully materializes input systems and intermediate automata. We present OmegaHyper, an overhaul of AutoHyper that keeps its algorithm but decomposes and reduces the size of the processed automata, and integrates the Kofola omega-automaton complementation tool. We compare OmegaHyper with existing explicit-state and symbolic HyperLTL model checkers, on 120 benchmarks from their published suites. OmegaHyper improves the performance of explicit-state HyperLTL model checking by up to orders of magnitude; bounded symbolic tools still reach further on violated instances with short counterexamples, as expected.
label: arXiv:2611.24210v1

summary.background:
- Model checking: automatically checking, by exhaustive search, that a system satisfies a specification.
- LTL (linear temporal logic): a language for describing how behaviour unfolds over time along a single run.
- HyperLTL: an extension of LTL that quantifies over several runs (traces) at once, so it can express properties like non-interference.
- Omega-automaton: a finite machine that accepts infinite sequences of events; used to encode temporal properties.
- Complementation: converting an automaton into one accepting exactly the inputs the original rejects; costly and central to handling quantifier alternations.
- Explicit-state vs. symbolic: explicit tools enumerate states one by one; symbolic tools encode sets of states compactly, often with bounded search depth.
summary.one_liner: OmegaHyper is a reworked version of the explicit-state HyperLTL model checker AutoHyper that decomposes and shrinks the automata it processes, integrates the Kofola complementation tool, and is benchmarked against existing explicit-state and symbolic checkers on 120 published benchmarks.
summary.plain: The paper is about checking whether a computer system meets rules that talk about several runs of that system at once, such as requirements about fairness or information leakage between runs. The existing tool AutoHyper can handle any combination of these rules, but it runs out of memory on large systems because it builds every intermediate piece in full. The authors built OmegaHyper, which keeps the same method but splits the work into smaller pieces, and report that it is up to orders of magnitude faster on explicit-state checking.
summary.why: Verifying properties that span multiple traces matters for security and concurrency, where single-trace checking is not enough. The text reports that symbolic bounded tools still go further on violated instances with short counterexamples, so OmegaHyper is a speedup within one family of methods rather than a general replacement for the others.

title: OmegaHyper: Explicit-State HyperLTL Model Checking on an omega-Automaton Diet

abstract: Multi-level compilers built on MLIR lower concurrent programs through many stages towards targets with potentially drastically different memory models, where an optimisation which appears reasonable, can silently change program behaviour. Testing these lowerings is hard: a concurrent program often has no single expected outcome, and existing MLIR fuzzers often assume determinism. We present MLIR-MRacle, a memory-model-aware metamorphic fuzzer for concurrent MLIR programs. MLIR-MRacle applies metamorphic relations gated by the target memory model, so that both the original and transformed programs remain well defined - executing both repeatedly, and comparing their outcome sets or distributions withone of two statistical oracles. A coverage guided campaign driver built on libafl is used to perform continuous fuzzing. MRs, memory models, oracles, and execution backends all provide extension points for future researchers and compiler engineers to build off this package. In a case study on Armv8 hardware, MLIR-MRacle ran over 145k trials across four configurations, reaching up to 93.6k compiler coverage edges, and found a bug in the OpenMP dialect verifier that has since been fixed upstream. Video: https://youtu.be/lKtGk0H97Ts?si=dWLUHl2CJ24ep6JY
label: arXiv:2611.24804v1

summary.background:
- MLIR: a compiler framework that lowers programs through a sequence of intermediate representations ("dialects").
- Memory model: the rules defining which reorderings of memory reads and writes a processor or language may observe across threads.
- Concurrent program: one with multiple threads whose interleavings can produce different outputs.
- Metamorphic testing: checking that a transformation preserves expected relationships between original and transformed programs, when no exact expected output exists.
- Fuzzing: automatically generating or mutating inputs to find failures.
- Statistical oracle: a rule that decides whether two observed outcome distributions are consistent, rather than comparing single outputs.
- Armv8: a widely used processor architecture with a relatively weak memory model.
- OpenMP dialect: an MLIR component for expressing parallel programs using OpenMP-style constructs.
summary.one_liner: MLIR-MRacle is a metamorphic fuzzer for concurrent MLIR programs that uses memory-model-gated transformation rules and statistical comparison of outcome sets to test compiler lowerings on Armv8 hardware.
summary.plain: Compilers often translate programs through several stages, and a change that looks harmless can quietly alter how a multi-threaded program behaves on a particular chip. This paper presents a testing tool that checks these translations by running the original and rewritten versions of a concurrent program many times and comparing the distribution of results, since such programs have no single correct output. In a case study on Armv8 hardware, the authors report over 145k trials and found a bug in the OpenMP dialect verifier, which has since been fixed upstream.
summary.why: Compiler bugs in concurrent code can be hard to notice because the wrong behaviour may appear only occasionally, so tools that compare outcome distributions address a real testing gap. The text does not show how broadly the approach would find bugs beyond the single reported case, so its wider impact is uncertain.

title: MLIR-MRacle: Memory-Model-Aware Metamorphic Fuzzing of Concurrent MLIR

abstract: Despite countless mitigation efforts, memory safety issues still prevail. The recently discovered security issues in PHP underline this fact. One of the most promising approaches to solving this problem is the concept of Capability Hardware Enhanced RISC Instructions (CHERI). There is a well-developed ecosystem of ISA simulators, compilers, operating systems, and hardware designs that support CHERI. However, the lack of a simulator modeling microarchitectural detail hinders efficient and fast design space exploration for CHERI-enhanced designs means the performance impact of CHERI remains understudied. Therefore, we present gem5-CHERI: a CHERI-enhanced adaptation of the gem5 simulator that can boot the CheriBSD operating system and run custom workloads. The simulator is available open-source on GitHub.
label: arXiv:2611.24460v1

summary.background:
- Memory safety: preventing programs from accessing memory beyond what they are meant to use, a common source of security flaws.
- CHERI (Capability Hardware Enhanced RISC Instructions): a processor extension where pointers carry hardware-checked permissions and bounds, called capabilities.
- ISA (instruction set architecture): the set of basic instructions a processor understands; simulators model these.
- gem5: an open-source simulator that models processor hardware in detail, used for architecture research.
- Microarchitecture: the internal organization of a processor (pipelines, caches) that determines speed.
- CheriBSD: a version of the FreeBSD operating system adapted for CHERI.
summary.one_liner: The paper presents gem5-CHERI, an extension of the gem5 microarchitectural simulator that adds CHERI capability-based memory protection and can boot the CheriBSD operating system and run custom workloads, with the code released open-source on GitHub.
summary.plain: Software often fails because programs read or write memory they should not touch, and many security bugs come from this. The authors describe CHERI, a hardware design approach that tags memory references with built-in limits, and they add it to gem5, a widely used computer simulator, so designers can test how such protection behaves in detailed models of processors. The text says the simulator can boot a CHERI-enabled version of FreeBSD (CheriBSD) and run custom programs.
summary.why: Before this, there was no detailed simulator for CHERI designs, so the speed cost of this protection was described as understudied. A tool like this could let researchers measure that cost and explore design choices, though the text does not report any performance results.

title: TechReport: Implementing CHERI in gem5

abstract: While popular operating systems such as Linux and Windows were originally designed as monolithic kernels, an increasing number of kernel subsystems have become extensible using eBPF. Users can now define custom policies for essential kernel mechanisms, such as the process scheduler, page cache, and network stack, without recompiling the kernel. These mechanisms give developers significant freedom to fit the kernel to their applications' workloads, but the question of which policy to deploy remains open. We study how to use agentic AI to automate kernel policy development, selection, and deployment, focusing on the page cache and the process scheduler as two representative subsystems. We show that existing approaches fall short: evolutionary and agentic search runs offline, is relatively expensive, and often fails to generalize to online workloads, while online knob tuners are encumbered by the knobs' lack of expressivity. In contrast, we propose Polymorph, which learns online: an AI agent writes a generalized, granular policy once, and a user mode tuner adjusts its parameters during runtime, with no LLM in the loop. For the page cache, Polymorph improves throughput over Linux's LRU by 8.4% on unseen data, nearly twice the gain of the best existing policy, while adapting to workload changes at runtime and costing only 16M tokens once, versus 125-240M tokens per workload for agentic offline search. For the process scheduler, it improves on Linux's default by 2.75x across six workloads, versus 2.27x for the best fixed sched_ext policy.
label: arXiv:2611.23644v1

summary.background:
- Kernel: the core software that manages a computer's hardware, memory and running programs.
- Page cache: memory the system uses to keep recently read disk data ready, so it doesn't have to be re-read from disk.
- LRU (least recently used): a simple rule that evicts the data that has gone unused the longest.
- Process scheduler: the part of the OS that decides which program gets the processor next.
- eBPF and sched_ext: mechanisms that let user-written code extend parts of the Linux kernel safely without recompiling it.
- Tokens: units of text processed by an AI model; the paper uses token counts as a proxy for AI cost.
- Throughput: how much work gets completed per unit time.
summary.one_liner: Polymorph uses an AI agent to write a generalized eBPF/sched_ext policy for the Linux page cache and process scheduler once, then lets a user-space tuner adjust its parameters online without an LLM in the loop.
summary.plain: Modern operating systems like Linux let developers plug in custom rules for how the computer manages memory caching and deciding which task runs next, without rebuilding the whole system. This paper asks whether an AI system can write those rules automatically. The authors report that their approach, Polymorph, gives a modest throughput gain for the page cache on data it was not trained on, and a larger speedup for the scheduler across six test workloads, at a lower AI cost than prior search methods.
summary.why: Choosing the right kernel policy for each workload is a practical problem for anyone running large servers, so automating it could matter. The text reports specific numbers (8.4% on unseen data, 2.75x versus 2.27x for the best fixed scheduler policy), but these come from the authors' own evaluation, and I cannot judge from the abstract alone how broadly they hold.

title: Polymorph: Operating System Kernel Optimization Through Artificial Intelligence

abstract: General-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) assistants are increasingly embedded in everyday life, transforming how people accomplish tasks and potentially reshaping how they interact with others. Prior research has focused on how using AI for explicitly social purposes affects users' psychological well-being and social lives. Yet such uses account for only a small portion of interactions with general-purpose AI assistants. Whether using AI for everyday, instrumental tasks affects users' psychological well-being and social behavior remains unclear. Here we investigate these effects through a longitudinal deactivation experiment with active ChatGPT users (N=625), in which participants were randomly assigned to abstain from using AI assistants for either fourteen days (treatment) or one day (control). Participants used AI predominantly for instrumental purposes, with 84.7% reporting productivity as their most frequent use case. Two weeks of deactivation significantly reduced loneliness relative to the control group ($β= -0.10$, $p=0.03$), with reductions persisting two weeks after participants resumed using AI ($β= -0.16$, $p=0.02$). Deactivation also significantly increased the number of people participants interacted with in person and the time they spent socializing over the intervention period. Open-ended responses indicate that during the deactivation period participants sought help from others for tasks they otherwise would have delegated to AI and redirected attention toward social interaction. Overall, our findings suggest that even when AI is used primarily to accomplish instrumental tasks, it may inadvertently reduce opportunities for social interaction and connection.
label: arXiv:2611.25263v1

summary.background:
- Deactivation experiment: participants are asked to stop using a tool for a set period, and outcomes are compared with a group that stops for less time (here, one day).
- Longitudinal: measurements taken over time, here including a follow-up two weeks after people resumed AI use.
- Loneliness and social interaction are measured through self-report and participants' descriptions of their time, as described in the text.
- β (beta) is a regression coefficient: the estimated size and direction of the effect. p-values indicate how likely a result this large would be by chance under the study's assumptions.
- Instrumental use means using a tool to get a practical job done, such as writing, planning, or research, as opposed to social or emotional use.
- Open-ended responses are free-text answers, used here to describe what people did instead of using AI, such as asking other people for help.
summary.one_liner: A randomized longitudinal deactivation experiment (N=625 active ChatGPT users) finds that a two-week break from general-purpose AI assistants, mostly used for instrumental tasks, reduced self-reported loneliness and increased in-person social interaction relative to a one-day control.
summary.plain: Many people now use AI chatbots like ChatGPT mainly for everyday work tasks rather than for companionship. This study asked whether giving those tools up for two weeks changes how lonely people feel and how much they socialize. Participants were randomly assigned to go without AI for either two weeks or one day, and the two-week group reported less loneliness and more in-person contact.
summary.why: Most research on AI and social life has looked at people using AI explicitly as companions, so this suggests that ordinary productivity use may also matter for connection. It is a single study as described in this text, and the authors' interpretation that AI may "inadvertently" reduce social contact is one reading of the data rather than a settled finding.

title: AI Deactivation Reduces Loneliness and Increases Social Interaction

abstract: Animating virtual opponents is an important yet challenging task in game development. In martial arts games, opponent motions must not only be physically plausible but also exhibit appropriate technique, timing, transitions, and target-directed intent. Traditional game animations often rely on handcrafted clips, state machine transitions, and procedural adjustments, which can be labor-intensive and may limit the behavioral diversity of non-player characters. This paper presents a martial arts motion skills learning framework for character animation in virtual sparring games. Inspired by Tang Soo Do, we collected a martial arts motion capture dataset containing isolated attacking and defending techniques, technique combinations and transitions, and contextual sparring variations. We first pretrained a reusable repertoire of martial arts motion skills from the captured data using reinforcement learning (RL) with adversarial style rewards, and then adapted these skills with task-specific rewards for target-directed striking and threat-aware evasion. We evaluated the motions generated by the learned policy through a user study, in which participants assessed their physical plausibility, smoothness, and martial arts form. To demonstrate their applicability to interactive gameplay, we developed a VR sparring prototype for Meta Quest headsets. The prototype combines policy-generated motion clips with lightweight state-based control to support interactive opponent behavior. Together, these findings support the feasibility of using a learned martial arts skill repertoire as a motion foundation for animating opponents in VR sparring games.
label: arXiv:2611.23825v1

summary.background:
- Character animation: making virtual figures move; games often use pre-recorded clips and state machines (rules for switching between clips).
- Motion capture: recording a real person's movements with sensors or cameras to use as reference data.
- Reinforcement learning (RL): training a program by rewarding behavior that achieves a goal; here a simulated character learns to move.
- Adversarial style rewards: a learned judge that rewards movements looking like the captured human motion.
- Task-specific rewards: extra scoring for goals such as hitting a target or evading an attack.
- Meta Quest: a consumer VR headset; the prototype runs on it.
- Tang Soo Do: a Korean martial art whose techniques informed the dataset.
summary.one_liner: A reinforcement-learning framework that pretrains a reusable repertoire of martial arts motion skills from motion-capture data and adapts them with task rewards to animate VR sparring opponents, evaluated by a user study and a Meta Quest prototype.
summary.plain: The paper looks at how to make computer-controlled fighters in virtual reality move like real martial artists, instead of relying only on hand-made animation clips. The authors recorded motion-capture data of Tang Soo Do techniques, learned a set of reusable movement skills from it, and then tuned those skills so the character can aim strikes at a target and dodge threats. Participants rated the resulting motions, and the team built a small VR sparring demo.
summary.why: Game opponents that move more varied and believable could reduce the labor of hand-authoring animations and make VR training or sparring feel more natural. The text reports a user study and a working prototype, but it does not give the study's results or sample size, so how strong the gains are cannot be judged from this text alone.

title: Learning Martial Arts Motion Skills for Animating Opponents in VR Sparring Games

abstract: Long-read sequencing technologies generate large volumes of data, creating substantial storage and transmission demands. Although reference-based compressors can achieve high compression, their reliance on an appropriate reference genome limits their use. We present LRCBench, a benchmark and survey of reference-free lossless compressors for long-read sequencing data. We review traditional and learning-based general-purpose and sequencing-specific methods, then evaluate 35 compressors on 16 real-world datasets from Oxford Nanopore and PacBio platforms. We compare compression ratio, storage savings, runtime, peak memory use, and robustness across datasets. Learning-based compressors are evaluated on six MinION datasets because of their high computational costs. CoLoRd achieves the best overall compression ratios in our experiments, while other methods offer trade-offs in speed, memory use, and robustness. We also examine multithreaded speedup and discuss future directions in parallel acceleration, privacy protection, adaptive parameter tuning, and hardware-algorithm co-design.
label: arXiv:2611.23794v1

summary.one_liner: A benchmark and survey of 35 reference-free lossless compressors (traditional and learning-based) evaluated on 16 real Oxford Nanopore and PacBio long-read sequencing datasets, comparing compression ratio, runtime, memory, and robustness.
summary.plain:
Modern DNA sequencing machines produce very large files, which are costly to store and send. This paper tests many software tools that shrink these files without needing a reference genome (a standard DNA text to compare against). The authors ran 35 such tools on 16 real datasets and compared how much they shrink the data, how fast they run, how much memory they use, and how consistent they are.</plain>
<parameter name="why">Storage and transfer costs are a practical bottleneck for long-read sequencing, so knowing which tools work best without a reference is useful to labs. The text reports that CoLoRd gave the best overall compression in these tests, but the results only cover the datasets and settings the authors used.</plain>
<parameter name="background">- Lossless compression: shrinking a file so it can be restored exactly, bit for bit.
- Compression ratio: original size divided by compressed size; higher means smaller output.
- Long-read sequencing: technology (Oxford Nanopore, PacBio) that reads DNA in long pieces, producing large files.
- Reference-based vs reference-free: reference-based tools compress by comparing to a known genome; reference-free tools do not need one, which matters when no suitable genome exists.
- Learning-based compressors: tools that use machine-learning models to predict the data, usually slower and more costly to run.
- Multithreading: running parts of a program on several processor cores at once to speed it up.

title: Benchmarking Traditional and Learning-Based Reference-Free Compressors for Long-Read Sequencing Data

abstract: Learning a Hamiltonian evolution time in Quantum Phase Estimation that produces phase distributions with low Shannon entropy circumvents the fundamental limit of digitization error of phase, independent of the number of phase qubits of accuracy. By introducing an optimization loop to minimize the Shannon entropy of measured eigenvalues produced by a QPE quantum circuit, minimum eigenvalue computation accuracy is greatly improved, which we show numerically on quantum magnet models. This technique works because standard QPE has a natural correspondence between entropy of the phase distribution and the analog accuracy of the minimum eigenvalue phase. This introduces for the first time a type of parameter learning to QPE, which makes near term practicality of QPE for fundamental sciences more feasible by using shorter depth QPE circuits.
label: arXiv:2611.25124v1

summary.background:
- Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE): a quantum algorithm that reads out an eigenvalue (energy level) of an operator as a phase angle.
- Hamiltonian: the operator describing a system's energy; evolving under it for a time t imprints phases tied to energies.
- Eigenvalue / minimum eigenvalue: the lowest energy level, often the target of ground-state calculations.
- Qubits and digitization error: the phase is stored in a finite number of binary digits, so precision is limited by the number of qubits.
- Shannon entropy: a measure of spread or uncertainty in a probability distribution; low entropy means outcomes cluster tightly.
- Quantum magnet models: standard test systems (spin lattices) used to benchmark quantum algorithms.
- Near-term quantum computing: work targeting current noisy hardware where shallow circuits are needed.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes learning the Hamiltonian evolution time in Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) by minimizing the Shannon entropy of the measured phase distribution, reporting improved minimum-eigenvalue accuracy on quantum magnet models.
summary.plain: Quantum Phase Estimation is a quantum-computing procedure for finding the lowest energy of a physical system, and its accuracy is normally limited by how finely the answer can be encoded in qubits. This paper adds an optimization loop that tunes the evolution time so the measured results are less spread out (lower Shannon entropy, a measure of how unpredictable a set of outcomes is). The authors report that this improves the estimate of the minimum energy in numerical tests on quantum magnet models.
summary.why: If the approach holds up, it could make QPE useful on near-term quantum hardware by allowing shorter, shallower circuits for physics problems. The text gives only a brief summary and numerical tests on magnet models, so its broader significance and how it compares with other methods are not established here.

title: Learning Integer Winding Evolution Times in Quantum Phase Estimation

abstract: We provide a rigorous definition of quasinormal modes (QNM) for the Majumdar--Papapetrou spacetimes with multiple extremal black holes. For certain configurations, the trapped set of the null geodesic flow contains stable (elliptic) orbits. We analyze this phenomenon in the case of two black holes of equal mass and show that it produces QNM converging exponentially fast to the real axis. QNM for black holes have been extensively studied for $\textit{single}$ black holes and this appears to be the first $\textit{mathematical}$ result for the case of multiple black holes.
label: arXiv:2611.24063v1

summary.background:
- Black hole "ringing" (quasinormal modes): damped oscillations a black hole gives off after being disturbed, each with a characteristic frequency and decay rate.
- Extremal black hole: a black hole with the largest charge or spin allowed for its mass, which here makes several of them can sit in equilibrium together.
- Majumdar–Papapetrou spacetime: an exact solution of Einstein's equations describing several charged black holes in static balance.
- Null geodesic: the path light takes through curved spacetime.
- Trapped set: the set of light paths that neither escape to infinity nor fall into a black hole.
- Elliptic (stable) orbit: a light path that stays bounded and returns near itself, like a stable planetary orbit; such orbits are why ringing decays slowly.
- Exponential convergence to the real axis: the modes' decay rates shrink toward zero very quickly, meaning long-lived ringing.
summary.one_liner: The paper gives a rigorous definition of quasinormal modes for Majumdar–Papapetrou spacetimes containing several extremal black holes, and shows that for two equal-mass holes, stable elliptic orbits in the trapped set produce quasinormal modes that approach the real axis exponentially fast.
summary.plain: When a black hole is disturbed, it "rings" like a bell at characteristic frequencies, called quasinormal modes, which fade away over time. This paper studies that ringing for a model universe containing several extremal (maximally charged) black holes rather than just one. The authors give a precise mathematical definition of these modes for this setting and find that, for two equal-mass holes, some light paths can circle stably between them, which yields ringing that decays very slowly.
summary.why: The text describes this as the first mathematical result on quasinormal modes for multiple black holes, which is why it is notable within a field that has mostly studied single black holes. The text does not say how these results would be checked against observations of gravitational waves, so any link to astronomy is unclear from this abstract alone.

title: Long lived QNM for multiple black holes

abstract: Static Love numbers of Schwarzschild black holes vanish at linear and quadratic order in General Relativity, while generic nonlinear tides remain less understood. We solve a specific non-axisymmetric octupolar tide at cubic order and, building on the symmetry of static General Relativity exploited by Parra-Martinez and Podo, match the result to a worldline effective field theory (EFT) using dimensional regularization. Surprisingly, we find a Love number that neither vanishes nor runs.
label: arXiv:2611.25059v1

summary.background:
- Tidal Love number: a number measuring how much an object deforms under an external tidal field; it characterises its internal response.
- Schwarzschild black hole: the simplest non-spinning, non-charged black hole in General Relativity.
- Linear, quadratic, cubic order: successively higher powers of the tidal strength; nonlinear effects enter at quadratic and cubic order.
- Worldline effective field theory (EFT): a method that treats a compact object as a point particle with extra terms describing its internal response, letting calculations be organised systematically.
- Dimensional regularization: a mathematical technique for handling divergent intermediate integrals by temporarily working in a non-integer number of dimensions.
- "Runs": a coupling that depends on the energy or length scale used in calculations; a non-running value is scale-independent.
- Octupolar: a tidal pattern with angular structure of degree three, more complex than the simple quadrupolar pattern.
summary.one_liner: The paper computes a cubic-order static Love number for Schwarzschild black holes under a non-axisymmetric octupolar tidal field, matching the result to a worldline effective field theory using dimensional regularization, and reports a nonzero value that neither vanishes nor runs with scale.
summary.plain: The paper asks how a black hole responds when it sits in an external gravitational "squeeze" that is stronger than the simple linear case. Earlier work found that a non-spinning black hole's static response vanishes at the first two orders, so the authors looked at the third order for one specific lopsided, non-symmetric pattern of squeezing. They report that the response at this order is nonzero and does not change with the mathematical scale used in the calculation.
summary.why: Love numbers describe how easily an object deforms under tides, and they can be read off from gravitational-wave signals of merging compact objects. A nonzero, scale-independent cubic value is notable because the text calls it surprising, but the text does not show how it would feed into observations, so its practical reach is unclear.

title: Nonzero cubic Love numbers of Schwarzschild black holes

abstract: Dissociation of molecular hydrogen increasing temperature or pressure may either occur gradually or abruptly, via a phase transition. Despite considerable experimental and theoretical efforts, the phase diagram of dense hydrogen at temperatures above solid melting is not precisely known. Here, we perform classical and quantum Path Integral molecular dynamics simulations of dense hydrogen using two machine-learned interatomic potentials both trained on quantum Monte Carlo energies and forces. The resulting phase diagram is constructed using state-of-the-art techniques. Both models show a first-order phase transition from the molecular to the atomic liquid terminating in critical points whose locations were determined using finite-size scaling techniques. Triple points, located at the highest temperature of the melting curve, are found at the intersection of the liquid-liquid lines with the melting curve and should lead to clear signatures in ramp compression experiments.
label: arXiv:2611.25178v1

summary.background:
- Hydrogen molecules are pairs of atoms; at high pressure and temperature they can dissociate into single atoms.
- A first-order phase transition is an abrupt change, like ice melting, with a jump in density; it ends at a critical point where the distinction between the two phases disappears.
- A triple point is where three phases (here, two liquids and a solid) coexist.
- Molecular dynamics simulates how atoms move over time; path-integral methods include quantum effects of light nuclei.
- Machine-learned interatomic potentials are fitted models that predict forces between atoms much faster than direct quantum calculations.
- Quantum Monte Carlo is a high-accuracy numerical method for solving the quantum many-body problem; finite-size scaling is a way to locate critical points from simulations of different system sizes.
- Ramp compression is an experimental technique that compresses a sample smoothly over time to high pressure.
summary.one_liner: Classical and quantum path-integral molecular dynamics with two machine-learned interatomic potentials trained on quantum Monte Carlo data map the liquid phase diagram of dense hydrogen near melting, reporting a molecular-to-atomic liquid transition, its critical points, and triple points.
summary.plain: This paper studies how hydrogen changes when it is squeezed and heated near its melting point, specifically whether its molecules (pairs of atoms) break apart in a sudden jump or gradually. The authors ran computer simulations using machine-learned models that were trained on very accurate quantum calculations. They report that both models show a sudden, first-order change from molecular liquid to atomic liquid, which ends at critical points, and that triple points lie where this change meets the melting curve.
summary.why: Dense hydrogen matters for planetary interiors such as those of giant planets, and the paper says its predicted triple points should produce clear signatures in ramp-compression experiments. The text does not go further, so the link to specific experiments or planetary models is something a reader should check in the full paper.

title: The phase diagram of fluid hydrogen near melting from machine-learned interatomic potentials trained on quantum Monte Carlo

abstract: Recently it was found that closely packed two-patch particles exhibit rich orientational ordering behaviors, e.g., nonmonotonic changes of the nematic order parameter and double BKT phase transitions [arXiv:2509.03981]. In this work, we show that, with repulsive patch-patch, attractive patch-nonpatch and intermediate nonpatch-nonpatch interactions, there exist frustrations in the system of closely packed two-patch particles. To investigate the ground states of the system, we design a Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithm with single-defect propagation. The simulation results show that the ground states are disordered and the correlation functions decay exponentially with the distance. These results demonstrate that in 2D close packing one could design patchy particles to explore orientationally disordered systems.
label: arXiv:2611.24560v1

summary.background:
- Patchy particles: particles with localized attractive or repulsive regions (patches) that control how they bond.
- Close packing: particles arranged so that they nearly touch with little empty space, here in two dimensions.
- Frustration: when interactions conflict so no single arrangement can satisfy all of them, often leaving many near-equal lowest-energy states.
- Ground state: the lowest-energy configuration of a system, here found by simulation rather than exact solution.
- Monte Carlo simulation: a computer method that makes random trial changes and accepts them by probabilistic rules to sample configurations.
- Orientational order and nematic order parameter: measures of how aligned particle directions are; disorder means no preferred alignment.
- BKT (Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless) transition: a two-dimensional phase transition involving vortex-like defects, referenced from an earlier paper.
- Correlation decay: how quickly the orientation of one particle stops influencing distant ones; exponential decay means a short correlation length.
summary.one_liner: A Monte Carlo study of closely packed two-patch particles in 2D, showing that competing (frustrated) patch and nonpatch interactions lead to disordered orientational ground states with exponentially decaying correlations.
summary.plain: This paper looks at tiny particles with two sticky spots ("patches") packed tightly on a flat surface, and asks how their orientations arrange themselves. The authors set up interaction rules that pull in competing directions, so the particles cannot satisfy all of them at once. They then used a computer simulation with a special update method to search for the lowest-energy arrangements and found that these arrangements are disordered, with the orientation links fading quickly with distance.
summary.why: It suggests that designing patchy particles could be a way to build orientationally disordered two-dimensional materials, which is a state that is otherwise hard to engineer. The text does not show how far this extends beyond the specific model studied, so its wider relevance is uncertain.

title: A Monte Carlo study of closely packed two-patch particles with frustrated interactions

abstract: We study the spin-1 Kitaev chain and, by analyzing its Hilbert-space connectivity in the Cartesian basis, show that it hosts an exponentially large number of exact zero-energy modes protected by chiral symmetry. For even-length periodic chains, their count is lower-bounded by the Jacobsthal number $(2^{L+1}+1)/3$, where $L$ is the chain length. We then construct an exponentially large number ($2^{L/2}$) of zero modes with an analytic expression that have a maximally mixed density matrix for a contiguous bipartition using the operator-state mapping. We further identify an embedded tight-binding structure governing defect dynamics that supports PXP-like quantum many-body scars (QMBS) in multiple sectors previously not reported. The associated forward-scattering approximation (FSA) Hamiltonian takes a universal form across the scarred sectors studied. A simple physical picture of defects propagating between walls provides an intuitive description of these dynamics and a structural guide to identifying sectors with fidelity revivals, while its limitations point to additional scarring mechanisms.
label: arXiv:2611.25051v1

summary.background:
- Quantum spin: a tiny magnetic degree of freedom; spin-1 means three possible states per site.
- Kitaev chain: a one-dimensional model of interacting spins with direction-dependent couplings.
- Zero modes: states with exactly zero energy; chiral symmetry is a mathematical symmetry that protects them.
- Hilbert-space connectivity: which basis states can be reached from which others by the dynamics.
- Quantum many-body scars: special non-thermal states that show slow, repeating dynamics instead of scrambling.
- PXP model: a standard toy model in which scars were first studied; FSA is an approximation that maps the dynamics onto a simpler effective hopping problem.
- Tight-binding: a simple model of particles hopping between neighbouring sites.
- Jacobsthal number: an integer sequence; here it gives a lower bound on the zero-mode count.
summary.one_liner: The paper finds exponentially many exact zero-energy modes protected by chiral symmetry in the spin-1 Kitaev chain, and identifies an embedded tight-binding defect structure that gives PXP-like quantum many-body scars in several sectors, described by a universal forward-scattering approximation Hamiltonian.
summary.plain: This paper studies a chain of tiny quantum magnets (spin-1 particles) arranged in a line, with a specific pattern of interactions. The authors show the chain has a very large number of special states that do not change energy over time, and they find that some other special states keep returning to their starting pattern when the system is run forward. They explain much of this with a simple picture of defects moving between barriers.
summary.why: Quantum many-body scars are unusual states that resist the usual tendency of isolated quantum systems to scramble and heat up, which matters for quantum simulation and quantum computing. The text reports a counting result and an analytic construction, but its wider significance beyond this model is not established in the excerpt provided.

title: Quantum many-body scars and zero modes in the spin-1 Kitaev chain

abstract: Chiral spin liquids (CSLs) are paradigmatic fractionalized phases, yet simple exact parent Hamiltonians for them remain scarce. In this work, we construct exact spin parent Hamiltonians for partially magnetized CSLs realizing various bosonic topological orders. Our construction relies on an exact Hubbard-type parent Hamiltonian for bosonic lattice fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states, valid at arbitrary repulsive interaction strengths. Taking the on-site repulsion to infinity and applying local boson-spin mappings yields exact parent Hamiltonians for the CSLs. Our two-spin construction generalizes the Kalmeyer-Laughlin spin Hamiltonian to a broader class of bosonic FQH model states, including Abelian states and non-Abelian parton states. We derive controlled microscopic realizations of these two-spin Hamiltonians via second-order superexchange in generalized spinful Hofstadter-Hubbard models with tailored hoppings and interactions. With more general local constraints and interactions, boson-spin mappings yield exact higher-spin and multispin parent Hamiltonians for partially magnetized CSLs.
label: arXiv:2611.24935v1

summary.background:
- Spin liquid: a magnet whose spins stay disordered and entangled even at very low temperature.
- Chiral spin liquid: a spin liquid that breaks time-reversal symmetry, giving it a definite handedness.
- Topological order: a kind of order described by global patterns of entanglement, not by local symmetry breaking; it can carry fractional excitations.
- Fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states: electron or boson states in strong magnetic fields with fractionally charged excitations; "Abelian" and "non-Abelian" refer to how those excitations exchange statistics.
- Parent Hamiltonian: an engineered local energy function whose exact ground state is a target wavefunction.
- Kalmeyer-Laughlin state: the original chiral spin liquid model, which this work generalizes.
- Hubbard model: a lattice model of particles hopping between sites with an on-site repulsion; the limit of infinite repulsion removes doubly occupied sites.
- Superexchange: an effective spin-spin interaction arising at second order from virtual electron hopping.
summary.one_liner: The paper constructs exact spin parent Hamiltonians for partially magnetized chiral spin liquids realizing bosonic topological orders, via a Hubbard-type parent Hamiltonian for bosonic lattice fractional quantum Hall states taken to infinite on-site repulsion and mapped onto spins.
summary.plain: The paper concerns a exotic magnetic state of matter called a chiral spin liquid, in which spins are strongly entangled and do not order, yet carry a built-in handedness. The authors write down simple, exactly solvable model rules (Hamiltonians) that have these states as their ground states, by starting from a known exactly solvable model of bosons in a lattice version of the fractional quantum Hall effect and translating it into spin language. They also outline how such spin models might be realized in electron systems with tailored hoppings and interactions, though the text presents these as derivations rather than experiments.
summary.why: Exact, solvable models are valuable benchmarks because they let researchers study topological order without approximations, and this work extends the classic Kalmeyer-Laughlin spin model to a wider family of bosonic states, including non-Abelian ones. Its relevance to real materials or quantum devices is not established by the text alone, so that connection should be treated as speculative.

title: Exact Parent Hamiltonians for Partially Magnetized Chiral Spin Liquids

abstract: Chan and Lee present a model where the AMS-02 positron excess is explained by dark matter (DM) annihilation in spike halos around nearby black holes A0620-00 and XTE J1118+480. Their model assumes a uniform magnetic and diffusive environment en route to Earth. Thus, it depends on the assumption that one can ignore the small-scale, near-horizon environment in the diffusion-loss equation. We demonstrate that this is not the case. An accurate magnetic field model near the horizon means, without increasing the required cross-section by a factor of roughly 500 to 1400, depending on the transport near the horizon, the positron flux from these sources cannot account for a significant fraction of the AMS-02 excess.
label: arXiv:2611.23983v1

summary.background:
- AMS-02: a particle detector on the International Space Station that measures cosmic rays, including positrons.
- Positron excess: more positrons observed at high energies than standard models of cosmic-ray production predict.
- Dark matter annihilation: hypothetical dark matter particles colliding and destroying each other, producing ordinary particles such as positrons.
- Dark matter spike: a dense, steeply peaked concentration of dark matter that can form around a black hole.
- X-ray binary: a system where a black hole or neutron star pulls matter from a companion star, emitting X-rays; A0620-00 and XTE J1118+480 are two nearby examples.
- Diffusion-loss equation: the standard equation describing how charged particles spread out through magnetic fields while losing energy.
- Event horizon: the boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing can escape.
- Cross-section: a measure of how likely particles are to interact; a larger required cross-section means the proposed process must be far more frequent.
summary.one_liner: A comment arguing that a dark-matter-annihilation explanation for the AMS-02 positron excess, based on spike halos around nearby black hole X-ray binaries, fails once the magnetic and diffusive environment near the black hole horizon is modelled accurately.
summary.plain: Cosmic-ray detectors such as AMS-02 on the International Space Station have measured more positrons (anti-electrons) arriving from space than simple models predict. One proposed explanation is that dark matter particles annihilate in dense clumps around nearby black holes and produce these positrons. This paper challenges that idea: the authors argue that the magnetic environment very close to a black hole changes how positrons escape, and that once this is included, the required dark matter annihilation rate would need to be hundreds to over a thousand times larger.
summary.why: The positron excess is one of the long-running hints that dark matter might be detectable through cosmic rays, so whether a specific proposed source survives scrutiny matters for that search. The text does not show how robust the factor of roughly 500 to 1400 is across all plausible models, so the conclusion should be read as the authors' estimate rather than settled fact.

title: Positron escape from dark matter spikes in black hole X-ray binaries

abstract: This work presents measurements of the total and single-differential electron neutrino charged-current cross sections on argon using the Short-Baseline Near Detector (SBND) at Fermilab. We present the highest statistics inclusive $ν_e + \bar ν_e$ (95.2% $ν_e$ and 4.8% $\barν_e$) charged-current cross section measurement on argon to date and the first inclusive $ν_e + \bar ν_e$ cross section measurement using the Booster Neutrino Beam. Direct measurements of this channel are crucial for future studies of both long- and short-baseline neutrino oscillations through electron neutrino appearance, which in turn are vital for answering open questions in neutrino phenomenology and searching for beyond the Standard Model physics at the intensity frontier. The data used for this work were collected with an exposure of $8.81 \times10^{19}$ protons on target, and 729 candidate events are selected with a minimum electron energy of 500 MeV. The single-differential cross sections are extracted in electron energy and angle with respect to the beam axis. The flux-averaged total cross section is measured to be $σ= [3.90 \pm 0.18\,\text{(stat)} \pm 0.41\,\text{(syst)}] \times 10^{-39}$ cm$^2$/nucleon for a predicted average neutrino energy of $\langle E_ν\rangle=1.8$ GeV for selected events. The total and differential cross sections are compared to predictions from common neutrino event generators. The data show a preference for generators that predict a lower overall cross section.
label: arXiv:2611.25098v1

summary.one_liner: A measurement, using the SBND detector at Fermilab's Booster Neutrino Beam, of the total and single-differential inclusive electron-neutrino (plus antineutrino) charged-current cross sections on argon, compared against common neutrino event generators.
summary.plain: This paper reports how often neutrinos of a specific type (electron neutrinos) interact with argon atoms when they hit a detector, and how that rate depends on the energy and angle of the electron that comes out. The team used the SBND detector at Fermilab, collecting data equal to about 8.81 × 10^19 protons aimed at a target, and selected 729 candidate events. They found a total interaction rate of about 3.90 × 10^-39 cm² per nucleon, and they report that the data favor simulation tools that predict a lower overall rate.
summary.why:
Neutrino experiments that look for oscillations, where neutrinos change type, depend on accurate models of how neutrinos interact, so direct measurements of this channel help check those models. The text links the result to future long- and short-baseline oscillation searches and to searches for physics beyond the Standard Model, but it does not itself show what effect the result will have on those searches.</why>
<parameter name="background">- Neutrinos: nearly massless, electrically neutral particles that interact very rarely with matter.
- Charged-current interaction: a neutrino exchanges a charged W boson with a nucleus and turns into a charged lepton (here an electron).
- Cross section: a measure of how likely an interaction is, expressed as an effective target area; the unit cm² per nucleon is per nucleon in the target.
- Argon: the liquid detector material used in SBND.
- Booster Neutrino Beam: a beam of neutrinos produced at Fermilab.
- Neutrino event generators: computer programs that simulate neutrino interactions; the paper compares its data with them.
- Oscillation: neutrinos changing from one type to another as they travel, which requires knowing interaction rates accurately.
- Statistical vs. systematic uncertainty: random counting error vs. errors from detector and modeling assumptions.</background>
<parameter name="difficulty">research-level

title: Measurements of the total and differential inclusive electron neutrino charged-current cross sections on argon with SBND

abstract: We discuss charmed mesons in heavy-ion collisions by focusing on their production from the quark-gluon plasma by quark recombination. We consider the production of not only the $D$, $D^*$, $D_s$, and $D_s^*$, but also the $D_{s0}^*(2317)$, $D_{s1}(2460)$, $D_{s1}(2536)$, and $D_{s2}^*(2573)$, thereby investigating the important role of heavier charm-strange resonances in understanding the measurements of the $D$ and $D_s$ mesons at the Large Hadron Collider at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=5.02$ TeV. We calculate their yields and transverse momentum distributions, and also evaluate ratios of the transverse momentum distribution between various charmed mesons, i.e., the $D_s$ and $D^0$, the $D_s$ and $D^+$, $D_s^*$ and $D^{*0}$, and $D_s^*$ and $D^{*+}$. Through this analysis, we attempt to understand in more detail the effects of strangeness enhancement on charmed meson production in heavy-ion collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=5.02$ TeV.
label: arXiv:2611.24303v1

summary.background:
- Heavy-ion collisions at the LHC create a quark-gluon plasma, a short-lived state of matter where quarks and gluons are not locked inside protons or neutrons.
- Charm quarks are heavy and are produced early in the collision, so they carry information about the plasma.
- Mesons are particles made of a quark and an antiquark; D mesons contain a charm quark, and D_s mesons also contain a strange quark.
- "Strangeness enhancement" means strange-containing particles are produced more often than expected in a plasma-free environment.
- Quark recombination (coalescence) is a model in which quarks that meet in the plasma bind together to form hadrons, instead of forming them one by one from scratch.
- Transverse momentum is the momentum sideways to the beam; the shape of its distribution reveals how particles were produced.
- Resonances are short-lived excited states that decay into lighter particles, so measured yields depend partly on these decays.
summary.one_liner: A theoretical study of how charm-strange hadrons, including heavier excited states such as D_s0*(2317) and D_s1(2460), are produced by quark recombination in the quark-gluon plasma formed in 5.02 TeV Pb-Pb-type heavy-ion collisions at the LHC, and how their yields and transverse-momentum ratios compare with D and D_s measurements.
summary.plain: When heavy atomic nuclei collide at very high energy, they briefly melt into a hot soup of free quarks and gluons, called the quark-gluon plasma. This paper asks how charmed particles, which contain a heavy "charm" quark, form out of that soup. The authors include not only the common charmed mesons but also several heavier, short-lived charm-strange particles, and they calculate how many of each are made and how fast they move. They then compare ratios between particle types with what the Large Hadron Collider has measured.
summary.why: Measurements of D and D_s mesons in heavy-ion collisions are a way to probe how the hot medium makes new particles and whether it favors strange quarks. The paper suggests that the heavier resonances, which are often left out of such models, may matter for matching the data; the text does not show how large this effect is beyond the stated comparisons.

title: Effects of charm-strange resonances on charmed meson production by recombination in relativistic heavy ion collisions

abstract: We report measurements of second-order cumulants and correlations of experimentally accessible baryon number, electric charge, and strangeness proxies in Ru+Ru and Zr+Zr collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 200$~GeV with the STAR experiment. The results exhibit similar centrality dependences in the two isobar systems within uncertainties. The baryon-strangeness correlation $C_{BS}$ is compared with lattice-QCD and UrQMD calculations. Motivated by recent lattice-QCD predictions for QCD matter in an external magnetic field, several ratios of conserved-charge correlations are studied as functions of centrality. In peripheral collisions, the measured ratios exhibit the same ordering as the lattice-QCD prediction. A qualitatively similar hierarchy is also found in UrQMD, although the model underpredicts the observed peripheral-to-central enhancement. These results motivate further quantitative studies of possible magnetic-field contributions and other sources of the observed centrality dependence.
label: arXiv:2611.24673v1

summary.background:
- Heavy-ion collisions: nuclei collided at high energy produce a short-lived hot, dense state of quarks and gluons.
- Conserved charges: baryon number, electric charge and strangeness are quantities conserved in the strong interaction; their fluctuations are studied as signals of the underlying matter.
- Isobars: nuclei with the same mass number but different proton counts (Ru and Zr), useful for comparing systems with nearly identical size.
- Cumulants and correlations: statistical measures of how much event-to-event counts vary and move together.
- Centrality: how head-on a collision is; peripheral means glancing, central means head-on.
- Lattice QCD: numerical simulation of quark-gluon theory on a grid; UrQMD: a transport model of hadronic collisions used as a baseline.
- Magnetic field: colliding heavy ions create very strong transient magnetic fields, which lattice calculations predict could affect charge correlations.
summary.one_liner: STAR measures second-order cumulants and correlations of proxies for baryon number, electric charge and strangeness in Ru+Ru and Zr+Zr collisions at 200 GeV, compares baryon-strangeness correlations with lattice QCD and UrQMD, and examines charge-correlation ratios versus centrality in light of a predicted magnetic-field signature.
summary.plain: Heavy nuclei are smashed together at high speed in the STAR detector at Brookhaven to briefly recreate the very hot, dense matter that filled the early universe. This paper uses two nearly identical isobar systems, ruthenium and zirconium, and tracks how the numbers of particles carrying different "charges" fluctuate and correlate from one collision to the next. The two systems look similar within uncertainties, and certain ratios in peripheral (glancing) collisions follow the ordering that lattice calculations predict for matter in a strong magnetic field.
summary.why: Fluctuations of conserved charges are a way to probe the phase structure of strongly interacting matter, and the magnetic-field angle connects this to extreme conditions in heavy-ion collisions and the early universe. The text reports only a qualitative match and says quantitative studies are still needed, so the magnetic-field interpretation remains open.

title: Fluctuations and Correlations of Conserved Charges in Isobar Collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 200 GeV with the STAR Detector

abstract: Scaling universal quantum computation and implementing quantum machine learning with protected logical qubits remain challenging. To harness the computational potential of existing fault-tolerant quantum platforms, we introduce topological quantum reservoir computing, a novel approach using protected degrees of freedom for storage and the host system's intrinsic dynamics for information processing. Using a one-dimensional Kitaev chain, we show how long-lived Majorana edge modes and fast bulk responses support these complementary functions within the same many-body system. We identify the tradeoffs governing access to protected memory and show how matched interfaces enable programmable writing and interactions enable autonomous information consolidation from the bulk to the edge. These mechanisms improve performance on tasks requiring long-term retention of temporal information. Our results establish topology as a new resource for quantum reservoir computing and open a route toward near-term quantum computing and quantum machine learning.
label: arXiv:2611.24013v1

summary.background:
- Quantum reservoir computing: feeding a signal into a complex physical system and reading out its response, with only a simple final readout trained.
- Qubit: the quantum version of a bit, and the basic unit of quantum information.
- Majorana edge modes: special states that sit at the ends of certain superconducting wires and are unusually resistant to local noise; they are a candidate for protected storage.
- Kitaev chain: a simple one-dimensional chain model that hosts Majorana edge modes.
- Bulk versus edge: the bulk is the interior of the chain; the edge is its end, where the protected states live.
- Fault tolerance: designing computation so that errors are corrected or suppressed faster than they accumulate.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes topological quantum reservoir computing, using protected Majorana edge modes of a one-dimensional Kitaev chain as memory and the bulk's fast dynamics as the processing step, and reports tradeoffs and improved performance on long-term temporal memory tasks.
summary.plain: Building large quantum computers is hard because the delicate quantum states that store information are easily disturbed. This paper proposes a way to use a special, well-protected part of a quantum system, the edge of a one-dimensional chain, as a long-lived memory, while the rest of the system handles fast processing of incoming signals. The authors work this out on a simple model and report that the arrangement helps with tasks that require remembering timing information for a long time.
summary.why: It suggests a way to make use of protected quantum states that are already being built, which could matter for near-term quantum machine learning. The text is a theoretical study on one model, so how far the idea carries to real hardware is not shown here.

title: Topological Quantum Reservoir Computing

abstract: Reliable assessment of quantum error correction requires understanding how coherent errors affect logical performance. Although tensor networks naturally capture coherent interference, entanglement growth and large qubit counts make repeated sampling costly. Here we develop a compiled Clifford-Augmented Matrix Product State (CAMPS) framework that reuses Clifford transformations across shots, recycles qubits released by measurements, evolves a compressed residual state, and accelerates sampling through rotation fusion and compilation tailored to the MPS layout. Surface-code benchmarks under fixed-sign coherent noise yield accurate logical error estimates at small bond dimensions, while random-sign simulations up to distance $d=9$ and on the $[[72,12,6]]$ bivariate bicycle code match the Pauli-twirling approximation results. Compared with uncompiled CAMPS, compiled CAMPS converges at smaller bond dimensions and achieves order-of-magnitude sampling speedups at equal bond dimension, opening a scalable route to studying coherent error propagation in larger fault-tolerant circuits.
label: arXiv:2611.24044v1

summary.background:
- Quantum error correction: encoding information across many physical qubits so that errors can be detected and fixed.
- Coherent noise: systematic, phase-like errors where small rotations add up, unlike random bit flips.
- Pauli twirling: a standard trick that converts coherent errors into simpler random errors for easier analysis.
- Tensor networks / matrix product states: a compressed way to represent quantum states of many qubits, whose cost grows with "bond dimension" (a measure of how much entanglement can be captured).
- Clifford circuits: a special class of quantum operations that can be simulated efficiently on classical computers.
- Sampling / shots: repeating a simulated experiment many times to estimate error rates.
- Surface code and bivariate bicycle code: two families of error-correcting codes; [[72,12,6]] denotes 72 physical qubits encoding 12 logical qubits with distance 6.
summary.one_liner: A compiled Clifford-augmented matrix product state (CAMPS) simulator that reuses Clifford transformations across shots, recycles measured qubits, and fuses rotations to speed up sampling-based simulation of quantum error correction under coherent noise.
summary.plain: Quantum computers are fragile, and error-correction schemes protect them, but errors that add up coherently (as smooth, consistent tilts rather than random flips) are hard to simulate on a classical computer. This paper presents a faster classical simulation method for this kind of noise, tested on surface-code and a larger bivariate bicycle code. The authors report that their compiled version reaches accurate answers with smaller computing budgets and samples about ten times faster than the uncompiled version at the same settings.
summary.why: Coherent errors can behave differently from the random errors that most error-correction estimates assume, so better tools for checking their effect on logical performance matter for designing fault-tolerant hardware. The text reports agreement with a standard approximation (Pauli twirling) on the tested cases, but says nothing about hardware experiments or how far the method scales beyond the tested sizes.

title: Accelerating Quantum Error Correction Simulations under Coherent Noise with Compiled Clifford-Augmented Matrix Product States

abstract: We study a network of three synchronized chaotic lasers and the radio frequency spectra of the intensity fluctuations. The position and morphology of the peaks are significantly different depending on the set of lasers being synchronized. The lasers and coupling paths are similar but not identical in all parameters, including their feedback and coupling delay times. The inverse of the delay mismatch between each pair of lasers introduces characteristic frequencies that shape the spectral response of the synchronized system. By studying two different three-laser configurations, we find that peaks appear whenever multiple harmonic contributions overlap in frequency, resulting in constructive enhancement of the spectral power. Numerical simulations performed with the same delay configurations show a clear agreement with the experimental measurements, reproducing both the peak positions and the overall spectral structure. These results indicate that the frequency content of the synchronized dynamics is largely determined by the delay-mismatch network and its harmonics.
label: arXiv:2611.24306v1

summary.background:
- Chaotic laser: a laser whose output brightness fluctuates irregularly, not in a steady or simply periodic way.
- Synchronization: coupled systems whose irregular signals end up matching each other in time.
- Delay (time lag): light takes a finite time to travel between lasers or back from a feedback mirror, so each link has a delay; a delay mismatch is a difference between these times.
- Radio-frequency spectrum: a breakdown of a signal's brightness fluctuations by how fast they oscillate, showing which frequencies are strongest.
- Harmonics: whole-number multiples of a base frequency; overlapping harmonics from different links can reinforce each other and create peaks.
summary.one_liner: Experiments and numerical simulations of three mutually coupled chaotic semiconductor lasers show that small mismatches in their coupling and feedback delay times set the characteristic frequencies and peak structure of the synchronized intensity spectra.
summary.plain: This paper looks at three lasers that are linked together so that their chaotic flickering in brightness falls into step with one another. The researchers measured the radio-frequency spectrum of that flickering, meaning which rates of fluctuation carry the most power. They found that the peaks depend on which lasers are synchronized and on tiny differences in the time delays between them, and simulations with the same delays matched the measured peak positions and overall shape.
summary.why: The text suggests a simple rule: peaks appear where several harmonic contributions line up in frequency, and the inverse of each delay mismatch sets a characteristic frequency. This may be useful for predicting or controlling the spectra of networks of coupled lasers, but the text does not say which applications it would affect.

title: Delay Mismatches Shape the Spectra of Three Synchronized Semiconductor Lasers

abstract: A squeezed laser undergoes a lasing transition into a squeezed cavity mode, where stimulated emission generates a bright coherent field with a laser-like coherence time while maintaining one field quadrature below the vacuum noise level. Here we propose an optical implementation that needs neither a nonlinear crystal nor injected squeezed light, based on engineered interactions between ensembles of rubidium atoms and a squeezed cavity mode via cavity-assisted Raman transitions. A first ensemble cools the cavity into a squeezed vacuum, a mechanism we term squeezed cooling, yielding up to 9 dB in the intracavity field, surpassing the 3 dB limit of optical parametric oscillators. Tuned for output instead, it reaches up to 18 dB of output squeezing. Incoherently pumping a second ensemble drives a lasing transition into the squeezed mode, emitting a bright beam with long coherence time and noise below vacuum spanning a megahertz-wide band, away from the sharp phase-diffusion peak of excess noise at the carrier frequency, and robust to relaxation oscillations. We characterize lasing thresholds, superradiant emission, and linewidth narrowing, and identify the experimentally accessible regime where the system exhibits the defining features of a squeezed laser.
label: arXiv:2611.24743v1

summary.background:
- Squeezed light: light whose noise is reduced in one measurable direction (a quadrature) below the vacuum noise floor, with extra noise in the conjugate direction.
- Optical cavity: two mirrors that trap light so it bounces back and forth and interacts repeatedly with atoms.
- Cold atoms: atoms cooled by lasers to very low temperatures, so they can be controlled precisely.
- Raman transition: a two-photon process that moves an atom between energy levels, here assisted by the cavity.
- Lasing threshold: the pumping level at which stimulated emission overtakes losses and a coherent beam appears.
- Coherence time and linewidth: how long a light wave stays in a stable phase, and how narrow its frequency spread is.
- Optical parametric oscillator (OPO): the standard nonlinear-crystal device for making squeezed light; the text cites its 3 dB limit for intracavity squeezing.
- Decibel (dB): a logarithmic scale for noise reduction; 3 dB is roughly halving the noise power.
summary.one_liner: A theoretical proposal for a squeezed laser built from cold rubidium atoms coupled to a squeezed cavity mode via cavity-assisted Raman transitions, using "squeezed cooling" to prepare squeezed light without a nonlinear crystal or injected squeezed light.
summary.plain: Light can be "squeezed," meaning the uncertainty in one of its two measurable properties is reduced below the normal background noise, at the cost of more noise in the other. This paper proposes a way to produce such light using clouds of cold rubidium atoms inside an optical cavity, instead of the usual nonlinear crystals. The authors report, from their modeling, that one atom ensemble can cool the cavity into a squeezed state, and a second pumped ensemble can produce a laser beam whose noise stays below the vacuum level over a band about a megahertz wide.
summary.why: Squeezed light is used in precision measurements such as gravitational-wave detectors, so a route that avoids crystals could matter for that kind of work. The text is a proposal and modeling study, and it does not show that the scheme has been built or tested, so its practical value is still uncertain.

title: Squeezed Cooling and Lasing with Cold Atoms in Cavity-QED

abstract: The inner heliosphere is permeated by fully developed, highly intermittent nonlinear turbulence. Conventional stochastic models synthesize these multiscale fluctuations by injecting additive noise within a flat Euclidean space. However, such approaches fundamentally violate the topological constraints of ideal magnetohydrodynamics, inadvertently breaking the kinetic incompressibility of the plasma and introducing spurious magnetic compressibility. To preserve the exact geometrical invariants of Alfvénic fluctuations, a novel mathematical framework is presented: the rotational p-model. By mapping a multifractal singular measure directly into the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ and integrating the associated stochastic differential equations in the Stratonovich sense on the spherical manifold $S^{2}$, the model generates highly intermittent, scale-dependent rotational dynamics. This Lie-group formulation conserves the magnetic field modulus while perfectly reproducing the fractional spectral envelopes and the non-Gaussian directional intermittency observed in space plasmas. Furthermore, by isolating purely directional reorientations, the framework provides exact analytical control over the waiting time statistics of magnetic intermittent bursts and the multifractal scaling exponents of angular deflections, offering a powerful new paradigm for the study of nonlinear turbulent phenomena.
label: arXiv:2611.24009v1

summary.background:
- Alfvénic fluctuations: wave-like ripples in a magnetized plasma (such as the solar wind) in which the magnetic field bends and twists while its overall strength stays roughly constant.
- Intermittency: turbulence that is not evenly spread out but arrives in sudden, concentrated bursts.
- Multifractal: a pattern whose scaling differs from place to place, so it needs a range of exponents rather than one.
- Spectrum: a breakdown of how much fluctuation energy sits at each timescale or size.
- Stochastic differential equation: an equation with random noise driving it; the Stratonovich form is a convention for handling that noise on curved surfaces.
- Lie group / Lie algebra so(3): the mathematics of 3D rotations; the sphere S² is the set of possible directions of a vector of fixed length.
- Waiting time statistics: the distribution of gaps between successive bursts.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes a "rotational p-model" that generates intermittent Alfvénic magnetic-field fluctuations by applying a multifractal measure to rotations in the Lie algebra so(3), integrated as Stratonovich SDEs on the sphere S².
summary.plain: Magnetic fields in the solar wind fluctuate in bursts across many scales, and simple random models of these fluctuations can accidentally make the field appear to compress, which real plasma does not do. This paper builds a new random model in which the magnetic field only changes direction by rotation, so its strength is kept fixed. The authors report that this approach reproduces the observed spectral shape and bursty directional behavior while preserving the field's magnitude.
summary.why: Solar-wind turbulence is a major open topic in space physics, and a model that respects the physical constraints of the plasma could be a useful tool for studying it. The text itself does not provide comparisons against spacecraft data beyond general claims, so the strength of the match with observations should be checked in the full paper.

title: A Lie-Group Approach to Alfvénic Turbulence: The SO(3) Rotational p-model

abstract: The tokamak, one of the mainstream approaches to magnetic confinement in nuclear fusion devices, will be the first approach to reach reactor class prototyping. Plasma start-up is expected to be more challenging in large superconducting next-step tokamaks such as ITER due to the low inductive toroidal electric field and potentially long durations in limiter configuration when plasma-wall interactions lead to easier impurity contamination of the confined plasma. Such limiter start-up is the standard way of early plasma formation in the vast majority of today's experimental devices and is planned on ITER. To mitigate these issues, a novel plasma start-up scheme with divertor geometry only (DIVO start-up) was recently developed for the first time on the EAST superconducting tokamak. The key breakthrough in this work is the use of a non-inductive, electron cyclotron wave generated plasma formed in a poloidal field configuration which is a superposition of a barrel-like geometry around the centre of the vacuum vessel and a mirror-like geometry across the whole vessel cross-section. Such a non-inductive discharge avoids the drawback of low inductive electric field which is unavoidable in large superconducting devices as a consequence of the relatively low voltages which can be applied to the magnet coils. In addition to the low toroidal electric field, the DIVO start-up scheme as demonstrated on EAST significantly reduces impurity sources compared to the conventional limiter phase approach, even in cases with relatively poorly conditioned plasma-facing surfaces. The robustness of the DIVO start-up has also been verified on EAST with varying prefill gas pressure, impurity level and inductive electric field. It thus offers a potential solution to one of the main issues facing routine successful start-up on large tokamak reactors.
label: arXiv:2611.23895v1

summary.background:
- Tokamak: a doughnut-shaped magnetic bottle used to confine plasma for nuclear fusion.
- Plasma start-up: the first phase where gas is ionised and heated into plasma.
- Limiter vs divertor: a limiter is a physical contact point on the inner wall; a divertor is a magnetic configuration that steers edge plasma to dedicated plates away from the core.
