Together, these findings reveal lipid- and domain-mediated mechanisms of ATP7B regulation and explain how specific WD variants disrupt them, providing a structural framework for mutation-directed therapeutic strategies, including pharmacological chaperones.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.766959 v1

summary.background:
- Copper is needed by enzymes but is toxic when unregulated.
- ATP7B is a P-type ATPase: a membrane pump that uses energy (ATP) to push metal ions across membranes.
- Wilson disease is caused by variants (mutations) in the ATP7B gene.
- Cryo-EM: a method that images frozen molecules to build 3D atomic structures.
- Nanodiscs: small lipid bubbles that hold a membrane protein in a membrane-like setting.
- Inward- and outward-facing conformations: the pump's two shapes, open to the cell interior or to the outside, alternating during transport.
- Salt bridge: an attraction between oppositely charged amino acids that helps hold a protein shape.
- Coarse-grained molecular dynamics: simplified computer simulations of how molecules move over time.
- Metal-binding domains: protein regions that grab copper ions and pass them along.
summary.one_liner:
A cryo-EM structure of human ATP7B in lipid nanodiscs, combined with coarse-grained simulations and mutagenesis, maps how Wilson disease variants (notably R969Q and W939C) disrupt a salt bridge, a cholesterol-binding site, and metal-binding domain dynamics in this copper transporter.</one_liner>
<parameter name="plain">Wilson disease is an inherited condition in which the body cannot get rid of extra copper, so the metal builds up in the liver, brain and other organs. This paper studies the ATP7B protein, a pump that moves copper and sends excess into bile, and asks how disease-linked mutations break it. The authors used a high-resolution 3D structure of the protein plus computer simulations and lab tests to find the specific parts that the mutations disturb.
summary.why: Current Wilson disease treatments mainly lower total copper, so a drug that repairs the faulty pump itself would be a different approach. The structural map of how particular mutations disrupt the protein could guide the design of pharmacological chaperones (small molecules that help a misfolded protein work), though the text does not show any such drug was tested.

title: Wilson disease mechanisms manipulate ATP7B activity

abstract: Controlling signaling enzymes with small molecules is a central goal in chemical biology and is of great utility for engineering cell-derived immunotherapies. Yet strategies for conferring selective small-molecule sensitivity without disrupting a protein's native function remain limited. Here we present a generalizable approach to engineering small molecule-controlled multidomain protein kinases. Using deep mutational scanning of full-length Lck, a tyrosine kinase essential for T cell receptor (TCR) signaling, we measured the effect of nearly all single amino acid substitutions in the kinase domain on phosphotransferase activity. The resulting activity landscape defined the domain's tolerance to substitution, mapped the regulatory interfaces that tune phosphotransferase activity, and, by treating bulky substitutions as ligand proxies, nominated cryptic pockets where covalent liganding is predicted to allosterically inhibit Lck. In parallel screens, we measured the sensitization of each variant to five clinically approved, reversible drugs: dabrafenib, erlotinib, gefitinib, imatinib, and nilotinib. Together, these landscapes identified substitutions that preserved or enhanced activity while sensitizing Lck to inhibition. Sensitizing substitutions were distributed throughout the kinase domain, including positions more than 30 [A] from the ATP-binding site, implicating long-range allosteric networks linking distal perturbations to ATP-binding site conformation and inhibitor potency. Integrating the activity and sensitization landscapes yielded a nilotinib-sensitized variant, I312S, that supports TCR signaling and, upon drug treatment, selectively suppresses proximal signaling and IL-2 production in Jurkat cells even in the presence of endogenous Lck.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.766442 v1

summary.background:
- Kinases are enzymes that add phosphate groups to other proteins, acting as switches in cell signaling.
- Lck is a kinase essential for T cell receptor signaling, the pathway by which T cells recognize targets.
- Deep mutational scanning: a method that makes and tests very large numbers of protein variants in parallel to see which changes matter.
- Reversible inhibitors bind a protein and can be removed; the drugs here (dabrafenib, erlotinib, gefitinib, imatinib, nilotinib) are approved for other diseases.
- Allosteric: affecting a protein's activity from a site far from where the drug or ligand binds.
- Jurkat cells: a standard immortalized T cell line used in laboratory experiments.
- IL-2: a signaling molecule T cells produce when activated.
summary.one_liner: Deep mutational scanning of full-length Lck kinase maps how nearly all single amino acid changes affect its activity and its sensitivity to five approved reversible inhibitors, yielding a nilotinib-sensitized variant (I312S) that can be switched off by drug in T cells.
summary.plain: Scientists wanted a way to switch off a specific signaling enzyme in immune cells using an ordinary drug, without breaking the enzyme's normal job. They tested nearly every single-letter change in one part of the enzyme Lck and measured how each change affected its activity and how easily five approved drugs could block it. One variant, I312S, kept working in T cells and was shut down selectively by nilotinib, reducing its signaling and interleukin-2 output.
summary.why: The approach offers a general route to making engineered signaling proteins drug-controllable, which may matter for designing cell-based immunotherapies that can be dialed up or down. The text reports the effect in Jurkat cells only, so its relevance to therapy in patients is not established here.

title: Paired Deep Mutational Scanning of Lck Activity and Inhibitor Sensitivity Enables the Engineering of Pharmacological Control of T Cell Receptor Signaling

abstract: Single-cell multi-omics data offer an opportunity to resolve how gene regulatory networks (GRNs) are rewired during cell-fate transitions, but most existing methods infer static snapshots, ignore temporal dependencies or assume linear regulation. Here we present DRAFT, a deep learning framework that combines graph attention with recurrent temporal memory to infer dynamic GRNs from time-resolved single-cell multi-omics data. On simulated data, DRAFT outperforms existing methods in accuracy and temporal smoothness. In mouse cellular reprogramming and Drosophila adult spermatogenesis, it recovers interactions supported by independent ChIP-seq, perturbation and Hi-C data, together with known stage-specific regulators. By inferring regulatory activity from dynamic network structure rather than expression alone, DRAFT identifies regulators whose activity precedes their transcriptional peak, including the candidate early germline regulator Mondo. Germline-specific Mondo knockdown alters germline stem cell number and expression of the predicted targets kuz and mamo. DRAFT also enables nonlinear alignment of co-developing lineages and reveals stage-specific cell-cell communication.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.767145 v1

summary.background:
- Gene regulatory network (GRN): a map of which genes or regulators control which other genes.
- Single-cell multi-omics: measuring several layers of molecular data (e.g., gene expression and chromatin accessibility) in individual cells.
- Cell-fate transition: a change in which cell type a cell is becoming, such as reprogramming a skin cell toward a stem-like state.
- Graph attention: a neural network technique that weighs connections between nodes (here, genes or regulators) by importance.
- Recurrent memory: a network design that carries information forward across sequential steps, here across time points.
- Validation evidence cited: ChIP-seq (maps where proteins bind DNA), Hi-C (maps 3D genome contacts), and perturbation experiments such as gene knockdown.
- Simulated data: artificial datasets with a known answer, used to test accuracy.
summary.one_liner: DRAFT is a graph attention plus recurrent memory deep learning framework that infers time-varying gene regulatory networks from time-resolved single-cell multi-omics trajectories, validated on simulated data and on mouse reprogramming and Drosophila spermatogenesis datasets.
summary.plain: Cells change their identity over time by switching genes on and off through networks of regulatory control. This paper presents a computer method, called DRAFT, that tries to reconstruct how those control networks rewire as cells move from one fate to another, using data that measure gene activity and chromatin accessibility in the same cells at several time points. The authors report that it performed better than existing methods on simulated data, and that in mouse reprogramming and fruit fly sperm-cell development it recovered interactions supported by outside evidence, including one candidate early regulator, Mondo, whose knockdown changed germline stem cell numbers.
summary.why: Most tools give a single static snapshot of regulation, so a method that tracks how regulation changes over developmental time could help explain cell-fate decisions. The experimental follow-up on Mondo is a concrete test of one prediction, but the text is a draft and gives few details, so the general claims should be treated as provisional until the full paper is available.

title: DRAFT: graph-recurrent learning of dynamic gene regulatory networks along single-cell multi-omics trajectories

abstract: Accurate protein complex structure modeling requires knowledge of complex stoichiometry, yet the copy numbers of individual subunits are often unknown. Consequently, predicting protein complex stoichiometry has emerged as a major challenge in recent years. Here, we present StoiAgent, a large language model (LLM)-powered AI agent that automates the retrieval and integration of sequence, structural, and literature evidence to predict stoichiometry while preserving interpretable reasoning traces (chain of thoughts) of its evidence assessment and ranking decision. An open-weight LLM model, Qwen3.6-27B, is used by StoiAgent as the LLM backbone to combine sequences, structural templates, AlphaFold3 structure predictions, and literature evidence, and perform stoichiometry candidate generation and ranking. On 56 CASP17 protein complex targets, it achieves top-1 accuracy of 75.0%, which represents a 23.2 percentage-point improvement over PreStoi with AlphaFold3 ranking (51.8%) and matches the top-1 accuracy of StoPred. Moreover, StoiAgent has a higher top-3 and top-5 accuracy than StoPred (85.7% versus 80.4% and 87.5% versus 85.7%, respectively). Furthermore, it outperforms general-purpose frontier LLMs, including ChatGPT and Gemini, in stoichiometry prediction. Case studies further illustrate how StoiAgent evaluates competing assembly hypotheses by integrating complementary evidence, with recorded reasoning traces documenting its decision-making process. Overall, StoiAgent demonstrates the potential of LLM-powered AI agents to improve protein complex stoichiometry prediction through the automated integration of diverse sources of evidence while providing interpretable explanations to guide downstream structure modeling.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.767325 v1

summary.background:
- Protein complex: several protein chains that assemble into one functional unit.
- Stoichiometry: how many copies of each chain are in the complex (e.g., 2 copies of A and 1 of B).
- AlphaFold3: an AI tool that predicts 3D protein structures from sequences.
- CASP: a biennial blind competition for testing structure prediction methods; CASP17 is a recent round.
- Large language model (LLM) agent: an AI system that plans steps, calls tools or databases, and reasons in text.
- Top-1/top-3/top-5 accuracy: whether the correct answer is the first, or among the first three or five, of the ranked candidates.
- Chain of thought: the written reasoning trail the model produces for its decisions.
summary.one_liner: StoiAgent is an LLM-driven agent that gathers sequence, template, AlphaFold3, and literature evidence to rank candidate subunit copy-number stoichiometries for protein complexes, reporting 75.0% top-1 accuracy on 56 CASP17 targets.
summary.plain: Proteins often work together as multi-part machines, and structure prediction tools need to know how many copies of each part are in the assembly, which is often unknown. This paper describes an AI agent that collects clues from protein sequences, known structures, AI-predicted structures, and scientific papers, then proposes and ranks possible copy-number arrangements while writing out its reasoning. On 56 benchmark targets from the CASP17 competition, it got the top answer right 75.0% of the time, about as well as a comparable method (StoPred) and better than the earlier PreStoi approach with AlphaFold3 ranking (51.8%).
summary.why: Getting the stoichiometry wrong can make structure models of protein complexes misleading, so a more accurate and explainable way to set this input could help downstream modeling. The text reports only top-1, top-3, and top-5 accuracy on a single benchmark set, so how well it generalizes to other complexes is not shown here.

title: Accurate and interpretable protein complex stoichiometry prediction through agentic AI with StoiAgent

abstract: Sensory representations fluctuate in precision from moment to moment, shaping the fidelity of perception and memory. Population-coding theory proposes that these fluctuations are constrained by correlated variability within neural populations, yet linking these mechanisms to behaviour and brain state in humans has remained challenging. Here we combined EEG with an encoding-decoding framework to reconstruct orientation-selective population responses and quantify representational precision dynamically over time. Precision predicted subsequent working-memory performance and evolved in close correspondence with the dynamics of correlated variability between decoded orientation channels. Following stimulus onset, correlated variability was selectively suppressed among similarly tuned channels, the pattern predicted to maximise coding fidelity. Prestimulus alpha power and pupil size independently predicted representational precision, linking these dynamics to endogenous cortical and neuromodulatory state. Together, these findings identify candidate mechanisms and accessible physiological markers of representational precision in humans.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767508 v1

summary.background:
- EEG: recording electrical activity of the brain through electrodes on the scalp; it is non-invasive but coarse in space.
- Population coding: the idea that information is carried by the joint activity of many neurons tuned to different features (here, orientation), not by one neuron alone.
- Encoding-decoding framework: a model is fit to predict brain signals from a stimulus, then inverted to estimate the stimulus or the tuned responses from new brain data.
- Correlated variability (noise correlations): trial-to-trial fluctuations that neurons share; when they are similar in tuning, they can limit how precisely a population encodes information.
- Alpha power: strength of roughly 8–12 Hz rhythmic EEG activity, often linked to cortical idling or gating.
- Pupil dilation: a non-invasive index of arousal and neuromodulatory state (e.g., noradrenergic activity).
- Working memory: holding information briefly in mind for later use.
summary.one_liner: Using EEG with an encoding-decoding approach, this paper reconstructs orientation-tuned population responses in humans and shows that moment-to-moment representational precision tracks correlated variability between decoded channels, prestimulus alpha power, and pupil size.
summary.plain: The brain's internal picture of what we see gets sharper or blurrier from moment to moment, and this affects how well we perceive and remember things. The authors recorded brain activity with EEG (electrodes on the scalp) while people viewed and remembered orientations, then used a statistical decoding method to reconstruct how groups of neurons were responding over time. They found that the sharpness of this internal picture predicted later memory performance, and that it was linked to a particular pattern of shared noise among similar neural channels and to two easily measured signals: alpha brain rhythms before a stimulus and pupil size.
summary.why: The work offers candidate mechanisms and non-invasive markers (alpha power, pupil size) for how precise sensory representations are, which could be useful for studying attention, memory and brain state in humans. The text does not show how far these markers generalise beyond this task, so their wider value remains to be tested.

title: Precision of sensory representations in cortex is indexed by alpha power and pupil dilation, and tracks the dynamics of correlated noise

abstract: Humans move in time with musical beats, yet how the brain builds the internal beat that guides movement is unknown. We recorded 4,719 neurons in six nodes of the audiomotor circuit while monkeys tapped in synchrony with auditory metronomes at different tempos. We found a clear functional dissociation in the temporal-frontal axis. Auditory cortex detected metronome clicks and contained local clocks that tiled each interstimulus interval, whereas parietal, striatal, and motor areas, most strongly the pre-supplementary motor area (preSMA), generated movement-aligned neural sequences that rescaled with tempo. Only in preSMA did population activity formed a cone-shaped manifold that jointly encoded tempo in its height, the produced interval in its width, and the timing of each tap relative to the beat in its position along the trajectory. During timing errors, preSMA activity kept conical shape but drifted toward shorter or longer tempos, revealing a hierarchical neural clock for beat synchronization.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.767170 v1

summary.background:
- Audiomotor circuit: brain areas linking hearing to movement.
- Neural population activity: the joint firing pattern of many neurons, analyzed as a single trajectory or shape.
- Manifold: a low-dimensional shape that population activity traces out; here described as cone-shaped.
- Interstimulus interval: the time gap between successive metronome clicks.
- Pre-supplementary motor area (preSMA): a frontal cortex region involved in planning and timing movements.
- Tempo: the speed of the beat.
- Synchronization-continuation tapping: tapping in time with a beat and then keeping the rhythm after the sound stops.
summary.one_liner: Recordings from 4,719 neurons across six nodes of the monkey audiomotor circuit show that the pre-supplementary motor area (preSMA) carries a population-level, cone-shaped timing manifold that encodes tempo, produced interval, and tap phase during beat-synchronized tapping.
summary.plain: Humans can tap along to a musical beat, but how the brain builds the internal sense of that beat is not well understood. The researchers recorded activity from thousands of nerve cells in monkeys tapping in time with metronomes at different speeds, and compared several brain regions involved in hearing and movement.
summary.why: The paper argues that a specific frontal region, preSMA, holds a hierarchical timing signal that sits above auditory and motor areas, which could help explain how rhythm guides movement. The text reports these findings from one study, so how well they generalize to other animals or to human timing is not shown here.

title: PreSMA population dynamics keep the beat atop the primate audiomotor hierarchy

abstract: Recent advances in single-cell and single-molecule sequencing have enabled high-resolution characterization of epigenetic states. However, methods that jointly measure multiple layers of epigenetic regulation within the same molecules and cells remain limited. Here, we developed Chromatin Immuno-Methylation sequencing (ChIMe-seq), a multimodal approach that simultaneously profiles histone modifications, DNA methylation, and nucleosome positioning genome-wide in single molecules and single cells. In contrast to recent approaches that rely on enzymatic fragmentation, ChIMe-seq preserves long DNA molecules by using a methyltransferase to deposit exogenous methylation marks that report on proximal histone modifications. This enables integration of multiple epigenetic features within individual molecules and supports short-read, long-read, and single-cell sequencing. These multimodal measurements are integrated into a novel mathematical framework that captures the coupling between nucleosome positioning, histone modifications, and DNA methylation. Both single-molecule and single-cell analyses reveal that DNA methylation is linked to nucleosome density in a manner modulated by local histone modifications, whilst differences in nucleosome:DNA structures are observed depending on epigenetic context and cell-type. Together, these results establish ChIMe-seq as a framework to investigate multifaceted epigenetic coordination across scales, from single-nucleotide resolution to long-range chromatin organization in single molecules and single cells.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.767085 v1

summary.background:
- Epigenetics: chemical marks that change how genes are read without altering the DNA sequence.
- Nucleosome: a unit of DNA wound around histone proteins; its position affects gene access.
- Histone modification: chemical tags on histone proteins that signal active or silent chromatin.
- DNA methylation: addition of a methyl group to DNA, often linked to gene silencing.
- Single-molecule and single-cell sequencing: reading the DNA of individual strands or cells rather than averaging over a mixed population.
- Methyltransferase: an enzyme that adds methyl groups; here it is used to write marks onto DNA near histones as a readout.
- Short-read vs long-read sequencing: short reads cover small DNA fragments; long reads cover much longer stretches, keeping more context.
summary.one_liner: ChIMe-seq is a method that uses an exogenous methyltransferase to tag histone-modification and nucleosome context on long DNA, allowing histone marks, DNA methylation and nucleosome positioning to be profiled together in single molecules and single cells.
summary.plain: Cells control which genes are active using several chemical layers that sit on or around DNA, such as tags on the histone proteins DNA wraps around and methyl marks on DNA itself. This paper describes a new lab method, ChIMe-seq, that reads several of these layers from the same DNA strand and from individual cells at once. The authors report that DNA methylation tracks how densely nucleosomes (DNA-packing spools) sit in a region, and that this relationship changes depending on nearby histone marks and cell type.
summary.why: Most existing methods measure only one epigenetic layer at a time, or chop DNA into short pieces that lose information about which marks occur together. Being able to see several layers on the same molecule may help explain how these controls coordinate, though the text does not show how broadly the method will be adopted or how it performs against existing tools.

title: ChIMe-seq enables multimodal epigenetic profiling in single molecules and single cells

abstract: Gene regulation is commonly modeled at the gene level, yet genes express multiple isoforms from distinct transcription start sites whose regulatory architecture is not resolved by current approaches. Here we introduce FULL-seq, a scalable single-cell multiomic platform that jointly profiles chromatin accessibility and full-length transcript coverage from the same cell, enabling direct coupling of regulatory elements to alternative first exon (AFE) usage. FULL-seq achieves high sensitivity for both transcriptome and chromatin accessibility while providing transcript-wide coverage across mRNAs up to 15 kb with precise exon-level mapping. We uncover diverse promoter-AFE regulatory architectures, revealing distinct transcription factor programs across alternative first exons of the same gene, and show that gene-level annotation frameworks can obscure regulatory relationships in multi-promoter genes. Applying FULL-seq to human cancer cells further reveals metastasis-associated AFE programs that are not apparent from gene-level expression. These AFE programs were reproduced in independent colorectal cancer cell-line datasets, and CALB1 AFE activation was observed in a subset of liver metastases from an independent patient cohort. Furthermore, CRISPRi-mediated repression of metastasis-associated CALB1 AFEs reduced colorectal cancer cell migration. Together, our findings establish alternative promoter and first-exon usage as a functionally relevant layer of gene regulation and demonstrate that FULL-seq enables regulatory relationships and cellular phenotypes to be connected at the promoter-isoform level.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.767299 v1

summary.background:
- Gene regulation: cells control how much of each gene is made, often by switching chromatin (DNA packaged with proteins) between open and closed states.
- Transcription start site (promoter): the position where a gene's copying into RNA begins.
- Isoform: alternative versions of a gene's product, here produced by different starting points.
- Alternative first exon (AFE): the first coding-region segment of an RNA, which differs depending on which promoter is used.
- Single-cell multiomics: measuring two or more kinds of molecular data from the same individual cell.
- Transcription factor: a protein that binds DNA to turn genes on or off.
- CRISPRi: a gene-silencing technique that blocks gene activity without cutting DNA.
- Metastasis: cancer spreading from its original site to other organs.
summary.one_liner: FULL-seq is a single-cell method that jointly measures chromatin accessibility and full-length transcripts in the same cell, linking promoter/regulatory elements to alternative first-exon usage in multi-promoter genes, and applies this to colorectal cancer metastasis-associated CALB1 programs.
summary.plain: Many genes can be switched on from several different starting points, producing different versions of the same gene product. This paper introduces FULL-seq, a method that reads, in each individual cell, both which parts of the DNA are open for switching on and which full-length versions of the messages are being made. Applied to cancer cells, it found programs tied to specific starting points that the usual gene-level view misses, including ones linked to metastasis, and reducing one of them (CALB1) slowed cell migration in lab tests.
summary.why: Standard gene-level measurements can average out differences between versions of a gene that behave differently, so this approach may reveal regulatory control hidden from current tools. The link to metastasis and the CRISPRi migration experiment are a potential route to new mechanistic or therapeutic questions, but the text alone does not establish clinical relevance, and the cohort and cell-line evidence is limited in scope.

title: FULL-seq reveals isoform-specific regulatory architecture in single cells

abstract: Background: REV-ERB nuclear receptors regulate gene expression and cellular metabolism, but their role in the response to hypoxia-associated stress remains unclear. We examined how the REV-ERB agonist STL1267 affects protein distribution and gene expression in HeLa cells exposed to cobalt chloride (CoCl2). Methods and Results: Immunofluorescence microscopy and RNA sequencing were used to compare vehicle-treated controls, cells exposed to CoCl2 plus vehicle, and cells exposed to CoCl2 plus STL1267. Representative images showed stronger nuclear HIF-1 staining after CoCl2 exposure. Nuclear staining was less pronounced with STL1267, while REV-ERB showed more extranuclear staining. CoCl2 exposure altered 267 genes, and STL1267 treatment during CoCl2 exposure altered 132 genes at a false discovery rate below 0.05. STL1267 increased ATF4 expression alongside genes involved in amino-acid synthesis and one-carbon metabolism, including ASNS, PHGDH, PSAT1, PSPH and MTHFD2. CTH and CHAC1 also increased, highlighting changes in sulfur-amino-acid metabolism and glutathione turnover. Among the genes induced by CoCl2, CA9, BNIP3 and LDHA decreased with STL1267, whereas HK2, PDK1 and VEGFA did not change significantly. Conclusions: STL1267 selectively reshapes hypoxia-associated gene expression and induces an ATF4-associated metabolic transcriptional program in CoCl2-treated HeLa cells, alongside qualitative changes in HIF-1 and REV-ERB distribution. These findings identify a potential connection between protein compartmentalization and metabolic stress responses, providing a basis for investigating how REV-ERB ligands influence cellular adaptation to oxygen limitation.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.767081 v1

summary.background:
- HIF-1α: a protein that accumulates when oxygen is low and switches on genes for adapting to hypoxia.
- CoCl2 (cobalt chloride): a chemical used in labs to mimic low-oxygen conditions.
- REV-ERB (REV-ERBα): a nuclear receptor, a protein that sits in the cell's nucleus and regulates gene activity, including circadian (daily) rhythm and metabolism.
- Agonist: a molecule that activates a receptor; STL1267 is described as a REV-ERB agonist.
- ATF4: a stress-response transcription factor that turns on amino-acid and one-carbon metabolism genes.
- RNA sequencing: a method that measures how active each gene is by counting its RNA messages.
- Immunofluorescence: staining proteins with fluorescent markers to see where they are in cells under a microscope.
- False discovery rate (FDR): a statistical threshold used to limit false positives when testing thousands of genes.
summary.one_liner: In CoCl2-treated HeLa cells, the REV-ERB agonist STL1267 shifted HIF-1α and REV-ERBα protein localization and reshaped hypoxia-linked gene expression, notably inducing an ATF4-associated amino-acid and one-carbon metabolism program.
summary.plain: Cells often respond to low oxygen by switching which genes they use and how they process nutrients. This study used cobalt chloride, a chemical that mimics low oxygen, on cultured cervical cancer cells, and tested a drug-like compound (STL1267) that targets REV-ERB, a protein that helps control daily rhythms and metabolism. The researchers looked at where certain proteins sat inside the cells and measured which genes switched on or off.
summary.why: It suggests a possible link between where regulatory proteins sit inside a cell and how the cell copes with metabolic stress, which could matter for understanding how cells adapt to low oxygen, such as in tumors. The text is a small study in one cell line, so any wider significance is uncertain and would need follow-up work.

title: STL1267 alters HIF-1α and REV-ERBα localization and transcriptional responses in CoCl2-treated HeLa cells

abstract: Mitochondria, the central axis of metabolism and energy transformation has emerged as a focal point for understanding the aging process and a plethora of human diseases. Yet, how the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes communicate is still unclear. This work aims to allow the analysis of such crosstalk by developing a genome-wide platform for studying genetic interactions between the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes. Using yeast as a model system in which mitochondrial homoplasmy and stable alterations in the mitochondrial genome can be generated by biolistic bombardment, we created a genome-wide library of yeast cells carrying nuclear deletions and temperature-sensitive mutations together with a superfolder-GFP reporter for the expression of the mitochondrial-encoded COX2 gene. Using this approach, we found links between nuclear-encoded processes and mitochondrial gene expression not previously anticipated, including a requirement for genes involved in MVB (multivesicular body) sorting/RIM signaling, vesicle trafficking/glycosylation, polarity, and peroxisome biogenesis, for maintaining mitochondrial COX2 expression. In contrast, defects in the autophagy machineries, ribosome biogenesis, and nuclear transcription and chromatin organization resulted in increased expression of COX2. While reduced COX2 expression correlated with a reduced expression of the nuclear-encoded TOM70 gene in mutants defect in mitochondrial functions, expression of the mitochondrial and nuclear genes responded differently to defects in cytoplasmic ribosome biogenesis and autophagy. When creating the COX2 expression library, we also found that cells devoid of mitochondrial DNA rely on the Rim101 signaling pathway, and many of its auxiliary regulatory factors, to maintain fitness. As mutations in the Rim101 signaling pathway also caused down-regulation of COX2 expression, it appears that Rim101 signaling is central for maintaining proper control of mitochondrial function. We believe the approach will allow for future genome-wide studies on how nuclear-encoded processes influence the translation, protein folding, and processing of mitochondria-encoded genes.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.766915 v1

summary.background:
- Mitochondria are organelles that produce cellular energy and have their own small genome, separate from the nuclear genome.
- COX2 is a mitochondrial gene that encodes part of a respiratory enzyme; its expression serves as the readout here.
- Yeast is a simple single-celled model organism widely used for genetic screens.
- Genetic interaction: when a mutation in one gene changes the effect of a mutation in another, suggesting the two gene products work together or in related processes.
- Homoplasmy means all copies of mitochondrial DNA in a cell are the same version.
- Biolistic bombardment is a method of firing DNA-coated particles into cells to introduce changes to mitochondrial DNA.
- Temperature-sensitive mutants work normally at one temperature but lose function at a higher one.
- Superfolder GFP is a bright, fast-folding green fluorescent protein used as a reporter of gene activity.
- Rim101 is a yeast signaling pathway that responds to environmental cues such as pH.
summary.one_liner: The authors built a genome-wide yeast library of nuclear gene deletions and temperature-sensitive mutants carrying a superfolder-GFP reporter for mitochondrial COX2 expression, and used it to map nuclear genes that raise or lower mitochondrial gene expression.
summary.plain: Mitochondria are the cell's energy-producing compartments, and they carry a small set of their own genes alongside the many genes stored in the cell nucleus. This paper asks how those two sets of genes talk to each other. The authors used baker's yeast, where they could change the mitochondrial DNA, and tagged a mitochondrial gene (COX2) with a fluorescent glow marker so they could measure its activity across thousands of nuclear gene mutants.
summary.why: The screen points to nuclear processes that were not previously expected to affect mitochondrial gene expression, such as the Rim101 signaling pathway and vesicle trafficking. Because mitochondrial dysfunction is linked to aging and many diseases, a platform like this could help future studies, though the text itself does not show how these links apply outside yeast.

title: Development of synthetic genetic arrays for studying interactions between the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes

abstract: Autoimmune disease is on the rise, and while no direct connection has been made, evidence suggests environmental toxins such as nanoplastics may be contributing to the increased incidence. A key factor in the onset of autoimmunity is inflammation; yet how nanoplastics impact innate immune function is unclear. Here, we exposed primary human neutrophils, macrophages, and endothelial cells to biocorona-coated polystyrene nanoplastics at physiologically relevant concentrations. All cells internalized nanoplastics without viability loss, but functional consequences diverged. Neutrophils increased myeloperoxidase release as nanoplastic concentration increased. Endothelial cells reduced leukocyte-recruiting mediator secretion and had decreased neutrophil adhesion following inflammatory stimulation. M1 macrophages broadly upregulated inflammatory cytokine secretion (including TNF- and IL-6), whereas M0 and M2 macrophages exhibited no significant secretory changes. Collectively, these findings indicate physiologically relevant nanoplastic concentrations do not universally increase inflammation but rather dysregulate innate immune populations in a manner that could contribute to autoimmunity.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.767123 v1

summary.background:
- Nanoplastics: plastic fragments smaller than about a micrometre, which can enter the body.
- Biocorona: a layer of proteins and other molecules that sticks to a particle once it is in body fluids, changing how cells see it.
- Innate immune system: the body's fast, general-purpose defenses, including neutrophils (first responders), macrophages (cells that engulf debris and signal to others) and endothelial cells (lining of blood vessels).
- M0, M1, M2 macrophages: macrophage states; M1 is pro-inflammatory, M2 is more anti-inflammatory and tissue-repairing, M0 is resting.
- Cytokines (e.g., TNF-α, IL-6): chemical messengers that signal inflammation.
- Myeloperoxidase: an enzyme released by neutrophils that can damage tissue.
- Autoimmunity: the immune system attacking the body's own tissues.
summary.one_liner: In primary human neutrophils, macrophages and endothelial cells, biocorona-coated polystyrene nanoplastics at physiologically relevant concentrations were internalized without loss of viability but produced cell-type- and activation-state-dependent changes in innate immune function, with M1 macrophages upregulating inflammatory cytokines (including TNF-α and IL-6).
summary.plain: Tiny plastic particles, far smaller than a grain of sand, are found in the environment and may be linked to the rise in autoimmune disease, though no direct link has been shown. The researchers exposed several types of human immune and blood-vessel cells grown in the lab to these particles at levels they considered realistic. The cells took the particles up without dying, but each cell type responded differently: some released more inflammatory signals, some released fewer, and some did not change much.
summary.why: Inflammation is a key step in the onset of autoimmunity, so knowing how everyday environmental particles change immune cell behavior is relevant to public health questions. The text itself does not establish a causal link to autoimmune disease, and the work is limited to cells in the lab, so its connection to disease in people remains a hypothesis.

title: Cell identity and activation state determine the innate immune response to nanoplastics

abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) offer a promising alternative to conventional antibiotics amid the growing global threat of antimicrobial resistance. Expanding AMP discovery requires both effective computational tools to accurately identify candidate peptides and access to underexplored biological resources that may harbor novel AMPs. However, the comparative performance of existing computational methods remains poorly understood, while ancient microbiomes have received limited attention as potential reservoirs of AMPs. Here, we systematically benchmarked six machine learning methods across with twelve feature configurations spanning sequence, structural, and protein language model features under a unified framework using eight curated AMP datasets. The best-performing methods were subsequently applied to three ancient metagenomic datasets representing the human gut (archaeological fecal sediments), human oral cavity (dental calculus), and mammoth-associated communities (teeth, skulls, and skin). In parallel, we employed reinforcement learning to select candidate peptides directly from ancient sequence pools without relying on modern AMP labels. Our benchmarking shows that protein language model embeddings provide the most informative features, and deep learning models, including convolutional, transformer-based, and recurrent architectures, outperform classical methods. Applying these models to ancient microbiomes identified candidates occupied the physicochemical space characteristic of AMPs but differed from those of candidates predicted from modern microbiome catalogs. We identified 111, 76, and 50 high-confidence candidate AMPs from the Neanderthal gut, ancient oral, and mammoth-associated communities, respectively. Reinforcement learning selected additional candidate AMPs with distinct properties compared with those predicted by models trained on modern AMP databases. Together, these findings establish a systematic benchmark for AMP prediction and highlight ancient microbiomes as an untapped source of antimicrobial peptide candidates. By integrating supervised machine learning with reinforcement learning, this study expands AMP discovery beyond modern microbiome catalogs and provides new opportunities to identify potentially novel AMPs.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.767431 v1

summary.background:
- Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs): short chains of amino acids produced by organisms that can kill or inhibit bacteria, fungi, or viruses.
- Metagenomics: sequencing all DNA from a sample (such as soil or teeth) to learn which organisms and genes are present, without culturing them.
- Machine learning classifiers: computer models trained on labeled examples to predict whether a new sequence is an AMP.
- Feature configurations: different ways of describing a peptide to a model, such as its sequence, predicted 3D structure, or embeddings from protein language models (models trained on protein sequences, analogous to language models trained on text).
- Reinforcement learning: a trial-and-reward approach where a program learns to pick good candidates by receiving feedback.
- Benchmarking: a fair side-by-side comparison of methods on the same data.
- Dental calculus: hardened dental plaque that preserves microbial DNA over long periods.
summary.one_liner: A systematic benchmark of six machine learning methods and twelve feature sets for predicting antimicrobial peptides, applied to ancient metagenomes (archaeological gut sediments, dental calculus, and mammoth-associated communities) and paired with reinforcement learning for candidate selection.
summary.plain: Antimicrobial peptides are small protein fragments that can kill microbes, and they are being studied as possible alternatives to antibiotics. This paper compares many computer methods for spotting these peptides in genetic data, then uses the best ones to search DNA-derived protein sequences from ancient samples such as old gut sediments, dental tartar, and mammoth remains. The authors report that protein language model features worked best and that deep learning models outperformed older classical methods.
summary.why: Finding new antimicrobial candidates matters because antibiotic resistance is a growing problem, and the paper suggests ancient microbiomes are a largely unexplored source. The main practical value is the comparison of methods, though the candidates themselves still need laboratory testing before any claim of antimicrobial activity can be made.

title: Benchmarking Machine Learning Methods for Antimicrobial Peptide Prediction and Discovery in Ancient Microbiomes

abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most lethal cancers in the western world and is largely resistant to treatment. A major barrier to effective treatment is the highly desmoplastic and immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment, where the organisation of tumour, stromal and resident immune cells limit immune infiltration. B7-H3 (CD276) is an emerging immune checkpoint marker investigated in phase I and Ib/2 clinical trials in PDAC, yet its biological role within the tumour environment remains poorly understood. We performed an integrated multiscale spatial profiling study to map B7-H3 expression across regional and single-cell spatial contexts in treatment-naive resected human PDAC. Furthermore, we explored the B7-H3 landscape in the neoadjuvant setting. Our results demonstrate that B7-H3 is not simply overexpressed in cancer but may act as a spatial organiser of the PDAC microenvironment, associated with a transition from epithelial-intrinsic tumour architecture to fibro-inflammatory immune states that underpin immune suppression, aggressive disease and poor prognosis. This fibro-inflammatory state appears conserved within the neoadjuvant landscape.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.762837 v1

summary.background:
- PDAC: the most common form of pancreatic cancer, usually diagnosed late and rarely responsive to treatment.
- Desmoplastic stroma: the dense, fibrous scar-like tissue that surrounds many pancreatic tumours and can block immune cells.
- Immune checkpoint: a molecule that can switch off immune responses; drugs targeting these are a major cancer therapy approach.
- B7-H3 (CD276): a checkpoint-type molecule being studied as a drug target in pancreatic cancer trials.
- Spatial profiling: measuring molecules while keeping track of where each cell sits in the tissue.
- Neoadjuvant: treatment given before surgery to shrink a tumour.
- Single-cell analysis: examining the features of individual cells rather than averaging across a tissue sample.
summary.one_liner: A multiscale spatial profiling study of treatment-naive resected human pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) that maps B7-H3 (CD276) expression across regional and single-cell contexts and proposes it as a spatial organiser linked to a fibro-inflammatory, immunosuppressive tumour state, with a similar state reported in neoadjuvant (pre-surgery treated) samples.
summary.plain: Pancreatic cancer is very hard to treat, partly because the tissue around the tumour is dense with scar-like support cells and immune cells that fail to fight it. This study looked at where a molecule called B7-H3 sits within pancreatic tumour tissue, both in broad regions and in individual cells. The authors report that B7-H3 may help shape how tumour, support and immune cells are arranged, and that this pattern is linked to poorer outcomes.
summary.why: B7-H3 is already being tested in early-phase clinical trials for pancreatic cancer, so understanding its role in the tissue layout could inform how those treatments are interpreted. The text does not establish causation, and it is only a description of tissue patterns in a limited set of samples, so the findings are best read as hypothesis-generating.

title: B7-H3 Orchestrates Fibro-Immune Spatial Organisation in Pancreatic Cancer

abstract: Metastasis requires cancer cells to overcome anchorage dependence and rewire mechanosensing pathways. Here, we identify the ERM proteins ezrin, radixin, and moesin as key but antagonistic regulators of breast cancer metastasis. Expression profiling across matched low- and high-metastatic breast cancer models revealed consistent upregulation of all three ERM proteins in highly metastatic cells. Despite this, ezrin depletion reduced colony formation, invasion, and lung metastasis, whereas radixin or moesin depletion enhanced these phenotypes. Loss of radixin or moesin increased ezrin localization at the cell edge, while ezrin depletion reduced membrane-associated moesin, indicating a dynamic balance among ERM proteins. Ezrin depletion also increased focal adhesion size and number, FAK activation, and force transmission to the extracellular matrix, whereas radixin or moesin silencing produced opposite effects. Cellular force magnitude was inversely correlated with invasion, and pharmacological modulation of contractility reverted the effects of ERM depletion. These findings reveal an ERM-dependent mechanosensing checkpoint that regulates metastasis through control of adhesion dynamics and force transmission.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.767111 v1

summary.background:
- Metastasis: the spread of cancer from its original site to other organs.
- ERM proteins: ezrin, radixin and moesin, which connect the cell's internal scaffold (actin) to its membrane.
- Focal adhesions: anchor points where a cell grips the surrounding matrix.
- Focal adhesion kinase (FAK): an enzyme that signals inside the cell when adhesions form and mature.
- Mechanosensing: how cells detect and respond to physical forces such as pulling and stiffness.
- Anchorage dependence: normal cells need to be attached to a surface to grow; metastatic cells often lose this need.
- Contractility: the cell's internal pulling force generated by its actin and myosin network.
- Models used: matched low- and high-metastatic breast cancer cell lines, with lung metastasis tested in animals.
summary.one_liner: In breast cancer cell models, the ERM proteins (ezrin, radixin, moesin) act as antagonistic regulators of invasion and lung metastasis, with ezrin promoting and radixin or moesin restraining these traits through effects on focal adhesions and cellular force transmission.
summary.plain: Cancer spreads when cells break away from a tumour, move through tissue, and form new tumours elsewhere, such as in the lungs. This study looked at three related proteins, ezrin, radixin and moesin, that link a cell's internal skeleton to its outer surface. The authors found that all three were raised in the more spreading breast cancer cells, yet removing ezrin reduced invasion and lung spread in their models, while removing radixin or moesin increased them.
summary.why: The paper suggests that these proteins help cancer cells sense and pull on their surroundings, and that the balance among the three may act as a checkpoint for spread. The text is only an abstract, so the size and generality of the effect are not clear from it; it may matter for thinking about mechanical targets in metastasis, but that link is a possibility rather than a demonstrated outcome.

title: ERM proteins antagonistically control cancer invasion and metastasis via mechanosensing regulation

abstract: Variation within populations is ubiquitous in nature, yet many models and frameworks in community ecology assume that all individuals within a population interact with the community identically. Modern coexistence theory is no exception; however, several subfields of ecology have independently been integrating coexistence theory, each asking the same underlying question: how do structured population dynamics shape coexistence outcomes? Here, I propose a unifying framework for integrating population variation into modern coexistence theory that is applicable across all fields of ecology. The application of this framework is presented in three case studies: niche overlap and fitness differences between influenza substrains, mutual invasibility between competing perennial plants, and fluctuation-dependent invasion outcomes in apparently competing prey with a foraging-predation risk tradeoff. Together, these examples illustrate the framework's broad applicability, power to resolve the interaction between population and community level processes, and its potential to reveal novel ecological phenomena.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.766574 v1

summary.background:
- Coexistence theory: the study of why competing species can persist together instead of one driving the others out.
- Population structure: differences among individuals within a species (such as strain, age, or life stage) that may change how they compete or are affected by predators.
- Niche overlap and fitness difference: two standard measures of how similar species are in their resource use and how unequal their competitive strengths are.
- Mutual invasibility: each species can increase when rare, which is a common test for stable coexistence.
- Apparent competition: two prey species that seem to compete only because they share a predator.
- Foraging-predation risk tradeoff: animals that feed more often tend to be more exposed to predators.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes a general framework for adding within-population variation (structured populations) to modern coexistence theory, and illustrates it with three case studies: influenza substrains, competing perennial plants, and apparently competing prey with a foraging-predation risk tradeoff.
summary.plain: Species in nature are not uniform: individuals differ in age, size, or type, and these differences can affect whether competing species can live together. This paper offers a common way to account for such differences when studying how species coexist, and tests it on three examples. The text describes the framework and examples only at a high level, so the specific findings are not given in this summary.
summary.why: Several subfields of ecology have been building similar tools separately, so a shared framework could help them compare results and link population-level and community-level processes. Its practical value depends on how well the three case studies work in detail, which the provided text does not show.

title: A unifying framework for structured population dynamics in modern coexistence theory

abstract: Enrichment is pivotal to captive animal welfare. Social enrichment is of particular importance for social animals who, due to laboratory space or protocols, are not housed in larger groups. The objective of our study was to see if caregivers could act as an additional source of social enrichment to pair-housed research macaques. 5 adult Rhesus (Macaca Mulatta) and 3 adult Cynomolgus macaques (Macaca fascicularis) were enrolled in the study. Every day, for 3 weeks, caregivers would spend 6 minutes interacting with the monkeys during afternoon feeding. Half the monkeys received human behaviour (HB), where the caregivers interacted with the monkeys using human body language and speaking softly. The other half received monkey-like behaviour (MB), in which caregivers would attempt to imitate monkey behaviour, all the while avoiding eye-contact or speaking (both of which may be perceived as aggressive). Our results showed that monkeys were more likely to engage in interactions before feeding, indicating that this may be an ideal time to provide social enrichment. Monkeys from both groups showed a 3.5 {+/-} 1.5 (F54 = 3.34, p = 0.058) decrease in the frequency of cage-directed abnormal behaviours and a 1.2 {+/-} 0.53 (F54 = 2.78, p = 0.067) decrease in the frequency of stereotypic abnormal over the course of the experiment. In addition, all monkeys saw a 12.9 {+/-} 6.1% (F54 = 2.40, p = 0.010) increase in the proportion of time spent interacting positively with cage-mates, including a 10.6 {+/-} 4.78% (F54.1 = 2.47, p = 0.077) increase in time spent grooming. This research contributes to the enhancement of animal care by helping to establish evidence-based guidelines for the proper care of non-human primates in research. It further deepens our understanding of social enrichment provided by humans as a cost-effective way of managing boredom.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.767050 v1

summary.background:
- Macaques (Rhesus and Cynomolgus) are monkeys widely used in biomedical research.
- Social enrichment means improving an animal's environment through social contact, which matters for highly social species.
- "Pair-housed" means two animals share a cage.
- "Abnormal behaviours" are repetitive or unusual actions, such as cage-directed behaviour or stereotypies (fixed repetitive movements), often taken as signs of stress or boredom.
- Grooming, picking through fur, is a common friendly interaction between monkeys.
- Statistical notes: the reported F values and p-values come from comparisons; p-values near or above 0.05 are weak evidence, and several reported effects are at or above that level.
- The study had only 8 animals, split between two groups.
summary.one_liner: A small study of eight lab-housed pair-housed macaques tests whether caregivers interacting with them during feeding, either using human-style or monkey-like body language, can serve as added social enrichment.
summary.plain: Monkeys kept in research labs often have little social contact, which can lead to boredom and unhealthy repetitive behaviours. The researchers tested whether caregivers spending six minutes a day with the animals during feeding, for three weeks, could act as a source of social stimulation. Half the monkeys were approached with human-style body language and soft speech, and half with monkey-like behaviour that avoided eye contact and talking.
summary.why: The work bears on animal welfare in research settings, where cheap ways to reduce boredom are useful and evidence-based care guidelines are still being developed. The reported findings are modest and based on very few animals, so they are best read as preliminary, not as proof that caregiver interaction works.

title: Making monkeys of caregivers: Evaluating the use of caregiver behaviour as social enrichment for lab-housed Rhesus and Cynomolgus Macaques

abstract: The level of fatty acid unsaturation of chloroplast lipids is a key determinant of plant acclimation to different environmental stresses. Though the enzymes catalysing fatty acid desaturation are well known, the regulatory mechanisms linking their activity to environmental signals remain poorly understood. In this work, we have addressed the role of chloroplast 2-Cys peroxiredoxins (Prxs), thiol peroxidases that play a central role in redox regulation, in {omega}-3 fatty acid desaturation in lipids of the organelle, and their contribution to plant acclimation to environmental stress. Genetic and lipidomic analyses of Arabidopsis (Arabidopsis thaliana) mutants lacking 2-Cys Prxs and/or the chloroplast {omega}-3 fatty acid desaturases FAD7 and FAD8 revealed that 2-Cys Prxs are required for the efficient synthesis of trienoic fatty acids in thylakoid membrane lipids, particularly in phosphatidylglycerol (PG). Different approaches show the in vivo interaction of 2-Cys Prxs with FAD7 and FAD8. However, no redox changes of these desaturases were observed regardless the contents of 2-Cys Prxs, thus indicating a regulatory mechanism independent of the classical cysteine-based redox switch. The combined absence of 2-Cys Prxs and chloroplast {omega}-3 desaturases severely compromised recovery from high-light photoinhibition, indicating that both systems act concertedly to maintain photosystem II (PSII) function under stress. Together, our results uncover a novel role of 2-Cys Prxs controlling the level of chloroplast PG cis-unsaturation and raise the possibility that the chaperone/scaffold activity of these enzymes links membrane lipid remodelling to photosynthetic stress response.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.766973 v1

summary.background:
- Chloroplasts are the organelles where photosynthesis happens; thylakoids are their internal membranes.
- Unsaturated fats have one or more carbon-carbon double bonds; more double bonds (trienoic = three) make membranes more fluid, which matters in cold and stress.
- Desaturases (FAD7, FAD8) are enzymes that add these double bonds.
- Phosphatidylglycerol (PG) is a lipid making up part of thylakoid membranes.
- Peroxiredoxins are enzymes that neutralise peroxides and help regulate cell redox (electron-balance) signals, typically via cysteine amino acids.
- Photosystem II (PSII) is the light-driven protein complex that splits water; high light damages it and it must be repaired.
- Arabidopsis thaliana is a small model plant; mutants lacking specific genes are used to test function.
summary.one_liner: In Arabidopsis, chloroplast 2-Cys peroxiredoxins are shown to promote trienoic fatty acid synthesis in thylakoid lipids, especially phosphatidylglycerol, via interaction with the FAD7/FAD8 omega-3 desaturases, and to help PSII recover from high-light damage, without a classical cysteine redox switch on the desaturases.
summary.plain: Plants build the fatty oils in their light-harvesting membranes, and how many double bonds these oils carry affects how well plants cope with stress. This study looked at a family of plant enzymes called 2-Cys peroxiredoxins and found that they help make one of these membrane fats, phosphatidylglycerol, more highly unsaturated. Plants lacking both these enzymes and the fat-making enzymes recovered poorly after being hit with too much bright light.
summary.why: It links two processes usually studied separately: membrane fat composition and the repair of the light-capturing machinery after strong sunlight. The text suggests the enzymes may act as helpers or scaffolds rather than through the usual redox switch, but this is a proposal the authors raise, not something established here.

title: 2-Cys peroxiredoxins facilitate phosphatidylglycerol unsaturation and contribute to PSII recovery from high-light photoinhibition

abstract: L-phenylalanine (Phe), an aromatic amino acid known to induce plant pathogen resistance at concentrations >4 mM, also functions as a broad-spectrum plant growth biostimulator in the total absence of biotic stress. To evaluate its biostimulatory potential, drench and foliar spray applications of Phe (1-16 mM) were tested on dicotyledonous (cucumber, tomato, lettuce) and monocotyledonous (wheat) crops grown under commercial-like net-house conditions with full NPK fertigation (150 mg/ L N). Weekly applications significantly enhanced vegetative growth across all species, increasing plant height by [≥]22-26%, node numbers by [≥]23-40%, and leaf/leaflet area by [≥]36-48% in cucumber and tomato, as well as expanding leaf area in lettuce. In reproductive stages, Phe treatments increased flower initiation, set fruits ([≥]23-27%), total fruit number ([≥]31%), and fruit yield per plant ([≥]30-36%) in cucumber and tomato. In wheat, Phe increased tiller formation, total spike counts by [≥]36%, and fresh/dry plant biomass. Growth enhancement required a strict concentration threshold of [≥]4 mM; lower concentrations (1-2 mM) were inconsistent, and applying 2 mM twice weekly failed to replicate the significant gains of a single 4 mM weekly treatment. Because background fertigation provided a continuous and ample nitrogen supply, periodic trace applications of Phe contributed negligible amounts of nutritional N or C. This supports the conclusion that Phe acts through concentration-dependent physiological and metabolic biostimulation rather than nutrient supplementation.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.766952 v1

summary.background:
- Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins; phenylalanine is one of them and is also a precursor for many plant defense and signaling compounds.
- A biostimulator is a substance that improves plant growth or yield through physiological effects, not by supplying nutrients or killing pests.
- Dicots (like cucumber, tomato, lettuce) and monocots (like wheat) are the two main groups of flowering plants; they differ in leaf and stem structure.
- A net-house is a mesh-walled growing structure that protects crops while allowing near-field conditions.
- Fertigation means delivering fertilizer dissolved in irrigation water; here nitrogen was supplied at 150 mg/L throughout.
- mM (millimolar) is a unit of concentration; 4 mM is a fixed amount of the compound per liter of solution.
- Previous work reportedly linked phenylalanine at higher concentrations to pathogen resistance; this study examined growth effects in the absence of disease pressure.
summary.one_liner: Field trials in net-houses show that weekly drench or foliar sprays of L-phenylalanine at or above 4 mM enhance vegetative and reproductive growth in cucumber, tomato, lettuce and wheat, with the authors attributing the effect to physiological biostimulation rather than added nutrition.
summary.plain: Farmers and researchers often use substances that help plants grow without fertilizing them directly. This study tested whether one common amino acid, L-phenylalanine, sprayed on or poured around plants, could make several crops grow bigger and yield more. In the reported trials, concentrations of 4 mM or higher gave clear gains in height, leaves, flowers, fruit and wheat tillers, while weaker doses were inconsistent.

title: L-Phenylalanine acts as a broad-spectrum plant growth biostimulator for both dicotyledonous and monocotyledonous crops

abstract: In vivo generation of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells could bypass the complex manufacturing required for conventional cell therapies, but systemic gene delivery remains limited by off target exposure and inefficient access to target immune cells. Here, we develop VINCIT (Virus Incorporated Niche for Cellular ImmunoTherapy), an injectable nanofiber hydrogel composite that establishes a localized immune-engineering niche for CAR T cell generation in vivo. VINCIT spatially retains viral vectors while recruiting endogenous immune cells, enabling local transduction of T cells, after which the engineered T cells enter the circulation. VINCIT spatially confines transgene expression compared with intravenous viral delivery and markedly enhances T cell transduction compared with subcutaneously injected free virus. VINCIT is compatible with both adeno-associated and lentiviral vectors, and CAR T cells generated in vivo exhibit antigen-specific effector responses and mediate CD19+ B cell depletion. In a humanized mouse model of lymphoma, a single VINCIT administration produces sustained tumor control and extends median survival from 32 to 110 days. Mechanistically, efficient CAR T cell generation requires coordinated interactions among multiple immune populations, with neutrophil depletion markedly reducing cellular recruitment and subsequent T cell programming. These findings establish a localized biomaterial niche for spatially controlled in vivo immune cell engineering.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.767176 v1

summary.background:
- CAR T cells: a patient's own immune T cells fitted with a synthetic receptor that lets them recognize and kill a specific target, here CD19 on B cells.
- Viral vectors: engineered viruses (adeno-associated and lentiviral) used as delivery vehicles to insert genes into cells; "transduction" means successful gene delivery into a cell.
- Hydrogel / nanofiber composite: a water-swollen, gel-like material built from very fine fibers that can be injected and act as a local depot.
- Humanized mouse model: a mouse given human immune cells or tissues so that human-like immune responses can be studied.
- Neutrophils: common white blood cells that help recruit other immune cells; the paper reports depleting them reduced recruitment and T cell programming.
- Preclinical: tested in animals or cells, not yet in human patients.
summary.one_liner: VINCIT is an injectable nanofiber hydrogel that retains viral vectors locally to recruit immune cells and generate CAR T cells in vivo, reporting spatially confined transgene expression, CD19+ B cell depletion, and extended survival in a humanized lymphoma mouse model.
summary.plain: Cell therapies that reprogram a patient's T cells to attack cancer usually require removing cells from the body and engineering them in a lab first. This paper describes a gel that is injected under the skin and holds gene-delivery viruses in one place, so immune cells that pass through can be modified there and then travel back into the bloodstream. In the mouse experiments described, this local approach confined gene expression to the site better than intravenous virus delivery and transduced more T cells than injecting free virus alone.
summary.why: Making CAR T cells inside the body could avoid the costly, slow manufacturing step and reduce off-target gene delivery to other tissues. The text reports a single treatment extending median survival in a mouse lymphoma model from 32 to 110 days, but this is preclinical work in mice, so its relevance to human therapy is not yet established.

title: VINCIT: A virus-incorporated biomaterial niche enables spatially controlled in vivo CAR T cell engineering

abstract: Objective: Conventional microelectrode arrays (MEAs) are suboptimal for long-term electrophysiology of three-dimensional (3D) excitable tissues, as limited oxygenation, nutrient diffusion, and tissue-electrode coupling compromise recording stability. Air-liquid interface (ALI) culture mitigates these constraints, but existing ALI MEA platforms are limited in channel count, flexibility, and compatibility with commercial multichannel acquisition systems. We developed and comprehensively characterized a next-generation ALI MEA for standardized, long-term recordings across multiple 3D excitable tissue models. Approach: The novel ALI MEA60 is composed of a porous polyimide membrane that integrates an array of 60 thin film microelectrodes (59 recording, one reference) and a basal perfusion chamber with Luer-lock connectors for controlled medium exchange and pharmacological wash-in/wash-out. It is compatible with the MEA2100-Mini data acquisition system (Multi Channel Systems). We characterized electrode impedance and noise across 41 ALI MEA60 devices, assessed 60-day stability with human iPSC-derived neural spheroids (N = 7 MEAs, 121 recordings) using a standardized longitudinal framework and linear mixed-effects models, and evaluated its versatility through pharmacological assays and recordings from human neural spheroids, brain organoids, ex vivo brain slices, and cardiac organoids. Main results: The platform showed reproducible electrical performance (median impedance 56 kOhms; at 1 kHz) and low noise (approx. 5uV Root Mean Square (RMS) in saline, 10-20 uV in medium), resolving spikes and local field potentials simultaneously. Recording remained stable for at least 60 days, with a stable noise floor and ~85% persistence of initial functional channels. Neural spheroids reproduced the standard qualitative signatures to gabazine, 4-aminopyridine (4-AP), and 6-Cyano-7-nitroquinoxaline-2,3-dione/D-2-amino-5-phosphonovalerate (CNQX/D-AP5), while cardiac organoids showed the expected beta-adrenergic response to isoproterenol. The ALI MEA60 can similarly record signals from human brain slices and organoids without hardware modification. Significance: The ALI MEA60 combines ALI culture, chronic recording stability, standardized pharmacological testing and cross-tissue compatibility in a single ready-to-use platform. It also establishes a reproducible framework for benchmarking long-term electrophysiological performance, thereby supporting disease modelling, drug discovery, organ-on-chip technologies and future chronic 3D electrophysiology systems. Keywords: microelectrode array (MEA); air-liquid interface (ALI); 3D excitable tissues; neural spheroids; cardiac organoids; chronic electrophysiology.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.766976 v1

summary.background:
- Microelectrode array (MEA): a flat dish or chip with many tiny electrodes that record electrical activity from cells sitting on it.
- Spheroid / organoid: a small 3D ball of cells grown in a dish that imitates some features of an organ, such as brain or heart.
- Excitable tissue: tissue, like nerve or heart muscle, that produces electrical spikes.
- Air-liquid interface (ALI) culture: the tissue sits on a porous membrane with its top exposed to air and its base fed by medium, which improves oxygen and nutrient supply.
- Spikes vs. local field potentials: spikes are fast signals from single neurons; local field potentials are slower signals from groups of cells.
- Impedance and noise: how much an electrode resists current and how much random electrical background it adds; lower values mean cleaner recordings.
- Pharmacological wash-in/wash-out: adding a drug to the tissue and then rinsing it away to see the effect.
- Linear mixed-effects model: a statistical method for tracking repeated measurements from the same samples over time.
summary.one_liner: A porous polyimide microelectrode array with 60 thin-film electrodes and a basal perfusion chamber, designed for long-term air-liquid interface recordings from 3D excitable tissues such as neural spheroids, organoids, and brain slices, characterized for impedance, noise, 60-day stability, and pharmacological responses.
summary.plain: Researchers built a small chip that listens to electrical signals from three-dimensional clumps of nerve or heart cells grown in the lab, and keeps them alive by exposing their top surface to air while feeding them from below. They tested it on 41 devices for electrical noise and resistance, and followed neural spheroids for 60 days, with about 85% of the working channels still working at the end. The chip also picked up the expected drug responses in neural and heart tissue and recorded from brain slices and brain organoids.
summary.why: Long-term recording from 3D tissue is hard, so a standardized, commercially compatible platform with a published stability benchmark could help disease modelling and drug screening. The text does not show how it compares with other devices beyond the authors' own characterization, and its value for those uses is still to be tested by others.

title: ALI MEA60: A porous thin-film microelectrode array for air-liquid interface electrophysiology of 3D excitable tissues

abstract: Chemotactic cells generate their own chemical gradients to form spatial patterns that support collective functions ranging from cooperative metabolism to immunity. Despite progress in understanding the optimality of chemotaxis in imposed chemical gradients, it remains unclear how close decentralized cell populations can come to maximizing the population-wide benefit of spatial organization through individual movement and local modulation of chemical gradients. We employ mean field game theory to characterize efficient spatial patterns achievable by decentralized populations as Nash equilibria: each agent optimizes its positioning given the spatial density of the other cells, whereas the population density is determined by the positioning of all individuals. We derive coupled dynamics of population movement and cue modulation that drive adaptation toward these equilibria and verify its structural correspondence to established phenomenological models of chemotactic pattern formation. We apply our framework to self-organized aggregation and numerically demonstrate that the dynamics can form multiple equilibrium patterns, some of which are comparable to the population-level optimum under moderate incentives to aggregate. We also show that the relative timescales of cue modulation and movement influence pattern selection and population-level efficiency: slower cue modulation can yield more coherent and efficient equilibrium patterns. Our framework thus highlights fundamental limits on collective optimization in decentralized cell populations, and suggests a functional role for timescales in self-organized coordination through environmental feedback.
label: arXiv:2611.24705v1

summary.background:
- Chemotaxis: cells moving up or down a chemical gradient.
- Self-organized patterning: group structures that emerge from local rules without a central planner.
- Nash equilibrium: a state where no individual can do better by changing its own strategy alone, given what others do.
- Mean field game theory: a method for modeling very large numbers of agents by using the average population density in place of each individual.
- Timescales: how fast the cue (chemical signal) changes compared with how fast cells move; the paper finds this ratio matters.
- Population-level optimum: the best overall arrangement for the group, which may differ from what individuals settle on.
summary.one_liner: A mean field game framework models chemotactic cells that both move and modulate the chemical cues they follow, showing how decentralized populations can reach Nash equilibrium spatial patterns, with cue-modulation timescale affecting which patterns are selected and how efficient they are.
summary.plain: Some cells create the chemical trails they follow, and together this can form spatial patterns that help the group, such as clustering for shared metabolism or immune defense. This paper asks how close such cell groups, acting only on local information, can get to the best pattern for the whole population. The authors model each cell as optimizing its own position given the others, and report that the resulting dynamics produce several stable patterns, some close to the best achievable when there is moderate incentive to aggregate.
summary.why: It offers a game-theoretic way to measure how efficient self-organized biological patterns can be, and it reports that the speed of cue modulation relative to movement can change which pattern forms. The text is theoretical and numerical only, so its relevance to real cell systems is not established here.

title: Chemotactic aggregation as cue-mediated adaptation toward Nash equilibrium in a spatial patterning game

abstract: Epizootic haemorrhagic disease virus serotype 8 (EHDV-8) emerged in France in September 2023 but its transmission dynamics remain poorly characterised. We adapted a stochastic, spatially explicit compartmental model developed for bluetongue to reconstruct the 2023-24 EHDV-8 epidemic in cattle in mainland France. The model represented transmission across cantons, incorporating cattle demography, pasture cover, relative Culicoides abundance and temperature-dependent vector processes. Three networks represented between-canton spread through short-range vector dispersal (pasture network), non-commercial cattle movements between pastures of the same farm (farm network), and cattle trade (trade network). Using approximate Bayesian computation with sequential Monte Carlo (ABC-SMC), we calibrated the model to canton-week seroprevalence estimates derived from bulk-tank milk measurements. Calibration narrowed the plausible range of the baseline vector-mediated transmission parameter and favoured higher movement intensities through the farm network, although movement intensity remained uncertain. Simulation-based parameter recovery showed that calibration generally identified parameter regions capable of reproducing epidemic patterns comparable to the pseudo-observed data, although predictive performance varied among datasets and was typically lower than that obtained with the generating parameters. When applied to observed data, the calibrated model captured several features of the observed weekly median seroprevalence across sampled cantons, although discrepancies remained at some sampling times and predictive uncertainty was substantial. These results demonstrate how bulk-tank milk surveillance can inform the reconstruction of EHDV-8 epidemic patterns within a national-scale transmission framework. This framework provides a basis for future evaluation and optimisation of vaccination strategies.
label: arXiv:2611.24620v1

summary.background:
- Epizootic haemorrhagic disease (EHD) is a viral disease of ruminants such as cattle and deer, spread by biting midges.
- Culicoides are tiny biting midges that act as vectors (carriers) of the virus; their abundance and activity depend on temperature.
