- Bluetongue is a closely related disease, and the model was originally built for it.
- Seroprevalence is the share of animals with antibodies, which indicates past infection.
- Bulk-tank milk testing checks milk pooled from a whole dairy herd for antibodies, a cheap surveillance method.
- A compartmental model sorts animals into groups (e.g. susceptible, infected, recovered) and simulates moves between them.
- A multilayer network represents several kinds of links between places (here: vector spread between pastures, movements within farms, and cattle trade).
- Approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) with sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) estimates which parameter values are consistent with observed data, by comparing simulations to data rather than computing likelihoods directly.
summary.one_liner: A stochastic, spatially explicit multilayer network model adapted from bluetongue work is calibrated with ABC-SMC to canton-week bulk-tank milk seroprevalence to reconstruct the 2023-24 EHDV-8 epizootic in mainland French cattle.
summary.plain: In September 2023 a virus called epizootic haemorrhagic disease (EHDV serotype 8) appeared in French cattle, and little is known about how it spread. The authors adapted an existing computer model of a related disease, bluetongue, and fitted it to antibody levels measured in milk from farms across France's cantons (regional districts) to rebuild how the 2023-24 outbreak likely unfolded.
summary.why: Animal disease outbreaks often spread through insect vectors and animal movements, and this paper shows one way to combine both with routine milk testing to reconstruct spread and inform future vaccination planning. The text reports that the fit was only partial, with notable discrepancies and wide uncertainty, so it is best read as a methods demonstration rather than a settled account of the outbreak.

title: A multilayer network-based modelling framework for epizootic haemorrhagic disease virus transmission in France

abstract: BackgroundCirrhosis is often diagnosed only at decompensation, making identification of high-risk groups important for prevention and early detection. Chronic liver disease mortality has fallen in southern Europe and France since 2010, but not in Germany. Whether the German plateau reflects birth-cohort alcohol exposure, metabolic liver disease or certification practice is unknown. MethodsDeaths by ICD-10 code, sex and age group were extracted from the WHO Mortality Database for 16 European countries (2000-2022), with Eurostat rates (2011-2023), German state-level mortality (1998-2024) and hospital diagnoses (2000-2023). Registry and Global Burden of Disease Study (GBD) 2023 estimates were summarised for ages 45-64, 65-74 and 75 years and over, with registry rates standardised to the European Standard Population 2013. FindingsGermanys age-standardised chronic liver disease mortality was 16.6 per 100 000 in 2011 and 16.0 in 2023, against declines of 21-37% in France, Italy and Spain. Between 2010 and 2022, alcoholic liver disease mortality at ages 45-64 fell by 17% in men and 25% in women, whereas fibrosis and cirrhosis (K74) mortality at ages 65-74 rose by 27% and 28%, with larger K70-K77 mortality increases in eastern than western Germany. Hospitalisation rates showed similar age-specific patterns, while in-hospital case fatality declined. Fewer than 0.5% of liver deaths were certified as fatty liver. GBD 2023 showed a similar age-specific increase but attributed rising mortality to all five modelled aetiologies. InterpretationThe German plateau reflects continued decline below age 65 and rising mortality at ages 65-74, compatible with cohorts born 1945-59 reaching this age band, particularly in eastern Germany. Consumption records and surveys indicate differing regional patterns of alcohol exposure. Much of the cirrhosis in these cohorts is certified without aetiology, and GBDs aetiological estimates cannot be verified in registration data. FundingNone. Research in context Evidence before this studyPubMed was searched without language restriction from inception to October 15, 2026, for registry-based analyses of cirrhosis or chronic liver disease mortality in Germany or in European comparisons, and for comparisons of GBD estimates with vital registration, using combinations of the terms cirrhosis, liver disease, alcohol-related liver disease, mortality, Germany, Europe, age-period-cohort, Global Burden of Disease and vital registration. Registry analyses have documented an east-to-west gradient of cirrhosis mortality across Europe and, in Germany, period and birth-cohort effects on alcohol-related mortality, with lower risks in later-born cohorts. A nationwide hospital study reported rising admissions for cirrhosis with falling in-hospital mortality. GBD publications acknowledge that ICD coding cannot reliably distinguish cirrhosis aetiologies, which are assigned using statistical models. We found no previous study combining detailed ICD-10 mortality analyses, age-specific European comparison, German federal-state trends and comparison with GBD aetiological estimates. Added value of this studyWe compared GBD 2023 estimates with European mortality registration data and examined German mortality by detailed ICD-10 code, age, sex and federal state, alongside hospital diagnosis statistics. The German plateau reflects rising mortality at 65-74 years, especially in eastern Germany, while mortality continues to decline at 45-64 years. The increase was concentrated in deaths coded as unspecified cirrhosis (K74.6) and accompanied by rising cirrhosis hospitalisation rates. At the same time, in-hospital case fatality and admissions for chronic viral hepatitis declined. GBD identified a similar age-specific increase but estimated rising mortality for all five aetiological sub-causes despite their differing representation in routine data. Implications of all the available evidenceThe absence of a decline in cirrhosis mortality in Germany is consistent with older birth cohorts with high cumulative alcohol exposure, although the aetiology of cirrhosis is often unspecified. Differences in alcohol consumption patterns, obesity and conditions after reunification may contribute to higher mortality in parts of eastern Germany. The findings support earlier detection and improved treatment access for older adults, age-specific surveillance in Germany and other European countries, and cautious interpretation of modelled aetiological fractions in countries without multiple-cause mortality data.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.26368157 v1

summary.background:
- Cirrhosis: scarring of the liver, often found only when it causes complications (decompensation).
- Age-standardised rate: a death rate adjusted to a standard age structure so populations can be compared fairly.
- ICD-10: the international coding system doctors and registries use to classify causes of death; K70–K77 covers liver disease, K74.6 is "unspecified cirrhosis."
- Birth cohort: a group of people born in the same years; comparing cohorts helps separate lifetime exposures from calendar-year effects.
- Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023: a modelled global estimate that assigns liver deaths to causes such as alcohol, viral hepatitis, and metabolic disease, partly using statistical models rather than recorded causes.
- Case fatality: the share of hospitalised patients who die during that stay.
summary.one_liner: A registry-based analysis of German and European liver disease mortality (2000–2024) by age, sex, federal state and detailed ICD-10 code, compared with Global Burden of Disease 2023 aetiology estimates, finds that Germany's cirrhosis mortality plateau reflects rising deaths at ages 65–74, concentrated in unspecified cirrhosis (K74.6) and in eastern Germany.
summary.plain: Germany's death rate from chronic liver disease has stopped falling while several neighbouring countries' rates have dropped. This paper looks at death certificates, hospital records and modelled global estimates to find where the plateau comes from. The authors report that deaths are still falling under age 65 but are rising among people aged 65 to 74, especially in the east, and that most of these cirrhosis deaths are recorded without a stated cause.
summary.why: The findings point to older cohorts with high past alcohol exposure as a possible driver, and suggest that older adults may need earlier detection and better treatment access. The authors also warn that global models assigning causes to cirrhosis deaths cannot be checked against routine death registration data, so those cause-specific figures should be read cautiously.

title: The plateau in liver disease mortality in Germany: contrasting trends by age, region and ICD-10 code, 2000-2024

abstract: BackgroundComprehensive influenza surveillance is conducted year-round in the United States to monitor changes in influenza activity. This report summarizes the 2025-26 U.S. influenza season. MethodsData from September 28, 2025 through October 3, 2026 were collected from national surveillance systems monitoring influenza through laboratory testing, outpatient and emergency department visits, hospitalizations, and mortality. Data modeled disease burden and assessed severity using established criteria. A subset of influenza positive specimens were genetically and antigenically characterized and assessed for antiviral susceptibility. ResultsInfluenza activity peaked during the week ending December 27, 2025, five weeks earlier than the 2024-25 season. There were two waves of influenza activity with influenza A(H3N2) subclade K viruses predominating the season overall and during the first wave followed by a smaller B/Victoria wave. The majority of circulating A(H3N2) and B/Victoria viruses were antigenically drifted from 2025-26 influenza vaccine reference strains. Season severity was classified as moderate overall, with children (0-17 years old) experiencing a high severity season and adults experiencing a moderate severity season. Children experienced the highest percent of influenza-associated outpatient and emergency department visits compared to other age groups. This seasons cumulative influenza-associated hospitalization rate in children is the highest hospitalization rate in the past 16 years. Additionally, there were 198 influenza-associated pediatric deaths reported to CDC as of October 29, 2026. ConclusionsAlthough antigenically drifted A(H3N2) viruses predominated, the 2025-26 U.S. influenza season occurred within historic norms for timing and severity. Year-round surveillance remains critical for detecting changes in influenza viruses and monitoring influenza-associated morbidity and mortality. Key PointsO_LICDCs severity assessment framework classified the 2025-26 U.S. influenza season as moderate across all age groups C_LIO_LINationally, peak influenza activity occurred in late December 2025 C_LIO_LIInfluenza A(H3N2) subclade K viruses predominated during the 2025-26 season C_LI
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.26367927 v1

summary.background:
- Influenza (flu) is a common respiratory virus; A and B are its main types for seasonal epidemics.
- Subclades are finer genetic groupings within a flu type; H3N2 is a specific A-type subtype.
- "Antigenically drifted" means the virus's surface proteins have changed enough that vaccine-induced immunity may match it less well.
- Vaccines are chosen each year from reference strains predicted to match the upcoming season's viruses.
- Surveillance means ongoing collection of case, hospital and death data to track disease.
- The severity rating here uses CDC's established framework, which grades the season as low, moderate or high for each age group.
- The text gives a data window ending October 3, 2026 and a pediatric death count as of October 29, 2026, which is inconsistent with a 2025-26 season report; readers should check these dates against the original source.
summary.one_liner: CDC's season summary of U.S. influenza activity for 2025-26, covering timing, two epidemic waves, dominant A(H3N2) subclade K viruses, vaccine mismatch, age-specific severity, and pediatric deaths.
summary.plain: This is an official government report on how the flu season went in the United States from late September 2025 onward. It tracks lab test results, doctor and emergency room visits, hospital stays and deaths, then rates how severe the season was. The main findings are that flu peaked in late December 2025, earlier than the previous season, and that a strain called A(H3N2) subclade K dominated, with a smaller second wave of a B-type strain.
summary.why: The report flags that children had their highest cumulative flu hospitalization rate in 16 years and that most circulating viruses differed antigenically from the vaccine strains, which matters for vaccine planning and child health. The text itself concludes the season was within historic norms for timing and severity, so the child-specific findings are the main point of interest.

title: Influenza activity in the United States during the 2025-26 influenza season

abstract: BackgroundHistorically, the Variola virus caused deadly smallpox epidemics in children. In Copenhagen, transmission was halted by 1810 when [~]90% of children were vaccinated following the introduction of a mandatory single-dose vaccine program. A 14-year honeymoon period followed, but in 1824 smallpox re-emerged as a milder disease of adults. We set out to study smallpox epidemics between 1824 and 1835 when all smallpox patients in Copenhagen were quarantined. MethodWe analyze data from 3795 smallpox patients reported by the treating physicians between 1824 and 1835. The data include age, vaccination status, and outcome. We estimate age-specific case fatality ratios (CFR) and vaccine effectiveness (VE) against mortality. FindingsFor the four outbreaks while quarantine was mandatory (1824-1834), the CFR was [~]1% among the vaccinated and [~]25% among the unvaccinated, corresponding to a VE of [~]95%. For the fifth outbreak in 1835, we found that CFR was low among the vaccinated but increased with age, which is evidence of waning vaccine protection. Almost no cases were over 40 years of age, suggesting lifelong immunity from smallpox infection. InterpretationAs the unvaccinated CFR was high and comparable to the pre-vaccine era, the milder post-honeymoon smallpox disease cannot be explained by genetic changes in the virus. Rather, high coverage with an effective vaccine combined with waning vaccine protection in adulthood explains the changing face of smallpox. We demonstrates how high vaccine coverage can disguise an outbreak of highly pathogenic smallpox as the milder Variola minor.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.26368180 v1

summary.background:
- Smallpox (caused by the Variola virus) was a deadly disease, especially for children, and was eradicated worldwide in 1980.
- Variola minor is the milder form of the virus; Variola major is the severe form.
- Case fatality ratio (CFR): the share of sick people who die.
- Vaccine effectiveness (VE): how much a vaccine reduces the chance of a bad outcome, here death, compared with the unvaccinated.
- Waning immunity: protection that weakens over time.
- Quarantine: isolating sick people to stop spread.
- Retrospective data: records collected in the past, analysed later.
summary.one_liner: Retrospective analysis of 3,795 Copenhagen smallpox patients (1824–1835) estimating age-specific case fatality and vaccine effectiveness against death, interpreting a milder "post-honeymoon" resurgence as a result of high vaccine coverage plus waning adult protection rather than viral change.
summary.plain: Smallpox was nearly stopped in Copenhagen by 1810, when about 90% of children had been vaccinated, but it returned in 1824 as a milder disease striking adults. This paper uses records from 3,795 patients treated by physicians between 1824 and 1835, when all patients were quarantined, to compare death rates among vaccinated and unvaccinated people. The authors report that the vaccine appeared to prevent most deaths in the first four outbreaks, and that protection seemed to fade with age in the fifth.
summary.why: It offers a rare historical natural experiment on how a vaccine and its waning protection shape which age groups a disease hits and how severe it looks. The authors argue that high vaccination can make a dangerous virus look like a milder one, which may matter for interpreting modern outbreak data, though the text does not spell out such links.

title: The effect of smallpox vaccination: unique insights gained from Danish post-honeymoon epidemics 200 years ago

abstract: Background-Synuclein seed amplification assay (Syn-SAA) has emerged as a promising biomarker for detecting underlying -synuclein pathology and predicting phenoconversion in prodromal Parkinsons disease (PD). However, its association with longitudinal clinical progression during the prodromal stage remains unclear. We investigated whether baseline Syn-SAA status and kinetic parameters were associated with motor and cognitive progression and subsequent phenoconversion in prodromal individuals. MethodsClinical progression was assessed using the Movement Disorder Society-Sponsored Revision of the Unified Parkinsons Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS) Part III motor scores, Hoehn and Yahr (H&Y) stage, and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores. Linear mixed-effects models were utilized to examine the associations between baseline Syn-SAA status, kinetic parameters, and longitudinal changes in these clinical measures. Additionally, time-to-event analyses were performed to assess the associations between SAA measurements and phenoconversion to PD or dementia with Lewy bodies. ResultsWe identified 2,532 participants with available baseline Syn-SAA status in the Parkinsons Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) prodromal cohort. This longitudinal study, which included up to 12 years of follow-up, comprised 1,714 Syn-SAA-positive and 818 Syn-SAA-negative individuals. Over the follow-up period, Syn-SAA-positive participants exhibited significantly faster motor progression measured by MDS-UPDRS Part III motor score than Syn-SAA-negative participants (0.611 vs. 0.139 points/year; P<0.001). This association persisted after excluding phenoconverters (0.430 vs. 0.202 points/year; P=0.014) and restricting follow-up to seven years (0.588 vs. 0.137 points/year; P<0.001). Among the 1,796 participants included in the time-to-event analyses, 181 phenoconversion events occurred. Baseline Syn-SAA positivity was associated with a significantly higher hazard of phenoconversion (adjusted hazard ratio 5.72, 95% confidence interval 3.78-8.68; P<0.001), whereas kinetic parameters showed no significant associations with phenoconversion risk. ConclusionsBaseline Syn-SAA positivity was associated with accelerated motor progression during the prodromal stage independent of phenoconversion. These findings support the potential utility of Syn-SAA positivity as a prognostic biomarker for motor progression and phenoconversion, with implications for risk stratification and participant selection in future disease-modifying trials.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.26368235 v1

summary.background:
- Parkinson's disease (PD) is a brain disorder involving loss of movement control; the "prodromal" stage is the period of early signs before a diagnosis is made.
- Alpha-synuclein is a brain protein that can misfold and clump; these clumps are thought to drive PD and related conditions.
- A seed amplification assay (SAA) copies tiny amounts of misfolded protein in a lab so they can be detected; "kinetic parameters" describe how fast the reaction proceeds.
- MDS-UPDRS Part III is a standard clinical motor exam score; Hoehn and Yahr is a 5-step disease stage scale; MoCA is a cognitive screening test.
- Phenoconversion means progressing from the prodromal state to a full diagnosis (here PD or dementia with Lewy bodies).
- Linear mixed-effects models track changes over time in repeated measurements; time-to-event analysis estimates the risk of an event over time, with hazard ratios comparing groups.
summary.one_liner: In the PPMI prodromal cohort, baseline alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay (Syn-SAA) positivity was associated with faster MDS-UPDRS Part III motor progression over up to 12 years, persisting after excluding phenoconverters, and with higher hazard of phenoconversion to Parkinson's disease or dementia with Lewy bodies, while assay kinetic parameters were not associated with phenoconversion.
summary.plain: This study looks at people who show early warning signs of Parkinson's disease but do not yet have a full diagnosis. A lab test that detects a misfolded protein clump (alpha-synuclein) was run at the start, and researchers tracked these people's movement scores, stage ratings and thinking scores for up to 12 years. Those who tested positive got worse on movement scores faster than those who tested negative, and they were much more likely to develop the disease later.
summary.why: If a blood or spinal-fluid test can flag who is likely to decline, it could help choose participants for future trials of treatments that aim to slow the disease. The authors suggest this as a prognostic marker, but the work is observational, so it shows association rather than proof that the test should guide care.

title: α-synuclein seed amplification assay positivity is associated with motor progression in the prodromal stage independent of phenoconversion

abstract: Background: Evidence linking social, behavioral, and environmental factors to dementia in Central Africa remains limited. Objective: To examine associations between 16 factors and dementia status in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), and quantify incremental model fit beyond age and sex. Methods: This cross sectional analysis included 721 participants (232 cognitively unimpaired; 489 with dementia, including 247 with suspected Alzheimers disease). Logistic regression jointly modeled 16 factors, age, sex, and missing-category indicators. Continuous covariates with missing values were mean-imputed and standardized. Model fit was assessed using Nagelkerke pseudo R squared, likelihood-ratio testing, and 1,000 bootstrap replicates. Results: Nagelkerke pseudo-R2 increased from 0.106 with age and sex to 0.368 after adding the factors (change in R2 = 0.262; bootstrap 95% CI: 0.241-0.371; chi-square(27) = 163.62, p < 0.001). Poverty (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 2.34, 95% CI: 1.52-3.60), low resilience (aOR = 1.84, 95% CI: 1.18-2.86), and depression (aOR = 1.53, 95% CI: 1.02-2.31) were associated with higher dementia odds. Higher education (aOR = 0.51, 95% CI: 0.39-0.66, per standard deviation increase) and obesity (aOR = 0.31, 95% CI: 0.10-0.90) showed inverse associations; obesity data were 79.9% missing. Alcohol consumption and PM2.5 exposure were not significantly associated with dementia. Conclusions: Poverty, lower resilience, depression, and education were associated with dementia status in this nonrepresentative cohort. Incremental model fit does not quantify preventable dementia burden, and causality cannot be inferred from these cross-sectional data.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.26368211 v1

summary.background:
- Dementia: a group of conditions causing progressive loss of memory and thinking skills.
- Cross-sectional study: data collected at one point in time; it can show that factors and conditions occur together but not which came first.
- Logistic regression: a statistical method that estimates how the odds of an outcome change with each factor; an adjusted odds ratio (aOR) above 1 means higher odds, below 1 means lower odds.
- Nagelkerke pseudo R-squared: a rough 0 to 1 measure of how much a model explains outcome differences, not the same as R-squared in ordinary regression.
- Bootstrap: a resampling method that re-runs the analysis many times to estimate uncertainty.
- Mean imputation: filling in missing values with the average; obesity data were 79.9% missing, so that result is weak.
- PM2.5: fine airborne particles from pollution.
summary.one_liner: A cross-sectional study of 721 community participants in the Democratic Republic of the Congo tests how 16 social, behavioral, and environmental factors relate to dementia status, and how much they add to a model that already includes age and sex.
summary.plain: This paper looks at what might be linked to dementia, a condition that affects memory and thinking, in people living in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The researchers compared 232 people without cognitive impairment with 489 people who had dementia, and checked 16 factors such as poverty, education, mood, and alcohol use. Poverty, low resilience, and depression were linked to higher odds of dementia, while more education was linked to lower odds.
summary.why: Evidence on dementia from Central Africa is scarce, so a study from this region adds data that most dementia research has not covered. The authors note the sample is not representative and that the data cannot show cause and effect, so the findings are best read as associations that may point to areas for further study.

title: Modifiable and Context-Specific Factors Associated with Dementia in the Democratic Republic of the Congo: A Community-Derived Cross-Sectional Study

abstract: Three mechanisms generate endogeneity in regressions under interference. We address them by constructing network-adaptive instrumental variables (NIV) for a spatial autoregressive (SAR) model with endogenous covariates and unknown network weights. Under network-conditional exclusion and information equivalence, the resulting instruments yield valid moments without knowing the true network. We establish joint identification of the structural mean coefficients and the network parameters, providing two sufficient routes. Then under additional covariance restrictions, we identify the disturbance spillover coefficient and the innovation variance. We develop NIV-GMM estimation, establish consistency and asymptotic normality, and give feasible inference and a test for mean network spillovers. Monte Carlo simulations examine their finite-sample performance.
label: arXiv:2611.25222v1

summary.background:
- Endogeneity: when an explanatory variable is correlated with the error term, so ordinary regression is biased.
- Instrumental variable (IV): an outside variable that affects the outcome only through the explanatory variable, used to isolate clean variation.
- Interference / spillovers: one unit's outcome depends on other units' outcomes or characteristics, often via a network.
- Spatial autoregressive (SAR) model: a regression where each unit's outcome depends on a weighted average of its neighbours' outcomes, with weights given by a network matrix.
- Network weights: numbers describing how strongly each unit is connected to each other unit; here they are unknown and must be estimated.
- GMM (generalized method of moments): an estimation method that chooses parameters so that sample averages of chosen moment conditions are close to zero.
- Identification: whether parameters can be uniquely recovered from the data under the assumptions.
- Consistency and asymptotic normality: estimates converge to the truth as data grow, and their spread is approximately bell-shaped, which justifies standard confidence intervals.
summary.one_liner: The paper constructs network-adaptive instrumental variables for a spatial autoregressive model with endogenous covariates and unknown network weights, and develops GMM estimation and inference for the resulting coefficients and spillover parameters.
summary.plain: When people or units influence one another through a network, a standard regression can give misleading answers because the variables are tangled together. This paper proposes a way to build helpful "instrument" variables that work even when the true pattern of who influences whom is not known. The authors show the model's key parameters can be identified under stated conditions, and they test their estimation method with computer simulations.
summary.why: Network interference shows up in many applied settings, such as peer effects, spillovers between regions, and contagion, so estimators that do not require the network to be known could be useful there. The text supports the theoretical claims and simulation tests, but it does not report how the method performs on real data, so its practical reach is still unclear.

title: Network-Adaptive Instrumental Variables

abstract: I study fuzzy difference-in-differences designs from a design-based perspective, in which potential outcomes and treatment decisions are fixed and only the assignment of a policy is random, with heterogeneous and possibly unknown assignment probabilities. The Wald-DiD design estimand equals an assignment-weighted complier effect plus contamination from switchers, from changes in always-takers' effects and from trends in untreated outcomes. I derive the conditions under which the estimand holds a clear causal interpretation. The conditions are weaker than parallel trends in both outcomes and treatments. We propose an Anderson--Rubin-type test with a conservative Neyman variance that remains valid under weak first stages, a sensitivity analysis for the complier effect, and estimators for designs with known assignment probabilities. An application to the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment illustrates the results.
label: arXiv:2611.24402v1

summary.background:
- Difference-in-differences: comparing the change over time in a treated group with the change in a comparison group.
- Parallel trends: the usual assumption that, without treatment, both groups would have changed at the same rate.
- Fuzzy design: assignment is random (for example, a lottery), but actual treatment uptake may differ from assignment.
- Wald estimator: the ratio of the outcome difference to the take-up difference, which recovers the effect for "compliers" (people whose uptake follows the assignment).
- Design-based inference: randomness comes only from the random assignment, not from sampling people from a larger population.
- Weak first stage: when assignment barely changes take-up, making estimates unstable and tests unreliable.
- Anderson–Rubin test: a test for effects that stays valid even when the first stage is weak.
summary.one_liner: The paper develops design-based inference for fuzzy difference-in-differences (where a policy is assigned at random but take-up is not), deriving when the Wald-DiD estimand has a causal reading, proposing an Anderson–Rubin-type test with a conservative Neyman variance valid under weak first stages, a sensitivity analysis for the complier effect, and estimators for known assignment probabilities, illustrated with the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment.
summary.plain: The paper looks at studies where a policy or program is offered to some people at random, but not everyone who is offered it signs up, and outcomes are compared before and after across groups. The author treats the people and their choices as fixed and only the random offer as the source of chance, and asks when the usual comparison-based estimate still means what we want it to mean. The paper gives conditions for that, proposes statistical tests and a sensitivity check, and applies the methods to the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment.
summary.why: Difference-in-differences is one of the most widely used tools for judging policy effects, and this work states its assumptions in a way that is weaker than the usual parallel-trends requirement. The Oregon experiment is a well-known health policy study, so the application makes the ideas concrete; the broader practical impact is not established by the text provided.

title: Design-Based Inference for Fuzzy Difference-in-Differences

abstract: We study repeated games with purely informational externalities. Each player observes a single conditionally independent signal and then repeatedly takes publicly observed actions to maximize their expected discounted payoff, which depends only on the state and their own action. We show that, when there are sufficiently many players and they are sufficiently patient, there exist equilibria where information is aggregated: the players' payoffs approximate the full-information payoff. This holds even if actions are uninformative under myopic play. Conversely, even if myopic play reveals the state, there also exist equilibria where information is not aggregated: payoffs approximate those under autarky. Our results speak to the range of possible outcomes of social learning games with forward-looking agents.
label: arXiv:2611.25280v1

summary.background:
- Repeated games: the same interaction happens many times, so players can reward or punish past behaviour.
- Folk theorem: a family of results saying that many payoff outcomes can be sustained as equilibria when players are patient enough.
- Conditionally independent signal: each player's private clue is independent of others' clues once the true state is known.
- Informational externality: a player's action affects what others learn, but not their own payoff directly.
- Autarky: the payoff from acting alone with only your own information, without learning from others.
- Myopic play: each player only optimizes the current period, ignoring future effects.
- Full-information payoff: the payoff if everyone's information were pooled.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves folk-theorem-style results for repeated social learning games with purely informational externalities, showing that both information-aggregating and non-aggregating equilibria can exist when there are many, patient players.
summary.plain: The paper studies a group of people who each get one private clue about an unknown state of the world, then make repeated public choices that others can see. It asks whether, if the players care about the long run and are patient, they can coordinate so that everyone's combined clues are effectively pooled, or alternatively so that they end up no better off than if each acted alone.
summary.why: The result matters for understanding when groups learn well from observing each other's actions, and it suggests that the outcome depends heavily on how forward-looking agents expect others to behave. The text does not indicate applications beyond this theoretical setting, so the wider relevance is uncertain.

title: Folk Theorems for Social Learning

abstract: This paper shows how the meet and join of any pair of equilibria in a super- modular game can be constructed. The method relies on two one-directional best-response processes that I call contagion up and contagion down. Starting from any action profile, applying this pair of processes in opposite orders produces two equilibria that define its equilibrium envelope. The endpoints of the envelope are precisely the least and greatest equilibria reachable through arbitrary asynchronous best-response dynamics, and can only move closer together as players revise their actions. These and other results show how appending one-directional adjustment processes to the familiar equilibrium lattice structure allows us to explore the relationships between equilibria further.
label: arXiv:2611.24614v1

summary.background:
- Game theory: a game is a set of players, each choosing an action to best respond to others' actions.
- Equilibrium: a set of actions where no player wants to change unilaterally.
- Supermodular game: a game where players' actions are complements, so raising one player's action tends to raise others' incentives to raise theirs.
- Lattice: a partially ordered set in which any two elements have a greatest lower bound (meet) and least upper bound (join); here the equilibria form such a structure.
- Best-response dynamics: a process where players repeatedly switch to their best reply to current play; "asynchronous" means players update one at a time, in any order.
- Fixed-point and order theory (e.g. Tarski's theorem) is helpful background but not required for the main idea.
summary.one_liner: The paper constructs the meet and join of any two equilibria in a supermodular game using two one-directional best-response processes ("contagion up" and "contagion down") and studies the resulting equilibrium envelope.
summary.plain: This paper is about games where several players each choose an action and want to respond to what the others do, and where the stable outcomes (equilibria) form a structured family. The author shows how to build two particular stable outcomes, the lowest and highest, from any starting point by repeatedly letting players adjust their actions in one direction only. The endpoints of this construction can only move closer together as players keep revising their actions.
summary.why: Knowing how equilibria relate to one another tells us how a strategic system might settle, and which outcomes are reachable through gradual adjustment. The text does not say what applications it may have beyond the theory itself, so its wider relevance is unclear from this passage alone.

title: On the equilibrium lattice of supermodular games

abstract: We study temporal fair division of indivisible items in both the goods and chores settings, with $n \ge 2$ agents and nonnegative additive values or costs. Items arrive one at a time and must be assigned immediately and irrevocably. The arrival order and all agents' values or costs are known in advance, and the cumulative allocation must satisfy the fairness requirements after each arrival. For goods, we give a polynomial-time algorithm that simultaneously achieves exact temporal proportionality up to one item (TPROP1), a $1/n$ approximation to temporal maximin share (TMMS), and a $1/(n-1)$ approximation to temporal envy-freeness up to one item (TEF1). The TMMS factor is optimal. For chores, we give a polynomial-time algorithm that simultaneously achieves exact TPROP1 and a $2-1/n$ approximation to TMMS. Classical scheduling lower bounds based on fixed sequences carry over to chores TMMS, establishing the optimality of this factor for $n=2,3$. For every $n \ge 2$, we further show that $2-1/n$ is the optimal TMMS factor subject to exact TPROP1. For every fixed $n \ge 3$ and every finite $β\ge 1$, we construct an instance of chores admitting no $β$-TEF1 allocation.
label: arXiv:2611.23782v1

summary.background:
- Fair division: splitting indivisible items among agents so that each feels treated fairly.
- Goods vs. chores: goods are things agents like to receive; chores are costs agents want to minimize.
- Temporal setting: items arrive one by one in a known order and each must be assigned immediately and permanently.
- Proportionality up to one item (PROP1): each agent gets at least their fair share, up to a single item's margin.
- Maximin share (MMS): the best guaranteed share an agent could secure by splitting items into groups themselves; a 'temporal' version requires this at every step.
- Envy-freeness up to one item (EF1): no agent prefers another's bundle after removing one item from it.
- Approximation factor: a multiplier showing how close a guarantee comes to the ideal; 1/n and 2-1/n are such factors.
- Scheduling lower bounds: known limits from job scheduling that transfer to this problem.
summary.one_liner: Online-style fair division of indivisible goods and chores where items arrive over time and must be assigned irrevocably, giving algorithms that simultaneously meet several temporal fairness notions (TPROP1, TMMS, TEF1) with tight approximation factors for chores.
summary.plain: This paper studies how to split a stream of items among several people when each item must be handed out right away and cannot be taken back, and the split has to look fair after every new item arrives. The items can be goods people want or chores people want to avoid. The authors give procedures that keep several fairness standards satisfied at once, and for chores they show some limits on how well those standards can be met.
summary.why: Many real allocation problems, such as assigning tasks or resources as they come in, work this way, so guarantees that hold at every step matter. The text gives tight bounds (the goods result for maximin share is stated as optimal, and the chores bounds are shown optimal for some cases), which makes the results more than just an algorithm; how these results apply outside the abstract model is not addressed in the text.

title: Temporal Fair Division: Simultaneous Guarantees for Goods and Chores

abstract: We construct a four-buyer online combinatorial auction with independent subadditive valuations and a fixed, known arrival order in which every online rule earns strictly less than $1/2$ of the expected offline optimum. A common partition, revealed at the third arrival, gives the first three buyers one unit of welfare per item. If the rule uses three distinct partitions, either an item allocated early contributes zero or the fourth buyer's expected value for the remaining bundle is one less than its size. We compute the optimal online and offline welfare exactly and show that a $1/2$ guarantee always holds with at most three buyers.
label: arXiv:2611.24920v1

summary.background:
- Combinatorial auction: a sale where buyers bid on bundles of items, not single items.
- Online: decisions must be made as each buyer arrives, without knowing future buyers.
- Competitive ratio: the worst-case fraction of the best possible (offline, all-knowing) value that an online rule guarantees.
- Subadditive valuation: a buyer's value for a bundle is at most the sum of its values for the separate items, so bundles have diminishing extra worth.
- Independent valuations: each buyer's values are drawn without depending on the others.
- Expected welfare: the average total value delivered to buyers under random values.
- Lower bound by construction: showing a ratio is impossible by exhibiting a hard instance.
summary.one_liner: The paper builds a four-buyer online combinatorial auction with independent subadditive valuations and a fixed arrival order, showing that no online allocation rule can guarantee half of the expected offline optimum, and that a 1/2 guarantee holds when there are at most three buyers.
summary.plain: This paper looks at a selling problem where buyers arrive one at a time and each must be given items immediately, without knowing who comes later. The authors build a specific example with four buyers and show that every possible online selling rule ends up with strictly less than half of the best total value an all-knowing seller could have achieved. They also state that the half-value target does hold when there are at most three buyers.
summary.why: It sharpens a known limit in online auction design by showing the best achievable guarantee is below one half for this setting, which matters for anyone hoping for a simple benchmark. The text does not say how this relates to wider applications, so its broader significance is uncertain from the abstract alone.

title: The Optimal Competitive Ratio for Subadditive Online Combinatorial Auctions is Less Than 1/2

abstract: Options on VXX bring the dynamics of the VIX futures curve into the joint SPX-VIX calibration problem. We construct a common model by specifying the VIX and then recovering instantaneous SPX variance from the requirement that its risk-neutral conditional expected average over the next thirty days equals the squared VIX. With truncated signatures of time-extended polynomial diffusions, this recovery reduces to finite-dimensional linear algebra and gives explicit access to the futures underlying VXX. The same specification therefore governs equity variance and rolling volatility exposure. To accommodate flexible specifications while respecting variance nonnegativity, we develop a regularized model and quantify the pricing errors of its tractable VIX and VXX proxies. Applications to short-dated option smiles illustrate joint calibration across the three markets, with Monte Carlo estimates of the proxy error bounds well below quoted bid-ask spreads.
label: arXiv:2611.25047v1

summary.background:
- Implied volatility: the market's forecast of future price swings, backed out from option prices.
- Variance: the square of volatility; a stochastic-volatility model lets this quantity itself move randomly.
- Risk-neutral measure: the pricing-world probability convention used to value derivatives, not real-world forecasts.
- VIX: a published index of expected 30-day S&P 500 volatility, derived from SPX option prices.
- VIX futures and VXX: futures contracts on the VIX, and an exchange-traded note whose value follows a rolling position in them.
- Calibration: adjusting model parameters so model prices match observed market prices.
- Signatures: a way of encoding the history of a random path as a sequence of numbers, truncated here to finitely many terms.
- Bid-ask spread: the gap between the price a buyer offers and a seller asks; a natural yardstick for acceptable pricing error.
summary.one_liner: The paper builds one stochastic-volatility model that jointly fits S&P 500 index options, VIX options and VXX options, using truncated signatures of polynomial diffusions to make the VIX-to-SPX variance recovery tractable, plus a regularized variant with quantified proxy pricing errors.
summary.plain: Traders price options on a stock index (SPX), on its fear gauge (the VIX), and on an exchange-traded note (VXX) that tracks VIX futures. The paper proposes one mathematical model that prices all three consistently: it starts from the VIX, then works backward to the index's instantaneous variance. The authors report that the resulting calculations reduce to finite-dimensional linear algebra, and that their approximation errors, estimated by simulation, are smaller than typical quoted bid-ask spreads.
summary.why: Calibrating one model to equity, volatility-index and volatility-product markets at once is a standard practical problem in derivatives pricing, and the text claims the approach gives explicit access to the VXX underlying futures. Whether it proves more accurate or easier to use than existing methods is not shown in the text provided.

title: A joint framework for SPX, VIX and VXX

abstract: Existing work suggests that markets can show volatility with paths rougher than those of Brownian motion. In theory this can happen when the order flow is close to instability with memory that decays as a power law. However, it is not fully clear how such order flow could arise from the predominantly algorithmic market making that characterizes order book dynamics. We show one such consistent mechanism. We treat each market maker as a desk that uses a first-order gradient rule to move the distances of its orders from the mid price toward target distances provided by an unknown oracle. We assume that distinct desks do not act synchronously in time but act whenever new information relevant to their respective oracles arrives, which each desk samples over its own characteristic lookback horizon. Across all desks the rule therefore takes the form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with information-driven (mini-batch) noise. In the continuum limit this update rule makes the volume of the order book follow a conservative stochastic partial differential equation (the Dean--Kawasaki equation) whose fluctuations drive the order flow. The distinct horizons of the desks further induce a persistent memory in the order flow that decays as a power law. Standard scaling arguments then lead to rough volatility. We confirm the key predictions of the model on simulated agents and on six months of Binance data with about 790 million orders. In liquid markets governed mainly by market makers, such as the perpetual futures of Binance, the order books are consistent with how our desks change the book.
label: arXiv:2611.24028v1

summary.background:
- Volatility: how much a price moves over time. "Rough" means the price path is more jagged than standard Brownian motion (the random walk model of particles).
- Order book: the list of buy and sell orders waiting at different prices; the mid price is halfway between best bid and best ask.
- Market maker: a participant, often algorithmic, that continuously posts buy and sell orders to provide liquidity.
- Gradient descent: a standard optimisation method that repeatedly moves a parameter a small step toward a better value; stochastic version uses noisy estimates.
- Power-law memory: influence of past events that fades slowly, like a heavy-tailed decay rather than an exponential one.
- Stochastic PDE: a differential equation with random forcing, here describing how order-book volume spreads and fluctuates over prices.
summary.one_liner: A model in which market makers adjust their order distances by stochastic gradient descent, with asynchronous information-driven noise, yields a Dean–Kawasaki-type conservative SPDE for order-book volume and, via power-law memory in order flow, rough volatility; checked on simulations and six months of Binance order data.
summary.plain: The paper asks whether the jagged, rough price moves seen in some markets can come from the way automated market makers place their orders. The authors model each market maker as a desk that repeatedly nudges its order distances from the mid price toward target distances it cannot observe directly, reacting only when new information arrives. They report that this setup produces the rough volatility seen in theory, and say the predictions match simulated agents and about 790 million Binance orders over six months.
summary.why: Rough volatility has been a productive idea in mathematical finance, but its microstructure origin was unclear; this paper proposes a concrete mechanism linking it to how market makers update orders. It may matter for modelling order books and market-maker behaviour, though the text alone does not show how general the result is beyond the liquid perpetual futures market studied.

title: Algorithmic Market Making Can Lead to Rough Volatility Through the Order Book

abstract: Existing AI agents can retrieve information, call tools, run experiments, and produce multi-step outputs. Yet most are built around relatively static workflows and struggle to preserve reliable state as the environment changes. Financial trading makes this limitation especially consequential: prices, news, market conditions, portfolio positions, and available capital evolve continuously. A result is useful only when it remains tied to the correct time, data snapshot, and execution context. We present Vibe-Trading, a comprehensive agent-native trading framework and all-in-one workspace for building, evaluating, and evolving agents for financial trading. It unifies market research, financial data, strategy generation, backtesting, portfolio analysis, paper trading, multi-agent collaboration, and optional broker execution. Its central contribution is an architecture that keeps results, evidence, research history, and trading authority connected throughout the research-to-action process. Each result retains its source, temporal scope, configuration, and producing run. Shared evidence grounding enables verification, versioned research records support reproducible continuation, and an explicit authority gate separates strategy research from live execution. Together, these designs provide a practical foundation for trading agents whose results can be traced, reproduced, and acted on only under explicit authority.
label: arXiv:2611.24845v1

summary.background:
- AI agent: a program that uses language models to plan steps, call tools, and produce outputs over several stages.
- Backtesting: running a trading strategy on historical prices to see how it would have performed.
- Paper trading: simulating trades with fake money on live market data, with no real orders.
- Broker execution: sending real buy and sell orders through a brokerage account.
- Provenance / reproducibility: recording where data and results came from so others can rerun and verify them.
- Authority gate: a control that decides which actions an agent is allowed to take, such as placing live trades.
summary.one_liner: Vibe-Trading is an all-in-one agent-native framework for financial trading that connects research results, evidence, run history, and an explicit authority gate between strategy research and live execution.
summary.plain: The paper describes a software workspace for building and testing AI agents that do financial trading work, such as researching markets, generating strategies, backtesting them on past data, and paper trading. Its main point is that each result is kept tied to where it came from, the time period it covers, its settings, and the run that produced it, so it can be checked and repeated later. It also separates testing a strategy from actually placing real trades, which only happens under explicit permission.
summary.why: Trading decisions depend heavily on timing and data, so a result that loses track of its context can be misleading; the paper targets this traceability problem for AI agents. The text is a system description and does not report measured performance, so its practical value is not established by what is given here.

title: Vibe-Trading: Towards Agent-Native Trading

abstract: High-altitude platform stations (HAPS) are expected to become an important component of sixth-generation (6G) and beyond wireless networks by providing wide-area wireless connectivity through massive multiple-input multiple-output (mMIMO) technology. As the communication performance of HAPS systems is fundamentally determined by the antenna array architecture, efficient antenna design has become a critical research topic. Motivated by these considerations, this article provides a comprehensive overview of antenna array design for mMIMO-enabled HAPS systems and proposes two novel antenna architectures to improve antenna-user alignment and communication performance. Specifically, the representative applications of mMIMO-enabled HAPS are first introduced, followed by the key design requirements for HAPS antenna arrays. Representative antenna architectures are then systematically reviewed and compared under a unified simulation framework based on the 3GPP NTN channel model. Finally, several promising research directions are discussed to provide insights into the design of next-generation intelligent HAPS antenna systems.
label: arXiv:2611.24064v1

summary.one_liner: A review of antenna array architectures for massive MIMO high-altitude platform stations (HAPS), comparing existing designs under a 3GPP non-terrestrial network channel model and proposing two new array architectures.
summary.plain: This paper looks at how to build the antennas for wireless base stations that fly in the stratosphere, roughly 20 km up, on balloons or aircraft. It surveys the main antenna layouts people have proposed and compares them in a common simulation setup. The authors also put forward two new antenna designs intended to point better at users on the ground and improve signal quality.
summary.why:
Flying base stations could extend mobile coverage to remote or underserved areas as part of future 6G networks, and the antenna is a key limit on how well they perform. The text does not report the size of the gains from the two proposed designs in the excerpt provided, so their practical value is not yet clear from this summary alone.</why>
<parameter name="background">- HAPS: aircraft or balloons that hover in the stratosphere and act as wireless towers in the sky.
- MIMO: using many antennas at once to send and receive several signal streams, improving speed and reliability; "massive" means very large numbers of antennas.
- Antenna array: a grid or line of small antennas whose combined signal can be steered toward a target.
- 6G: the next generation of cellular networks after 5G, still under development.
- 3GPP NTN channel model: a standard mathematical model, from the mobile industry's standards body, of how radio signals behave between satellites or platforms and phones.
- Antenna-user alignment: keeping the antenna's beam pointed at the right ground area as the platform moves.</background>
<parameter name="difficulty">intermediate

title: Toward Massive MIMO HAPS Networks: Antenna Architectures and Design

abstract: Emerging integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) systems reuse the communications signal for radar-like sensing to provide environmental awareness. However, this integrated design imposes conflicting constraints on the modulation format, as communications systems use higher-order modulation formats while sensing systems use unit-modulus signals, making constellation shaping a key performance driver in ISAC systems. This paper develops a unified analytical and experimental framework for constellation shaping in monostatic orthogonal frequency division multiplexing ISAC systems and systematically analyzes its interaction with the three canonical sensing channel estimators (SCEs): the matched filter, the reciprocal filter, and the Wiener filter (WF). We begin by deriving constellation-dependent image signal-to-interference-and-noise ratio (ISINR) expressions for the SCEs that account for practical effects such as windowing and multi target scenarios. Based on this, we derive the corresponding entropy-maximizing channel input distributions. We generalize an autoencoder framework to optimize geometric, probabilistic, including conventional and generalized low-complexity probabilistic amplitude shaping (PAS), and joint constellation shaping across all three SCEs. Extensive simulations and hardware-in-the-loop experiments validate the derived ISINR and show that sensing performance is governed by the SCE choice, while communications performance is dominated by the shaping method. Notably, the WF combined with joint shaping achieves the best ISAC trade-off. Low-complexity PAS variants closely approach this performance, offering a flexible trade-off and outperforming legacy modulation formats.
label: arXiv:2611.24271v1

summary.background:
- Integrated sensing and communications (ISAC): one radio signal used both to transmit data and to detect objects by their reflections, like radar.
- Monostatic: the transmitter and receiver sit in the same place, so the device listens to echoes of its own signal.
- OFDM: a modulation scheme that splits data across many narrow frequency subcarriers.
- Constellation shaping: choosing which signal points (symbols) are used and how often each is sent, to improve performance.
- Unit-modulus signal: a signal whose strength stays constant, which radar prefers.
- Sensing channel estimators (matched, reciprocal, Wiener filters): methods for estimating the echo response from the transmitted and received signals.
- Entropy and probabilistic amplitude shaping (PAS): measures of information content and a technique for sending some symbols more often than others.
- Autoencoder: a neural network trained to compress and reconstruct data, here used to search for good constellations.
- Hardware-in-the-loop: testing with real radio hardware connected to a simulated environment.
summary.one_liner: This paper analyzes how constellation shaping (choosing the set and probabilities of transmitted symbols) interacts with three sensing channel estimators in monostatic OFDM integrated sensing and communications, using analytical derivations, autoencoder-based optimization, simulations, and hardware-in-the-loop experiments.
summary.plain: Wireless systems are being designed to both send data and sense their surroundings using the same radio signal, but the best way to shape the transmitted signal for communication can conflict with what sensing needs. This paper studies how to shape that signal and how it interacts with different sensing methods, using both mathematical analysis and tests on hardware. The authors report that the sensing result mainly depends on which sensing estimator is used, while data performance mainly depends on the shaping method, with one combination (Wiener filter with joint shaping) giving the best overall trade-off.
summary.why: As radio devices such as future mobile networks and vehicles try to combine communication and radar-like sensing on one signal, the choice of modulation affects both jobs at once, so this trade-off matters for practical design. The text reports both simulations and hardware experiments, but the summary given here does not show the size of the gains, so the practical impact is best judged from the full paper.

title: Constellation Shaping for OFDM-ISAC Systems: A Systematic and Experimental Comparison

abstract: Accurate assessment of dysarthric speech is vital for clinical diagnosis and rehabilitation, yet existing automated methods rely heavily on isolated, single-task models or generic speech quality metrics that fail to disentangle heterogeneous neuromotor deficits. This work presents the first systematic investigation into adapting auditory large language models (ALLMs) for multi-dimensional dysarthric speech assessment under a unified, prompt-conditioned framework. Four representative ALLMs are benchmarked across five clinical perceptual dimensions from the Speech Accessibility Project (SAP): naturalness, monopitch, intelligibility, imprecise consonants, and inappropriate silences. To bridge generic perceptual quality and clinical evaluation, a two-stage training paradigm is explored, leveraging out-of-domain pre-training followed by in-domain clinical adaptation. Experimental results demonstrate that leading ALLMs reliably capture fine-grained pathological variations, exhibiting distinct and complementary strengths across prosodic and articulatory attributes. These findings establish ALLMs as a scalable foundation for clinical speech evaluation and provide practical insights into model selection and multi-task transfer potential.
label: arXiv:2611.23768v1

summary.background:
- Dysarthria: a speech disorder caused by weakness or poor coordination of the muscles used for speaking, often after neurological conditions.
- Perceptual assessment: expert listeners rating speech on traits like clarity and naturalness.
- Auditory large language model (ALLM): a large AI model that takes audio as input and responds in text, guided by written prompts.
- Speech Accessibility Project (SAP): a dataset effort collecting speech from people with speech differences.
- Two-stage training: first train on broad, related data (out-of-domain), then fine-tune on the target clinical data (in-domain).
- Multi-task transfer: whether learning one rating task helps with the others.
summary.one_liner: Benchmarks four auditory large language models (ALLMs) on five clinical perceptual dimensions of dysarthric speech from the Speech Accessibility Project, using a prompt-conditioned setup with two-stage (out-of-domain then in-domain) training.
summary.plain: This paper looks at whether AI models that can listen to audio and answer questions about it can judge the speech of people with dysarthria, a condition where muscle control makes speech hard to understand or unnaturally flat. The authors tested four such models on five things clinicians listen for, such as how natural the speech sounds, whether pitch is flat, how clear it is, whether consonants are imprecise, and whether there are inappropriate pauses. They report that the leading models pick up these fine-grained differences and that each model has different strengths across the prosody (rhythm and pitch) and articulation (sound formation) measures.
summary.why: Clinicians currently rely on slow, subjective listening, and most automated tools only score one thing or use generic quality measures, so a single model that rates several clinical traits could be useful for diagnosis and rehabilitation tracking. The text does not show clinical trials or validation against clinicians' outcomes, so its practical value is still unproven.

title: Beyond Intelligibility: Fine-Grained Perceptual Assessment of Dysarthric Speech with Auditory Large Language Models

abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) seeks to decode neural network computations into human-understandable logic. A core methodology in MI is circuit discovery: identifying the information flow in sub-networks that drive specific model behaviors. While circuit discovery has matured within Natural Language Processing (NLP), the interpretable circuits in music models remain largely unexplored. In this work, we identify a music-functional circuit within two symbolic music generative models: ChatMusician and MuPT. The music function we consider is the prediction of the terminal tonic root in a classical harmonic progression pattern $I \ldots V \rightarrow I$. We use the Auto-Emergence algorithm to extract a principal sparse sub-network as the identified circuit. Validation via causal intervention confirms that this identified circuit is a primary driver of harmonic progression behaviors in the symbolic music models. To our knowledge, this represents the first systematic circuit-discovery study conducted within the music domain. Our demo page is available at: https://ukiyo23rui.github.io/auto-emergence-demo/.
label: arXiv:2611.24453v1

summary.background:
- Mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering what the parts of a neural network compute.
- Circuit discovery: finding the subset of connections that carries out a specific behavior.
- Symbolic music: music represented as text-like tokens (notes, chords) rather than audio.
- Tonic/dominant: the home chord (I) and the chord a step away from it (V) that tends to lead back home.
- Causal intervention: altering or disabling parts of the model to test whether they really drive the behavior.
- Sparse sub-network: a small fraction of the model's components that the method selects.
summary.one_liner: The paper uses circuit discovery (extracting a sparse sub-network via the Auto-Emergence algorithm) to locate the part of two symbolic music generative models, ChatMusician and MuPT, that predicts the closing tonic in a I…V→I chord progression, and checks it with causal interventions.
summary.plain: Researchers studied two computer models that generate music written as symbols, and asked which internal parts of the model handle a basic music rule: after a chord moves from the home chord to the dominant and back, the model should land on the home chord again. They pulled out a small, sparse subset of the network that seems to carry this behavior, and reported that switching that subset off or changing it disrupts the harmonic pattern, according to the text's causal-intervention check.
summary.why: Most interpretability work on circuits has been done on language models, so applying it to music is a new direction, and the authors say it is the first systematic circuit-discovery study in music. Its wider relevance is uncertain from this text alone, since it covers two models and one chord pattern.

title: Harmonic Circuit: Chord Progression Lies in a Sparse Principal Information Flow in Symbolic Music Models

abstract: Safe control around dynamic obstacles requires information about both distance and relative motion. Range-based filters commonly reconstruct the required range rate from successive range measurements or from obstacle-state estimators, which can introduce estimator delay or sensitivity to range noise when obstacle motion changes. A frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar measures radial relative velocity directly through Doppler. We use this measurement as the derivative of an ego-centered range control barrier function (CBF) and obtain a closed-form filter on the robot's forward velocity. A measurement margin constructed from sensor error bounds accounts for errors in range, Doppler, ego velocity, and bearing. In 508 paired encounters within the platform's retreat capability, direct Doppler produces two buffer incursions, compared with 15 for a constant-acceleration and 25 for a constant-velocity Kalman filter. On a Unitree Go1, the controller stops at $0.777 \pm 0.015$ m against the predicted $0.758$ m and reacts to a farther approaching object while a nearer static return remains. The guarantee covers the longitudinal range channel under bounded measurement errors and continuously available detections. Direct Doppler removes the need to reconstruct range rate in the safety loop, reducing the delay between a change in obstacle motion and its effect on the safety command.
label: arXiv:2611.23654v1

summary.background:
- Control barrier function (CBF): a mathematical safety boundary; a controller is kept so that the distance to an obstacle never drops below a safe limit.
- Range rate: how fast the distance to an object is changing.
- FMCW radar: a radar that sends a continuously varying signal; it reports distance and, via the Doppler effect (the frequency shift of reflected waves from moving objects), radial speed.
- Kalman filter: a standard method that estimates hidden quantities such as speed from noisy measurements; the paper compares against constant-velocity and constant-acceleration versions.
- Buffer incursion: entering the safety margin around the robot.
- Ego-centered: measured relative to the robot itself.
- Unitree Go1: a small quadruped (four-legged) robot used in the experiment.
summary.one_liner: The paper uses an FMCW radar's direct Doppler velocity measurement as the time derivative of an ego-centered range control barrier function, yielding a closed-form forward-velocity safety filter with a sensor-error margin.
summary.plain: Robots that move near other objects need to know how far away each object is and how fast it is closing in. This paper tests a radar that measures closing speed directly, rather than estimating it from a series of distance readings, and uses that speed to limit how fast the robot can drive forward. In 508 paired encounters, the direct-speed approach caused 2 buffer incursions, versus 15 for one estimator and 25 for another; a small quadruped robot also stopped at about 0.78 m where 0.76 m was predicted.
summary.why: It addresses a concrete delay in safety control: range-rate estimates lag behind changes in obstacle motion, and a sensor that measures velocity directly may shorten that lag. Its scope is narrow (longitudinal range channel, bounded errors, continuously available detections), so its relevance to other settings is not established by the text.

title: Radar-Native Control Barrier Functions: Doppler Range Rate as a Measured Barrier Derivative

abstract: Separating hyperplanes are widely used in Control Barrier Function (CBF)-based collision avoidance, yet their orientations strongly govern control intervention-the deviation of the applied control from the robot's nominal command. Existing methods typically select hyperplane orientations from geometry alone. Jointly optimizing orientations and control yields a continuous, non-convex problem in which local nonlinear solvers suffer from initialization sensitivity, local minima, and unpredictable latency, while discretized orientation grids scale exponentially with obstacle count. For planar navigation of a polygonal robot among polygonal obstacles, we present a solver-free, control-aware separating hyperplane selection method that directly computes a global optimum of this joint problem at each step whenever it is feasible. Exploiting the geometry of Minkowski difference polygons, we reduce this continuous non-convex optimization to evaluating a polynomial-size set of candidate control interventions via closed-form algebraic checks, selecting the feasible candidate of minimum norm. Across 250 simulated navigation scenarios, our method reduces cumulative intervention cost by 3.6% at the median and 27.3% at the 90th percentile compared to a local nonlinear solver, and completion time by 0.6% and 5.6%, respectively. In scalability benchmarks, it achieves a 6.1x per-step speedup at 16 simultaneous obstacles.
label: arXiv:2611.23867v1

summary.background:
- Control barrier function (CBF): a safety condition that a controller must keep a robot inside a safe region, enforced by modifying its commands.
- Separating hyperplane: a straight line (or plane) that divides the robot's safe space from an obstacle; its angle affects how the safety rule acts.
- Control intervention: how much the applied command must differ from the robot's originally intended command to stay safe.
- Minkowski difference: a geometric shape formed by subtracting one shape from another, used to express when two shapes collide.
- Non-convex optimization: finding the best choice when the problem has many local best points, so local solvers can get stuck.
- Polynomial-size candidate set: the number of options checked grows at a manageable rate as obstacles are added, unlike grids that grow exponentially.
summary.one_liner: A solver-free method that picks control-aware separating hyperplane orientations for control barrier function collision avoidance by enumerating a polynomial set of candidate control interventions and choosing the feasible one of minimum norm, for planar polygonal robots among polygonal obstacles.
summary.plain: Robots that steer around obstacles often use a safety rule that depends on how a imaginary dividing line (a "separating hyperplane") is angled between the robot and each obstacle. This paper shows how to choose those angles so that the robot deviates as little as possible from where it wanted to go, without running a slow, possibly unreliable optimizer at each step. The authors report that, across 250 simulated navigation scenarios, the method lowered total control deviation cost by 3.6% at the median and 27.3% at the 90th percentile compared with a local nonlinear solver, and reported a 6.1x per-step speedup with 16 obstacles.
summary.why: Collision avoidance for autonomous robots and vehicles depends on how safety constraints are set up, and this work targets a specific trade-off between safety and deviation from the intended path. It may matter for real-time planning where solver latency is a concern, but the text only covers simulations of planar polygon scenarios, so transfer to real or 3D systems is unknown.

title: Control-Aware Separating Hyperplanes for Control Barrier Functions in Planar Navigation

abstract: Arm separation is an important technical tool in the study of critical and near-critical planar percolation systems. When combined with RSW estimates, it proves quasi-multiplicativity of arm-event probabilities, links the derivatives of different events and allows the identification of universal arm exponents. We provide a very generic statement of arm separation that applies to arbitrary planar percolation models. Our argument is based on exploring configurations conditioned on the existence of arms in such a way that "exposed" arms are revealed with positive probability. The exploration algorithm is independent of the percolation model and applies to all polychromatic arm events. As an application, we prove a strong arm-separation result for critical planar FK-percolation.
label: arXiv:2611.26458v1

summary.background:
- Percolation: random open/closed sites or edges on a grid; at the critical point, large connected clusters appear but only just.
- Arm events: the event that several disjoint open or closed paths reach from a point out to a distance, with a given color pattern.
- Quasi-multiplicativity: arm probabilities over different scales multiply up to constant factors, which lets one compare them across scales.
- RSW (Russo–Seymour–Welsh) estimates: bounds that stop open crossings from becoming too unlikely in a box, a basic input to such arguments.
- Universal arm exponents: scaling exponents that depend only on the arm pattern, not on the specific model.
- FK-percolation: a random cluster model linking percolation to the Potts model in physics.
summary.one_liner: A generic arm-separation statement for arbitrary planar percolation models, proved via a model-independent exploration algorithm, with a strong arm-separation result applied to critical planar FK-percolation.
summary.plain: This paper is about random patterns of connected and disconnected regions on a flat plane, the sort of thing that models how fluid seeps through a porous material. The authors prove a general rule saying that several separate paths ("arms") running out from a point can be kept apart from one another in a controlled way, and they show that the rule works for a broad class of such models. They then apply it to a specific model called critical FK-percolation, which is closely tied to statistical physics.
summary.why: Tools like arm separation are standard steps for deriving precise exponents that describe how likely such paths are at the critical point, so a result that holds for any planar model rather than one at a time is useful to researchers in this area. The text does not say how far the result extends beyond the cases it treats, so its wider reach is uncertain.

title: Generic arm separation for planar percolation models

abstract: We prove dynamical edge universality for three families of interacting particle systems for every $β>0$: $β$-Dyson Brownian motion with an analytic potential, weighted $β$-corners processes, and a class of discrete-time Markov chains. Our results apply to general non-equilibrium initial data and show that the Airy$_β$ line ensemble emerges at positive times whenever the limiting density has a regular square-root edge. More precisely, after centering at the moving deterministic edge and rescaling space and time on the $n^{-2/3}$ and $n^{-1/3}$ scales, respectively, the trajectories of the top $k$ particles converge jointly in distribution to the top $k$ curves of the Airy$_β$ line ensemble, for every fixed $k$, in the topology of uniform convergence on compact time intervals. The proof combines dynamical loop equations with characteristic-flow estimates to establish local laws near the moving edge and upper bounds on the extremal particle. We then identify the stochastic evolution of every subsequential limit of the rescaled Stieltjes transform and establish convergence through the pole-evolution characterization of the Airy$_β$ line ensemble.
label: arXiv:2611.25364v1

summary.background:
- Interacting particle system: many random particles whose motion depends on the others, here with a repulsion parameter β>0.
- Dyson Brownian motion: eigenvalues of a random matrix evolving in time, the standard model of repelling particles.
- Edge universality: the statement that local behavior at the extreme edge of a particle cloud does not depend on fine details of the model.
- Airy line ensemble: a family of random curves (for β=1,2,4 tied to classical random matrix ensembles) describing the edge after rescaling.
- Stieltjes transform: an analytic tool that encodes the particle density; loop equations are identities used to control it.
- Square-root edge: the density vanishes like the square root of distance at the boundary of the cloud.
- Uniform convergence on compact time intervals: the convergence holds uniformly over bounded time windows.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves that three families of interacting particle systems (β-Dyson Brownian motion with analytic potential, weighted β-corners processes, and a class of discrete-time Markov chains), for every β>0, have their top particles near the moving edge converge to the Airy_β line ensemble at positive times, starting from general non-equilibrium initial data.
