summary.plain: The paper studies systems of many randomly moving particles that repel each other, and asks what the leading particles at the edge look like over time. It shows that, for three broad families of such systems, once the particle density has a regular square-root shape at its edge, the top few particles, zoomed in on the right scale in space and time, follow a single universal family of random curves called the Airy_β line ensemble. The text indicates this holds regardless of how the system started.
summary.why: Universality results like this explain why very different random systems show the same edge behavior, and the Airy line ensembles are central objects in random matrix theory and probability. The text does not spell out wider applications, so any connection beyond this area is uncertain.

title: Dynamical edge universality and the Airy$_β$ line ensemble

abstract: In this paper we prove a theorem on the unique solvability of the Cauchy problem for a stochastic partial differential equation driven by the fractional Brownian motion with Hurst index $H>\frac{1}{4}$.
label: arXiv:2611.26580v1

summary.background:
- Partial differential equation: an equation relating a function of space and time to its rates of change.
- Stochastic (random) forcing: a term in the equation that is driven by randomness.
- Brownian motion: the random jittery path of a particle; fractional Brownian motion generalises it with a memory parameter.
- Hurst index H: a number in (0,1) controlling how rough the noise path is; larger H means smoother paths.
- Mild solution: a solution written through an integral formula involving the equation's semigroup (the operator that propagates the system forward in time), rather than requiring classical derivatives.
- Existence and uniqueness: showing a solution exists and that only one such solution exists.
- Cauchy problem: the equation together with an initial condition at time zero.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves existence and uniqueness of mild solutions to a stochastic partial differential equation driven by fractional Brownian motion with Hurst index H > 1/4.
summary.plain: The paper studies equations that describe how a quantity changes over space and time when it is also pushed around by random noise. The noise here is a special kind of random motion (fractional Brownian motion) whose smoothness is set by a number called the Hurst index. The authors show that, when that index is above 1/4, the Cauchy problem (an equation with a given starting state) has one well-defined solution in the mild sense.
summary.why: Noise with memory, like fractional Brownian motion, appears in models of physics, finance and networks, where ordinary random noise is too simple. The text itself is short and gives only the main statement, so its wider impact is not clear from it alone.

title: Existence and Uniqueness of Mild Solutions to Rough Stochastic Partial Differential Equations driven by Fractional Brownian Motion with Hurst Index $H > 1/4$

abstract: In this note, we improve the regularity of Hölder continuous stationary solutions with respect to inner variations which are harmonic outside their zero set. We obtain a $\sqrt{\log}$-Lipschitz estimate for a class of solutions allowing a generalized phase variable and including the two-phase problem. In the case of the one-phase problem, we can improve to Lipschitz regularity. In particular, we show that the initial Lipschitz assumption in the class of variational solutions considered by Kriventsov and Weiss can be replaced by any positive Hölder exponent
label: arXiv:2611.25345v1

summary.background:
- Partial differential equation (PDE): an equation relating a function to its rates of change in space.
- Free boundary problem: a problem where the region where the solution is nonzero (or the interface between regions) is itself unknown and must be solved for.
- Stationary solution: a configuration that does not change under small allowed deformations, as in an energy-minimizing state.
- Hölder continuity: a measure of smoothness weaker than differentiability; the exponent indicates how regular the function is.
- Lipschitz continuity: a stronger smoothness condition meaning the function's slope is bounded.
- Harmonic function: a function whose Laplacian is zero, the basic smooth "balanced" function in PDE theory.
- Two-phase vs one-phase problem: whether the setting has two competing states or one state against a background of zero.
summary.one_liner: The paper sharpens regularity results for Hölder continuous stationary solutions of free boundary problems that are harmonic off their zero set, obtaining sqrt(log)-Lipschitz estimates for a class with a generalized phase variable (including the two-phase problem) and full Lipschitz regularity in the one-phase case, which lets the initial Lipschitz assumption in Kriventsov–Weiss's variational class be weakened to any positive Hölder exponent.
summary.plain: This is a mathematical note about "free boundary problems," where a solution to an equation has to be found together with the unknown edge that separates two regions (for example, a boundary between two phases of a material). The author asks how smooth such solutions must be when they are stationary, meaning they are balanced against small deformations of the shape. The text reports that the smoothness can be improved: the solutions are shown to be Lipschitz, which means they cannot change too steeply, up to a mild logarithmic correction in the two-phase case, and fully Lipschitz in the one-phase case.
summary.why: Regularity results like these decide whether the boundary between regions is well behaved enough for further analysis, so they matter for the theory of such problems. The text itself only states the improvement over an earlier assumption from Kriventsov and Weiss; it does not claim wider applications, and I have not checked how it fits into the broader literature.

title: On the regularity of stationary solutions to free boundary problems

abstract: We consider Hörmander oscillatory integral operators on $\mathbb{R}^n$. In particular, we are interested in proving bounds with dependence on the signature of the phase. The sharp universal range of $L^p\to L^p$ estimates was obtained for any given signature by the second author and Iliopoulou. Under the mild non-compression hypotheses on the phase introduced in Chen et al., we prove $L^p\to L^p$ estimates that go beyond this universal range in odd dimensions. We also obtain the sharp universal range of $L^p\to L^q$ estimates for odd $n$. The techniques are based on the breakthrough work of Wang--Wu on the Fourier restriction conjecture.
label: arXiv:2611.26265v1

summary.background:
- Oscillatory integral operator: an integral whose kernel is a fast-oscillating exponential e^{i·phase}, used to measure how smoothing or spreading a function occurs.
- L^p bounds: statements that the operator keeps a function's size measured in the L^p norm within a constant factor, for a given exponent p.
- Signature of a phase: an integer-valued summary of the curvature of the phase function (how many directions curve positively versus negatively).
- Hörmander class: a standard family of phase functions with controlled smoothness and nondegeneracy assumptions.
- Fourier restriction conjecture: a central open problem asking how the Fourier transform of a function restricted to a curved surface behaves; Wang–Wu's recent work is a major advance on it.
- Universal range: the set of exponents p for which the estimate holds regardless of the particular phase, given its signature.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves L^p-to-L^p and sharp L^p-to-L^q bounds for Hörmander oscillatory integral operators on R^n, with constants that depend on the signature of the phase, under a non-compression hypothesis, in odd dimensions, using techniques from Wang–Wu's work on the Fourier restriction conjecture.
summary.plain: This paper studies a family of averaging operators that weight a function by a rapidly wiggling phase, a standard object in harmonic analysis. The authors ask how well these operators behave when the wiggling is described by a "signature," a count of how the phase curves in different directions. They show that, under a mild condition on the phase, some estimates can be pushed beyond the best previously known general range, but only in odd dimensions.
summary.why: Sharp bounds for oscillatory integrals feed into questions about Fourier restriction and related wave and dispersive equations, so improvements in this area matter to specialists. The text does not show wider applications, so beyond the specialist setting its reach is uncertain.

title: Oscillatory integral operators of arbitrary signature: beyond the universal estimates

abstract: Let $\mathscr{M}$ and $\mathscr{N}$ be non-trivial closed subspaces of a separable Hilbert space $\mathscr{H}$ such that $\mathscr{M}\cap\mathscr{N}=\{0\}$ and $\mathscr{M}+\mathscr{N}$ is dense in $\mathscr{H}$. We characterize when there exists an invertible operator on $\mathscr{H}$ which maps $\mathscr{M}$ onto $\mathscr{N}$ and $\mathscr{N}$ onto $\mathscr{M}$. We prove that such an operator exists if and only if $\mathscr{M}$ and $\mathscr{N}$ have a common algebraic complement. This happens if and only if either neither of the operators $(I-P)Q$ and $(I-Q)P$ is compact, or $P-Q$ is compact and $\dim(\mathscr{M}\cap\mathscr{N}^\perp)=\dim(\mathscr{M}^\perp\cap\mathscr{N})$, where $P$ and $Q$ are the orthogonal projections onto $\mathscr{M}$ and $\mathscr{N}$. Moreover, the operator can be chosen to be an involution. Consequently, the group of collineations of the diamond lattice $\{\{0\},\mathscr{M},\mathscr{N},\mathscr{H}\}$ which fix $\mathscr{M}$ and $\mathscr{N}$ is always complemented in the group of all its collineations.
label: arXiv:2611.25622v1

summary.background:
- Hilbert space: a complete space of vectors with inner products, generalizing ordinary geometry to infinite dimensions.
- Closed subspace: a linear slice of the space that is closed under limits.
- Orthogonal projection: the operator that drops a vector perpendicularly onto a subspace.
- Algebraic complement: a subspace that together with another subspace spans the whole space with no overlap, without requiring perpendicularity.
- Compact operator: a map that is "nearly finite-dimensional" in the sense that it turns bounded sets into nearly compact sets.
- Involution: an operator that equals its own inverse when applied twice.
- Lattice of subspaces and collineations: the diamond lattice is the four-element structure {0, M, N, whole space}; collineations are its structure-preserving maps.
summary.one_liner: Characterizes when two non-trivial closed subspaces M and N of a separable Hilbert space, with trivial intersection and dense sum, can be swapped by an invertible operator (which can be taken to be an involution), in terms of a common algebraic complement and compactness conditions on projections.
summary.plain: This paper is about pairs of "flat slices" (subspaces) inside an infinite-dimensional space of functions or vectors, and whether a single reversible transformation can swap them. The author gives a precise test for when such a swap exists. The test asks whether the two slices share a common way of being completed to the whole space, or equivalently checks certain compactness conditions on how the slices are projected.
summary.why: The result settles exactly when a symmetric swap of two subspaces is possible, and it shows the group of symmetries of this small lattice of subspaces is always complemented. It is a structural statement in operator theory; the text does not indicate applications beyond this area.

title: Collineations of the diamond lattice in a Hilbert space

abstract: In 1926, Nevanlinna (Acta Math. {\bf 48} (1926), no. 3-4, 367-391) proved that if two distinct and non-constant meromorphic functions $f$ and $g$ share $a_1,$ $a_2,$ $a_3,$ $a_4$ CM in the complex plane, where $a_1,$ $a_2,$ $a_3,$ $a_4$ are four distinct complex values in the extended complex plane, then $f$ is a Möbius transformation of $g$, two of the shared values, say $a_1$ and $a_2$, are Picard exceptional values, and the cross ratio $\left(a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4\right)=-1.$ Later on, Gundersen (Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. {\bf 277} (1983), no. 2, 545-567. Correction: {\bf 304} (1987), 847-850) proved that if two non-constant meromorphic functions share two values CM and share two other values IM, then the functions share all four values CM. In 1992, Gundersen (Complex Var. Elliptic Equ. {\bf 20} (1992), no. 1-4, 99-106) proposed the following famous question: if two non-constant meromorphic functions share three distinct values IM and share a fourth value CM, then do the functions necessarily share all four values CM? This question is a long-standing question in the studies of the Nevanlinna's value distribution theory of meromorphic functions, and has not been completely resolved by now. In this paper, we completely resolve the question, and prove that if two distinct and non-constant meromorphic functions $f$ and $g$ share $a_1,$ $a_2,$ $a_3$ IM and $\infty$ CM, where $a_1,$ $a_2,$ $a_3$ are three distinct and finite complex values in the complex plane, then $f$ and $g$ also share $a_1,$ $a_2,$ $a_3$ CM.
label: arXiv:2611.25948v1

summary.background:
- Meromorphic function: a function of a complex variable that is analytic except for isolated poles (points where it blows up).
- Sharing a value: f and g both take a given value a at the same points.
- CM (counting multiplicity) versus IM (ignoring multiplicity): CM also requires the same order of contact at those points.
- Infinity as a value: the point where a function has a pole, treated as a value in the extended complex plane.
- Nevanlinna theory: the study of how often meromorphic functions take given values, from 1926 onward.
- Gundersen's question (1992): whether sharing three values IM and a fourth CM forces sharing all four CM.
- Only the abstract-level statement is given here; the proof details are not in the text provided.
summary.one_liner: The paper settles Gundersen's long-standing question (1992) on meromorphic functions sharing three values IM and a fourth CM, by proving that when f and g share three finite values IM and infinity CM, they also share the three finite values CM.
summary.plain: The paper concerns pairs of functions defined on the complex numbers that take the same values at the same points. Two functions "share" a value if they hit it at the same places, either with multiplicity counted (CM) or ignoring multiplicity (IM). The author proves that a known open question, whether sharing three values loosely and a fourth value tightly forces tight sharing of all four, has a positive answer in the case described.
summary.why: This question had been open since 1992 and sits at the core of Nevanlinna's value distribution theory, a classical area of mathematics. The text itself does not discuss applications beyond this theory, so its wider significance is uncertain to me.

title: On the solution of a question for meromorphic functions sharing three values IM and a fourth value CM in the complex plane

abstract: We study the single matrix point interpolation problem for positive real matrix valued functions on the right half-plane, both in the single variable setting and in the noncommutative multivariable setting. In the single variable case, a careful analysis is done for when the solution may or must have a pole at infinity. In the multivariable setting, as the pole structure at infinity can be more complicated, we focus on the case when there is no pole at infinity. The results also yield numerical algorithms for finding a solution.
label: arXiv:2611.26240v1

summary.background:
- Complex analysis: functions of a complex variable, defined on the complex plane.
- Right half-plane: the set of complex numbers with positive real part.
- Positive real function: a function whose values have nonnegative real part on the half-plane; these model passive physical or electrical systems.
- Interpolation: finding a function that takes prescribed values at prescribed points.
- Matrix-valued function: outputs are grids of numbers rather than single numbers.
- Pole at infinity: a point where the function's size grows without bound as the input goes to infinity.
- Noncommutative multivariable setting: several inputs whose order of multiplication matters, as with matrices.
summary.one_liner: The paper studies matrix-point interpolation for positive real matrix-valued functions on the right half-plane, in both single-variable and noncommutative multivariable settings, with attention to when a pole at infinity can or must occur.
summary.plain: The paper looks at a problem of finding a smooth function with prescribed values at given points, where the function's outputs are grids of numbers (matrices) and the function must stay "positive" on a half of the complex plane. The authors analyse when the solution may or must blow up at infinity in the one-variable case. In the multivariable case, where the structure at infinity is more complicated, they restrict to solutions that do not blow up there.
summary.why: Problems of this kind arise in systems and control theory and in operator theory, where positive real functions describe passive systems. The text says the results also yield numerical algorithms for computing a solution, but it does not give details of those algorithms or their performance, so the practical reach is unclear from this text alone.

title: Matrix-point interpolation for positive real odd functions in one and several variables

abstract: We consider vector-valued magnetic Schrödinger operators $-Δ_{a} +V$ with magnetic potential ${a}\in C^2(\mathbb{R}^d;\mathbb{R}^d)$ and electric potential $V$ given by a symmetric and positive semidefinite $m\times m$ matrix-valued function whose entries belong to $L^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^d)$. Assuming that $\|\operatorname{curl} {a}(\cdot)\|\operatorname{Id}_{\mathbb{R}^m} + V$ belongs to a certain matrix reverse Hölder class, we characterize necessary and sufficient conditions under which the spectrum of $-Δ_{a} +V$ is discrete, and study the eigenvalue asymptotics and exponential decay of eigenfunctions.
label: arXiv:2611.26479v1

summary.one_liner:
The paper gives necessary and sufficient conditions for discrete spectrum, plus eigenvalue asymptotics and exponential eigenfunction decay, for matrix-valued magnetic Schrödinger operators whose electric potential is only assumed locally integrable and whose combined magnetic-curl and potential term satisfies a matrix reverse Hölder condition.</one_liner>
<parameter name="plain">The paper studies a standard model from quantum physics: a particle with several internal states that moves under a magnetic field and an electric potential. The question is when the allowed energy levels form a discrete list rather than a continuum, and how those levels and the associated wave functions behave. The text indicates the authors identify exact conditions for discreteness and study how the energy levels grow and how the wave functions decay at large distances.
summary.why:
Discreteness of the spectrum and the rate at which eigenvalues grow are basic questions for Schrödinger operators, and the setting (vector-valued, with only locally integrable potentials) is more general than the usual scalar, smooth case. The abstract does not say how the results compare with earlier work or what applications they have, so the wider significance is unclear from this text alone.</why>
<parameter name="background">- Schrödinger operator: the energy operator of quantum mechanics, here "kinetic energy" (the Laplacian) plus a potential.
- Magnetic potential a: a vector field describing a magnetic field; the curl of a measures the field's strength and direction.
- Matrix-valued (vector-valued) potential V: an m-by-m array of functions, so the particle has m internal states that can interact.
- Spectrum and eigenvalues: the set of allowed energy levels; "discrete" means they form an isolated list that can be counted.
- Eigenvalue asymptotics: how the counted energy levels grow as the level index increases.
- Locally integrable (L^1_loc): functions whose integral is finite on bounded regions, allowing fairly rough potentials.
- Reverse Hölder class: a technical regularity condition on how a function's averages behave across scales.
- Exponential decay: wave functions fall off rapidly, like exp(-c|x|), far from the origin.</background>
<parameter name="difficulty">research-level

title: Spectral asymptotics for vector-valued magnetic Schrödinger operators

abstract: We prove that every unital surjective complex-linear spectral isometry between complex unital semisimple Banach algebras is a Jordan isomorphism, thereby giving an affirmative answer to the spectrum-preserving form of Kaplansky's conjecture. We also characterize surjective complex-linear maps between arbitrary unital Banach algebras that preserve invertibility in either direction, satisfy either spectral inclusion, or preserve the spectral radius. In particular, for a complex-linear bijection between semisimple Banach algebras, preservation of invertibility in either direction implies preservation in both directions, and either spectral inclusion implies equality of spectra, even without assuming unitality. As an application, we study preservers of the Fredholm essential spectrum and essential spectral radius.
label: arXiv:2611.26462v1

summary.background:
- Banach algebra: a complete normed space of operators (or functions) that can be multiplied, such as bounded operators on a Hilbert space.
- Spectrum: the set of complex numbers λ for which (a − λ·1) is not invertible; it generalizes eigenvalues.
- Spectral radius: the largest absolute value in the spectrum; a measure of the "size" of an element's powers.
- Semisimple / unital: semisimple means no nonzero part is "invisible" to the spectrum; unital means the algebra has a multiplicative identity.
- Jordan isomorphism: a bijection that preserves the symmetrized product ab+ba and squares, a weaker form of multiplicative preservation than a full algebra isomorphism.
- Kaplansky's conjecture: a question on whether isometries between such algebras must be Jordan-type maps; the paper addresses a spectrum-preserving version.
- Fredholm essential spectrum: a refined spectrum that ignores finite-dimensional perturbations, used in operator theory.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves that unital surjective complex-linear spectral isometries between unital semisimple Banach algebras are Jordan isomorphisms (answering a spectrum-preserving form of Kaplansky's conjecture), and characterizes surjective linear maps preserving invertibility, spectral inclusion, or spectral radius, with an application to Fredholm essential spectra.
summary.plain: This paper studies structure-preserving maps between algebras of operator-like objects, where the key question is whether a map that keeps each object's "spectrum" (the set of numbers that describe when it can be inverted or fails to be invertible) intact must respect the algebra's multiplication. The authors show that, under the stated conditions, such maps are essentially the familiar kind that respect products in a symmetrized way (Jordan isomorphisms). They also find that for certain maps, preserving invertibility in one direction already forces preserving it in both directions.
summary.why: It settles, in the spectrum-preserving setting, a long-standing question associated with Kaplansky's conjecture about isometries of operator algebras, so it is of interest to specialists in the area. The abstract does not say how the results are used beyond the stated application to Fredholm essential spectra, so their wider impact is unclear from the text alone.

title: Spectral isometries and invertibility preservers on Banach algebras

abstract: Let $H$ be a quasi-triangular Hopf algebra of sqaure-free dimension over $\mathbb{C}$. In this note, we show that $H$ is semisimple and cocommutative. Equivalently, a braided finite tensor category $\mathcal{C}$ of square-free Frobenius--Perron dimension with a fiber functor is tensor equivalent to the representation category of a finite group.
label: arXiv:2611.25676v1

summary.background:
- Hopf algebra: an algebraic object that generalizes symmetry groups, with a way to multiply and to split elements.
- Quasi-triangular: carries an extra structure (an R-matrix) that gives a consistent way to swap tensor factors, which is the "braiding."
- Semisimple: decomposes cleanly into simple building blocks, with no tricky nilpotent parts.
- Cocommutative: the splitting operation does not depend on the order of factors, which is the signature of a group.
- Tensor category and fiber functor: a category of representations with a way to multiply objects; a fiber functor identifies it with vector spaces, which is what makes it a group's representations.
- Frobenius–Perron dimension: a generalized notion of size for such categories.
- Square-free: an integer not divisible by any square greater than 1 (e.g. 6, 30 but not 12).
summary.one_liner: The paper proves that a quasi-triangular Hopf algebra over the complex numbers whose dimension is square-free is semisimple and cocommutative, and hence that a corresponding braided finite tensor category with a fiber functor comes from a finite group.
summary.plain: This is a pure-mathematics note about a family of algebraic structures that describe symmetries, specifically those whose size (dimension) is not divisible by any perfect square other than 1. The author shows that, for these structures, a certain "braided" refinement collapses to the simplest case: the structure behaves like the symmetries of an ordinary finite group. The text itself is short and gives only the main statement, not the detailed argument.
summary.why: It strengthens the classification picture for finite tensor categories by showing that a extra braiding condition forces a square-free-dimensional case to be group-like. Its broader significance is unclear from the abstract alone, and I have not checked how it relates to other classification results.

title: On quasi-triangular Hopf algebras of square-free dimensions

abstract: We construct super analogues of the quantum groups of divided powers introduced by Lusztig. We call them super analogues because the Lie-theoretical data governing their structure is comparable to that of contragredient Lie superalgebras. Indeed, we show that they admit PBW-type bases parametrized by root systems of super type, and that they also have Lusztig isomorphisms giving a representation of the corresponding Weyl groupoids. Moreover, we prove that our super objects are equipped with a Frobenius-type morphism whose kernel is the Drinfeld double of a finite-dimensional Nichols algebra of super type, a super analogue of Lusztig's small quantum group, and whose cokernel is the enveloping algebra of the semisimple Lie algebra determined by the Cartan roots of the Nichols algebra. We carry out our construction within the framework of Nichols algebras of diagonal type, specifically, those whose braiding is obtained by specializing at a root of unity. This allows us to consider a divided power integral form inside a large quantum group of De Concini--Kac--Procesi type and then, via specialization, obtain our desired object.
label: arXiv:2611.26505v1

summary.background:
- Lie algebra: a mathematical structure describing continuous symmetries, such as rotations.
- Lie superalgebra: a generalization where some components are "odd" and anticommute, used in physics for supersymmetry.
- Quantum group: a deformed version of a symmetry structure, depending on a parameter q, often at a root of unity.
- Divided powers: a way of building integral forms (versions defined over the integers) of algebras, avoiding division.
- PBW basis: a Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt basis, an ordered set of building blocks spanning the algebra.
- Root system and Weyl groupoid: combinatorial data encoding symmetries of a Lie-type structure.
- Nichols algebra: a graded algebra arising from braided vector spaces, used to build quantum groups.
- Frobenius morphism: a map in characteristic-type settings whose kernel and cokernel are smaller, simpler pieces of the structure.
summary.one_liner: The paper constructs super analogues of Lusztig's quantum groups of divided powers, with PBW-type bases indexed by super-type root systems, Lusztig isomorphisms realizing the Weyl groupoid, and a Frobenius-type morphism relating a small quantum group (a Drinfeld double of a finite-dimensional Nichols algebra) and the enveloping algebra of a semisimple Lie algebra.
summary.plain: This is a piece of abstract algebra about "quantum" versions of symmetry structures, the kind that describe how systems can be transformed while keeping track of their internal rules. The authors build a new family of such structures that behaves like objects built from "super" symmetries, which mix ordinary and sign-flipping (odd) components. They show these objects have organized bases and symmetry-like maps, and they relate them to a smaller finite version and to a classical Lie algebra via a Frobenius-type map.
summary.why: The work extends Lusztig's divided-power quantum groups, a central framework in representation theory, to the super setting, where the usual Lie-algebra tools need modification. The connections it draws between finite-dimensional quantum objects and classical Lie algebras are the kind of link that matters in this area, but the text alone does not show how far these results reach beyond the authors' framework.

title: Super quantum groups of divided powers à la Lusztig

abstract: We determine the algebraic relations among full de Rham comparison periods of elliptic curves over finite extensions of $\mathbb Q_p$. The connected local monodromy group gives the transcendence degree and an explicit affine linear relation ideal for the full matrix in Fontaine's field $B_{\mathrm{dR}}$. After normalizing the holomorphic row and reducing to $\mathbb C_p$, the transcendence degree drops by one and the normalized determinant supplies the additional relation. Every polynomial relation of degree at most $d$ is detected modulo $t^{d+1}$. For $d\ge1$ this bound is sharp for each elliptic curve. A rational quasi-period row gives a Galois-stable Tate line. Together with an algebraic holomorphic period ratio it forces potential splitting, which identifies the exact ordinary CM obstruction. We compute the full Tate matrix. For ordinary non-CM curves with $p\ge5$, the standard quasi-period row is rational precisely at a zero of Katz's $E_{2,p}$. Away from the zeros the two full ratios are algebraically independent. At the zeros, a nonzero quasi-period and the normalized holomorphic ratio have algebraically independent images in $\mathbb C_p$. The complex question that motivates these results, the analogue for Drinfeld modules, and a conditional arithmetic consequence for Katz values complete the comparison.
label: arXiv:2611.25399v1

summary.background:
- Elliptic curve: a smooth cubic curve with a group law; its periods are integrals that encode its geometry.
- p-adic numbers (Q_p) and C_p: number systems built from a prime p, with a different notion of closeness than the real numbers; C_p is the completed algebraic closure of Q_p.
- Transcendence degree: the maximum number of algebraically independent quantities, i.e. how many values can be "free" with no polynomial relation among them.
- de Rham comparison periods: numbers relating two cohomology theories (algebraic de Rham and étale/Betti-type) for the same curve; they live in Fontaine's ring B_dR.
- Galois-stable line: a line of vectors fixed as a set by the symmetries of the field of definition.
- Ordinary and CM curves: "ordinary" is a condition on the reduction mod p; "CM" (complex multiplication) means the curve has extra symmetries.
- Katz's E_{2,p}: a p-adic modular form whose zeros are studied; the text uses its zeros as the special locus.
- Drinfeld modules: an analogue of elliptic curves over function fields.
summary.one_liner: The paper determines the algebraic relations among the full de Rham comparison periods of elliptic curves over finite extensions of Q_p, works out the transcendence degree and the Tate matrix, and analyzes ordinary non-CM curves at zeros of Katz's E_{2,p}.
summary.plain: The paper studies a family of numbers attached to elliptic curves (smooth cubic curves) when they are viewed through p-adic numbers, a different way of measuring size from the usual real one. It asks which polynomial equations these numbers must satisfy and which ones they can be free of. The text reports that the answers depend on the curve's structure, and it singles out special points, the zeros of a known function called Katz's E_{2,p}, where a rational quasi-period appears.
summary.why: The results give exact counts of independent quantities and sharp bounds on the degrees of relations, which is the kind of precise statement specialists look for in transcendence theory. The text also mentions an analogue for Drinfeld modules and a conditional arithmetic consequence for Katz values, but I have not checked how these connect to wider open problems, so the broader significance is unclear from the text alone.

title: Rational Elliptic Period Relations Across Realizations: Complex Lattices, Local p-adic Periods, and Drinfeld Modules

abstract: The modular properties of holomorphic Eisenstein series for $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ and its congruence subgroups do not carry over to their primitives. Instead, the transformation of iterated Eisenstein integrals under congruence subgroups of level $N$ introduces inhomogeneous terms comprising (among others) cyclotomic multiple zeta values of level $N$. We combine iterated Eisenstein integrals for the congruence subgroups of level $N=2$ of arbitrary iteration depth with their complex conjugates and (single-valued) level-2 cyclotomic multiple zeta values such that they define non-holomorphic modular forms. Our construction of these so-called equivariant iterated Eisenstein integrals for $Γ(2)$ and $Γ_0(2)$ proceeds at the level of generating series that take values in an infinite-dimensional (pro-unipotent) Lie group and closely follow Brown's analogous construction in the $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ case. The required insertions of cyclotomic multiple zeta values are controlled by zeta generators for level 2 that normalise the corresponding (pro-nilpotent) Lie algebra of the generating series and whose Lie-bracket relations we determine systematically. Upon restriction to Eisenstein series of modular weight~2, we recover single-valued multiple polylogarithms on the genus 0 modular curve $Γ(2)\backslash \mathbb{H}$.
label: arXiv:2611.26597v1

summary.background:
- Modular forms: functions on the upper half-plane that transform in a controlled way under a group of symmetries (here Γ(2) and Γ_0(2), subgroups of level 2).
- Eisenstein series: a standard family of modular forms; iterated Eisenstein integrals are repeated antiderivatives of them.
- Multiple zeta values: special real numbers defined by nested sums; cyclotomic versions involve roots of unity, and level 2 uses the simplest such case.
- Non-holomorphic: not complex-differentiable everywhere, involving complex conjugates.
- Single-valued polylogarithms: multi-valued functions adjusted so they have no ambiguity when going around loops.
- Lie algebra / Lie group: algebraic structures describing continuous symmetries; the paper works with generating series valued in such groups.
summary.one_liner: The paper constructs non-holomorphic "equivariant" iterated Eisenstein integrals for the level-2 congruence subgroups Γ(2) and Γ_0(2), built from level-2 cyclotomic multiple zeta values, and determines the Lie-bracket relations of the associated zeta generators.
summary.plain: The paper studies a family of special functions tied to symmetries of a geometric space (the upper half-plane, with rules for how its transformations act). Ordinary Eisenstein series behave well under these symmetries, but their antiderivatives do not, and the paper repairs this by adding correction terms built from certain special numbers and their complex conjugates. The construction is done for two specific symmetry groups of "level 2", and the result is checked by restricting to a particular weight, where it recovers known single-valued multiple polylogarithms.
summary.why: It extends Brown's known construction for the full modular group SL_2(Z) to smaller symmetry groups of level 2, which is a natural step in a long-running line of work on how modular forms and multiple zeta values fit together. The text does not claim wider applications, so its reach beyond this area is unclear from the abstract alone.

title: Equivariant iterated Eisenstein integrals for congruence subgroups of level 2

abstract: We study the specialization of Donaldson-Thomas virtual cycles for surface sheaves on a Calabi Yau threefold degenerating to a simple normal crossing threefold, composed of two quasi Fano threefolds glued along a common (double) divisor. The compactification of the two relative sheaf moduli spaces involves construction of suitable moduli space of sheaves on expanded degenerations of each quasi Fano variety. On a fixed expanded fiber the matching datum is an equivalence of the derived restrictions of the component sheaves. We identify the corresponding deformation complexes and give valuative and obstruction-theoretic hypotheses under which the specialized virtual class is a sum over marked joining divisors. When a marked space is the full fiber product of proper relative factors over a smooth simple boundary moduli space, its class is a refined diagonal pullback. For the case of sheaves supported on hyperplane sections of the threefold we discuss construction of the proper relative family by descending the chartwise stable loci, and identify both marked pieces, including the one with zero boundary. To provide some examples, we carry out explicit constructions for the moduli space of surface structure sheaf and its twists. We also prove valuative results for specified sheaves with noninvertible hulls. In a sequel, Part II, we use the construction of degeneration technique in this article to compare quintic invariants with the predicted S-duality modularity of "M5-brane modified elliptic genus" provided by string theorists, Gaiotto Strominger and Yin.
label: arXiv:2611.26207v1

summary.background:
- Calabi-Yau threefold: a special six-real-dimensional shape with trivial canonical class, central to string theory.
- Quintic: a Calabi-Yau threefold given by a degree-five polynomial in projective four-space.
- Sheaf: a systematic way of assigning algebraic data (like functions or bundles) to pieces of a space; a surface sheaf is supported on a surface inside the threefold.
- Moduli space: a space whose points parametrize a family of geometric objects.
- Donaldson-Thomas invariant / virtual cycle: a counting tool that produces a well-defined count even when the moduli space is singular or of unexpected dimension.
- Degeneration / simple normal crossing variety: a limit where a smooth space splits into pieces meeting along a common divisor.
- Quasi-Fano: a variety whose anticanonical class is positive in a weak sense, a standard class of building blocks.
- Derived restriction and deformation complex: homological-algebra tools that track obstructions to deforming objects.
- Elliptic genus and modularity: invariants from physics that should satisfy symmetry under transformations of a modular group.
summary.one_liner: The paper studies how Donaldson-Thomas virtual cycles for surface sheaves on a Calabi-Yau threefold behave under degeneration to a simple normal crossing threefold made of two quasi-Fano pieces, using expanded degenerations and virtual gluing, with examples on the quintic.
summary.plain: The paper looks at a standard geometric object, a Calabi-Yau threefold (a higher-dimensional analogue of a torus-shaped surface used in string theory), and asks what happens to counts of certain sheaves on it when the space is pinched apart into two pieces glued along a shared divisor. The authors build a compactified moduli space for the pieces, state conditions under which the counting class splits into a sum over marked joining divisors, and work out explicit examples such as the surface structure sheaf. The text says the results are partly conditional on valuative and obstruction-theoretic hypotheses.
summary.why: Degeneration formulas let hard invariants of a space be computed from simpler pieces, and the text says a sequel uses this to compare quintic invariants with a predicted modularity from string theory (Gaiotto, Strominger and Yin). Whether that comparison succeeds is not shown in this text, so its value to physics is only a stated aim here.

title: Surface sheaves on the quintic I. Expanded degenerations and virtual gluing

abstract: We prove uniform bounds for the Stein degrees of boundary divisors on generalised log Calabi-Yau fibrations of Fano type over arbitrary fields of characteristic zero. The main ingredient is the birational case for which we provide two approaches.
label: arXiv:2611.25501v1

summary.background:
- Algebraic geometry studies solution sets of polynomial equations, called varieties.
- A birational map is an invertible correspondence between two varieties that is defined on most of their points.
- A fibration is a map from one variety to another whose fibres (preimages of points) are the pieces of interest.
- Log Calabi-Yau and Fano type are technical classes of varieties with controlled curvature-like properties, used to describe when a variety is well-behaved.
- A boundary divisor is a special hypersurface removed or marked on the variety.
- The Stein degree is a specialised numerical invariant from the paper's setting; the abstract does not define it.
- Characteristic zero means the underlying number field behaves like the rational or real numbers, without the arithmetic quirks of prime characteristic.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves uniform bounds on the Stein degrees of boundary divisors on generalised log Calabi-Yau fibrations of Fano type over fields of characteristic zero, with the birational case as the main ingredient, approached in two ways.
summary.plain: This paper is about shapes defined by polynomial equations, specifically how certain boundary pieces of a family of such shapes can be controlled. The authors prove that a particular numerical measure of these pieces, called the Stein degree, is bounded by a quantity that does not depend on the particular shape, and they do this for fields of characteristic zero. The key step is a special "birational" case, for which they give two separate arguments.
summary.why: Uniform bounds of this kind tell specialists that a complicated family of geometric objects has a limit on how wild its boundary behaviour can get. The text does not say what wider applications this has, so its connections beyond algebraic geometry are unclear from the abstract alone.

title: Stein degree on birational log Calabi-Yau fibrations

abstract: We construct a homotopy coherent product structure extending the Chas-Sullivan product on chains of the free loop space of a manifold. Our construction uses the framework of Morse homology with DG coefficients and perturbed Morse gradient trees. We define an operad given by moduli spaces of Morse gradient trees with a twisted differential. This Morse tree operad receives a map from a suspended A$\infty$-operad and in turn acts on Morse homology with DG coefficients associated to a fibration over a manifold with a fibrewise monoidal structure.
label: arXiv:2611.25890v1

summary.background:
- Manifold: a space that locally looks like ordinary Euclidean space, such as a surface.
- Free loop space: the space of all closed loops in a manifold.
- Chains and homology: a way of assigning algebraic invariants to a space by counting cycles of shapes.
- Morse homology: computing topology by studying critical points of a smooth function and the gradient paths between them.
- Chas-Sullivan product: an existing multiplication on loop-space homology.
- A-infinity algebra: a multiplication that is associative only up to coherent higher corrections.
- Operad: a formal framework for collecting ways to combine inputs into outputs.
- Moduli space: a space parametrizing families of geometric objects, here trees of gradient flow lines.
summary.one_liner: The paper builds a homotopy-coherent (A-infinity) product on Morse homology with DG coefficients that extends the Chas-Sullivan product on chains of the free loop space of a manifold, using an operad of moduli spaces of perturbed Morse gradient trees.
summary.plain: The paper is about a way of multiplying certain shapes-of-loops measurements in a manifold (a smooth curved space) so that the multiplication stays consistent up to a controlled set of higher-order adjustments. The authors do this with a tool called Morse theory, which studies a space by following the paths of a smooth "height" function, and they extend an existing multiplication known as the Chas-Sullivan product. The text says they build an operad (a bookkeeping structure for how many inputs combine into one output) from moduli spaces of Morse gradient trees.
summary.why: The Chas-Sullivan product is a known structure linking the topology of a space to the topology of its loop space, so a fuller, more consistent version may matter to researchers in algebraic topology and string topology. The abstract does not describe applications beyond this, so the wider significance is unclear from the text alone.

title: An A $\infty$ -algebra structure for enriched Morse complexes

abstract: We prove that the set of invertible Koopman operators attached to the usual interval probability space is dense (and hence dense $G_δ$) in the space of bistochastic operators in the polynomial weak topology. This extends the non-polynomial analogue (due to Brown/Vershik/Ryzhikov/Eisner). We also show that the plain and polynomial weak topologies are distinct on bistochastic operators, confirming the distinction between the two results.
label: arXiv:2611.26151v1

summary.background:
- Bistochastic operator: a linear map that preserves total mass and maps non-negative functions to non-negative functions in both directions, a generalization of doubly stochastic matrices.
- Koopman operator: an operator built from a measure-preserving transformation that acts on functions by composing them with the map; invertibility means the underlying process can be run backwards.
- Topology (weak topology): a rule for when a sequence of operators counts as converging; "polynomial" refers to a variant that tests convergence against polynomial expressions.
- Dense: every member of the larger set can be approximated arbitrarily closely by members of the subset.
- Dense G-delta: a set that is a countable intersection of open sets and is dense; such sets are often regarded as "large" in Baire category sense.
- Non-polynomial analogue: the earlier result by Brown, Vershik, Ryzhikov and Eisner, which the abstract cites as the version under the ordinary weak topology.
summary.one_liner: The paper shows that invertible Koopman operators from the interval probability space are dense in the bistochastic operators under the polynomial weak topology, extending a known non-polynomial result, and that the plain and polynomial weak topologies differ on bistochastic operators.
summary.plain: The paper studies a family of mathematical objects called bistochastic operators, which generalize how randomness and mixing move mass around a space. It asks how "typical" the reversible ones (those coming from invertible changes of the underlying random process on the unit interval) are within the whole family, when closeness is measured in a particular way. The authors find that these reversible examples are dense, meaning they can approximate any member of the family arbitrarily well, under this measure of closeness.
summary.why: Density results like this tell us which kinds of dynamical behaviour are generic rather than rare in a large space of operators. The paper also separates two closely related notions of convergence, which clarifies how much the choice of topology matters; its broader connections are not spelled out in the text.

title: Power topologies and uniformities on bistochastic operators

abstract: This paper is devoted to study the convergence behavior of the most probable transition paths in a class of multiscale stochastic dynamical systems. First, based on Euler-Lagrange equations, we establish proximity and convergence results in the space of continuous functions endowed with the supremum norm. These results compare the most probable paths of the multiscale system with those of averaged system derived from the averaging principle. Next, we utilize a variational framework and analyze the Onsager-Machlup functionals using $Γ$-convergence. Together with the equi-coercivity of the functional family, we prove the convergence of both their minima and minimizers. Specifically, we show weak convergence of the minimizers in the Cameron-Martin space $H^1$, which implies their strong convergence in $L^2$.
label: arXiv:2611.26205v1

summary.background:
- Stochastic differential equations: dynamics driven by random noise.
- Multiscale systems: parts of the system evolve at very different speeds.
- Averaging principle: replacing fast fluctuations by their average effect to get a simpler slow equation.
- Most probable transition path: the route a noisy system is most likely to take between two states, found by minimizing an action or cost.
- Onsager-Machlup functional: the cost function whose minimizer gives that most likely path.
- Euler-Lagrange equations: the differential equations a minimizing path must satisfy.
- Γ-convergence and equi-coercivity: tools from calculus of variations for showing that minimizers of a family of functions converge to a limit minimizer.
- Cameron-Martin space H¹ and L² norms: function spaces describing smooth paths and average-square size of functions.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves that most probable transition paths of multiscale stochastic systems converge to those of an averaged system, using Euler-Lagrange equations in the sup-norm and Γ-convergence of Onsager-Machlup functionals with equi-coercivity, yielding convergence of minima and minimizers (weakly in the Cameron-Martin space H¹, hence strongly in L²).
summary.plain: Random systems that move on two speeds, a fast jittery one and a slow overall one, often have a most likely route between two states. This paper asks whether that route for the full system settles down to the route of a simpler averaged system as the speed gap grows. The authors show it does, using two approaches: one based on the equations that describe the most likely path, and one based on minimizing a cost function.
summary.why: Knowing when a complicated noisy system can be replaced by a simpler averaged model makes it easier to predict rare transitions, such as a chemical reaction or a climate tipping event. The text does not discuss specific applications, so any link to those is an inference rather than a claim of the paper.

title: Convergence of the Most Probable Transition Paths in Multiscale Systems

abstract: Data assimilation (DA) in partially observed nonlinear systems requires repeated estimation of both hidden states and their uncertainty. Conventional nonlinear filtering can be computationally expensive and often relies on an explicit dynamical model. In this paper, we develop the Neural Conditional Gaussian Model (Neural CGM), a data-driven dynamical model that maps unobserved physical states into a learned latent space, where the dynamics of the latent states follow a conditional Gaussian structure. This structure allows closed-form DA updates in the latent space, while nonlinear encoder-decoder mappings retain the flexibility needed to represent complex dynamics in physical space. A key feature of Neural CGM is its treatment of uncertainty in DA. The latent posterior mean and covariance are mapped to the physical variables through a Gaussian decoder that combines local moment propagation with learned nonlinear corrections. The resulting physical-space posterior statistics depend on the sequentially updated latent distribution rather than on a separate post-processing estimate. The same statistics enter a Gaussian negative log-likelihood during training, so both the posterior mean and uncertainty affect the learned model. Because Neural CGM learns the dynamical model itself, it can also be used for state forecasting and simulation without explicit knowledge of the governing equations. Numerical experiments on benchmark nonlinear dynamical systems show accurate state estimation and forecasting while substantially reducing online assimilation cost relative to conventional nonlinear DA methods. Neural CGM is therefore suited to repeated state estimation, uncertainty quantification, and prediction from partial observations.
label: arXiv:2611.26463v1

summary.background:
- Data assimilation: combining a model's prediction with incoming noisy observations to update the best estimate of a system's current state.
- Hidden (latent) state: quantities that drive a system but are not directly measured.
- Nonlinear filtering: estimation methods for systems where the relationships are not straight-line; these can be expensive to run repeatedly.
- Conditional Gaussian structure: a model in which, given some variables, the remaining ones follow a bell-shaped (Gaussian) distribution, so updates can be computed exactly with formulas.
- Encoder-decoder: a neural network that compresses data into a simpler internal representation and then reconstructs it in the original form.
- Uncertainty quantification: stating not just an estimate but how confident or spread-out it is.
- Negative log-likelihood: a training score that rewards predictions that are both accurate and appropriately confident.
summary.one_liner:
The paper proposes Neural CGM, a learned latent-space dynamical model whose latent dynamics follow a conditional Gaussian structure, enabling closed-form sequential data assimilation with uncertainty propagated to physical-space posterior statistics via a Gaussian decoder trained with a Gaussian negative log-likelihood.</one_liner>
<parameter name="plain">The paper addresses how to keep track of a system's hidden state and how uncertain that estimate is, when we only see partial, noisy measurements of a nonlinear system. The authors build a neural network that maps the hidden physical state into a simpler latent space where the update step can be computed in closed form, then map back to physical variables with uncertainty included. According to the text, this gives accurate estimates and forecasts on benchmark systems while cutting the online cost of assimilation compared with conventional nonlinear methods.
summary.why: Data assimilation is used in weather forecasting and similar fields, where repeated state updates are costly, so a cheaper method with explicit uncertainty could be useful there. The text reports only benchmark experiments, so how well it transfers to real, large-scale systems is not established here.

title: Neural Conditional Gaussian Model: Efficient Data Assimilation with Sequential Uncertainty Quantification for Nonlinear Dynamics

abstract: A fundamental result in Ramsey theory due to Alon, Frankl and Lovász gives an exact formula for the $q$-colour Ramsey numbers of matchings in $r$-uniform hypergraphs: if $n\ge\mathsf{AFL}_r(\mathbf{t})=(r-1)\|\mathbf{t}\|_\infty+1+\sum_{j=1}^q(t_j-1)$ then in any $q$-edge-colouring of $K^r_n$ there is some colour $j$ with a matching of size $t_j$. We show that a very weak quasirandomness assumption suffices for this Ramsey property: we can replace $K^r_n$ by any $r$-graph $H$ on at least $\mathsf{AFL}_r(\mathbf{t})+o(n)$ vertices that is a sublinear connector, meaning that it has no balanced $r$-partite holes of linear size. This generalises the result for $r=2$ (ordinary graphs) that we proved previously using a compression algorithm based on Gallai-Edmonds decompositions. This structure theory is unavailable in the hypergraph setting, so we combine two other proof methods, namely (a) simultaneous optimisation in all colours by clustering vertices using fractional cover weights from LP duality, and (b) local-to-global structure via random sampling and Kahn's matching theorem.
label: arXiv:2611.25893v1

summary.background:
- Ramsey theory: guarantees that sufficiently large structures contain a monochromatic pattern under any colouring.
- Hypergraph: like a graph, but each link (edge) can join any number r of vertices; r-uniform means every link has exactly r vertices.
- Matching: a set of links with no shared vertices; size t means t disjoint links.
- Q-colour Ramsey number: the threshold size needed so that any q-colouring forces a monochromatic object.
- Sublinear connector: a hypergraph with no large, balanced r-partite "hole" (a big missing block of links) at linear scale.
- LP duality and fractional cover weights: a linear-programming tool that assigns weights to vertices to bound matchings.
- Kahn's matching theorem: a probabilistic result about when random hypergraphs contain near-perfect matchings.
- The authors previously proved the graph case (r=2) using Gallai–Edmonds structure theory, which does not generalise to hypergraphs.
summary.one_liner: The paper extends the Alon–Frankl–Lovász exact formula for multicolour Ramsey numbers of matchings in r-uniform hypergraphs from complete hypergraphs to any sublinear connector on at least AFL_r(t)+o(n) vertices, using clustering via LP-duality cover weights and a random-sampling argument built on Kahn's matching theorem.
summary.plain: Ramsey theory asks how large a structure must be before any colouring of its connections is forced to contain a monochromatic pattern. This paper studies the case where you colour the connections of a hypergraph (a network where links can join more than two items) and ask for a large set of disjoint links all in one colour. The authors show that the known exact size threshold still works when the network is only required to be fairly well mixed, with no large lopsided gaps, rather than complete.
summary.why: It sharpens a classical exact result by showing it holds under a much weaker structural condition, which indicates the threshold is robust rather than an artefact of complete networks. The text does not state wider applications, so the connection to other areas is not established here.

title: A very robust Ramsey theorem for hypergraph matchings

abstract: For every strength, we prove the existence of rational designs on spheres, orthogonal and unitary groups, real and complex Grassmannians, and ellipsoids that are defined by positive-definite quadratic forms with rational coefficients and have a rational point. This answers Bannai's Problem for these spaces, solves the problem of Cui--Xia--Xiang on rational spherical $4$-designs on the unit circle, and proves Xiang's conjecture in the stronger form of existence in every dimension. To this end, we introduce the $(G,\mathcal{S})$-Prouhet--Tarry--Escott problem for an abelian group $G$ and a finite set of characters $\mathcal{S}$ and develop its existence and minimality theory. We also prove a general theorem transforming integer-weighted rational designs into equi-weighted designs on distinct rational points. On the unit circle $\mathbb{S}^1$, we determine the minimum sizes of rational spherical designs of strengths $4,5,6,7$ and show that they are respectively $2304,4608,9216,9216$. We also show that the minimum size of a rational spherical $5$-design on $\mathbb{S}^2$ is $192$. We further apply our framework to prove a conjecture of Thuswaldner--Ziegler on sums of distinct units and to answer Mahabaduge's problem on convex equilateral lattice polygons affirmatively.
label: arXiv:2611.25516v1

summary.one_liner: The paper proves existence of rational designs (weighted point sets with rational coordinates that average polynomials exactly, in the sense of spherical designs) on spheres, classical groups, Grassmannians and ellipsoids, introduces a group-character generalization of the Prouhet–Tarry–Escott problem, and determines minimum sizes of rational spherical designs on the circle and a 5-design on the 2-sphere.
summary.plain:
The paper asks whether certain evenly-spread sets of points on curved shapes, such as circles, spheres and ellipsoids, can be chosen with rational (fraction-valued) coordinates while still averaging test functions exactly. The authors show such sets exist for a broad range of these shapes and every strength they consider. They also pin down the smallest possible number of points for some small cases, for example 2304 points for strength 4 on the circle and 192 points for strength 5 on the 2-sphere.</plain>
<parameter name="why>Rational versions of these designs are a natural number-theoretic counterpart to classical design theory, and the paper claims to resolve several open questions (Bannai's problem, a problem of Cui–Xia–Xiang, Xiang's conjecture, Thuswaldner–Ziegler, Mahabaduge). The text does not say how these results are used outside pure mathematics, so their wider significance is unclear from this text alone.</plain>
<parameter name="background">- Spherical t-design: a finite point set on a sphere whose average of every polynomial of degree at most t equals its average over the whole sphere; "strength" means t.
- Rational design: a design whose points (and weights) have rational coordinates.
- Prouhet–Tarry–Escott problem: find two different multisets of integers with equal sums of powers up to some degree; a classical problem in number theory.
- Characters of an abelian group: basic symmetry-measuring functions; the paper's generalized problem is phrased with a finite set of them.
- Grassmannian: the space of k-dimensional subspaces of n-dimensional space; orthogonal and unitary groups are the symmetry groups of real and complex inner-product spaces.
- Positive-definite quadratic form: a formula defining an ellipsoid-type shape whose values are positive except at the origin.</background>
<parameter name="difficulty">research-level

title: Rational Designs and Prouhet--Tarry--Escott Problems

abstract: Adding constraints obtained by integrating governing equations to the loss has been reported to improve the accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in several applications, but mathematical understanding of these benefits remains limited. For several partial differential equations (PDEs), we derive stability estimates for losses with and without integral constraints. The comparison reveals that in certain parameter regimes, the standard loss has very weak control over specific error components, and that the integral constraints restore uniform control of these components. This explains when and why the constraints improve accuracy. Finally, numerical experiments support this interpretation. In parameter regimes where the standard loss is predicted to have weak control over those components, the two losses indeed show clear differences in accuracy. Conversely, in regimes where the standard loss retains sufficient control, both losses yield similar accuracy.
label: arXiv:2611.25515v1

summary.background:
- PDE (partial differential equation): an equation relating a function to its rates of change in several variables, used to model physical processes like heat or flow.
- PINN (physics-informed neural network): a neural network trained with a loss function that penalizes violations of the governing equation.
- Loss function: a score measuring how wrong the network is; training pushes it down.
- Integral constraint: an extra condition obtained by integrating (summing over space or time) the governing equation, added to the loss.
- Stability estimate: a mathematical bound showing that small errors in the loss cannot produce arbitrarily large errors in the solution.
- Error components: separate parts of the total error; the paper argues the standard loss controls some of these weakly.
summary.one_liner: The paper derives stability estimates for physics-informed neural network (PINN) losses with and without integral constraints for several PDEs, showing when integral constraints restore uniform control over certain error components, and checks this with numerical experiments.
summary.plain: Neural networks can be trained to approximate solutions of physics equations, such as heat or fluid flow equations, by penalizing them when they break those equations. Some researchers have found that also adding rules obtained by summing the equation over a region improves accuracy, but the reason was not well understood. This paper works out mathematically when that extra rule helps and shows that experiments agree with the explanation.
summary.why: It gives a theoretical reason for a practical training trick that has been reported to help in several applications, so users can predict when it is worth the effort. The text does not say how broadly the results extend beyond the PDEs studied, so that wider reach is uncertain.

title: When and why can integral constraints improve the accuracy of physics-informed neural networks?

abstract: We develop fixed-step variational integrators for time-dependent Lagrangian systems on Lie groups, derive their reduced dynamics, and analyze their long-time behavior by backward error analysis. We derive the continuous Euler-Lagrange equations, energy balance, and Noether conservation laws, and construct time-indexed discrete Lagrangians using retractions, with the midpoint-Cayley scheme treated explicitly. On their regularity domains, the resulting phase-space maps are symplectic. For left-invariant discrete Lagrangians, they reduce to Lie-Poisson maps that preserve coadjoint orbits and, when $G$ is connected, every Casimir function. A variational error analysis establishes second-order accuracy of the midpoint-Cayley method. We also construct an exactly symplectic, projectable extension on $T^*(\mathbb R\times G)$ whose formal modified Hamiltonian is affine in the momentum conjugate to time and admits symmetry reduction. Under uniform analyticity, coefficient bounds, and domain-containment assumptions, optimal truncation yields exponentially accurate interpolation and near-conservation of the modified extended Hamiltonian over exponentially long intervals. For a connected attitude network on $SO(3)^N$ with damping and uniformly positive, non-increasing coupling weights, we prove local asymptotic stability of the static consensus set for the continuous dynamics and exact preservation of total spatial momentum by the discrete scheme. Numerical experiments on the network and on a time-dependent rigid body on $SO(3)$ illustrate second-order convergence and the extended energy balance.
label: arXiv:2611.25313v1

summary.background:
- Lagrangian mechanics: motion is derived from an action (integral of kinetic minus potential energy) whose stationary paths give the equations of motion.
- Lie group: a smooth space with a compatible group multiplication, such as rotations SO(3); a Lie group is used to describe orientations.
- Variational integrator: a discrete-time scheme obtained by applying the action principle to a discretized action, which tends to inherit conservation laws.
- Symplectic map and Hamiltonian/momentum: geometric structure of phase space that conserved quantities (energy, momentum) respect.
- Noether's theorem: each continuous symmetry gives a conserved quantity.
- Backward error analysis: interprets a numerical scheme as the exact flow of a nearby "modified" system, explaining long-time accuracy.
- Consensus/synchronization: coupled agents reaching a common state; "local asymptotic stability" means nearby states converge back to that state.
summary.one_liner: The paper builds fixed-step variational integrators for time-dependent Lagrangian systems on Lie groups, analyzes their reduced dynamics, backward error, and long-time behavior, and proves stability and momentum-preservation results for an attitude consensus network on SO(3)^N.
summary.plain: The paper studies how to simulate on a computer the motion of rotating or orientation-like systems whose governing rules change over time, such as a spinning body or a group of coupled orientations. The authors design step-by-step numerical schemes built from a "discrete action" principle, which is meant to keep the simulation faithful to the underlying physics. They report that the schemes preserve key geometric structures, that the midpoint-Cayley version is second-order accurate, and that an extended energy quantity is nearly conserved over exponentially long times under stated assumptions.
summary.why: Structure-preserving integrators matter when simulations must run for long times without drifting away from physical laws, and the paper links this to attitude synchronization among coupled rotating bodies. The text does not show how widely these methods would be adopted, so their practical reach beyond the stated examples is uncertain.

title: Variational integrators for time-dependent Lagrangian systems on Lie groups

abstract: This contribution focuses on bisimulation invariance as the hallmark of modal model theory and of modal modelling. It exemplifies traditional as well as more recent ramifications \&\ extensions of classical results -- involving variant modes of bisimulation equivalence and matching modalities also beyond plain Kripke structures, and emphasising especially the technical challenges in finite model theory and other non-elementary settings. Main results to be discussed revolve about the theme of expressive completeness phenomena: beside expressive completeness under bisimulation invariance in relation to first-order background logics, in the style of van Benthem--Rosen characterisations, this also concerns maximality results under criteria form abstract model theory, in the style of Lindstroem theorems.
label: arXiv:2611.26244v1

summary.background:
- Modal logic: a logic with "necessarily" and "possibly" operators, read over graphs of states and transitions (Kripke structures).
- Bisimulation: a back-and-forth matching between two state graphs such that matched states agree on their local facts and can mirror each other's moves; the two are then indistinguishable in the logic.
- Bisimulation invariance: a property of a formula or query whose truth is unchanged by such matchings.
- Expressive completeness: the claim that a logic can define every property of a given kind that has the relevant invariance.
- van Benthem–Rosen characterisation: the theorem that, on finite structures, modal logic is exactly the bisimulation-invariant fragment of first-order logic.
- Lindström theorem: a result saying a logic is maximal among logics satisfying certain abstract criteria.
- Finite model theory: the study of logic restricted to finite structures, where many standard tools fail.
summary.one_liner: A survey-style overview of bisimulation invariance in modal logic, covering variant bisimulation notions, matching modalities beyond Kripke structures, and expressive completeness results in the style of van Benthem–Rosen and Lindström theorems.
summary.plain: This is a survey-style paper about when a formal language for describing systems (modal logic) can only tell apart situations that are "the same" under a particular kind of matching between them, called bisimulation. It reviews classical results and newer extensions, including variants of that matching and settings where the usual tools of finite model theory are hard to apply. The main theme is expressive completeness: showing that a logic captures exactly the properties that respect this matching, and that it is maximal in a suitable sense.
summary.why: The text is an abstract-level description, so the specific results are not shown here. It may matter to researchers in logic and computer science who use modal logic to model systems, since expressiveness limits tell you what a language can and cannot say about them.

title: Invariance and Expressiveness: Modal Variations

abstract: In this paper, we will argue that the notion of computational trust can be understood as a form of fallible intuitionistic knowledge grounded in verification. This approach naturally captures a key aspect of trust: it involves vulnerability. Specifically, it validates the principle that verification leads to trust but does not validate the opposite principle that trust leads to verification. Thus, we can trust on good grounds that some program will perform according to its specification but the program might still fail. We present a simple logic for capturing this notion of computational trust based on constructive modal propositional logic extended with a trust modality, which will be specified in an inferential fashion and by utilizing the proofs-as-programs correspondence.
label: arXiv:2611.25799v1

summary.background:
- Intuitionistic logic: a version of logic in which a claim counts as known only when you have a constructive proof of it, not merely because its denial leads to contradiction.
- Modal logic: an extension of ordinary logic with operators such as "it is necessary that" or, here, "one trusts that."
- Proofs-as-programs correspondence: the idea that a formal proof can be read as a program, and a program as a proof of its specification.
- Verification: checking, by formal reasoning or testing, that a program meets its specification.
- Fallible knowledge: knowledge that can turn out to be false, unlike infallible knowledge.
summary.one_liner: The paper argues that computational trust can be modeled as fallible intuitionistic knowledge grounded in verification, and gives a simple constructive modal logic with a trust modality, specified inferentially via proofs-as-programs.
summary.plain: The paper asks what it means to trust a computer program. Its answer is that trust can be treated as a kind of knowledge that rests on having verified the program, but that is open to being wrong. The authors build a small formal logic to capture this idea.
summary.why: The logic is designed so that verification leads to trust, but trust does not automatically lead to verification, which matches the everyday idea that one can rely on a program on good grounds and still be let down. The abstract does not say how this connects to practical software assurance or other applications, so that link is unclear from the text.

title: Computational trust as intuitionistic knowledge

abstract: The one-loop dilatation operator of a superconformal planar gauge theory can be written as a sum of local generators. The algebra these generators satisfy is a powerful organising principle for the spectrum. For SU(2)-like bosonic subsectors we show that this algebra can be read off directly from Feynman diagrams, which we identify as a natural graphical language for it. For N=4 super Yang-Mills this simply reproduces the Temperley-Lieb (TL) algebra of the XXX spin chain. After orbifolding and marginally deforming to N=2 superconformal quiver theories, the same recipe yields dynamical generalisations of the TL algebra. In these theories, the faces of the diagrams are coloured according to the quiver nodes, and separated by domain walls corresponding to bifundamental fields. There are two inequivalent SU(2)-like subsectors, which lead to two different TL algebras. One sector is built from the two bifundamental scalars and (in the simplest case) gives a dynamical TL algebra with a colour-dependent loop fugacity in its quadratic relation. The other sector is built from one bifundamental and one adjoint scalar, and (always) gives a novel algebra, in which the cubic TL relation becomes dynamical. In this latter case, we show that each generator of this new algebra is related to a standard XXZ TL generator by a colour-dependent twist. This twist is local and not an algebra homomorphism, and can be written as a dynamical Drinfeld twist. In both sectors, the TL structure provides a natural graphical approach to the spectral problem, as well as clarifying the structure of the irreducible representations of these chains. Finally, we give a preliminary description of the loop models associated to these algebras.
label: arXiv:2611.26285v1

summary.background:
- Gauge theory: a physical theory of forces in which particles are described by fields that transform under a symmetry group (here SU(2)).
- Superconformal / N=4 and N=2 theories: highly symmetric supersymmetric theories; N=4 SYM is the most symmetric case.
- Quiver theory: a theory whose gauge groups are arranged as nodes of a graph, with "bifundamental" fields as links between nodes; orbifolding is a way of building such theories from simpler ones.
- Dilatation operator: the operator that generates how quantum corrections change the scaling of operators; at one loop it acts locally on neighbouring fields, like a spin chain Hamiltonian.
- Temperley-Lieb algebra: an algebra with generators satisfying a quadratic and cubic relation, with a loop fugacity parameter; it underlies the XXZ spin chain and loop models.
- Dynamical algebra, Drinfeld twist: relations whose constants depend on a label (here the quiver node colour), and a change of basis used to relate algebras.
- Spin chain: a row of quantum spins with nearest-neighbour interactions, a model for the spectrum of the gauge theory.
summary.one_liner: The paper derives the algebra of the one-loop dilatation operator of SU(2)-like bosonic sectors directly from Feynman diagrams, recovering the Temperley-Lieb algebra for N=4 SYM and obtaining dynamical (colour-dependent) Temperley-Lieb generalisations for orbifolded N=2 quiver gauge theories.
summary.plain: The paper studies a family of quantum field theories whose particles interact in a structured way, described by a "quiver" diagram of interacting groups. The authors show that a set of algebraic rules governing how the interaction acts on particle states can be read straight from Feynman diagrams, a standard pictorial bookkeeping for particle interactions. Applied to two kinds of quiver theories, this gives two new families of algebras, one of which has a twist that links it to a known algebra.
summary.why: Temperley-Lieb algebras appear in statistical mechanics, knot theory and spin chains, so a graphical, diagram-based route to their colour-dependent generalisations may help in finding the spectrum and the associated loop models. The text does not show how far these structures extend beyond the cases treated, so the wider significance is uncertain.

title: Dynamical Temperley-Lieb algebras from Quiver CFTs

abstract: In a Hilbert space, we consider the Cauchy problem for an evolutionary equation with the operator $A+B(t)$, where $A$ is a self-adjoint positive definite operator and $B(t)$ is a bounded operator depending on time. By means of the perturbation algorithm, the purely implicit four-layer semi-discrete scheme of the third order of approximation (the three-step backward differentiation formula) is reduced to three two-layer schemes, whose solutions are used to construct an approximate solution of the original problem.
