The authors report that their system won first place in the competition, runs in under 10 milliseconds per prediction on average, and matches the ordinary (unprotected) model's output to within 0.02%.
summary.why: Private AI predictions that are fast enough to use in practice could let companies share or screen sensitive compounds without exposing them. The text reports a competition result and speed figures, but it does not show how the approach would perform outside this benchmark setup.

title: GPU-Accelerated Secure Inference for Drug--Target Interaction Prediction

abstract: We revisit running-time lower bounds historically based on the Exponential Time Hypothesis. Our case study asks how much of their quantitative content can be recovered under the assumption FPT $\neq$ W[1]. The reductions encode the choice of a clique in few bits and control the target parameter in terms of that encoding. This makes a sufficiently fast algorithm for the target problem yield a fixed-parameter algorithm for deciding whether a graph has a clique of the requested size. We obtain twelve lower bounds for deterministic algorithms across graph, string, and integer feasibility problems, including bounds that hold under structural restrictions. In several cases the same function of the parameter appears in the exponent as in the historical bound, with the additional requirement that the cutoff for any prescribed saving in the exponent be computable.
label: arXiv:2611.26080v1

summary.background:
- Running-time lower bound: a proof that no algorithm for a problem can run faster than a given function of input size, under some assumption.
- Clique: a set of nodes in a network where every pair is directly connected; deciding whether a clique of a given size exists is a classic hard problem.
- Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH): a belief that certain problems cannot be solved in subexponential time (time growing slower than any exponential).
- Parameterized complexity: studies problems where one input quantity (the parameter) is kept small; FPT (fixed-parameter tractable) means solvable in time f(parameter) times a polynomial in input size.
- W[1]: a harder-looking class of parameterized problems; FPT ≠ W[1] is the belief that these are not the same, i.e., W[1]-hard problems have no FPT algorithm.
- Reduction: a method of transforming one problem into another so that a fast solver for the second yields a fast solver for the first.
- Deterministic algorithm: one that always follows the same steps, with no random choices.
summary.one_liner: The paper asks how much of the quantitative running-time lower bounds usually derived from the Exponential Time Hypothesis can instead be obtained from the weaker assumption FPT ≠ W[1], via reductions from clique with few-bit encodings, yielding twelve bounds for deterministic algorithms on graph, string, and integer feasibility problems.
summary.plain: Computer scientists often prove that certain problems cannot be solved faster than some speed limit, and they base these limits on a widely believed conjecture called the Exponential Time Hypothesis. This paper asks how many of those speed limits can still be proved using a different, more basic assumption, namely that a certain class of "parameterized" problems is not efficiently solvable. The authors do this by converting a search for a group of mutually connected nodes in a network into instances of other problems, and report twelve such lower bounds.
summary.why: It matters because it tests how far a standard family of hardness results can be carried under a different, arguably less specific assumption, which affects how confidently researchers can claim certain problems are hard. The text does not say how these results compare with the strength of the original conjecture-based bounds beyond the stated similarity in exponents, so the broader significance is uncertain.

title: Running-Time Lower Bounds under FPT $\neq$ W[1]

abstract: Asymmetric Multi-Path TSP is the generalization of the Asymmetric Traveling Salesperson Problem where we are looking for $k$ walks, each with prescribed start $s_i$ and prescribed end $t_i$, such that every vertex is visited by at least one of the walks. The objective is to minimize the total length of all walks. In general, it is NP-hard to find any approximation for this problem in polynomial time (even if the approximation factor is allowed to depend on the number of vertices). We show that one can obtain an $O(k)$-approximation in time $n^{O(k)}$, answering an open question by Friggstad [2013]. For the special case where all tour start vertices $s_i$ are identical and all end vertices $t_i$ are identical, we obtain an $O(k)$-approximation in polynomial time, as well as an $(O(\frac{1}ε), 1+ε)$-bicriteria approximation. For the multi-depot setting, where $s_i =t_i$ for all $i$, we obtain a constant-factor approximation in polynomial time. Finally, our results imply improved constant-factor approximation algorithms for Asymmetric Regret-Bounded Vehicle Routing and unit-weight Path ATSP.
label: arXiv:2611.26188v1

summary.background:
- Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP): find the shortest tour visiting every point.
- Asymmetric: distances depend on direction (going A to B may cost differently than B to A), like one-way streets.
- Approximation algorithm: a fast method that guarantees a answer within a known factor of the best possible, rather than the exact optimum.
- NP-hard: a class of problems believed to have no fast exact solution in general.
- O(k)-approximation: the cost is at most a constant times k (the number of walks) times the optimum.
- Bicriteria approximation: the solution may use slightly more walks or budget than allowed, in exchange for a better cost guarantee.
- Multi-depot: all walks start and end at the same depot.
summary.one_liner: The paper gives approximation algorithms for Asymmetric Multi-Path TSP, where k walks with fixed start and end points must jointly cover all vertices of a directed graph, minimizing total length, including an O(k)-approximation in time n^{O(k)} that answers an open question of Friggstad [2013].
summary.plain: This paper studies a route-planning puzzle: several travelers each have a set starting point and ending point, and together they must visit every location while keeping the total distance as short as possible. The one-way-street version of this problem is hard to solve exactly, and no good approximation is possible in general. The authors give methods that come within a factor proportional to the number of travelers, and they get stronger results for special cases where all travelers share starting and ending points.
summary.why: It settles an open question posed by Friggstad in 2013 and gives improved constant-factor results for related routing problems such as vehicle routing with regret bounds and unit-weight Path ATSP. The text does not say how these results compare with other recent work, so their wider significance is uncertain.

title: Approximation Algorithms for Asymmetric Multi-Path TSP

abstract: Static analyzers are cheap and widely deployed, which makes their reports a candidate feedback signal for secure LLM code generation. Existing approaches place the analyzer inside an iterative repair loop with intermediate steps, which is costly and makes it hard to isolate the report's effect on the model. We introduce two strategies that give the finding to the model during generation. When the analyzer raises an alert, generation is rolled back, and the finding is inserted either as a code comment (Comment) or in the user message (Steering). We compare them with two iterative approaches and a control without the analyzer, across three models and three Python benchmarks, and we measure security using each benchmark's oracle. Guidance during generation is cheap and can be effective, at 0.9 to 1.9 times the baseline's output tokens against up to 24.1 times for iterative approaches. With DeepSeek-V4.1-flash on RiskyPy, Steering raises the share of functional and secure programs from 52.5% to 64.4%, close to the best iterative approach (66.2%) while using less than a fifth of the tokens. A per-rule analysis shows that rules with a local fix benefit most, and replacing the XML parser is net-positive on two of the three models. The study also identifies when guidance should not be applied. Analyzers flag at most 5.6% of the functional but insecure programs on SecEvalPlus, leaving little guidance to act on. When a static analysis alert (warning or error) contradicts the task, models tend to follow the analyzer and break the program. The two Qwen2.5 models often fail when the fix requires restructuring the code. These results indicate that static-analysis guidance is worth applying with a capable model, on rules with a local fix, and after filtering alerts that conflict with the task specification.
label: arXiv:2611.26312v1

summary.background:
- Static analyzer: a tool that inspects code without running it and reports possible bugs or security issues (alerts).
- LLM code generation: a language model writes programs token by token; "output tokens" is a rough measure of how much text it produces, and so of cost.
- Iterative repair loop: generate code, check it, feed the report back, and regenerate, repeating several times.
- Rollback: undoing the partly written output back to the point where the alert fired, then continuing with the finding included.
- Functional and secure: the program does what the task asks and passes the benchmark's security test.
- Benchmarks used: RiskyPy and SecEvalPlus are Python test sets for insecure code; the paper's results depend on their oracles (automatic checkers).
- Qwen2.5, DeepSeek: names of the language models tested.
summary.one_liner: The paper tests two ways of feeding static-analyzer warnings to an LLM during code generation (rolling back at an alert and inserting the finding as a comment or in the user message), comparing them against iterative repair loops and a no-analyzer control on three Python security benchmarks.
summary.plain: AI models that write code often produce insecure programs, and cheap automatic checking tools (static analyzers) can flag problems. This paper asks whether those warnings can be handed to the model while it is writing the code, instead of running a slower check-and-fix loop afterward. The authors found that this in-generation guidance costs much less extra text than repair loops and can help, but it works best with a capable model and fixes that are local, and it can backfire when the warning conflicts with the task.
summary.why: Static analyzers are widely used and inexpensive, so a method that uses their output cheaply could matter for AI-assisted coding. The text reports results on three models and three benchmarks, so how well it generalizes beyond these is not established here.

title: Static Analysis Guidance for Secure LLM Code Generation

abstract: Motivated by the non-standard interpretations of if-then-else in probabilistic and quantum programs we review the different semantics of conditional branching and propose a unifying categorical structure for the interpretation of if-then-else. We show that many semantically important categories possess this structure, covering inter alia classical, probabilistic, quantum or non-deterministic computations. We examine algebraic structures related to and generated by this categorical structure, in particular on collections of predicates. In this setting we show that the skew-associativity rules of GKATs and barycentric algebras are two instances of a common skew-associativity rule.
label: arXiv:2611.26400v1

summary.background:
- Programming semantics: the mathematical meaning assigned to a piece of code.
- Conditional branching: a program choosing one of two paths based on a test (if-then-else).
- Categories (category theory): an abstract way of describing mathematical objects and the structure-preserving maps between them.
- Probabilistic and quantum programs: programs whose outputs are random or involve quantum measurement, so a branch is not simply true or false.
- Non-deterministic computation: a program where several outcomes are possible and the choice is not fixed.
- Predicates: yes/no tests or properties whose outcomes are collected and combined algebraically.
- GKAT and barycentric algebra: named algebraic systems for reasoning about programs and convex mixtures; "skew-associativity" is a rule about how grouping of operations can be reordered in a non-symmetric way.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes a unifying categorical structure for interpreting if-then-else across classical, probabilistic, quantum and non-deterministic computation, and studies the algebra of predicates it generates, including a shared skew-associativity rule for GKATs and barycentric algebras.
summary.plain: The paper looks at what "if this, then that, otherwise the other" means in computer programs. In probabilistic and quantum programs, this basic branching step does not behave the way it does in ordinary programs, so researchers have used different definitions. The authors compare these definitions and propose one shared abstract framework that covers many of them.
summary.why: Giving several different kinds of computation one common description of branching may make it easier to reason about them together. The text does not say how far this framework will be used in practice, so its wider impact is uncertain from this abstract alone.

title: On the semantics of conditional branching

abstract: Embedded computing demands high performance and energy efficiency across workloads with widely different computational characteristics. Choosing the most suitable execution model therefore requires a quantitative understanding of how each model maps to different workload classes. In this paper, we compare three execution models for energy-efficient embedded computing: scalar multicore, stream ing multicore, and vector processing. We use three open-source RISC-V accelerators as representative implementations: the PULP Cluster, the Snitch Cluster, and Spatz, respectively. Their open-source hardware and software stacks enable a controlled comparison based on implementations in the same 12 nm technology and a common benchmark suite. Our results reveal that no single execution model performs best across all workload classes. Spatz delivers the greatest benefits for regular and highly vectorizable compute-intensive applications, achieving up to 4.29x higher performance and 5.17x greater energy efficiency than the other architectures. However, its effectiveness strongly depends on the availability of data-level parallelism and regular computation and memory-access patterns, making it the most sensitive to workload characteristics. The Snitch Cluster performs particularly well on applications with limited parallelism and streamable memory-access patterns, providing up to 5.53x higher performance and 1.45x greater energy efficiency. Conversely, the PULP Cluster is most effective on irregular and control-dominated applications, achieving improvements of up to 5.66x in performance and 2.80x in energy efficiency. Compared with Spatz, however, the greater flexibility offered by PULP and Snitch comes at a non-negligible cost in terms of both area and power.
label: arXiv:2611.25947v1

summary.background:
- Embedded computing: processors built into everyday devices, where power use and chip area matter as much as speed.
- Multicore: several processing cores working in parallel on one chip.
- Vector processing: one instruction operates on a whole row of numbers at once, which suits regular, repetitive math.
- Streaming access: the hardware fetches data in predictable sequences ahead of time, so the processor waits less for memory.
- RISC-V: an open, free instruction set that anyone can build chips around.
- PULP, Snitch, Spatz: three open-source RISC-V accelerator designs, each representing one of the execution models above.
- 12 nm: a chip manufacturing process size, used here so the three designs are compared on equal footing.
- Energy efficiency: how much useful work is done per unit of energy consumed.
summary.one_liner: A controlled comparison, all in 12 nm technology on a common benchmark suite, of three RISC-V parallel accelerator designs (PULP scalar multicore, Snitch streaming multicore, Spatz vector) for energy-efficient embedded workloads.
summary.plain: Small chips inside devices like sensors and wearables often need to do heavy number crunching while using very little power. This paper compares three different ways of organizing the processing cores on such chips, using open-source designs built on the same manufacturing technology and tested on the same set of benchmark programs. The authors find that no single design wins everywhere: one is best for regular, number-heavy tasks, another for tasks with little parallel work, and a third for irregular, control-heavy tasks.
summary.why: Choosing the right processor design for a given job can change both speed and battery use considerably, so these measured trade-offs are useful for anyone designing embedded hardware. The text reports peak gains but does not give the full benchmark breakdown, so the headline numbers should be read as best cases rather than typical results.

title: Matching Architecture to Workload: Comparing RISC-V Parallel Accelerators for Energy-Efficient Embedded Computing

abstract: Improving microprocessor performance while meeting ASIC implementation constraints like area and frequency is a complex and labor-intensive task that requires expertise across computer architecture, hardware design, and performance analysis and profiling. While large teams in industry can afford the engineering resources to target this problem across performance modeling, RTL design, and ASIC implementations, small teams of researchers and engineers cannot take on this huge engineering burden while keeping up with the pace of advancement in processor microarchitecture. Recent advancements in large language model (LLM) agents present a promising substrate to accelerate this traditionally human-intensive process. In this work, we build and evaluate MiracleGro, an agentic AI-based system that, without human intervention, analyzes cycle-level RTL behavior and synthesis results, identifies performance bottlenecks, and translates architectural ideas into RTL implementation in a leading open-source out-of-order superscalar application core, the Berkeley Out-of-Order Machine (BOOM). Taking into account cycle-exact performance, area, and critical path, MiracleGro automatically produces improved BOOM designs that drastically increase the human-optimized BOOM's performance on substantial workload suites such as SPEC CPU2017 with full reference inputs. MiracleGro achieves an 85% IPC speedup and a frequency improvement of 27% in SkyWater 130nm, resulting in a 2.34x wall-clock time speedup on the full SPEC CPU2017 intspeed benchmarks (30 trillion instructions). This result demonstrates the enormous opportunity to harness frontier models to improve state-of-the-art RTL-driven platforms for implementation-grounded microarchitecture research across hardware designs.
label: arXiv:2611.26517v1

summary.background:
- Processor core: the central computing block of a CPU that executes instructions.
- Out-of-order superscalar: a design that runs several instructions at once and reorders them to keep hardware busy.
- BOOM: the Berkeley Out-of-Order Machine, an open-source processor design written in hardware description code.
- RTL (register-transfer level): the code that describes what hardware does each clock cycle.
- Synthesis and ASIC: converting that code into a physical chip layout; the reports give area and critical-path (maximum clock speed) estimates.
- IPC (instructions per cycle): a measure of how much work a core completes per clock tick.
- SkyWater 130nm: an older, open chip manufacturing process used for the evaluation.
- SPEC CPU2017: a standard benchmark suite of real programs; wall-clock time combines IPC and clock frequency.
- LLM agent: a language model that plans and carries out multi-step tasks with tools.
summary.one_liner: MiracleGro is an LLM-agent system that autonomously analyzes cycle-level RTL behavior and synthesis results of the open-source BOOM out-of-order RISC-V core, then implements architectural changes that the paper reports as improving IPC, clock frequency and wall-clock time on SPEC CPU2017 in SkyWater 130nm.
summary.plain: Designing a faster computer chip takes teams of experts many months of work. This paper describes an AI system that tries to do much of that work on its own: it looks at how a chip design behaves cycle by cycle and at synthesis reports, spots slow spots, and writes new hardware code to fix them. The authors report that the resulting modified processor ran a large standard benchmark suite about 2.34 times faster in wall-clock time than the original human-designed version.
summary.why: It is a concrete attempt to use frontier AI models for hardware design, a task that usually needs large engineering teams, so small research groups could potentially benefit. The text does not show how general the gains are beyond this one core, one process technology and one benchmark suite, so the wider impact remains to be seen.

title: From Seed to BLOOM: Autonomously Growing a Better Out-of-Order Core

abstract: Differential privacy (DP) is increasingly adopted to protect sensitive data in visualization, but understanding how privacy-induced noise affects visual representations remains fragmented. Prior work has examined the impact of DP noise on specific chart types, yet these findings are typically tied to particular chart types and evaluation settings, making it difficult to generalize across contexts. In parallel, visualization research has long established that visual channels, the visual properties of marks that encode data attributes, differ in perceptual effectiveness under noise-free conditions. However, these principles have not been systematically revisited under DP, where noise is deliberately introduced into the data to protect privacy. In this paper, we present a channel-centric perspective to reframe prior empirical and theoretical results. Our synthesis drawson prior findings to motivate a channel-read-mechanism hypothesis: the utility of DP visualizations may depend on the task-relevant reads made salient by visual channel configurations and DP mechanism choice jointly. Moreover, this perspective highlights the role of channel choice throughout the privacy-preserving visualization pipeline, from disclosure framing and DP algorithm design to utility evaluation and interpretation of noisy outputs. The synthesis also identifies gaps in the existing evaluation literature and highlights research opportunities for channel-aware DP visualization.
label: arXiv:2611.26396v1

summary.background:
- Differential privacy (DP): a method that adds carefully calibrated random noise to data or results so that no single person's record can be identified, at a cost to accuracy.
- Visualization: turning data into charts or graphics for people to read.
- Visual channels: the visual properties that carry data values, such as position, length, angle, area, or color.
- Utility: how useful or accurate a privatized output remains for the reader's task.
- Perceptual effectiveness: how reliably people read a given visual property accurately.
- Channel-read-mechanism hypothesis (from the paper): the idea that usefulness depends jointly on which reading a chart makes easy and on which DP mechanism adds the noise.
summary.one_liner: A position-style synthesis that reframes prior findings on differentially private (DP) visualization through the lens of visual channels (position, color, size, etc.), proposing a channel-read-mechanism hypothesis and identifying gaps in evaluation research.
summary.plain: Protecting private data often means adding random noise to it before it is charted, and that noise can make charts harder to read. This paper looks across earlier studies of how this noise affects different charts and argues that the way information is visually encoded, such as by position, length, or color, matters as much as the privacy method used. It proposes a working hypothesis for this and points to gaps in how these charts are currently tested.
summary.why: As more organizations publish charts built from sensitive data, knowing which visual designs stay readable under privacy noise helps both designers and privacy engineers. The text is a synthesis and hypothesis rather than a set of new experiments, so its claims are proposals to be tested, not established results.

title: Rethinking Utility in Differentially Private Visualization: A Channel-Centric Perspective

abstract: People often watch videos to find information, but locating relevant moments can be difficult and time-consuming. Existing strategies like scrubbing rely primarily on visual scanning and linear search, providing limited support for goal-directed navigation. We present VideoTrail, an AI-powered browser extension that supports information seeking in videos through a hierarchical visualization. Inspired by information foraging theory, VideoTrail surfaces semantic and structural cues as information scent, creating an explorable roadmap of segments. The system is multimodal and adaptive, prioritizing visual or textual scent based on the video's content. In a user study (N=16), VideoTrail helped participants efficiently locate key moments and enabled new navigation strategies compared to traditional timelines, highlighting how exposing an adaptive video structure can enhance goal-directed viewing.
label: arXiv:2611.25377v1

summary.background:
- Information foraging theory: a model from HCI that treats information seeking like animals hunting for food, following "scent" (cues that suggest where useful content lies).
- Scrubbing: dragging the playback bar to skip around a video.
- Hierarchical visualization: showing content at multiple levels of detail, such as broad sections that break down into smaller segments.
- Multimodal: using more than one kind of signal, here visual and text content.
- User study: an experiment where people perform tasks with a system, compared against a baseline; N=16 means 16 participants, a small sample.
summary.one_liner: VideoTrail is a browser extension that uses a hierarchical, multimodal visualization, framed through information foraging theory, to help users navigate and locate information in videos, evaluated in a 16-person user study against standard timelines.
summary.plain: People often watch videos to find a specific piece of information, but scrubbing through a progress bar is slow and hit-or-miss. This paper presents VideoTrail, a browser add-on that builds a map of a video's sections, with labels and structural cues, so viewers can jump toward the parts most likely to matter. In a study with 16 participants, the authors report that it helped them find key moments more efficiently than a traditional timeline and supported new ways of navigating.
summary.why: Video is a common but hard-to-search medium, and better navigation tools matter for learning, research, and everyday viewing. The work is a small-sample user study, so its findings are preliminary, but it connects human-computer interaction design with ideas about how people forage for information.

title: VideoTrail: Interactive Video Foraging Through Hierarchical Visualization

abstract: Quantum locally recoverable codes with $(r,δ)$-locality ($(r,δ)$-qLRCs) are quantum error-correcting codes in which $δ-1$ erased qudits can be recovered by accessing only $r$ other qudits. The minimum locality of a qLRC is the least $r$ such that it has $(r,δ)$-locality. This paper aims to construct optimal impure $(r,δ)$-qLRCs with disjoint recovering sets and explicit minimum localities, where the optimality is measured by the Singleton-like bound of Guruswami, Kshirsagar, and Trivedi (GKT-optimal). Such qLRCs have particular advantages in recovering as many quantum erasures as possible while operating in parallel and with minimal qudit access overhead. We first characterize the recovering sets and the minimum locality of any CSS code by local relative distances, which are relative minimum distances of punctured codes with respect to shortened codes. We then construct impure qLRCs as CSS codes from nested pairs of generalized monomial-Cartesian codes. Grouping the monomials by their degree in the last variable, we reduce both their minimum distances and their local recovery to nested pairs of codes in the remaining variables, and the coordinates with the same values of these variables form disjoint recovering sets. In this way, we obtain four infinite families of GKT-optimal impure $(r,δ)$-qLRCs with disjoint recovering sets, and determine their minimum localities and the recovering sets attaining them for every admissible $δ$, except for a partial range of $δ$ in one family. These minimum localities need not be monotone in $δ$. In particular, two of the families contain GKT-optimal impure subfamilies of CSS codes CSS$(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{C})$ with $(r,δ)$-locality for some $r<n-δ+1$ at values of $δ$ for which $\mathcal{C}$ has no classical $(r',δ)$-locality for any $0<r'<n$, where $n$ is the length of $\mathcal{C}$.
label: arXiv:2611.25859v1

summary.background:
- Error-correcting codes: adding redundancy so that erased or corrupted symbols can be recovered.
- Erasure and qudit: a qudit is a quantum unit with d levels (a generalization of a qubit); an erasure is a known loss of such a unit.
- Locality (r, δ): any δ−1 erased units can be recovered by reading only r others; the minimum locality is the smallest such r.
- Recovering sets: groups of units that can be used together to repair a loss; disjoint sets mean the groups do not overlap.
- CSS codes: a construction of quantum codes built from two classical linear codes, here a nested pair C and its relative.
- Singleton-like bound: a theoretical upper limit on how good a code can be; GKT-optimal means a code meets this limit.
- Monomial-Cartesian codes: algebraic evaluation codes built from polynomial monomials on a grid.
summary.one_liner: The paper builds quantum locally recoverable codes with disjoint recovering sets from nested generalized monomial-Cartesian CSS code pairs, obtaining four infinite families that are optimal under the GKT Singleton-like bound and determining their minimum localities.
summary.plain: This paper is about quantum error-correcting codes, which protect quantum information by spreading it across many storage units (qudits) so that lost units can be rebuilt. The authors design a family of such codes where a missing unit can be restored by reading only a small number r of other units, with the goal of recovering as many lost units as possible at once. They report four infinite families of codes that meet a known theoretical limit (the GKT bound) and work out, for each allowed level of protection, the smallest such r and which units to read.
summary.why: Locality, meaning how few other units must be read to repair a loss, matters for storage and distributed systems where reading data is costly, and the paper gives exact answers rather than only bounds. The text does not indicate applications beyond coding theory, so the practical reach is unclear from the abstract alone.

title: Optimal Impure $(r,δ)$-Quantum Locally Recoverable Codes with Explicit Minimum Localities

abstract: How many independent quantum systems does it take to hide one system that is correlated with a reference? An observer can measure all the systems together with the reference to detect the correlation. We turn any such measurement into binary tests on a single system and the reference. For each test we bound the probability of declaring a signal when an independent pair was prepared. Averaging the largest signal acceptance probabilities allowed by these bounds controls the normalized trace distance in the convex-split lemma. A second bound gives a sufficient number of systems by minimizing the hypothesis-testing relative entropy over the state of the reference. Both bounds hold for density operators on separable Hilbert spaces. Comparing two distributions for the location of the hidden system gives one-shot bounds for private communication and one-way secret key distillation, including the public information available to an eavesdropper. For a fixed finite-alphabet model with separable quantum outputs and positive information advantage and variances, we recover the known Gaussian corrections to the attainable number of private or key bits from $n$ independent repetitions and bound the remaining loss by $\log_2 n+O(1)$ at fixed errors. The position-based key distillation protocol attains this bound with $O(n)$ public bits.
label: arXiv:2611.25496v1

summary.background:
- Quantum state: a mathematical description of a quantum system, written as a density operator.
- Reference system: a second system whose correlation with the hidden system is what the observer tries to detect.
- Trace distance: a measure of how distinguishable two quantum states are (0 means identical, 1 means perfectly distinguishable).
- Convex split lemma: a statement that a mixture of correlated states can be made close to a product of independent copies, given enough copies.
- Binary hypothesis testing: deciding between two possible states using one measurement with two outcomes; relative entropy here measures how hard this is.
- Secret key distillation: turning correlated, partly eavesdropped randomness into shared secret bits.
- Asymptotic repetitions and log terms: results for n independent uses, where the leftover loss grows like log n.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves one-shot quantum convex-split bounds via binary hypothesis testing, and applies them to private communication, one-way secret key distillation, and a position-based key protocol with a log n loss term.
summary.plain: The paper asks how many separate quantum systems are needed to hide one system that is linked to a reference system, so that an observer measuring all of them cannot tell the hidden one apart from an unrelated pair. The authors turn this into a set of simple yes-or-no tests and derive bounds on how many systems suffice. They then use these bounds to estimate how many secret bits can be sent or shared, including what an eavesdropper might learn publicly.
summary.why: The results give explicit one-shot bounds for private communication and key distillation, which connects quantum information theory to practical secret-key questions. The text does not show how these bounds compare with other methods in practice, so their practical reach is unclear.

title: Convex splitting by binary quantum hypothesis testing

abstract: We study the dynamics of the most general metric teleparallel spacetimes of Bianchi types II, III and IX, which admit a four-dimensional symmetry group, in the 1-parameter family of New General Relativity. We first show that in each of these classes the most general metric teleparallel geometry is described by four free functions of time, while another four functions of time describe the most general energy-momentum tensor compatible with the same symmetries. We then derive the field equations of New General Relativity for this class of geometries. Finally, we present some solutions to these field equations. Our results show that both solutions resembling features of the standard Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker cosmology of General Relativity and deviations thereof exist.
label: arXiv:2611.26474v1

summary.background:
- General Relativity: Einstein's theory of gravity, in which gravity is curvature of spacetime.
- Teleparallel gravity: an equivalent-style reformulation that describes gravity using torsion (a twisting of the geometry) instead of curvature.
- New General Relativity: a one-parameter family of teleparallel theories; the parameter selects a particular member of the family.
- Bianchi types: classes of spatially uniform but possibly anisotropic (direction-dependent) universe models, labelled by roman numerals.
- Symmetry group of motion: a set of transformations (such as translations and rotations) that leave the universe unchanged; more symmetries mean fewer free functions.
- Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) cosmology: the standard isotropic model of an expanding universe.
- Free functions of time: unknown quantities depending on time that the equations determine.
summary.one_liner: Derives and partially solves the field equations of one-parameter New General Relativity (a teleparallel gravity theory) for spatially homogeneous Bianchi II, III and IX universes that have a four-dimensional symmetry group.
summary.plain: This paper studies model universes that look the same everywhere in space, described by a rival formulation of gravity called New General Relativity, which describes gravity through a different geometric bookkeeping than Einstein's theory. The authors write down the most general versions of three such universe shapes (Bianchi types II, III and IX) that keep a four-dimensional set of symmetries, and derive the equations that govern them. They then present some solutions, finding some that resemble the standard expanding universe of Einstein's theory and some that deviate from it.
summary.why: Testing whether alternative formulations of gravity give cosmologies that differ from General Relativity is a way to probe what observations could distinguish them. The text does not indicate any direct link to observational data, so the practical significance is uncertain from this abstract alone.

title: Bianchi cosmologies with four-dimensional groups of motion in New General Relativity

abstract: We study quantum-gravitational corrections to the planar integrable structure of the symmetric product orbifold $\text{Sym}^N(\mathbb{T}^4)$ that is dual to tensionless string theory on AdS$_3\times$S$^3\times \mathbb{T}^4$. We consider the deformation that switches on R-R flux in the bulk, and analyze the associated level spacing statistics. The leading non-planar corrections lift the planar degeneracies and produce signs of random-matrix behavior. Our results provide a controlled example of string interactions driving the onset of quantum chaos.
label: arXiv:2611.25576v1

summary.background:
- AdS3×S3×T4 is a specific string theory background; AdS is a curved space with negative curvature, and holography relates it to a lower-dimensional quantum theory on its boundary.
- Tensionless string theory: a limit where the string's tension (stiffness) goes to zero, making the theory tractable.
- Symmetric product orbifold Sym^N(T^4): a conformal field theory built from N copies of a four-torus theory with copies permuted; it is the proposed dual description.
- Planar limit: the leading-order approximation where only the simplest interactions count, analogous to the leading term in a large-N expansion; non-planar corrections are the subleading ones.
- R-R flux: a background field (Ramond-Ramond) threaded through the bulk space.
- Integrability vs. chaos: integrable systems have many conserved quantities and regular spectra; chaotic systems show level repulsion and random-matrix-like spacing statistics.
- Level spacing statistics: the study of gaps between neighboring energy levels, used as a fingerprint of chaos.
summary.one_liner: The paper studies non-planar (quantum-gravitational) corrections to the integrable planar structure of the symmetric product orbifold Sym^N(T^4), dual to tensionless string theory on AdS3×S3×T4 with R-R flux switched on, and examines level spacing statistics for signs of random-matrix behavior.
summary.plain: This paper asks how a highly structured, exactly solvable model of string theory becomes chaotic once quantum gravity effects are included. The authors add a deformation that turns on a background field in the bulk (the higher-dimensional space) and look at how the energy levels are spaced. They report that the leading corrections break the exact degeneracies of the simple planar model and show some signs of the spacing patterns typical of random matrices.
summary.why: It offers a concrete, controlled setting in which string interactions are argued to drive the onset of quantum chaos, which is a question of interest across quantum gravity and holography. The text itself is limited to an abstract, so the strength of the evidence and how far the result generalizes are not something I can judge from it.

title: From Integrability to Chaos in Tensionless AdS3 String Theory

abstract: As anything not in equilibrium is, by definition, nonequilibrium, there is no universally agreed-upon set of topics that can constitute an exhaustive presentation of nonequilibrium statistical mechanics. At the same time, nonequilibrium statistical mechanics has transcended traditional physics to become a powerful language for complex systems. Prompted by an enthusiastic curiosity about complex systems, these cursory lecture notes attempt to elucidate some introductory concepts and techniques used in classical nonequilibrium statistical mechanics, which find successful applications not only in foundational physics, but also across other fields such as biology, ecology, economics, and sociology. Except for the specific synthesis and presentation of the material, which assumes basic familiarity with equilibrium statistical mechanics, the author claims no originality.
label: arXiv:2611.26394v1

summary.background:
- Equilibrium: a state where a system's large-scale properties no longer change over time, as with a cup of coffee reaching room temperature.
- Statistical mechanics: explaining large-scale behavior by averaging over the huge number of tiny particles involved.
- Nonequilibrium: any situation not in such a balanced state, including systems that flow, are driven, or are still relaxing.
- Familiarity with equilibrium statistical mechanics is assumed by the notes.
summary.one_liner: Informal lecture notes introducing core concepts and mathematical tools of classical nonequilibrium statistical mechanics, assuming prior knowledge of equilibrium statistical mechanics.
summary.plain: These are lecture notes about the physics of systems that are not settled into a steady, balanced state, such as systems that are still changing or are being driven by outside forces. The author says they aim to explain basic ideas and techniques used in this area, and to show how the same tools are applied beyond physics, in fields like biology, ecology, economics, and sociology. The author states that the material is a selection and presentation of known work, with no claim of originality.
summary.why: The text suggests the methods are being used as a common language for complex systems outside physics, which is why the notes may be useful to readers in those fields. The text does not give specific results or examples, so the actual reach of these tools in other fields cannot be judged from this excerpt alone.

title: Nonequilibrium Statistical Mechanics: Physical Concepts & Mathematical Tools

abstract: Attention heads specialize into distinct functions during training, often emerging in stages together with sharp changes in model behavior. While this phenomenon has mostly been studied as a function of training time, we ask how head specialization depends on the amount of available training data. Empirically, we find that heads specialized to syntactic relations in BERT emerge as the dataset size increases. We then study this phenomenon in a solvable high-dimensional model of multi-head attention and establish that, in this model, head specialization is a genuine phase transition in sample complexity, corresponding to a non-analyticity in the test error and other observables. Depending on data structure and regularization, specialization can follow uninformative head differentiation or occur through a cascade of phase transitions that progressively recover weaker latent features, providing a statistical form of simplicity bias. Finally, we relate these statistical transitions to the stagewise emergence of specialized heads during online learning, disentangling statistical from dynamical origins of head specialization.
label: arXiv:2611.26228v1

summary.background:
- Attention head: a component of a transformer network that learns which other parts of the input to focus on.
- BERT: a widely used pretrained language model based on transformers.
- Phase transition: an abrupt qualitative change in behavior at a critical point, as with water freezing; here, a sudden change as data increases.
- Sample complexity: how much training data is needed to learn something reliably.
- Non-analyticity: a mathematical kink or jump in a smooth curve, which signals a phase transition.
- High-dimensional solvable model: a simplified mathematical model with many parameters whose behavior can be computed exactly in a limit.
- Simplicity bias: a tendency to learn simple features first and more complex ones later.
- Online learning: training on data one example at a time as it arrives.
summary.one_liner: The paper studies how attention heads in transformers come to specialize as a function of training-set size rather than training time, showing in a solvable high-dimensional multi-head attention model that specialization appears as a genuine phase transition in sample complexity.
summary.plain: Large language models contain many "attention heads," each of which can end up handling a different job, such as tracking grammar relations. Most prior work has looked at how this specialization unfolds over training time; this paper asks how it depends on how much data the model sees. The authors report that in BERT, heads specialized to syntactic relations appear as the dataset grows, and that in a simplified mathematical model the change is sharp, like a phase change in physics.
summary.why: It reframes head specialization as something governed by how much data is available, not only by training duration, which could inform how much data is needed before internal structure forms. The text does not establish how far these simplified-model results carry over to large real models, so that link remains open.

title: Attention Head Specialization: Phase Transitions in Sample Complexity

abstract: Accurate simulations of strongly correlated electrons remain a central challenge in computational physics. We introduce neural-network Gaussian projected entangled-pair states (NN-GPEPS), which exploit the locally-entangled subspace of Gaussian states to give an architecture more compatible with modern neural networks and an exact contraction cost of $O(N^{3/2})$ on two-dimensional lattices. For the Hubbard model at $U/t=8$ and $1/8$ hole doping, we obtain state-of-the-art variational energies in large lattices of up to 1024 sites. These results demonstrate an accurate approach to strongly correlated fermions by connecting neural networks with Gaussian tensor networks.
label: arXiv:2611.26604v1

summary.background:
- Hubbard model: a simple lattice model of electrons that hop between sites and repel each other when two share a site; U is the repulsion and t the hopping strength.
- Strongly correlated electrons: electrons whose interactions are too strong for simple single-particle pictures to work.
- Hole doping: removing some electrons from a half-filled system, here 1/8 of the expected filling.
- Variational energy: an upper bound on the ground-state energy from a trial quantum state; lower is better.
- Tensor networks (PEPS): a way of compressing a many-particle quantum state into a grid of small linked arrays; contraction cost is the computing effort needed to evaluate it.
- Gaussian states: quantum states whose correlations follow simple pairing rules, easy to compute with but limited in expressiveness.
- Neural network quantum states: using a neural network as a trial wavefunction optimized numerically.
summary.one_liner: The paper introduces neural-network Gaussian projected entangled-pair states (NN-GPEPS), a tensor-network ansatz with exact contraction cost O(N^{3/2}) on 2D lattices, and applies it to the Hubbard model at U/t=8 and 1/8 hole doping on lattices up to 1024 sites.
summary.plain: Physicists want to predict how many interacting electrons behave inside a material, but exact calculations blow up quickly as the system grows. This paper proposes a new mathematical form for describing the electrons' quantum state that mixes neural networks with a simpler "Gaussian" building block. The authors report that it gives low-energy estimates on grids of up to 1024 sites for a standard model of electrons (the Hubbard model).
summary.why: Strongly correlated electrons underlie phenomena such as high-temperature superconductivity, which is why accurate simulations matter, though the text itself does not make that link. The reported scaling and the large system sizes suggest the method may be practical where many existing approaches struggle, but the text does not compare costs or accuracy against specific alternatives in enough detail to judge its importance.

title: Scalable Simulation of Strongly Correlated Fermions with Neural Gaussian Tensor Networks

abstract: The scaling of multi-element quantized Hall array resistance standards necessitates rigorous validation that internal quantization has not broken down without relying on the verification of dissipationless edge state transport. One proposed solution is to use a Symmetric Precision Quantization Reliability criterion, a mathematical framework that statistically assures such validation strictly through outer terminal measurements of Cn-symmetric designs. This criterion essentially bounds the likelihood of hidden localized defects arising from quantum Hall breakdown and has potential uses in quantum computing and semiconductor testing but is presented in the context of its application toward quantum electrical standards.
label: arXiv:2611.26016v1

summary.background:
- Quantum Hall effect: in a two-dimensional electron system at low temperature and strong magnetic field, resistance takes exact, universally reproducible values set by fundamental constants.
- Resistance array standard: many quantum Hall elements wired together to reach resistance values useful for calibration.
- Quantization breakdown: a localized failure where the exact quantized value stops holding inside part of the device.
- Edge states: conducting channels along the device boundary that carry current without loss; verifying them directly is the conventional check the paper aims to avoid.
- Cn symmetry: a design with n-fold rotational symmetry, which the proposed criterion relies on.
- Outer terminal measurements: electrical readings taken only at the device's external contacts.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes a statistical reliability criterion, the Symmetric Precision Quantization Reliability (SPQR) criterion, that aims to verify quantum Hall array resistance standards using only outer-terminal measurements of Cn-symmetric device designs.
summary.plain: Quantum Hall devices are used as very precise electrical resistance references, and larger arrays of them are harder to check for hidden faults where the quantized behavior breaks down inside the device. This paper describes a mathematical framework that aims to give statistical assurance of such faults being unlikely by measuring only at the outer terminals, rather than relying on checking the edge-state currents directly.
summary.why: Precision resistance standards underpin electrical measurement, so a way to validate large arrays without invasive checks could matter for metrology. The text also suggests possible uses in quantum computing and semiconductor testing, but it does not show results for those areas, so that connection remains unverified.

title: Topology-Enabled Self-Verification of Quantum Hall Resistance Standards

abstract: Pulsar-timing accelerations point to a localized mass concentration near the Sun, consistent with a dark matter sub-halo. We work out what such an object implies for the nature of dark matter, organizing the implications by their observable effect: suppression or enhancement of structure formation, internal structure and survival after formation, and emission or scattering by the constituents. We discuss ultralight wave dark matter, thermal and nonthermal warm dark matter, dark acoustic oscillations and dark matter-baryon scattering, elastic and inelastic self-interactions, invisible decays with recoil, primordial black holes, indirect detection, and a possible connection to the LUX-ZEPLIN high-energy recoil candidate. We then ask what new data would discriminate among these models. The existing accelerations are measured outside the tidal radius, where they are blind to the interior mass distribution, to the object's velocity, and to the sub-halo population. We identify four routes that lift these degeneracies: accelerations measured inside the halo, which separate point-mass, cuspy, and cored profiles; lensing and accretion, which test whether the mass is compact; the morphology of annihilation or decay emission, which probes the inner profile; and a search for a comoving stellar population, which tests whether the object is dark and measures its velocity. We also contrast this program with pulsar-timing-array searches for transiting dark matter substructure, which probe vastly lighter objects through a different observable.
label: arXiv:2611.25359v1

summary.background:
- Dark matter: unseen matter that is inferred from its gravity; its particle identity is unknown.
- Sub-halo: a smaller, dense clump of dark matter within a larger dark matter halo.
- Pulsar timing: precise tracking of the regular pulses from spinning neutron stars; tiny unexpected drifts can reveal nearby gravity.
- Acceleration measured outside the tidal radius: the data only sense the total pull from outside the object, so the interior structure cannot be read off.
- Candidate models named in the text: ultralight wave dark matter, warm dark matter, self-interacting dark matter, primordial black holes, and others.
- LUX-ZEPLIN: an underground detector searching for dark matter particles by their recoils.
- Cusp vs. core: whether density rises sharply toward the centre or stays flat.
summary.one_liner: A theory-organized survey of what a candidate dark matter sub-halo near the Sun, inferred from pulsar-timing accelerations, would imply for dark matter models, and which future measurements could tell those models apart.
summary.plain: Timing signals from distant pulsars (rapidly spinning dead stars) seem to be nudged by a hidden concentration of mass near the Sun, which could be a clump of dark matter. The paper goes through many candidate dark matter types and asks what each would predict for that clump. It then lists four kinds of new observations that could tell the candidates apart, since the current data cannot.
summary.why: If a dark matter clump is really this close to Earth, it would be a rare direct handle on what dark matter is made of, which is an open question in physics. The text is a framework and does not establish that the clump exists, so its value depends on whether the pulsar-timing signal holds up.

title: Dark Matter Model Implications of a Candidate Sub-halo Near the Sun, and the Data Needed to Discriminate Among Them

abstract: To study the early-universe production of dark matter particles beyond thermal equilibrium often requires solving several coupled Boltzmann equations at the phase-space level. We present a new method to address this challenge using Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) based on stochastic interactions of an ensemble of particles. We implement and validate efficient algorithms to describe freeze-out, decays, elastic scattering and number-changing processes within the dark sector. These algorithms do not require a discretisation of momentum space on a pre-defined grid and do not rely on approximations such as thermally averaged cross sections. As illustrative example, we consider a scenario with two-step dark matter production, leading to a bimodal phase-space distribution, and consider the subsequent evolution under elastic and number-changing processes. We show that DSMC is a flexible approach to explore out-of-equilibrium processes and solve Boltzmann equations at the phase-space level in order to predict the abundance of dark matter particles and their effect on structure formation.
label: arXiv:2611.25812v1

summary.background:
- Dark matter: unseen matter that makes up most of the mass of galaxies; its origin is studied through its early-universe history.
- Freeze-out: the point when particles stop interacting enough to keep up with the cooling universe, fixing how many remain.
- Boltzmann equations: equations that track how many particles exist and how their energies are spread out over time.
- Phase space: the combined description of where particles are and how fast they move; here, the distribution of momenta.
- Thermal equilibrium: a state where particles share a common temperature-set energy spread; out-of-equilibrium means this does not hold.
- Monte Carlo method: estimating results by simulating many random events and averaging them.
- Bimodal distribution: a distribution with two distinct peaks.
summary.one_liner: The paper introduces Direct Simulation Monte Carlo, a particle-based stochastic method, to solve phase-space Boltzmann equations for dark matter production, freeze-out, decays, and scattering without a fixed momentum grid or thermally averaged cross sections.
summary.plain: The paper looks at how dark matter particles could have been produced in the hot early universe and how their speeds and energies evolved afterwards. Instead of tracking the full distribution of particle energies on a fixed grid, the authors simulate a large group of individual particles that collide and change at random according to probabilities. They test the method on a scenario with two production steps, which gives a two-peaked energy distribution, and show how it handles scattering and particle-number changes.
summary.why: Dark matter abundance and its speed distribution affect how structure forms in the universe, so more flexible tools for these calculations matter. The text presents the method as a general approach for out-of-equilibrium cases, but it does not report a broader comparison with existing solvers, so its practical advantage is not established here.

title: Direct simulation Monte Carlo for dark matter production and phase-space evolution

abstract: Massive neutron stars (NSs) require a sufficiently stiff core equation of state (EOS), while the relatively small tidal deformability inferred from GW170817 favors softer nuclear matter at intermediate densities. Given the importance of the nuclear symmetry energy in neutron-rich matter, an intriguing question arises: Can the symmetry energy become supersoft at high densities while remaining compatible with these seemingly competing constraints? Within the nonlinear Walecka framework, we demonstrate that nucleon short-range correlations (SRCs), manifested as a high-momentum tail (HMT) in the nucleon momentum distribution, can accommodate such behavior without introducing additional interaction parameters. We derive for the first time analytical expressions for the symmetry energy curvature $K_{\rm{sym}}$ for both free Fermi gas (FFG) and HMT momentum distributions. Using model parameter sets that reproduce empirical nuclear matter properties around saturation density, we find that SRC-HMT yields substantially more negative $K_{\rm{sym}}$ than the FFG case, allowing the symmetry energy to reach a maximum at low supra-saturation densities and subsequently decrease while the total pressure remains sufficient to support massive NSs. The resulting EOSs also predict smaller NS radii and tidal deformabilities consistent with GW170817. These results connect the microscopic nucleon momentum distribution with the density dependence of the symmetry energy and macroscopic NS properties.
label: arXiv:2611.25913v1

summary.background:
- Neutron stars: extremely dense stellar remnants; their size and mass depend on the equation of state (pressure versus density).
- Massive neutron stars need a stiff equation of state; GW170817 (a neutron-star merger observed in gravitational waves) constrains the tidal deformability, favoring softer matter at intermediate density.
- Symmetry energy: the extra energy per nucleon when neutrons outnumber protons; its density dependence is summarized by the curvature parameter K_sym.
- Free Fermi gas: the simple baseline model in which nucleons fill momentum states up to a sharp edge.
- Short-range correlations (SRCs): pairs of nucleons close together that briefly carry high momentum, producing a high-momentum tail beyond the Fermi edge.
- Nonlinear Walecka model: a standard relativistic mean-field model of nuclear matter with meson exchange.
- Tidal deformability: how easily a neutron star is stretched by a companion's gravity, measured in the merger signal.
summary.one_liner: Using the nonlinear Walecka model, this paper shows that a high-momentum tail in nucleon momentum distributions from short-range correlations can make the nuclear symmetry energy turn over and decrease at high density, while keeping neutron stars massive and tidal deformabilities consistent with GW170817.
summary.plain: Neutron stars must be stiff enough to support about twice the Sun's mass, yet the gravitational-wave event GW170817 suggests they are not too squishy at intermediate densities. This paper asks whether the energy cost of making neutron-rich matter (the symmetry energy) can drop at high density while both constraints still hold. The authors find that short-range pairs of nucleons, which give a high-momentum tail to how nucleons are distributed, can produce this behavior without adding new free parameters.
summary.why: It links a microscopic feature of nuclei (short-range correlations) to macroscopic observations of neutron stars and gravitational waves, which is a useful bridge between the two fields. The text reports model-based results only, so how strongly they hold for real matter depends on the chosen parameter sets and the assumed momentum distribution, which the abstract alone does not settle.

title: Nucleon Short-Range Correlations and Supersoft Nuclear Symmetry Energy: Compatibility with Massive Neutron Stars and GW170817

abstract: u3lib is a C++ library for U(3)/SU(3) representation-theory calculations in nuclear structure and related applications. It evaluates Wigner coupling and Racah recoupling coefficients using the procedure proposed in 2024 by Dang et al., which avoids the binomial coefficients and alternating sums used in earlier formulations. The library also provides irreducible representations (irreps), dimensions, Casimir invariants, conjugation, and tensor-product decompositions with outer multiplicities. It supports the canonical Gelfand-Tsetlin basis and the physical SU(3) $\supset$ SO(3) basis, including inner multiplicities and the transformation between the two bases. Generator routines return matrix elements in the canonical basis and reduced matrix elements in the physical basis. Python bindings mirror the C++ API. Domain skills supplied with the repository allow an AI assistant with code-execution access to call these routines from natural-language requests.
label: arXiv:2611.26558v1

summary.one_liner: u3lib is a C++ library (with Python bindings) for U(3)/SU(3) representation-theory calculations in nuclear structure, computing Wigner and Racah recoupling coefficients via the 2024 Dang et al. procedure and handling Gelfand-Tsetlin and SU(3)⊃SO(3) bases, generators, and tensor-product decompositions.
summary.plain:
This paper describes a software toolkit for doing a specific kind of symmetry bookkeeping used in nuclear physics, where the arrangement of protons and neutrons is described by groups of mathematical transformations. The authors built a library that calculates the numerical coefficients needed to combine and regroup these symmetry states, using a recently proposed method that avoids some long formulas that are error-prone to compute. The library also includes an option for an AI assistant to call its routines from plain-language requests.</plain>
<parameter name="why">Calculations of this kind sit underneath models of atomic nuclei, so a reliable, documented tool can save researchers effort and reduce mistakes. The text does not report any new physical results or benchmark comparisons, so its practical value depends on how well the code performs, which the description alone does not show.</why>
<parameter name="background">- Symmetry groups: U(3) and SU(3) are families of mathematical rotations that describe how nuclear states can be organized.
- Representation theory: a way of labeling and classifying these symmetry states (irreducible representations, or "irreps").
- Wigner and Racah coefficients: numerical factors used when combining angular momenta or regrouping quantum states; they appear in many quantum calculations.
- Gelfand-Tsetlin basis: a standard labeling scheme for SU(3) states; the physical SU(3)⊃SO(3) basis is another labeling tied to rotational angular momentum.
- Casimir invariants: quantities that label an irrep and stay constant within it.
- Python bindings: a wrapper that lets code written in C++ be called from Python.</background>
<parameter name="difficulty">research-level

title: u3lib: An AI-Ready Computational Framework for U(3) Symmetry Algebra, Wigner Coupling, and Racah Recoupling Coefficients

abstract: Experimental demonstrations of quantum error correction often exhibit noise that varies across space and time, and attempting to characterize this disorder has been shown to substantially improve decoding performance. However, theoretical studies of quantum error correction typically assume fixed, perfectly known, homogeneous noise. Here we model decoding with incomplete or inaccurate knowledge of disordered noise channels by treating physical error rates as random variables. We show that the decoding performance is set by a small number of information-theoretic functionals of the noise distribution: the entropy determines the threshold while Bhattacharyya coefficients bound the deep sub-threshold decay rate of logical failures. Furthermore, our results give a quantitative measure of the benefits of characterizing this noise. We numerically investigate both maximum-likelihood and minimum-weight-error decoding of surface codes, showing good agreement with theory across the code-capacity, phenomenological, and circuit-level noise settings, including with noise distributions seen in open-access superconducting devices. When it comes to error correction in realistic settings, reporting the average entropy and Bhattacharyya coefficient of noise distributions could therefore be more informative than the mean or median error rates of a device's components.
label: arXiv:2611.26506v1

summary.background:
- Quantum error correction: encoding information across many physical qubits so errors can be detected and corrected.
- Surface code: a common error-correcting layout of qubits arranged on a grid.
- Decoder: an algorithm that takes error-detection measurements and infers which errors occurred.
- Noise threshold: the physical error rate below which making the code larger reduces logical (encoded) errors.
- Entropy (information-theoretic): a measure of uncertainty or spread; here it summarizes how spread out the error rates are.
- Bhattacharyya coefficient: a number measuring how much two probability distributions overlap; here it bounds how quickly logical failures fall off at low noise.
- Code-capacity, phenomenological, and circuit-level noise: increasingly realistic models that add measurement errors and gate errors.
- Maximum-likelihood and minimum-weight decoding: two standard ways of choosing the most probable error explanation.
summary.one_liner: The paper models quantum error-correcting surface codes decoded with incomplete or inaccurate knowledge of disordered, spatially and temporally varying physical error rates, and shows that the entropy and Bhattacharyya coefficients of the noise distribution govern threshold and sub-threshold performance.
summary.plain: Quantum computers make errors, and error correction tries to spot and fix them. Real hardware has error rates that differ from one component to another and drift over time, but theory usually assumes every component has the same, perfectly known error rate. This paper treats the error rates as random quantities and asks how well a decoder, the software that infers errors from measurements, can do when it only partly knows them.
summary.why: The authors argue that reporting the average entropy and Bhattacharyya coefficient of a device's error rates may be more useful than reporting mean or median rates, which is a practical suggestion for how hardware performance is described. The text does not show how widely this reporting practice would be adopted, so its impact remains to be seen.

title: When the Noise Gets Noisy: Quantum Error Correction with Disordered Noise and Misinformed Decoding

abstract: We introduce a unified framework for sensing time-dependent fields through the lens of classical and quantum algorithms. First, we develop three pulse sequence protocols, namely randomized, matched, and pooled spectroscopy, which outperform established approaches such as dynamical decoupling across a wide range of tasks. These protocols attain the optimal sensitivity for linear and nonlinear AC sensing on conventional spin or qubit platforms, improving existing devices by changing only their pulse sequences. We then introduce quantum computational spectroscopy (QCS), which couples quantum sensors to a quantum processor. QCS combines two new primitives: a quantum computational frequency comb that coherently converts any classical signal into a quantum oracle, and a family of quantum algorithms that use the oracle to extract signal information in superposition. Variations can be implemented on current platforms with only one memory ancilla. We show that the ultimate limit imposed by quantum mechanics lies polynomially beyond the Heisenberg limit, and that QCS achieves it. Attaining this new limit requires quantum computation, establishing a fundamental separation between conventional and quantum computational sensing. Moreover, QCS retains beyond-Heisenberg scaling for broadband signals under constant-strength sensor depolarization, while we prove that the same noise limits any protocol lacking quantum computation to standard-quantum-limit scaling. Our result provides the first asymptotic, beyond-quadratic quantum advantage in AC metrology when noise is aligned with the signal, proving that Lindblad span conditions do not apply to broadband quantum sensing. Our work builds an algorithmic theory for designing sensing protocols and establishes quantum sensing as a new frontier for quantum algorithms, with quantum advantages that surpass the Heisenberg limit and that persist under noise.
label: arXiv:2611.25572v1

summary.background:
- Quantum sensor: a single quantum system (such as a spin or qubit) whose state changes when it is exposed to an external field.
- AC sensing: measuring a field that oscillates over time, as opposed to a constant one.
- Dynamical decoupling: a standard technique that repeatedly flips a sensor's state with pulses to protect it from noise while it senses a signal.
- Heisenberg limit: the best precision scaling allowed by quantum mechanics for many sensing tasks; the paper claims to exceed it in this setting.
- Standard quantum limit: the weaker precision scaling reachable without quantum entanglement or advanced control.
- Quantum oracle and quantum algorithm: an oracle is a black-box operation that encodes information; a quantum algorithm is a procedure that processes such operations on a quantum computer.
- Lindblad span conditions: mathematical constraints describing which noise patterns limit quantum advantage in open quantum systems.
- Depolarization: a noise process that randomly scrambles a quantum state.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes randomized, matched, and pooled pulse-sequence protocols for AC sensing and a quantum computational spectroscopy scheme that couples a quantum sensor to a quantum processor, claiming a beyond-Heisenberg-limit scaling that requires quantum computation and persists under aligned noise.
summary.plain: The paper is about using quantum devices to measure signals that change over time, such as weak oscillating magnetic or electric fields. The authors first show that changing only the pulse sequences used to control a sensor can beat a standard technique called dynamical decoupling. They then propose coupling the sensor to a quantum processor, which they argue can reach a precision limit that goes beyond the usual Heisenberg limit, although the text itself does not show experimental results.
summary.why: If the claims hold, this would suggest that quantum computation itself, not just entanglement or better control, can improve sensing precision, and it links sensing to the design of quantum algorithms. The text is an abstract only, so the strength of the claims, the assumptions behind them, and whether they survive realistic hardware cannot be judged from it.

title: Algorithmic Quantum Sensing

abstract: We calculate numerically energy spectra and angular distributions of photoelectrons and X-ray photons emitted in the process of tunnel photoionization of argon by a focused laser beam of multi-petawatt power. By scanning the beam power and varying the degree of focusing and the field polarization, we show these distributions to be sensitive both to the peak laser intensity and to the field configuration in the focal spot. Investigated parameters of the laser beam correspond to those of several recently commissioned lasers of multi-petawatt power. These findings, in line with the earlier reported proposals, provide a basis for the development of a reliable ionization diagnostics of extremely intense laser fields.
label: arXiv:2611.26496v1

summary.background:
- Tunnel ionization: in a very strong laser field, the electric field bends the atom's binding barrier so an electron can leak out of the atom.
- Petawatt: one quadrillion watts of power, though the pulse lasts only a very short time.
- Peak intensity: the power concentrated per unit area at the focus, which sets how strongly the atoms are driven.
- Focal spot field configuration: the shape and structure of the electric field in the small region where the beam is focused, which is not uniform.
- Polarization: the direction in which the laser's electric field oscillates.
- Photoelectrons and X-ray photons: electrons and light quanta emitted by the atom during ionization; higher-energy photons are X-rays.
- The work is numerical (computer simulation), not an experiment.
summary.one_liner: Numerical calculations of photoelectron and X-ray photon spectra and angular distributions from tunnel ionization of argon in multi-petawatt focused laser fields, showing sensitivity to peak intensity and focal-spot field configuration.
summary.plain: This paper looks at how to measure how intense a very powerful laser beam is, by watching the fast electrons and high-energy X-ray photons that the laser knocks out of argon atoms. The authors simulated these emissions for laser powers in the multi-petawatt range, varying the power, how tightly the beam is focused, and its polarization. They report that the energies and directions of the emitted particles change with these settings, so they could in principle serve as a diagnostic.
summary.why: Multi-petawatt lasers are newly built facilities, and their peak intensity is hard to measure directly at the focus, so a reliable diagnostic would be useful to those facilities. The text says the findings agree with earlier proposals, but it does not report any experimental test, so the practical reliability remains to be shown.

title: Fast electrons and high energy photons produced in strong-field ionization of atoms as diagnostics of multi-petawatt laser beams

abstract: Laser-plasma accelerators reach gradients a thousand times above radio-frequency cavities, but need joule-class femtosecond lasers firing about once per second, and electrons outrun the wave. A comb of laser lines spaced by the plasma frequency, each in its own mode of a matched channel, drives a wake moving at the speed of light. In particle-in-cell simulations a 175\,mJ, 0.5\,ps drive holds 21\,GV/m over 10\,mm with a 0.15\,rad phase drift; a test electron gains 208\,MeV, 2.6 times more than in one mode. Because the wave builds up resonantly, the required energy falls steeply with density: a 29\,mJ drive sustains 20\,GV/m, and a 10\,mJ drive, within reach of kilohertz industrial lasers, gives a test electron 170\,MeV over 30\,mm. A simulated stage transfers 5\,\% of the laser energy to the wake; the Manley--Rowe limit is about 18\,\% for five lines.
label: arXiv:2611.26032v1

summary.background:
- Laser-plasma acceleration: a laser pulse creates a wave in a plasma that can carry and accelerate electrons, reaching gradients far above conventional radio-frequency cavities.
- Dephasing: accelerated electrons eventually outrun the wave that is accelerating them, which limits the energy gain.
- Plasma frequency: the natural oscillation rate of electrons in a plasma; here laser colors are spaced by this amount.
- Particle-in-cell (PIC) simulation: a computer method that tracks particles and fields together; the results here come from such simulations.
- Manley–Rowe limit: a physical bound on how much laser energy can be converted into the plasma wave, given the photon energies involved.
- Units: GV/m is accelerating gradient (energy gained per meter); MeV is an energy unit; mJ and ps are millijoules and picoseconds.
summary.one_liner: A proposed laser-plasma accelerator driven by a comb of laser lines spaced at the plasma frequency, each in its own mode of a matched channel, reports simulated gradients of about 21 GV/m with millijoule-to-175 mJ picosecond drives and reduced dephasing.
summary.plain: Particle accelerators usually need very large, expensive lasers to push electrons to high energy inside a plasma, a hot gas of charged particles. This paper proposes a way to do this with much less laser energy, using a set of closely spaced laser colors that build up a wave in the plasma that keeps pace with the electrons. In computer simulations only, the authors report accelerating test electrons to about 170 to 208 MeV with drives as small as 10 to 175 millijoules.
summary.why: If the simulated results hold up in experiments, laser-driven accelerators could become far cheaper and run at higher repetition rates, which would matter for compact accelerator applications. The text presents only simulation results, so practical feasibility is unverified.

title: Dephasing-free plasma acceleration with millijoule picosecond lasers

abstract: Ice-cloud retrievals from polarimetric radar, lidar and submillimeter radiometry commonly assume random orientation, horizontal alignment or a prescribed flutter angle. We link the orientation dynamics of ice crystals to their scattering.
