Fluid-inertial torque turns small settling crystals broadside on, and turbulent velocity gradients turn them away, so their orientation depends on the dissipation rate. We combine a closed-form orientation distribution for overdamped spheroids, including rotational diffusion and turbulence intermittency, with orientation-averaged Rayleigh, Rayleigh--Gans, T-matrix and specular scattering. Turbulence enters the scattering only through the Legendre moments of the orientation distribution. In the Rayleigh regime the specific differential phase follows crystal alignment, so assuming perfectly horizontal crystals biases ice-water-content retrievals low. Combining the specific differential phase with differential reflectivity limits this bias to $25\%$ for a single size of the shapes studied. For size distributions that span the alignment transition the bound can fail, because the two observables weight sizes differently. Depolarization adds sensitivity to higher-order moments and to intermittency. At finite size the second orientation moment mainly controls the scattering cross sections and the asymmetry parameter, and for optically soft crystals its contribution vanishes $54.7^\circ$ from the vertical. Specular returns from partly aligned plates should persist for lidars pointed $3^\circ$ from nadir. An exploratory analysis of EarthCARE lidar data finds a weakly depolarizing, low-lidar-ratio signature most frequent near $-11^\circ$C, where plates grow. Degree-scale tilt widths inferred from glints and lidar require larger crystals, near or beyond the validity range of the model.
label: arXiv:2611.25750v1

summary.background:
- Ice crystals in clouds are small, non-spherical particles; their shape and orientation change how they scatter light and radio waves.
- Polarimetric radar sends and receives waves with different polarizations; differential reflectivity and specific differential phase are standard measures of particle shape and alignment.
- Lidar is a laser-based instrument; depolarization and lidar ratio describe how particles change light's polarization and how strongly they backscatter.
- "Ice water content" is the mass of ice per volume of air, a key quantity retrieved from these measurements.
- Rayleigh, Rayleigh–Gans, T-matrix and specular scattering are approximations of varying accuracy for particles of different sizes relative to the wavelength.
- Orientation is described by Legendre moments, which are averages of a tilt-dependent function; turbulence enters the scattering only through these averages.
- Turbulent dissipation rate measures how fast turbulent energy is lost as heat in the air.
summary.one_liner: A closed-form orientation distribution for small settling ice spheroids, combined with several scattering approximations, shows how turbulence-driven tilt changes polarimetric radar, lidar and radiometer signals and the retrievals built on them.
summary.plain: Ice crystals falling through clouds tilt in a way that depends on how turbulent the air is, but many radar and lidar retrievals assume the crystals are randomly oriented or lying flat. This paper models how the tilt is set by turbulence and fluid drag, then works out how that tilt changes what the instruments measure. It reports that assuming perfectly flat crystals can bias estimates of ice water content low, and that a combined radar measurement limits this bias to 25% for the single crystal size studied.
summary.why: Retrievals of ice in clouds from satellites and ground radars feed weather and climate models, so a systematic bias from wrong orientation assumptions matters. The exploratory EarthCARE lidar analysis hints at a link to crystal growth near -11 °C, but the text presents this as tentative, and the paper notes that some tilt widths need larger crystals than the model is valid for.

title: Scattering by Small Ice Crystals in Turbulence: From Orientation Statistics to Retrieval Biases

abstract: We present a systematic study of energy transfers in three-dimensional (3D) decaying Hall-magnetohydrodynamics (HMHD) turbulence. Our study has been designed to investigate the dependence of these transfers on initial energy spectra, the ion-inertial length $d_{i}$, and the magnetic Prandtl number $Pr_{m}$. Using shell-to-shell decomposition, we compute the energy transfer rates for (a) kinetic-to-kinetic, (b) magnetic-to-magnetic, (c) kinetic-to-magnetic, and (d) magnetic-to-kinetic interactions by carrying out extensive pseudospectral direct numerical simulations (DNSs) of 3D HMHD and its MHD counterpart. Furthermore, we examine the magnetic-to-magnetic and current-density-to-magnetic energy transfers arising from the Hall term in this framework. Energy transfers between like fields -- namely, kinetic-to-kinetic and magnetic-to-magnetic -- are predominantly local and forward in direction, cascading energy from large to small length scales. This behavior is consistent with a self-similar flow structure in the inertial range. Cross-field transfers, between kinetic and magnetic energy, are found to be forward but non-local in character. At low and high $Pr_{m}$, the transfers become local, and the nonlinear energy transfer is significantly suppressed. Moreover, we observe that the Hall term drives both inverse and forward transfers of magnetic energy, associated with local and non-local transfer, respectively.
label: arXiv:2611.25686v1

summary.background:
- Turbulence: chaotic, swirling motion across many sizes of eddies; energy typically flows from large to small scales.
- Magnetohydrodynamics (MHD): a model treating an electrically conducting fluid or plasma as a fluid coupled to magnetic fields.
- Hall term: an extra correction in Hall-MHD that matters when ions and electrons decouple at small scales; it is governed by the ion-inertial length d_i, a characteristic length scale.
- Magnetic Prandtl number Pr_m: the ratio of how fast momentum diffuses to how fast magnetic fields diffuse; it sets the relative size of viscous and magnetic dissipation.
- Shell-to-shell decomposition: a way of splitting the flow into wavenumber bands ("shells") to measure transfers between scales.
- Pseudospectral direct numerical simulation (DNS): solving the governing equations numerically on a grid without turbulence modelling.
- Decaying turbulence: turbulence with no forcing, so its energy declines over time.
summary.one_liner: A set of 3D pseudospectral simulations of decaying Hall-MHD turbulence maps how kinetic and magnetic energy move between length scales, varying initial spectra, the ion-inertial length d_i, and the magnetic Prandtl number Pr_m.
summary.plain: This paper studies how energy moves between big and small swirling structures in a conducting fluid or plasma that carries magnetic fields, where the flow is slowly losing energy over time. The authors ran many detailed computer simulations and tracked energy passing between fluid motion and magnetic fields at different scales. They report that energy usually cascades from large scales to small ones locally, while exchanges between fluid motion and magnetic energy tend to be forward but spread across scales, and that the Hall term can push magnetic energy in either direction.
summary.why: Energy transfer across scales is central to how turbulent plasmas heat up and dissipate, which matters for space and astrophysical plasmas and for laboratory fusion. The text does not establish how these results apply to any specific observed system, so the connection to real plasmas should be treated as a possibility rather than a demonstrated result.

title: Energy transfers in decaying three-dimensional Hall-magnetohydrodynamics turbulence: Dependence on the Ion-Inertial Length and the Magnetic Prandtl Number

abstract: Quantitative measurement of complex coloration patterns is essential for many biological studies and practical applications. Although color perception depends on the observer's visual system, an objective characterization is possible by measuring the spectral reflectance across the sample surface. Traditional methods for measuring spectral reflectance are either limited in spatial resolution, as with spectrometer probes, or limited in spectral detail, as with digital cameras. We present a method for reconstructing spatially resolved spectral reflectance of samples from multiple images taken under different illuminants with known spectral irradiance. Using an optimization scheme that minimizes pixel-value error while regularizing for the smoothness of the reflectance spectrum, our method generates high-resolution hyperspectral images. We tested our method using both existing spectral reflectance datasets and original multi-illumination images taken in a custom photo-box, demonstrating high accuracy and simple implementation of the method, as well as the ability to infer how samples are perceived by different visual systems. Our method can be a useful tool for objective quantification of complex visual patterns in color-related biological research and imaging applications.
label: arXiv:2611.25520v1

summary.background:
- Spectral reflectance: the fraction of each wavelength of light a surface bounces back; it describes color objectively.
- Hyperspectral imaging: capturing reflectance at many wavelengths for each point of an image, rather than just red, green and blue.
- Digital cameras record only three broad color channels per pixel, so much spectral detail is lost.
- Spectrometer probes measure detail at one small spot at a time, so they are slow for whole surfaces.
- Illuminant: a light source with a known spectrum; using several known lights gives the method more information to work with.
- Regularization: a mathematical constraint that favors smooth spectra, helping the solution stay realistic when data are limited.
- Visual system: different animals perceive the same reflectance differently, which the method is said to help infer.
summary.one_liner: A method that reconstructs spatially resolved spectral reflectance from several digital photographs taken under different known illuminants, using a pixel-error minimization with a smoothness regularizer on the spectrum.
summary.plain: Scientists studying animal or plant coloration often need to know exactly what colors a surface reflects, not just how it looks to a camera. This paper describes a way to get that detailed color information across an entire sample by taking several ordinary digital photos of it under different known lights and combining them mathematically. The authors report that the approach was accurate on existing reflectance datasets and on their own photos taken in a custom photo box.
summary.why: Objective color measurement matters for studies of how colorful patterns look to different animal visual systems, and a low-cost camera-based method could make such measurements easier. The text does not give a comparison against other methods in detail, so its advantage over existing tools is claimed by the authors rather than shown in the summary here.

title: Multi-Illumination Spectral Reflectance Reconstruction: A method for hyperspectral imaging using digital photography

abstract: This work investigates deep convective self-aggregation in the space of scales, extending the physical-space analysis of Part I. We introduce a novel theoretical framework by examining and deriving a generalized Yaglom equation for the second-order structure function $\langle δh_f^{\prime 2} \rangle$, the scale-dependent variance of Frozen Moist Static Energy (FMSE). Self-aggregation is found to be sustained by an inverse energy cascade driven by boundary-layer production and mediated by mesoscale circulations with horizontal scales $r \sim$(100-250 km). The inverse cascade of energy is found to be realized through a series of shallow and mid-level mesoscale circulations which behave in a self-similar way. Accordingly, the scale-energy variance exhibits an extraordinary collapse across all atmospheric layers onto a robust self-similar power law, $\langle δh_f^{\prime 2} \rangle \sim r^{6/5}$. In contrast, horizontal velocity increments show a degree of self-similarity ($\langle δu_r^{\prime 2} \rangle \sim r^{2/5}$) that retains a residual height dependence. Interestingly, the FMSE scaling breaks down at elevations lower than 750 m and at small local scales below 100 km, allowing us to identify the boundary layer top as a scale-dependent dividing layer where the strong stratification filters the interactions between the surface and free-troposphere, so that small scale dynamics of the low and high atmospheric layers are decoupled while those at large mesoscale are coupled. The derived scaling laws are also used to quantify the moisture-convection feedback via scale-dependent correlation coefficients that show that vertical transport strengthens with scale ($ρ_{mc\perp} \sim r^{2/5}$), while horizontal convergence weakens at the exact inverse rate ($ρ_{mc\parallel} \sim r^{-2/5}$).
label: arXiv:2611.25829v1

summary.background:
- Deep convection: tall thunderstorm-type clouds driven by rising warm, moist air.
- Self-aggregation: moist convective regions clustering into large dry and moist areas without an external cause.
- Frozen moist static energy (FMSE): a combined measure of heat and moisture in air, used to track energy in the atmosphere.
- Structure function and Yaglom equation: statistical tools that measure how much a quantity differs between two points separated by a distance r, and how energy is transferred across scales.
- Energy cascade: the transfer of energy between scales of motion; an inverse cascade moves energy from small to large scales.
- Power law (r^(6/5), r^(2/5)): a relationship where a quantity scales as a fixed power of distance.
- Boundary layer: the lowest part of the atmosphere, in contact with the surface.
- Part I: the companion paper analysing the same phenomenon in physical space rather than scale space.
summary.one_liner: A scale-by-scale (Yaglom-equation) energy budget of deep convective self-aggregation, finding an inverse energy cascade sustained by boundary-layer production with self-similar power-law scalings of frozen moist static energy and horizontal velocity increments at mesoscales of roughly 100-250 km.
summary.plain: Tropical storm clouds often bunch together into moist clusters instead of spreading evenly, a process called self-aggregation. This paper, the second of a two-part study, looks at how that clustering is distributed across different sizes of the atmosphere, from small patches to large regions. It reports that energy appears to move from small scales toward larger mesoscale circulations (about 100-250 km), with the energy-related variance following a simple power law in distance.
summary.why: Self-aggregation of convection affects how clouds, humidity and rainfall are organised in the tropics, which matters for climate and weather models. The text does not say how directly these scaling laws would change those models, so the practical reach is uncertain.

title: Multi-scale dynamics of deep convective self-aggregation. Part II: scale-by-scale budget and mesoscale self-similarity

abstract: Differentiable programming enables online calibration of numerical models by minimizing errors accumulated along simulated trajectories. This includes estimating physical parameters and training neural sub-models in hybrid configurations. Gradients are typically computed using adjoint methods, or backpropagation through time (BPTT), whose computational and memory costs grow with the length of the training window. This limits the duration and resolution of hybrid-model training, a major bottleneck for realistic geophysical applications. Approaches like truncated BPTT reduces memory use by discarding sensitivities across truncation boundaries, introducing gradient bias and neglecting long-range dependencies. We propose a class of gradient approximation methods that preserve the adjoint recurrence over the full trajectory while approximating only the pullback operators within it. Exact pullbacks are computed by automatic differentiation at sparse anchor states only. Between anchors, sensitivities propagate either through the identity (Zero-order) or through a reused, frozen pullback (Pullback Reuse). This approximation makes the parameter pullback constant within each chunk, allowing the gradient sum to factorize so that a single evaluation per chunk replaces one per time step. We evaluate both on three systems of increasing complexity, an incomplete Lorenz-63 model, a large-eddy closure for two-dimensional quasi-geostrophic turbulence, and bias correction in a multilayer quasi-geostrophic ocean model. Peak memory falls by up to an order of magnitude and runtime up to fourfold, with Pullback Reuse staying closest to the exact gradient direction. In all three cases, approximate gradients support hybrid-model training at comparable accuracy, showing that effective online learning does not require exact gradients.
label: arXiv:2611.26095v1

summary.background:
- Hybrid model: a physics-based simulation with some parts replaced or corrected by a neural network.
- Online learning / calibration: adjusting model parameters while the simulation runs, using errors that build up along the trajectory.
- Gradient: the direction in which to nudge parameters to reduce error.
- Adjoint method and backpropagation through time (BPTT): standard ways to compute these gradients by running the calculation backward through time; their memory cost grows with the length of the training window.
- Truncated BPTT: a cheaper shortcut that cuts the backward pass into pieces, which biases the gradient and drops long-range effects.
- Automatic differentiation: software that computes exact derivatives of a program.
- Lorenz-63 and quasi-geostrophic models: simplified chaotic systems used as testbeds for atmosphere and ocean dynamics.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes approximate adjoint gradient methods (Zero-order and Pullback Reuse) that keep the full-trajectory adjoint recurrence but compute exact pullbacks only at sparse anchor states, to cut memory and runtime when online-training hybrid physics-plus-neural models on geophysical systems.
summary.plain: Scientists often tune computer models of weather and ocean flow by checking how far the simulation drifts from observations and adjusting it as it runs. Computing the correction signal exactly for long runs needs a lot of memory and time. This paper proposes cheaper approximations that keep the overall bookkeeping intact but only do the expensive exact calculation at a few checkpoints, and tests them on three test systems.
summary.why: Training hybrid models over longer and finer simulations is a stated bottleneck for realistic geophysical work, so cheaper gradients could matter for that. The text reports peak memory cuts of up to tenfold and runtime cuts of up to fourfold, with comparable accuracy, but these are the authors' results on three test systems and their wider applicability is not shown here.

title: Approximate Adjoint Models for Memory and Compute-Efficient Online Learning of Hybrid Models

abstract: We show that the traditional approach of parameterizing the background and linear-perturbation evolutions, through the equation-of-state parameter $w(a)$ and a time-dependent sound speed squared $\bar{c}^2_s(a)$, does not fully specify the cosmological behavior of dark energy theories. Using a new, fully nonlinear fluid framework, we perform spherical-collapse simulations of two clustering dark energy models with identical $w(a)$ and $\bar{c}^2_s(a)$, finding that their central dark-energy densities differ by up to 50\% for cluster-sized dark matter halos. We identify the departure of the local sound speed from $\bar{c}_s$ as the main driver of these differences. In contrast, all other theory-specific quantities in the fluid equations can be described by their background values to a very good approximation. The results demonstrate that nonlinear structure formation encodes critical additional information about the underlying dark energy theory, opening an avenue for discriminating between models using observables on small scales.
label: arXiv:2611.26460v1

summary.background:
- Dark energy: the unknown component thought to drive the accelerating expansion of the universe.
- Equation of state w(a): the ratio of a dark energy's pressure to its density, which may change over cosmic time (a is the scale factor, a stand-in for time).
- Sound speed squared: sets how quickly disturbances spread through a fluid; here it is a time-dependent quantity.
- Linear vs. nonlinear perturbations: small density ripples grow in a simple way at first; once they become dense, the behaviour must be simulated in full.
- Spherical collapse: a simplified model of a clump of matter contracting under its own gravity to form a halo.
- Dark matter halo: a dense clump of dark matter in which galaxies and clusters form.
summary.one_liner: Shows that dark energy models with identical equation-of-state w(a) and effective sound speed can still differ in nonlinear spherical-collapse simulations of clustering dark energy, with the local sound speed identified as the main driver.
summary.plain: The paper asks whether the standard way of describing dark energy, a single number for how its pressure relates to its density plus a sound-speed value, fully pins down how dark energy behaves. Using a new fully nonlinear fluid framework, the authors simulate the collapse of large clumps of matter in two dark energy models that share those same two descriptors. They report that the dark energy density at the centre of cluster-sized halos can differ by up to 50% between the two models.
summary.why: If the result holds, small-scale structure such as galaxy clusters could carry information that large-scale measurements miss, which would be a new route to telling dark energy models apart. The text does not show observational tests, so the practical impact is still an open question.

title: Breaking the background and linear degeneracies: Using nonlinear clustering to discriminate between dark energy models

abstract: While the background evolution of dark energy is relatively straightforward to model, its perturbations, especially on nonlinear scales, generally require significantly more sophisticated treatment. Existing simulation methods for clustering dark energy --- a large class of interesting theories which are until now not well studied --- usually rely on grid-based solvers and perturbatively derived equations, whose validity in the nonlinear regime remains unknown. In this paper, we introduce a novel fluid method based on splitting the dark energy action into two parts: a kinetic part and a potential part. The resulting fluid equations are fully nonlinear and not reliant on simplifying approximations, making them suitable to describe the small-scale evolution of clustering dark energy theories, such as $k$-essence models with small sound speeds. We demonstrate the numerical implementation of this framework through spherical-collapse simulations of two representative $k$-essence models, evolving dark matter and dark energy simultaneously. The simulations are able to follow the development of dark-energy density perturbations throughout halo collapse, to $\mathcal{O}(\textrm{1}-10)$. By investigating their dependence on the dark-energy sound speed and dark-matter halo mass, we illustrate how dark-energy clustering responds to variations in the competing effects of pressure support and gravitational pull. These results demonstrate the applicability of this new framework to study nonlinear dark-energy clustering across a range of physical conditions, providing the foundation for its future extension to fully three-dimensional cosmological simulations through particle-based algorithms such as smooth particle hydrodynamics (SPH).
label: arXiv:2611.26461v1

summary.background:
- Dark energy: a hypothesized component causing the universe's accelerated expansion; its "perturbations" are small local density variations.
- k-essence: a class of dark-energy theories where the energy depends on the kinetic term of a scalar field; the "sound speed" sets how quickly pressure perturbations propagate.
- Clustering: whether dark energy gathers into lumps like dark matter, rather than staying smooth.
- Nonlinear regime: when density contrasts are large, so linear approximations break down (e.g., inside collapsing halos).
- Spherical collapse: a simplified model of a uniform spherical overdensity collapsing under gravity, used as a test case.
- Action: a quantity from which field equations are derived; splitting it means separating the kinetic and potential contributions.
- Fluid method / SPH: ways of simulating matter as a fluid, either on grids or with particles.
summary.one_liner: The paper introduces a fully nonlinear fluid method, built by splitting the dark-energy action into kinetic and potential parts, and uses spherical-collapse simulations of two k-essence models to study dark-energy clustering around dark-matter halos.
summary.plain: Dark energy is the unknown component thought to drive the accelerating expansion of the universe, and some versions of it may clump together under gravity like matter does. Existing computer methods for modeling this clumping rely on approximations whose accuracy in the strongly nonlinear regime is unclear. The authors propose a new way to write the equations of dark energy as a fluid, and test it on simplified spherical collapses of two example models.
summary.why: Simulating how dark energy clusters on small scales matters for interpreting future cosmological surveys, but the text only shows a proof-of-concept on spherical collapse, not full 3D cosmological results. The authors frame it as groundwork for later particle-based (SPH) simulations, which the text does not demonstrate.

title: Splitting the action: A fully nonlinear fluid method for clustering dark energy

abstract: Mapping the distribution of elements in the Milky Way and understanding how that distribution has changed over time can give us insight into the formation and evolution of our Galaxy. Here we use homogeneously estimated atmospheric parameters, elemental abundances, distances, and ages for ~580,000 giants from five major spectroscopic surveys---all simultaneously placed on a single, self-consistent scale by one model---allowing us, for the first time, to use a large sample of stars with uniform labels and ages that cumulatively span much of the disk to trace how the metallicity structure of the Milky Way depends on stellar age. Our chrono-chemical analysis shows that the radial metallicity gradient of the disk depends non-monotonically on age: it is shallow for the youngest stars, steepening to a maximum of ~-0.07 dex/kpc at intermediate ages (~5-6 Gyr), and flattening to near zero for the oldest stars. This "U-shaped" age dependence is driven largely by the low-alpha (thin-disk) population, with the high-alpha (thick-disk) sequence having weak gradients at all ages. In contrast to [Fe/H], the radial [Mg/Fe] gradient is weak (<~0.01 dex/kpc) at all ages. Together, these trends are consistent with an inside-out formation scenario in which the gradient of the star-forming gas has flattened over at least the last ~6 Gyr, while the near-zero gradient of the oldest stars reflects their formation in a well-mixed disk, efficient radial migration, or both.
label: arXiv:2611.26550v1

summary.background:
- Galaxy disk: the flat, spinning part of the Milky Way where most stars, including the Sun, sit.
- Giant stars: evolved, bright stars whose light can be measured across large distances, which makes them useful for mapping.
- Metallicity ([Fe/H]): the share of elements heavier than hydrogen and helium in a star, here measured through iron relative to hydrogen. Stars formed later usually have more of it.
- Radial gradient: how a quantity changes with distance from the galactic centre, quoted here in dex per kiloparsec (dex is a logarithmic unit; a kiloparsec is about 3,260 light-years).
- Alpha elements ([Mg/Fe]): a chemical ratio used to separate the older, puffier thick disk (high-alpha) from the younger thin disk (low-alpha).
- Inside-out formation: the idea that the inner disk formed first and the outer disk later.
- Radial migration: stars drifting from their birthplace to other radii over time.
- Spectroscopic survey: a project that measures the light spectrum of many stars to infer their temperature, composition and other properties.
summary.one_liner: Using about 580,000 giant stars from five spectroscopic surveys, placed on one consistent parameter scale, the paper maps how the Milky Way's radial metallicity gradient and [Mg/Fe] gradient vary with stellar age.
summary.plain: The paper asks how the chemical makeup of our Galaxy varies from its centre outward, and whether that pattern has changed over time. The authors combined star measurements from five large sky surveys, all put on one common scale with one model, so their ages and element measurements can be compared directly. They report that the outward change in iron-to-hydrogen content is gentle for the youngest stars, steepest for stars of roughly 5 to 6 billion years, and nearly flat for the oldest stars.
summary.why: The result constrains how the Milky Way's disk built up, which matters for models of galaxy formation in general. The authors interpret it as consistent with inside-out growth, with the oldest stars possibly formed in a well-mixed disk or moved by radial migration; the text does not settle which explanation is right.

title: Chemical Cartography Across Time: The Age-Dependent Chemical Structure of the Milky Way with a Homogeneous Sample of 580,000 Giants from Five Surveys

abstract: We investigate the cosmic infrared background (CIB) that is expected to arise from the Population (Pop) III.1 supermassive black hole (SMBH) formation scenario, which involves early SMBH seeding via supermassive primordial star formation enabled by dark matter annihilation heating. We model the emission from Pop III.1 supermassive stars, including their growth phase, flash ionization phase, and early black hole accretion phase, as well as accompanying emission from lower-mass Pop III.2 stars. The CIB is composed of stellar and SMBH accretion disk continuum radiation, nebular continuum emission, and Ly$α$ radiation redistributed through scattering in the neutral intergalactic medium. Based on the feedback regulated Pop III.1 model of Petkova et al. (2026), our fiducial model assumes $\sim 10^5\,M_\odot$ Pop III.1 stars forming by $z_{\rm flash}=20$ with a comoving number density of $\sim0.2\,{\rm cMpc}^{-3}$. For this model, the combined stellar contribution is less than $1\%$ of existing direct and diffuse CIB measurements. However, the contribution to the CIB from $z\sim6-20$ SMBH accretion is expected to be larger than the Pop III.1 stellar component for average Eddington ratios $λ_{\text{Edd}} \sim 0.01$. Latest CIB observations place constraints of $λ_{\text{Edd}} \lesssim 0.3$ for the fiducial Pop III.1 model during these epochs.
label: arXiv:2611.25355v1

summary.background:
- Cosmic infrared background (CIB): the diffuse glow of infrared light from all sources over cosmic history, which is hard to separate into individual sources.
- Population III stars: the first generation of stars, made of pristine hydrogen and helium with no heavier elements.
- Supermassive black hole (SMBH): a black hole with millions to billions of times the Sun's mass, found at the centres of large galaxies.
- Seeding: the idea that early black holes grew from smaller "seed" black holes formed from collapsing early stars.
- Dark matter annihilation heating: dark matter particles colliding and releasing energy, which can keep early gas clouds hot and stop them fragmenting into small stars, allowing very massive stars to form.
- Eddington ratio: how fast a black hole is accreting matter compared with the maximum rate its radiation pressure allows; 0.01 means accreting at about 1% of that limit.
- Redshift z: a measure of distance and lookback time; z of about 6 to 20 corresponds to the first few hundred million to about a billion years after the Big Bang.
- Lyman-alpha: a specific ultraviolet/optical emission line of hydrogen that can be scattered by neutral hydrogen in intergalactic space.
summary.one_liner: This paper models the cosmic infrared background expected from a hypothesized Pop III.1 pathway in which supermassive primordial stars, heated by dark matter annihilation, seed early supermassive black holes, and tests the predicted background against existing observational limits.
summary.plain: The paper asks how much faint infrared light the universe should contain if the first giant black holes formed from enormous early stars powered partly by dark matter. The authors model light from those stars, from the black holes' accretion disks, from surrounding glowing gas, and from hydrogen Lyman-alpha radiation scattered through the neutral gas between galaxies. They then compare the totals with existing measurements of this background.
summary.why: Measurements of the infrared background are a rare indirect check on very early star and black hole formation that is hard to see directly. The text says the stellar part of the signal in its fiducial model is under 1% of existing measurements, while black hole accretion could be larger at average Eddington ratios near 0.01, and current data limit that ratio to about 0.3 or less. Whether this scenario holds up depends on the underlying model of Petkova et al. (2026), which this text does not evaluate.

title: The Cosmic Infrared Background from Population III.1 Supermassive Stars and Black Holes

abstract: We performed one-dimensional calculations to investigate how the magnetorotational instability (MRI) affects dust growth in protoplanetary disks. We simultaneously solved the evolution of the dust size distribution and the vertical magnetic field. The dust size distribution is evolved taking into ac- count coagulation and fragmentation. For the magnetic field evolution, we considered both ambipolar diffusion and Ohmic dissipation. The MRI-driven turbulent viscosity was estimated self-consistently from the local magnetic field strength and non-ideal magnetohydrodynamics diffusivities. We found that MRI-driven turbulence becomes stronger for smaller initial plasma beta, and the enhanced tur- bulence promotes dust growth in MRI-active regions. However, dust growth is ultimately limited by radial drift, and the dependence of dust size on the magnetic field strength is significant only in the outer regions of the disk. In other words, over most of the disk, radial drift remains the dominant factor controlling the maximum dust size, and the magnetic field strength plays only a minor role in determining the overall dust size distribution.
label: arXiv:2611.25602v1

summary.background:
- Protoplanetary disk: a rotating disk of gas and dust around a young star, where planets form.
- Dust growth: tiny grains stick together (coagulation) or shatter on collisions (fragmentation).
- Radial drift: gas pressure makes dust slowly spiral inward toward the star, capping how large grains can get.
- Magnetorotational instability (MRI): a process in which a weakly magnetized, rotating gas becomes turbulent, which transports angular momentum and stirs dust.
- Plasma beta: ratio of gas pressure to magnetic pressure; a smaller value means a stronger field relative to gas pressure.
- Non-ideal magnetohydrodynamics: effects (ambipolar diffusion, Ohmic dissipation) by which weakly ionized gas lets magnetic fields drift or decay.
- One-dimensional calculation: the model varies along only one coordinate (here, distance from the disk midplane or radius, as simplified in the model), not a full 3D simulation.
summary.one_liner: A one-dimensional study coupling dust coagulation and fragmentation with the evolution of a vertical magnetic field, including ambipolar diffusion and Ohmic dissipation, to test how magnetorotational-instability-driven turbulence sets dust growth in protoplanetary disks.
summary.plain: This paper looks at how the magnetic field inside a young, gas-and-dust disk around a newborn star affects how small dust grains clump into larger particles, the raw material for planets. The authors ran computer simulations in which the dust sizes and the magnetic field evolve together, and the turbulence the field stirs up is calculated from the field's own strength. They found that a stronger magnetic field (a lower "plasma beta," a measure of how much gas pressure compares with magnetic pressure) makes the turbulence stronger, which helps dust grow in the regions where it is active.
summary.why: The result suggests that magnetic turbulence matters for dust growth mainly in the outer disk, while inward radial drift (dust spiraling toward the star) still limits the maximum grain size over most of the disk. This is relevant to understanding how planetary building blocks form, though the text describes only a one-dimensional model, so its broader applicability is uncertain.

title: Dependence of Dust Growth on Magnetic field Strength in Protoplanetary Disks

abstract: The formation of gas giant planets by the gas disk gravitational instability (GDGI) mechanism depends sensitively on the thermodynamics of the protoplanetary disk gas: disk gas must be able to cool on orbital timescales for dense clumps to become gravitationally unstable and contract to form protoplanets. Since disk cooling is regulated by the opacity of the dust grains embedded in the gas, the properties of these dust grains are critical for the GDGI mechanism. Grain growth to larger sizes than assumed in traditional opacity models for solar metallicity, as well as protostars with sub-solar metallicity, should have lower opacity disks that are more conducive to planet formation by GDGI. Here we use a three dimensional radiative hydrodynamics and gravitation code to compute the evolution of the GDGI in $0.091 M_\odot$ disks with varied initial minimum values (1.3 to 2.7) of the Toomre criterion orbiting solar-mass protostars. Three sets of eight models are computed: one with the standard opacity, and two more with the opacity reduced by arbitrary factors of 10 or 100. As expected, the reduced opacity models result in enhanced disk fragmentation by the GDGI and the production of more self-gravitating clumps than the standard opacity models. Nevertheless, all three opacities form similar self-gravitating clumps at this early phase of clump evolution, with masses of 0.2 to 0.7 $M_{Jup}$ and semimajor axes between 6 and 13 au. Significant dust grain growth should enhance the ability of the GDGI to form protoplanets around super-solar metallicity protostars.
label: arXiv:2611.26804v1

summary.background:
- Protoplanetary disk: a rotating disk of gas and dust around a young star, where planets form.
- Gravitational instability: when a disk's self-gravity overcomes its internal pressure and forms dense clumps that can contract into planets.
- Toomre criterion: a stability measure for rotating disks; lower values mean the disk is more prone to clumping.
- Opacity: how strongly material blocks radiation; dust grains raise opacity, slowing cooling.
- Grain growth: small dust particles clumping into larger ones, which changes opacity.
- Metallicity: the fraction of elements heavier than helium in a star; solar metallicity is the Sun's value.
- Jupiter mass (M_Jup) and astronomical unit (au): units for planet mass and orbital distance.
summary.one_liner: Three-dimensional radiative hydrodynamics simulations test how lower dust opacity (from grain growth or sub-solar metallicity) affects gas giant planet formation by gravitational fragmentation of protoplanetary disks around solar-mass stars.
summary.plain: This paper asks how giant planets can form quickly from the gas around a young star by the disk breaking into clumps under its own gravity. Such clumps need the gas to cool fast enough, and cooling depends on how much the tiny dust grains in the gas block heat from escaping. The authors ran computer simulations with standard dust opacity and with opacity reduced by factors of 10 and 100, and found that lower opacity produced more fragmentation, but all cases formed clumps of similar mass and distance.
summary.why: It links grain growth and star chemistry (metallicity) to whether disk instability can make giant planets, a question of how planets like those seen in exoplanet surveys form. The text suggests the effect may matter most around metal-rich stars, but this is a modelling study of early clump evolution only, so its broader implications remain uncertain.

title: The Effect of Dust Grain Growth and Stellar Metallicity on Gas Giant Planet Formation by Disk Instability

abstract: We investigate how the effective nucleon mass and symmetry energy affect pasta phase properties and the unified equation of state (EOS) of neutron stars. The nonuniform pasta structure is described within the self-consistent Thomas-Fermi approximation, while nucleonic interactions are treated in the relativistic mean-field framework with several typical parameter sets adopted. Our results indicate that the symmetry energy and its slope are crucial in determining the onset of pasta phases and their geometric configurations. In the high-density region where matter becomes uniform, the effective nucleon mass plays a dominant role. A larger effective nucleon mass tends to soften the EOS, which yields a smaller radius for a canonical $1.4 M_{\odot}$ neutron star and reduces the corresponding tidal deformability.
label: arXiv:2611.25666v1

summary.background:
- Neutron star: a stellar remnant about 1.4 times the Sun's mass packed into roughly 20 km across.
- Equation of state (EOS): the rule relating pressure to density; it determines how big and how compressible a star is.
- Nuclear pasta: non-spherical clumps, rods, or sheets of dense nuclear matter predicted in the star's inner crust.
- Thomas-Fermi approximation: a simplified quantum-statistical method for estimating how matter arranges itself in space.
- Relativistic mean-field framework: a theory describing nucleon interactions via exchanged effective fields, with fitted parameter sets.
- Symmetry energy: the extra energy cost of making nuclear matter unbalanced between neutrons and protons; its slope describes how that cost changes with density.
- Effective nucleon mass: the apparent mass of protons and neutrons inside dense matter, which can differ from their free mass.
- Tidal deformability: how easily a star is stretched by a companion's gravity, an observable in merging neutron-star signals.
summary.one_liner: Using self-consistent Thomas-Fermi calculations with relativistic mean-field nucleon interactions, this paper examines how the effective nucleon mass and the nuclear symmetry energy (and its slope) shift the onset and geometry of nuclear pasta phases and the resulting unified neutron-star equation of state, including the 1.4 solar-mass radius and tidal deformability.
summary.plain: Neutron stars are extremely dense collapsed stars, and the deep crust of such a star may contain clumpy or sheet-like shapes of nuclear matter called "pasta." This paper studies how two properties of nuclear matter, the apparent mass of nucleons and how the energy of nuclear matter changes when neutrons outnumber protons, affect when this pasta forms and what the overall pressure-density relation of the star looks like. The authors report that the symmetry energy controls where pasta appears and what shape it takes, while the effective nucleon mass matters most in the denser uniform core. A heavier effective mass makes the matter softer, giving a smaller star radius and a smaller tidal deformability for a 1.4 solar-mass star.
summary.why: Radius and tidal deformability of neutron stars are constraints that gravitational-wave and X-ray observations try to measure, so the link between nuclear inputs and these observables is of interest for testing dense-matter models. The text does not report comparisons with specific observations, so its direct bearing on those measurements is unclear from this abstract alone.

title: Impact of Effective Nucleon Mass and Symmetry Energy on Nuclear Pasta Phases and the Unified Equation of State of Neutron Stars

abstract: We study tidal disruptions of rotating solar-type stars by a rapidly spinning supermassive black hole with general-relativistic smoothed-particle hydrodynamics. To capture strong-field effects, we place the pericentre at a few gravitational radii of a black hole, and compare with weak-field encounters at a larger pericentre around a lighter black hole. We vary the black hole spin, the orbital inclination and the stellar rotation, using rigidly and differentially rotating stars with spin aligned, anti-aligned or perpendicular to the orbital angular momentum. In the strong field, the black hole spin decides whether a core survives on equatorial and inclined orbits, and stellar rotation reduces the surviving core in every partial disruption. At the larger pericentre, as in Newtonian studies, anti-aligned rotation instead protects the star from disruption. In both cases the tide reverses an anti-aligned spin just before pericentre. The outcome differs because in the strong field the tide keeps acting on the reversed core long after pericentre. Deep encounters leave cores spinning above break-up, which shed mass and angular momentum as they settle. Full disruptions approach the canonical fallback law, whereas the late-time slope of partial disruptions is not universal and is set by the debris energy distribution near the surviving core.
label: arXiv:2611.26043v1

summary.background:
- Tidal disruption: a star passing near a black hole is stretched and partly torn apart by the gravity difference across its body.
- Pericentre: the closest point of an orbit to the black hole.
- Gravitational radius: a length scale set by the black hole's mass; a few of them means very close to the hole, where general relativity matters.
- Spin and inclination: the black hole's rotation and the tilt of the star's orbit relative to it.
- Smoothed-particle hydrodynamics: a simulation method that represents gas as moving particles.
- Partial vs full disruption: whether a dense core of the star survives the encounter.
- Fallback law: the rate at which torn-off debris returns to the black hole, often described as a power law in time.
summary.one_liner: General-relativistic smoothed-particle hydrodynamics simulations of rotating solar-type stars tidally disrupted by a rapidly spinning supermassive black hole, comparing strong-field (close pericentre) and weak-field (Newtonian-like) encounters across black hole spin, orbital inclination and stellar spin alignment.
summary.plain: This paper looks at what happens when a star passes too close to a supermassive black hole and gets torn apart. The authors simulate stars that already spin, and vary how the black hole spins and how the star's spin lines up with its orbit. They compare very close passes, where Einstein's gravity matters strongly, with gentler passes that behave more like classic Newtonian physics.
summary.why: Tidal disruption events are one of the few ways to probe black holes and their surroundings from afar, so how much of a star survives and how the debris falls back affects what telescopes might see. The text reports that strong-field encounters can differ from Newtonian expectations, for example in whether anti-aligned stellar spin protects the star; how far this carries over to real observed events is not something the text establishes.

title: Strong Field Tidal Disruptions of Rotating Stars by Spinning Black Holes

abstract: As single-aged populations containing stars spanning a range of masses but otherwise with similar properties, star clusters provide valuable testbeds for stellar evolution theory. The old, metal-rich, open cluster NGC 6791 is well studied, but the availability of asteroseismic observations of individual cluster members allows for a more in-depth analysis. Driven by mounting evidence that the solar assumption for convection used in almost all 1D stellar models is not adequate, and in light of the increased precision provided by modern data and asteroseismic constraints, we built and compared custom isochrones with varying values of the convective mixing length, $α_\text{MLT}$, to two clusters with well-determined ages: NGC 6791 and the well-studied, metal-poor globular cluster M92. For both clusters, we found that the best-fitting mixing length parameter decreases monotonically as a function of evolutionary phase, finding values between $0.98-1.10α_{\odot}$ for NGC 6791 and $1.16-1.21α_{\odot}$ for M92. In NGC 6791, this corresponds to an 18% decrease in the best fitting mixing length between the main sequence turn-off and upper end of the red giant branch. The degree of variation found within this one object is therefore comparable to variation across the literature in $α_\text{MLT}$ fits for other non-solar targets, calling single-valued $α_\text{MLT}$ fits to clusters into question. It is also consistent with $\log g$-$α_\text{MLT}$ trends predicted by higher-fidelity, 3D convection analyses. Our results therefore illustrate the need for more flexibility in our treatment of the mixing length in isochrones to properly model clusters.
label: arXiv:2611.25306v1

summary.background:
- Isochrone: a theoretical curve showing where stars of one age and composition sit on a brightness-versus-colour diagram.
- Star cluster: a group of stars born together, so they share an age and starting composition; useful as a test bed.
- Mixing length (alpha_MLT): a tunable parameter in 1D stellar models describing how far rising hot gas travels in convection, expressed relative to the Sun's value.
- Convection: heat transport by churning motion of gas inside a star, which simple models can only approximate.
- Asteroseismology: studying stars by their vibrations, which gives precise measurements of their interiors and surface gravity (log g).
- Main sequence turn-off and red giant branch: the bend where stars leave the main sequence and the later phase of swollen, cooler giant stars.
- Metal-rich vs metal-poor: astronomers' term for stars with more or fewer elements heavier than helium.
summary.one_liner: Custom stellar isochrones with varying convective mixing length are fitted to the old open cluster NGC 6791 and globular cluster M92, finding the best-fit mixing length drops steadily along the evolutionary sequence, which challenges single-valued mixing-length calibrations.
summary.plain: This paper looks at groups of stars that all formed at the same time, using them as test cases for models of how stars age. The authors compared model tracks that use different values of a setting describing how hot gas churns inside stars, for an old open cluster (NGC 6791) and an old globular cluster (M92). They found the best-fitting setting changes as stars move from the turn-off point to the upper red giant branch, rather than staying constant.
summary.why: Most stellar models assume one fixed convection setting, calibrated on the Sun, and this work suggests that assumption may be too rigid, which could affect ages and properties derived from clusters. The text says the trend is consistent with predictions from more detailed 3D convection simulations, but the broader implications are not tested in the text.

title: Sherlock 'Chrones: The Curious Case of NGC 6791 and Asteroseismic Targets Therein Reveals Mixing Length Dependence on Evolutionary Stage

abstract: Mass transfer is a highly dynamical 3D process that spans evolutionary timescales in binary stars. It is key to the production of gravitational waves through formation of binary black holes and other double compact objects. We integrate global 3D hydrodynamics into stellar evolutionary modeling to resolve mass transfer across nuclear timescales. We employ the shellular approximation in the stellar evolution code MESA to map a 3D spatial structure by equipotential shells in the Roche geometry to maintain hydrostatic equilibrium across tidally-distorted surfaces. We employ the method of time-incremented multiscale evolution to alternate between stellar evolution and 3D hydrodynamics to span large timescales with dynamical feedback. We employ this framework to examine a likely merging binary black hole progenitor system of a low-metallicity 30Msol donor star and 9.3Msol black hole from the end of the main sequence to core Carbon depletion. We modeled two complete mass transfer phases in 3D while self-consistently accounting for stellar evolution. These comprised a thermal-timescale early Case B phase and a nuclear-timescale late Case B phase. The prescription of Kolb & Ritter (1990) closely predicted the results of 3D evolution, except at the end of the first phase of mass transfer; our 3D model remained well-contained by the outer Lagrange point, despite 1D predictions of substantial L3 overflow during this stage. We find incorporating 3D hydrodynamics during Case B mass transfer did not significantly impact expected merger times. Our model never overflowed L3 as predicted by 1D prescriptions. L2/L3 outflows formed even while underflowing those equipotentials. Our model suggests these outflows can be neglected for the evolution of similar systems, but were dense enough to potentially impact X-ray observations.
label: arXiv:2611.25310v1

summary.background:
- Binary star: two stars orbiting each other; one can pull gas off the other through mass transfer.
- Black hole merger: two compact remnants spiral together and emit gravitational waves, ripples in spacetime.
- Case A/B/C mass transfer: labels for when in its life the donor star overflows its boundary (Case B means after core hydrogen runs out, during shell burning).
- Roche lobe and Lagrange points: the teardrop-shaped region around each star where gravity is dominated by that star; L2 and L3 are points outside it where gas can escape.
- Hydrodynamics: computer modeling of how fluids (here, stellar gas) flow and push.
- Metallicity: the fraction of elements heavier than helium in a star; low metallicity stars lose less mass to winds.
- MESA: a widely used open-source 1D stellar evolution code.
- Equipotential/hydrostatic equilibrium: the gas is assumed to sit in balance under gravity and pressure.
summary.one_liner: A 3D hydrodynamics model, coupled to the MESA stellar evolution code via the shellular approximation and time-incremented multiscale evolution, follows mass transfer in a likely merging binary black hole progenitor (30 Msun donor, 9.3 Msun black hole, low metallicity) through two Case B mass-transfer phases and compares it with the 1D Kolb & Ritter (1990) prescription.
summary.plain: This paper looks at a pair of stars in which a massive star is slowly feeding gas onto a black hole that orbits it. Such pairs are thought to be the ancestors of black hole mergers that send gravitational waves through space. The authors simulated this exchange in full 3D, alternating between a stellar evolution model and a fluid-flow model, from the end of the star's main life until its core runs out of carbon.
summary.why: Mass transfer between stars is a key step in making merging black hole pairs, but simpler 1D models have to approximate it. The text reports that the 3D run matched a standard 1D prescription closely except at one stage, that the gas did not spill past the outer balance point (L3) as 1D models predicted, and that merger timing was not significantly changed. The authors also suggest the outflows could matter for X-ray observations, though the text does not show that directly.

title: 3D Binary Evolution of a Merging Binary Black Hole Progenitor

abstract: Molecular conformation plays a central role in determining molecular properties and dynamics. Here, we report the production and conformer-resolved spectroscopy of cold calcium 3-hydroxyphenoxide radical (CaOC$_6$H$_4$-3-OH) in a cryogenic buffer-gas cell. Internal rotation of the hydroxyl group gives rise to distinct $anti$- and $syn$-conformers. The CaO moiety acts as an optical cycling center (OCC), enabling the $\widetilde A - \widetilde X$ and $\widetilde B - \widetilde X$ transitions of both conformers to be resolved by laser-induced fluorescence spectroscopy. Dispersed fluorescence measurements reveal diagonal vibrational branching fractions of 0.91-0.93, indicating favorable optical cycling characteristics. Following excitation of off-diagonal vibronic transitions near the calculated torsional barrier in the $\widetilde A$ state, the emission remains predominantly conformer specific, indicating that conformational identity is largely preserved over the excited-state fluorescence lifetime. These results demonstrate that a metal-centered OCC can serve as an intrinsic, site-specific optical reporter of molecular conformation, providing a foundation for repetitive optical readout and studies of conformational dynamics at the single-molecule level.
label: arXiv:2611.25851v1

summary.background:
- Conformer: different 3D shapes of the same molecule that interconvert by rotation around a bond; here, the twist of the OH group.
- Radical: a molecule with an unpaired electron, here a calcium-oxygen unit attached to a benzene-based ring.
- Optical cycling center (OCC): a metal-containing unit that can be excited by light and emit it back many times with little loss to other states, allowing repeated readout.
- Laser-induced fluorescence: exciting molecules with a laser and recording the light they emit.
- Vibrational branching fraction: the share of emitted light that returns the molecule to its original vibrational (internal motion) level; higher values mean fewer leaks.
- Buffer-gas cell: a cold chamber filled with inert gas used to cool molecules before measurement.
- Torsional barrier: the energy hill a molecule must cross to twist from one conformer to the other.
summary.one_liner: Cold CaO-tagged 3-hydroxyphenoxide radicals in a buffer-gas cell are shown to have resolvable anti and syn conformers whose laser-induced fluorescence is conformer-specific, with diagonal vibrational branching of 0.91-0.93 supporting optical cycling.
summary.plain: This paper studies a molecule that has a flexible hydroxyl (OH) group that can twist into two shapes, called conformers. The authors attach a calcium-oxygen unit to it, cool the molecules very cold in a gas-filled chamber, and shine laser light on them. Each twisted shape glows in its own way when excited, so the glow tells you which shape the molecule had.
summary.why: The work shows that a metal-containing tag can act as a built-in, site-specific light reporter of molecular shape, which could help in tracking how molecules change shape over time. Its broader relevance to single-molecule readout is suggested by the authors but has not been tested in this text.

title: Witnessing Molecular Conformation via Optical Cycling Centers

abstract: We present three global adiabatic potential energy surfaces (PESs) for the O($^3$P) + C$_2$(X $^1Σ_g^+$, a $^3Π_u$) to CO(X$^1Σ^+$) + C($^3$P) reaction, computed at the icMRCI+Q/aug-cc-pVTZ level. This reaction is relevant to combustion chemistry, atmospheric processes, and astrochemistry. Since the energy difference between the $^1Σ_g^+$ and $^3Π_u$ states of C$_2$ is smaller than the zero-point energy, both states mix upon interaction with the approaching O atom. Consequently, the PESs exhibit a double-well topography in the reactant valley. Beyond this feature, the three PESs display markedly different topographies. The 1 $^3A''$ PES features a deep minimum 7.16 eV below the O + C$_2$ entrance channel. In contrast, the 2 $^3A''$ and 1 $^3A'$ surfaces possess shallower collinear wells ($\approx$ 5.7 eV) and strong angular anisotropy arising from avoided crossings with higher-lying triplet states. The analytical fits reproduce the \textit{ab initio} data with root-mean-square (RMS) deviations of 0.022--0.028 eV over an energy interval exceeding 13 eV. Quasiclassical trajectory (QCT) calculations reveal higher reactivity on the barrierless $1\,^3A''$ surface compared to the $2\,^3A''$ PES, where an angle-dependent entrance barrier reduces the cross sections. Furthermore, cross sections for reactions initiated from C$_2$(X $^1Σ_g^+$) and C$_2$(a $^3Π_u$) are remarkably similar for the three PESs, regardless of the initial rovibrational state.
label: arXiv:2611.26233v1

summary.background:
- Potential energy surface (PES): a map of how the energy of a set of atoms changes with their positions; reactions proceed across it.
- Adiabatic surface: an energy surface for one electronic state, assuming electrons adjust instantly as nuclei move.
- Triplet state: an electronic configuration with two unpaired electron spins; O(3P) and C(3P) are ground-state atoms of this kind.
- C2 states: X 1Σg+ (singlet ground state) and a 3Πu (lower triplet state); their small energy gap lets them mix.
- Zero-point energy: the minimum vibrational energy a molecule keeps even at absolute zero.
- ab initio / icMRCI+Q: quantum-chemistry calculations done from first principles, without fitted experimental data.
- Quasiclassical trajectory (QCT): simulation that follows atoms along classical paths with quantum-derived starting conditions, used to estimate reaction cross sections.
- Cross section: an effective target area describing how likely a reaction is at a given collision energy.
- Analytical fit: a mathematical formula reproducing the computed energies; RMS deviation measures the average fit error.
summary.one_liner: Three global triplet adiabatic potential energy surfaces are computed at the icMRCI+Q/aug-cc-pVTZ level for O(3P) + C2 reacting to CO + C(3P), with quasiclassical trajectory dynamics showing reactivity differences between surfaces and between the two C2 electronic states.
summary.plain: The paper studies a chemical reaction in which an oxygen atom collides with a C2 molecule and forms carbon monoxide plus a carbon atom. Reactions like this matter in flames, the atmosphere and interstellar space. The authors built three detailed maps of the energy landscape the atoms move across, then ran simulated collisions on them to estimate how often the reaction happens.
summary.why: The text reports that the two low-lying states of C2 mix because their energy gap is smaller than the zero-point energy, which gives a double-well shape in the reactant region, and that the surfaces differ strongly in shape. Such surface maps are the input for combustion and astrochemical models, so the work may be useful there, though the text does not itself test any model.

title: Triplet adiabatic potential energy surfaces for the O($^3$P) + C$_2$(X$^1Σ_g^+$, a$^3Π_u$) reaction and quasiclassical trajectory dynamics

abstract: Reward misalignment is usually regarded as a failure of artificial intelligence. In materials discovery with generative AI models, however, disagreement between predefined rewards and expert judgment may reveal materials that the rewards overlook. We investigate this possibility using electronic flat bands as a prime example. Experts mostly agree with a numerical bandwidth score, but their disagreements are systematic and cannot be explained by an estimated 5% rate of mistaken labels. We learn the experts' preferences from pairwise comparisons and use them to guide a crystal diffusion model. The learned preferences and numerical score agree on the flattest bands but diverge elsewhere. For example, the preferences favor KCo2As2 and CoGa, reported compounds with partially flat bands that the score would discard. The framework also extends to synthesizability and phonon properties. Our findings suggest that reward misalignment can expose opportunities for materials discovery beyond what fixed rewards are designed to find.
label: arXiv:2611.26186v1

summary.background:
- Electronic flat band: an energy band that is nearly horizontal, so electrons in it have very similar energies regardless of their momentum; such bands are of interest for strongly correlated electronic behavior.
- Bandwidth score: a single number summarizing how spread out a band is; a smaller number means flatter.
- Reward misalignment: when the score an AI system is optimized for does not match what people actually want.
- Pairwise comparison: asking an expert which of two options they prefer, then inferring a overall preference scale from many such choices.
- Crystal diffusion model: a generative model that proposes atomic crystal structures by iteratively refining random arrangements.
- Synthesizability and phonon properties: whether a material can plausibly be made, and how its atoms vibrate, both mentioned as extensions.
summary.one_liner: The paper argues that disagreements between a fixed numerical reward and expert judgment can point to promising materials, using electronic flat bands as the test case and learning expert preferences to steer a crystal diffusion model.
summary.plain: Computer models that design new materials are usually scored by a fixed rule, and this paper asks what happens when that rule disagrees with human experts. The authors ask experts to compare pairs of candidate materials, learn their preferences from those comparisons, and use them to guide a generative model. They report that experts mostly agree with the numerical score on the flattest electronic bands but disagree systematically elsewhere, and that the learned preferences favor some reported compounds with partially flat bands that the score would have discarded.
summary.why: It reframes a mismatch between AI objectives and expert judgment as a possible source of new candidates rather than only a failure, which may matter for AI-guided materials search. The text does not show that the flagged materials have been synthesized or validated beyond the stated comparisons, so the practical payoff is still unclear.

title: Reward misalignment as an opportunity for materials discovery

abstract: The ability to measure thermal properties and visualize heat transport processes with high spatial resolution is becoming increasingly important for materials discovery, next-generation electronics, and advanced manufacturing. As critical dimensions and architectures of novel materials and high performance electronics shrink and become more heterogeneous, thermal transport is no longer governed by bulk material properties alone, but by local variations in microstructure, such as interfaces and defects, while the operating conditions can also play a role. With the development of non-contact pump-probe thermoreflectance techniques, specific heat, thermal conductivity, and interface conductance can be mapped either through wide-field thermos-reflectance images or by scanning technique. However, key challenges remain such as the balance between imaging throughput and measurement accuracy, the extraction of multiple parameters with high confidence, and non-intrusive subsurface characterization, etc. This Review highlights recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI)-assistance in high-throughput data processing, visualizing interfacial thermal transport, and nonintrusive subsurface analysis, and offers outlooks for future research directions such as spectral mapping of heat carriers, three-dimensional property mapping, and AI-agentic experimental designs. We anticipate this Review will motivate future efforts in combining AI with experimental techniques to achieve unprecedented capabilities for thermal characterization of nanoscale materials and device characterization, facilitating materials discovery and electronics revolution.
label: arXiv:2611.25779v1

summary.background:
- Thermoreflectance: a non-contact optical method that uses a laser pulse to heat a surface and a second beam to detect small changes in reflected light, revealing how fast heat spreads.
- Thermal conductivity: how readily a material conducts heat.
- Interface conductance: how easily heat passes across a boundary between two materials; a bottleneck in many devices.
- Specific heat: how much heat a material stores per unit of temperature change.
- Wide-field vs. scanning imaging: capturing a whole area at once versus building a map point by point.
- Subsurface characterization: probing structure beneath the surface without cutting or destroying the sample.
- Machine learning / AI-agentic design: algorithms that learn from data, and systems that propose and run experiments with limited human direction.
summary.one_liner: A review of how artificial intelligence is being applied to pump-probe thermoreflectance imaging for mapping thermal properties, interfacial heat transport, and subsurface structure in nanoscale materials and devices.
summary.plain: This is a review article about using artificial intelligence to make heat-flow measurements of very small materials and electronic devices faster and more informative. The authors describe recent work that uses AI to process large volumes of thermal images, to visualize how heat crosses boundaries between materials, and to look beneath surfaces without damaging them. They also outline possible next steps, such as mapping which heat-carrying vibrations dominate, building three-dimensional property maps, and using AI to plan experiments.
summary.why: As devices and materials shrink and become more varied internally, heat behaves differently at local defects and interfaces, so fast, accurate thermal mapping matters for electronics and materials design. The text is a general overview and does not report new experimental results, so its practical impact is best judged by the specific studies it surveys.

title: Intelligent Imaging of Thermal Transport in Nanostructures

abstract: Soft biological materials are a fascinating kind of matter characterized by the unique ability of consuming internal energy to perform complex tasks to preserve the life of the single organism or a whole community. Moreover, biologically inspired materials able to mimic specific features of biological systems can be exploited to design novel materials with vast potential applications in areas ranging from healthcare and robotics to energy and environmental sustainability. In this review, we focus on the modeling approaches used to capture the dynamics of this peculiar kind of active matter, starting from the observation of orientational symmetries and reviewing the basis of the so-called active liquid crystal theory, a celebrated model that was successfully used to interpret and investigate a number of different phenomena occurring in both biological and artificial realizations. We review the role of topological defects in biological systems and discuss the complex phenomenon of active turbulence, a chaotic dynamical regime observed in a variety of different realizations of systems of both biological and synthetic origin. Finally, we discuss how geometrical and topological confinement can also play an important role in many biological processes, from cellular apoptosis in epithelial tissue, to animal morphogenesis.
label: arXiv:2611.25959v1

summary.background:
- Active matter: systems whose parts consume energy to move on their own, unlike passive materials such as water or rubber.
- Liquid crystals: materials whose building blocks share a preferred direction, like the molecules in an LCD screen; "orientational symmetry" refers to this alignment.
- Topological defects: points or lines where the alignment pattern cannot be smoothly continued, similar to a knot or a vortex in a fluid.
- Active turbulence: chaotic, swirling flow driven by energy input at small scales rather than by a push from outside.
- Confinement: restricting a system to a certain shape or space, such as cells inside a tissue or a droplet in a container.
- Apoptosis: programmed cell death; morphogenesis: the process by which an organism's body takes shape.
summary.one_liner: A review of continuum modeling of active matter in soft biological and bio-inspired materials, centred on active liquid crystal theory, topological defects, active turbulence, and confinement effects in tissues and morphogenesis.
summary.plain: This is a review article about how materials that are alive, or copy living systems, behave when they keep consuming their own internal energy to move and organise themselves. It surveys mathematical models, mainly one called active liquid crystal theory, that describe these systems. It also covers swirling chaotic flow known as active turbulence, and how confining shapes can influence processes such as cell death in tissue and the development of animal body shapes.
summary.why: The text suggests possible links to healthcare, robotics, energy and environmental uses, but it does not give specific applications or results, so these links are broad aims rather than demonstrated outcomes. It is mainly useful as an overview of modeling approaches for living and bio-inspired active matter.

title: Soft biological and bio-inspired materials

abstract: Branched macromolecular architectures are ubiquitous in living systems and synthetic polymeric systems, create topologically complex media that strongly influence tracer dynamics beyond simple packing fraction-driven crowding effects. Motivated by biological systems such as amoebae, astrocytes, cytoskeletal assemblies, and cyclic bottlebrushes, we investigate active and passive tracer transport in polymeric environments of topologically distinct architectures. Here, using Langevin dynamics simulations, we focus on how polymer topology alters diffusion behavior in a branched-ring polymeric (BRP) environment. To isolate the role of intramolecular topology from monomer density, we specifically benchmark the BRP dynamics against an unlinked linear-ring polymer mixture (LRM). In general, we find that while passive tracers are largely unaffected by the polymer connectivity and bending rigidity, the self-propelled active tracers strongly distinguish between the two architectures. Increasing chain rigidity facilitates active diffusion in the unlinked LRM but strongly restricts mobility in the BRP matrix, driving a transition to pronounced long-time subdiffusion that becomes more prominent with propulsion strength. Different physical observables reveal that interconnected topological cages are formed in the stiff limit, leading to transient weak ergodicity breaking and leptokurtic displacement statistics. Further, the self-intermediate scattering function confirms that the short-range dynamics remain unaltered by the matrix connectivity, while relaxation at large spatial length scales is governed by the topological caging. Finally, varying the branch length and number, we identified an optimal branch architecture that maximizes active trapping. Our results establish that macromolecular connectivity and stiffness dominate the active transport even in the system of identical packing fraction.
label: arXiv:2611.25528v1

summary.background:
- Tracer: a small particle followed to measure how a medium moves it.
- Passive vs active tracer: passive ones are only pushed around by thermal jiggling; active ones have their own propulsion, like a swimming microbe.
- Subdiffusion: motion that slows down over time, getting stuck more than random wandering would predict.
- Packing fraction: the share of space filled by the polymer material; here the study holds it fixed.
- Ring polymer: a closed loop of linked units; branched rings have side arms attached to the loop.
- Langevin dynamics: a simulation method that models particle motion with friction and random kicks.
- Weak ergodicity breaking: a particle's long-run average depends on its starting situation, so it does not explore the whole space evenly.
- Leptokurtic displacement: most steps are short but occasional long jumps occur, giving heavy-tailed statistics.
- Intermediate scattering function: a measure of how long a pattern of particle positions persists at a given length scale.
summary.one_liner: Langevin dynamics simulations show that self-propelled tracers are trapped and driven into long-time subdiffusion by branched ring polymer matrices, with stiffness and connectivity mattering more than packing density, while passive tracers are largely unaffected.
summary.plain: This study asks how the tangled shape of large molecules affects the movement of tiny particles that swim or move on their own, such as cells or motile microbes moving through a crowded gel. The researchers used computer simulations of branched ring-shaped polymers and compared them with a mixture of unlinked linear rings at the same density. They found that ordinary passive particles hardly notice the difference, but self-propelled ones get trapped much more in the branched network, especially when the polymer chains are stiff.
summary.why: The results suggest that how polymers are connected and how stiff they are can matter more than how crowded the space is, which may be relevant to how cells and active particles move through biological tissue or synthetic materials. The text is a simulation study, so its relevance to real biological systems is suggested by the authors' motivation rather than shown directly.

title: Topological trapping of active tracers in branched ring polymer matrices

abstract: Identifying active molecules for known targets and potential targets for existing drugs is central to drug discovery and repurposing. Drug-target interaction (DTI) models can rank vast numbers of drug-target pairs, but limited experimental capacity restricts testing to a small number of candidates. We compared the bidirectional recommendations of 13 released systems across 711 molecular structures of FDA-approved drugs and 614 human proteins. For the same target or drug, pairs of models produced completely disjoint Top-10 molecule and protein lists in 77.8% and 70.1% of comparisons, respectively. Even where recommendations overlapped, agreement between some systems largely reflected recurring preferences for the same candidates. Published inhibition measurements for 79 molecules and 65 kinases revealed that some systems enriched active candidates, yet their hit yields changed little when recommendations were matched to different drugs or targets, whereas other systems lost substantially more hits. Some of the former systems also rarely ranked both molecules and kinases correctly when two drugs favoured different kinases. We further retrained the same architecture on the same data, with the training objective fixed and random seeds varied. Despite similar test performance, mean pairwise Top-10 overlap on a separate screening catalogue was about two candidates. Our study moves DTI model evaluation beyond benchmark performance to assess whether model predictions can guide meaningful experimental decisions in drug discovery and target identification.
label: arXiv:2611.26369v1

summary.background:
- Drug-target interaction (DTI) model: software that predicts how strongly a drug molecule will bind a protein.
- Benchmark performance: a model's accuracy score on a fixed test dataset; it may not reflect real-world usefulness.
- Top-10 overlap: how many of the 10 highest-ranked candidates two models share; low overlap means they disagree.
- Kinases: a protein family often used as drug targets; inhibition measurements show whether a molecule blocks them.
- Random seed: a starting number for training a model; changing it can yield a different model even with identical data and settings.
