- Bidirectional screening: asking both which proteins suit a given drug and which drugs suit a given protein.
summary.one_liner: A bidirectional benchmark of 13 published drug-target interaction models on FDA-approved drugs and human proteins finds that their top-ranked recommendations often disagree sharply, and that some models' hit rates depend on matching, while retraining with different random seeds changes top-10 lists substantially.
summary.plain: Computer models are used to guess which drugs might act on which proteins, so that scientists know what to test in the lab. This paper compares 13 such released models on about 711 approved drugs and 614 human proteins, and asks whether their suggestions are consistent and useful. The authors found that the models often gave very different top-10 lists, and that some models found more active compounds against kinases (a family of proteins) than others, though not all of them held up when the drugs or targets were swapped.
summary.why: Drug-repurposing and target-finding pipelines depend on these rankings, and the paper suggests that good scores on standard benchmarks do not guarantee that the top picks are reliable for real lab decisions. The text is a preprint-style summary, so the scope of its conclusions is limited to the datasets and models it tested.

title: From Benchmarks to the Bench: Preference, Correspondence and Selectivity in Bidirectional Drug-Target Screening

abstract: Rare events drive transformations across physics, chemistry and biology, yet predicting their mechanisms and rates remains a fundamental challenge. Here we introduce Pharos, a framework that learns to make rare transitions accessible while predicting how frequently they occur under physical dynamics. Through stochastic optimal control, Pharos jointly learns the probability of completing a transition and how to steer simulations toward it, allowing sampling and learning to improve one another. Across biomolecular benchmarks, Pharos learns accurate transition probabilities with order-of-magnitude gains in convergence speed over previous algorithms. It transfers across ion assembly systems in explicit solvent while maintaining accurate reaction rate predictions, scales to host-guest binding systems that span millisecond timescales, and enables chemical reaction studies with a computationally demanding machine learning interatomic potential. By combining efficient sampling, quantitative kinetics, and transferability, Pharos opens a route toward foundation models of rare event mechanisms and rates across molecular systems.
label: arXiv:2611.26765v1

summary.background:
- Rare event: a change that happens very infrequently relative to the time step of a simulation, such as a protein folding or a drug molecule binding.
- Molecular dynamics: computer simulation of how atoms move under physical forces over time.
- Transition rate / kinetics: how often an event occurs per unit time; the quantity this work aims to estimate accurately.
- Stochastic optimal control: a mathematical framework for choosing how to steer a random process (here, a simulation) to reach a target at low cost.
- Machine learning interatomic potential: a learned model that approximates the energy and forces between atoms, cheaper than quantum calculations but still costly to run.
- Host-guest binding: one molecule (guest) fitting into a larger molecule (host), a standard test system for binding kinetics.
summary.one_liner: Pharos uses stochastic optimal control to learn both the probability of completing a rare molecular transition and how to bias simulations toward it, aiming for faster and quantitatively accurate rate estimates under physical dynamics.
summary.plain: The paper deals with rare events, such as a molecule changing shape or two molecules binding, which happen so seldom that ordinary computer simulations almost never see them. The authors built a method, called Pharos, that learns how to nudge a simulation toward these events while still estimating how often they happen. The abstract reports faster convergence on biomolecular test cases and applications to ion assembly, host-guest binding and chemical reactions, though the abstract gives only limited detail on these results.
summary.why: Estimating how fast rare events occur is a long-standing bottleneck in chemistry, biology and materials design, so a faster route to accurate rates would matter if it holds up. The abstract's claims of an order-of-magnitude speedup and use with a machine learning interatomic potential are reported by the authors and are not independently checked here; the stated goal of "foundation models" for rare events is an aspiration rather than a demonstrated result.

title: Pharos: Learning to Control Rare Events at Scale

abstract: Radical S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) enzymes that synthesize structurally constrained ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs) with therapeutic potential mostly do so by employing a dedicated RiPP recognition element (RRE). With the growing number of RRE-free maturases discovered, how these enzymes engage their substrates remains largely unexplored. In this work, we mapped substrate-enzyme interactions in DarE, an RRE-free radical SAM enzyme that installs the C-C and C-O-C crosslinks of the antibiotic darobactin during the first step of darobactin biosynthesis. Using anaerobic hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS), we simultaneously resolved specific regions within the enzyme and its precursor peptide substrate, DarA, across five complex states. The N-terminal extension and part of the TIM-barrel domain of DarE, along with the leader region of DarA, become protected, revealing the peptide-engagement interface. Additional protection emerged only in the presence of SAM, identifying SAM as a key contributor to precursor-peptide engagement in an RRE-free RiPP maturase. Electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy further demonstrated precursor peptide-dependent perturbations of the chemical environment of the iron-sulfur clusters. These findings suggest that SAM-dependent peptide engagement, mediated in part by the N-terminal extension of the radical SAM enzyme, provides an alternative mechanism for precursor-peptide recognition in RRE-free RiPP maturases. Our work also demonstrates the utility of anaerobic HDX-MS for characterizing protein-peptide-small molecule interactions in oxygen-sensitive metalloenzymes.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.767387 v1

summary.background:
- RiPPs (ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides): small peptides made by ribosomes and then chemically modified; many become drugs or antibiotics.
- Radical SAM enzymes: enzymes that use an iron-sulfur cluster and S-adenosylmethionine (SAM, a common cofactor) to make radical chemistry possible.
- RRE (RiPP recognition element): a separate protein module that many such enzymes use to bind their peptide; DarE lacks one.
- Darobactin: an antibiotic whose structure contains C-C and C-O-C crosslinks installed by DarE.
- HDX-MS: a method that measures how fast backbone hydrogens swap with deuterium from water; regions that are shielded (for example by binding) swap more slowly. Anaerobic use protects oxygen-sensitive iron-sulfur clusters.
- EPR spectroscopy: a technique that detects unpaired electrons and reports on the local chemical environment of metal clusters.
summary.one_liner: Using anaerobic hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry and EPR spectroscopy, this study maps how the RRE-free radical SAM maturase DarE engages its precursor peptide DarA, and finds that the cofactor SAM contributes to peptide binding.
summary.plain: Bacteria make some antibiotics by first building a peptide chain and then having an enzyme stitch parts of it together with chemical crosslinks. This paper looks at how the enzyme DarE grabs its peptide partner, DarA, in the making of the antibiotic darobactin. The authors used a method that tracks which parts of the protein and peptide become shielded when they bind, and found that a region at the front of the enzyme, plus the leader part of the peptide, come together, with extra shielding only when the cofactor SAM is present.
summary.why: Most enzymes of this family use a separate helper module to recognise their peptide, but DarE does not, so the paper offers a different recognition route that may apply to other RRE-free enzymes. The text does not establish how general this mechanism is beyond DarE, and the study is limited to a single enzyme-peptide pair.

title: SAM-Dependent Precursor Peptide Engagement by Darobactin Maturase DarE

abstract: A key question in the RNA world hypothesis for the origin of life is the nature of the compartment that separates and protects the RNA from its environment. While membranes are a leading candidate for the initial compartment, biomolecular condensates have been proposed as an alternative, possibly simpler route to compartments. Here we show that bona fide liquid condensates form spontaneously when nucleotides (such as ATP) are mixed with divalent cations and a short-chain alcohol or diol in water. These condensates do not require any polymer to form, but can concentrate polymers like RNA and DNA, which show unexpected chemical behavior inside the condensates. Most surprisingly, RNA survives for days inside nucleotide condensates under acidic conditions that cause rapid and extensive hydrolysis in bulk. This effect is also observed for a phosphate-ester model substrate and therefore likely reflects the suppression of backbone cleavage. Coarse-grained simulations suggest that the condensate interior is bound together by magnesium-phosphate bridging interactions and is therefore highly depleted of water. At neutral pH, the same compartment reverses the course of a hammerhead ribozyme reaction, shifting it from cleavage toward religation. Finally, we observe that nucleotide droplets also spontaneously organize phospholipids at their surface, suggesting a possible evolutionary route from biomolecular condensates toward membranes. Thus, we believe that nucleotide condensates, which are built from the same building blocks as the genetic polymers themselves, overcome long-standing challenges with the RNA world hypothesis for the origin of life by protecting nucleic acids and reshaping their chemistry.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767475 v1

summary.background:
- RNA world hypothesis: the idea that RNA came before DNA and proteins, carrying both genetic information and some catalysis.
- Biomolecular condensate: a droplet that forms by molecules separating from water, like oil in vinegar, without a membrane around it.
- Hydrolysis: water breaking a chemical bond; RNA's backbone is vulnerable to this, especially in acid.
- Ribozyme: an RNA molecule that catalyses a chemical reaction. The hammerhead ribozyme cuts RNA; religation is the reverse, joining the pieces back together.
- Divalent cations: positively charged metal ions with a 2+ charge, such as magnesium, that bridge negatively charged phosphate groups.
- Coarse-grained simulation: a simplified computer model that represents groups of atoms as single beads to study large-scale behaviour.
summary.one_liner: Nucleotides such as ATP, mixed with divalent cations and a short-chain alcohol or diol in water, form liquid condensates that concentrate RNA and DNA, protect RNA from acid hydrolysis, and shift a hammerhead ribozyme reaction from cleavage toward religation.
summary.plain: This paper asks how the earliest RNA-based life could have been kept apart from its surroundings before cell membranes existed. The authors report that simple nucleotide molecules, such as ATP, form droplet-like liquid compartments when mixed with metal ions and a small alcohol in water. Inside these droplets, RNA lasted for days under acidic conditions where it would normally break down quickly, and a ribozyme (an RNA that acts as an enzyme) reacted in the reverse direction.

title: Unexpected properties of nucleotide condensates could facilitate the RNA world

abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the deadliest cancers, largely due to its poor response to chemotherapy and the development of drug resistance. Survivin (BIRC5), an inhibitor of apoptosis frequently overexpressed in PDAC, contributes to tumor cell survival and gemcitabine resistance, making it an attractive therapeutic target. Here, we developed a lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-based platform for the delivery of preassembled spCas13b ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) to achieve transient and sequence-specific RNA silencing in pancreatic cancer cells. We optimized ionizable lipid formulations for Cas13b RNP encapsulation and identified a formulation achieving approximately 80% encapsulation efficiency, with sustained colloidal stability and gene-silencing activity during seven days of storage at 4{degrees}C. LNP-delivered Cas13b RNPs efficiently silenced endogenous BIRC5 in three pancreatic cancer cell lines, reducing survivin protein levels and inducing apoptosis. In gemcitabine-resistant PANC-1 cells, BIRC5 silencing synergistically enhanced the cytotoxic effect of gemcitabine in vitro. This therapeutic combination was further evaluated in a PANC-1 xenograft model, where only the combined administration of BIRC5-targeting Cas13b RNP-LNPs and gemcitabine significantly inhibited tumor growth, without apparent systemic toxicity. Intratumoral administration also restricted nanoparticle distribution to the injected tumors. These findings establish LNP-mediated delivery of Cas13b RNPs as a new strategy for transient RNA-targeted therapy and provide proof of concept for combining survivin silencing by Cas13b with chemotherapy to address gemcitabine resistance in pancreatic cancer.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767627 v1

summary.background:
- Gemcitabine: a standard chemotherapy drug for pancreatic cancer; tumor cells can become resistant to it.
- Survivin (BIRC5): a protein that blocks programmed cell death (apoptosis); it is often overexpressed in pancreatic tumors.
- RNA silencing: reducing how much of a specific protein a cell makes by destroying its messenger RNA.
- Cas13b: a bacterial enzyme that can be guided to cut specific RNA molecules; "ribonucleoprotein" (RNP) means the enzyme is delivered pre-bound to its guide RNA.
- Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs): tiny fat-based carriers that deliver molecules into cells; ionizable lipids help them load and release cargo.
- Xenograft: human cancer cells grown as tumors in mice, used to test treatments before human trials.
- Encapsulation efficiency: the share of the cargo that is successfully packed inside the particles.
summary.one_liner: Preassembled Cas13b ribonucleoproteins delivered in ionizable lipid nanoparticles silence BIRC5 (survivin) RNA transiently in pancreatic cancer cells and, in a PANC-1 xenograft model, combine with gemcitabine to slow tumor growth.
summary.plain: Pancreatic cancer is very hard to treat, partly because tumors stop responding to the chemotherapy drug gemcitabine. This study packaged a molecular "scissors" protein complex (Cas13b, which cuts a specific messenger RNA) inside fatty nanoparticles, then used it to switch down a survival gene called survivin. In lab cells and in mice with pancreatic tumors, switching down survivin together with gemcitabine slowed tumor growth more than either alone, according to the authors.
summary.why: Gemcitabine resistance is a central problem in pancreatic cancer, and the paper offers a proof-of-concept way to pair an RNA-targeting tool with chemotherapy. Because the silencing is meant to be transient, it may suit safer, temporary treatments, but the text is a single preclinical study in one xenograft model, so clinical relevance is unproven.

title: Lipid nanoparticle-delivered Cas13b ribonucleoproteins targeting survivin overcome gemcitabine resistance in pancreatic cancer

abstract: Antibody-antigen structure prediction commonly relies on sampling a single co-folding predictor deeply and selecting its highest-confidence output using model-specific confidence scores. We introduce AbPoolRank, a predictor-agnostic structural selector that ranks mixed pools using cross-pose agreement, within-source reproducibility and interface geometry, without native confidence, predictor identities or predictor-specific parameters. On 103 cluster-disjoint, post-2021 antibody-antigen complexes from SAbDab2, three structures each from Boltz-2, Promera, Protenix-v2, ESMFold2-Fast and OpenDDE form a 15-structure pool that reaches 58.0% medium-or-better Success@1 (DockQ [≥] 0.49), exceeding confidence-based selection from every individual predictor sampled 100 times (26-52%). Existing ranking methods did not rescue deep single-predictor sampling or surpass our selector on mixed pools, with no method exceeding 51.5% on 100 structures from one co-folder and AbPoolRank matching the strongest single-structure methods while significantly outperforming consensus methods. AbPoolRank trained without one predictor lost at most 3.0 percentage points, and the frozen model accepted full MSA-conditioned ESMFold2, a sixth predictor absent from method development, without retraining or loss of accuracy. Diversification also improved the accuracy-compute frontier, with the 15-structure pool using 1.8-fold less aggregate GPU time than the most accurate single-predictor setting in our compute benchmark and 3.3-fold less than sampling that predictor 100 times. Together, these results show that shallow sampling across complementary co-folders, coupled with a confidence-free selector, provides an accurate and computationally efficient inference strategy for antibody-antigen structure prediction.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.767212 v1

summary.background:
- Protein structure prediction: AI tools that predict a molecule's 3D shape from its amino acid sequence.
- Antibody-antigen complex: an antibody bound to the molecule it targets (the antigen).
- Co-folding predictor: a model that predicts the shapes of several molecules together, such as an antibody and its target.
- Confidence score: a number a predictor outputs to rate its own answer; the paper's method avoids relying on it.
- DockQ and Success@1: a quality score for how well a predicted binding pose matches the real one, and the share of cases where the top-ranked answer is good enough (DockQ at least 0.49 for medium quality).
- Consensus and sampling: generating many candidate structures and picking those that agree with one another, versus generating many from one model.
- GPU time: the computing cost measured on graphics processors.
summary.one_liner: AbPoolRank is a confidence-free, predictor-agnostic selector that picks the best antibody-antigen complex structure from a mixed pool of outputs from several co-folding predictors, reaching 58.0% medium-or-better Success@1 on 103 post-2021 SAbDab2 complexes and beating deep sampling of any single predictor (26-52%).
summary.plain: Antibodies are immune proteins that stick to a target molecule, and predicting the 3D shape of the antibody bound to its target is useful for drug design. This paper argues that instead of running one AI structure predictor many times and trusting its own confidence score, it is better to collect a small set of answers from several different predictors and use a separate scoring method to pick the best one. On 103 recent antibody-target complexes, the mixed pool of 15 structures picked correctly more often than any single predictor sampled 100 times, and it also used less computing time.
summary.why: Choosing the right answer from many AI predictions is a practical bottleneck in structure prediction, and the paper reports both better accuracy and lower compute cost. The text reports results only on the benchmark described; how well it transfers to real drug-discovery workflows is not shown here.

title: Breadth over Depth: Predictor-Agnostic Consensus for Improved Antibody--Antigen Structure Prediction

abstract: Motivation: Pathogen phylogenies are useful for monitoring the evolution of pathogens and for detecting new variants, as it provides information that can aid public health decisions and outbreak response. Since not all infections are sequenced, certain pathogen lineages may be missing or only poorly represented in reconstructed phylogenies. Identifying these gaps could help to determine where additional data collection is required. Results: We developed a computational method to locate regions of missing samples from the observed tree alone, without sequences from those samples. A machine learning model predicts which branches lead toward the missing region. Beam search then identifies three representative paths and estimates a candidate most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of the missing region for each path. We tested this framework on 5,000 simulated phylogenies where we controlled which tips were deleted. On an independent test set, the best candidate recovered an average of 89.9% of deleted tips, increasing to 90.7% when all three candidates were combined. Predicted and true MRCAs lay on the same ancestral-descendant lineage in 91.3% of cases. We further evaluated the approach on an empirical SARS-CoV-2 phylogeny with introduced missingness. By identifying potentially underrepresented lineages, this framework could help real-time identification of missing infections and improve outbreak response.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767590 v1

summary.background:
- A phylogeny is a tree diagram showing how sampled genomes are related by descent; tips are the sampled sequences and branches are the lineages connecting them.
- The most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of a group is the earliest point on the tree from which all members of that group descend.
- Machine learning here means a model trained on example trees to predict which branches lead toward missing data.
- Beam search is a method that keeps a small set of the most promising paths while exploring a tree, rather than checking every path.
- Simulated phylogenies are computer-generated trees where the true answer is known, so the method can be scored against it.
- Sampling gaps are common because not every infection is sequenced, so the observed tree can misrepresent the full outbreak.
summary.one_liner: A machine learning and beam-search method that infers, from an observed pathogen phylogeny alone, which branches lead toward unsampled regions and estimates the most recent common ancestor of each missing region, evaluated on simulated and introduced-missingness SARS-CoV-2 trees.
summary.plain: Genetic family trees of viruses are built from the genomes that labs have actually sequenced, but many infections are never sequenced, so some virus lineages may be missing or underrepresented. This paper describes a computer method that looks only at the tree that was built and tries to point to where those gaps are, without seeing any sequences from the missing cases. On 5,000 simulated trees with deliberately removed tips, the best of its candidate locations recovered on average about 90% of the deleted tips.
summary.why: Knowing where sampling is thin could guide where public health teams collect more samples during outbreaks, which matters for spotting new variants. The text reports results only on simulated trees and one SARS-CoV-2 tree with artificially introduced gaps, so its real-world usefulness is not yet shown.

title: Localizing Unsampled Regions in Partially Sampled Pathogen Phylogenies Using Machine Learning

abstract: Neuroscience relies on diverse model species to understand animal behavior and brain function. Yet, tools for rapid, high-resolution brain connectivity mapping remain unavailable in most vertebrate species, slowing progress in many neuroscience models and rendering cross-species circuit comparisons challenging. Here, we overcome this barrier by establishing sequencing-based barcoded connectomics for rapid single-neuron tracing in seven vertebrate species ranging from frogs to birds to non-human primates. We develop a general solution to viral tropism and barcode trafficking, validate our reagents by mapping the projections of thousands of neurons in the songbird HVC, and discover a single set of reagents that functions across highly divergent species. Together, we provide ready-to-use barcoding reagents for diverse species and a simple framework for further adapting them if necessary, enabling high throughput single-neuron tracing across vertebrates.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767886 v1

summary.background:
- Connectomics: mapping which brain cells connect to which others.
- Projection mapping: following a neuron's long output fibres to their target regions.
- Barcoding: labelling each neuron with a unique short DNA sequence, delivered by a virus, so that sequencing the target tissue reveals which barcodes arrived where.
- Viral tropism: a virus's preference for infecting certain cell types; the paper addresses limits here that block the method in some species.
- HVC: a songbird brain region tied to song production, used here as a test system.
- Vertebrates: animals with a backbone, including fish, amphibians, birds, and mammals.
summary.one_liner: The paper reports sequencing-based barcoded connectomics, a method that tags individual neurons' projections with DNA barcodes, adapted to work across seven vertebrate species and validated by mapping thousands of songbird HVC neurons.
summary.plain: Scientists want to know which parts of the brain each nerve cell connects to, but good mapping tools exist mainly for a few lab animals. This paper adapts a DNA-barcoding approach so that it works in seven vertebrate species, from frogs and birds to non-human primates. The authors tested it by tracing the projections of thousands of neurons in the songbird HVC, a brain region involved in birdsong, and found one set of reagents that worked across very different species.
summary.why: Being able to trace single neurons in many species at once could make it easier to compare brain wiring across animals, which is hard when each species needs its own tools. The text presents ready-to-use reagents and a framework for adapting them, but it does not show how far these results will carry to other brain regions or species.

title: Universal barcoded connectomics for massively parallel single-neuron projection mapping in diverse vertebrate species

abstract: Adaptive behavior is commonly framed as an optimization problem, in which organisms learn to maximize reward. Here we show that simple networks with local, Hebbian-like learning rules, which have no reward objective, nonetheless reproduce hallmark features of animal reward-seeking when placed in closed-loop environments where rewards arrive as ordinary sensory input. Six canonical local learning rules were tested under these conditions, and despite most rules being designed for unsupervised representation learning, all rules learned to seek out signal. However, at the parameters tested, only one rule, prospective configuration, robustly captured all of a set of tested phenomena: reward-magnitude-dependent learning rates, probability matching, memory retention across contexts, and switching between exploration and exploitation with heavy-tailed statistics. In these networks, actions that produce input become self-sustaining states (attractors) of network dynamics. Attractors reside in an activity-weight space and mediate behaviors, and adapt to their environments rather than being fixed properties of the networks. These flexible geometries provide a parsimonious account of how heavy-tailed runs of repeated choices, which resemble Levy flights seen in foraging, also change with the environment. A single framework then makes predictions about behavior and neural population geometries that can be used to investigate the learning dynamics of the brain.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767638 v1

summary.background:
- Hebbian learning: a rule where connections between neurons strengthen when they are active together, roughly "cells that fire together wire together."
- Local learning rule: an update that uses only information available at the connection itself, with no global reward signal.
- Closed-loop environment: the network's actions change what sensory input it receives next, which then feeds back into learning.
- Attractor: a stable pattern of activity a network settles into and tends to stay in; here, actions that produce input become self-sustaining.
- Probability matching: choosing options in proportion to how often they pay off, rather than always picking the best one.
- Heavy-tailed runs / Levy flights: movement patterns with many short steps and occasional very long ones, often seen in animal foraging.
- Reward optimization: the standard framing in which an agent is assumed to learn to maximize a reward value.
summary.one_liner: Simulated networks trained only with local Hebbian-like learning rules, with no reward objective and rewards delivered as ordinary sensory input, show reward-seeking features, with the prospective configuration rule matching the tested phenomena most consistently and behaviour explained by flexible attractors in activity-weight space.
summary.plain: The paper asks whether animals must be maximizing a reward to behave adaptively, or whether simple learning rules that strengthen connections between co-active neurons can produce similar behaviour. The authors built small networks, placed them in closed-loop environments where rewards appear as ordinary sensory input, and tested six standard learning rules. All of them learned to seek out the signal, but only one rule, prospective configuration, consistently reproduced the full set of tested behaviours.

title: Adaptive behaviors emerge from Hebbian-like plasticity through flexible attractors

abstract: Motivation: Genetic diseases are complex phenomena that are currently defined by their clinical symptoms, rather than by the combinations of variants that give rise to them. Incomplete penetrance and phenotypic variability indicate that the genomic background contributes to the effect of variants. Recent advancements in genomics have produced vast amounts of data and created new opportunities to study genetic diversity across human populations. Much of this variation is inherited as recombination-defined contiguous segments, called haploblocks. We previously introduced a novel methodology for genomic hash encoding, the Genomic Cluster Engine, which groups individuals into clusters using phased haploblock sequences. By encoding each haploblock sequence as a compact hash, the characterization of genomic backgrounds, the subtyping of etiologies and the inference of local ancestry become fast and scalable. Results: We have optimized the Genomic Cluster Engine pipeline for large genomic datasets through parallelization and improved memory management. We applied our pipeline to 2,548 individuals across 26 populations from the 1000 Genomes Project and produced a dataset of haploblock-based genomic hashes for the resulting clusters. The genomic hashes and clusters can be used for investigating variant effects in the context of their haplotype backgrounds or for genotype-phenotype association studies. This comprehensive dataset is now publicly available, providing a valuable resource for both academic and industry researchers worldwide. Availability: The haploblock boundaries, sequences, clusters and genomic hashes for the 1000 Genomes Project are available under the CC0 license at https://data.haploblocks.org and on the Registry of Open Data on AWS https://registry.opendata.aws.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767536 v1

summary.background:
- Genome: the full set of DNA instructions in a person.
- Variant: a difference in DNA sequence between people.
- Haplotype: the set of variants inherited together on one copy of a chromosome.
- Haploblock: a long stretch of DNA passed down largely intact between generations, because recombination (the shuffling of chromosomes during reproduction) rarely breaks it up.
- Phased: sequence data where variants are assigned to the correct chromosome copy.
- Hash: a fixed-length code computed from data, used here to make comparisons fast.
- Penetrance: how often a genetic variant actually produces its associated trait or disease.
- 1000 Genomes Project: a public catalogue of genomes from people across many populations.
summary.one_liner: This paper describes an optimized run of the Genomic Cluster Engine, a hash-based method that groups people by phased haploblock sequences, applied to 2,548 1000 Genomes individuals across 26 populations, and releases the resulting public dataset of haploblock boundaries, sequences, clusters and genomic hashes.
summary.plain: Genetic diseases are usually defined by their symptoms rather than by the specific gene variants behind them, and the surrounding DNA can change how a variant behaves. This paper reports on a computing pipeline that summarizes each stretch of inherited DNA as a compact code and groups people with similar stretches together. The authors ran it on 2,548 people from 26 populations in the 1000 Genomes Project and made the resulting data freely available.
summary.why: The main contribution is a public, reusable resource rather than a new biological finding, and the text does not report results from disease studies. It may be useful for researchers studying how a variant's effect depends on the genetic background it sits in, though the text does not show this being done yet.

title: Generation of a Public Dataset for Etiological Subtyping with the Genomic Cluster Engine

abstract: Vertebral fracture risk is influenced by trabecular bone (Tb) microarchitecture, a phenotype that is regulated by genetic and environmental factors. We examined the genetic architecture of Tb microarchitecture in the fifth lumbar vertebra (L5) and its modification by dietary calcium (Ca). Male mice from 51 BXD recombinant inbred lines were fed adequate (0.5%) or low (0.25%) Ca diets from 4 to 12 weeks of age. Micro-computed tomography (CT) was used to assess seven L5 Tb phenotypes, and the response to Ca restriction (RCR) was calculated for each phenotype. Quantitative trait loci (QTL) were identified by composite interval mapping and compared with previously reported femoral Tb QTL from the same mice. Genetic background significantly influenced all L5 phenotypes and their responses to Ca restriction. We identified 127 QTL distributed across 61 loci. First, very few L5 QTL overlapped those previously identified in the femur, providing strong evidence for skeletal site-specific genetic regulation of Tb microarchitecture. Second, QTL detection was strongly dependent on dietary Ca, with only 4 of 33 loci identified under adequate Ca intake also detected under low Ca intake. Third, QTL controlling the RCR were largely distinct from those controlling L5 phenotypes under either dietary condition. Many loci affected multiple phenotypes, suggesting shared genetic regulation of Tb characteristics. Integration of genetic variation, expression QTL, and existing functional evidence identified plausible candidate genes at several high-priority loci. Together, these findings demonstrate that genetic regulation of Tb microarchitecture is both skeletal site-specific and diet-dependent, and that adaptation to dietary Ca restriction has a distinct genetic component.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767695 v1

summary.background:
- Trabecular bone: the spongy, porous inner part of bone, whose struts and spacing (microarchitecture) affect strength.
- Micro-computed tomography (micro-CT): X-ray imaging that builds 3D pictures of bone structure at very fine scale.
- BXD recombinant inbred lines: a fixed panel of mouse strains derived from crossing two parent strains, so each line has a stable, shared mix of their genes; this lets researchers link genetic regions to traits across repeated measurements.
- QTL (quantitative trait locus): a chromosome region statistically associated with variation in a measurable trait.
- Composite interval mapping: a statistical method for locating QTL while accounting for nearby QTL.
- Expression QTL (eQTL): a genetic region that influences how much a nearby gene is switched on, used to narrow down candidate genes.
- Response to calcium restriction (RCR): how much a bone trait changes when dietary calcium is lowered, computed per phenotype.
summary.one_liner: In 51 BXD recombinant inbred mouse lines fed adequate or low dietary calcium, the authors mapped 127 QTL across 61 loci for L5 vertebral trabecular bone microarchitecture and its response to calcium restriction, finding little overlap with femoral QTL and strong diet dependence.
summary.plain: This study asks how genes and diet together shape the internal lattice of spongy bone in the lower back bones of mice, which relates to how easily vertebrae can fracture. Male mice from 51 related inbred strains were raised on normal or low-calcium food, their vertebrae were scanned in 3D, and the chromosome regions linked to each bone trait were mapped. The authors report that most of these regions differed from those previously found in the thigh bone, differed between the two diets, and that the response to low calcium had its own genetic pattern.
summary.why: Vertebral fractures are a major concern in bone disease, and the text suggests that genetic studies done in one bone may not carry over to another or to different diets. The paper identifies candidate genes at several high-priority loci, but the text does not show whether these hold up in humans, so the link to clinical bone health remains unestablished.

title: Site-Specific and Diet-Dependent Genetic Architecture of Trabecular Bone in Male BXD Recombinant Inbred Mice

abstract: We propose a semi-mechanistic ODE-based transcription model for zebrafish embryogenesis that captures common baseline expression dynamics by integrating the maternal-to-zygotic transition mechanism. We fitted this model to a time-course RNA-seq dataset of D. rerio spanning early developmental stages until 120 hpf. Using the inferred model parameters, we identified common gene expression pattern using fuzzy c-means clustering and compared these with clusters stemming from a shape-based approach using smooth trajectories. We show that the ODE-parameter-based approach improves to biological interpretability by linking clusters to underlying regulatory mechanism, such as the timing of zygotic genome activation, thereby generating more precise expression clusters. However, the results also revealed technical biases of the time-course data, originating from the poly(A) enrichment step.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.767246 v1

summary.background:
- Maternal-to-zygotic transition: early embryos rely on RNA and proteins deposited by the mother until their own genome switches on (zygotic genome activation).
- RNA-seq: a method that counts how much of each gene's RNA is present in a sample, used here over a time course.
- ODE (ordinary differential equation) model: a set of equations describing how quantities such as RNA levels change over time, with parameters fitted to data.
- Clustering: sorting genes into groups with similar behaviour; fuzzy c-means allows a gene to partly belong to several groups.
- Poly(A) enrichment: a lab step that selects messenger RNA by its tail; it can bias which transcripts are measured.
- hpf: hours post fertilization, a standard embryo age unit.
summary.one_liner: A semi-mechanistic ODE model of zebrafish maternal-to-zygotic transition is fitted to time-course RNA-seq data, and its inferred parameters are used with fuzzy c-means clustering to group genes by shared expression baselines, compared against a shape-based smooth-trajectory clustering.
summary.plain: Early zebrafish embryos first run on molecules supplied by the egg, then switch to making their own genetic instructions. This paper builds a mathematical model of that handover and fits it to measurements of gene activity in zebrafish from early stages up to 120 hours after fertilization. The authors then group genes by patterns the model predicts, and compare these groups with groups formed from the plain shape of each gene's activity curve.
summary.why: The authors report that grouping genes by model parameters gives clusters linked to the timing of zygotic genome activation, which they describe as more precise than shape-only grouping. The paper also reports that the data carry technical bias from the poly(A) enrichment step, a caveat that matters for anyone interpreting such time-course sequencing data. The text does not say how large or general these gains are.

title: Modelling Maternal-to-Zygotic Transition Dynamics to Identify Common Gene Expression Baselines in Zebrafish Development.

abstract: Chiral organs such as the gut develop complex, stereotyped shapes, despite variability in the molecular and cellular processes that build them. How cell activity specifies tissue-scale handedness and reproducibly shapes whole organs remains unclear. Here, we use the embryonic Drosophila midgut to understand how a symmetric tubular organ reliably coils into a complex loop of alternating handedness, without any known left-right asymmetric gene expression.Through multi-view light-sheet imaging, 3D geometric analysis, and physical modeling, we show that midgut handedness is specified by epithelial cells in a neighboring organ, relayed across all three germ layers, and finally amplified and canalized by the mechanics of confined gut elongation. Myosin 1C expression in the hindgut epithelium controls midgut handedness up to hundreds of microns away, transmitting chiral bias to the midgut through migratory cells that form the longitudinal muscle. As the midgut elongates, a buckling instability then amplifies early left-right asymmetric constrictions, and confinement funnels the organ into a stereotyped coil. Tissue mechanics thus canalizes organ shape into one of two chiral forms, selected by an inter-organ cellular relay.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.766015 v1

summary.background:
- Chirality (handedness): an object that cannot be superimposed on its mirror image, like a left vs. right hand.
- Left-right asymmetry: normally, body organs are patterned to one side by specific genes; here the authors say no known asymmetric gene expression is involved in the gut.
- Myosin 1C: a motor protein that helps cells generate and shape mechanical force.
- Epithelium: a sheet of tightly joined cells that lines organs and tubes.
- Longitudinal muscle: muscle fibers running along the length of the gut, built by migrating cells.
- Buckling instability: the tendency of a stretched tube or rod to bend sideways under compression, like a bent straw pressed at its ends.
- Light-sheet imaging: a microscopy method that illuminates a thin slice of a living sample to image it over time with little damage.
summary.one_liner: In the embryonic Drosophila midgut, handedness is set by Myosin 1C in the neighboring hindgut epithelium, relayed through longitudinal muscle precursors, and then amplified into a stereotyped coil by buckling and confinement during elongation.
summary.plain: Many organs in animal bodies are not symmetrical, and they twist into a consistent left-handed or right-handed shape. This paper studies the fruit fly embryo's gut, which coils into a looped shape with alternating handedness, even though no known left-right genes are switched on in it. The authors used multi-angle microscopy, 3D shape measurements, and physical models to trace the handedness back to a nearby organ, the hindgut, where the protein Myosin 1C is expressed.
summary.why: It shows how a tiny, early bias passed between neighboring tissues can be turned into a reliable large-scale body shape by physical forces alone. The text does not discuss implications beyond fly development, so any link to vertebrate left-right patterning or human organ malformations would be speculative.

title: Mechanical canalization of chiral gut morphogenesis

abstract: Giardia duodenalis infection is associated with diarrhea and dysbiosis in dogs, while metronidazole treatment can further disrupt the microbiota. We evaluated adjunctive LB fermentate HF (LBHF), a Lactobacillus-derived postbiotic, in a randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled study of 30 naturally infected dogs (Terriers). Animals received metronidazole (50 mg/kg/day) with LBHF (50 mg/kg/day) or microcrystalline cellulose placebo (70 mg/kg/day) for 21 days. Clinical outcomes, fecal biomarkers, canine dysbiosis index, and cyst shedding were monitored over 45 days. Fecal shotgun metagenomics was performed at baseline and day 45. After baseline covariate adjustment, LBHF was associated with significantly lower Giardia burdens during treatment, particularly at days 10 and 20, improved fecal consistency, and reduced odor. No significant effects were found for fecal calprotectin, secretory IgA, blood biomarkers of digestive function, or canine dysbiosis index. Overall microbiome turnover was similar between groups, but multivariate analyses identified distinct treatment-associated community trajectories. LBHF was associated with increased Bacteroidota representation and functional capacity for plant polysaccharide degradation, alongside depletion of gene sets involved in flagellar assembly, quorum sensing, biofilm formation, and epithelial-cell signaling. Baseline microbiome composition also predicted Giardia burden, highlighting an association between parasite load and bacterial community structure. Adjunctive LBHF supplementation was associated with faster resolution of canine giardiasis, improved fecal quality, and coordinated microbiome remodeling. Further mechanistic studies are needed to establish whether the observed microbiome functional changes contribute to parasite clearance and recovery of intestinal health.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.767253 v1

summary.background:
- Giardia duodenalis: a single-celled intestinal parasite that causes diarrhea in dogs and other animals.
- Metronidazole: an antibiotic/antiparasitic drug used to treat it; it can disturb beneficial gut bacteria.
- Postbiotic: a preparation of substances made by bacteria (here, Lactobacillus fermentation), not live bacteria.
- Randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled: dogs were assigned to groups by chance, and handlers or assessors did not know who got the real product versus filler.
- Microbiome and shotgun metagenomics: sequencing all DNA in stool to identify which bacteria are present and which genes they carry.
- Dysbiosis index: a score summarizing how far the gut bacterial community departs from a healthy profile.
- Calprotectin and secretory IgA: stool markers of gut inflammation and local immune defense.
summary.one_liner: A randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled trial in 30 naturally Giardia-infected Terrier dogs testing whether an adjunctive Lactobacillus-derived postbiotic (LBHF) alongside metronidazole improves parasite clearance, stool quality, and gut microbiome function.
summary.plain: Giardia is a microscopic gut parasite that causes diarrhea in dogs, and the usual antibiotic treatment, metronidazole, can further upset the gut's bacterial community. In this study, 30 infected dogs got metronidazole plus either a bacterial-derived supplement (LBHF) or a placebo filler for 21 days, and researchers tracked symptoms, parasite shedding, and gut bacteria over 45 days. The supplement group had lower parasite levels during treatment, firmer stools, and less odor, but other gut and blood markers did not differ.
summary.why: Giardia is common in dogs and treatment can be hard to get right, so a low-cost adjunct that speeds recovery would matter if it holds up. The paper only reports associations and says mechanistic studies are still needed, so the link between the observed microbiome changes and parasite clearance is unproven.

title: EFFECT OF A LACTOBACILLUS POSTBIOTIC ON DIGESTIVE HEALTH IN DOGS RAISED IN CONDITIONS AT RISK OF GIARDIA DUODENALIS INFECTION

abstract: Plant-based diets are usually defined by what they exclude, overlooking which plant foods are eaten and how processed they are. Here we examine whether this overlooked dimension is related to the gut microbiome. In a cross-sectional study of 172 omnivorous, lacto-ovo-vegetarian and vegan adults profiled by shotgun metagenomics, vegetarians and vegans harboured fewer gut species than omnivores. Within this group, however, each standard deviation increase in minimally processed plant-food intake was associated with 27 additional species (p = 0.001), independently of fibre intake, and richness in participants with the highest intake approached that of omnivores. No such association was seen among omnivores. Higher intake was also linked to more species previously associated with favourable cardiometabolic health and to better health-related quality of life. Dietary labels alone may therefore conceal meaningful variation in the gut microbiome, and characterising how plant foods are processed may help in understanding how plant-based diets relate to health.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767798 v1

summary.background:
- Gut microbiome: the community of bacteria and other microbes living in the intestine.
- Species richness: how many different microbial species are present; higher is often, though not always, linked to better health.
- Shotgun metagenomics: sequencing all the DNA in a stool sample to identify which microbes are present and roughly what they carry.
- Cross-sectional study: data collected from many people at one time, so it shows correlation, not cause and effect.
- Minimally processed plant foods: foods such as whole fruits, vegetables, legumes and grains that have been little altered from their natural state.
- Standard deviation: a unit of spread in the data; the paper reports associations per one standard deviation increase in intake.
- Lacto-ovo-vegetarian: a vegetarian who eats dairy and eggs but no meat or fish.
summary.one_liner: A cross-sectional shotgun metagenomics study of 172 omnivorous, lacto-ovo-vegetarian and vegan adults finds that intake of minimally processed plant foods is positively associated with gut microbial species richness within the vegetarian and vegan group, but not among omnivores.
summary.plain: Diets labelled "vegetarian" or "vegan" describe only what people leave out, not what they eat or how much their food is processed. This study asked whether the amount of minimally processed plant food people eat relates to the variety of microbes in their gut. Among 172 adults, vegetarians and vegans had fewer gut species than omnivores, but within that group, those eating more minimally processed plant foods had more species.
summary.why: It suggests that a diet label alone may hide differences in gut microbes that matter for health, which could help explain mixed results on plant-based diets. The study is observational and cross-sectional, so it shows an association at one point in time and cannot establish that these foods cause the change.

title: Not all plant-based diets are alike: intake of minimally processed plant foods is associated with gut microbial richness among vegetarians and vegans.

abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) exhibits bidirectional transcriptional reprogramming following standard-of-care (SoC) treatment, yet the direction cannot be predicted from primary tumours. Using independent longitudinal bulk and single-cell datasets, we show that this response is captured by a framework, the JARID2 Binding Site (JBS) axis. Tumours and cells can be positioned along this axis according to expression of JBS genes, with responder subtypes defined by movement along the axis from primary to recurrent states. The JBS axis aligns with established GBM ecosystems and their constituent cell populations, and recurrent tumours polarise towards opposite ends. Changes in tumour microenvironment composition strongly influence this polarisation and drive adaptive transcriptional responses more profoundly than chemoradiation alone. Mechanistically, JBS genes are enriched for promoters marked by persistent bivalent chromatin and neurodevelopmental regulatory programmes. These findings suggest that JARID2-associated Polycomb regulation maintains a reservoir of developmental plasticity that enables treatment-driven ecosystem adaptation and represents a potential therapeutic vulnerability.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.766938 v1

summary.background:
- Glioblastoma: the most common and aggressive primary brain tumour in adults; standard care is surgery, radiation and chemotherapy, and tumours usually recur.
- Transcriptional reprogramming: a change in which genes a cell switches on or off, without changing the DNA sequence itself.
- Bulk vs single-cell sequencing: bulk measures the average activity of a whole tumour sample; single-cell measures each cell separately.
- Polycomb / JARID2: protein complexes that add chemical marks to chromatin (DNA packaged with proteins) to keep developmental genes silenced.
- Bivalent chromatin: a mark combining both "on" and "off" signals at a gene promoter, often seen at developmental genes that are poised to be activated.
- Tumour microenvironment: the non-cancer cells and tissue surrounding the tumour cells.
- Abstract only: the text given is a short summary, so methods, sample sizes and statistics are not available to check.
summary.one_liner: Using longitudinal bulk and single-cell glioblastoma datasets, the authors define a JARID2 Binding Site (JBS) gene-expression axis that tracks how tumours shift from primary to recurrent states after standard chemoradiation, and link this shift to bivalent chromatin marks at neurodevelopmental genes.
summary.plain: Glioblastoma is an aggressive brain cancer that often returns after standard treatment, and the tumour's genetic activity changes in ways that are hard to predict from the first biopsy. This paper describes a scoring scheme, the JBS axis, based on a set of genes that positions tumours and individual cells along a line, and shows that recurrent tumours tend to move toward opposite ends of that line. The authors report that changes in the surrounding tumour environment shape this movement more than chemoradiation alone does.
summary.why: It offers a way to describe why treated glioblastoma can change in different directions, which matters because treatment choices may depend on that direction. The text suggests a link to Polycomb regulation (a system that keeps genes switched off during development) as a possible therapeutic target, but this is a proposal from the abstract and has not been tested in the text provided.

title: Glioblastoma exhibits bidirectional adaptation to treatment through JARID2-associated developmental plasticity

abstract: Metabolic flexibility helps cancer cells survive targeted therapy, and BRAF-mutant melanoma rewires mitochondrial metabolism in response to BRAF/MEK inhibitors (BRAF/MEKi). We previously showed that connexin43 (Cx43) acts as a tumour suppressor in BRAF-mutant melanoma and enhances the response to BRAF/MEKi. Here, we investigated whether mitochondrial remodelling contributes to these effects. Cx43 upregulation promoted mitochondrial biogenesis including selective increase of CI and CV, enhanced oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), and increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, alongside DRP1-associated mitochondrial fragmentation. Despite enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis and OXPHOS, Cx43 upregulation was associated with respiratory chain remodelling, characterised by loss of complex IV, increased ER and mitochondrial stress, and enhanced mTORC1-associated signalling. These changes were accompanied by an adaptive unfolded protein response that did not engage the pro-apoptotic ATF4-CHOP axis. Notably, BRAF/MEK inhibition largely attenuated the mitochondrial biogenesis phenotype and most of the stress markers associated with Cx43 upregulation, while promoting mitochondrial network elongation and markedly increasing mitochondrial ROS. Despite this impact, Cx43-expressing tumour cells retained higher membrane potential, ROS levels and survival under glucose-limiting conditions. Collectively, these findings reveal a dissociation between the mitochondrial effects of Cx43 and its enhancement of the response to BRAF/MEKi, highlighting the complexity of Cx43-mediated metabolic regulation in BRAF-mutant melanoma. By distinguishing mitochondrial remodelling from therapeutic sensitisation, this study provides new insights into the response to BRAF/MEK inhibition and highlights mTORC1-associated signalling and mitochondrial oxidative stress as potential therapeutic vulnerabilities for further investigation.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767001 v1

summary.background:
- BRAF is a gene whose mutation drives many melanomas; BRAF and MEK inhibitors are drugs that block its signalling pathway.
- Connexin43 is a protein that forms channels between cells and was previously described here as acting as a tumour suppressor.
- Mitochondria are the cell's energy-producing compartments; oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) is their main energy-making chain, with complexes such as CI, CIV and CV as parts of it.
- Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are chemically reactive oxygen molecules that can damage cells at high levels.
- DRP1 is a protein that splits mitochondria into fragments; mTORC1 is a growth-signalling pathway that regulates cell metabolism.
- The unfolded protein response is a cell stress program triggered when proteins fold improperly in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
- Experiments are cell-culture studies; the text does not report animal or patient data.
summary.one_liner: In BRAF-mutant melanoma cells, raising the gap-junction protein connexin43 boosts mitochondrial biogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation and reactive oxygen species, while BRAF/MEK inhibitor treatment largely reverses these mitochondrial changes but not Cx43's sensitising effect.
summary.plain: Skin cancer cells with a common BRAF mutation often survive drug treatment by changing how their energy-producing structures, the mitochondria, work. This study looked at whether a protein called connexin43, which the same group had previously linked to better drug response, reshapes those mitochondria. The authors found that more connexin43 led to more mitochondria and more energy and oxidative stress, but that these changes were not what made the cells more responsive to the drugs.
summary.why: It suggests that mitochondrial stress and the mTORC1 signalling pathway could be possible targets for future cancer treatments, though the text only flags them for further investigation. It also shows that a link between a protein and drug response does not necessarily run through the mitochondria, which matters for interpreting such results.

title: Connexin43 drives mitochondrial biogenesis and organelle stress in BRAF-mutant melanoma cells

abstract: Animal populations globally are suffering significant declines; many species are social, and individuals are likely to adjust their social behaviour as they lose associates. Therefore, social networks may respond to population decline as individuals adjust their social connections in response to changing social environments. Our understanding of how individual responses to loss of their associates alters the structure of their social networks is rudimentary. To quantify how social responses to individual loss can alter network structure, we simulated individual loss and compensatory formation of new social ties across 268 empirical animal social networks. Compensation changed the structural effects of individual loss, though these effects often depended on which individuals were removed. Loss of central, peripheral or random individuals produced different network responses, while social compensation had similar effects regardless of compensation strategy. Together, these results suggest that compensatory social behaviour can reorganise social networks as populations decline, even if departing from the original structure. Accounting for these responses may improve predictions of how demographic change affects social structure, particularly when losses are socially patterned and without knowing the compensation strategy. Broadly, our findings highlight compensation as a potentially important process linking individual social behaviour to the reorganisation of animal societies.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767549 v1

summary.background:
- Social network: a map of who interacts with whom, where animals are points and their associations are links.
- Central vs. peripheral individuals: well-connected animals versus those with few links.
- Simulation: testing "what if" scenarios on computer models built from observed networks, rather than in the field.
- Compensation: remaining animals forming new social links to replace lost ones.
- Network structure: measurable features of a map, such as how connected or clustered it is.
summary.one_liner: Using 268 empirical animal social networks, the authors simulate removal of individuals and compensatory formation of new ties to show how compensation alters the structural effects of losing central, peripheral or random individuals.
summary.plain: Many animal populations are shrinking, and animals that remain may change who they associate with. This study used computer simulations on 268 real animal social networks to remove individuals and let the remaining animals form new social ties. It found that these new ties changed how much the network's structure was affected by losses, though the effects still depended on which individuals were removed.
summary.why: Population declines are widespread, and the way animals rebuild their social connections after losing companions could change how groups hold together. The abstract suggests this matters most when losses are concentrated in well-connected or otherwise socially patterned individuals, but the text does not show how well the simulated responses match what happens in real populations.

title: Social compensation changes predicted effects of individual loss in animal societies

abstract: Climate change is imposing strong selection pressures on many wild populations, forcing them to adapt or face extinction. Conservation biology attempts to predict evolutionary responses to inform management but is hampered by a poor understanding of how variation arises. For many populations, responses to warming may rely substantially upon phenotypic plasticity, with cues from parental and offspring environments shaping development. However, how information from the environment, the genome, and the epigenome interacts to produce phenotypic variation is poorly understood. We investigated these factors, and their interactions, by using Icelandic populations of threespine stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) that have adapted to geothermal warming. Using a split-temperature F1 to F2 hybrid cross, a novel morphometric approach, and reduced representation bisulphite sequencing, we elucidated the genetic architecture of transgenerational plasticity (TGP), within-generation plasticity (WGP), and that of morphological and methylation variation. This revealed that TGP and WGP have distinct genetic architectures involving different biological functions. The genetic architecture of traits was strongly influenced by both the parental and offspring thermal environments, potentially exposing different genetic variation to selection. Finally, we showed that TGP is favoured by selection and driven by the exposure of allelic variation by methylation. Our results suggested that predicting climate change responses should move beyond assessments of standing genetic variation to understand how TGP, WGP and the environment interact. More broadly, these findings improve our understanding of the processes that generate variation during adaptive divergence.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767529 v1

summary.background:
- Phenotypic plasticity: one organism's ability to change its traits in response to environment, without a change in its genes.
- Within-generation plasticity (WGP): change in traits from the conditions an individual itself experiences.
- Transgenerational plasticity (TGP): change in offspring traits driven by the environment their parents experienced.
- Epigenome and DNA methylation: chemical marks on DNA that influence gene activity without altering the DNA sequence; they can sometimes be inherited.
- Genetic architecture: the set of genes and their interactions that underlie a trait.
- F1 to F2 hybrid cross: breeding two genetically different populations, then breeding their offspring, to mix and sort their genetic variants.
- Reduced representation bisulphite sequencing: a lab method that reads methylation marks across a subset of the genome.
- Ectotherm: an animal whose body temperature depends largely on its surroundings, such as fish.
summary.one_liner: A split-temperature F1-to-F2 hybrid cross of Icelandic threespine stickleback from geothermally warmed and cooler sites, combined with morphometrics and reduced-representation bisulphite sequencing, examines how transgenerational and within-generation plasticity, genetics and DNA methylation jointly shape morphological variation.
summary.plain: Climate change pushes wild animals to cope with new temperatures, either by changing their genes over time or by adjusting how they develop within their own lifetime and across generations. This study used stickleback fish from Iceland, where some populations have lived in warm geothermal water for generations, and bred their offspring under different temperatures. The authors report that the genetic basis of changes that carry over from parents (transgenerational plasticity) and changes that occur within one generation appear to differ, and that DNA methylation, a chemical tag on DNA that can switch genes on or off, helps expose some genetic variation to selection.
summary.why: It bears on whether conservation forecasts of how species will respond to warming should account for parental effects and epigenetics, not just standing genetic variation. The text reports the findings without independent replication or wider context, so their generality beyond this system is not established.

title: Within- and transgenerational plasticity evolve separately in a thermally adapted ectotherm

abstract: Pattern-triggered immunity (PTI) is classically associated with an extracellular respiratory burst generated by plasma membrane-localized NADPH oxidases (RBOHs). Here, we identify an ancient RBOH-independent intracellular respiratory burst driven by central carbon metabolism. Using in vivo biosensors, we demonstrate that receptor activation rapidly triggers sugar catabolism via glycolysis, shifting the NAD pool toward its reduced state. This redox pressure drives a burst in mitochondrial respiratory flux and oxygen consumption. Consequent mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) production activates ANAC017-mediated retrograde signaling to induce broader PTI gene expression. This intracellular respiratory burst represents a conserved early hallmark of immunity across land plants and links cellular carbon status to immune activation. It reveals functional parallels between plant immune metabolism and metabolic reprogramming during mammalian immune-cell activation.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767486 v1

summary.background:
- Pattern-triggered immunity (PTI): the plant's first-line immune response, switched on when cell-surface receptors detect microbial molecules.
- Respiratory burst: a rapid release of reactive oxygen species (ROS), molecules that act as signals and can damage microbes.
- RBOHs: plasma-membrane enzymes that produce the classic surface burst.
- Glycolysis: the cell's breakdown of sugar into smaller molecules, producing energy carriers.
- NAD pool: a shared set of molecules that carry electrons; its "reduced" form stores energy and electrons.
- Mitochondria: organelles that generate cellular energy through respiration, which consumes oxygen.
- Retrograde signaling: messages sent from organelles back to the nucleus to change gene expression.
- ANAC017: a plant transcription factor involved in stress and mitochondrial signaling.
- Biosensors: genetically encoded probes that report metabolite or redox levels in living cells.
summary.one_liner: The paper reports an RBOH-independent, intracellular respiratory burst in plant pattern-triggered immunity, in which glycolysis-driven NADH buildup boosts mitochondrial respiration and mitochondrial ROS that activate ANAC017-dependent retrograde signaling.
summary.plain: Plants fight off microbes partly by releasing a quick burst of reactive oxygen molecules, which is usually attributed to enzymes on the cell surface. This paper describes a second, internal burst: when immune receptors are switched on, the cell rapidly breaks down sugar, and the energy-producing power plants inside the cell (mitochondria) then use more oxygen and make reactive oxygen signals that switch on defense genes. The authors used biosensors inside living plants to track these changes.
summary.why: It challenges the standard picture of the plant immune burst as purely a surface-enzyme event and links cellular sugar and energy status directly to immune activation. The text also suggests a parallel with metabolic shifts in mammalian immune cells, but how far that parallel holds is not established in this summary.

title: The intracellular respiratory burst of plant immunity signaling

abstract: The plant nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) immune receptors are known to play a crucial role in plant host defence against a variety of biotic stresses. Several NLR proteins contain integrated domains (NLR-ID) like ankyrin (ANK) and WRKY transcription factor domains and are important evolutionary adaptations in plant immunity. They are responsible for the perception of effector molecules from invading pathogens and pests and subsequent activation of plant immune responses. However, the functional roles these ANK-NLR-WRKY proteins play in wheat (Triticum aestivum) against various pathogens and pests remain poorly understood. Computational tools employed for comparative sequence and phylogenetic analyses revealed that TaAdnr1 is highly conserved across diploid (T. urartu), tetraploid (T. dicoccoides), and hexaploid (T. aestivum) wheat species, including its well characterised orthologue YrU1 from T. urartu. Three-dimensional (3D) protein structural modelling using AlphaFold2 supported strong conservation in the multiple domains of these NLR orthologues, more specifically within the integrated WRKY domain. This conservation may suggest a strong evolutionary maintenance of TaADNR1. Furthermore, this may also suggest TaADNR1 reflects specificity in effector recognition and regulation. Therefore, the integration of functional genomics studies, sequence analysis, evolutionary analysis and structural modelling possesses the potential to provide new insights into the pleiotropic roles of integrated domain NLRs in wheat.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767528 v1

summary.background:
- NLR proteins: plant immune receptors that detect signals from invading pathogens and trigger defence.
- Integrated domain (NLR-ID): an extra protein region added to an NLR that may bind pathogen molecules; here ANK (ankyrin) and WRKY domains.
- Orthologues: versions of the same gene in different species that descend from a common ancestor.
- Wheat ploidy: diploid (two sets of chromosomes), tetraploid (four) and hexaploid (six); T. urartu, T. dicoccoides and T. aestivum are the diploid, tetraploid and hexaploid examples.
- Phylogenetic analysis: comparing sequences to infer evolutionary family trees.
- AlphaFold2: an AI tool that predicts a protein's 3D structure from its sequence.
- YrU1: a known, well-characterised orthologue from T. urartu that provides a reference point.
summary.one_liner: A computational comparison of an ANK-NLR-WRKY immune receptor (TaADNR1) and its orthologues across diploid, tetraploid and hexaploid wheat, using sequence, phylogenetic and AlphaFold2 structural analysis.
summary.plain: Wheat plants defend themselves against disease-causing microbes and pests using immune proteins called NLRs. This paper looks at one such protein, TaADNR1, and its matching versions in wild and cultivated wheat relatives. The authors used computer tools to compare the gene sequences, trace evolutionary relationships, and predict the 3D shapes of the proteins, finding that the versions are highly similar, especially in the WRKY part.
summary.why: Immune receptors like these help determine which pathogens a crop can resist, so understanding how they are conserved across wheat species may matter for breeding. The text is a computational study only and does not test disease resistance directly, so any link to real-world crop protection is still an open question.

title: Comparative Analysis of Orthologous ANK-NLR-WRKY Proteins in Wheat Species: Evolutionary Divergence and Structural Characteristics

abstract: Cannabidiol (CBD) is an important medicinal cannabinoid which accumulates in the Cannabis sativa plant as the precursor cannabidiolic acid (CBDA). Measurement of CBDA levels is important for crop valuation, harvest optimisation, and quality control. However, its quantification typically requires laboratory-based analytical methods that are not readily deployable at the point of need. Here, we report the development of an engineered protein biosensor for selective CBDA detection based on chemically induced dimerization of engineered nanobody domains. Here a cannabidiol-responsive nanobody pair was incorporated into a two-component beta-lactamase-based biosensor architecture, such that ligand binding ultimately results in reconstitution of beta-lactamase activity quantified in a simple colorimetric assay. The resulting sensor displayed high affinity for CBD (KD = 1.9 +/- 0.2 nM) and CBDA (KD = 32 +/- 4 nM). Structure analysis informed a single substitution mutation of ligand-binding nanobody to shift its selectivity in favour of CBDA. This minimal modification inverted sensor specificity, generating a CBDA-selective biosensor that showed no detectable activation either by CBD or the immediate biosynthetic precursor, cannabigerolic acid (CBGA). The engineered sensor exhibited nanomolar affinity for CBDA (KD = 21 +/- 2.4 nM), an 8.4-fold dynamic range, and a limit of detection of 0.5 nM. Sensor performance was validated using crude extracts from CBDA-producing biomass and achieved 95.6% agreement with LCMS-based quantification.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.767439 v1

summary.background:
- CBD is a medicinal compound from Cannabis sativa; CBDA is the acid form the plant makes first and that converts to CBD.
- A biosensor is a molecule or system that signals when it binds a target, here via a color change.
- Nanobodies are small antibody fragments that can be engineered to bind specific molecules.
- Beta-lactamase is an enzyme; in this design, two halves of it are brought together by the ligand so that the enzyme works again and produces a color in a simple assay.
- KD (dissociation constant) measures binding strength; lower nanomolar values mean tighter binding.
- LCMS (liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry) is the standard lab method used as the reference here.
- Limit of detection is the smallest amount reliably measured.
summary.one_liner: A two-component, beta-lactamase-based protein biosensor built from engineered nanobodies is reported that detects cannabidiolic acid (CBDA) selectively, with a single mutation shifting specificity away from CBD and read out by a simple colorimetric assay.
summary.plain: Cannabis growers and quality-control labs need to know how much CBDA, the precursor of the medicinal compound CBD, is in a plant, but the usual measurements need lab equipment. This paper describes a protein-based sensor that binds CBDA and produces a color change, and the authors tested it on crude plant extracts. Their results matched the standard lab method (LCMS) in 95.6% of cases.
summary.why: A cheap, field-deployable test for CBDA could help with crop valuation, harvest timing and quality checks. The text reports the validation only on crude extracts from CBDA-producing biomass, so its performance in real field or industrial settings is not shown here.

title: Quantification of cannabidiolic acid in Cannabis sativa using a two-component allosteric protein biosensor

abstract: Inherited retinal diseases are leading candidates for gene therapy, but photoreceptor-directed adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors still require subretinal injection, which treats only part of the retina and carries surgical risk. Intravitreal delivery is simple and panretinal, yet inner-retinal barriers block most capsids, and capsids selected in one species rarely translate. Mapping retinal glycans across seven mammals, we found heparan sulfate (HS) marking the inner limiting membrane and terminal N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) enriched on photoreceptor segments. These invariants defined a two-part design principle, attenuated HS binding with strong terminal GlcNAc engagement, implemented as a sequential in vitro selection, Conserved Receptor-Selection Technology (CReST). Its lead GlcNAc-selected capsid, AAV2.IvtB, increased retinal transgene expression 6.5-fold over AAV2.7m8 in mice and photoreceptor transduction 2.5-fold in pigs, acting through terminal GlcNAc engagement. It partially preserved photoreceptors in rd10 mice and suppressed laser-induced choroidal neovascularization. CReST is a receptor-guided, animal-free route to capsids with a defined, conserved mechanism.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.767272 v1

summary.background:
- AAV (adeno-associated virus): a small, non-disease-causing virus widely used as a gene delivery vehicle; its outer shell (capsid) determines which cells it enters.
- Retina: the light-sensing tissue at the back of the eye; photoreceptors are the cells that detect light.
- Intravitreal vs. subretinal injection: injection into the eye's vitreous gel is simpler and reaches more of the retina, but the inner retinal layers block many vectors; subretinal injection is surgically riskier and treats only part of the retina.
- Glycans: chains of sugar molecules on cell surfaces that viruses often use as docking points. Heparan sulfate (HS) and N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) are two such sugars.
- Directed evolution / in vitro selection: generating many capsid variants and picking those that perform best, here guided by receptor binding.
- rd10 mice: a mouse model of inherited retinal degeneration. Laser-induced choroidal neovascularization: an experimental model of abnormal blood vessel growth under the retina.
summary.one_liner: A paper describing CReST, a receptor-guided in vitro selection method that yielded the AAV2.IvtB capsid, which transduces retina more efficiently after intravitreal injection across mice and pigs by engaging terminal GlcNAc on photoreceptors while attenuating heparan sulfate binding.
summary.plain: Gene therapy vectors (harmless viral shells used to carry genes) usually have to be injected under the retina, a surgery that reaches only part of it. This paper looks for a version that can be injected into the eye's gel-filled center instead and still reach the light-sensing cells across the whole retina.
