The authors mapped sugar-based molecules in the retinas of seven mammals and used those shared features to guide a lab selection method, producing a vector that worked better in mice and pigs.
summary.why: The reported gains are measured in mice and pigs and include partial rescue of photoreceptors in a mouse degeneration model and reduced laser-induced blood vessel growth, so they are preliminary and not yet tested in patients. If the approach holds up, it could make retinal gene therapy simpler to deliver, but the text does not show clinical safety or efficacy.

title: Biochemical selection on conserved glycans yield a cross-species AAV capsid for efficient panretinal intravitreal delivery

abstract: When a fractional order improves the fit of an epidemic model, it is usually taken as evidence of memory. We ask whether the order of the Caputo susceptible-infectious-removed (SIR) model can actually be recovered from incidence data. If the transmission rate is allowed to vary freely in time, as in hybrid forecasting models, every admissible order, removal rate and initial count reproduces the data exactly. With constant transmission and exact data the order is identifiable in principle, but the dominant term of early linearized growth depends on only two parameter combinations: the growth rate r = (beta - gamma)^(1/alpha) and the amplitude beta*I0/alpha. What is left is transient, and it is limited. We prove that parameter sets sharing these two combinations give Poisson count distributions whose Kullback-Leibler divergence stays bounded no matter how long the linear phase is observed, and that the nonlinear model inherits this bound as the population grows. In simulations, wrong orders were rejected in at most 5% of replicates when the data ended two weeks or more before the epidemic peak, and in 95-100% once the peak was included; separation began only a few days before the peak. With mild overdispersion the order was identified only once about 60% of the population had been infected, and with stronger overdispersion not even then. Fits that the early data could not tell apart predicted peaks that differed by 75%, and plug-in forecasts that ignored parameter uncertainty were badly overconfident. Data generated without any memory produced fitted orders below one when transmission changed and when the fitted model was discretized in daily steps. In early COVID-19 data from Bangladesh and the United States, orders from 0.6 to 1 gave almost the same growth rate, whatever value we assumed for the removal rate.
label: arXiv:2611.25440v1

summary.background:
- SIR model: splits a population into susceptible, infectious and removed (recovered) groups, with transmission and removal rates.
- Caputo fractional derivative: a generalization of ordinary rates of change, with an order alpha (1 means ordinary dynamics); values below 1 are often read as slow fading of past effects, or "memory".
- Identifiability: whether the data can, in principle, distinguish between different parameter settings.
- Kullback-Leibler divergence: a measure of how different two probability distributions are; near zero means hard to tell apart.
- Poisson counts and overdispersion: standard models for case counts; overdispersion means the variance is larger than the Poisson model allows.
- Plug-in forecast: a prediction that treats estimated parameters as exact, ignoring their uncertainty.
summary.one_liner: The paper asks whether the fractional order of a Caputo SIR epidemic model can be recovered from incidence data, showing it is weakly identifiable from early-phase data and that fitted orders can be confounded with transmission changes and overdispersion.
summary.plain: Researchers often read a better fit from a "fractional" epidemic model as proof that an outbreak has memory, meaning past infections affect later spread in a slow-fading way. This paper checks whether the memory setting (the order) can actually be pinned down from case counts. Using theory and simulations, it finds that early case data mostly reveal only two combinations of parameters, and that the order is recoverable only after the epidemic peak or after a large share of the population is infected.
summary.why: If a fitted memory parameter cannot be separated from other settings, claims of "memory" in outbreak data, and forecasts built on them, may be overconfident. The paper also reports that early COVID-19 data from Bangladesh and the United States fit orders from 0.6 to 1 about equally well, which bears on how such models should be interpreted; the wider impact beyond this setting is not assessed in the text.

title: Fractional Order or False Memory: Identifiability of Caputo SIR Models from Incidence Data

abstract: Demographic fluctuations can drive finite epidemic populations into an absorbing disease-free state even when the corresponding infinite system supports sustained activity. By means of Monte Carlo simulations, we investigate how spatial coupling of two distinct subsystems modifies stochastic extinction and epidemic spreading in susceptible-infectious-susceptible (SIS) and susceptible-infectious-recovered (SIR) models on inhomogeneous two-dimensional square lattices. For isolated SIS systems, extinction times exhibit approximate power-law scaling near the epidemic threshold even for small systems. Traversal times characterize the distinct propagation dynamics of SIS and SIR infection clusters. We consider diffusively coupled regions with different transmission characteristics in coupled SIS-SIS, SIR-SIS, and SIR-SIR configurations. Invading fronts can reactivate a vulnerable SIS region after its initial infection has disappeared and establish a long-lived active epidemic state. This stabilization can be induced by either a sustained SIS source or a single transient SIR epidemic wave. Spatial correlation measurements support a mechanism in which the invading activity generates an extended correlated infectious population, effectively providing favorable initial conditions for renewed epidemic spreading. Correlations develop particularly strongly parallel to the subsystem interfaces. Decoupling the regions after some elapsed period demonstrates that autonomous persistence requires sufficient coupling time beyond the first interface arrival for this correlated population to become established. Increasing system size delays invasion but enhances the probability of ultimate successful stabilization. In two coupled SIR regions, transmission can initiate a macroscopic secondary outbreak, while permanent immunity restricts both epidemics to transient activity.
label: arXiv:2611.26792v1

summary.background:
- Compartmental models: populations are split into susceptible, infected and recovered groups, with rules for moving between them.
- SIS model: infected individuals return to susceptible after recovery, so the disease can persist indefinitely.
- SIR model: recovery brings permanent immunity, so each outbreak eventually burns out.
- Epidemic threshold: the transmission level above which infection can sustain itself in an infinite population.
- Absorbing state: a condition from which the system cannot escape, here a disease-free population.
- Stochastic extinction: chance fluctuations in a small population can kill off an infection even when it would persist in a large one.
- Monte Carlo simulation: repeated random runs of a model used to estimate typical outcomes.
- Spatial correlation: how strongly infection status at one site predicts status at another nearby site.
summary.one_liner: Monte Carlo study of stochastic extinction and invasion-driven reactivation in two diffusively coupled, spatially inhomogeneous 2D lattices running SIS and SIR epidemic dynamics.
summary.plain: This paper asks how a disease in a small, finite population can die out by chance, and how neighbouring areas can revive it. The authors ran computer simulations of two linked regions on a grid, each following a simple infection rule, either infected people can become susceptible again (SIS) or they recover with lasting immunity (SIR). They report that an incoming wave of infection can restart a dormant region and keep it active for a long time, provided the two regions stay coupled long enough.
summary.why: The work looks at how chance and spatial contact together decide whether an epidemic persists, which matters for small or patchy populations. The text does not show how directly the findings apply to real disease data, so any practical link should be treated as a hypothesis.

title: Infection Spreading and Stochastic Extinction in Finite Spatially Inhomogeneous Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible and Susceptible-Infected-Recovered Systems

abstract: Purpose Suicide during pregnancy or after birth (the perinatal period) represents a leading, preventable cause of United States maternal deaths. This study aimed to understand the complex relationship between perinatal status and life circumstances among perinatal suicide decedents in the United States and generate insights regarding suicide risk. Methods This cross-sectional study used decedent data from the 2003-2023 National Violent Death Reporting System suicide mortality registry (N=20,217). We applied psychometric network analysis using 18 binary life circumstances indicators representing four domains: relationships, health, socioeconomic status, and risk factors for suicide. We generated two networks for the overall sample and perinatal sample and assessed network structure, bridge centralities, and stability. Results The analytic sample included 1,297 perinatal and 18,920 non-perinatal decedents. The network of the overall sample was stable. Perinatal status did not appear at the center of the network but connected primarily with intimate partner problems. The network of the perinatal sample was modestly stable. Postpartum status was not at the center of the network but connected to depressed mood and mental health diagnoses. In both networks, depressed mood had the highest bridge betweenness, and there was a consistent link between physical health domains and socioeconomic domains. Conclusion Suicide prevention strategies targeting childbearing-aged women should incorporate factors beyond pregnancy, including physical health, intimate partner relationships, and socioeconomic challenges.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.26368387 v1

summary.background:
- Perinatal period: pregnancy and the first year after birth.
- National Violent Death Reporting System: a US database of details gathered from death investigations and records.
- Cross-sectional study: a snapshot of many cases at one point in the data, which cannot establish cause and effect.
- Network analysis: a method that treats each factor as a point and each statistical association as a line, showing which factors cluster together.
- Bridge centrality: how strongly a factor links otherwise separate clusters of factors.
- Network stability: whether the map holds up when the data are slightly resampled. The paper reports the overall network as stable and the perinatal network as only modestly stable, which means its details deserve more caution.
- Binary indicator: a yes-or-no record of whether a circumstance was present.
summary.one_liner: A cross-sectional psychometric network analysis of 2003–2023 National Violent Death Reporting System suicide decedents (N=20,217) comparing 18 binary life-circumstance indicators between perinatal and non-perinatal women, with attention to bridge centrality and network stability.
summary.plain: This paper looks at women who died by suicide while pregnant or within the first year after giving birth, a period that is a leading preventable cause of maternal death in the United States. Using death records from 2003 to 2023, the researchers mapped how 18 everyday circumstances, such as relationship problems, health issues, money troubles, and known suicide risk factors, tend to occur together. They then compared that map for perinatal deaths (1,297 cases) with the map for all other deaths (18,920 cases).
summary.why: Maternal suicide is a preventable cause of death, and the paper suggests that prevention for women of childbearing age should look beyond pregnancy itself to health, partner relationships, and finances. The findings describe associations in death records, not causes, so they point to where prevention might focus rather than proving what works.

title: Perinatal suicide risk factors: A network analysis

abstract: Background: We aimed to investigate the association between moderate-to-vigorous leisure-time physical activity (MVLTPA) and longitudinal trajectories of systolic (SBP) and diastolic (DBP) blood pressure, as well as the incidence of high blood pressure and antihypertensive drug initiation, in adults aged 60-80 years at high cardiovascular risk. Methods: In participants from the PREDIMED trial (61% women; 5,254 participants), MVLTPA was assessed using the Minnesota Leisure Time Physical Activity Questionnaire and expressed as cumulative average metabolic equivalent of task-minutes/day. SBP and DBP trajectories were modelled using mixed-effects models with cubic splines (>100 [adequate] vs <100 [insufficient] metabolic equivalent of task-minutes/day). First occurrence of high blood pressure (SBP >140 mmHg or DBP >90 mmHg) and antihypertensive drug initiation were assessed with Cox models (adequate vs insufficient, and continuous MVLTPA). Results: SBP and DBP declined with increasing age, with no clinically meaningful differences between MVLTPA groups. The association between adequate MVLTPA and incident high blood pressure was null (HR 1.11, 95% CI 0.94-1.32). However, adequate MVLTPA was associated with a 17% lower risk of antihypertensive drug initiation (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.71-0.98). The association appeared stronger in women (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.58-0.94) than in men (HR 0.98, 95% CI 0.78-1.22) (p-value for sex interaction = 0.058). A modest inverse linear dose-response association between MVLTPA and risk of antihypertensive drug initiation was also observed (per 25 metabolic equivalent of task-minutes/day: HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.97-1.00; p-value = 0.022). Conclusions: In older adults at high cardiovascular risk, MVLTPA was not associated with clinically meaningful differences in SBP or DBP trajectories or incident high blood pressure, but was associated with a lower risk of antihypertensive drug initiation. These findings support promoting habitual physical activity as part of cardiovascular risk management in older adults.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.26368306 v1

summary.background:
- PREDIMED was a large Spanish trial testing Mediterranean-style diets in people at high cardiovascular risk; this paper analyses its data.
- Blood pressure is reported as two numbers: systolic (pressure when the heart beats) and diastolic (pressure between beats). High blood pressure here means above 140 or 90 mmHg.
- Physical activity was self-reported with a questionnaire and summarised as MET-minutes per day (MET is a unit of activity intensity); over 100 MET-minutes/day was labelled "adequate".
- Mixed-effects models track repeated measurements in each person over time; Cox models estimate the relative rate of an event (hazard ratio, HR) over follow-up. An HR below 1 means a lower rate of the event.
- Observational cohort findings show association, not cause.
summary.one_liner: In a secondary analysis of the PREDIMED trial (5,254 adults aged 60-80 at high cardiovascular risk), higher moderate-to-vigorous leisure-time physical activity was not linked to clinically meaningful differences in blood pressure trajectories or new high blood pressure, but was associated with lower risk of starting antihypertensive drugs, with a possible sex difference.
summary.plain: This study asks whether being more physically active in your free time, such as brisk walking, cycling or sports at a moderate-to-vigorous effort, is linked to healthier blood pressure in older adults who already face high heart risk. The researchers followed over 5,000 people over time and tracked their blood pressure, new high blood pressure diagnoses, and when they began taking blood pressure medication. Activity did not change blood pressure readings in a meaningful way or the chance of new high blood pressure, but people who were more active were less likely to start blood pressure medicine.
summary.why: Starting blood pressure medication is a practical, clinically important event, so a link to activity suggests exercise may matter in day-to-day cardiovascular care. The sex difference was not clearly established (interaction p = 0.058), so it should be treated as a hint rather than a finding, and the study is observational, so it cannot prove activity caused the difference.

title: Moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, longitudinal blood pressure trajectories, and hypertension-related outcomes in older adults at high cardiovascular risk: a cohort study

abstract: The upper respiratory tract (URT) microbiome modulates the local mucosal immune environment, with potential implications for respiratory viral infection susceptibility and outcomes. We leveraged a first-in-human SARS-CoV-2 challenge study in 34 healthy young adults, 18 of whom became infected, to characterize host gene expression and microbiome composition and dynamics in nasal and throat samples collected before viral inoculation and over the subsequent 14 days. Compared with participants who remained uninfected, participants who became infected had elevated baseline nasal expression of gene modules related to interferon, innate inflammatory, and neutrophil responses, as well as a delayed transcriptional response to viral challenge. Baseline nasal microbiome composition differed modestly by subsequent infection status, with lower relative abundances of Corynebacterium accolens and higher abundances of Dolosigranulum pigrum and Staphylococcus aureus among participants who became infected. Integrated analyses of microbiome and host gene expression data identified coordinated networks of microbiome features and host immune modules that distinguished infected from uninfected participants, including prior to inoculation. Notably, immune modules associated with infection susceptibility were positively correlated with S. aureus abundance and negatively correlated with the abundances of common nasal commensals, Corynebacterium spp. and Staphylococcus epidermidis, linking altered nasal microbiome community structure with the heightened inflammatory state associated with infection susceptibility. Symptom burden and viral load were similarly linked to distinct networks of microbiome and host gene expression features within nasal samples. Taken together, these findings highlight potential microbiome-host interactions within the nasal mucosa that may contribute to differences in respiratory viral infection outcomes.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.26368138 v1

summary.background:
- Upper respiratory tract: the nose and throat, where many respiratory viruses first enter the body.
- Microbiome: the community of bacteria and other microbes that normally live on body surfaces.
- Human challenge model: a study where volunteers are intentionally infected under controlled conditions, which allows timing of exposure to be known.
- Gene expression: measurement of which genes are switched on in tissue samples, used here as a readout of immune activity.
- Interferon and neutrophil responses: parts of the immune system's early alarm and first-responder activity against viruses and bacteria.
- Corynebacterium, Staphylococcus, Dolosigranulum: genera of common bacteria found in the nose; S. aureus is a species that can cause infections.
- Viral load: the amount of virus measured in a sample.
summary.one_liner: In a first-in-human SARS-CoV-2 challenge study of 34 healthy young adults (18 infected), baseline nasal and throat microbiome composition and host gene expression were linked to infection susceptibility, symptoms, and viral load.
summary.plain: Researchers looked at why some people catch COVID-19 and others do not, even when exposed to the same virus. In a study where healthy volunteers were deliberately given the virus, they compared the bacteria living in the nose and throat, and the nose's immune activity, before the virus was given. People who later became infected differed modestly in both.
summary.why: The paper suggests that the mix of bacteria in the nose and the local immune state before exposure may relate to who gets infected and how sick they get. These are associations from a small study, so they point toward possible mechanisms rather than establishing cause.

title: Upper respiratory microbiome and host immune signatures associated with SARS-CoV-2 susceptibility and illness in a human challenge model

abstract: Background Tuberculosis (TB) remains a leading infectious cause of death, with drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) challenging disease control. Brazil has a high TB burden, and Rio Grande do Sul state reports persistently high incidence and drug-resistance rates. The drivers shaping the regional DR-TB burden remain poorly characterised. Methods We conducted genomic surveillance of confirmed DR-TB cases in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, from January 2023 to September 2024. Clinical isolates underwent genotypic (gDST) and phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (pDST) and whole-genome sequencing (WGS). We analyzed 33 newly sequenced genomes and 267 historical Mycobacterium tuberculosis genomes collected in 2011-2019 to characterize resistance, transmission, and spatiotemporal patterns and estimate the contributions of transmitted and acquired rifampicin resistance. Findings Molecular testing detected rifampicin resistance missed by pDST, including borderline rpoB mutations in 18.2% and emerging resistance-associated variants in 3% of the 33 analyzed isolates. Conversely, pDST detected baseline bedaquiline resistance missed by WGS in one newly diagnosed case. Among 300 genomes, 181 (60.3%) clustered into 32 genomic clusters at a 5-SNP threshold, including 12 with long-term circulation and several spanning prisons and communities. Sublineage frequencies remained stable over time, whereas we observed marked geographic structuring and localized clonal expansion. Among 178 rifampicin-resistant isolates, transmission accounted for an estimated 79.2-88.2% of resistance, corresponding to 11.8-20.8% of cases arising through de novo acquisition during treatment. Interpretation Our findings identify active transmission as the main driver of rifampicin-resistant TB in Rio Grande do Sul, with long-term transmission chains extending across both incarcerated and community settings. These results underscore the urgent need to strengthen timely TB case detection and resistance testing, enhance contact investigations, and implement targeted interventions aiming to interrupt persistent transmission chains.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.26368293 v1

summary.background:
- Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, a bacterium spread through the air.
- Drug-resistant TB does not respond to some or all standard drugs; rifampicin is a key first-line drug.
- Whole-genome sequencing reads the bacterium's full genetic code, allowing researchers to tell whether cases are closely related.
- A "5-SNP threshold" means genomes differing by five or fewer single-letter genetic changes are grouped as likely linked.
- Drug susceptibility testing comes in two types: genotypic (detecting resistance genes) and phenotypic (growing bacteria with drugs in the lab).
- "Acquired" resistance develops during treatment; "transmitted" resistance is caught from another person.
summary.one_liner: Whole-genome sequencing of 33 new drug-resistant TB isolates plus 267 historical genomes from Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, indicates that transmission between people, including in prisons and communities, drives most rifampicin resistance in the region.
summary.plain: This paper looks at drug-resistant tuberculosis, a lung infection that resists standard antibiotics, in the Brazilian state of Rio Grande do Sul. The researchers sequenced the bacteria's genomes from recent patients and compared them with older samples to trace how the infection spreads. They found that most resistance came from the disease passing from person to person, rather than from patients becoming resistant during treatment.
summary.why: Tracing transmission chains tells public health teams where to focus case finding, resistance testing and contact tracing, including in prisons. The study covers one region over a limited period, so its findings may not apply directly elsewhere.

title: Long-term transmission chains fueling the drug-resistant tuberculosis burden in Southern Brazil

abstract: Brazil is one of the higher meat producer and consumer worldwide. Recently, the sustainability of the meat market is questioned on regard to its high contribution to climate change and public health concerns such as obesity. Hence, further public policies are likely to regulate the meat market and simultaneously reduce meat production and consumption. However, in the context of middle-income countries marked by strong inequalities such as Brazil, the nutritional effect of such market regulation is uncertain. Indeed, one can hypothesize that meat intake plays a protective role against poor nutritious food intake and weight gain among underprivileged settings. To test this hypothesis, this study analyzes household cross-sectional yearly surveys collected from 2018 to 2023 in the 27 Brazilian State capitals. As expected, multivariate estimates show education-specific associations between meat intake and obesity. Among the most educated individuals, declaring not consuming any meat the previous day before the survey is associated with lower body mass index (BMI) and obesity risk, as observed in previous epidemiological studies. By contrast, declaring consuming meat the previous day before the survey appears to be protective against weight gain among poorly educated individuals. We also observe education-specific meat substitution behaviors that help explain these findings. In facts, meat is more likely to be replaced by sweets and ready-to-eat meals among poorly educated individuals compared to more educated ones. We conclude that, everything being equals, meat market regulation policy might worsen public health concerns for under-privileged individuals. Important investments in the education sector and anti-poverty programs are thus needed to limit the raise of nutritional inequalities.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.26368245 v1

summary.background:
- Cross-sectional survey: data collected from many households at one point in each year, showing associations rather than cause and effect.
- Body mass index (BMI): a weight-to-height measure used to classify obesity.
- Multivariate estimates: statistical models that adjust for other factors (such as age or income) at the same time.
- Effect modification: when the link between two things (meat intake and obesity) differs depending on a third factor (education).
- Meat substitution: what people eat instead of meat, here sweets and ready-to-eat meals.
- Ultra-processed/ready-to-eat foods: packaged, convenience foods that are often high in fat, sugar, or salt.
- Middle-income country: a nation with moderate average income but large gaps between rich and poor.
summary.one_liner: A cross-sectional study of household surveys from 27 Brazilian state capitals (2018–2023) examining whether education level modifies the association between previous-day meat intake and BMI/obesity, with meat-substitution patterns as a possible explanation.
summary.plain: Brazil eats and produces a lot of meat, and some policymakers want to cut meat production and consumption for climate and health reasons. This study asks whether such cuts would help or hurt health across different groups, using yearly household surveys from Brazil's capital cities. The authors report that among better-educated people, not eating meat the day before was linked to lower body weight and obesity risk, while among less-educated people, eating meat was linked to lower weight gain, with meat more often replaced by sweets and ready-to-eat meals in that group.
summary.why: It bears on whether market or dietary regulation aimed at health and climate has uneven effects across income and education groups. The text is a single observational study, so its associations do not establish that meat causes lower obesity, and the authors' policy conclusion is a suggestion rather than a tested result.

title: Does educational attainment change the association between meat intake and obesity? A case-study from urban Brazil.

abstract: Background: Tuberculosis Diagnosis delays among tuberculosis patients can worsen infection transmission, disease severity, and mortality risk. Identifying factors influencing delays is crucial due to its persistence across healthcare levels and communities. The study identify determinants of tuberculosis diagnosis delay among patients attending public health facility of Metekel zone, Northwest Ethiopia:2023 Methods: An unmatched case-control study was conducted in Metekel zone health facilities from March to April 2023, involving 210 tuberculosis patients (103 cases, 107 controls) selected through systematic sampling. Data collected through structured questionnaires and STATA used for analysis, including bi-variable and multi-variable logistic regressions. Variables with p-value < 0.25 in bi-variable analysis were included in the final model after checking model fitness and multicollinearity. Results: Overall, 210 tuberculosis patients were included in the study. The following independent variables were associated diagnosis delay of tuberculosis: TB patients who travel greater than 10km (AOR: 2.941, (95 % CI: 1.509, 5.731); TB patients who are living at rural area (AOR: 4.135, 95 % CI :1.759, 9.723); TB patients who prior visit in holly-water and traditional medicine [AOR: 2.978, (95% CI: 1.292, 6.863); poor knowledge about TB [AOR: 2.826, (95% CI: 1.404, 5.687)]. Conclusion: Tuberculosis diagnosis delay is a major challenge to eliminate tuberculosis by breaking the chain of transmission. This study can be attributed to factors including place of residence being rural, poor knowledge about tuberculosis, non-health facility initial actions upon symptom onset, and far distance to health institutions. Recognizing these determinants helps in identifying and addressing barriers inhibiting early diagnosis, potentially improving healthcare access and promoting more timely diagnosis and treatment for tuberculosis patients.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.26368197 v1

summary.background:
- Tuberculosis (TB): a bacterial infection, mainly of the lungs, that spreads through coughing and breathing.
- Diagnosis delay: time between first symptoms and the start of proper TB diagnosis; the paper's exact cut-off for "delay" is not stated in the text provided.
- Case-control study: compares people with an outcome (cases, here delayed diagnosis) with people without it (controls) and looks back at what differed between the groups.
- Unmatched: cases and controls were chosen without pairing them on specific traits.
- Logistic regression: a statistical method that estimates how strongly each factor is linked to the outcome; "AOR" (adjusted odds ratio) above 1 means higher odds of delay after accounting for other factors; the 95% CI gives the range of uncertainty.
- Metekel Zone: an administrative area in Northwest Ethiopia.
summary.one_liner: An unmatched case-control study of 210 tuberculosis patients in Metekel Zone, Northwest Ethiopia (2023 data collection), identifying factors associated with delayed TB diagnosis: longer travel distance, rural residence, prior visits to holy water or traditional medicine, and poor TB knowledge.
summary.plain: Tuberculosis (TB) is a lung infection that spreads through the air, and it is harder to control when people are diagnosed late. This study looked at 210 TB patients at public clinics in one zone of Ethiopia to find out what made diagnosis take longer. It found that living in a rural area, travelling more than 10 km to a health facility, going first to holy water or traditional healers, and having poor knowledge about TB were each linked with a longer delay.
summary.why: Diagnosis delay keeps TB spreading and raises the risk of severe illness and death, so knowing which barriers matter can guide local services. The study is a single small local survey, and its findings are associations rather than proof of cause, so they should be read as pointers for local action rather than settled results.

title: Determinants of Tuberculosis Diagnosis Delays among Patients Attending Public Health Facility of Metekel Zone, Northwest Ethiopia, 2024 unmatched Case-Control Study

abstract: Background: According to the -Synuclein Origin site and Connectome (SOC) model, idiopathic Parkinson's Disease (iPD) is classified into two distinct subtypes: symmetric body-first, with diffuse spread and early non-motor clinical manifestations, and asymmetric brain-first, with initially circumscribed motor manifestations. Evidence regarding the application of this model to genetic PD remains limited. Objective: To investigate imaging and motor asymmetry in genetic vs iPD and idiopathic REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (iRBD), addressing thus indirectly the SOC model in genetic PD. Methods: We analyzed demographic, imaging and clinical data from 85 GBA PD, 166 LRRK2 PD, and 912 iPD patients, as well as 30 iRBD participants with abnormal DATSCAN from the PPMI database. Imaging asymmetry was assessed both by Asymmetry Index and absolute Asymmetry difference. Motor asymmetry was calculated as the absolute difference between the MDS-UPDRS III scores of the right and left sides. Results: GBA- and LRRK2-PD patients exhibit more symmetric putaminal radioligand uptake than iPD patients, but greater imaging asymmetry than iRBD subjects in the caudate. iRBD is more symmetric than iPD in both caudate and putamen. Consistent with the imaging data, GBA- and LRRK2-PD exhibit greater clinical motor symmetry than iPD. Conclusion: GBA- and LRRK2-PD are more symmetric than iPD on imaging and clinical grounds. GBA-PD appears to be a predominantly symmetric diffuse synucleinopathy, as predicted by the SOC model. The SOC model may not be applicable to LRRK2-PD, with its predominantly circumscribed motor phenotype, possibly because in this case -Synuclein pathology does not determine lateralization of motor manifestations.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.26368329 v1

summary.background:
- Parkinson's disease (PD) involves loss of dopamine-producing nerve cells, which is seen on DaT scans (a radioactive tracer that binds dopamine transporters in the striatum: caudate and putamen).
- Alpha-synuclein is a protein that clumps abnormally in PD; the SOC model proposes two subtypes: a symmetric "body-first" form with widespread spread and early non-motor symptoms, and an asymmetric "brain-first" form with early, localized motor symptoms.
- GBA and LRRK2 are genes; variants in them raise the risk of PD.
- iRBD (idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder) is a sleep condition where people act out dreams and often later develop a synucleinopathy.
- PPMI is a large public research database of Parkinson's patients and controls.
- MDS-UPDRS III is a standard clinical rating scale for motor symptoms.
- Asymmetry index and absolute asymmetry difference are ways of quantifying left-right imbalance.
summary.one_liner: Cross-sectional PPMI analysis comparing the left-right symmetry of dopamine-transporter imaging and MDS-UPDRS III motor scores in GBA-PD, LRRK2-PD, idiopathic PD and iRBD, used to test whether the SOC subtype model applies to genetic PD.
summary.plain: Parkinson's disease often starts on one side of the body and can differ in how it spreads through the brain. This study looked at people with Parkinson's caused by two known gene changes (GBA and LRRK2), compared them with people with no known genetic cause, and with people at risk who have a sleep disorder that often precedes Parkinson's. The researchers measured how evenly brain scan signals and motor symptoms were split between the left and right sides.
summary.why: It tests whether a proposed model that sorts Parkinson's into two subtypes also holds for genetic forms, which matters for how patients might be grouped in future studies and trials. The text reports that GBA-PD looked more symmetric and LRRK2-PD did not fit the model, and suggests a possible reason, but this is an observational association and the authors' explanation is speculative.

title: Imaging and Motor Asymmetry in Parkinson's Disease associated with GBA and LRRK2 mutations: Data from the PPMI study

abstract: White matter (WM) pathology is increasingly recognized as an early, mechanistically relevant feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet sensitive in-vivo biomarkers remain limited. Here, we introduce an MRI-based Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging (RKI) technique sensitive to WM microstructure. RKI metrics differentiate two distinct phenotypes of white matter that follow divergent microstructural trajectories in preclinical and early symptomatic AD. We examined their relationships to AD progression, gray matter (GM) pathology, and clinical impairment in 305 adults spanning amyloid-negative to amyloid-positive stages with normal cognition, preclinical AD, and early symptomatic AD. Pathological changes in one phenotype reflected axonal alterations without myelin loss and were anatomically coupled to GM cortical pathology, strengthening with disease stage - a signature of Wallerian degeneration. Alterations in the other phenotype represented WM demyelination. A model incorporating RKI-metrics, age, sex, amyloid status, APOE genotype, and brain volume classified Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR)-based impairment with an area under the receiver operating curve (AUC) = 0.933, with the RKI-metrics contributing 27% (second only to amyloid at 40%). While both phenotypes related comparably to concurrent cognition (each ~27%), the "axonal" phenotype showed the strongest relationship to subsequent cognitive decline (41% of explained variance), with the "myelin" phenotype contributing 31%. These RKI-defined dual white matter phenotypes provide new insight into AD pathology, adding diagnostic and prognostic value for tracking both current cognitive status and future cognitive decline.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.26368344 v1

summary.background:
- Alzheimer's disease (AD): a progressive brain disease that causes memory and thinking decline; amyloid protein buildup is an early hallmark.
- Preclinical AD: amyloid or other brain changes are present but symptoms are not yet obvious.
- White matter: the brain's wiring (nerve fibers), which is wrapped in myelin, a fatty insulating layer.
- Demyelination: loss of myelin insulation, which slows nerve signals.
- Axonal damage: injury to the nerve fiber itself.
- Wallerian degeneration: nerve fibers degenerating after their connected cell bodies are damaged, so damage spreads along the wiring.
- Gray matter: the outer layers of brain tissue where nerve cell bodies sit.
- APOE genotype: a gene variant linked to Alzheimer's risk.
- Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR): a standard scale for staging dementia severity.
- AUC (area under the curve): a 0 to 1 score of how well a model separates groups; 0.933 is high.
summary.one_liner: A study introducing Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging (RKI), an MRI method sensitive to white matter microstructure, which separates two white matter phenotypes (axonal versus myelin changes) with different trajectories across the Alzheimer's disease continuum in 305 adults.
summary.plain: Alzheimer's disease damages the brain's wiring as well as its gray matter, but the wiring damage is hard to measure in living people. This paper describes an MRI-based technique that splits white matter changes into two types: damage to the nerve fibers themselves, and loss of their myelin insulation. The researchers tracked these in 305 adults ranging from people without amyloid to those with early symptoms.
summary.why: The text reports that the two phenotypes relate differently to later cognitive decline, with the axonal type showing the strongest link (41% of explained variance), and that the RKI metrics added to a model classifying clinical impairment. This may help with earlier tracking of disease, but the text does not show clinical use, and the findings come from a single cohort reported in the abstract only.

title: Distinct Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging-Derived White Matter Microstructural Phenotypes Tracking Alzheimer's Disease Pathology and Cognitive Decline

abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) genomic studies have largely underrepresented African populations, limiting understanding of disease biology in these groups. This study addressed this gap by generating integrated genomic and transcriptomic data from South African (SA) CRC patients, establishing a foundation for future cancer studies. Bulk RNA sequencing of 32 samples identified several differentially expressed genes between tumour and normal samples, with AGAP3, AMPD2, ANKRD10, and SALL4 showing strong diagnostic performance (average sensitivity 99.9%, specificity 94.22%, PPV 99.9%, NPV 89.5%). SALL4 performed best and was validated using TCGA data and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis. Consensus Molecular Subtype classification revealed a distinct distribution, with enrichment of metabolic (CMS3, 30%) and mesenchymal (CMS4, 30%) subtypes and under-representation of canonical CMS2 (21%). APC mutation rates were lower than in European patients (~55% vs ~75%). Functional analysis identified inflammatory pathways as primary drivers of carcinogenesis, with viral influences exacerbating the inflammatory tumour microenvironment. Altered neural pathways in tumour samples suggested a consequential gut-brain axis loop as cancer infiltrates enervated tissue, an increasingly relevant field to which these data contribute. Whole-genome sequencing of 12 samples revealed pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants with transcriptomic differential expression; SMPD1, PERM1, PRRT2, and RP1 emerged as potential multi-omics markers, while novel mutations (KDM6A, C2CD2, TAF2, SLC6A16, OR5M10, PITRM1, TRIM64B, CARD11) were identified as previously unrecognised contributors to CRC progression in African samples. These findings expand genomic resources for African cancer research and provide new insights into the molecular landscape and tumourigenesis mechanisms of CRC in SA patients, supporting the development of population-specific precision oncology approaches.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.26368287 v1

summary.background:
- Colorectal cancer: cancer of the colon or rectum (the large bowel).
- RNA sequencing: measures which genes are switched on and how strongly in a tissue sample.
- Whole-genome sequencing: reads the full DNA of a sample to find genetic variants (changes).
- Differentially expressed genes: genes that are more or less active in tumour than in normal tissue.
- Sensitivity / specificity / PPV / NPV: measures of how well a marker separates cancer from normal tissue.
- Consensus Molecular Subtypes (CMS): a classification of colorectal tumours into four groups based on gene activity patterns.
- APC mutation: a change in the APC gene, common in bowel cancer and an early driver of it.
- TCGA and Kaplan-Meier analysis: a public cancer genome database and a method for comparing survival over time.
summary.one_liner: Bulk RNA sequencing of 32 and whole-genome sequencing of 12 South African colorectal cancer samples identifies candidate diagnostic genes, tumour subtype distribution, APC mutation rates and novel variants in an underrepresented population.
summary.plain: Bowel cancer genetics have mostly been studied in people of European descent, so less is known about patients in Africa. This study sequenced the genes and their activity in tumour and healthy tissue from South African bowel cancer patients. It reports several genes that could help tell tumour from normal tissue, a different spread of tumour subtypes than in European studies, and some gene changes not previously linked to this cancer.
summary.why: Genetic studies that leave out African populations may miss biology and treatment targets that matter there, so this adds data to a gap. The text is a small study (32 and 12 samples), so the findings are best seen as leads for larger work rather than settled results; the link to a gut-brain axis is described by the authors as an emerging area and is not established by these data.

title: Transcriptomic and Genomic Sequencing of South African Colorectal Cancer Patients Reveal Population-Specific Insights and Variants

abstract: Publicly deposited stable-isotope-resolved metabolomics data can be reanalyzed independently, but small patient-derived experiments may produce treatment effects with limited statistical resolution. We reanalyzed a public isotope-resolved metabolomics dataset from patient-derived lung cancer tissue cultures to quantify treatment- and tissue-specific labeling patterns and their uncertainty. We used 38 tissue samples from two patients: matched tumor and non-tumor slices from UK131 treated with vehicle or pembrolizumab and traced with U-13C6-glucose or U-13C5,15N2-glutamine (n = 3 per cell), and a pembrolizumab x WGP {beta}-glucan factorial experiment in UK2035 tumor tissue (n = 3/3/3/2). We recomputed protein-normalized pools, isotopologue distributions, atom-percent excess and pathway summaries. Effects were estimated with log2-scale linear models, Hedges' g, and exact randomization tests that enumerated all assignments compatible with each design; Benjamini-Hochberg q values were calculated within endpoint families. Sixteen macrophage samples were examined only descriptively. In UK131 tumor tissue, labeled non-oxidative pentose phosphate pathway intermediates increased 1.84-fold (model P = 0.036; exact tumor P = 0.10; exact interaction P = 0.16; q = 0.32). Weighted isotopic scrambling increased 1.31-fold (exact interaction P = 0.04; q = 0.20), and glutamine-derived glutathione diversion increased 1.66-fold (exact interaction P = 0.09; q = 0.22). In UK2035, the combination increased the labeled IMP/(ATP+GTP+UTP) ratio 3.64-fold (model interaction P = 3.2 x 10-4; exact P = 0.016; q = 0.097). No endpoint survived Benjamini-Hochberg correction at q < 0.05 in the exact analyses. The reanalysis reproduced the direction of the source study's principal labeling patterns but showed that their statistical support is weaker than model-based P values imply. These results should be treated as hypothesis-generating estimates for larger patient-derived studies, not as evidence of a validated metabolic bottleneck.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.26368161 v1

summary.background:
- Patient-derived tissue: tissue taken from patients and kept alive in a dish or slice culture.
- Stable isotope tracing: feeding cells sugars or amino acids containing heavy, non-radioactive atoms (such as carbon-13) to follow how they are used in metabolism.
- Metabolomics: measuring many small chemical molecules in a sample.
- Pembrolizumab: an immunotherapy drug that blocks the PD-1 immune checkpoint.
- Beta-glucan (WGP): a fungal sugar polymer that can stimulate immune cells.
- P value: the probability of seeing a result at least this extreme if there were no real effect.
- Exact randomization test: a test that checks every possible way of assigning samples to groups, rather than relying on model assumptions.
- Benjamini-Hochberg q value: an adjustment that controls the share of false positives when many tests are run.
- Hedges' g: a standardized size-of-effect measure that corrects for small samples.
summary.one_liner: An independent reanalysis of a public isotope-tracing metabolomics dataset from small patient-derived lung cancer tissue cultures, testing how pembrolizumab and a beta-glucan treatment change labeling patterns, with exact randomization tests and multiple-comparison correction.
summary.plain: Researchers took a publicly shared set of lab measurements from lung tumor tissue slices grown outside the body and checked the analysis again from scratch. The tissue was fed sugar and amino acids tagged with a heavy carbon or nitrogen isotope, so scientists could follow where those atoms went inside cell chemistry. The reanalysis found the same general direction of effects as the original study, but with much weaker statistical support.
summary.why: It is a useful example of how small patient-derived experiments can produce effects that look more certain in standard model-based p values than they are under stricter tests. The authors describe the results as hypothesis-generating only, and the text does not show any link to clinical outcomes.

title: # Treatment- and tissue-context-specific isotope labeling patterns in patient-derived lung cancer tissues: an independent reanalysis of public metabolomics data

abstract: Objectives: To examine how quickly software vulnerabilities are exploited after public disclosure, and whether hacking breaches at US health care providers changed in size after 2021, a period in which earlier studies had found attacks concentrating on large organizations. Methods: Retrospective analysis of public data. We linked the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (1,748 entries) with CVE publication dates to measure time to confirmed exploitation by half-year of publication (2021-2025). We also analyzed 8,029 breach reports submitted to the HHS Office for Civil Rights, focusing on hacking/IT incidents at health care providers. Results: Median time to confirmed exploitation was 24 days for vulnerabilities published from late 2021 to mid 2022, 0 days for those published in the second half of 2022, and 6 days in 2023-2025, with no further shortening across 2023-2025 (P = .40). About a quarter were exploited on or before the day of disclosure. Among provider hacking breaches, the share affecting fewer than 5,000 people fell from 42% in 2016 to 32% in 2022 (trend P = .004) and rose to 46% in 2025 (P < .001). Conclusions: The window between disclosure and exploitation had narrowed to about a week before generative AI was widely available. After 2022, breaches moved toward smaller events, reversing the earlier concentration on large organizations. Defenses that depend on patching speed will not protect small providers.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.26368300 v1

summary.background:
- CVE: a public identifier for a specific software vulnerability, with a publication date.
- CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog: a US government list of flaws confirmed to be used in real attacks; the paper uses its 1,748 entries.
- Time to exploitation: days between public disclosure of a flaw and its first confirmed use in attacks. A median of 0 days means many were exploited on or before the day they were announced.
- HHS Office for Civil Rights breach portal: US federal reports of health data breaches affecting 500 or more people; the paper analyzes 8,029 reports.
- Hacking/IT incident: the category of breach caused by an outside attack or IT failure, as opposed to theft of paper records or internal misuse.
- Trend test (P value): a statistical check of whether a change over time is likely to be real; P = .40 means no clear further change, while P < .001 means a very unlikely chance result.
- Patching: installing software updates that fix known flaws.
summary.one_liner: A retrospective analysis of CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and HHS breach reports examines how fast software flaws are exploited after disclosure and how the size of hacking breaches at US health care providers changed from 2016 to 2026.
summary.plain: Software flaws are often announced publicly before criminals start using them, and this paper asks how long that gap has been. It also checks whether hacks on US health care providers, as reported to federal regulators, have been getting bigger or smaller over time. The authors found the gap shrank to a median of about a week by 2023-2025, and that the share of provider hacks affecting fewer than 5,000 people rose from 32% in 2022 to 46% in 2025.
summary.why: The findings suggest that small clinics may be hit by attacks that quickly follow public disclosure of a flaw, which bears on how much a patching-based defense can protect them. The text does not show what caused either trend, so the link to generative AI in the conclusions is the authors' suggestion rather than something the data establish.

title: The Shrinking Grace Period and the Downsizing of Ransomware Victims: Exploitation Timelines and Breach Size Among US Health Care Providers, 2016-2026

abstract: Background: Patients' difficulties with illness and care (not understanding a result, distress, daily restrictions, not knowing where to go, family strain) may not surface in clinical encounters or records. Regulatory guidance on patient-focused drug development recognizes social-media listening as a source of patient experience data, but no systematic framework exists for Traditional Chinese discussions in Taiwan, and keyword pipelines measure such content poorly. Objective: To characterize patient-expressed needs, burdens and barriers ("frictions") in Taiwanese online health discussions with an eight-domain, Taiwan-contextualized framework, identify whose frictions they are, and assess how securely each is measured. Methods: From a 13.6-million-unit archive of the PTT forum and three ask-a-physician services, seeded samples of 9,131 pipeline-flagged units and 1,000 unflagged forum articles (10,130 distinct units) were read in full by a large language model under rubrics for relevance, author (patient or family member) and eight domains: information gap, emotional burden, lifestyle burden, medication experience, system navigation, access barrier, caregiver burden and cost burden. Profiles were reported separately for forum articles and physician submissions and checked against a second vendor, two physicians' independent labels of 160 accepted and rejected units, and the archive's keyword pipeline. Results: Among 2,395 model-confirmed forum articles, 83.1% voiced at least one friction: information gap 59.5% (physicians 86%-93%), emotional burden 39.0%, medication experience 24.1%, lifestyle burden 22.2% and system navigation 16.3%; access barrier, caregiver burden and cost burden were each below 7%. Of 3,105 submissions, nearly all were questions and 53.8% also carried a burden. Navigation rarely concerned insurance (9.1%). Family-authored forum articles (14.5%) more often voiced emotional burden (54.9% vs 36.3%), navigation (34.8% vs 13.2%; instrument-dependent) and access barriers (16.4% vs 4.7%), and patient-authored articles lifestyle burden (24.8% vs 6.9%); caregiver burden came with emotional burden in 86.0% of articles voicing it. Emotional and lifestyle burden were commoner in forum articles than submissions under the model, a second vendor and both physicians; medication experience and navigation were instrument-dependent, and physicians disagreed on cost (32% vs 4%). The keyword pipeline had stored its information-gap output for 29.9% of model-confirmed reference-stratum units and over-counted insurance navigation 2.9-fold; its relevance flag was 50.5% precise for forum articles and reached an estimated 42.9% of patient-voice articles. Conclusions: Systematic listening organized Taiwanese patients' and families' online accounts into eight clinically interpretable friction domains, led by the need to understand and by emotional burden, with family-authored posts more often voicing navigation and access difficulty. These expressed concerns may not surface in routine encounters; they identify candidate targets for patient-centred communication and services, which require evaluation. Some domain levels depended on the reader, and keyword pipelines missed or distorted them, so such work needs full-text reading, explicit definitions and clinician checks. Keywords: social media; patient experience data; patient-focused drug development; unmet needs; caregivers; natural language processing; large language models; content analysis; Taiwan; national health insurance
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.26365957 v1

summary.background:
- "Social listening" means systematically reading public online posts to learn what people experience.
- "Patient-focused drug development" is a regulatory approach that gathers patients' own views of their conditions and treatments.
- A "large language model" is an AI system trained on text that can label or summarise written material; here it was used as a reader and coder.
- "PTT" is a large Taiwanese forum; "ask-a-physician" services let users submit health questions to doctors.
- A "keyword pipeline" is an automated filter that flags posts containing certain words, a simpler method than reading the full text.
- Agreement checks used a second AI vendor and two physicians' independent labels on 160 posts.
- Taiwan's National Health Insurance is the public system that frames many of the cost and access questions.
summary.one_liner: A large language model was used to read full Traditional Chinese posts from Taiwan's PTT forum and physician Q&A services and code them into eight patient-friction domains, with checks against a second model, physician labels and a keyword pipeline.
summary.plain: Patients and their families often describe struggles online, such as not understanding a diagnosis, feeling distressed, or not knowing where to go, that rarely come up in a doctor's visit. This study read about 10,000 Taiwanese online health posts and questions with an AI language model, sorting them into eight kinds of difficulty. The most common concern was not understanding their condition, followed by emotional strain; family members more often wrote about navigating the system and access problems.
summary.why: It offers a way to hear patient and family concerns at scale, which regulators already recognise as a possible source of patient experience data. The paper also reports that a common keyword-based method missed or distorted several categories, which matters for anyone building similar monitoring tools; its usefulness for actual services still needs testing, as the authors themselves note.

title: Patient-Expressed Needs, Burdens and Barriers in Taiwanese Online Health Discussions: A Taiwan-Contextualized Friction Framework Applied With Large Language Model-Based Social Listening

abstract: Productivity improvements in digital industries could massively reshape the structure of production networks and drive significant labour reallocation across sectors. We examine these adjustments using a calibrated agent-based model of the global economy. We consider two scenarios with the same cumulative increase in digital-supplier productivity, which differ in how digital inputs in exposed industries are incorporated into production. The key difference is whether digital inputs enter as standard intermediate inputs (low embeddedness) or are combined directly with primary factors (high embeddedness). Across economies, both scenarios generate gains in gross output, household utility, and GDP, although value-added gains are more modest and unevenly distributed across sectors. High embeddedness generally amplifies production responses, particularly in industries highly exposed to digital inputs. Structurally, as digital industries become central in the production network and attract labour from other activities, other industries move further upstream and downstream. Persistent labour reallocation pressures also indicate potential unemployment risks where workers cannot move to expanding industries. These findings stress that, beyond productivity gains derived from advances in digital technologies, economic and social consequences depend on how digital inputs integrate into production and on workers' possibilities to adapt to structural change.
label: arXiv:2611.26338v1

summary.background:
- Agent-based model: a simulation where many interacting units (here, industries and households) follow rules, and aggregate outcomes emerge from their interactions.
- Calibrated: parameters are set so the model reproduces observed economic data.
- Intermediate inputs: goods and services one industry buys from another to make its own output.
- Value added: output minus intermediate inputs; roughly the income created at each stage, closely tied to GDP.
- Embeddedness: how deeply digital inputs are woven into production, here either as ordinary purchased inputs (low) or combined directly with labour and capital (high).
- Upstream/downstream: positions in a supply chain, closer to raw inputs or to final consumers.
- Labour reallocation: workers moving between industries as demand and productivity shift.
summary.one_liner: A calibrated agent-based model of the global economy compares two ways digital inputs can enter production after a common productivity gain in digital-supplier industries, tracing effects on output, value added, utility, and sectoral labour reallocation.
summary.plain: The paper asks what happens to whole economies if the industries that supply digital goods and services become much more productive. It simulates this in a computer model of the global economy under two scenarios that differ in how digital inputs are used by other industries. Gross output, household well-being, and GDP rise in both cases, but value added gains are smaller and uneven across sectors, and workers may struggle to move into growing industries.
summary.why: It addresses how technology gains spread through supply chains and labour markets, a question relevant to policy on automation and job transitions. The text does not show how well the model's assumptions match real data, so its quantitative conclusions should be read cautiously.

title: Structural economic change under the digital transformation

abstract: How should a predictor trained on historical data be adapted to a new economic environment or task when few target observations are available? We propose structural fine-tuning, a framework that introduces economic restrictions to guide the adaptation of pretrained predictors. The framework does not require a complete structural model; instead, it utilizes constraints based on economic knowledge, ranging from simple, ubiquitous assumptions to particular workhorse models. Theoretically, we characterize conditions when economic restrictions improve prediction over the original model and ordinary fine-tuning. Then, we illustrate the framework through a simulation exercise of a credit issuer's credit-limit decision following a Medicaid-style expansion in medical payments. Imposing restrictions based on eligibility, outstanding medical bills, cash flows, and group-level risk bounds, our framework lowers the root mean squared error of predicted risk by 28 to 39 percent and the issuer's policy regret by 3 to 10 percent relative to ordinary neuron gating, LoRA, and full fine-tuning.
label: arXiv:2611.25420v1

summary.background:
- Pretrained predictor: a model fit on historical data, then reused.
- Fine-tuning: updating a trained model on a smaller new dataset.
- LoRA and neuron gating: lightweight fine-tuning methods that change only a small part of the model.
- Root mean squared error (RMSE): a standard measure of prediction error; lower is better.
- Policy regret: the loss a decision-maker incurs compared with the best possible decision.
- Economic restrictions: constraints derived from economic theory or institutional rules that the adapted model must respect.
- Simulation exercise: results come from synthetic data built to mimic a setting, not from observed outcomes.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes "structural fine-tuning," which adapts a pretrained predictor to a new economic setting by imposing economic restrictions (ranging from simple assumptions to workhorse models) during fine-tuning, and reports theory plus a simulation of a credit-limit decision.
summary.plain: The paper asks how a prediction model trained on past data should be adjusted when a new environment or task has only a few new observations. The authors suggest adding rules drawn from economic knowledge, such as who is eligible or how cash flows work, to guide that adjustment. They test this in a simulated case where a credit issuer sets credit limits after a change resembling a Medicaid-style expansion of medical payments.
summary.why: Adapting models with little new data is a common practical problem in economic forecasting and policy evaluation, so combining model-adaptation methods with economic knowledge is worth attention. The reported gains come from a simulation rather than real data, so how far they carry to actual credit markets is an open question the text does not settle.

title: Structural Fine-Tuning under Economic Restrictions

abstract: In this note, I provide a direct and self-contained proof of Koray's (2000) theorem, by which a neutral and unanimous social choice function is universally self-selective if and only if it is dictatorial. Koray's (2000) original proof relies on results by Sen (1970) and Houthakker (1950) to construct a social welfare function for each alternative set. He then shows that these functions are Paretian and independent of irrelevant alternatives, allowing him to apply Arrow's (1950, 1951) impossibility theorem. Instead, I construct a cyclic preference profile and show that the voter who ranks the chosen alternative first is the dictator on every finite nonempty alternative set.
label: arXiv:2611.25748v1

summary.background:
- Social choice function: a rule that takes each voter's ranking of options and picks a winner from any menu of options.
- Neutrality: the rule does not favor any option by its label.
- Unanimity (Pareto): if every voter ranks one option above another, the rule does not choose the lower one.
- Self-selection: the chosen option from a menu stays chosen when the menu is narrowed to include it.
- Dictatorship: one specific voter's ranking alone determines the outcome.
- Arrow's impossibility theorem: a classic result showing that no ranking-based voting rule with basic fairness properties avoids dictatorship when there are three or more options.
- Cyclic preferences: rankings that loop, such as A above B, B above C, and C above A.
summary.one_liner: A short note giving a direct, self-contained proof of Koray's (2000) result that a neutral, unanimous social choice function is universally self-selective if and only if it is dictatorial.
summary.plain: This note is about how groups make collective choices, such as picking one option from a set when each member has their own ranking. The author re-proves a known result: if a group's choice rule treats all options equally, respects unanimous agreement, and has the property that the chosen option is always picked again when the menu shrinks (self-selection), then the rule must be dictatorial, meaning one fixed voter's ranking always decides. The new proof builds a special arrangement of voter rankings and shows that the voter who ranks the chosen option first must be the dictator.
summary.why: It offers a shorter route to an existing impossibility result, avoiding the earlier proof's reliance on several older theorems. The text does not claim wider consequences, so its value is mainly as a cleaner argument for specialists in social choice theory.

title: A Simple Proof of Koray's Theorem

abstract: We revisit the classic chain-store paradox by introducing exogenous public signals about the incumbent's private type that arrive each period over a finite horizon. We fully characterize perfect Bayesian equilibria in terms of sequences of reputation cutoffs that increase over time: entrants enter below their cutoff, while the normal incumbent mixes below its cutoff and fights above it. The equilibrium outcome is generically unique. Information arrival dampens the incentive to build a reputation, so full deterrence need not emerge as the horizon grows arbitrarily long, even when the incumbent is very patient. We characterize exactly when there is full deterrence in the limit, along with the limiting equilibrium when there is not.
label: arXiv:2611.26452v1

summary.background:
- Chain-store paradox: a monopolist facing a sequence of entrants may fight early entrants to build a reputation for toughness, a result that seems paradoxical under strict backward-induction logic.
- Incumbent's private type: the incumbent knows whether it is a "normal" (profit-driven) or a "tough" (always-fight) type; entrants only know the probabilities.
- Perfect Bayesian equilibrium: a solution concept in which each player best-responds to beliefs that are updated correctly from observed play.
- Reputation cutoff: a threshold belief about the incumbent's toughness above which the incumbent fights and below which entry is accepted.
- Mixing: randomizing between actions (here, fighting or not) with set probabilities.
- Finite horizon and patience: the game has a fixed number of periods, and patience measures how much the incumbent values future payoffs.
- Full deterrence: entry is never attempted in equilibrium.
summary.one_liner: This paper extends the chain-store reputation game to a finite horizon with exogenous public signals about the incumbent's private type, characterizing perfect Bayesian equilibria via increasing reputation cutoffs and identifying when full deterrence arises in the limit.
summary.plain: The paper studies a standard story about a dominant firm that faces a series of potential competitors and wants to look tough so newcomers stay out. It adds a twist: public news about the firm arrives over time, independent of what the firm does. The authors work out how firms and entrants should behave in this setting and find that this steady flow of news weakens the firm's incentive to build a tough reputation.
summary.why: The chain-store paradox is a well-known benchmark for how reputation can deter entry, so showing that outside information can undercut that reputation effect is a useful refinement. The text does not indicate applications beyond this theoretical setting, so its wider relevance is unclear from the excerpt alone.

title: Entry Deterrence with Public Signals: Revisiting the Chain-Store Paradox

abstract: We give a polynomial-time algorithm for exact equilibrium computation in atomic splittable polymatroid congestion games with integral ranks and rational player-specific affine latencies with positive slopes. The algorithm first computes equilibria of associated integer-splittable games, in which demands are allocated in multiples of a common packet size. For arbitrary polymatroid bases, no polynomial-time algorithm for these discrete equilibria was previously known. We provide such an algorithm and use progressively finer packets to recover the continuous equilibrium exactly. Our proof uses the multiple-exchange theorem of Oki and Schwarcz (2025) to obtain two exchange matchings that yield equilibrium proximity under changes of packet sizes and ranks, independently of cost coefficients. We then bound the matching deficiency caused by rank changes and construct compatible submodular rank roundings. Together these give a polynomial-time packet-halving algorithm using polynomially many submodular-function minimizations and exact rational arithmetic. The analysis rests on a uniqueness theorem of independent interest: for arbitrary real polymatroid ranks and continuously differentiable, strictly increasing, convex latencies, we prove uniqueness of equilibria, resolving a previously open problem.
label: arXiv:2611.25757v1

summary.background:
- Congestion game: players choose resources; each resource's cost rises with the number of users.
- Equilibrium: a split where no player can lower its own cost by changing its choice alone.
- Splittable demand: a player can divide its demand across several resources rather than picking one.
- Atomic: each player is a single, non-negligible participant, not a tiny crowd member.
- Polymatroid: a combinatorial structure generalizing capacity limits on sets of resources, defined by a rank function.
- Affine latency: a cost that rises linearly with load (a constant plus slope times load); positive slope means cost increases with load.
- Submodular function minimization: a standard polynomial-time optimization tool over these structures.
- Polynomial time: the running time grows at most as a polynomial in the input size.
summary.one_liner: The paper gives a polynomial-time exact algorithm for equilibria in atomic splittable polymatroid congestion games with affine latencies, via integer-packet approximations and proximity arguments built on an Oki–Schwarcz multiple-exchange theorem, and proves equilibrium uniqueness for arbitrary real polymatroid ranks with convex, strictly increasing latencies.
summary.plain: The paper studies a model where several players share a network of resources and each splits its demand across them, with congestion making each resource slower as more load lands on it. The authors show how to compute the stable split (the equilibrium) exactly and efficiently, by first solving a version where demand moves in fixed-size chunks and then shrinking the chunks step by step. They also prove that, under broad conditions, this stable state is the only one.
summary.why: Equilibrium computation in congestion-type games matters for traffic, network routing, and resource sharing, where it is useful to know both that a stable outcome can be found and that it is unique. The uniqueness result is stated as resolving a previously open problem, though the text alone does not show how widely that problem was discussed. Connections beyond this specialist setting are not established in the text.

title: Uniqueness, Proximity, and Scaling in Atomic Splittable Polymatroid Congestion Games

abstract: We study the fair division of indivisible chores that must be assigned in a prescribed order. The complete instance is known in advance, but assignments cannot be changed. Temporal envy-freeness up to one chore (TEF1) requires envy-freeness up to one chore after every arrival. For goods, TEF1 allocations need not exist, and deciding whether one exists is NP-hard. For chores, Elkind et al. (AAMAS 2025) showed that TEF1 allocations exist for two agents, but left open whether they always exist, conjecturing that they do not, and whether deciding their existence is hard. We resolve both questions, confirming the conjecture in a strong form: for every $n\ge3$ and every finite factor, some $n$-agent instance admits no allocation satisfying TEF1 even up to that factor. This holds even when all agents have the same multiset of individual chore costs, with nine chores sufficing for three agents. Deciding TEF1 existence is NP-complete for every fixed $n\ge3$, even when all costs lie within a factor $1+2^{-m}$ of one another, where $m$ is the number of chores. Instances without TEF1 allocations exist arbitrarily close to the uniform cost matrix with $O(n\log n)$ chores, and just nineteen for three agents. We then relate fairness to social cost. Even when a TEF1 allocation is supplied, minimizing social cost subject to TEF1 admits no polynomial-time approximation within any factor polynomial in the number of chores unless P$=$NP, already for three agents with strictly positive normalized costs. In contrast, for every fixed number of agents, we give an FPTAS for the optimal temporal EF1 factor, the smallest factor up to which TEF1 can be satisfied, whose output has social cost no larger than that of the cheapest allocation attaining this factor. Thus a slight relaxation of fairness permits a social-cost guarantee that, unless P$=$NP, no polynomial-time algorithm can provide under exact TEF1.
label: arXiv:2611.25892v1

summary.background:
- Indivisible chores: tasks that cannot be split and that each agent dislikes doing (each has a cost to each agent).
- Envy-freeness up to one chore (EF1): no agent would prefer another's bundle after removing one task from that bundle.
- Temporal fairness: the fairness condition must hold after every prefix of arrivals, not just at the end, and assignments are fixed once made.
- NP-hardness / NP-completeness: a standard notion from computational complexity meaning no known efficient algorithm is expected; "unless P = NP" is the usual caveat.
- Approximation and FPTAS: an algorithm that gets within a guaranteed factor of the best answer; an FPTAS does so in time polynomial in the input and in 1/error for fixed parameters.
- Social cost: the total cost all agents incur under an allocation.
summary.one_liner: The paper settles open questions on temporal EF1 fairness for indivisible chores: it shows such allocations need not exist for three or more agents, that deciding their existence is NP-complete, and that minimizing social cost under TEF1 is hard to approximate, while an FPTAS exists for the optimal temporal EF1 factor.
summary.plain: The paper studies how to split up unpleasant tasks (chores) among several people when the tasks arrive in a fixed order and cannot be reassigned. It asks whether a split exists where nobody ever feels they have a clearly worse share, up to the removal of one task, at every point in time. The authors show that for three or more people such splits sometimes do not exist, that checking whether one exists is computationally hard, and how this interacts with the total cost of the tasks.
summary.why: This settles a question that an earlier paper left open and conjectured, so it matters for anyone designing fair task-sharing rules over time. The link to social cost is a concrete trade-off: a small loosening of the fairness requirement permits efficient computation, which may be relevant to practical scheduling or allocation systems, though the text itself does not discuss applications.

title: Closing Gaps in Temporal Fair Division for Chores

abstract: Calibrating a volatility surface from sparse option prices requires repeated solutions of a pricing equation as the volatility parameters change. We implement a hybrid quantum and classical method for this inverse problem using the Dupire local-volatility model. A positive coefficient representation specifies the local variance, and linear combinations of Hamiltonian simulations approximate the associated pricing evolution. The circuit propagates through successive maturity intervals and evaluates discrepancies at the observed strikes. Measurement counts provide the objective values used by a classical optimiser to update the volatility coefficients. We implement this calibration cycle in a logical gate simulator and assess it alongside classical pricing solvers and alternative surface models. Multiple-maturity synthetic examples illustrate the reconstruction of smiles and skews, while a separate small circuit experiment tests the complete measured calibration. The comparisons quantify the effects of model flexibility, pricing approximation and measurement precision. Recorded gate counts and sampling budgets identify the main computational costs of the implementation.
label: arXiv:2611.25344v1

summary.background:
- Option: a contract whose price depends on future stock price and a strike level; option quotes at several strikes and maturities are the data.
