abstract: Across their development, clonal multicellular organisms generate new cell types from less differentiated cell types. Differentiation pathways arrange into a hierarchical, tree-like organization: regressions from specialized to undifferentiated cell types rarely occur and undifferentiated cell types often have the potential to produce, when subject to distinct stimuli, two or more differently specialized cell types. How cell type transitions acquire such a peculiar disposition requires an explanation that must reside in the properties of gene regulatory networks (GRNs); after all, GRNs orchestrate the changes in gene activity that define cell types. We studied vast numbers of small dynamic model networks to search for elementary GRNs that could yield the simplest hierarchical, developmental-like, differentiation patterns. We found that only a small minority of GRNs are compatible with hierarchical cell type transitions. Importantly, GRNs that yielded developmental-like differentiation patterns shared common traits: One is the presence of tangles of cycles of positive interactions. Genes in such a tangle produce an all-or-none one-way response to a signal. Another such trait is mutual inhibition between genes associated to different specialized cell types, enforcing their mutually exclusive activation. Moreover, these regulatory patterns are more abundant in published experimentally sustained developmental GRNs than as expected by chance. In addition, we show that it is easy to maintain hierarchical cellular differentiation throughout evolution, even when undergoing changes in gene regulatory interactions and developmental mechanisms. Our work supports the prevalence of design principles that organize hierarchically differentiation pathways in clonal multicellular organisms.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767571 v1

summary.background:
- Gene regulatory network (GRN): a set of genes whose activity switches others on or off; modeled as a diagram of positive (activating) and negative (inhibiting) links.
- Cell differentiation: the process by which a less specialized cell becomes a specialized cell type, such as a skin or nerve cell.
- Hierarchical (tree-like) differentiation: a branching pattern where each step narrows possible cell fates and reversal is rare.
- Dynamic model: a mathematical simulation of how gene activity levels change over time under given inputs.
- Positive feedback cycle: a loop in which genes activate each other, which can lock a cell into a stable state.
- Mutual inhibition: two genes that suppress each other, so only one tends to be active.
- Clonal multicellular organism: an organism that develops from a single cell that divides, such as animals and plants.
summary.one_liner: The paper uses small dynamic gene regulatory network models to identify the network features (positive-feedback cycles and mutual inhibition between cell-type genes) that produce hierarchical, tree-like cell differentiation, and checks these features against published developmental networks.
summary.plain: Cells in a growing animal or plant usually become more specialized in a branching, one-way pattern: a less specialized cell can give rise to two or more specialized types, but specialized cells rarely turn back. The authors asked which simple wiring patterns among genes could produce this pattern, by simulating large numbers of small model networks. They report that only a small minority of such networks behave this way, and that the ones that do share a few recurring features.
summary.why: The work offers a possible explanation for why developmental pathways are so consistently tree-shaped, grounding it in the wiring of gene networks rather than in assumption. The text reports that these features are more common in published experimental developmental networks than chance would predict, and that hierarchy can persist through evolutionary change; how far these model results carry over to real organisms is not established in the text.

title: Gene regulatory networks and the organization of cell differentiation in multicellular organisms

abstract: Training RNA secondary structure predictors is limited by scarce reference annotations, even as chemical probing produces abundant nucleotide-level measurements. These measurements inform pairing states without identifying base-pairing partners. Here we extend MXfold2, which combines neural and thermodynamic folding scores, to learn from probing profiles and predict RNA secondary structures from sequence alone. We introduce three training objectives. One learns from probing-assisted target structures. The other two use implicit maximum-likelihood estimation to pass surrogate gradients from reactivity-ranking and likelihood losses through discrete folding. Simulations, RNAgym measurements and external structural tests show improved chemical agreement and gains in exact base-pair prediction when chemical supervision is combined with structural pretraining and replay. Probing profiles can thus broaden the range of RNAs that inform sequence-only structure prediction, including RNA populations with few complete structure annotations.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767577 v1

summary.background:
- RNA is a chain of four bases (A, C, G, U); bases pair with partners to form a folded "secondary structure."
- Structure prediction software estimates the folding from sequence, often combining learned neural scores with thermodynamic energy rules.
- Chemical probing uses reagents that react differently with paired and unpaired bases, giving a reactivity value per nucleotide, but it does not say which base pairs with which.
- Training a model normally needs reference structures; here, probing profiles stand in for part of that supervision.
- Implicit maximum-likelihood estimation is a technique for training models through discrete choices (such as picking a fold) by approximating gradients.
- Exact base-pair prediction means the predicted pairs match the reference pairs precisely.
summary.one_liner: MXfold2, a hybrid neural-thermodynamic RNA folding model, is extended to learn from chemical probing profiles using three training objectives, two of which use implicit maximum-likelihood estimation to pass gradients through discrete folding.
summary.plain: RNA molecules fold into shapes defined by which of their bases pair up, and predicting that shape from the sequence alone usually requires scarce, carefully annotated examples. This paper shows how chemical probing experiments, which measure how reactive each position of an RNA is, can be used as extra training signal. The authors report improved agreement with the chemical measurements and some gains in predicting exact base pairs, in simulations, RNAgym data and external structural tests.
summary.why: Chemical probing data are far more abundant than full structure annotations, so using them could widen the set of RNAs for which sequence-only structure prediction is practical, including RNA families with few known structures. The text does not say how large the gains are or how far they transfer beyond the tested datasets, so the practical reach remains to be judged.

title: Learning RNA secondary structure from chemical probing with MXfold2

abstract: Multiunit threshold crossings support high-performance brain-computer interfaces and preserve the low-dimensional trajectories that summarize population dynamics, raising the question of when spike sorting is still necessary. Using previously published recordings from four rhesus monkeys, we analyzed areas 3b and 1 of primary somatosensory cortex and ventral premotor cortex during a bimodal detection task, and ventral premotor cortex during an interval comparison task. From the same spikes, we built three representations: putative single units obtained with nonlinear sorting (UMAP and HDBSCAN), intermingled units obtained with linear sorting, and unsorted multiunit activity. Nonlinear sorting resolved up to three times more units than multiunit activity. In area 1, mixing discarded the periodicity information carried by phase-locked neurons, lengthened intrinsic timescales by about 40%, increased trial-to-trial variability, and raised neurometric detection thresholds by 33%. In premotor cortex, mixing reduced the task-related information recovered from the population and hid significant dimensions of its dynamics. After geometric alignment, the overall shape of population trajectories was nearly identical across representations, but distances between population states were distorted, and the approximately linear representation of interval duration saturated for longer intervals. Multiunit activity is therefore sufficient for analyses that rely on the dominant, shared structure of population activity, such as decoding, whereas analyses of single-neuron coding, variability, timescales, dimensionality, and parametric representations often require spike sorting.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767959 v1

summary.background:
- Spike sorting: separating the electrical spikes recorded on one electrode into the individual neurons that produced them.
- Multiunit activity: the combined spike signal from many neurons, without separating them.
- Population trajectories: paths traced through a high-dimensional space by the activity of many neurons over time, often reduced to a few dimensions.
- Intrinsic timescale: how quickly a neuron's activity fluctuations decay over time.
- Neurometric threshold: the smallest stimulus difference an ensemble of neural responses can reliably detect.
- UMAP and HDBSCAN: computational tools for grouping spike waveforms into clusters.
- Decoding: predicting what a subject is doing or perceiving from recorded brain activity.
summary.one_liner: Compares nonlinear (UMAP/HDBSCAN) spike sorting, linear sorting, and unsorted multiunit threshold crossings from the same monkey recordings in somatosensory and premotor cortex, asking which analyses need single-neuron identity.
summary.plain: Brain recordings pick up electrical spikes from many nearby nerve cells mixed together, and researchers must decide whether to separate them into individual neurons or just use the combined signal. Using previously published data from four monkeys, the authors built three versions of the same spikes and compared them. They found that the combined signal is good enough for analyses of the shared overall pattern of activity, such as decoding, but separating individual neurons was needed for measures like timing, variability and how neurons individually encode information.

title: When spike sorting matters: single-neuron identity in the quantification of neural circuits

abstract: Learning is commonly explained by changes in synaptic strength. In animals, however, learning also engages intrinsic plasticity -- changes in how readily neurons convert synaptic input into firing. Its contribution to human learning has been unclear, because conventional non-invasive measures of cortical excitability primarily reflect synaptic strength. Here we used controllable-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation to estimate two biophysical indices of intrinsic excitability in human motor cortex, before and after motor training. Training produced signatures of increased intrinsic excitability, selectively in the cortical representation of the trained muscle, but not an untrained muscle. Individuals showing larger intrinsic excitability changes learned faster, independently of changes in motor-evoked potential amplitude, an index of synaptic excitability that increased following training but did not predict learning rate. An axon model reproduced the measured changes through small shifts in membrane excitability. These findings provide evidence that intrinsic plasticity is expressed in the intact human brain, and that it represents a behaviourally relevant component of learning-related cortical adaptation.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767269 v1

summary.background:
- Synaptic strength: how strongly one neuron influences another; the usual explanation for learning.
- Intrinsic excitability/plasticity: how readily a neuron itself turns incoming signals into firing; changes here are seen in animals.
- Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS): a coil over the scalp that briefly stimulates the brain; the motor-evoked potential (MEP) is the muscle twitch it produces and is mainly a measure of synaptic excitability.
- Controllable-pulse TMS: a TMS variant that shapes the pulse, allowing indirect estimates of neuron-level properties.
- Motor cortex representation: the brain area controlling a given muscle; the trained muscle was compared with an untrained one as a control.
- Axon model: a computer simulation of a nerve fibre, used here to check whether small membrane changes could explain the measurements.
summary.one_liner: Using controllable-pulse TMS to estimate two biophysical indices of intrinsic excitability in human motor cortex, the paper reports training-related increases specific to the trained muscle's representation, with larger intrinsic changes linked to faster learning independent of synaptic-type MEP changes.
summary.plain: Learning is usually explained by changes in how strongly brain cells connect to each other. In animals, though, learning also changes how easily individual neurons fire, and this study asks whether that happens in people. The researchers measured two indirect indices of how easily motor-cortex neurons fire, before and after motor training, using magnetic stimulation of the scalp.
summary.why: If confirmed, this would suggest that a second, cell-level mechanism (intrinsic plasticity) contributes to human motor learning alongside connection-strength changes, which matters for how we understand skill learning and recovery. The text does not show follow-up work or clinical applications, so these links remain speculative.

title: Motor learning engages intrinsic plasticity in the human cortex

abstract: Co-transcriptional chromatin regulation is widely recognized as a mechanism that reinforces active gene expression, yet transcriptionally active genes must also be able to transition into stable epigenetic silencing during developmental transitions and environmental responses. Whether and how ongoing transcription is coupled to the initiation of epigenetic silencing remains unclear. Here we show that elongating RNA polymerase II phosphorylated at Ser2 (RNAPII-Ser2P) functions as an instructive signal for epigenetic silencing initiation. At actively transcribed genes, RNAPII-Ser2P positions and spatially constrains the FLD-LD H3K4me1 demethylase complex near transcription termination regions, separating the complex from its gene-body H3K4me1 substrate. We found that both chemical perturbation of transcription and physiological silencing cues induce a redistribution of RNAPII-Ser2P into the gene body, accompanied by FLD relocalization and subsequent gene-body H3K4me1 erasure. FLD disengages from chromatin upon gene silencing, indicating that active transcription is required for its continued chromatin association. We further show that LD tethers FLD to RNAPII through an N-terminal HOX domain that binds the C-terminal region of FLD and an adjacent TFIIS domain that contacts the RNAPII CTD in a Ser2P-sensitive manner. This FLD-LD-RNAPII bridge is essential to promote H3K4me1 erasure and gene silencing. Together, these findings reveal a mechanism by which active transcription licenses the initiation of epigenetic silencing.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.766859 v1

summary.background:
- Gene transcription: a polymerase enzyme reads DNA to make RNA; its tail (CTD) carries chemical marks such as Ser2 phosphorylation that change along the gene.
- Chromatin: DNA wrapped around proteins; chemical tags (methyl groups) on these proteins help switch genes on or off.
- H3K4me1: a methyl tag on histone H3 associated with active genes; a demethylase removes it.
- Epigenetic silencing: a stable, heritable switching-off of a gene without changing its DNA sequence.
- Terminators and gene body: the gene's 3' end where transcription ends, and the body between start and end.
- The paper's system is a plant (FLD is the Arabidopsis-type demethylase), so findings are from that model.
summary.one_liner: In plants, elongating RNA polymerase II phosphorylated at Ser2 recruits and spatially positions the FLD-LD H3K4me1 demethylase complex near gene ends, and its redistribution into gene bodies during transcription perturbation or silencing cues triggers H3K4me1 erasure and gene silencing via an FLD-LD-RNAPII bridge.
summary.plain: Cells sometimes switch a gene off for good, a process called epigenetic silencing, and this paper asks how a gene that is currently being read out gets set up for that switch. The authors report that the molecular machine copying the gene (RNA polymerase II, in a form marked at Ser2) acts as a signal: it holds a demethylase complex (FLD-LD) near the end of the gene, away from the chemical tags it removes, and when the machine's marker shifts into the gene body, the complex moves there, removes a activating chemical mark (H3K4me1), and the gene goes quiet. Experiments described in the text link this to a physical bridge between the complex and the machine, which is needed for silencing.
summary.why: It offers a mechanistic answer to how active transcription can lead to stable silencing rather than only reinforcing activity, which is a question relevant to development and stress responses. The text reports this in a plant model, so how far it generalises to other organisms is not something the text establishes.

title: Intragenic redistribution of RNA polymerase II licenses epigenetic silencing

abstract: High levels of lipoprotein(a) (Lp(a)) increase risk of cardiovascular diseases. Lp(a) concentration is primarily determined (>80%) by genetic variation at LPA, particularly by its large, size-polymorphic kringle IV-2 (KIV-2) repeat. However, because variation of the KIV-2 repeat is difficult to measure, the precise ways that genetic variants at LPA and other loci determine Lp(a) levels have been unclear, especially in individuals of non-European ancestry. Here, we developed new computational techniques to accurately genotype KIV-2 variation in whole-genome-sequenced population cohorts. Applying these methods to UK Biobank (n=490,414) and All of Us (n=245,394) provided insights into the genetic determinants of Lp(a) and the mutational dynamics of the KIV-2 repeat, which we found expands or contracts intra-allelically once every [~]500 generations. Variation in Lp(a) levels among people of all genetic ancestries was accurately predicted by a single, transferable genetic model capturing cis-epistatic effects of KIV-2 length and protein-altering polymorphisms in LPA. Controlling for predicted effects of LPA alleles revealed an additional, highly polygenic contribution to Lp(a) variation: LPA-adjusted Lp(a) levels associated with genetic variation at over 300 loci (P<5x10-8), much like other blood lipids. These results elucidate the genetic architecture and mutational origins of Lp(a) variation, showing how detailed characterization of a largely monogenic trait can provide surprising insights for complex trait genetics.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.767202 v1

summary.background:
- Lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a): a cholesterol-carrying particle in the blood; high levels are linked to heart disease.
- LPA gene: the gene that mostly determines Lp(a) levels, with over 80% of variation attributed to it.
- KIV-2 repeat: a segment of LPA that repeats a varying number of times; its length differs between people and is hard to measure with standard sequencing.
- Genotyping: reading a person's genetic variants from their DNA.
- Polygenic: influenced by many genes, each with a small effect.
- Cis-epistasis: interactions between variants on the same chromosome copy that affect the trait together.
- Whole-genome sequencing and biobanks (UK Biobank, All of Us): large databases of sequenced genomes linked to health data.
- Mutation dynamics: how often the repeat length changes over generations; the text reports changes roughly every 500 generations.
summary.one_liner: A genome-wide study that computationally genotypes the size-variable KIV-2 repeat in LPA across UK Biobank and All of Us, modeling how repeat length and protein-altering variants shape lipoprotein(a) levels, estimating the repeat's mutation rate, and finding over 300 loci associated with LPA-adjusted Lp(a).
summary.plain: Lipoprotein(a) is a blood fat particle that raises the risk of heart and blood-vessel disease, and its level is mostly set by genes. The hard part is a repetitive stretch of the LPA gene that is difficult to measure, so researchers developed new computer methods to read it from whole-genome sequences of large population studies. They then used these methods to build a model that predicts Lp(a) levels across people of many ancestries and to show that many other genetic regions also contribute.
summary.why: Lp(a) is a known, hard-to-treat cardiovascular risk factor, so a more accurate genetic picture could inform risk prediction and future drug targets, though the text does not itself address clinical use. The finding that a mostly single-gene trait also has a large polygenic component may matter for how complex traits are studied more generally.

title: The genetic architecture of lipoprotein(a): simplicity, complexity, and mutability

abstract: Gametogenesis, the process of meiosis coupled to gamete formation, transforms diploid progenitor cells into haploid gametes through extensive cellular remodeling and rewiring of gene expression. Several stress-responsive transcription factors (TFs) are upregulated during gametogenesis, but whether the cellular mechanisms that handle environmental stress also support the success of this developmental process is largely unexplored. Here, we show that four stress-responsive TFs, Hsf1, Skn7, and the paralogs Msn2 and Msn4, are endogenously active during budding yeast gametogenesis in the absence of external stress and drive distinct gene expression programs. Simultaneous meiotic depletion of Msn2, Msn4, and Skn7 compromise the fitness of the resulting gametes. We identified just two TF-dependent targets, the antioxidant genes TSA1 and AHP1, as important for gamete fitness, directly connecting TF activity to the protection of meiotic progeny. Our results demonstrate that the activation of canonical stress-response regulators is built into the meiotic program and suggest that such pathways can be repurposed during development to safeguard cellular health.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767631 v1

summary.background:
- Transcription factors: proteins that switch genes on or off; they are the control switches this paper studies.
- Meiosis: the cell division that produces haploid gametes (sperm, egg, or yeast spores) from diploid cells.
- Gametogenesis: the full process of making gametes, including meiosis and the packaging of gametes.
- Stress-response pathways: built-in cellular systems that respond to heat, oxidative damage and similar threats.
- Antioxidant genes (TSA1, AHP1): genes whose products help neutralize reactive oxygen molecules that can damage cells.
- Gamete fitness: how well a gamete survives and can contribute to the next generation; the text measures this only indirectly through yeast experiments.
- Budding yeast: a single-celled fungus widely used as a model organism in cell biology.
summary.one_liner: In budding yeast, four stress-responsive transcription factors (Hsf1, Skn7, Msn2 and Msn4) are active during gametogenesis without any added stress, and depleting Msn2, Msn4 and Skn7 together lowers gamete fitness, with the antioxidant genes TSA1 and AHP1 identified as key targets.
summary.plain: When yeast cells make sex cells (gametes), they halve their chromosomes and reshape themselves in a major developmental process called meiosis. This paper asks whether the cell's built-in stress-defense switches also help that process succeed. The authors found that several of these switches turn on during meiosis even without any outside stress, and that turning off three of them at once makes the resulting gametes less fit. Two antioxidant genes, TSA1 and AHP1, appear to be the important downstream helpers.
summary.why: It suggests that the machinery cells use to cope with environmental damage is also part of normal development, not only an emergency response. This may matter for understanding how gametes stay healthy, though the text does not show how broadly the idea applies beyond yeast.

title: Endogenous activation of multiple stress-response pathways during meiosis promotes gamete fitness

abstract: The vitreous, the largest intraocular tissue, provides a transparent light path and maintains the intraocular homeostasis. The reconstitution of the vitreous in vitro or in vivo remains an unsolved biomedical challenge. Here, we discovered a common feature, the "growth edge", constituted primarily of fibroblasts and their secreted proteins in human and mouse vitreous development. By leveraging the transforming growth factor beta signaling, we then generated centimeter-scale vitreous-like organoids (VOs) through stepwise differentiation from human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs). The VOs exhibited striking similarity to human vitreous in terms of physical transparency, vitreoretinal interface, molecular composition, biological profiles and regenerative transplantability. Lines of evidence supported that fibroblasts are the key cell hub for vitreous development. Finally, VOs with a transthyretin (TTR) mutation recapitulated the vitreous phenotypes of human patients with vitreous amyloidosis. Together, vitreous organoid technology opens avenues for future studies of human vitreous development, disease modeling, and regenerative therapeutics for a broad spectrum of human vitreoretinal diseases.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767433 v1

summary.background:
- The vitreous is the transparent gel that fills the large chamber behind the lens of the eye.
- Organoids are small, three-dimensional tissue cultures grown from stem cells that mimic parts of an organ.
- Pluripotent stem cells can develop into many cell types; here they are human cells made to form eye-like tissue.
- Fibroblasts are connective-tissue cells that make structural proteins and scaffolding.
- TGF-beta is a signaling protein that directs cell growth and specialization.
- Transthyretin (TTR) is a protein that, when mutated, can misfold and build up as amyloid deposits; vitreous amyloidosis is a clouding of the vitreous caused by such deposits.
- Mouse development data were used as a comparison, per the text.
summary.one_liner: The authors identify a fibroblast-rich "growth edge" in human and mouse vitreous development and use TGF-beta signaling to differentiate human pluripotent stem cells into centimeter-scale vitreous-like organoids that model a TTR-linked vitreous amyloidosis.
summary.plain: The vitreous is the clear, jelly-like filling of the eye that lets light reach the retina and helps keep the eye's pressure and shape stable. Scientists have not yet been able to rebuild it in the lab or repair it in the body. Here, the authors grew stem-cell-derived clumps of tissue that they call vitreous organoids, reaching about a centimeter in size, and report that they looked and behaved in ways similar to human vitreous.
summary.why: A lab model of the vitreous could help study how this tissue forms and how it fails, and may eventually inform repair strategies for eye diseases. The text reports that the organoids carried a disease-linked gene mutation and reproduced features of a patient condition, but whether this translates to treatment is not shown in the text, so its clinical reach remains uncertain.

title: Centimeter-sized Human Vitreous Organoids from Pluripotent Stem Cells

abstract: The emergence of plasmid-mediated resistance to critically important antimicrobials poses a growing threat to global health. Here we report the first genomic evidence of plasmid-mediated fosA3 and blaCTX-M-65 coexisting with mcr-1.1 and tet(X4) in multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli from clinically healthy broiler chickens in Pakistan. Among 1,677 high-quality genomes collected through antimicrobial resistance surveillance in Punjab, Pakistan, three isolates recovered between 2022 and 2024 harboured all four resistance determinants. Hybrid genome assemblies showed that fosA3 and blaCTX-M-65 were co-located on IncHI2A plasmids, whereas mcr-1.1 and tet(X4) were carried on separate IncI2 and IncFIA/IncFIC plasmids, all predicted to be conjugative; in one isolate the tet(X4) contig did not circularise. The isolates belonged to sequence type 93 and exhibited resistance to fosfomycin, colistin, tigecycline and cefotaxime. Comparative genomic analysis revealed highly conserved IncHI2A plasmid backbones, with an additional integron-associated resistance region in the 2024 isolates, suggesting acquisition of accessory resistance determinants. Resistance to three last-line antimicrobial classes and a canonical virulence profile now coexist on conjugative plasmids in poultry E. coli, a combination that favours co-selection and argues for plasmid-resolved surveillance in poultry production.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767496 v1

summary.background:
- E. coli is a common gut bacterium; avian pathogenic strains cause disease in poultry.
- Plasmids are circular, extra DNA molecules that can be copied and transferred between bacteria, carrying resistance genes.
- Conjugative plasmids can transfer themselves to other bacteria by direct contact.
- Resistance genes named here: fosA3 (fosfomycin), blaCTX-M-65 (cephalosporins such as cefotaxime), mcr-1.1 (colistin), tet(X4) (tigecycline and related tetracyclines).
- Colistin, tigecycline and fosfomycin are considered last-line or critically important drugs for human medicine.
- Hybrid assembly combines short- and long-read sequencing to reconstruct complete plasmids.
- Sequence type (ST93) is a label for a bacterial lineage; IncHI2A, IncI2, IncFIA/IncFIC are plasmid families.
summary.one_liner: Genomic study of three multidrug-resistant avian pathogenic E. coli from Pakistani broiler chickens, reporting fosA3, blaCTX-M-65, mcr-1.1 and tet(X4) co-located on conjugative plasmids (IncHI2A, IncI2, IncFIA/IncFIC).
summary.plain: Bacteria that cause disease in chickens were found carrying genes that resist several antibiotics, including last-resort drugs. The genes sit on small, mobile pieces of DNA called plasmids that can pass between bacteria. The authors sequenced the full genomes of three isolates from healthy broilers in Punjab, Pakistan, and mapped where each gene sits.
summary.why: Plasmids that carry resistance to several last-line drug classes are a concern because they can spread resistance between bacteria, including those that affect people. The paper is a small genomic case report, so it shows the combination exists in these isolates rather than how widely it has spread.

title: Emergence of mobile fosA3-blaCTX-M-65 with mcr-1.1 and tet(X4) on conjugative plasmids in avian pathogenic Escherichia coli from industrial poultry in Pakistan

abstract: Precision-cut lung slices (PCLS) preserve native three-dimensional lung architecture and cellular complexity, providing a valuable ex vivo platform for studying pulmonary host-pathogen interactions. However, existing PCLS infection models typically introduce microorganisms into previously uninfected tissue, while fresh PCLS prepared from infected lungs have limited experimental flexibility and scalability. To our knowledge, cryopreserved PCLS generated from lungs with an established in vivo pulmonary infection have not been described. Herein, we evaluated cryopreserved PCLS from mice with established Pneumocystis murina pneumonia (PCP) as an ex vivo platform for infection and therapeutic studies. PCLS were prepared from dexamethasone-immunosuppressed mice with established PCP, rested for 24 h, cryopreserved in a novel freezing medium for 12 days in liquid nitrogen, rapidly thawed, recovered for 24 h, and treated with pentamidine for 72 h. Viability was assessed in uninfected and PCP-infected PCLS before and after cryopreservation. Although post-thaw viability decreased in both groups, substantial viability was still retained, allowing further experimentation. qPCR showed that cryopreservation did not alter expression of the type I and type II alveolar epithelial markers podoplanin (Pdpn) and surfactant protein C (Sftpc) in either group. Importantly, pentamidine significantly reduced Pneumocystis mitochondrial small subunit (mtSSU) rRNA levels in thawed PCP-infected PCLS, demonstrating suitability for anti-Pneumocystis drug testing. These findings establish the first cryopreserved ex vivo PCP model using infected mouse PCLS, preserving endogenous fungal burden and infection-associated host responses while enabling flexible, scalable studies of Pneumocystis biology, host-pathogen interactions, therapeutic efficacy, and potentially other pulmonary infections.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767844 v1

summary.background:
- Precision-cut lung slices (PCLS): very thin slices of lung tissue kept alive in culture, preserving the lung's structure and cell mix outside the body.
- Pneumocystis murina: a fungus that infects mouse lungs and is used as a model for Pneumocystis pneumonia in people.
- Dexamethasone: a steroid used here to suppress the mice's immune systems so the infection establishes.
- Cryopreservation: freezing tissue in liquid nitrogen (about -196 °C) to store it long-term.
- Viability and qPCR: viability measures how many cells are still alive; qPCR measures how much of a specific gene's RNA is present. Here, mtSSU rRNA signals fungal load and Pdpn and Sftpc are markers for lung lining cells.
- Pentamidine: an existing anti-Pneumocystis drug used as the test treatment.
summary.one_liner: The authors describe a cryopreserved mouse precision-cut lung slice model, prepared from animals with established Pneumocystis murina pneumonia, and show that pentamidine reduces fungal rRNA in thawed infected slices.
summary.plain: Pneumocystis is a fungus that causes serious pneumonia in people with weakened immune systems, and studying it usually requires live animals. This paper describes thin slices of mouse lung that were already infected in the animal, frozen for 12 days, thawed, and kept alive in the lab for testing. When the researchers treated the thawed infected slices with the drug pentamidine, the fungal genetic material dropped significantly.
summary.why: A frozen, ready-to-use lung tissue model could allow more flexible and scalable testing of anti-fungal drugs and infection biology without repeated animal work. The text reports only one drug and a single readout, so its usefulness for other pathogens or drugs is not yet shown.

title: An Infected Cryopreserved Precision-Cut Lung Slice Model for Drug Susceptibility Testing in Pneumocystis murina Pneumonia

abstract: KRAS is the most frequently mutated proto-oncogene in human cancers. Progression to advanced disease is frequently associated with allelic imbalance of the KRAS locus with gain of the mutant allele and loss of the wild-type allele through clonal and sub-clonal loss of heterozygosity (LOH). While a large body of literature has focused on the effects of allelic imbalance on oncogene addiction through gain of the mutant allele, the role of the wild-type KRAS proto-oncogene in malignant progression has not been fully elucidated. To capture this phenomenon, we developed a first-in-class somatic mosaic and lineage tracing genetically engineered mouse model (smGMLT) of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma allowing for real time in vivo tracing of Kras-LOH. Longitudinal characterization of the smGMLT demonstrated the presence of a strong evolutionary bottleneck towards the selective loss of the wild-type allele at metastatic sites. Cross species analysis leveraging research autopsies and surgical specimens revealed that KRAS-LOH is associated with metastatic dissemination and shorter overall survival. Transcriptomic analysis through single-cell RNA sequencing uncovered a conserved phenomenon whereby KRAS-LOH is paralleled by an immune evasive phenotype through loss of the tumor-cell interferon response and reduced CD8+ T cell infiltration. In line with this evidence, orthotopic transplants of isogenic tumor populations differing for the Kras allelic status demonstrated that only cancer cells with Kras-LOH are are able to form tumors in immune competent animals. Restoration of the wild-type allele abrogates tumorigenesis in KrasLOH transplants in immunocompetent through activation of the TBK1-IRF axis. Altogether, these studies demonstrate that the KRAS proto-oncogene is a functional tumor suppressor in pancreatic cancer exerting its function through interferon-mediated, cell-extrinsic modulation of the tumor immune microenvironment.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767567 v1

summary.background:
- KRAS is a gene that normally helps control cell growth; mutated versions drive many cancers, and pancreatic cancer is among the most affected.
- A "proto-oncogene" is a normal gene that can become cancer-promoting; a "tumor suppressor" normally holds cancer back.
- Loss of heterozygosity (LOH) means a cell loses one of its two copies of a gene, here the normal KRAS copy.
- Interferons are signaling proteins that alert the immune system; CD8+ T cells are immune cells that kill tumor cells.
- Genetically engineered mouse models, lineage tracing (following cells' descendants over time), single-cell RNA sequencing, and orthotopic transplants (implanting cancer cells into the same organ in mice) are the main tools used.
- TBK1 and IRF are signaling molecules in the interferon pathway.
summary.one_liner: In a mouse model of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, loss of the wild-type Kras allele during tumor progression is linked to metastasis, poorer survival, reduced interferon signaling and CD8+ T cell infiltration, and tumors lacking the wild-type allele form only in immune-competent hosts when the wild-type allele is absent, suggesting wild-type KRAS acts as a tumor suppressor.
summary.plain: Most cancers with a KRAS mutation keep one normal copy and one mutated copy of the gene. As tumors spread, they often lose the normal copy, leaving only the mutant one. This study tracked that loss in mice and in patient samples, and found that tumors missing the normal copy spread more, were harder for the immune system to attack, and lost a key immune-alarm signal called the interferon response.
summary.why: It challenges the common view that KRAS works only as a cancer-driving oncogene, suggesting the normal copy may restrain tumors by helping immune cells find them. If confirmed, loss of the normal copy could serve as a marker of how aggressive a tumor is or of whether immune-based treatments might work, but the text alone does not show clinical implications.

title: The tumor suppressor role of the KRAS proto-oncogene in metastatic pancreatic cancer.

abstract: Spatially organized tumor-stromal interactions contribute to metabolic remodeling and immune suppression in bladder cancer (BLCA). Using spatial transcriptional programs to define single-cell states, we identified a niche comprising SPINK1-high epithelial cells (E2) and TPM2-high cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) (C1). SPINK1 promoted tumor growth and myofibroblastic CAF programs, with EGFR and TGF-{beta} signaling implicated in tumor-CAF communication. Inferred metabolic reactions and spatial metabolite distributions supported a candidate circuit linking tumor-derived lactate to CAF oxidative metabolism and glutamine provision, followed by tumor glutamine utilization for reductive carboxylation and fatty acid synthesis. SPINK1 perturbation altered extracellular glutamine and lactate concentrations. Predicted chemokine interactions implicated C2/C3 CAFs in T cell recruitment, whereas the E2-C1 niche exhibited checkpoint and exhaustion-associated features. RHCG-positive tumor regions contained higher proportions of TOXCXCR4 cells among CD3 T cells, suggesting a possible association between ammonia handling and T cell dysfunction. In vivo, Spink1 loss attenuated tumor progression, increased cytotoxic CD8 T-cell infiltration, and enhanced tumor control during PD-1 blockade. These findings identify a spatially organized tumor-stromal niche associated with metabolic cooperation and immune restriction, supporting SPINK1 as a candidate therapeutic target in combination with immunotherapy.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767479 v1

summary.background:
- Bladder cancer (BLCA): a cancer of the bladder lining.
- Tumor microenvironment: the non-cancer cells and tissue around a tumor, such as fibroblasts (supporting connective-tissue cells) that can be reprogrammed by cancer.
- Spatial transcriptomics: a method that measures which genes are active at specific locations in a tissue slice, so neighborhoods can be identified.
- SPINK1: a secreted protein found at high levels in some tumor cells here; the paper tests it in mice.
- Metabolic reactions: chemical conversions cells use for energy and building materials; lactate and glutamine are nutrients or byproducts that cells exchange.
- Reductive carboxylation and fatty acid synthesis: pathways by which cells build fats from glutamine-derived molecules.
- T cells and exhaustion: immune cells that lose effectiveness after prolonged exposure to tumors; CD8 T cells are cytotoxic killers.
- PD-1 blockade: an immunotherapy that releases a brake on T cells.
- Note: several links (metabolic circuit, ammonia handling, chemokine signaling) are predicted or associative in the abstract, not directly shown.
summary.one_liner: A spatial transcriptomics-based study identifying a SPINK1-high tumor epithelial and TPM2-high cancer-associated fibroblast niche in bladder cancer, linking proposed lactate-glutamine metabolic exchange to T-cell restriction and PD-1 blockade response in mice.
summary.plain: The paper looks at how bladder cancer cells and the supporting tissue around them (fibroblasts) work together in specific neighborhoods of a tumor, and how that teamwork may help the tumor avoid the immune system. The authors mapped these neighborhoods using spatial gene-activity data and computer-predicted metabolic flows, then tested the gene SPINK1 in mice. In those mice, removing Spink1 slowed tumor growth, brought in more killer T cells, and improved response to PD-1 immunotherapy.
summary.why: Bladder cancer immunotherapy does not work for everyone, so a candidate target that could be combined with PD-1 blockade is of interest. The metabolic and spatial links are mostly inferred from computer predictions and correlations, so they remain hypotheses that need direct experimental confirmation.

title: Spatial organization of a SPINK1-associated tumor-stromal ecosystem links metabolic remodeling to immune restriction in bladder cancer

abstract: Modern coexistence theory (MCT) has been the mainstay of recent research on coexistence of competing species. Competition not only drives evolutionary changes in traits that affect coexistence, but also induces rapid plastic changes. However, a generalised framework that integrates plasticity and evolution into MCT is lacking. We formulate such a framework for a system of two competing species and analyse how breadth of available resources modulates the effect of competition-induced plasticity on the evolution of coexistence components (niche and fitness difference). We find that, in broad environments, divergent plasticity accelerates evolution towards positive invasion growth rates for both species, facilitating coexistence, whereas convergent plasticity hinders this process. Surprisingly, in narrower environments, divergent plasticity can hinder coexistence, leading to exclusion, whereas convergent plasticity can facilitate coexistence. Our results show that plasticity reshapes the eco-evolutionary trajectories to coexistence, highlighting the importance of integrating short-term plastic responses with long-term evolutionary dynamics.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767819 v1

summary.background:
- Competing species can coexist if they differ in their niches (how they use resources) more than they differ in overall fitness (competitive strength).
- Modern coexistence theory (MCT) is the standard framework that splits coexistence into these two components.
- Phenotypic plasticity means one genotype changes its traits in response to its environment within its own lifetime, unlike evolution, which changes trait frequencies across generations.
- "Divergent" plasticity means the two species shift their traits in different directions under competition; "convergent" means they shift toward each other.
- Invasion growth rate: a rare species' per-capita growth when it is scarce; positive values mean it can recover and persist.
- Resource breadth: how many or how varied the resources available are, here treated as a key environmental setting.
summary.one_liner: A theoretical framework that adds competition-induced phenotypic plasticity and evolution to modern coexistence theory for two competing species, examining how resource breadth changes whether niche and fitness differences evolve toward coexistence.
summary.plain: This paper asks whether two species competing for the same resources can keep living together, and how quick, individual-level changes in behaviour or traits (plasticity) interact with slower evolutionary change. The authors build a mathematical model of two competing species and vary how many kinds of resources are available. They report that plasticity can help or hurt coexistence depending on whether the species' responses move apart or together and on how broad the environment is.
summary.why: Coexistence of competitors is a central question in ecology, and the paper argues that short-term plastic responses should be included alongside long-term evolution when predicting it. The text is a model-based study with no empirical data shown in the abstract, so its relevance to real populations is untested here.

title: Phenotypic plasticity reshapes the evolution of species coexistence

abstract: A central goal of evolutionary genetics is to determine how environmental pressures maintain adaptive genetic variation, and evaluate how this variation is encoded in the genome. We leveraged two powerful approaches to identify genomic regions associated with climatic adaptation, test the genetic basis of climatic adaptation, and predict genomic responses to novel climates: genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of climate niche parameters derived from demographic models and genome-environment associations (GEA) of climatic factors with 2,737,409 loci. The GWAS found 319 unique single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with climate niche parameters derived from demographic models using multi-year manipulative field experiments with Boechera stricta. The GEA detected 154 unique SNPs linked to climatic variation, with only one SNP found in both approaches. Local adaptation via adult survival arose primarily through conditional neutrality, as local alleles outperformed foreign alleles at only one end of the climatic gradient, rather than genetic trade-offs. Candidate genes near these loci were implicated in stress responses. Contrary to expectations, increasing temperatures and accelerating snowmelt timings did not augment the absolute fitness of low elevation genotypes. We found non-linear fitness functions for seedling recruitment at multiple SNPs detected via GWAS, with both conditional neutrality and genetic trade-offs evident in different portions of the climatic gradient. Local maladaptation arose exclusively in GEA SNPs. Our analyses revealed that the hot and dry conditions projected under climate change may rapidly exceed the tolerance of this species. However, we identified 47 SNPs at which evolutionary rescue or assisted migration could ameliorate the reduction in fitness under climate change.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767859 v1

summary.background:
- Local adaptation: populations evolve traits that suit their own environment, so a variant that helps at one site may hurt at another.
- SNP (single nucleotide polymorphism): a single-letter difference in DNA sequence used as a genetic marker.
- GWAS (genome-wide association study): scans the genome for variants that track with a measured trait.
- GEA (genome-environment association): scans the genome for variants that track with environmental factors such as temperature.
- Demographic models: mathematical models of birth, death and survival rates, here used to summarise climate niche parameters from field data.
- Conditional neutrality: a variant helps in some environments and has no effect in others.
- Genetic trade-off: a variant helps in one environment but costs fitness in another.
- Evolutionary rescue and assisted migration: a population adapts fast enough to survive, or humans move individuals to better-suited locations.
- Fitness: the number of surviving offspring or the chance of surviving and reproducing.
summary.one_liner: A genome-wide study in the wildflower Boechera stricta combines field-experiment demographic models with genome-environment associations to map the genetic basis of climate adaptation and to project how populations may fare under warmer, drier conditions.
summary.plain: Plants that grow along a climate gradient, such as from low to high elevation, carry genetic variants suited to their local conditions. The authors asked which parts of the genome drive this local adaptation and how well those variants would cope with the hotter, drier climates expected later this century. They combined multi-year field experiments on the wildflower Boechera stricta with genome scans and found a few hundred candidate variants, along with signs that the species may struggle under projected climate change.
summary.why: Predicting whether wild populations can keep pace with climate change depends on knowing which genetic variants matter and how they affect survival and reproduction. The paper links field-measured fitness to specific genome regions and suggests that some variants might help through evolutionary rescue or assisted migration, though the practical reach of these predictions for other species is not established in the text.

title: The genetic basis of adaptation to continuous environmental gradients informs predictions about climate change responses

abstract: Orchids are a large and diverse group of plants with unique adaptations that have enabled the utilization of many different environmental habitats across almost all continents. These adaptations are mediated by an as-yet-underexplored genetic resource. Nearly all sequenced orchid genomes are of Asian origin and represent less than 0.1% of all orchid species, limiting the ability to explore and mine the gene space of this complex plant family. Greater representation of orchids in genome databases could provide important insights into the genes responsible for adaptive phenotypes, which could be useful for targeted crop improvement and in orchid conservation efforts. To begin to expand the palette of orchid genomes, an effort was undertaken to sequence the genome of a North American terrestrial orchid, Tipularia discolor. K-mer analysis estimated a haploid genome size of approximately 1.7 Gb, with a high proportion of repetitive sequences. Although a complete genome was not obtained, the implementation of a conservative gene mining approach and the generation of a candidate gene mining pipeline led to the identification of 68 consensus contig objects containing whole or partial genes related to sucrose, trehalose, terpenoid, and phenylpropanoid metabolism. Of note, two bibenzyl synthase homologs were identified with high confidence and clustered with characterized orchid bibenzyl synthases in a CHS/BBS phylogeny, indicating that T. discolor, like its Asian and South American relatives, has the capacity to produce this distinct class of phenylpropanoids. Thus, despite substantial fragmentation, the T. discolor assembly contains sufficient gene space representation for targeted candidate gene discovery. This works lays the foundation for functional characterization of selected candidates and development of a more complete genome assembly for comparative genomic studies.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.767051 v1

summary.background:
- Genome: the full set of an organism's DNA; sequencing it is often done by stitching short reads into longer pieces called contigs.
- Fragmented assembly: a genome reconstruction broken into many unlinked pieces, so whole genes or their arrangement may be missing.
- K-mer analysis: a counting method that estimates genome size from repeated short DNA strings, without assembling the full genome.
- Repetitive sequences: DNA that appears many times over, which makes assembly harder.
- Specialized (secondary) metabolites: plant chemicals not needed for basic growth, such as those in flavors, defenses or medicines.
- Phenylpropanoids and bibenzyls: a chemical family and a subclass produced by plant enzymes like chalcone synthase (CHS) and bibenzyl synthase (BBS).
- Phylogeny: a family tree built from sequence similarity; "clustered with" means the genes are closely related in that tree.
- Homolog: a gene in one species that descends from a similar gene in another.
summary.one_liner: A fragmented draft genome of the North American terrestrial orchid Tipularia discolor, mined with a candidate-gene pipeline, yields 68 contigs for sugar, terpenoid and phenylpropanoid genes, including two bibenzyl synthase homologs that cluster with known orchid bibenzyl synthases.
summary.plain: Orchids are a huge plant family, but only a tiny fraction of their species have had their genetic blueprint (genome) sequenced, and nearly all of those come from Asia. This study tried to sequence the genome of a North American orchid, Tipularia discolor. The genome came out broken into many pieces, so it is not complete, but the researchers could still search the pieces for specific genes and found 68 fragments linked to sugar, plant-chemical and pigment-type pathways.
summary.why: Two candidate genes resemble enzymes that make bibenzyls, a distinct class of plant chemicals, which suggests this orchid can make them too, as some related orchids do. The fragmented assembly is a foundation for later lab testing of these genes and for a better genome, but the text does not show any practical application yet.

title: Candidate gene mining of a fragmented Tipularia discolor Pursh (Nutt.) genome assembly reveals genes putatively associated with specialized metabolite production.

abstract: Root-knot nematodes (RKNs) are a major concern for tomato growers worldwide. Management relies heavily on the plant resistance gene Mi-1, which has been bred into most processing tomato cultivars. However, repeated use of Mi-1 has placed strong selection pressure on nematode populations, promoting the emergence of resistance-breaking isolates. Despite the growing impact of resistance-breaking RKNs, their frequency, distribution, and species identity across California remain poorly understood. In this study, we isolated RKN isolates from processing tomato fields at 14 sites across California, identified them to species, and evaluated their reproduction on current rotation crops to determine whether crop rotation could suppress these populations. All 14 sites yielded resistance-breaking populations, and most isolates were M. incognita. A SNP-based principal component analysis revealed substantial genetic diversity among several isolates, suggesting that resistance-breaking emerged independently in multiple fields rather than all spreading from a single population. In greenhouse assays, alfalfa displayed the lowest reproduction of both wild-type and resistance-breaking M. incognita, whereas reproduction on other rotation crops varied by isolate. Together, these results show that rotation decisions should be guided by local RKN population identity and host compatibility rather than generalized strategies across fields.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767369 v1

summary.background:
- Root-knot nematodes are tiny roundworms that infect plant roots and cause galls, reducing crop yield.
- Mi-1 is a plant resistance gene bred into most processing tomatoes to block these worms.
- "Resistance-breaking" means a worm population can reproduce on Mi-1 tomatoes despite the gene.
- Crop rotation means planting non-host or poor-host crops between tomato seasons to lower worm numbers.
- M. incognita is one of the most common root-knot nematode species.
- SNP (single-nucleotide polymorphism) analysis compares small DNA differences between samples to estimate how related they are.
- Greenhouse assays test reproduction under controlled conditions, which may not match field results.
summary.one_liner: Survey of root-knot nematode isolates from 14 California processing tomato fields, testing species identity, SNP-based genetic diversity, and reproduction of wild-type and Mi-1 resistance-breaking M. incognita on rotation crops in greenhouse assays.
summary.plain: Microscopic worms that live in plant roots, called root-knot nematodes, are a major problem for tomato growers. Tomato varieties carry a resistance gene, Mi-1, that normally keeps them in check, but some worm populations have adapted to overcome it. This study sampled 14 California tomato fields, identified the worm species, and tested how well each population reproduced on crops that farmers might rotate into the field.
summary.why: Resistance that fails under heavy use is a recurring problem in farming, and this work suggests that rotation choices may need to be tailored to each field's worm population rather than applied as one general rule. The text does not describe effects on yields or on field-scale outcomes, so the practical impact is not established here.

title: Resistance-Breaking Root-knot Nematode Isolates Across California Tomato Fields Show Virulence Differences on Rotation Crops and Genomic Polymorphisms

abstract: Continuous oxygen delivery is essential for cerebral tissue function, yet its local supply characteristics remain incompletely understood. Quantifying oxygen transport in microvascular networks (MVNs) requires a physiologically consistent description of oxygen exchange between vascular compartments via mass transfer coefficients (MTCs). We investigate how different MTC formulations influence oxygen availability and hypoxic burden in realistic MVNs, and whether they produce relevant local differences in tissue oxygenation. A multicompartment oxygen transport model describing exchange between red blood cells (RBCs), plasma, and tissue in realistic MVNs was developed and evaluated against in vivo measurements. Three RBC-plasma MTC formulations were compared: constant, hematocrit-dependent, and hematocrit- and saturation-dependent. Additionally, a double-flux formulation incorporating a direct RBC-to-tissue flux was compared with standard single-flux formulations. Global tissue oxygen distributions were comparable across RBC-plasma MTC formulations, but hematocrit- and saturation-dependent MTC formulations predicted larger hypoxic tissue fractions. The largest differences occurred under low hematocrit, with local plasma oxygen partial pressure PO2 differing by {approx}6 mmHg along representative vascular paths. Introducing the direct RBC-tissue exchange reduced tissue PO2 at low hematocrit and enhanced it at high hematocrit, with the largest differences observed in small vessels. Sensitivity analysis revealed that RBC oxygen diffusivity can alter the double-flux effect magnitude. MTC assumptions substantially influence predicted oxygen availability and hypoxic burden, particularly under low-hematocrit conditions and in small vessels, underlining the need for their accurate definition. The proposed model provides a basis for evaluating these effects, improving the interpretation of oxygen transport predictions in realistic MVNs.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767880 v1

summary.background:
- Microvascular network: the web of very small blood vessels (capillaries and nearby vessels) that delivers oxygen to tissue.
- Hematocrit: the fraction of blood volume made up of red blood cells; low hematocrit means fewer red cells carrying oxygen.
- Partial pressure of oxygen (PO2): a measure of how much oxygen is available, in mmHg; low values indicate hypoxia.
- Mass transfer coefficient: a parameter describing how quickly oxygen passes between compartments (red cells, plasma, tissue).
- Single-flux vs double-flux: whether oxygen exchange goes only through plasma to tissue, or also directly from red cells to tissue.
- Sensitivity analysis: testing how much results change when an input assumption is varied.
summary.one_liner: A computational study comparing how different mass transfer coefficient formulations for oxygen exchange between red blood cells, plasma and tissue, including a direct red-cell-to-tissue flux, change predicted tissue oxygenation in realistic cerebral microvascular networks.
summary.plain: Brain tissue needs a steady supply of oxygen, which travels through tiny blood vessels and leaks out into surrounding tissue. This paper builds a computer model of oxygen moving through a realistic network of these small vessels, checks it against in vivo measurements, and tests how the choice of equations for oxygen exchange changes the answer. The authors found that the exchange assumptions matter most when red blood cells are sparse and in the smallest vessels, where they shift predicted low-oxygen tissue areas and local oxygen levels.
summary.why: Predictions of how much oxygen reaches brain tissue depend on these modelling choices, so the results suggest that model assumptions can change conclusions about hypoxia (too little oxygen). The text does not describe applications beyond model evaluation, so its practical impact is uncertain.

title: Mass Transfer Formulations Shape Oxygen Transport and Tissue Oxygenation in Microvascular Networks

abstract: Bone morphogenetic protein-2 (BMP-2) is a potent osteoinductive growth factor; however, its burst release from clinical collagen sponge carriers can cause inflammation and ectopic bone formation. Alternative delivery vehicles slow BMP-2 protein release through increased crosslinking density, which stiffens the polymer network and can restrict cell infiltration required for bone formation. Here, we introduce a BMP-2 delivery system in which a hyaluronic acid (HA) hydrogel containing BMP-2-specific affibodies is formed within clinically used collagen sponges to retain BMP-2 through protein-material affinity interactions rather than physical entrapment. We developed a maleimide functionalized, hydrazone crosslinked HA hydrogel such that affibody conjugation is chemically orthogonal to network formation, allowing affibody density to be varied independently of crosslinking density. Forming this hydrogel within a collagen sponge produced composite scaffolds with improved surgical handling and BMP-2 retention. Moreover, in vitro, composite scaffolds exhibited minimal swelling while retaining more BMP-2 than the collagen sponge alone. In vivo, composite scaffolds conjugated with BMP-2-specific affibodies improved ectopic mineralization in a BMP-2 dose-dependent manner. In a critically sized femoral defect, composite scaffolds with and without affibodies significantly increased bone volume relative to the collagen sponge. Thus, this composite scaffold effectively integrates the clinically used collagen sponge with a tunable HA hydrogel and BMP-2-specific affibodies to improve BMP-2-mediated bone regeneration and expand the use of naturally derived biomaterials for bone healing.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767909 v1

summary.background:
- BMP-2 (bone morphogenetic protein-2): a signaling protein that tells cells to form bone.
- Collagen sponge: a clinically used porous scaffold that carries BMP-2 but releases it quickly ("burst release").
- Ectopic bone formation: bone growing where it is not wanted, such as soft tissue.
- Hydrogel: a water-swollen network of polymer chains; crosslinking density controls how tightly the network is linked and how stiff it is.
- Hyaluronic acid: a natural sugar polymer abundant in connective tissue.
- Affibody: a small engineered protein that binds a specific target, here BMP-2.
- Critically sized defect: a bone gap too large to heal on its own, used as a demanding test model.
summary.one_liner: A hydrazone-crosslinked, maleimide-functionalized hyaluronic acid hydrogel carrying BMP-2-binding affibodies, formed inside clinical collagen sponges, is tested for controlled BMP-2 retention and bone regeneration in ectopic and critically sized femoral defect models.
summary.plain: Doctors often use a protein called BMP-2 to help bones heal, but the collagen sponge that carries it tends to release it all at once, which can cause swelling and bone growth in the wrong places. This paper describes a new carrier made by growing a gel of hyaluronic acid (a natural sugar-based material found in the body) inside the collagen sponge, with small protein binders that hold BMP-2 in place. The authors report that the composite handled better in surgery, kept more BMP-2 than the sponge alone, and increased bone formation in animal tests.
summary.why: Controlling how long a bone-healing protein stays where it is put could reduce side effects of current treatments, and the design lets binding density be tuned separately from gel stiffness. The text reports animal results only, so whether this helps patients remains open.

title: Affibody-conjugated hyaluronic acid hydrogels within collagen sponges enhance dose-dependent BMP-2-mediated bone formation and repair of critically sized femoral defects

abstract: Sequence similarity has long been a strong signal for protein function prediction, whereas the predictive value of network topology has been difficult to verify. Since a protein's function is largely defined by its interaction partners, and since similar interactions are expected across species, aligning protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks by topology alone should uncover functionally related proteins. Topology-only global network alignment has recently produced high-quality functional predictions, but it has yet to be shown that local regions of topological similarity can do the same. We introduce DijSLA (Dijkstra-inspired Stochastic Local Alignment), the first local network alignment algorithm designed from the ground up to use only topology. We adopt a seed-and-extend strategy: starting from seed pairs of proteins with similar network topology, we expand the alignment in a Dijkstra-inspired manner, following edges out of the aligned set to node pairs with near-maximal similarity. Rather than expanding deterministically, we inject randomness so that we can sample many high-quality alignments, in which node pairs with robust topological similarity "rise above" the noise and reveal functional similarity. Using networks and GO annotations from April 2010, we predict annotations validated against those from April 2020. With Network Alignment Frequency (NAF), a robustness measure that correlates with prediction precision, we make predictions with precision on par with or better than the best sequence-based methods and broadly similar to that of global topological alignment. Compared with existing local aligners, DijSLA produces larger, topologically high-quality alignments, which yield dramatically more predictions with higher validation rates, while using less CPU time and far less memory. Code is available at https://github.com/waynebhayes/BLANT/tree/master/CDijkstra.
label: arXiv:2611.26926v1

summary.background:
- Protein-protein interaction (PPI) network: a graph where proteins are nodes and physical or functional interactions are edges.
- Network alignment: finding a mapping between nodes of two networks so that matched nodes have similar neighborhoods; local alignment finds small matched regions rather than one whole-network mapping.
- Seed-and-extend: start from a small trusted match, then grow it outward one step at a time.
- Dijkstra-style expansion: a greedy search that always adds the best-scoring next candidate, here made stochastic.
- Gene Ontology (GO) annotations: standardized labels describing protein function; predictions are checked against later annotations.
- Precision: the fraction of predicted annotations that turn out to be correct.
- Sequence-based methods: function prediction using amino acid sequence similarity, the usual baseline.
summary.one_liner: DijSLA is a topology-only local network alignment algorithm that seeds and greedily extends matches between protein-protein interaction networks of different species, using randomized Dijkstra-style expansion and a network-alignment-frequency robustness score to predict Gene Ontology annotations.
summary.plain: Proteins inside cells work through their interaction partners, and the same kinds of interaction patterns tend to appear across species. This paper asks whether comparing only the shape of protein interaction maps, without using protein sequences, can reveal which proteins share a function. The authors build a method that grows small matched regions between two species' networks, adds randomness to sample many possible matches, and keeps the matches that recur often.
summary.why: The text reports that predictions from this topology-only local method reach precision comparable to or better than the best sequence-based methods, and that it yields more validated predictions than existing local aligners while using less CPU time and memory. Its relevance to wider protein function prediction is plausible but the text does not test beyond the April 2010 to April 2020 GO comparison described.

title: Topology-only Local Network Alignment, Part 2. DijSLA: Stochastic Greedy Extension for Cross-Species GO Annotation Prediction

abstract: Human visual perception is dynamically shaped by the recent past, a phenomenon known as serial dependence. Mechanistic models show that a residual memory trace can generate this dependency, yet its functional purpose (why the visual system should carry information forward in time at all) remains debated. We tested the hypothesis that serial dependence emerges as a normative consequence of optimizing vision for robustness against sensory noise. We trained recurrent autoencoders (a CNN encoder, a ConvGRU memory module, and a CNN decoder) to reconstruct natural videos corrupted by Gaussian noise, with no objective referring to perceptual history. Models that used their temporal memory achieved lower reconstruction error than memory-free counterparts, and this advantage widened as training noise increased, indicating that integrating past context is an adaptive denoising strategy. Probing the trained models with Gabor and dot sequences, we found that memory gave rise to serial dependence spontaneously: an attractive bias toward previous orientations and a spatial "continuity field" toward recently seen locations, both strengthening with training noise. Across temporal delays, the model's serial dependence was strongest for the immediately preceding stimulus and decayed monotonically. This profile quantitatively matched human orientation judgments, including an independent public dataset, once a known response-autocorrelation confound was controlled: an apparent non-monotonicity in one dataset reflected this measurement artifact rather than a genuine model-human mismatch. These findings suggest that serial dependence need not be an idiosyncratic quirk but can arise as a byproduct of optimizing for noise robustness, offering a normative account of perceptual history-dependence that complements existing mechanistic explanations and links behavior to an underlying computational objective.
label: arXiv:2611.26949v1

summary.background:
- Serial dependence: the tendency of current perception to be biased toward recent stimuli.
- Autoencoder: a neural network that compresses an input and then tries to rebuild it; here it rebuilds clean video from noisy video.
- Recurrent memory (ConvGRU): a component that carries information from earlier video frames forward to later ones.
- Gaussian noise: random, bell-curve-distributed static added to each pixel.
- Gabor patch: a striped image patch often used to test orientation perception.
- Response autocorrelation: a measurement artifact where a participant's answer on one trial depends on their previous answer, which can distort the apparent pattern across delays.
summary.one_liner: Recurrent autoencoders trained only to denoise natural video develop serial dependence (perceptual bias toward recently seen orientations and locations) that quantitatively resembles human orientation judgments, including on an independent public dataset.
summary.plain: People's perception of what they see now is pulled toward what they saw a moment ago; researchers have debated why the brain does this. The authors trained small neural networks with a memory to clean up noisy video, with no goal about past perception, and found the networks that used memory cleaned up noise better, especially when the noise was stronger. Those same networks then showed a pull toward recent orientations and locations that matched human-like patterns in their timing.
summary.why: It offers a normative explanation: a bias that looks like a quirk may follow from the goal of handling noisy input well, which links behaviour to a computational objective. Whether this explains the human brain, rather than just matching some data, is not settled by this text alone.

title: Serial Dependence Emerges from Optimizing Vision for Noise Robustness

abstract: Background Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is an increasingly prevalent neurodevelopmental condition with multifactorial origins, including potential prenatal environmental contributions. Maternal anemia (decreased hemoglobin [Hb] levels) has long been associated with adverse offspring neurodevelopmental outcomes. Yet, evidence regarding elevated levels of antenatal hemoglobin levels, in relation to ASD risk remains limited. This study evaluated the association between maternal Hb levels during pregnancy and the risk of ASD diagnosis in offspring. Methods This large-scale, population-based retrospective cohort study used electronic health records from births of members of Clalit Health Services (CHS), the largest health maintenance organization in Israel, between 2011 and 2021. The study included 303,234 singleton live births to Jewish mothers who had at least one measured prenatal Hb value and were CHS members. Exclusion criteria were children with known genetic disorders and births <25 weeks of gestation. Maternal Hb, and red blood cells (RBC) levels during the first and second trimesters were categorized as low (<2.5th percentile), normal (reference), or high (>97.5th percentile). The main outcome was a diagnosis of ASD in the offspring, as recorded in medical files. Statistical analyses adjusted for maternal age, socioeconomic status, gestational diabetes, BMI, and other clinical and demographic factors. Results Among the 303,234 births, 8,106 (2.7%) children were diagnosed with ASD. High maternal Hb levels were associated with elevated odds of ASD diagnosis (aOR=1.22; 95% CI=1.08:1.37), with the strongest association observed for first-trimester measurements (aOR=1.31; 95% CI=1.14-1.49). This association persisted in the sibling-matched analysis (aOR=1.64; 95% CI=1.08-2.47) and was not modified by maternal RBC levels, suggesting that it was not explained by familial factors or RBC counts. The main limitations of this study include the lack of available data on maternal smoking, and the absence of detailed information on maternal nutritional status. Conclusions These findings suggest that elevated antenatal Hb levels may be relevant to offspring neurodevelopment. Further studies are needed to replicate these findings and clarify the biological mechanisms underlying this association.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.26368133 v1

summary.background:
- Autism spectrum disorder (ASD): a neurodevelopmental condition affecting social communication and behavior; diagnosed from medical records here.
- Hemoglobin (Hb): the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells; measured in routine prenatal blood tests.
- Anemia: low hemoglobin; prior research links it to worse offspring neurodevelopment.
- Trimesters: the three roughly three-month stages of pregnancy.
- Cohort study: follows a defined group over time to see who develops an outcome.
- Adjusted odds ratio (aOR): a measure of how much more likely an outcome is in one group versus a reference group, after accounting for other factors; 1.22 means about 22% higher odds.
- Sibling-matched analysis: compares siblings from the same mother to reduce the influence of shared family factors.
- Limitations noted by authors: no data on maternal smoking or detailed nutrition; population is Jewish mothers in one HMO.
summary.one_liner: A large Israeli health-records cohort (303,234 singleton births, 2011–2021) found that high maternal hemoglobin in the first or second trimester was associated with higher odds of a later autism spectrum disorder (ASD) diagnosis in offspring, with the strongest signal for first-trimester values.
summary.plain: Researchers looked at whether a mother's blood hemoglobin level during pregnancy, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen, is linked to whether her child later receives an autism diagnosis. Using electronic medical records from one large Israeli health organization, they compared children whose mothers had unusually high hemoglobin readings with children whose mothers had typical readings. They found that high readings were associated with somewhat higher odds of an autism diagnosis, though this is an association and does not show that high hemoglobin causes autism.
summary.why: Most prenatal blood research has focused on low hemoglobin (anemia), so the question of whether unusually high levels matter is less explored. The result is worth following up, but it comes from one observational study, and the authors themselves call for replication and for clarifying the biological mechanisms.

title: Elevated maternal hemoglobin levels during pregnancy are associated with autism spectrum disorder in the offspring: A population-based cohort study

abstract: Background: Maternal immune activation is a robust risk factor for autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Current evidence relies on specialized immunological markers not routinely measured, limiting population-level risk identification. We investigated the association between maternal white blood cell (WBC) counts, a ubiquitous component of routine prenatal care during pregnancy, and offspring ASD risk. Methods: We conducted a retrospective population-based cohort study of 303,234 singleton live births (51% male) between 2011 and 2021 from Clalit Health Services in Israel. Exposures were maternal total and differential WBC counts from routine testing during the 1st and 2nd trimesters. High and low exposures were defined as >97.5th and <2.5th percentiles, respectively.
