The primary outcome was clinical ASD diagnosis. Analyses included multivariable logistic regressions, matched-sibling analyses (n=2,894 discordant pairs), and chronicity analyses in multiparous mothers (n=72,102). Results: Among 303,234 children, 8,106 (2.7%) were diagnosed with ASD. Elevated maternal total WBC counts were associated with increased odds of ASD (adjusted odds ratio [aOR]=1.59; 95% CI, 1.43-1.75), with the strongest association in the 1st trimester (aOR=1.64; 95% CI, 1.45-1.85). Similar associations were seen with elevated neutrophils, lymphocytes, and monocytes. While most associations were attenuated in matched-sibling analyses, chronicity analysis revealed increased ASD odds in offspring of mothers with persistently elevated WBC counts across multiple pregnancies (aOR=1.49; 95% CI, 1.08-2.01). Conclusions: Persistently elevated maternal WBC counts across pregnancies are associated with increased offspring ASD risk. These routinely collected hematologic markers support the maternal immune activation hypothesis and may contribute to future prenatal risk assessment models.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.26368136 v1

summary.background:
- Autism spectrum disorder (ASD): a neurodevelopmental condition diagnosed through clinical assessment; here, diagnoses recorded in health records.
- Maternal immune activation hypothesis: the idea that immune activity in a pregnant woman can affect the developing brain of the fetus.
- White blood cells (WBCs): immune cells in the blood; total counts and subtypes (neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes) are routinely measured in prenatal care.
- Odds ratio (OR): how much the odds of an outcome change for an exposure; 1.59 means roughly 59% higher odds, not a 59% higher probability.
- Retrospective cohort: following existing health records over time rather than enrolling and following participants forward.
- Matched-sibling analysis: comparing siblings born to the same mother with different exposures, which helps control for shared family factors.
- Chronicity analysis: checking whether the same mother had high counts across multiple pregnancies.
- Percentiles: high and low exposures were defined as the top and bottom 2.5% of counts.
summary.one_liner: A retrospective Israeli cohort of 303,234 singleton births finds that elevated maternal white blood cell counts from routine first- and second-trimester tests are associated with higher odds of clinically diagnosed autism, with weaker support from sibling-matched and repeated-pregnancy analyses.
summary.plain: Autism is linked to the mother's immune system during pregnancy, but the specialized immune tests used in past studies are not part of routine care. This study checked whether ordinary blood counts (white blood cells, which fight infection) taken during pregnancy relate to a child's later autism diagnosis. It found that mothers with unusually high counts had somewhat higher odds of having an autistic child, and that this was most visible when the counts were high across several pregnancies.
summary.why: If routine blood counts carry a real signal, they could be used cheaply across whole populations to help flag pregnancies at higher risk, and they add support to the idea that maternal immune activation plays a role in autism. The text does not show that the counts cause autism, and most associations shrank in the sibling comparison, so the link is best treated as an association that needs confirmation.

title: Chronic Maternal White Blood Cell Elevation During Pregnancy and Offspring Autism

abstract: The PfSPZ Vaccine induces both humoral and cellular immunity. While T cells are likely critical for protection, previous analyses of antibody correlates have focused on select antigens. Here, we apply a proteome-wide approach to examine antibody responses across the entire Plasmodium falciparum (Pf) proteome. Sera from malaria-naive volunteers immunized with high doses of PfSPZ Vaccine were probed using whole proteome Pf protein microarrays and high-density Pf peptide microarrays. Both platforms identified antibody responses that significantly correlated with protection, including responses to the immunodominant Pf circumsporozoite protein (CSP). Multiple reactive epitopes within non-CSP proteins shared homology with the central repeat and junctional regions of CSP, suggesting broad intra-proteome cross-reactivity. Greater breadth of seropositive responses was associated with protection. Cross-reactivity was confirmed by off-target binding of well-characterized memory B cell- and plasmablast-derived monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) targeting CSP. What began as a search for antibody correlates of protection and potential vaccine candidate antigens led to the surprising discovery of probable promiscuous CSP antibody responses that bind non-CSP proteins. The association between protection and greater levels of intra- and extra-Plasmodium cross-reactivity raises new questions about parasite biology and microbial evolution.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.26367676 v1

summary.background:
- PfSPZ Vaccine: a malaria vaccine made of live but radiation-attenuated sporozoites (the infective form of the Plasmodium falciparum parasite) given to volunteers.
- Antibodies: immune proteins that bind specific molecular targets (antigens); "seropositive" means antibodies to a target were detected in blood serum.
- CSP (circumsporozoite protein): the most abundant surface protein on sporozoites and the main target of the vaccine's antibody response; it has repeated central sequences.
- Proteome-wide arrays: chips carrying most of the parasite's proteins (or overlapping peptide fragments) to test which ones antibodies bind.
- Cross-reactivity: one antibody binding several unrelated targets that share similar sequence pieces.
- Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs): identical antibodies cloned from single immune cells, used to test specific binding.
- Correlate of protection: a measurable immune marker statistically associated with being protected; it does not by itself prove causation.
summary.one_liner: A proteome-wide antibody survey of sera from PfSPZ-vaccinated malaria-naive volunteers finds that antibodies to many non-CSP Plasmodium falciparum proteins, which share sequence homology with CSP's central repeat and junctional regions, correlate with protection and are partly cross-reactive with CSP-targeting monoclonal antibodies.
summary.plain: Malaria vaccine researchers wanted to know which antibodies in people's blood best predict protection after being immunized with a whole-parasite vaccine. They tested volunteers' blood against nearly the entire malaria parasite's set of proteins, using protein and peptide arrays. They found that antibodies aimed at the main vaccine target, CSP, were linked to protection, but so were antibodies that stuck to other parasite proteins with similar sequence fragments.
summary.why: The vaccine is known to protect, but its antibody correlates have mostly been studied for a few antigens, so a broader view could point to new vaccine candidates. The finding that CSP-type antibodies also bind unrelated parasite proteins is unexpected and raises questions about parasite biology and cross-reactivity, though the text does not establish how these off-target bindings affect protection.

title: Proteome-wide antibody responses to PfSPZ Vaccine include cross-reactive antibodies that correlate with protection from malaria

abstract: Abstract Background: Culture-negative TB is a major diagnostic challenge, and the lack of a reliable reference standard hinders evaluation of non-sputum diagnostic tests. We compared composite reference criteria and Bayesian latent class analysis to examine how different culture-negative TB definitions affect disease classification and evaluations of two non-sputum biomarkers: urine lipoarabinomannan (uLAM) and host transcriptional response signatures (HRS). Methods: Urine and blood samples from 112 sputum culture-negative and 55 culture-positive symptomatic adults evaluated for tuberculosis from South Africa, Uganda, and Kenya, alongside 17 controls with other respiratory conditions, were analyzed using uLAM and HRS assays. Sensitivity and specificity were estimated for each assay based on three reference criteria: composite microbiological, composite clinical, and a latent class model. Results: Positive classification proportions were 0.29 (32/112) and 0.46 (51/112) for the composite criteria and 0.20 (22/112) for the latent class model, with the Bayesian model estimating a prevalence of 0.31 (95%CrI 0.11-0.64). Sensitivity and specificity for uLAM ranged from 0.06-0.13 and 0.92-0.96, respectively. Sensitivity and specificity for HRS ranged from 0.47-0.78 and 0.56-0.69, respectively. uLAM results were significantly associated with microbiological positivity (OR=5.38, 95%CI=1.63-13.02). Conclusion: Three distinct reference frameworks identified different individuals as having culture-negative TB while producing index assay sensitivity and specificity estimates with overlapping confidence and credible intervals, leading to similar conclusions regarding biomarker utility. This supports the use of complementary reference approaches to assess robustness to disease classification uncertainty in heterogeneous conditions such as culture-negative TB.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.26368340 v1

summary.background:
- Tuberculosis (TB) is a bacterial lung infection; culture grows the bacteria in a lab to confirm it.
- "Culture-negative" means the usual lab test did not find the bacteria, even though TB may still be suspected.
- Sensitivity is the share of true cases a test catches; specificity is the share of non-cases it correctly clears.
- A reference standard is the benchmark used to judge a test; without a perfect one, researchers use composite criteria (combining several clinical or lab findings) or latent class analysis (a statistical method that infers hidden true disease status from patterns across tests).
- Bayesian analysis gives a credible interval, the Bayesian counterpart of a confidence interval.
- Urine lipoarabinomannan is a bacterial-cell-wall molecule detected in urine; host transcriptional response signatures are patterns of gene activity in the blood.
- Sample sizes are modest (112 culture-negative and 55 culture-positive adults, plus 17 controls).
summary.one_liner: Compares three ways of defining culture-negative tuberculosis (composite microbiological, composite clinical, and Bayesian latent class model) to estimate how well urine lipoarabinomannan (uLAM) and host transcriptional response signatures (HRS) detect the disease.
summary.plain: Tuberculosis (TB) is sometimes present even when standard lab culture of sputum (phlegm) comes back negative, and there is no reliable gold-standard test to confirm these cases. This study looked at urine and blood samples from people with suspected TB in Africa and tested two non-sputum tests on them. The main finding is that the three ways of defining the disease sorted people differently, yet the tests' accuracy estimates overlapped enough to lead to similar overall conclusions.
summary.why: Diagnosing TB without sputum culture matters because many people who are ill cannot produce good sputum samples, and better non-sputum tests could help. The paper also shows that how the reference standard is chosen can change the picture, which is relevant to how any new diagnostic is judged.

title: Evaluation of urine lipoarabinomannan and host response signatures for culture-negative tuberculosis using composite criteria and Bayesian Latent Class Analysis

abstract: Background The opioid crisis is the leading driver of overdose mortality in the United States. While overdose deaths have decreased in recent years, the reporting lag in official overdose deaths presents a hurdle in implementing public health interventions to combat the crisis. Objective To address these data-reporting delays and improve prediction during highly volatile periods, we developed a Bayesian hierarchical spatiotemporal model using real-time drug overdose data sources to predict quarterly overdose deaths across Ohio counties from 2020 to 2024. Methods We implemented a Bayesian spatiotemporal model using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA). Rapid-reporting surveillance metrics, specifically urine drug test (UDT) positivity rates and Emergency Medical Services (EMS) naloxone administration events, were incorporated as fixed covariates. Models were constructed stepwise by first optimizing the spatiotemporal random effect structure and then sequentially adding fixed effects to minimize prediction error. A rolling training window was implemented and evaluated across different training window sizes. Results were assessed overall and stratified by county population size. Results We found that the optimal predictive model structure consists of a two-year training window, a random walk temporal effect, a structured spatial effect, and fentanyl UDT positivity and EMS naloxone events. Incorporating these UDT and EMS data significantly enhanced predictive performance, with the most pronounced accuracy gains occurring during the unprecedented overdose increase associated with the COVID-19 pandemic in the second quarter of 2020. While predictive performance was highly robust in large, urban counties, predictive capability in smaller counties was limited by low data availability. Conclusion Our spatiotemporal prediction model successfully bridges the administrative reporting lags and offers near-real-time quarterly overdose prediction. The study also showed that integration of real-time data sources is especially beneficial for capturing sudden, volatile spikes in overdose deaths.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.26368445 v1

summary.background:
- Opioid overdose deaths: the leading cause of overdose death in the US; fentanyl is a major driver.
- Reporting lag: official death certificates and final counts take months to be finalized.
- Urine drug test (UDT) positivity: the share of tested urine samples that show a drug, here fentanyl.
- EMS naloxone events: emergency medical service calls where naloxone, a drug that reverses opioid overdoses, was given.
- Bayesian hierarchical spatiotemporal model: a statistical model that borrows information across neighboring areas (space) and across time periods, and expresses uncertainty as probabilities.
- INLA (Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation): a fast computational method for fitting such Bayesian models.
- Rolling training window: the model is refit using the most recent years of data, moving forward over time, to test predictions.
- Random walk and structured spatial effects: model components that assume each period (or area) is similar to the one before (or next to it).
summary.one_liner: A Bayesian spatiotemporal INLA model for Ohio counties, 2020–2024, that uses urine drug test fentanyl positivity and EMS naloxone events as real-time covariates to predict quarterly opioid overdose deaths, with a two-year training window and random-walk temporal and structured spatial effects.
summary.plain: Official overdose death counts often arrive months after the fact, which makes it hard for health officials to respond in time. This study builds a statistical model for Ohio's counties that uses faster signals, such as drug test results from patients and emergency medical calls where naloxone (an overdose reversal drug) was given, to estimate overdose deaths each quarter. The authors report that adding these faster signals improved predictions, especially during sudden spikes like the early 2020 COVID-19 surge, and that predictions were reliable in large urban counties but weaker in small ones with less data.
summary.why: Reporting lags are a real obstacle to timely response in the overdose crisis, so a method that gives near-real-time estimates could help local planning. The text does not show how well the approach would work in other states or in practice, so its usefulness beyond Ohio remains to be tested.

title: Predicting county-level opioid overdose mortality in Ohio through multimodal data: A spatiotemporal study using toxicology and EMS indicators, 2020-2024

abstract: Medical crowdfunding allows for funding for needs not covered by the local healthcare system. We aimed to characterize the crowdfunding campaigns for the needs of Polish individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF). In our study, we analyzed data from a leading medical crowdfunding webpage in Poland, focusing on campaigns for individual medical needs initiated between 2009 and 2017. We characterized the features of individuals with CF and the declared goals for which the funds from the online campaigns were intended. Of all 2,656 campaigns, 96 (3.6%) were related to individuals with CF. Approximately two-thirds of these campaigns reached their target amount. Individuals with CF primarily raised funds to cover treatment costs, medical equipment, and entertainment. The successful collection had a significantly lower financial target than unsuccessful campaigns. If the receivers were living in a city or fundraising to gather funds for an inhaler, these were also associated with the campaign's success. However, these associations were slightly above the threshold of statistical significance. Crowdfunding campaigns can be an effective funding source for the needs of patients with CF that are not covered by the public healthcare system. Analyzing crowdfunding efforts for specific patient groups can help reveal their unmet health needs.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.26368008 v1

summary.background:
- Cystic fibrosis (CF): an inherited condition that causes thick mucus in the lungs and digestion, requiring lifelong treatment.
- Medical crowdfunding: people raise money from the public online for health costs, often because public insurance does not pay for them.
- Unmet needs: health-related costs or services that patients must pay for themselves or go without.
- Statistical significance: a rough test of whether a pattern is likely more than chance; "slightly above the threshold" means the evidence is weak.
- Descriptive study: it reports what happened in the data and does not test cause and effect.
- Campaigns come from one website, so the results may not represent all Polish patients or all fundraising.
summary.one_liner: A descriptive analysis of 96 Polish crowdfunding campaigns (out of 2,656 individual medical campaigns, 2009–2017) for people with cystic fibrosis, examining campaign goals, outcomes, and factors associated with reaching the funding target.
summary.plain: People with cystic fibrosis, a inherited lung and digestive disease, in Poland sometimes raise money through public online fundraising pages to pay for things the national health system does not cover. This study looked at 96 such campaigns from a major Polish crowdfunding site between 2009 and 2017. About two-thirds reached their goal, and the funds mostly went to treatment costs, medical equipment, and some non-medical needs such as entertainment.
summary.why: The study suggests that crowdfunding records can show gaps in what public healthcare covers for a specific patient group. The authors report that smaller funding targets were linked to success, while the links for city residence and inhaler purchases were only slightly above the threshold of statistical significance, so these should be treated as tentative.

title: Unmet needs of Polish patients with cystic fibrosis seen through the lens of crowdfunding

abstract: Deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus (STN-DBS) effectively treats motor and non-motor symptoms in advanced Parkinson's disease (PD). However, 15-20 % of patients experience postoperative cognitive decline and identifying preoperative markers remains an unmet clinical need. In this prospective open-label study, we employed NODDI-DTI to investigate whether cerebral microstructure predicts cognitive outcomes following STN-DBS. Forty PD patients underwent diffusion MRI and neuropsychological assessments at preoperative baseline and 6-month follow-up. A whole-brain voxel-wise analysis related microstructural metrics to postoperative cognitive change. Compromised microstructure within three large-scale networks - the frontoparietal/attentional, default mode/limbic, and ventral associative/visual networks - was associated with greater postoperative cognitive decline. These findings suggest that both disease-related network degeneration and stimulation acting on compromised circuits may contribute to postoperative cognitive decline. In conclusion, preoperative evaluation of microstructural integrity may help identify patients at risk for postoperative cognitive decline, supporting individualised counselling and targeted behavioural monitoring after STN-DBS.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.26368410 v1

summary.background:
- Parkinson's disease: a progressive neurological disorder affecting movement, with growing non-motor symptoms including cognition.
- Deep brain stimulation (DBS): surgically implanted electrodes that send electrical pulses into a deep brain target; here the subthalamic nucleus (STN).
- Cognitive decline: worsening of thinking skills such as attention, memory and planning.
- Diffusion MRI: an MRI technique that measures how water molecules move in brain tissue, reflecting tissue structure.
- NODDI-DTI: two diffusion-MRI models; they estimate fibre organisation and tissue density/complexity in more detail than standard imaging.
- Brain networks: groups of regions that work together, here frontoparietal/attentional, default mode/limbic, and ventral associative/visual.
- Voxel-wise analysis: comparing brain imaging values at every small 3D point across the brain.
- Open-label: patients and clinicians knew the treatment given; no control group blinding is implied.
summary.one_liner: A prospective open-label study of 40 Parkinson's patients using NODDI-DTI diffusion MRI finds that preoperative white-matter and grey-matter microstructure within three large-scale brain networks is associated with greater cognitive decline six months after subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation.
summary.plain: Deep brain stimulation is an implanted electrode treatment that eases movement and other symptoms in advanced Parkinson's disease, but about 15 to 20 percent of patients have thinking abilities worsen afterward. Researchers scanned 40 patients' brains with a special MRI method before surgery and again tested their thinking six months later. They found that poorer tissue quality in several brain networks before surgery was linked to bigger declines in cognition.
summary.why: If brain scans taken before surgery can flag who is at risk of thinking decline, clinicians could counsel patients more individually and monitor them more closely. The text suggests the findings point to both existing disease damage and the stimulation itself as contributors, but the study's size and open-label design mean the predictive value still needs confirmation in other groups.

title: Microstructure predicts cognition following deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease

abstract: Objectives: Plasma neurodegeneration biomarkers offer an opportunity to characterize Parkinson's disease (PD) biology. The objective of this study was to investigate such biomarkers in deeply-phenotyped participants in Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI). Methods: Baseline plasma samples from early (<2 years since diagnosis) sporadic PD participants with a positive CSF alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay (aSyn-SAA) and healthy controls (HC) with a negative aSyn-SAA test were utilized. Plasma P-tau217 (Roche Diagnostics), neurofilament light chain (NfL, Quanterix), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP, Quanterix), and (PD only) amyloid-beta (A{beta}) levels (40 and 42, C2N Diagnostics) were measured. Clinical features at baseline and over up to 11 years were compared across biomarker tertiles in models controlling for age, sex, and baseline outcome variable. Results: The cohort was 97 HC and 523 PD and participants. Median [IQR] biomarker values (pg/mL) for HC and PD were P-tau217: 0.14 [0.06 -0.75], 0.15 [0.06 -0.90]; NfL: 10.6 [3.13 -49.85], 12.26 [3.77-62.67]; GFAP: 66.56 [19.75 -403.48], 87.19 [14.55 -531.82]; and in PD A{beta}40: 391.32 [209.95 -538.38]; A{beta}42: 42.74[27.75 -68.55]. No biomarkers differed between HC and PD. In PD, biomarkers were associated with age. In PD only, higher baseline levels of P-tau217 and NfL were associated with greater hazards of a worse cognitive and balance outcome. P-tau217, NfL, and GFAP levels were associated with change in cognitive score over time. Interpretation: Plasma P-tau217, NfL and GFAP levels in early, sporadic PD with confirmed synucleinopathy predict future cognitive and functional impairment, and these findings can inform clinical research design and clinical care.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.26368420 v1

summary.background:
- Parkinson's disease: a progressive brain disorder affecting movement, with cognitive and balance problems over time.
- Alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay (aSyn-SAA): a lab test on spinal fluid that detects misfolded alpha-synuclein protein, used here to confirm the disease biology.
- Sporadic: not caused by a known inherited gene change.
- Plasma biomarkers: molecules measured in a blood sample that reflect activity or damage in tissues such as the brain.
- P-tau217: a form of tau protein linked to brain changes, often studied in Alzheimer's disease.
- NfL (neurofilament light chain): a protein released when nerve fibres are damaged.
- GFAP: a protein from support cells (astrocytes) in the brain, rising with injury or inflammation.
- Amyloid-beta (Aβ40, Aβ42): proteins that can accumulate in the brain; measured only in the Parkinson's group.
- PPMI (Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative): a large longitudinal study that collects detailed clinical and biological data.
- Tertiles: dividing participants into three equal-sized groups by biomarker level.
- Hazard: the instantaneous risk of an event occurring over time, used in time-to-event models.
summary.one_liner: In early sporadic Parkinson's disease with confirmed alpha-synuclein seeding in CSF, baseline plasma P-tau217, NfL and GFAP levels were associated with later cognitive and balance decline in PPMI participants compared with healthy controls.
summary.plain: This study looks at simple blood tests that measure signs of nerve-cell damage in people with early Parkinson's disease, compared with healthy people. Researchers measured several proteins in blood samples taken at the start of the study and then tracked participants' thinking and balance for up to 11 years. They found that higher levels of three of these markers were linked to worse later outcomes in the Parkinson's group, though the blood levels themselves did not differ between the two groups.
summary.why: If blood markers can flag which early patients are likely to decline, they could help design clinical trials and guide care, but the text is an association study and does not show that the markers cause or can reliably predict decline for individuals. Its relevance to treatment decisions remains to be tested.

title: Plasma neurodegeneration biomarkers and clinical progression in early sporadic Parkinson's disease

abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains a leading cause of cancer mortality, with a minority of patients experiencing durable responses to first-line immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Currently, there are no easily accessible tools to predict clinical benefit to first-line immunotherapy. To address this gap, we developed LCatlas (https://www.lcatlas.org), a point-of-care web application designed to predict immunotherapy outcomes and inform evidence-based treatment decisions. Using data from 79 NSCLC patients receiving first-line immunotherapy, we extracted demographic, clinical, and molecular features from electronic medical records and compared three independent approaches, statistical model (logistic regression), machine learning (XGboost), and AI model (TabTransformer) to identify the most effective predictor. LCatlas accepts nine variables, gender, smoking history, bone/pleura/liver metastasis, PDL1 tumor staining, albumin level, hemoglobin level, lymphocyte count, neutrophil count, and platelet count, to predict responses to both immunotherapy and immunotherapy plus chemotherapy. LCatlas cross-validation yielded an area under the curve (AUC) of 79% [72% - 85%], with sensitivity of 87% [72% - 95%] and specificity of 78% [64% - 89%], outperforming previous studies including high-volume data-driven deep-learning approaches. In a validation cohort consisting of 28 individuals, it demonstrated a prediction accuracy of 82%. LCatlas may serve as a valuable point-of-care tool by identifying patients likely to experience extended immunotherapy or combination therapy using readily available medical data. Its evidence-based approach can optimize personalized treatment planning and thereby promote quality and safety of care.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.26368446 v1

summary.background:
- NSCLC: non-small cell lung cancer, the most common type of lung cancer.
- Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs): drugs that release the brakes on the immune system so it attacks tumours; "first-line" means the first treatment given.
- PD-L1 staining: a lab test on tumour tissue measuring a protein that affects immune response; higher levels often predict better response.
- Albumin, hemoglobin, lymphocytes, neutrophils, platelets: routine blood measures reflecting nutrition, oxygen-carrying capacity and immune status.
- AUC: area under the ROC curve, a 0–100% score of how well a model separates responders from non-responders (50% is chance).
- Sensitivity and specificity: the share of true responders correctly flagged, and the share of non-responders correctly flagged.
- Logistic regression, XGBoost, TabTransformer: three ways to build prediction models, from simple statistics to machine learning to an AI model for tabular data.
- Cross-validation: testing a model by repeatedly holding out parts of the same dataset; it is less convincing than testing on fully new patients.
summary.one_liner: A small retrospective study (79 first-line immunotherapy NSCLC patients) that builds LCatlas, a web tool using nine routine blood, clinical and molecular variables to predict response to first-line immunotherapy with or without chemotherapy, comparing logistic regression, XGBoost and TabTransformer models.
summary.plain: Lung cancer treatment with immune-boosting drugs works well for only some patients, and doctors currently lack an easy way to predict who will benefit. The authors built a free web tool, LCatlas, that takes nine details already in medical records (such as blood counts, albumin, smoking history and where the cancer has spread) and estimates the chance of a good response. In a small group of 79 patients, the tool's predictions were moderately accurate, and it was also tested on 28 other people.
summary.why: Predicting who benefits from expensive, sometimes toxic immunotherapy could help guide treatment choices if it holds up. However, the study is small, the accuracy figures come from cross-validation within the same 79 patients, and the claim of outperforming earlier studies, including deep-learning ones, rests on the authors' own comparison, so it needs external validation before clinical use.

title: LCatlas: A Point-Of-Care Tool for Predicting Immunotherapy Outcomes in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer

abstract: Background: Pathological complete response (pCR) after pembrolizumab-based neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy predicts improved outcomes in early triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), but circulating immune determinants of response remain poorly characterized. Methods: The study included 64 patients with early TNBC treated with pembrolizumab-based neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy. Flow cytometry analyzed 125 peripheral-blood specimens collected at baseline, during treatment and before surgery. Baseline PBMCs from 22 patients underwent scRNA-seq, generating 135,271 quality-controlled cells. Analyses used nonparametric tests, effect sizes, FDR correction and sensitivity analyses. Results: Baseline scRNA-seq identified response-associated transcriptional differences. Patient-level pseudo-bulk analysis revealed enrichment of TNF-alpha/NF-kappaB signaling in cytotoxic T/NK and B cells from non-pCR patients (global q<=3.94e-7), together with MYC targets and mTORC1 signaling in cytotoxic T/NK cells (both global q=7.00e-5). T-cell analyses suggested preserved naive/memory features in pCR, while a higher proportion of CX3CR1-expressing cells within the CD4 memory/activation-like compartment was associated with pCR (q=0.0157; AUC=0.949). In B cells, pCR was associated with a nominally higher naive-like program score (P=0.029; q=0.059), supported by higher IGHM and IGHD signals, whereas XBP1 was higher in non-pCR. Flow cytometry identified treatment-associated B-cell remodeling. At pre-surgery, switched-memory B-cell CD38 balance was higher in pCR than non-pCR patients (62.6% versus 50.0%; P=0.0086; q=0.0667; Cliff's delta=0.651; AUC=0.825) and remained nominally significant in leave-one-patient-out analyses. Early increases in unswitched-memory B-cell CD38 balance were numerically greater in non-pCR patients, whereas pre-surgery switched-memory B-cell CD38 balance was higher in pCR patients. Conclusions: Baseline inflammatory and metabolic pathway enrichment was associated with non-pCR, whereas pCR-associated T-cell findings included a CD4 memory/activation-associated CX3CR1 signal and trends towards preserved naive/memory features. Together with time- and compartment-dependent B-cell remodeling, these findings nominate circulating transcriptional states and CD38-defined B-cell dynamics for prospective validation as candidate biomarkers of pathological response.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.26368490 v1

summary.background:
- Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC): a subtype lacking the hormone and HER2 receptors that common targeted drugs act on, so it is treated largely with chemotherapy and immunotherapy.
- Neoadjuvant therapy: treatment given before surgery; pathological complete response (pCR) means no invasive cancer is seen in the removed tissue afterward.
- Pembrolizumab: an immune checkpoint inhibitor that releases the brakes on the immune system so it can attack tumor cells.
- Flow cytometry: a lab method that counts and sorts individual cells by surface markers.
- Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq): measures which genes are active in each individual cell.
- Pseudo-bulk analysis: averages single-cell data within each patient to compare patients rather than cells.
- CD38, IgM/IgD, CX3CR1, XBP1: cell-surface or internal molecular markers used to label immune cell types and states.
- False discovery rate (q value) and AUC: statistical measures of how likely a result is a chance finding and how well a marker separates two groups.
summary.one_liner: In 64 early triple-negative breast cancer patients given pembrolizumab-based neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy, baseline single-cell RNA profiling and serial flow cytometry of blood immune cells were used to nominate circulating signals (inflammatory pathway enrichment, a CX3CR1 CD4 memory signal, and CD38-defined B-cell dynamics) associated with pathological complete response.
summary.plain: Some breast cancer patients have all visible tumor removed by surgery after pre-operative drug treatment, and this "complete response" tends to predict better outcomes. This study looked at immune cells in the blood of 64 patients with a hard-to-treat breast cancer subtype to see whether patterns in those cells differ between patients who did and did not achieve complete response. The authors report several candidate patterns, but these are exploratory findings that still need confirmation in future studies.
summary.why: If confirmed, blood-based markers could help doctors anticipate who responds to immunotherapy without waiting for surgery, which is a real clinical need. The text presents these as candidate biomarkers only; several results are borderline after multiple-comparison correction (q values near 0.06 to 0.07), so they should be treated as hypotheses rather than established predictors.

title: CIRCULATING IMMUNE DYNAMICS DURING NEOADJUVANT CHEMOIMMUNOTHERAPY IN EARLY TRIPLE-NEGATIVE BREAST CANCER

abstract: Transformer-based foundation models have shown strong potential for modeling longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs), yet existing models focus primarily on risk prediction rather than treatment effect estimation, which limits evidence generation. Here, we introduce the ITE-Transformer, a transformer-based framework that combines self-supervised representation learning from longitudinal patient trajectories with doubly robust causal machine learning for predicting individualized treatment effects (ITEs). As a result, our ITE-Transformer allows to study counterfactual questions of how an individual patient's outcome may differ under alternative treatment strategies. The ITE-Transformer learns temporally contextualized representations of patients' diagnosis and medication histories and subsequently uses these representations to predict treatment assignment, treatment-specific outcome risks, and patient-specific ITEs. The ITE-Transformer is trained using structured EHR data from ~350,000 participants in the All of Us Research Program and evaluated in two clinically different comparative-effectiveness tasks: (i) GLP-1 receptor agonists versus DPP-4 inhibitors among patients with type 2 diabetes, with major adverse cardiovascular events as the outcome, and (ii) immunotherapy versus chemotherapy in a pan-cancer cohort, with all-cause mortality as the outcome. Across both applications, the ITE-Transformer improves the discrimination and calibration of treatment assignment and outcome models compared with existing tabular machine learning approaches and an otherwise identical transformer trained without self-supervised pre-training. The ITE-Transformer further identifies substantial heterogeneity in predicted ITEs and yields interpretable patterns of treatment response associated with patients' diagnoses, medication histories, and comorbidities. Together, our work demonstrates how clinical foundation models can be developed for analyzing heterogeneity in treatment effects and thus support real-world evidence generation.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.26368479 v1

summary.background:
- Electronic health records (EHRs): routine clinical databases of diagnoses, prescriptions and visits.
- Foundation model: a large model first trained on broad data with no specific task in mind, then reused for particular tasks.
- Transformer: a neural network architecture, widely used in language models, that processes sequences such as a patient's history of events.
- Self-supervised pre-training: learning from the data's own structure (for example, predicting hidden parts of a record) without manual labels.
- Individualized treatment effect (ITE): an estimate of how much one specific patient's outcome would change under one treatment versus another; it cannot be observed directly, since each patient receives only one treatment.
- Doubly robust estimation: a causal method that stays reliable if either of two underlying models (treatment or outcome) is reasonably correct.
- Comparative effectiveness: research comparing two existing treatments in routine practice.
- Discrimination and calibration: how well a model ranks patients by risk, and how closely its predicted probabilities match observed rates.
- All of Us Research Program: a large US research cohort with linked health data.
summary.one_liner: A transformer-based foundation model, pre-trained with self-supervision on longitudinal EHR diagnosis and medication histories and combined with doubly robust causal learning, is proposed to estimate individualized treatment effects in two comparative-effectiveness tasks using All of Us data.
summary.plain: This paper asks how a patient's health outcome might differ depending on which treatment they receive, using years of patient records from electronic health systems. The authors built a model that first learns general patterns from patients' diagnosis and medication histories, then estimates treatment effects for individuals. They tested it on two comparisons: diabetes drugs (GLP-1 agonists versus DPP-4 inhibitors) and cancer treatments (immunotherapy versus chemotherapy).
summary.why: The text reports that the model predicted treatment assignment and outcomes somewhat better than standard tabular machine learning and a transformer without pre-training, and that it found varying predicted effects across patients. Whether this improves real-world evidence generation depends on validation the summary does not describe, such as evaluation against randomized trial results.

title: The ITE-Transformer: A pre-trained foundation model for predicting individualized treatment effects from electronic health records

abstract: This study evaluated machine learning models for screening elevated generalized anxiety symptoms from remotely collected neutral read speech in 1,788 adults from Botswana, Ghana, Nigeria, and Tanzania. Elevated symptoms were defined by Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item (GAD-7) questionnaire scores [≥] 5. Nine classifiers were assessed across nine scenarios defined by speech-task configuration (short sentence, long passage, or both tasks) and sex stratification under participant-separated, repeated nested cross-validation (CV). Acoustic-only models used the extended Geneva Minimalistic Acoustic Parameter Set, and context-augmented models added age, self-reported health, and sex where applicable. With feature selection, the highest mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCROC) was 0.594 for acoustic-only models and 0.699 for context-augmented models, the latter in the female-only combined-task scenario. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) identified fundamental frequency descriptors as prominent acoustic predictors, while health status and age were the leading predictors in context-augmented models. Performance varied across scenarios, and feature selection provided no consistent benefit. Secondary regression poorly estimated continuous symptom severity. These findings indicate limited discrimination from neutral speech acoustics alone and improved performance with participant context, warranting external validation.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.26367837 v1

summary.background:
- Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD): persistent, excessive worry; screened here with the GAD-7, a 7-item questionnaire where a score of 5 or more was treated as "elevated" symptoms.
- Acoustic features: measurable properties of sound such as pitch (fundamental frequency), loudness and timing; the eGeMAPS set is a standard compact list of these.
- Machine learning classifier: a model that learns from labelled examples to sort new cases into groups (here, elevated vs not elevated).
- AUC-ROC: a 0.5 score means chance-level sorting and 1.0 means perfect; the best acoustic-only model reached 0.594, and the best context-augmented model 0.699.
- Nested cross-validation: a way of testing models on data held out from training, repeated to reduce over-optimistic results; "participant-separated" means no person appears in both training and test sets.
- SHAP: a method that estimates how much each input feature pushes a model's prediction up or down.
summary.one_liner: Machine-learning classifiers trained on acoustic features of neutral read speech, with and without demographic and health context, were evaluated for screening elevated GAD-7 anxiety scores in 1,788 adults from four African countries under participant-separated nested cross-validation.
summary.plain: Researchers asked whether a short recording of someone reading text aloud could help flag possible generalized anxiety. They analysed voice recordings from 1,788 adults in Botswana, Ghana, Nigeria and Tanzania, collected remotely, and compared nine computer models. Voice features alone gave weak results, while adding simple personal information such as health status and age helped more.
summary.why: Remote, low-cost screening could matter in places with few mental health clinicians, but this study reports only modest performance and the authors themselves say external validation is needed. It is a useful check on how far voice alone can go, not evidence that voice screening is ready for use.

title: Automated Screening for Generalized Anxiety Disorder Using Voice Analysis and Machine Learning

abstract: Securing hundreds of billions of dollars in decentralized finance (DeFi) requires both cryptographically secured collateral and economic capital to absorb losses that collateral alone cannot cover. Composability makes both the amount and location of this protection matter: Kelp's nearly \$300 million April 2026 bridge exploit showed how an attacker could borrow against stolen assets across lending markets. We study how to allocate junior capital that absorbs losses before users incur losses in lending protocols. The main object we study is a tripartite graph that records user assets, their covered liabilities, and the junior capital permitted to pay them. Cuts in this graph determine what protection is missing, while a static security game on the graph defines how much such protection should cost. We call this cost the adversarial default premium (ADP), which can be viewed as the excess cost of insurance in composable financial systems. We then study the joint cost of funding loans and protecting their creditors via this insurance. In a tripartite graph with $N$ borrowers and $M$ lenders, we show that existing systems such as Aave and Morpho have an insurance cost that is $Θ(N)$. Under mild assumptions, we show that the optimal graph has an insurance cost that is $Θ(\sqrt{N})$ with small constants. We apply our model to numerous 2026 DeFi cyber attacks and estimate ADP and the performance of optimized graphs. We find practical capital cost savings of up to 34.5% for our optimized design versus designs that resemble Aave and Morpho. Our results suggest that new lending protocols can improve capital efficiency by treating junior capital as a first-class constraint in protocol design.
label: arXiv:2611.26948v1

summary.background:
- DeFi: lending and borrowing run by smart contracts on public blockchains, without a traditional bank.
- Collateral: assets locked up to secure a loan.
- Composability: protocols can be stacked, so one protocol's assets can be reused as collateral in another, letting a single exploit spread.
- Junior capital: a first-loss buffer that absorbs losses before senior creditors (here, users) are hit; similar to a deductible or insurance layer.
- Tripartite graph: a three-part network linking user assets, the liabilities they cover, and the junior capital available to pay them.
- Static security game: a game-theory model in which an attacker picks a strategy against fixed defenses, used here to price the protection.
- Θ(N) vs Θ(√N): asymptotic growth rates; as the number of borrowers N grows, the optimized design's insurance cost grows much more slowly.
- Kelp exploit (April 2026): an attack, cited in the paper, in which roughly $300 million in stolen bridged assets was used as borrowed collateral across lending markets.
summary.one_liner: The paper models how junior (first-loss) capital should be allocated across a tripartite graph of user assets, covered liabilities, and protecting capital in DeFi lending, defines an adversarial default premium via a static security game, and shows an optimized graph can scale insurance cost as Θ(√N) versus Θ(N) for Aave- and Morpho-like designs.
summary.plain: Decentralized lending protocols hold large sums, and when hackers exploit them, losses can spread across linked lending markets. This paper asks how much backup money (a first layer of capital that takes losses before users do) such systems need, and where it should be placed. The authors model this as a network diagram, define a cost for the protection, and report that an optimized layout could cut the capital cost by up to 34.5% compared with designs resembling Aave and Morpho, based on estimates applied to 2026 attacks.
summary.why: Losses from DeFi exploits are large and can cascade through composable protocols, so how much capital to hold and where is a practical design question. The idea of treating junior capital as a core design constraint may be useful for protocol designers, though the results rest on the authors' model and assumptions, which the summary text does not fully spell out.

title: Bottlenecked: The Capital Cost of Protected DeFi Lending

abstract: We examine whether social trust shapes the pricing of lottery-like stocks by influencing investors' beliefs regarding optimistic information associated with extreme future payoffs. We argue that higher social trust reduces investors' skepticism toward optimistic information associated with extreme future payoffs, increasing demand for lottery-type stocks and leading to overpricing and lower subsequent returns. Using a sample of 8,875 firms across 49 US states over the period 1996-2018 and MAX as a proxy for lottery-like characteristics, we show that the MAX effect is concentrated in regions with relatively high trust and is weak or absent in regions with relatively low trust. We further find that this trust conditioning is stronger in regions with lower education or income levels, consistent with social trust playing a relatively more important role when investors have more limited access to private information. The results are robust to alternative lottery proxies and a range of robustness checks. Our findings identify social trust as a novel determinant of the pricing of lottery-like stocks and provide evidence that social capital may amplify belief-driven mispricing in assets with highly skewed payoffs.
label: arXiv:2611.27020v1

summary.background:
- Lottery-like stocks: shares whose returns are highly skewed, so most outcomes are poor but a few are very large.
- MAX: a common measure of lottery-likeness, based on a stock's highest recent daily return in a period.
- MAX effect: the tendency for stocks with high past MAX to earn lower later returns, often read as overpricing driven by demand for lottery-style payoffs.
- Social trust: the general willingness of people in a community to believe others, often measured by survey responses aggregated to regions.
- Overpricing and skepticism: investors who doubt optimistic news demand less of such stocks; the paper argues trust reduces that doubt.
- Robustness checks: tests that repeat the analysis with different measures or assumptions to see whether results hold.
summary.one_liner: Using 1996–2018 US firm data across 49 states, this paper tests whether regional social trust amplifies the mispricing of lottery-like stocks (proxied by MAX), with the MAX effect concentrated in high-trust regions.
summary.plain: Some stocks behave like lottery tickets: they rarely pay off but occasionally pay off enormously, and investors often overpay for them, which tends to be followed by weak returns. This paper asks whether the general level of trust among people in a region changes how strongly investors pay for such stocks. The authors find that the pattern appears mainly in high-trust regions and is weak or absent in low-trust ones.
summary.why: It suggests that a broad social attitude, trust, may shape how people form beliefs about risky, highly skewed investments, linking finance to social capital research. The text does not show how far the result generalizes beyond US states and the chosen proxies, so it should be read as evidence of an association rather than a settled cause.

title: Trust and Lottery-Related Anomalies

abstract: Uplink channel estimation can be severely degraded by hybrid-field interference, where strong near-field intra-site interference is coupled with far-field inter-site interference. Although a joint near-/far-field dictionary can capture this interference structure, it requires dense angle--distance matching that may incur high complexity and performance degradation. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a hybrid-field interference suppression framework for uplink channel estimation. First, we formulate a hybrid-field interference model and analyze its sparse reconstruction. Then, to avoid exhaustive near-field dictionary matching, we propose a low-complexity interference-parameter estimation method based on the angle--domain diffusion pattern of the dominant interference. Using the estimated parameters, the proposed parametric interference-nulling orthogonal matching pursuit (PIN-OMP) algorithm suppresses the dominant interference components and reconstructs the desired uplink channel from the interference-suppressed observation. Furthermore, a physical critical-distance bound is derived to characterize the feasible distance-inversion region, and a conditional hybrid Cram'er--Rao bound (HCRB) is established to quantify the desired channel reconstruction limit under a reconstructed interference basis. Finally, numerical results are provided to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed scheme.
label: arXiv:2611.27185v1

summary.background:
- Uplink channel estimation: measuring how a device's radio signal travels to a base station, needed to decode data.
- Far-field vs. near-field: far-field assumes signals arrive as parallel waves (depends only on direction); near-field, typical of very large antenna arrays, also depends on distance to the source.
- Intra-site vs. inter-site interference: unwanted signals from the same cell site versus from neighboring sites.
- Sparse reconstruction / dictionary: representing a signal as a few terms chosen from a large table of candidate directions and distances; orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP) is a standard greedy search through that table.
- Cramér–Rao bound: a theoretical lower limit on the error any unbiased estimator can achieve.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes a low-complexity method (PIN-OMP) that estimates and nulls strong near-field intra-site and far-field inter-site interference before reconstructing the desired uplink channel, and bounds the achievable channel reconstruction error with a conditional hybrid Cramér–Rao bound.
summary.plain: Wireless base stations receive signals from phones and devices, and a nearby interferer plus a distant one can corrupt the measurement of the channel a device is actually using. This paper describes a way to first estimate the pattern of the strongest interference, cancel it out, and then recover the wanted channel, without the heavy computation of searching over every possible position. The text reports that the approach is effective in numerical simulations, but the abstract alone does not give the size of the gains.
summary.why: Future large antenna arrays will create near-field conditions where the old far-field models break down, so cleaner channel estimates at lower computational cost matter for practical systems. Whether the method holds up in realistic deployments is not shown in the provided text.

title: Hybrid-Field Interference Suppression for Low-Complexity Uplink Channel Estimation

abstract: ISAC systems enable simultaneous data transmission and environmental sensing using a common waveform. Characterizing their fundamental estimation-information performance limits is of core interest in information theory. In this paper, the achievable data rate for communications and the Miller-Chang-type CRB on sensing distortion are adopted as ISAC performance metrics, both of which are functionals of the ISAC waveform distribution. Our aim is to characterize the optimal input distributions across the entire CRB-rate Pareto boundary, corresponding to different sensing-communication tradeoff preferences. Three types of power constraint on input waveform are considered, namely, i) general power (GP), ii) maximum amplitude (MA), and iii) constant modulus (CM) constraints. Under these constraints, Pareto-optimal input distributions are shown to exhibit a common structural property: the directional component is uniformly distributed over the complex unit sphere; the power distribution is discrete (excluding the communication-optimal point under GP, where it follows a Gamma distribution induced by Gaussian inputs). We further investigate and characterize their Pareto-optimal sensing-communication preference dependent support structures. Finally, numerical algorithms are developed under GP and MA to trace their Pareto boundaries and determine corresponding optimal power distributions based on their respective support characteristics. From both analytical and numerical results, we conclude sensing prefers deterministic power while communication benefits from a richer distribution of power levels, thereby revealing the sensing-communication waveform uncertainty tradeoff in the fundamental power domain.
label: arXiv:2611.27022v1

summary.background:
- ISAC: one transmitted waveform serves both data delivery and radar-like sensing.
- Achievable rate: the amount of data per second that can be reliably sent, a standard information-theory measure.
- Cramér-Rao bound (CRB): a lower limit on the error of any unbiased estimate; here it measures sensing accuracy.
- Pareto boundary: the set of designs where you cannot improve one goal (sensing or communication) without worsening the other.
- Input distribution: the statistical pattern of signal values and power the transmitter uses.
- Power constraints: general average power, a maximum amplitude cap, or constant modulus (fixed signal magnitude).
- Gaussian and Gamma distributions: common probability patterns; the communication-optimal case under general power follows a Gamma pattern of power.
summary.one_liner: The paper characterizes the optimal input waveform distributions along the full communication-rate versus Miller-Chang-type CRB sensing-distortion Pareto boundary for ISAC under general power, maximum amplitude, and constant modulus constraints, and gives numerical algorithms for the general-power and maximum-amplitude cases.
summary.plain: Integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) is about using one radio signal to both send data and detect objects in the environment. This paper studies the best possible trade-off between how well the signal can carry data and how accurately it can measure its surroundings, and what kind of signal power pattern achieves each trade-off. The authors find that the best sensing signals keep a fixed power level, while the best communication signals use a varied spread of power levels.
summary.why: The work gives a theoretical answer to a design question for future wireless systems that must both communicate and sense, and it links sensing and communication through a shared notion of waveform uncertainty. The text does not report practical system tests, so its direct impact on real deployments is unclear.

title: On Pareto-Optimal Estimation-Information Limits-Achieving Distributions for Integrated Sensing and Communications

abstract: Music theory enables performers, composers, and listeners to engage more deeply with music. Schenkerian analysis (SchA) is a particularly illustrative and widely used approach for modeling tonal structure, organizing music into hierarchical layers of harmonic and voice-leading relationships. Despite its importance in pedagogy and scholarship, producing well-formatted Schenkerian graphs remains difficult. A typical workflow might involve writing the Schenkerian analysis on paper, and then manually, painstakingly, entering each symbol by hand into music software, exporting to vector graphics, and manually refining layouts in graphical editors. Existing optical music recognition (OMR) systems for handwritten common western music notation (CWMN) can be leveraged for their ability to recognize small-scale symbols common to those in SchA. However, CWMN OMR models generally fail to recognize large symbols such as phrase slurs, struggle with dense notation, and do not recognize Schenkerian analysis markings. Thus, these models do not extend well to digitizing SchA. This paper introduces a novel framework for optical music recognition of both CWMN and SchA. Our novel contributions include (1) an ensemble model in which each individual model follows a different image-cropping scheme for improved object detection, (2) a topological neural network architecture for notation assembly, where candidate hyperedges attend to one another and perform hierarchical message passing, (3) the first dataset of labeled handwritten SchAs, gathered with novel model integration to the OMR-annotation software, MuNG Studio, and (4) the first algorithm for converting semantic Schenkerian graphs into typeset format.
label: arXiv:2611.26958v1

summary.background:
- Optical music recognition (OMR): software that reads images of sheet music and recovers the notes and symbols.
- Common Western music notation (CWMN): standard printed staff notation.
- Schenkerian analysis: a method that reduces a piece to layers of harmonic and voice-leading structure, shown as graphs with slurs and other markings.
- Ensemble model: several models combined so their outputs are merged for better results.
- Hypergraph / topological neural network: a network that links groups of symbols together rather than only pairs, so it can model how symbols belong together.
- Message passing: a process where nodes in a network exchange information with neighbors to refine their predictions.
- MuNG Studio: annotation software used to label OMR data.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes an optical music recognition framework for handwritten Schenkerian analysis graphs and common Western notation, combining a cropping-based model ensemble, a topological neural network for assembling notation, a new labeled dataset of handwritten Schenkerian analyses, and an algorithm that converts semantic graphs into typeset output.
summary.plain: Music theorists often sketch Schenkerian analysis, a way of diagramming the underlying structure of a piece, by hand, then re-enter it into music software one symbol at a time. This paper describes software that reads scanned handwritten versions of these diagrams and turns them into clean, typeset digital graphs. The authors also built a new collection of labeled handwritten analyses and a method for converting the recognized structure into a standard print format.
summary.why: Handwriting-to-digital tools for music notation are a practical aid for teaching and scholarship, and the text notes that existing systems miss large symbols like phrase slurs and Schenkerian markings. The released dataset and conversion algorithm may be useful to others working on this niche, though the text does not report how well the system performs.

title: A Novel Dataset and Framework for Schenkerian Optical Music Recognition

abstract: Urban mixed traffic networks provide diverse mobility options, yet conventional routing guidance with fixed travel modes leaves the benefits of coordinating travel modes and route planning largely unexploited. This paper proposes an integrated mode recommendation and dynamic routing guidance framework for urban mixed traffic networks comprising private vehicles, autonomous vehicles, and buses. We formulate a dynamic trip index (DTX) that incorporates mode-specific travel time, monetary cost, and convenience, enabling consistent evaluation of trip quality across travel modes. Using this measure, we develop a mode recommendation method that selects feasible autonomous vehicle or bus services based on predicted DTX for travelers without private vehicles, while preserving service capacity for travelers with known demand. We integrate this method with dynamic routing guidance for private and autonomous vehicles to improve the average trip quality of all travelers. Simulation studies involving $1{,}500$ travelers on a real-world road network in Shanghai, China, show that the proposed framework increases the mean realized DTX by $13.01\%$ compared with dynamic routing guidance alone and by $19.68\%$ compared with fixed travel modes with preplanned routes, highlighting the value of mode flexibility in improving trip quality beyond route adaptation.
label: arXiv:2611.27091v1

summary.background:
- Dynamic routing guidance: real-time advice to drivers about which road to take, updated as traffic changes.
- Mixed traffic network: a road system shared by several vehicle types, here private cars, autonomous vehicles (self-driving cars offered as a service), and buses.
- Trip index (DTX): a single score combining travel time, money cost, and convenience so that different modes can be compared on one scale.
- Mode recommendation: suggesting which travel option a person should take; here, autonomous vehicles or buses are offered to travelers who have no private car, while capacity is kept for travelers with known demand.
- Simulation: testing the method on a computer model of traffic rather than on real travelers, so results depend on the model's assumptions.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes a joint mode-recommendation and dynamic routing-guidance framework for mixed urban traffic (private cars, autonomous vehicles, buses), built around a dynamic trip-quality index (DTX), and evaluates it in a simulation of 1,500 travelers on a real Shanghai road network.
summary.plain: Cities offer several ways to get around, such as driving your own car, riding a self-driving car, or taking a bus, but navigation advice usually fixes the mode and only suggests routes. This paper builds a system that also suggests which mode a traveler should use, scoring each option by travel time, cost, and convenience. In a computer simulation of 1,500 travelers on a real Shanghai road network, the authors report that this combined approach raised the average trip score by 13.01% over route guidance alone and by 19.68% over fixed modes with pre-planned routes.
summary.why: It treats choice of travel mode and choice of route as one problem rather than two, which matters as self-driving cars and buses share roads with private cars. The gains are simulation results only, so they show what the method can do under the modeled assumptions rather than how travelers would respond in practice.

title: Mode Recommendation and Dynamic Routing Guidance for Improved Trip Quality in Mixed Traffic Networks

abstract: Grid operators now require dynamic models of data centers and other large computational loads, and new ride-through rules assume that these models predict how facilities respond to disturbances. This review asks what evidence supports that assumption. We coded 160 documents, screened from 1,424 de-duplicated database and seed records plus 65 added documents, by the strongest reference object each presents, from grid-side records to simulation only. Across 19 field-evidence entries, 15 requirement documents from three continents and nine model classes, we find two comparisons of a standard library model with measured data-center events: with default parameters the model failed both, and refitting it to each event separately reduced the error but was never tested on an unseen event. Among the sources reviewed, we found no successful held-out validation of a frozen, facility-specific data-center model against an independent measured disturbance, and 25 of the 33 model-phenomenon combinations with any evidence involve no electrical measurement. The features that distinguish the new rules (memory of repeated dips, recovery within 0.5-3 s, proportional power reduction during the sag, overvoltage response) are those current phasor models cannot represent or have never been tested against. In the operator procedures examined, simulations and model-to-model benchmarks are accepted as evidence of model fidelity, unlike the measured validation required of generators, and proposed mitigations have mostly been evaluated on unvalidated facility models. We propose context-of-use gates that separate calibration from validation, release labels for model claims, a minimum validation protocol with acceptance criteria, and a research agenda.
label: arXiv:2611.27169v1

summary.one_liner: An evidence-graded review of 160 documents finds that dynamic models of large data-center loads are rarely validated against measured disturbances on unseen events, and proposes context-of-use gates, release labels, and a minimum validation protocol.
summary.plain: Grid operators now ask for computer models of big data centers, and new rules assume those models can predict how the facilities behave when the power grid is disturbed. This review checks whether the evidence supports that assumption. The authors found very little: the one standard model they could test failed with default settings, and refitting it to single events was never checked on a different event.
summary.why:
Data centers draw very large and fast-changing amounts of power, so how their models are trusted affects grid stability and the rules that govern connections. The paper is a careful critique of evidence rather than a new model, so its main value is in showing where validation is missing and what would count as adequate.</background>
<parameter name="background">Ride-through: a load's ability to stay connected during a brief voltage dip instead of dropping off. Dynamic model: a mathematical simulation of how equipment responds over time to grid changes. Phasor model: a simplified grid-simulation approach that tracks slow-changing voltage and current averages rather than the full waveform. Calibration vs. validation: calibration fits model settings to one dataset; validation tests the frozen model against a separate, independent measurement. Held-out event: a disturbance not used in fitting. Context-of-use: the specific question a model is meant to answer.

title: Which Data-Center Load Models Can Be Trusted? An Evidence-Graded Review of Dynamic Modeling and Validation for Large Computational Loads

abstract: We created a list of the most notable AI agents that can live in your text messages, from general assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.
label: AI News & Artificial Intelligence | TechCrunch

summary.background:
- An "AI agent" is a program that can carry out tasks for you, such as booking, reminders, or answering questions, rather than only chatting.
- Text messaging here means SMS or messaging apps where you converse with the AI as you would with a person.
- The article is a consumer-oriented list, not a research study or product review with testing.
- Details such as specific product names, features, prices, and privacy terms are not included in the provided text.
summary.one_liner: A news roundup listing notable AI agents that can be reached through text messaging, grouped into general assistants and agents aimed at families, travel, and work.
summary.plain: This article is a short list of AI tools you can talk to by sending text messages, much like messaging a contact on your phone. It groups them by purpose, such as general helpers, family organizers, travel planners, and work assistants. The text itself is only a brief introduction, so it does not describe how each agent performs or what they cost.
summary.why: It shows a growing trend of AI assistants moving into everyday messaging apps rather than separate websites or apps. Whether this becomes a lasting habit is not something the article can tell us.

title: Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages

abstract: We got two very different pictures of Nvidia — the company’s latest earnings report vs. the tech executives loudly calling for Jensen Huang’s return.
label: AI News & Artificial Intelligence | TechCrunch

summary.background:
- Nvidia makes graphics processors (GPUs), which are widely used to build and run AI models.
- Jensen Huang is Nvidia's co-founder and long-serving chief executive.
- An earnings report is a regular financial statement a public company releases with its sales, profit, and outlook.
- "Calling for someone's return" suggests that person had stepped back from a role, but the article's text does not say in what capacity or why.
- The piece is a short commentary; it gives no figures, quotes, or named executives.
summary.one_liner: A short opinion-style news piece contrasting Nvidia's latest earnings report with public calls from tech executives for Jensen Huang to return to a leadership role.
summary.plain: The article looks at Nvidia, the chipmaker that makes the processors used to train and run AI systems, and compares two signals about it. One is the company's recent financial earnings report, which describes how well the business performed. The other is a set of public statements from tech executives urging its co-founder and chief executive, Jensen Huang, to come back into a leading role.
summary.why: Nvidia is a central supplier in the AI boom, so questions about its leadership and financial health matter to investors and the wider industry. The text is very brief and does not give the specifics of the earnings numbers or the executives' reasons, so it is hard to judge how much weight the contrast deserves.

title: A tale of two Nvidias

abstract: Macrophages perform a wide array of distinct and crucial functions, and therefore tightly regulate their responses to external stimuli. These cells must integrate sequential signals over time to mount an appropriate response to their immunological niche. How prior cytokine stimulation shares macrophage responses to a subsequent stimulus remains poorly understood, yet has important implications for pathogen clearance as well as tissue repair and homeostasis. Here, we systematically characterize transcriptional responses to sequential cytokine stimulation in primary human macrophages, as well as demonstrate the effect of interactions with bacterial pathogens on macrophage transcriptional responses and plasticity. We find that prior stimulation history constrains subsequent transcriptional responses in a stimulus-specific and asymmetric manner. Across the cytokines we tested, we observe that IFN{beta} is a dominant regulator of subsequent responses to other cytokines. We observe that this plasticity restriction is concentration dependent, rapidly established, and persists after cytokine removal. Additionally, we show that endogenous IFN{beta} produced during infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis restricts subsequent cytokine responses in a manner that is dependent on the activity of the bacterial secretion system ESX-1. Taken together, these findings establish a hierarchical model of macrophage responses to cytokines that depends on cytokine identity and order.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.14.765729 v1

summary.background:
- Macrophages: immune cells that engulf microbes and coordinate responses in tissues.
- Cytokines: signaling proteins that cells use to communicate and trigger responses.
- Transcriptional response: changes in which genes a cell switches on or off, measured here as the cell's gene-expression response.
- Interferon-beta (IFN-beta): a cytokine involved in antiviral and antibacterial defense.
- Mycobacterium tuberculosis: the bacterium that causes tuberculosis.
- ESX-1: a secretion system the bacterium uses to inject molecules into host cells; it is a known virulence factor.
- "Plasticity" here means the cell's ability to change its response to new signals.
summary.one_liner: Using primary human macrophages, this paper shows that prior cytokine exposure asymmetrically constrains later transcriptional responses, with IFN-beta acting as a dominant regulator, and that Mycobacterium tuberculosis-induced IFN-beta restricts later cytokine responses in an ESX-1-dependent way.
summary.plain: Immune cells called macrophages receive many chemical signals (cytokines) in sequence, and what they received earlier can change how they react later. This study tested that in human macrophages, showing that the order and identity of earlier signals limit how the cells respond to later ones. It also found that interferon-beta, a signal produced when tuberculosis bacteria infect the cells, restricts later responses, and that this depends on a bacterial secretion system called ESX-1.
summary.why: Infected tissue sees signals arrive one after another, so how earlier signals shape later reactions bears on pathogen clearance and tissue repair. The text does not show clinical consequences, so the link to treatment or disease outcomes remains a question for future work.

title: Macrophage signaling history constrains subsequent transcriptional responses to cytokine stimulation

abstract: In the last twenty years, the microbiome has become a central focus of biomedical research, with amplicon sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene considered the industry standard for taxon identification of prokaryotes due to its cost-effectiveness. However, common target regions in 16S amplicons often do not uniquely distinguish closely related species, restricting many analyses to the genus level. Additionally, curated databases such as NCBI's 16S curated database often do not contain all intragenomic variants of the 16S gene and lack annotation of the 16S genomic composition and gene structure. To address these limitations, our team created RADSuite, a collection of tools which includes a more robust database of 16S gene copies (RADlib), an application that identifies which V regions will allow for species level identification (RADx), and a step-by-step guide for how to integrate RADlib within existing metagenomic profiling software tools. Here we demonstrate the utility of using RADSuite as a guide for designing 16S amplicon sequencing experiments. For example, RADx can be used to recommend 16S components that enable species-level resolution for most microbes of interest, even when industry-standard default amplicon choices (V3/V4) are insufficient. These findings suggest that targeted variable region selection is critical for reliable species identification. As researchers use RADSuite to improve the quality of their experiments, we anticipate improved experimental accuracy in fields of microbiome research from human health to environmental conservation.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767742 v1

summary.background:
- 16S rRNA gene: a stable gene found in bacteria and archaea, used as a barcode to identify them.
- Amplicon sequencing: copying and reading just one targeted region of DNA, cheaper than sequencing everything in a sample.
- V regions: variable stretches within the 16S gene; different stretches differ in how well they distinguish species.
- Genus vs. species: a genus is a broader group that can contain several species; species-level resolution is more precise.
- Intragenomic variants: a single bacterial genome can carry several slightly different copies of the 16S gene, which reference databases may not fully capture.
- Metagenomic profiling: estimating which microbes are present in a mixed sample.
summary.one_liner: RADSuite is a toolkit (a curated 16S rRNA gene copy database, RADlib; a variable-region selector, RADx; and an integration guide for metagenomic profilers) aimed at improving species-level identification in 16S amplicon sequencing.
