summary.plain: Scientists often identify bacteria by reading a short, standard piece of their genetic code called the 16S gene. This paper describes a set of software tools that work out which parts of that gene can tell closely related bacterial species apart, rather than only their broader genus group. The authors report that their tool can recommend regions that give species-level results for most microbes of interest, even where the commonly used default regions (V3/V4) fall short.
summary.why: Many microbiome studies, in areas from human health to environmental monitoring, can only name bacteria to the genus level, so better species-level naming could sharpen their conclusions. The paper's claims are about the tools' usefulness as a guide for experiment design; the text alone does not show how well they perform in practice against other methods.

title: RADSuite: Improving Species-Level Identification in Microbiome Research

abstract: Astrocytes contribute to hippocampal cognitive functions, but how astrocyte-derived factors regulate memory formation remains unclear. Here, we identify astrocyte-secreted Cathepsin D (CtsD) as a regulator of hippocampal learning and memory. Proteomic profiling of hippocampal astrocytes upon learning identified candidates predicted to be secreted, among which we focused on CtsD, whose extracellular brain functions are unknown. Neutralizing extracellular CtsD or astrocyte-selective CtsD knockdown (aCtsD-KD) impaired hippocampal long term potentiation (LTP) and memory acquisition, suggesting an extracellular role for astrocytic CtsD. In aCtsD-KD mice, these deficits were accompanied by alterations in excitatory transmission and synaptic structures. aCtsD-KD also caused abnormal extracellular matrix (ECM) accumulation, and its partial digestion by chondroitinase ABC rescued the memory deficit, indicating that astrocytic CtsD-dependent ECM degradation contributes to hippocampal memory. Together, our findings suggest a CtsD-dependent astrocyte-matrix-synapse axis regulating hippocampal memory.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.768232 v1

summary.background:
- Astrocytes: star-shaped glial cells that support neurons and release signaling molecules.
- Hippocampus: a brain region essential for forming new memories.
- Long-term potentiation (LTP): a lasting strengthening of connections between neurons, widely used as a cellular model of learning.
- Extracellular matrix (ECM): the mesh of sugar-protein molecules outside cells that helps hold tissue structure and regulates synapses.
- Cathepsin D: an enzyme that usually breaks down proteins, here studied for a role outside cells.
- Chondroitinase ABC: an enzyme that cuts down certain ECM sugar chains, used here as a tool to test the matrix's role.
- Knockdown: reducing how much of a gene's product a cell makes.
summary.one_liner: Astrocyte-secreted Cathepsin D is reported to shape hippocampal LTP and memory acquisition in mice, apparently by remodeling the extracellular matrix around synapses.
summary.plain: Brain support cells called astrocytes release proteins that may influence how memories form. This study focuses on one such protein, Cathepsin D, which is normally known for breaking down material inside cells. The authors found that blocking it outside astrocytes, or knocking it down in astrocytes of mice, weakened a measure of synaptic strengthening (LTP) and impaired memory acquisition, and that partially digesting a surrounding matrix material restored memory in these mice.
summary.why: It points to a possible link between astrocytes, the extracellular matrix that surrounds neurons, and synapse strength in memory, a mechanism that has received less attention than neuron-to-neuron signaling. The text does not establish how broadly these findings apply beyond the mouse experiments described.

title: Astrocyte-secreted Cathepsin D regulates hippocampal memory through extracellular matrix remodeling

abstract: Adeno-associated virus vectors (AAVs) have broad utility in neuroscience. A variety of features, such as titer, capsid, enhancers and promoters, coding and non-coding elements, can be utilized to pursue diverse experimental ends. The net effects of titer and capsid have been used experimentally to pursue retrograde and anterograde studies, such as through the monosynaptic spread of high-titer AAV1. The literature on AAV8 is conflicting, with evidence for and against its long-range action outside of the infected starter population. Using the mouse corticopontocerebellar tract, we report that AAV8, when used at high titers, can be associated with long range recombination outside of the starter population. This phenomenon depended upon the viral titer and was influenced by the presence of other experimental injections. Surprisingly, separate injections of high-titer AAV8 recombinase and recombinase-reporter AAV8s gave rise to recombination across long distances in populations not known to be monosynaptically connected. Given the possibility of long range and emergent effects, we suggest that investigators empirically determine titer, capsid, and injection designs that reduce false positives and/or indirect effects.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.767967 v1

summary.background:
- AAV (adeno-associated virus) is a harmless, engineered virus used to deliver genes into specific cells.
- Titer is the concentration of virus particles in an injection; higher titer usually means more cells are infected.
- Capsid is the protein shell around the virus that influences which cells it infects and how it spreads.
- Recombinase (such as Cre) is an enzyme that cuts and rearranges DNA in engineered cells; a reporter then reveals which cells had that activity.
- Starter population means the cells directly infected by the injection.
- Monosynaptic means a direct, single-step connection between two neurons; tracing methods aim to label only these.
- The corticopontocerebellar tract is a brain pathway running from the cortex through the pons to the cerebellum, used here as a test system.
summary.one_liner: In mice, high-titer AAV8 injected into the corticopontocerebellar pathway produced recombination outside the injected starter cells, depending on titer and on other co-injections, including across regions not known to be monosynaptically connected.
summary.plain: Researchers use harmless viruses to carry genetic tools into brain cells, and they often assume the virus only affects the cells it was injected into. This paper reports that a common virus type, AAV8, given at high concentration, can switch on genetic reporters in distant cells that were not directly infected. The effect depended on the dose and on what other virus injections were made at the same time.
summary.why: This matters for anyone who uses viral tools to map brain circuits, because labeled cells far from the injection site could be mistaken for directly connected cells. The text suggests that the effect may come from spread beyond the starter cells, but the mechanism is not established here.

title: Unexpected Long Range Actions of AAV8

abstract: 5-methylcytosine (5mC) and 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) are genome-wide epigenetic modifications involved in chromatin organization and transcriptional regulation. Although Enzymatic Methyl-seq (EM-seq) can enable the combined profiling of 5mC and 5hmC, Enzymatic 5hmC-seq (E5hmC-seq) can provide selective profiling of 5hmC at single-base resolution. In this context, we systematically validated E5hmC-seq using diverse genomic DNA samples. Next, we integrated E5hmC-seq with EM-seq to distinguish between 5mC and 5hmC landscapes during neuronal differentiation of mouse embryonic stem cells. First, we observed dynamic remodeling of both modifications throughout differentiation, with pronounced changes during the transition from embryoid bodies (EBs) to neural progenitor cells (NPCs), characterized by a global decrease in 5hmC accompanied by an increase in 5mC. Subsequently, differentially hydroxymethylated regions (DhMRs) exhibiting 5hmC depletion frequently showed a concurrent increase in 5mC, whereas regions gaining 5hmC displayed an opposing trend, reflecting the genome-wide relationship. Mapping these modifications to transcriptional profiles revealed an association between cytosine modification dynamics and gene expression, where transcriptional downregulation correlated with 5hmC depletion with concomitant 5mC enrichment. In summary, combined mapping of EM-seq and E5hmC-seq can decipher the dynamic interplay between 5mC and 5hmC at single-base resolution and provide insights into the relationships among cytosine modification dynamics, genomic context and transcriptional regulation during differentiation.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.768104 v1

summary.background:
- DNA is a chain of four letters; some C letters carry a methyl chemical tag (5mC).
- 5hmC is a related tag made by oxidizing 5mC; it is thought to be an intermediate in removing or changing methylation.
- Epigenetic marks are chemical changes that affect gene activity without altering the DNA sequence itself.
- Single-base resolution means the method measures the tag at each individual C position, not in averaged blocks.
- EM-seq is an enzyme-based sequencing method that distinguishes methylation marks; E5hmC-seq is a related enzyme-based method specific to 5hmC.
- Embryonic stem cells can be guided to form embryoid bodies and then neural progenitor cells, which are early precursors of nerve cells.
- Differentially hydroxymethylated regions (DhMRs) are DNA stretches where 5hmC levels differ between conditions.
summary.one_liner: The paper validates Enzymatic 5hmC-seq (E5hmC-seq) and combines it with EM-seq to map 5mC and 5hmC at single-base resolution during neuronal differentiation of mouse embryonic stem cells, linking shifts in these marks to gene expression.
summary.plain: Cells carry chemical tags on their DNA that help control which genes are switched on. This study tracked two of these tags, one called 5mC and a related one called 5hmC, as mouse stem cells turned into brain-type progenitor cells. The authors report that 5hmC fell and 5mC rose at the key early step, and that genes which were turned down tended to lose 5hmC and gain 5mC.
summary.why: Mapping these DNA tags precisely over time helps show how cell identity changes are wired to gene activity, which matters for developmental biology and for reading epigenetic data. The text reports correlations between modification changes and expression, so it does not by itself show that the tag changes cause the expression changes.

title: Single-base 5mC and 5hmC profiling identifies a dynamic 5hmC-to-5mC transition at gene bodies and transcription end sites during neuronal differentiation of mouse embryonic stem cells.

abstract: The global resurgence of syphilis poses a major public health challenge, even in the era of effective antibiotic therapy. Following treatment, some patients achieve seroreversion, whereas others remain serofast with persistent nontreponemal antibody reactivity. Although nontreponemal antibody titers guide clinical follow-up, it remains unclear how closely they reflect the resolution of inflammation and recovery of immune function. We integrated single-cell transcriptomics, immunophenotyping in clinical samples, and functional assays to characterize circulating monocytes and natural killer (NK) cells across seroreversion and low- and high-titer serofast states, and further examined the impact of HIV coinfection. CD14+ monocytes retained inflammatory and CD163-associated scavenging programs after seroreversion, whereas serofast patients showed additional IFN-STAT1 activation in this subset. NK cells from serofast patients exhibited reduced JUN expression and impaired degranulation. JNK inhibition reduced the magnitude and altered the kinetics of NK cell degranulation, IFN-{gamma} production, and amphiregulin (AREG) induction. Among low-titer serofast patients, HIV coinfection was associated with higher mitochondrial complex I gene expression and partially restored NK cell degranulation compared with patients with syphilis alone. Complex I inhibition also reduced NK cell degranulation. These findings suggest that seroreversion does not necessarily indicate immune normalization and identify post-treatment immune alterations not fully captured by conventional serological monitoring, providing a rationale for investigating cellular immune markers as complementary measures of recovery after syphilis treatment.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.766608 v1

summary.background:
- Syphilis is a sexually transmitted bacterial infection (Treponema pallidum) treated with antibiotics.
- Nontreponemal antibody titer: a blood antibody level measured to follow treatment response; falling levels suggest cure.
- Seroreversion: antibody levels returning to normal after treatment. Serofast: antibodies remaining detectably elevated.
- Single-cell transcriptomics: measuring which genes are active in individual cells.
- Monocytes and NK (natural killer) cells: types of white blood cells involved in inflammation and killing infected or abnormal cells.
- Degranulation: NK cells releasing stored toxic granules to kill targets; a common measure of NK function.
- JNK/JUN and STAT1: intracellular signalling pathways that switch genes on; mitochondrial complex I is part of the cell's energy-producing machinery.
- HIV coinfection: many syphilis patients also carry HIV, which affects immunity.
summary.one_liner: Single-cell transcriptomics and functional assays of circulating CD14+ monocytes and NK cells across syphilis seroreversion, low- and high-titer serofast states, and HIV coinfection, linking JUN/JNK signalling and mitochondrial complex I to impaired NK degranulation.
summary.plain: Syphilis is treated with antibiotics, and blood tests for antibodies are then used to check recovery. Some patients' antibody levels drop back to normal (seroreversion), while others stay stuck at a detectable level (serofast). This study looked at two types of immune cells in the blood to see whether patients whose antibody tests look normal have fully recovered immune function, and found signs that they may not have.
summary.why: Antibody titers are the main tool for deciding whether syphilis treatment has worked, so finding immune changes that persist after antibodies normalize suggests cell-based markers could complement them. The text does not show how these findings would translate into clinical testing, so this remains a research-stage observation.

title: Distinct innate immune states associate with divergent serological outcomes after syphilis treatment

abstract: Bacteria use sophisticated mechanisms to defend themselves against antibiotics and bacteriophages, yet how they combat toxins deployed during interbacterial competition remains poorly understood. Bacteria use type VI secretion, bacteriocins, and contact dependent inhibition systems to deliver antibacterial toxins that inhibit growth by antagonizing essential processes. Here, we discover that Pseudomonas aeruginosa uses homologs of the eukaryotic major vault protein and a tRNA-like noncoding RNA to defend against RNA-damaging ribotoxins. Using an engineered pyocin delivery system, we showed that P. aeruginosa sensed ribotoxin damage and activated transcription of an RNA repair operon, which included band7, a homolog of the major vault protein. Genetic analyses demonstrated that band7-expressing bacteria were significantly more protected against growth inhibition by a ribotoxin that cleaved the anticodon loop of specific tRNA. Band7 was necessary but not sufficient, and defense also required a non-coding band7 RNA (bRNA). bRNA was cleaved by the ribotoxin, suggesting a mechanism for specificity and defense. Bioinformatic analyses revealed that band7 and candidate bRNA are widely distributed within RNA repair systems across diverse bacteria. Our data suggest that bacteria use structures related to the eukaryotic vault complex to respond to RNA damage thereby providing a hypothesis for the function of the enigmatic human vault.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.768214 v1

summary.background:
- Bacteria compete with each other using toxins delivered by systems such as type VI secretion, bacteriocins, and contact-dependent inhibition.
- Ribotoxins are toxins that damage RNA; here, one cuts the anticodon loop of specific transfer RNAs (tRNAs), which are needed to read genetic code into proteins.
- A major vault protein is a component of a large, barrel-shaped particle found in eukaryotic (animal) cells whose function is still unclear.
- Band7 proteins are a family that includes this vault-related protein homolog.
- Non-coding RNA is RNA that is not translated into protein but has regulatory or structural roles.
- A transcriptional response means cells switching genes on or off in reaction to a signal.
summary.one_liner: In Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a band7 homolog of the major vault protein and a candidate non-coding RNA (bRNA) are required, together with the ribotoxin's target site, for defense against a tRNA-anticodon-cleaving ribotoxin, with bioinformatic evidence that these components are widespread in bacterial RNA repair systems.
summary.plain: Bacteria often fight each other with toxins that attack their cells, and this paper looks at how one bacterium, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, protects itself against toxins that chop up RNA, the molecule cells use to build proteins. The authors found that when such damage occurred, the bacterium switched on a set of repair genes, including one related to a protein found in human cells called the major vault protein. Bacteria carrying this gene were better protected against a toxin that cuts a specific tRNA, and a short non-coding RNA made from the same region was also needed.
summary.why: It offers a possible clue to the long-unexplained function of the human vault, a large cell structure, and suggests a general way bacteria may repair RNA damage caused by rivals. The text does not show how far these findings extend beyond the bacteria tested, so the link to human vaults remains a hypothesis that the authors themselves propose.

title: Homologs of the Major Vault Protein defend bacteria against ribotoxins

abstract: We propose a framework for simplex-valued diffusion processes, formulated as solutions to stochastic differential equations driven by antisymmetric Brownian motion. Our edge-wise representation includes the multivariate Jacobi processes and the general class of continuous simplex-valued polynomial diffusions. Also, it allows bounded, locally Lipschitz state-dependent drift rates and edge weights. We establish weak solutions, as well as global strong existence and pathwise uniqueness for strictly positive initial states under a sufficient boundary non-attainment condition.
label: arXiv:2611.27309v1

summary.background:
- Simplex: the set of non-negative numbers that sum to one (e.g., proportions of a whole).
- Brownian motion: the mathematical model of continuous random jiggling, as in pollen particles in water.
- Stochastic differential equation (SDE): an equation describing how a quantity changes over time with both a steady push (drift) and random noise.
- Diffusion process: a random process whose solution is described by such an SDE.
- Weak vs. strong solution: a weak solution exists in some probabilistic sense; a strong solution is defined pathwise on a given noise source.
- Pathwise uniqueness: for a given noise path, there is only one solution.
- Jacobi process: a known diffusion living on an interval, here generalised to the simplex.
summary.one_liner: The paper builds a class of simplex-valued diffusion processes as solutions to stochastic differential equations driven by antisymmetric Brownian motion, covering multivariate Jacobi processes and general simplex polynomial diffusions, and proves weak existence plus global strong existence and pathwise uniqueness from strictly positive starting states under a boundary non-attainment condition.
summary.plain: This paper studies random processes that move around inside a simplex, meaning a set of numbers that are all non-negative and add up to one, like a split of a whole into shares. The authors describe such moving shares as solutions to a type of random-motion equation, using a specific kind of random noise that keeps the total fixed. They show that these processes exist and are uniquely determined when they start with every share strictly positive, under a stated condition that they never reach the edge of the simplex.
summary.why: Shares that evolve randomly over time, such as portfolio weights or population proportions, are a natural setting for these models, so a general, well-posed framework matters for that kind of modelling. The text does not discuss applications, so any link to specific fields is my inference rather than something the paper states.

title: Stochastic Differential Equations on the Simplex

abstract: We study isolation in the binomial random graph $G(n,p)$. When $p=o(1)$ and $np\to\infty$, allowing an $F$-free graph on the undominated vertices gives the same first-order asymptotics for every fixed forest $F$ as the domination number $\gamma(G)$ in $G(n,p)$. For the ordinary isolation number $\iota(G)$ ($F$ is an edge) we prove two-point concentration when $p$ is bounded away from $1$ and $np^2/(\log n)^3\to\infty$. We also identify a transition in the gap $\gamma(G)-\iota(G)$ when $\log(1/p)=o(\log n)$. This gap tends to infinity in probability when $p$ is well below $(\log\log n/\log n)^2$ and is at most one with high probability when $p$ is well above this scale. Finally, for every fixed graph $F$, we show that the classical minimum degree bound for domination is asymptotically sharp for $F$-isolation, even for regular host graphs.
label: arXiv:2611.26781v1

summary.background:
- A random graph G(n,p): n vertices, each pair joined by an edge independently with probability p.
- "Asymptotic" / "with high probability": statements about what happens as n grows large, holding with probability tending to 1.
- Domination number γ(G): the fewest vertices that together touch or include every vertex (each vertex is chosen or adjacent to a chosen one).
- Isolation number ι(G): the fewest vertices whose removal leaves a graph with no edges; the paper's F-isolation generalises this to leaving a graph with no copy of F, where F is a fixed forest (F = an edge gives ordinary isolation).
- Two-point concentration: the value is, with high probability, one of two adjacent integers.
- Minimum degree bound: a classical lower bound on domination in terms of the smallest number of neighbours any vertex has.
- Probability asymptotics, including log and little-o notation.
summary.one_liner: Studies the isolation number, domination number and F-isolation of the binomial random graph G(n,p) for p = o(1) and np → ∞, giving two-point concentration results, a transition in the gap between domination and isolation, and asymptotic sharpness of the minimum-degree bound for regular hosts.
summary.plain: This paper looks at random networks where each possible link between n points appears independently with some small probability p. It asks how few "chosen" vertices are needed so that every other vertex is either chosen or next to a chosen one, and how that changes when the goal is weakened to leaving behind only vertices that do not contain a given shape (such as a tree-like pattern). The authors give fairly precise answers on how these numbers behave as the network grows, and show how the gap between two related counts depends on how sparse the network is.
summary.why: These are questions about how precisely typical large random networks can be covered or dominated, and the text reports sharp thresholds where the behaviour of this gap changes. The text does not say what applications it may have, so its wider relevance is unclear from the abstract alone.

title: Isolation in Random Graphs

abstract: In this paper, we study projectively flat spherically symmetric sprays of constant curvature. We derive a system of equations that is equivalent to the constant-curvature condition for such sprays and solve it to obtain a complete classification of the projective factor \(p(r,s)\) into four explicit families. We further show that the sprays induced by projectively flat spherically symmetric Finsler metrics of constant flag curvature \(K=0\), \(K=-1\), and \(K=1\) are all special cases of our classification, thereby confirming that the sprays induced by these constant-flag-curvature Finsler metrics are fully contained in our framework.
label: arXiv:2611.27723v1

summary.background:
- Manifold: a space that looks locally like ordinary Euclidean space, on which calculus can be done.
- Finsler metric: a way of measuring length in which the length of a vector can depend on its direction, generalizing Riemannian metrics.
- Spray: a geometric object on the space of directions that determines the "natural paths" (geodesics) of a Finsler metric.
- Projective flatness: the spray's paths match straight lines up to reparametrization, the Finsler analogue of a flat-looking geometry.
- Spherical symmetry: the spray looks the same in all directions around a point, so it depends only on the radius r and a direction variable s.
- Flag curvature: a measure of how curved the space is along a given 2-dimensional direction; constant means the same everywhere and in all directions.
- Projective factor p(r,s): the function that encodes the spray's projective structure and is solved for in the paper.
summary.one_liner: The paper classifies projectively flat, spherically symmetric sprays of constant curvature by solving the equations that constant curvature imposes on the projective factor p(r,s), obtaining four explicit families that include the spray cases for constant flag curvature K = 0, -1, and 1.
summary.plain: This is a pure mathematics paper about "sprays," which are rules describing how straight-line-like paths behave on a curved space, the kind used in Finsler geometry (a generalization of Riemannian geometry where distances can depend on direction). The authors write down the conditions that make such a spray have constant curvature, solve them, and sort every possible solution into four explicit families. They also check that the known constant-curvature examples with curvature 0, -1, and 1 fall inside these families.
summary.why: The result gives a complete list rather than a set of examples, which matters for anyone studying which curved geometries of this type exist. The text does not describe applications outside geometry, so its wider relevance is uncertain.

title: Projectively Flat Spherically Symmetric Sprays of Constant Curvature

abstract: We prove that a projectively induced Kahler-Einstein metric has positive Einstein constant as soon as it admits one nonzero local real-holomorphic Killing field. Neither completeness nor a prescribed global group action is assumed. This gives a partial answer, under a local symmetry hypothesis, to the general positivity problem for Kahler-Einstein submanifolds of (finite-dimensional) projective space. The key observation is that, by Calabi rigidity, a local real-holomorphic Killing field is induced by a projective unitary vector field whose tangency propagates along any connected global Kahler immersion, without a simple-connectivity assumption. Applied to Hulin's complete continuation, this produces a global Killing field with a bounded Hamiltonian potential given by the ambient projective moment map. The resulting Laplace equation, the Omori--Yau maximum principle and Yau's Liouville theorem exclude both negative and zero Einstein curvature. We also prove a non-Einstein obstruction under uniformly negative Ricci curvature and obtain compact equivariant continuations.
label: arXiv:2611.27345v1

summary.background:
- Kähler manifold: a complex geometric space with a compatible notion of distance and angle.
- Kähler–Einstein metric: a Kähler metric whose Ricci curvature is a constant multiple of the metric; the sign of that constant (positive, zero, negative) is the key quantity.
- Projective space and submanifold: the complex analogue of the sphere-like space of lines through the origin; a submanifold is a smaller shape embedded inside it.
- Killing field: a smooth vector field whose flow preserves the metric, i.e. a continuous symmetry.
- Real-holomorphic vector field: a flow that respects the complex structure.
- Calabi rigidity: a result saying that local symmetries of such embeddings extend in a controlled way.
- Omori–Yau maximum principle and Yau's Liouville theorem: standard tools for showing that certain bounded functions on non-compact spaces must be constant.
- Hulin's continuation: a known construction extending the embedded metric; the text uses it as an input.
summary.one_liner: The paper shows that a projectively induced Kähler–Einstein metric must have positive Einstein constant whenever it has at least one nonzero local real-holomorphic Killing field, with no completeness or global group-action assumption, and extends this to a non-Einstein obstruction and compact equivariant continuations.
summary.plain: The paper studies curved geometric shapes that sit inside a flat-style projective space and carry a specific kind of balanced, evenly curved structure. The authors show that if such a shape has even a local symmetry (a smooth flow that preserves the geometry in a neighbourhood), then its curvature must be strictly positive, so negative and zero curvature are ruled out. The argument uses a global extension of the local symmetry, which the text describes as coming from a known rigidity result of Calabi.
summary.why: The general question of whether such embedded Kähler–Einstein submanifolds of projective space must have positive curvature is open, and this gives a partial answer under a local symmetry hypothesis. The text does not say how far the method extends beyond this setting, so its wider reach is uncertain.

title: A local symmetry forces positivity for projectively induced Kahler-Einstein metrics

abstract: This survey gives an overview of the Bernoulli or one-phase free boundary problem, with emphasis on recent progress.
label: arXiv:2611.26636v1

summary.background:
- A partial differential equation (PDE) describes how a quantity, such as temperature or pressure, varies across space.
- A free boundary is an edge of a region whose position is unknown and must be solved for along with the function.
- The Bernoulli (one-phase) problem is a classic example in which the function is zero on one side of the boundary and the rate of change across the boundary is tied to the boundary's shape.
- A survey is a review that collects and organizes existing work rather than presenting new results.
summary.one_liner: A survey of the classical Bernoulli (one-phase) free boundary problem in PDE theory, emphasizing recent progress.
summary.plain: This is an overview article about a mathematical problem where a function is defined in a region, but the edge of that region is not known in advance and must be found as part of the solution. The text is a short abstract that says the survey covers the Bernoulli or one-phase version of this problem and highlights recent progress. The abstract does not list specific results, so details of what was found cannot be taken from it.
summary.why: Free boundary problems model settings such as fluid flow, heat spread and phase changes, where the shape of a boundary is part of the answer. The abstract gives no specific results or links to applications, so its wider relevance cannot be judged from the text alone.

title: Overview and recent progress on the classical Bernoulli free boundary problem

abstract: We study the fully nonlinear degenerate parabolic free boundary problem $$|Du|^\kappa F(D^2u)-u_t=u^{\gamma-1} \qquad \textrm{in} \quad \{u>0\},$$ where $\kappa>0$, $0<\gamma<1$, and $F$ is a convex or concave uniformly elliptic operator with $F(0)=0$. We establish the existence of a nonnegative viscosity solution with prescribed continuous nonnegative boundary data and prove its optimal upper growth along the free boundary, together with matching non-degeneracy estimates in parabolic cylinders adapted to the scaling. Our approach combines a weak Bernstein estimate with barrier arguments to obtain local compactness and boundary attainment. To obtain the optimal growth rate, we further use persistence of positivity for limits with vanishing absorption coefficients to identify the homogeneous equation across the zero set, and then combine the optimal spatial regularity estimate of \cite{LLYZ25} with an iteration argument.
label: arXiv:2611.27774v1

summary.background:
- Parabolic equation: an equation describing evolution in time, like heat spreading, with u_t the rate of change in time.
- Free boundary: the edge between the region where the solution is positive and where it is zero; its location is part of the answer.
- Fully nonlinear, degenerate operator: the equation depends non-linearly on the second derivatives (and here on the size of the gradient |Du|), and can lose ellipticity in some directions; convex or concave uniformly elliptic F means F is bounded in a controlled way.
- Viscosity solution: a weak notion of solution that works when classical derivatives may not exist.
- Growth rate and non-degeneracy: how fast the solution rises away from the edge and a lower bound ensuring it does not flatten out.
- Scaling: parabolic cylinders are regions adapted to the equation's time-space scaling, so estimates hold at every size.
- Barrier arguments and compactness: standard tools for building comparison functions and extracting convergent subsequences of solutions.
summary.one_liner: The paper studies a fully nonlinear, degenerate parabolic quenching (free boundary) problem with a gradient-dependent operator, proving existence of nonnegative viscosity solutions with prescribed boundary data, an optimal upper growth rate along the free boundary, and matching non-degeneracy estimates.
summary.plain: The paper looks at a time-dependent equation in which a quantity u must stay nonnegative, and the region where u is positive has a moving edge called the free boundary. The authors show that a suitable solution exists for given nonnegative boundary values, and they pin down how fast u can grow as one approaches that edge. They also prove that u cannot be too flat near the edge, with estimates matched to the natural time-and-space scaling of the problem.
summary.why: Free boundary problems of this type model situations where a process turns off or saturates once a quantity reaches zero, so the sharp growth and non-degeneracy bounds describe how the solution behaves at that switching edge. The text does not describe specific applications, so any wider connection is uncertain; the work is mainly a technical contribution to the theory of fully nonlinear equations.

title: On the fully nonlinear degenerate parabolic quenching problem

abstract: The functional calculus allows for the rigorous analysis of functions of matrices or even operators. The free functional calculus gives the natural class of functions over any category. We initiate the representation theory for taking a generic free functional calculus to the classical nc functional calculus going back to Taylor, Voiculescu and many others, with an eye towards learning of categories. The functional calculus on direct sum closed and locally similarity (i.e. change of coordinates) invariant domains inherits the niceties of complex analysis and large-scale parallel networks, such as automatic analyticity, free universal monodromy, which gives a hypothetical explanation for beneficial overfitting.
label: arXiv:2611.27943v1

summary.background:
- Functional calculus: a way of plugging a matrix or operator into a function (like a polynomial or power series) and getting a matrix or operator back.
- Matrices do not generally commute (AB may differ from BA), so "noncommutative" versions of these ideas are harder than the usual scalar case.
- Similarity (change of coordinates): rewriting a matrix in a different basis; a domain is "similarity invariant" if the property is preserved under such rewriting.
- Direct sum: stacking matrices block-diagonally.
- Category: an abstract framework of objects and maps between them, used here as the setting for the free calculus.
- Analyticity: a function that is locally given by a convergent power series; "monodromy" refers to how analytic continuation around loops can change a function.
- Overfitting: a machine learning model fitting training data very closely, including noise.
summary.one_liner: The paper begins a representation theory that relates a generic free functional calculus (for matrices and operators, over categories) to the classical noncommutative functional calculus of Taylor and Voiculescu, and notes consequences for domains that are closed under direct sums and similarity changes of coordinates.
summary.plain: The paper is about a way of applying functions to grids of numbers (matrices) and to more abstract operators, where the inputs can be non-commuting. It starts a general framework that links a newer "free" version of this calculus to the older classical version. The abstract only states that this framework is initiated and gives some properties of the resulting function classes; it does not give the detailed results.
summary.why: The abstract connects the framework to complex analysis and to large parallel networks, and it suggests a possible but explicitly "hypothetical" explanation for why overfitting can sometimes be harmless in such networks. That link is speculative as stated, and the text alone does not show how far it goes.

title: Freedom is all you need

abstract: We give an affirmative solution to the Ritt problem.
label: arXiv:2611.27008v1

summary.background:
- Polynomials: sums of powers of a variable, such as x^2 + 3x.
- Functional decomposition: writing a function as a composition of simpler functions, e.g. f(g(x)).
- Ritt's theory: classical results by Joseph Ritt (1920s–1930s) on when and how such decompositions can be rearranged.
- Decidability: whether a yes/no question can be answered by a fixed, always-terminating algorithm.
- Harmonic analysis is the listed field, but the abstract itself concerns algebraic decomposition problems; the link is not explained in the text.
summary.one_liner: The paper claims a positive answer to the Ritt problem, which asks whether a certain algorithmic decision question about functional decompositions of polynomials and related functions is solvable.
summary.plain: This paper settles a long-standing question about how complicated formulas can be broken into simpler pieces. The Ritt problem asks whether there is a reliable procedure that can decide if two such breakdowns of a formula are equivalent. The text says the authors give a positive answer, meaning such a procedure exists, but the short summary does not spell out the method.
summary.why: The text is only a one-sentence abstract, so its importance cannot be judged from it alone. Results of this kind matter to researchers in algebra, dynamics and computer algebra, since they settle whether a class of questions can be answered by computation at all.

title: The Ritt problem is decidable

abstract: We construct a smooth complex affine surface $Y$ such that $\pi_1(Y)$ is virtually $3$-step nilpotent, but not virtually $2$-step nilpotent. This gives a negative answer to the quasi-projective version of Campana's nilpotency problem.
label: arXiv:2611.27475v1

summary.background:
- Complex affine surface: a smooth solution set of polynomial equations in two complex variables, with the points at infinity removed.
- Fundamental group: a group recording which loops on a space can be continuously deformed into one another.
- Nilpotent group: a group that becomes trivial after repeatedly taking commutators; "k-step nilpotent" measures how many such levels are needed.
- Virtually nilpotent: the group has a finite-index subgroup that is nilpotent.
- Campana's nilpotency problem: a conjectural link between the loop structure of a space and its nilpotency, asked in the projective and quasi-projective settings.
- Quasi-projective: a space that is an open subset of a projective (compact-type) algebraic variety.
summary.one_liner: The paper constructs a smooth complex affine surface whose fundamental group is virtually 3-step nilpotent but not virtually 2-step nilpotent, giving a negative answer to the quasi-projective version of Campana's nilpotency problem.
summary.plain: The paper is about the shapes that complex algebraic surfaces can have, as seen through their "loops" (the fundamental group, a way of recording which closed paths can be deformed into one another). The author builds a specific smooth surface of this kind whose loop structure is nested three levels deep but not two, which settles a question in the negative.
summary.why: The result answers a specific open question (a version of Campana's nilpotency problem) by showing the answer is no in the quasi-projective setting. Beyond that, the text does not say more about wider implications, so its significance beyond this question is unclear from the summary alone.

title: An affine surface with 3-step nilpotent fundamental group

abstract: We study the Newton maps of $\sin z$, $\cos z$, $\sinh z$, and $\cosh z$, each of which is transcendental meromorphic and has infinitely many unbounded immediate attracting basins. We first verify directly that, for the cosine Newton map $N_{\cos}(z) = z + \cot z$, the half-planes $\{\pm \operatorname{Im} z > M\}$ are repelling petals at infinity for every $M \ge 2$. These explicit petals allow us to apply the tame-basin criterion of Bara\'nski, Fagella, Jarque, and Karpi\'nska and obtain local connectivity of the spherical boundary of each immediate basin of $N_{\cos}$. We also show that the Newton map of $Ae^{\lambda z} + Be^{-\lambda z}$, where $AB\lambda \neq 0$, is affinely conjugate to the sine Newton map $N_{\sin}(z) = z - \tan z$. The published local-connectivity theorem for $J(N_{\sin})$ therefore applies to this entire family, including the cosine and the two hyperbolic Newton maps. We describe the invariant lines and basin geometry of the four maps and illustrate the corresponding dynamical planes numerically.
label: arXiv:2611.26654v1

summary.background:
- Newton's method: an iterative rule for approximating roots of an equation; each starting point is mapped step by step.
- Julia set: the boundary between starting points whose iterates behave tamely and those that behave chaotically.
- Basin of attraction: the set of starting points that converge to a given attracting point; "immediate" means the component touching that point directly.
- Transcendental meromorphic function: a complex function that is not a polynomial or rational function, with poles allowed, such as sin or cos.
- Local connectivity: a topological property saying the boundary is not pinched in a way that makes it hard to approach locally; here it is stated for the boundary of each basin.
- Repelling petal: a region near infinity where iteration pushes points away, used as a technical tool.
- Affine conjugacy: two maps are the same up to a linear change of coordinates.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves local connectivity of Julia sets (the boundaries between stable and chaotic behaviour) for Newton maps of sin, cos, sinh and cosh, by verifying repelling petals at infinity for the cosine map and showing the hyperbolic family is affinely conjugate to the sine case.
summary.plain: The paper studies a method for finding roots of equations, called Newton's method, applied to four standard trigonometric and hyperbolic functions, and asks how the boundary between starting points that converge and those that do not is shaped. The authors show that for the cosine version, certain half-plane regions far from the origin behave in a way that lets an existing mathematical criterion apply, giving a clean boundary shape. They also show that a whole family of hyperbolic functions is, after a change of coordinates, the same as the sine version, so a previously published result covers them too.
summary.why: It settles a structural question about the boundaries of these dynamical systems for a whole family of maps by reducing them to one known case. Its wider relevance is mainly to specialists in complex dynamics; the text does not claim applications beyond that field.

title: Local connectivity of Julia sets of Newton maps of trigonometric and hyperbolic functions

abstract: This article gives a survey of the AF-embedding problem for $C^*$-algebras. The problem asks when a given $C^*$-algebra $A$ embeds into an \emph{approximately finite dimensional} (AF) $C^*$-algebra (a direct limit of finite dimensional $C^*$-algebras). This is largely based on my paper ``Subalgebras of simple AF algebras,'' which shows that separable, exact $C^*$-algebras satisfying the UCT and admitting a faithful, quasidiagonal trace embed into a unital, simple AF algebra. Some other results are also discussed.
label: arXiv:2611.27471v1

summary.background:
- A C*-algebra is a collection of bounded linear operators on a Hilbert space (a space of possible states or waves), closed under addition, multiplication, and taking adjoints.
- An AF (approximately finite dimensional) algebra is a limit of a growing chain of finite-dimensional matrix-type algebras.
- "Embedding" means placing one algebra inside another as a copy of a subalgebra.
- Terms like exact, UCT, quasidiagonal, faithful trace, and simple are technical properties of these algebras; each is a condition restricting which algebras qualify.
- Familiarity with linear algebra and basic functional analysis is needed.
summary.one_liner: A survey of the AF-embedding problem for C*-algebras, centred on the author's result that separable, exact, UCT C*-algebras with a faithful quasidiagonal trace embed into a unital simple AF algebra.
summary.plain: This paper is a survey about when a mathematical object called a C*-algebra can be placed inside a simpler kind of algebra, one built up step by step from finite-dimensional pieces. The main content, based on the author's earlier paper, is a sufficient condition for this kind of embedding to exist. The text also mentions some other results but gives only a brief outline of them.
summary.why: Embedding a complicated algebra into a simpler, well-understood one is a standard way to learn about the original, so results of this type help organise the field. The text does not say how far these results reach beyond operator algebras, so any wider connection is uncertain.

title: On the AF embedding problem

abstract: We give an operator-algebraic characterization of Cayley graphs that are partial cubes, that is, embed isometrically into a hypercube. More precisely, noncommutative versions of the Lichnerowicz inequality control the spectral gap of the generator of a quantum Markov semigroup by the constant in the complete $\Gamma_2$-criterion of Junge and Zeng or the constant in the geometric Ricci criterion of Junge, LaRacuente and Li. We show that for word-length semigroups on group von Neumann algebras, equality in either of these inequalities occurs exactly when the Cayley graph is a partial cube.
label: arXiv:2611.27204v1

summary.background:
- Group von Neumann algebra: an operator-algebra version of a discrete group, used to model quantum systems built from a group.
- Quantum Markov semigroup: a family of maps describing how a quantum system evolves randomly over time, analogous to a random walk.
- Spectral gap: the smallest nonzero eigenvalue of a generator; it controls how fast the process mixes toward equilibrium.
- Lichnerowicz inequality: a classical bound relating spectral gap to curvature-like geometric quantities; here its noncommutative versions are studied.
- Cayley graph: a graph whose vertices are group elements, with edges given by multiplying by generators.
- Partial cube: a graph that embeds isometrically (distances preserved) into a hypercube.
- Word-length semigroup: a semigroup of operators generated by the length of group elements measured in generators.
summary.one_liner: The paper shows that, for word-length semigroups on group von Neumann algebras, equality in two noncommutative Lichnerowicz-type spectral gap inequalities (the complete Γ2 constant of Junge–Zeng and the geometric Ricci constant of Junge–LaRacuente–Li) holds exactly when the group's Cayley graph is a partial cube.
summary.plain: The paper studies a rate at which a random-walk-like process on a group settles down to equilibrium, and how that rate compares with a geometric bound. The authors ask when the bound is exactly tight, and they find that tightness happens precisely when the group's Cayley graph (the picture of the group's elements linked by generator steps) can be drawn isometrically inside a hypercube, a class called partial cubes. The text given is only the abstract, so the details of the proofs are not visible here.
summary.why: It gives a precise graph-theoretic characterization of when a noncommutative geometric inequality is sharp, linking operator algebras to discrete geometry. The abstract alone does not show how broadly the result extends beyond word-length semigroups.

title: Rigidity in the Lichnerowicz inequality for word-length semigroups

abstract: We investigate when the universal enveloping algebra $U(\mathfrak{g})$ of an infinite-dimensional Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ is coherent. We show that if $\mathfrak{g}$ is the loop algebra of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra $\mathfrak{h}$ then $U(\mathfrak{g})$ is coherent exactly when $\mathfrak{h}$ is nilpotent. As a consequence, we show that $U(\mathfrak{g})$ is not coherent if $\mathfrak{g}$ is complex, simple, $\mathbb{Z}$-graded, of polynomially bounded growth, and not isomorphic to the Witt algebra $W = \mathrm{Der} \mathbb{C}[t,t^{-1}]$ or its one-sided version. We also demonstrate that the homomorphic image of $U(W)$ used to prove non-Noetherianity of $U(W)$ in previous work of the first author and Walton is not coherent. On the other hand, we establish that two closely related connected graded rings are graded coherent. Finally, we prove that any exhaustively filtered ring is coherent if its Rees ring is graded coherent.
label: arXiv:2611.27824v1

summary.background:
- Lie algebra: a vector space with a bracket operation, used to describe continuous symmetries.
- Universal enveloping algebra U(g): a ring built from a Lie algebra g that encodes its representations.
- Loop algebra: functions from a circle (or Laurent polynomials) with values in a finite-dimensional Lie algebra.
- Witt algebra: the derivations of Laurent polynomials, an infinite-dimensional example.
- Coherent ring: a ring where finitely generated one-sided ideals are finitely presented; a finiteness property.
- Noetherian ring: every ideal is finitely generated; coherence is a weaker related condition.
- Nilpotent: a Lie algebra whose repeated brackets eventually vanish.
- Graded and filtered rings: rings split into pieces indexed by integers or ordered by a size-like filtration; the Rees ring links the two.
summary.one_liner: The paper determines when universal enveloping algebras of infinite-dimensional Lie algebras (notably loop algebras and the Witt algebra) are coherent, and studies coherence of related graded and filtered rings.
summary.plain: The paper studies a property called "coherence" for a family of algebraic structures built from infinite-dimensional symmetry-like objects (Lie algebras). Coherence is a tidy-behaviour condition: roughly, certain systems of equations have solutions that are finitely described. The authors show that for loop algebras the property holds exactly when the underlying finite-dimensional algebra is nilpotent, and they find that several specific examples fail it.
summary.why: It sharpens what is known about which infinite-dimensional algebras behave well under standard finiteness conditions, and it extends earlier work on non-Noetherianity of the Witt-algebra enveloping algebra. The text does not indicate further applications beyond this algebraic classification.

title: On coherence of enveloping algebras of infinite-dimensional Lie algebras

abstract: Let $P$ be a $p$-group that acts faithfully and coprimely on a finite group $H$. In a previous paper it was shown that if $H$ is solvable, then there exists a conjugacy class $c$ of $H$ whose stabilizer in $P$ has order at most $|P|^{1/2}$, and that this bound is best possible. In this paper we remove the hypothesis that $H$ is solvable. As a consequence, there always exists an irreducible character of $H$ whose inertia group in $P$ has order at most $|P|^{1/2}$. The proof depends on the classification of finite simple groups. Its main new ingredient is a result on quasiprimitive linear actions of $p$-nilpotent groups which shows that the elements acting as field automorphisms can be ignored when one looks for vectors with small stabilizers. We also present a new family of examples, with nonsolvable $H$, in which the bound is attained.
label: arXiv:2611.27916v1

summary.background:
- Finite group: a group with finitely many elements, such as the symmetries of a finite object.
- p-group: a group whose size is a power of a prime p.
- Acting coprimely and faithfully: P applies symmetries to H in a way that is nontrivial and does not share prime factors with H's order in a problematic way.
- Conjugacy class: a set of elements of H that are equivalent under relabeling by H itself.
- Stabilizer / orbit: the stabilizer is the set of symmetries in P fixing a given class; the orbit is the set of classes it moves it to. Large orbit means small stabilizer.
- Solvable group: a group built up by stacking simple pieces that are abelian; nonsolvable groups contain more complex simple pieces.
- Classification of finite simple groups: a large completed classification of the basic building blocks of finite groups, used as a tool here.
- Irreducible character and inertia group: basic objects of representation theory; the inertia group is the set of symmetries that preserve a given character.
summary.one_liner: The paper extends a known result on large orbits of coprime p-group actions from solvable to arbitrary finite groups, showing via the classification of finite simple groups that some conjugacy class (or irreducible character) has stabilizer of order at most |P|^{1/2}, with a new nonsolvable family attaining the bound.
summary.plain: This paper is about symmetries of finite groups: a small group P of symmetries (of prime-power size) acts on a finite group H, and the question is how many elements of H P can leave mostly in place. The author-level result is that, for every such action, some conjugacy class of H has a stabilizer in P of size at most the square root of |P|. A previous paper had proved this only when H is solvable, and this paper removes that restriction, using the classification of finite simple groups.
summary.why: The bound is sharp: the text says it is attained, and the paper gives a new family of nonsolvable examples where it is reached. The result also gives, as a consequence, an irreducible character of H whose inertia group in P is small, which links the question to representation theory; the text does not say more about wider applications.

title: Large orbits of $p$-groups on conjugacy classes of arbitrary finite groups

abstract: We give a proof of the $n!$ theorem based on the representation theory of Cherednik algebras and an analog of the rotation of complex structures arising from an action of the quaternions.
label: arXiv:2611.27113v1

summary.background:
- Representation theory: studying abstract groups or algebras by how they act on vector spaces.
- Symmetric group: the group of all rearrangements of n objects; it has n! elements.
- Cherednik algebras: a family of algebras depending on parameters, built from reflection groups, used to study such representations.
- The n! theorem: a known result in this area, which the paper re-proves; the text does not state its exact form.
- Quaternions: an extension of the complex numbers with three imaginary units; "rotating complex structures" means changing which linear map plays the role of multiplication by i.
- Background in abstract algebra at the graduate level is assumed.
summary.one_liner: The paper gives a new proof of the n! theorem (a result about the dimension of certain representations of Cherednik algebras, which are algebras attached to symmetric groups and related reflection groups), using an analogue of rotating complex structures coming from a quaternion action.
summary.plain: This is a mathematics paper about a known result called the "n! theorem," which concerns a family of algebraic objects built from symmetric groups (the groups of ways to rearrange n items). The authors give a new proof of it. Their method uses a trick borrowed from geometry: rotating the structure that makes a space "complex," using an action of the quaternions, a number system extending the complex numbers.
summary.why: The text is short, so it does not say what new consequences the new proof gives or how it compares to earlier proofs. Its value is mainly as an alternative route to a known theorem, which may connect representation theory with geometry, though the text does not spell out these links.

title: The $n!$ theorem via quaternionic rotation of Cherednik algebras

abstract: In this work, we prove the Weighted Fundamental Lemma for Lie algebras for general (quasi-split) unramified $G$. The strategy is to adapt the proof of Chaudouard--Laumon from the split case. In particular, we define the notion of a $\xi$-stable Higgs bundle for a quasi-split reductive group scheme $G$ on a curve, and prove that the stack of such form a proper, finite-type Deligne--Mumford stack over the Hitchin base when $G$ has anisotropic center. We then adapt the global cohomological theorem of Chaudouard--Laumon to the quasi-split setting, and perform the required Frobenius-point count to obtain an identity of adelic orbital integrals. A local-to-global argument deduces the WFL for Lie algebras. In the last chapter, we perform a parallel reduction to deduce Waldspurger's nonstandard WFL from a global version which follows from the same geometric theory. Our work implies the Twisted Weighted Fundamental Lemma in good characteristic, which completes Moeglin--Waldspurger's stabilization of the twisted Arthur--Selberg trace formula. We therefore render unconditional the endoscopic classification for classical groups and an array of downstream consequences in automorphic theory.
label: arXiv:2611.26750v1

summary.background:
- Reductive group: a continuous symmetry group of algebraic type, such as matrix groups.
- Quasi-split and unramified: a special, relatively tame class of such groups over local number fields.
- Orbital integral: an averaged quantity over conjugacy classes, used to compare different trace formulas.
- Fundamental lemma: a identity comparing orbital integrals on a group and on an associated endoscopic group; the "weighted" and "Lie algebra" versions are refinements.
- Higgs bundle and Hitchin base: geometric objects on a curve and their parameter space, used as a tool for counting.
- Trace formula and endoscopy: frameworks in automorphic representation theory for classifying automorphic forms by comparing groups.
- Frobenius point count: counting solutions over finite fields as a route to an identity.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves the Weighted Fundamental Lemma for Lie algebras over unramified quasi-split groups by adapting the Chaudouard–Laumon geometric method (via ξ-stable Higgs bundles and a Frobenius point count), and derives Waldspurger's nonstandard version and a twisted version in good characteristic.
summary.plain: This is a paper in pure mathematics about symmetry groups and the counting identities that link them, which underpin the study of automorphic forms (highly symmetric functions on number-theoretic spaces). The authors extend a known result, the Weighted Fundamental Lemma, from split groups to a wider class called quasi-split groups. They do this by adapting an existing geometric proof, building a suitable family of algebraic objects over a curve and counting points on them.
summary.why: The text says the result is a step needed to complete Moeglin–Waldspurger's stabilization of the twisted trace formula, and that it makes the endoscopic classification for classical groups unconditional. Its wider significance rests on those downstream consequences, which I have not checked and which the text only asserts.

title: The weighted fundamental lemma for non-split groups

abstract: A factorization $f=uvw$ of a square-free sextic over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ of odd characteristic into three monic quadratics defines a genus-2 curve with a rational $(2,2)$-isogeny kernel, and the Richelot construction attaches to it three dual quadratics $U,V,W$. We determine, for every odd prime power $q$, the number of such factorizations with prescribed splitting behaviour over $\mathbb{F}_q$ of all six quadratics. Each of the $64$ counts is $q(q-1)(q+1-n_f)/64$ times $C(q)\pm t_q$, where $n_f$ is the number of roots of $f$ in $\mathbb{F}_q$, $C$ is an explicit monic cubic, and $t_q$ is the trace of Frobenius attached to the newform $\eta(2z)^{4}\eta(4z)^{4}$ of weight $4$ and level $8$. The proof reduces the counts by elementary means to a twisted second moment of the Legendre family of elliptic curves, which is a value of a hypergeometric function over $\mathbb{F}_q$ evaluated by Ahlgren and Ono for primes. As consequences, the number of factorizations whose three pairwise resultants lie in one square class is a polynomial in $q$, with proportion $1/4+3/(4q^{2})+O(q^{-4})$. When the quotient is a product of two elliptic curves conjugate over $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$, we prove that the splitting of the factors $u,v,w$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ decides which points of order two of the elliptic factor are divisible by two.
label: arXiv:2611.27775v1

summary.background:
- A finite field F_q is a set with q elements, where q is a prime power; arithmetic is done modulo the field's structure.
- A square-free sextic is a degree-six polynomial with no repeated roots; splitting it into three monic quadratics is a factorization.
- A genus-2 curve is a curve of "genus" (number of holes) two; its Jacobian splits or relates to elliptic curves.
- A (2,2)-isogeny is a structure-preserving map between abelian varieties with a kernel of order four; the Richelot construction produces the dual quadratics.
- Splitting behaviour refers to whether a quadratic has roots in F_q or not.
- A newform is a special modular form; its trace of Frobenius is an integer tied to counting points mod p.
- The Legendre family is a standard family of elliptic curves; a twisted second moment is an averaged sum over that family.
- The paper says the value was evaluated for primes by Ahlgren and Ono.
summary.one_liner: Counts factorizations of square-free sextics over finite fields into three quadratics, with splitting conditions, via Richelot isogenies of genus-2 curves, with the answer expressed through the trace of a weight-4 newform of level 8 and a twisted second moment of the Legendre family.
summary.plain: This paper studies a counting problem: how many ways a polynomial of degree six, over a finite field with q elements, can be split into three quadratic pieces, when we also track which of those pieces factor further over the field. The authors give an exact formula for each of the 64 possible splitting patterns. The formulas involve a known number-theoretic quantity tied to a specific modular form, and the proof reduces the counting, by elementary means, to a known hypergeometric value.
summary.why: The result links a concrete counting question about polynomials and genus-2 curves to a specific modular form, which is a meaningful connection between two areas of number theory. The text does not say much about wider applications, so its broader significance is best judged by specialists.

title: Splitting types of Richelot isogenies over finite fields and a newform of weight four

abstract: Let $K$ be a global field of characteristic $2$ and $\varphi\colon E\to E'$ the Verschiebung of an ordinary elliptic curve $E/K$ with a rational point of order $2$. We prove an explicit formula for the homogeneous-space Cassels--Tate pairing on $\Sha(E/K)[\varphi]$ as a sum of local Artin--Schreier symbols, show that it coincides with Kramer's descent pairing and, on $\Sha(E/K)[\varphi]$, with the pairing induced by Milne's flat duality, and deduce that it is non-degenerate on $\Sha(E/K)[\varphi]/\hat\varphi(\Sha(E'/K)[2])$. For every ordinary elliptic curve $A/K$ we express the parity of $\mathrm{rk}\,A(K)+\dim\Sha(A/K)[2]$ by local terms (after Kramer), and identify these with local root numbers at places of semistable or potentially multiplicative reduction, and in further cases using curves with finite $\Sha$. We determine $\Sha$ in examples, and extend the formula to rational points of any prime order $\ell$, the new case being $\ell=\operatorname{char}K$.
label: arXiv:2611.27040v1

summary.background:
- Elliptic curve: a cubic curve with a group law on its rational points.
- Global field of characteristic 2: a function field or number field-like object where arithmetic is done modulo 2.
- Rank of A(K): the number of independent rational points of infinite order.
- Sha (Tate–Shafarevich group): obstructions to local solutions being global; its size is largely conjectural.
- 2-Selmer group and Cassels–Tate pairing: tools that detect elements of Sha and whose structure constrains ranks.
- Isogeny (Verschiebung) and 2-torsion: maps between curves and points of order 2.
- Artin–Schreier symbols: local pairing values used in characteristic 2.
- Local root numbers: local signs from the functional equation of L-functions, linked to parity of rank.
summary.one_liner: For ordinary elliptic curves over global fields of characteristic 2 with a rational 2-torsion point, the paper gives an explicit local-symbol formula for the Cassels–Tate pairing on the 2-torsion of Sha, relates it to Kramer's descent pairing and Milne's flat duality, and uses it to express the parity of rk A(K) + dim Sha(A/K)[2] via local terms and root numbers.
summary.plain: This paper studies elliptic curves, smooth curves defined by cubic equations, over number-like fields where arithmetic works in characteristic 2 (a setting where numbers behave like binary digits). It concerns a hidden group called Sha that measures how far certain rational solutions fail to exist globally despite existing locally. The authors give an explicit formula for a pairing that organises this hidden group and show it matches other known descriptions, which lets them determine the parity (even or odd) of a key count in terms of local data.
summary.why: Parity questions about ranks of rational points are central to arithmetic geometry, and the paper ties an algebraic pairing to local root numbers, a link that is of interest to specialists. The text does not indicate wider consequences beyond this setting, and the extension to prime order rational points, including the new case where the prime equals the characteristic, is presented as a technical advance.

title: An explicit Cassels--Tate pairing in characteristic $2$ and the parity of $2$-Selmer ranks

abstract: Many problems in enumerative geometry are solved by computing the degree of the top Chern class of a suitable vector bundle. Results from $\mathbb{A}^1$-homotopy theory allow to answer enumerative questions over arbitrary fields, replacing the top Chern class by the Euler class in Chow-Witt groups. For its degree to be well-defined, one needs the vector bundle to be relatively oriented. Another way to solve enumerative problems is to translate them to tropical geometry, where they become combinatorial problems. In this paper, we give a combinatorial description of relative orientability for vector bundles over smooth proper toric varieties. We show that it behaves well under tropicalization, establishing a tropical version of relative orientability, which will allow to the use of tropical geometry to answer enumerative questions over arbitrary fields. As a demonstration, we prove a quadratically enriched version of the Bernstein-Khovanskii-Kushnirenko theorem via tropical geometry. Lastly, we define the notion of $k$-phase structures on tropical hypersurfaces, generalizing the real case.
label: arXiv:2611.27238v1

summary.background:
- Enumerative geometry: counting solutions to geometric problems, such as how many curves satisfy given conditions.
- Vector bundle: a family of vector spaces attached smoothly to each point of a space; "relatively oriented" means a consistent choice of orientation is possible, which is needed for the count to be well-defined.
- Chern class and Euler class: invariants of vector bundles whose degree gives a count of solutions; the Euler class lives in Chow-Witt groups, a refined version that works over any field.
- A^1-homotopy theory: a framework from modern algebraic topology that lets topological tools be applied to algebraic varieties over arbitrary fields.
- Toric variety: an algebraic variety built from combinatorial data (a fan of cones), so its geometry can be read off from polytopes and lattices.
- Tropical geometry: a piecewise-linear shadow of algebraic geometry, where polynomial problems become problems about polyhedral complexes.
- Bernstein-Khovanskii-Kushnirenko theorem: a classical result counting solutions of polynomial systems via the volumes of their Newton polytopes.
- Quadratic enrichment: refining an integer count into a count valued in quadratic forms, which keeps track of extra arithmetic information.
- Phase structure: extra data on a tropical hypersurface that records signs; the real case is the classical version that the paper generalizes to k phases.
summary.one_liner: The paper gives a combinatorial criterion for relative orientability of vector bundles on smooth proper toric varieties, shows it is preserved under tropicalization, and applies this to a quadratically enriched Bernstein-Khovanskii-Kushnirenko theorem and to k-phase structures on tropical hypersurfaces.
summary.plain: Many counting problems in geometry ask how many solutions a system of equations has, and modern methods answer these by computing a single numerical invariant. This paper works on making that invariant well-defined over any field, and it translates the question into a simpler combinatorial setting called tropical geometry, where the problem reduces to counting on piecewise-linear shapes. The authors give a checkable combinatorial test for when the needed geometric data is consistent, and they show that the test carries over to the tropical setting.
summary.why: It offers a route for using tropical geometry, which turns hard algebra into combinatorics, to answer enumerative questions over arbitrary fields, not only over the complex numbers. The text itself only indicates this as a goal and a demonstration, so the broader impact is something to judge from the full paper.

title: Combinatorial relative orientability for toric and tropical geometry

abstract: We study strongly $F$-regular and $F$-pure normal surface singularities whose residue fields are not necessarily perfect. We characterize strong $F$-regularity in terms of the weighted dual graph and geometric reducedness of the exceptional components of the minimal resolution, extending Hara's classification over algebraically closed residue fields. We also determine the possible dual graphs of $F$-pure surface singularities and give converse criteria. Notably, the exceptional components of an $F$-pure surface singularity are geometrically reduced unless the singularity is a rational double point.
label: arXiv:2611.27597v1

summary.background:
- Singularity: a point where a surface fails to be smooth, e.g. a cone tip.
- Minimal resolution: a way of replacing the singular point by a smooth surface with a chain or tree of curves, the exceptional components.
- Dual graph: a diagram with one node per exceptional curve and edges for intersections, weighted by numerical data.
- Characteristic p and Frobenius: working with arithmetic where adding p copies of 1 gives 0; Frobenius raises functions to the p-th power.
- F-regular / F-pure: technical "good behaviour under Frobenius" conditions indicating mild singularities.
- Residue field: the field of values at the singular point; "imperfect" means Frobenius is not surjective on it.
- Geometric reducedness: a curve stays reduced (no repeated components) after passing to an algebraic closure.
- Rational double point: a simple, well-classified type of surface singularity.
summary.one_liner: The paper classifies strongly F-regular and F-pure normal surface singularities over possibly imperfect residue fields, via weighted dual graphs and geometric reducedness of exceptional components of the minimal resolution, extending Hara's algebraically closed case.
summary.plain: The paper studies a family of "mild" singular points on surfaces, the kind of points where a shape folds in on itself, and asks when these points behave well under a specific arithmetic operation (the Frobenius map, which raises coefficients to a power p) in characteristic p. It works in a more general setting where the underlying number field need not be perfect, which the earlier classical results did not cover. The authors give a description of these singularities using the pattern of a graph built from the resolved surface, and they also list which graphs can occur for the weaker F-pure version.
summary.why: The work extends a known classification by Hara from algebraically closed fields to imperfect residue fields, so it covers a broader class of cases. The text also states a specific consequence: for F-pure surface singularities, the exceptional components are geometrically reduced unless the singularity is a rational double point. How far this reaches beyond surfaces is not stated in the text.

title: Classification of strongly $F$-regular and $F$-pure surface singularities with imperfect residue fields

abstract: In topological data analysis, path homology accounts for directed graph while combinatorial Laplacian extends homology groups to spectral theory. However, these approaches are built on a boundary operator with condition $\partial^2=0$. Mayer homology replaces this condition with $N$-nilpotent boundary map $\partial^N=0$. By using the primitive $N$-th root of unity in the boundary operator, it relates each degree $n$ to the degrees $n-q$ and $n+N-q$. This work introduces persistent Mayer path homology. We show that Mayer path homology is functorial for strict digraph maps, which gives persistent Mayer path homology for filtered digraphs, and prove that its barcodes are stable under perturbations. For $N=3$ we derive formulas that reduce $\beta_0^{3,1}$ and $\beta_2^{3,2}$ to the classes of vertices identified by squares and the rank of a small matrix indexed by triangles. We also introduce the Mayer path Laplacian and its persistence theory, prove that their kernels recover (persistent) Mayer path homology, show that they distinguish digraphs with the same Mayer path Betti numbers, and prove a stability bound for the eigenvalues of the persistent up-Laplacian. We demonstrate that persistent Mayer path homology detects the formation of feed-forward loops, whose formation is not detected by ordinary path homology. In an application to cucurbit[7]uril, filtered by an interatomic distance normalized by van der Waals radii, Mayer path homology separates contacts that only close cycles from contacts that close feed-forward triangles, and changes at almost four times as many filtration values as path homology after the bonded framework is formed.
label: arXiv:2611.26982v1

summary.background:
- Directed graph: a network whose edges have a one-way direction.
- Homology: a counting method from topology that records loops and holes in a space; Betti numbers are the counts.
- Boundary operator: a rule that maps a structure to its outline; in ordinary homology applying it twice gives zero, and Mayer homology relaxes this to applying it N times gives zero.
- Persistent homology: tracking these counts as a distance threshold (filtration) grows, producing barcodes that show when features are born and die.
- Laplacian (combinatorial): a matrix whose kernel and eigenvalues encode the same homology information in spectral form.
- Feed-forward loop: a three-node directed motif where one node points to a second, which points to a third, and the first also points to the third.
- Filtration by van der Waals radii: distances between atoms scaled by their typical contact size, used to decide when atoms count as connected.
summary.one_liner: The paper introduces persistent Mayer path homology and Mayer path Laplacians for filtered directed graphs, extending path homology built on a nilpotent boundary map with N-th roots of unity, with stability results and an application to cucurbit[7]uril molecular contacts.
summary.plain: The paper studies shape-like invariants of networks where connections have a direction, such as one-way links between points. It builds a new version of these invariants, called Mayer path homology, that tracks how structures appear and disappear as a distance threshold grows. The authors report that it can detect feed-forward loops, which the older standard method misses, and in a molecule example it changes at more filtration values than the older method.
summary.why: Tracking directed structures across scales could help analyze networks where direction matters, such as chemical contact graphs or signalling networks. The text shows the method is applied to one molecule, so its wider usefulness is not established here.

title: Persistent Mayer Path Homology and Mayer Path Laplacian

abstract: In this note we give an alternative definition of the Freudenthal end-compactification of a non-compact manifold by defining ends to be the filters of open subsets with compact boundaries that have a base of connected subsets. We start by defining these notions and proving that the resulting compactification is equivalent to the Freudenthal compactification. In particular, we explicitly discuss the equivalence between our definitions and those from two different approaches: maximal binding families and inverse limits. After that, we give an example of a non-metrizable manifold, showing how these new definitions make it easier to identify ends and understand the topology of the end-compactification. We also prove a well-known metrization theorem, showing an application of our definition. Finally, we also give an alternative proof of the topological characterization of the Freudenthal compactification.
label: arXiv:2611.26989v1

summary.background:
- Manifold: a space that locally looks like ordinary Euclidean space, such as a surface.
- Compact set: a set that is closed and bounded in a strong sense; in everyday terms, it does not leak off to infinity.
- Compactification: adding points to a space so that it becomes compact, in a controlled way.
- Ends of a space: the different ways of escaping to infinity; the Freudenthal compactification adds one point per end.
