- Filter: a family of sets that is closed under taking supersets and finite intersections, used here to pick out "directions toward infinity."
- Metrizable: a space whose topology can be described by a distance function.
summary.one_liner: The paper gives a new, more streamlined definition of the Freudenthal end-compactification of non-compact manifolds, via filters of open sets with compact boundary that have a base of connected subsets, and shows it agrees with the older constructions.
summary.plain: The paper is about how a non-compact shape (a manifold, such as an infinitely long surface) can be closed up by adding points that describe the different ways it "goes off to infinity." The author proposes a simpler way to define these added points, using collections of open regions with compact boundaries, and checks that this gives the same result as the standard construction. The text also gives an example of a non-metrizable manifold, and uses the new definitions to prove a known metrization theorem and to give an alternative proof of a known characterization.
summary.why: The Freudenthal compactification is a standard tool in topology, so a cleaner definition that is proven equivalent to the usual ones can make it easier to teach and apply. The text does not indicate further connections beyond the metrization and characterization results it mentions.

title: A simple approach to ends of manifolds and the Freudenthal compactification

abstract: The aim of this survey is to clarify the intimate relations between Lyapunov functions and chain recurrent sets. The study of this subject comes from a seminal paper by Conley and has had recent advances by the so-called Weak KAM Theory for homeomorphisms. We provide a survey of the state of the art, presenting recent improvements and connections with the stationary Hamilton-Jacobi equation. Finally, in order to illustrate the distinctions between recurrent sets in a non-trivial case as well as their dependence on a parameter, we discuss a compartmental model from mathematical epidemiology and a fast-slow version of a prey-predator model with Allee effect.
label: arXiv:2611.27887v1

summary.background:
- Dynamical system: a rule that describes how a state evolves over time.
- Recurrent set: a region a system keeps coming back to, at least approximately, after leaving it.
- Chain recurrence (Conley): a way to track returns using short jumps that allow small errors.
- Lyapunov function: a measuring function that decreases along trajectories, like an energy that settles, used to prove stability.
- Homeomorphism: a continuous, reversible change of a space, used as the discrete-time analogue of a flow.
- Hamilton-Jacobi equation: a partial differential equation from mechanics and optimal control; its stationary form is time-independent.
- Weak KAM theory: a generalized framework from Hamiltonian mechanics relating dynamics to solutions of this equation.
- Compartmental model: an epidemiology model that splits a population into groups such as susceptible and infected.
- Allee effect: a condition where populations grow poorly when they are very small.
summary.one_liner: A survey linking Lyapunov functions and Conley's chain recurrent sets in topological dynamics, including recent weak KAM results for homeomorphisms, connections to the stationary Hamilton-Jacobi equation, and examples from epidemiology and predator-prey dynamics.
summary.plain: This survey looks at how to describe where a system that changes over time can keep returning near its starting points, and how "energy-like" measuring functions (Lyapunov functions) can reveal that structure. It reviews existing results, including newer ones from a field called weak KAM theory, and links them to a classical equation from physics and mathematics. To show how these sets change with a parameter, it works through a disease compartment model and a predator-prey model with an Allee effect (where small populations struggle to grow).
summary.why: The text presents this as a review of the current state of the field rather than a single new finding, so its value lies mainly in organizing known results. It may matter to researchers connecting stability analysis of dynamical systems with Hamilton-Jacobi equations, though the text does not spell out specific applications beyond the two examples.

title: Recurrent sets and Lyapunov functions: from topological dynamics to weak KAM theory

abstract: We consider the direct product of two symplectomorphisms, one of which exhibits a basic set and the other one acts on a compact surface and has a non-degenerate elliptic equilibrium. Under a local domination condition we show that a typical real-analytic perturbation of this system displays a large normally hyperbolic lamination on which the natural invariant measure is ergodic. The proof, which introduces a novel geometric source of semi-local ergodicity, combines tools ranging from KAM theory to geometric measure theory and is robust enough to be of interest in more general configurations.
label: arXiv:2611.27429v1

summary.background:
- Symplectomorphism: a transformation that preserves the area/volume structure of phase space, the basic symmetry of Hamiltonian mechanics.
- Ergodic measure: a natural invariant measure under which almost every trajectory explores the set evenly over time.
- Basic set: a compact invariant set with chaotic, hyperbolic dynamics, a building block in the theory of dynamical systems.
- Elliptic equilibrium: a fixed point around which nearby orbits circle rather than run away or collapse.
- Normally hyperbolic lamination: a layered family of invariant sets where motion transverse to the layers grows or shrinks at a controlled rate.
- KAM theory: the body of results showing that many quasi-periodic motions survive small perturbations of a Hamiltonian system.
- Real-analytic perturbation: a small change to the system's rules that is smooth in a strong, power-series sense.
summary.one_liner: For a product of two symplectomorphisms (one with a basic set, the other with a non-degenerate elliptic equilibrium on a compact surface), the paper shows that under a local domination condition a typical real-analytic perturbation yields a large normally hyperbolic lamination on which the natural invariant measure is ergodic.
summary.plain: This paper studies a mathematical model of a system that moves in a way that preserves a kind of "volume" from classical mechanics. The authors build a combined system from two simpler pieces and show that, after a small generic nudge to the rules, the system has a large structured set on which its typical behavior mixes thoroughly, so a long-run average over the set matches the average over the whole set. The text does not give the full statements, so details of the mixing claim are limited to the abstract.
summary.why: Ergodicity, the property that a system's time averages match its space averages, is a central question in dynamics, and this work addresses it for systems that are not uniformly hyperbolic, where such results are harder. The abstract says the technique, which combines KAM theory with geometric measure theory and introduces a new geometric source of "semi-local" ergodicity, may apply to more general settings, but how far it extends is not stated here.

title: Non-local ergodic measures in symplectic dynamics

abstract: For every prime $p\ge 29$, we construct an antipodal spherical $7$-design on $S^{p-1}$ with $42(p-1)(p+2)^2$ points. The construction uses eigenlines of finite Weil operators.
label: arXiv:2611.26879v1

summary.background:
- Sphere S^{p-1}: the surface of a ball in p-dimensional space.
- Spherical t-design: a finite point set whose average of any polynomial of degree at most t equals the average over the whole sphere; here t = 7.
- Antipodal: the point set is symmetric, so for every point x its opposite -x is also included.
- Prime dimension p: the construction works only when the dimension is prime and at least 29.
- Weil operator / eigenline: a finite-field object from number theory whose special eigen-directions give the point set; the abstract does not explain the details.
- Point count: the bound 42(p-1)(p+2)^2 is an upper bound on how many points are used.
summary.one_liner: The paper constructs antipodal spherical 7-designs on the unit sphere S^{p-1} for every prime p ≥ 29, using at most 42(p-1)(p+2)^2 points, via eigenlines of finite Weil operators.
summary.plain: The paper is about placing a finite set of points evenly over the surface of a high-dimensional sphere so that they average out the way a truly uniform spread would, at least for polynomial functions up to degree 7. The author builds such point sets for every prime dimension p at least 29, with a stated point count of 42(p-1)(p+2)^2. The construction draws on a mathematical tool called Weil operators, which are used to find special directions (eigenlines) that supply the points.
summary.why: Small, explicit designs of this kind matter for numerical integration, coding and quantum state sampling, where fewer well-spread points save work. The text does not state which applications, if any, this result affects, so its wider relevance is uncertain from the abstract alone.

title: Small spherical 7-designs in prime dimensions

abstract: The binding number of a graph, introduced by Woodall [J. Combin. Theory, Ser. B, 1973], is a central topic in structural and extremal graph theory. Recently, Chen et al. introduced the $k$-th binding number $\beta^k(G)$. Anderson [J. Combin. Theory, Ser. B, 1971] proved that every graph $G$ of even order with $\beta^1(G)\ge\frac43$ contains a perfect matching, and that the bound $\frac43$ is best possible. For $k\ge2$, Chen et al. proved that $\beta^k(G)\ge1$ guarantees a $k$-factor whenever $kn$ is even, and that the bound $1$ is best possible. The above facts reveal a fundamental distinction between the higher-order binding number and the classical binding number. This distinction makes extremal problems for graphs with bounded $k$-th binding number particularly intriguing. For positive integers $n,$ $k$ and $r$, we in this paper determine the maximum size and spectral radius among all graphs $G$ of order $n$ satisfying $\beta^k(G)<r$, and characterize the corresponding extremal graphs, respectively. In particular, when $k=1$, our results imply the corresponding extremal results of Fan and Lin [Electron. J. Combin., 2024] and Liu, Chen and Fan [Electron. J. Combin., 2026]. Our proofs develop a structural framework that relates higher-order neighborhood inequalities to the structure of the complements of graphs. This framework may provide an approach to Tur\'{a}n-type problem involving the $k$-th binding number, and the approach may be of independent interest.
label: arXiv:2611.27699v1

summary.background:
- Graph: vertices (points) joined by edges (lines); order n means number of vertices, size means number of edges.
- Perfect matching / k-factor: a way to pair up all vertices (or cover them by k-regular spanning subgraphs) using edges.
- Binding number: a graph parameter (Woodall, 1973) measuring how much the neighborhoods of vertex sets expand; Anderson (1971) showed binding number at least 4/3 forces a perfect matching.
- k-th binding number: a higher-order version introduced by Chen et al.; the text notes that score at least 1 guarantees a k-factor when kn is even.
- Extremal problem (Turán-type): find the largest graph (by edges or spectral radius) that avoids a given property.
- Spectral radius: the largest eigenvalue of the graph's adjacency matrix, a single number summarizing its structure.
- Complement graph: the graph on the same vertices with exactly the missing edges.
summary.one_liner: The paper determines the maximum number of edges and the maximum spectral radius over n-vertex graphs with k-th binding number below r, and characterizes the extremal graphs, generalizing known k=1 results.
summary.plain: This paper is about graphs, which are networks of points joined by lines, and a score called the k-th binding number that measures how well every group of vertices is connected to the rest. The authors ask: if a graph's score is kept below a fixed value r, how many connections can it have at most, and what does the densest such graph look like? They answer this for both the number of edges and a matrix-based measure called the spectral radius, and identify the graphs that reach the maximum.
summary.why: Extremal questions like this show how a structural condition limits how dense a network can be, which is the core of Turán-type graph theory. The authors say the proof method, which links neighborhood inequalities to the complement of the graph, may carry over to other Turán-type problems, but the text does not show how far that reaches.

title: Extremal problems for graphs with bounded $k$-th binding number

abstract: We analyze a fully discrete finite element projection method for the stochastic incompressible Navier--Stokes equations with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions and multiplicative noise. We show solvability and uniform moment estimates for the intermediate and the corrected velocity approximations under the assumption that the initial data is square-integrable and divergence free, and that the deterministic forcing term is bounded in $L^{q}(0,T;H^{-1}(D))$ for a sufficiently large $q$. Under standard stability and approximation assumptions on the finite element spaces and a coupling condition on the spatial and temporal discretization parameters, we prove convergence of a subsequence to a martingale solution of the stochastic Navier--Stokes equations. The analysis combines the complementary spatial and temporal estimates of the predicted and the corrected velocity approximations and uses the numerical dissipation to identify their common limit. We establish tightness of the piecewise constant temporal interpolations of the velocity field approximations using Aldous' criterion combined with the uniform discrete moment estimates. The convergence result holds in two and three space dimensions as it does not rely on any additional regularity of the limiting martingale solution beyond the one naturally available from the energy inequality. Finally, we demonstrate the performance of the scheme in numerical experiments in two space dimensions for smooth and vortex sheet initial data.
label: arXiv:2611.27969v1

summary.background:
- Navier--Stokes equations: the standard equations describing how viscous fluids move.
- Incompressible: the fluid's density stays constant, so its velocity must be divergence free (no net sources or sinks).
- Stochastic / multiplicative noise: random forcing whose strength depends on the current state of the flow.
- Finite element method: splitting a domain into small pieces and approximating the solution with simple functions on them.
- Chorin projection method: a two-step time-stepping trick that first moves the flow forward, then corrects it to restore incompressibility.
- Martingale solution: a weak notion of a random solution, defined on a possibly different probability space, which need not be unique.
- Moment estimates and tightness: bounds on average sizes of the random quantities and a way to guarantee that a sequence of random paths has convergent subsequences.
- Aldous' criterion: a standard test for tightness of random processes.
- Vortex sheet: an idealized flow with a concentrated jump in velocity across a curve, a hard test case.
summary.one_liner: Proves that a fully discrete finite element Chorin projection scheme for the stochastic incompressible Navier--Stokes equations with multiplicative noise and Dirichlet boundary conditions converges (along a subsequence) to a martingale solution in two and three dimensions, under a coupling of space and time step sizes.
summary.plain: This paper studies a computer method for simulating fluid flow (like water or air) that is randomly disturbed by noise, where the fluid is kept incompressible and sits inside a container with fixed walls. The authors show that their step-by-step numerical scheme stays well-behaved and, as the grid gets finer, its results settle toward a valid random-solution of the underlying equations. They also test the method numerically in two dimensions on smooth and vortex-sheet starting conditions.
summary.why: Random fluid models are used when uncertainty or noise matters, so a convergence proof gives some confidence that the computed results mean something. The text does not say how the method compares with other schemes or what applications it targets, so its wider impact is uncertain.

title: Convergence of a finite element Chorin projection method for the stochastic Navier--Stokes equations

abstract: Mesh-free partial differential equation (PDE) solvers construct discrete systems from residuals at sampled points. These solvers fit coefficients in a parameterized trial representation and select solver-design parameters governing the representation, training-residual weighting, and regularization. These parameters strongly affect solution accuracy, yet existing selection strategies are largely tailored to particular solver classes. To address this limitation, we formulate a unified validation-driven bilevel optimization framework applicable across different solver classes, in which the lower level fits coefficients using training collocation residuals, while the upper level selects solver-design parameters using held-out validation residuals. For nonlinear PDEs, however, solving the nonlinear lower-level problem to high accuracy is costly, while the adjoint system is typically ill-conditioned and indefinite. To address this issue, we propose an efficient implicit hypergradient method that approximates the lower-level response using finite, warm-started damped Gauss-Newton (GN) updates. For the adjoint solve, we use the damped GN matrix to compute an initial adjoint and to precondition a finite number of minimum residual iterations. To quantify the errors introduced by these approximations, we derive local hypergradient error bounds that separate the contributions of the finite lower-level solve, adjoint damping, and the final adjoint residual. Combining this analysis with validation sampling bounds and residual stability, we relate validation residuals to PDE solution accuracy and establish error bounds for the computed PDE solution. Numerical experiments on several nonlinear PDEs, including a high-dimensional problem, demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed method across Kansa, random feature and extreme learning machine, and physics-informed neural network solvers.
label: arXiv:2611.27347v1

summary.background:
- PDE (partial differential equation): an equation relating a function to its rates of change, used to model physical processes such as heat or waves.
- Mesh-free solver: a numerical method that works from scattered points rather than a fixed grid of cells.
- Residual: how far a candidate solution misses satisfying the equation at chosen points.
- Bilevel optimization: an outer problem (choose settings) wrapped around an inner problem (fit the solution to the settings).
- Validation set: held-out points used to score choices without fitting to them.
- Hypergradient: the gradient of the outer score with respect to the settings, which lets the outer choice be improved by gradient steps.
- Gauss-Newton method: an iterative method for nonlinear least-squares fitting; "damped" means step sizes are tempered for stability.
- Adjoint system: an auxiliary linear system used to compute hypergradients efficiently.
- Preconditioning: transforming a linear system so an iterative solver converges faster.
- Physics-informed neural network (PINN): a neural network trained to satisfy a PDE and its boundary conditions.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes a validation-driven bilevel optimization framework for tuning design parameters of mesh-free PDE solvers (Kansa, random feature/extreme learning machine, and physics-informed neural network methods), using an efficient implicit hypergradient with warm-started damped Gauss-Newton and preconditioned minimum-residual adjoint solves, and derives local error bounds linking validation residuals to solution accuracy.
summary.plain: Mesh-free methods solve equations like heat or fluid flow by checking the equation at scattered sample points instead of on a grid. These methods have settings, such as network shape or regularization strength, that strongly affect accuracy and are hard to choose. The authors choose these settings by fitting the solution on training points and scoring it on separate held-out validation points, and they make the search for good settings computationally cheaper for nonlinear equations.
summary.why: Choosing solver settings is a practical bottleneck for these methods, and a single selection framework that works across several solver families could be useful. The text reports numerical experiments, including a high-dimensional nonlinear problem, but I cannot judge from the abstract alone how large the practical gains are.

title: A Validation-Driven Bilevel Optimization Method for Mesh-Free PDE Solvers and Its Error Analysis

abstract: This article develops a second stage of an argument begun in 2013, revisiting Alain Badiou's use of topos theory in Being and Event and Logics of Worlds. The previous article diagnosed Badiou's reduction of topos theory to its atomistic, localic form as the scientific scapegoat in his attack on 'democratic materialism'. Now I ask what follows when this logicist illusion is dispelled and the categorical alternative is taken seriously, particularly with respect to forcing, semantic expression, and mathematical subjectification that constitute the key elements of Badiou's earlier work. I thus reconstruct Badiou's own arguments in a corrected form, while transferring them to a categorical framework. The aim is not to introduce new mathematical results, but to identify what is conceptually lost through their reduction to set-theoretic formalism. In particular, I describe Cohen's forcing argument in the context of Grothendieck topoi and Kripke-Joyal semantics, thereby explicating the geometric structures implicit in Badiou's thinking. This reconstruction further brings into view a different way of understanding Badiou's concepts of subject, body, and change. Rather than treating a topos as merely a formal container for mathematical objects, I propose reading it as a body of mathematical expression, aligning with Johnstone's characterization of a topos as a 'universe of discourse'. At the same time, the geometrization of logic allows Badiou's own four-fold typology of change - when applied to topos theory itself as a mathematical 'event' - to be anchored to various historical definitions of a topos. In this way, the article bridges Badiou's two major works while clarifying how his own limited expression of mathematical formalism embodies his 'dialectical', ultimately singular concept of the event, and the way it clouds his philosophical understanding of locality and temporality.
label: arXiv:2611.27280v1

summary.background:
- Badiou: a French philosopher whose works Being and Event and Logics of Worlds use set theory and topos theory to describe truth, events and change.
- Topos (plural topoi): a mathematical structure from category theory that generalises set theory and can serve as a setting for logic.
- Category theory: a framework that studies mathematical objects through the relationships (maps) between them rather than their internal contents.
- Forcing: Paul Cohen's technique for building new models of set theory, used to show certain statements cannot be proved or disproved from the standard axioms.
- Kripke-Joyal semantics: a way of giving meaning to logical statements inside a topos.
- Localic: a more restricted, point-based form of topos, which the author argues Badiou relied on.
- Grothendieck topos: a general notion of topos introduced in algebraic geometry.
- Johnstone's "universe of discourse": a description of a topos as a setting in which mathematical reasoning takes place.
summary.one_liner: A philosophical reconstruction of Alain Badiou's use of topos theory (forcing, Kripke-Joyal semantics, and his typology of change) recast in a categorical framework, arguing that a topos can be read as a "body of mathematical expression."
summary.plain: The paper revisits how the philosopher Alain Badiou used a branch of advanced mathematics, topos theory, in his books Being and Event and Logics of Worlds. The author argues that Badiou shrank this mathematics down to a narrow, set-based version, and asks what is lost when it is restored to its fuller categorical form. The author says the aim is conceptual clarification rather than new mathematical results.
summary.why: It connects philosophy of mathematics, the foundations of logic, and the reception of category theory in continental philosophy, and it is a second part of an argument begun in 2013. The text itself does not show how much influence the argument has, so its wider significance is uncertain.

title: Bridging Badiou's Gaps: Topos Theory and the Bodies of Mathematical Expression

abstract: We study the computational strength of enumerations of generic and random sets, particularly its interplay with computing these `typical' sets. We show that, while enumerations of $2$-generics can compute $2$-generics, this fails at higher levels---every $3$-generic has an enumeration which computes no weak $3$-generic. The analogous statement holds for randoms---every weak $2$-random has an enumeration which computes no $1$-random. We then analyze the total degrees above a quasiminimal enumeration degree, showing certain restrictions as well as certain positive results on the possible Turing degrees in such a cone. This answers a question of Slaman and Sorbi, by showing that there are quasiminimals with no minimal Turing degrees above them. We also show that while every total degree above some quasiminimals compute dimension $1$ sets, the total degrees above any quasiminimal fail to be a subset of the PA degrees.
label: arXiv:2611.27239v1

summary.background:
- Computability theory asks which infinite sets of numbers can be computed from which others.
- Turing degree: a class of sets that are equally hard to compute from one another, under ordinary Turing computation.
- Enumeration degree: a coarser-to-finer notion where a set is computed by listing its members (positive information only), not by deciding membership.
- Generic and random sets: "typical" infinite sets that avoid all definable special properties (genericity) or are incompressible/unpredictable (randomness). Levels (2-generic, 3-generic, 1-random, weak 2-random) measure how strongly typical.
- Quasiminimal: an enumeration degree with no non-computable (total) degrees strictly below it, apart from trivial ones.
- PA degrees: degrees that compute a solution to a certain combinatorial principle (Peano arithmetic-related), and dimension 1 sets are a measure of how much of the set's information is free.
summary.one_liner: The paper studies the computational strength of enumeration reducibility for generic and random sets, showing limits on what enumerations of 3-generics and weak 2-randoms can compute and mapping which Turing degrees can lie above quasiminimal enumeration degrees.
summary.plain:
The paper is about how much information can be extracted from "typical" infinite sets of binary digits, using a way of computing called enumeration, which asks whether a set can be listed out from another set rather than decided item by item. The authors show that some such listing-based constructions cannot recover typical sets at higher levels of typicality. They also answer an open question of Slaman and Sorbi by showing that some quasiminimal degrees have no minimal Turing degrees above them.</plain>
<parameter name="why">It sharpens the picture of how randomness and genericity behave under computability reductions, a central topic in the study of what can be computed from what. The text itself does not say how these results bear on wider applications, so their broader significance is unclear from this text alone.

title: The Power Of Enumerations

abstract: We fully classify the brane tilings and the 4d N=1 supersymmetric quiver gauge theories corresponding to toric Calabi-Yau 3-folds whose toric diagrams are convex lattice polygons with two interior lattice points. There are 45 such polygons up to GL(2,Z) transformations and lattice translations: 5 triangles, 19 quadrilaterals, 16 pentagons and 5 hexagons. We identify all 323 toric phases corresponding to these toric Calabi-Yau 3-folds. For every toric phase, we present the brane tiling with its quiver and superpotential, the perfect matching matrix and the F- and D-term charge matrices. For each brane tiling, we study the mesonic moduli space of the corresponding abelian 4d N=1 theory through its Hilbert series and plethystic logarithm, and identify its generators and their leading relations. We also identify the mesonic global symmetry for each brane tiling and determine the superconformal U(1)R charges.
label: arXiv:2611.27861v1

summary.background:
- Toric diagram: a small lattice polygon (points on a grid) that encodes a toric Calabi-Yau 3-fold, a special higher-dimensional geometric space used in string theory.
- Interior lattice point: a grid point strictly inside the polygon; here, polygons with exactly two.
- Brane tiling (dimer model): a tiling of a torus by polygons that encodes a gauge theory's particles and interactions.
- Quiver gauge theory: a diagram of nodes (gauge groups) and arrows (matter fields) describing a 4d supersymmetric theory.
- Superpotential: a polynomial describing the interactions among the fields.
- Toric phase: one of the distinct gauge theories that share the same underlying geometry.
- Moduli space, Hilbert series, plethystic logarithm: tools for counting the gauge-invariant quantities and their relations in a theory.
- U(1)R charge: a symmetry charge used to fix the theory's superconformal behaviour.
summary.one_liner: A complete classification of brane tilings and their associated 4d N=1 quiver gauge theories for toric Calabi-Yau 3-folds whose toric diagrams are convex lattice polygons with exactly two interior lattice points (45 polygons, 323 toric phases), including Hilbert series and mesonic moduli space data.
summary.plain: This paper is a catalogue in theoretical physics and geometry. It looks at a family of shapes that encode certain higher-dimensional geometric spaces, and at the physics theories (built from particles and their interactions) linked to each one. The authors list every such shape with two interior points, find all 323 physical versions of them, and record the matching diagrams and mathematical data for each.
summary.why: The text presents this as a complete classification, which makes it a useful reference for anyone studying the link between string-theory gauge theories and the geometry of Calabi-Yau spaces. The text does not say what broader consequences follow, so its wider importance is unclear from this text alone.

title: Brane Tilings and Polygons with Two Interior Points

abstract: In this paper, we study random density matrices constructed by taking partial traces of projections onto random subspaces of a bipartite Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_{B}$ distributed according to the pushforward measure of the action of the unitary group on the Grassmannian $\text{Gr}_{n}(\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_{B})$. This ensemble models a `typical' quantum subspace. All tracial moments of the density operator, as well as mixed tracial moments of reduced density operators, are computed explicitly using Weingarten calculus. There are several consequences of these results. In particular, we prove that the empirical spectral distribution of the density operator converges almost surely to a rescaled Marchenko-Pastur law. We also prove that this ensemble can be written as a sum of asymptotically free random density operators, leading to an alternative proof of the convergence of the spectral distribution. Finally, we compute the asymptotic expansion of the average entanglement entropy.
label: arXiv:2611.27914v1

summary.background:
- Density matrix: a matrix describing a quantum state; its eigenvalues are nonnegative and sum to one.
- Partial trace: averaging out one subsystem to get the state of the other.
- Grassmannian: the space of all subspaces of a fixed dimension, here sampled uniformly via the unitary group.
- Tracial moments: averages of powers of the matrix's trace, which encode the eigenvalue distribution.
- Weingarten calculus: a systematic method for integrating polynomial functions of random unitary matrices.
- Marchenko-Pastur law: the limiting eigenvalue distribution of certain large random matrices.
- Asymptotic freeness: a notion from free probability describing when large random matrices behave independently in a specific algebraic sense.
- Entanglement entropy: a measure of how correlated the two subsystems are, computed from the reduced density matrix.
summary.one_liner: The paper computes all tracial moments and mixed reduced-state moments of random density matrices obtained by partial traces of projections onto random subspaces drawn from the Grassmannian, using Weingarten calculus, and derives almost-sure convergence of the spectrum to a rescaled Marchenko-Pastur law, an asymptotic freeness decomposition, and the asymptotic average entanglement entropy.
summary.plain: The paper studies a model of a "typical" quantum state: pick a random subspace of a two-part quantum system, then look at the state of just one part by averaging out the other. The authors work out the statistical averages of the eigenvalue pattern of these random density matrices exactly, using a counting technique called Weingarten calculus. From these results they show that the pattern of eigenvalues settles into a known shape (a rescaled Marchenko-Pastur law) as the system grows, and they estimate the average entanglement entropy.
summary.why: Random density matrices like these are used as benchmarks for what generic quantum states look like, which matters for quantum information and statistical physics. The text offers two routes to the same spectral result, one of which goes through asymptotic freeness, a link to random matrix theory; the broader impact beyond this setting is not addressed in the text.

title: The moments and asymptotic spectral distribution of the Grassmannian ensemble

abstract: We study second order variational mean-field games with quadratic Hamiltonian. In analogy with entropic optimal transport, Benamou, Carlier, Di Marino and the second author recently proposed an entropy-minimization formulation of the problem, which could be interpreted as the Lagrangian counterpart of the classical Eulerian approach. We investigate the small-noise $\Gamma$-limit for the Lagrangian entropy-minimization formulation and establish $\Gamma$-convergence of second order mean-field games towards their deterministic first order counterpart. This also translates into another (dynamical) proof of the convergence of the Schr\"odinger problem to optimal transport. Moreover, we study the original Eulerian problem and prove a first order energy expansion, which establishes a selection principle for minimizers of the deterministic problem.
label: arXiv:2611.27695v1

summary.background:
- Mean-field game: a model of a very large population of agents, each optimizing a cost that depends on the population's overall distribution.
- Second-order vs first-order: second-order models include random noise (diffusion); first-order models are deterministic.
- Entropy: a measure of spread or randomness; entropy minimization here penalizes deviation from a reference random motion.
- Schrödinger problem: a noisy, entropy-regularized version of optimal transport (finding the cheapest way to move one distribution of mass to another).
- Optimal transport: the least-cost way to rearrange one distribution into another.
- Γ-convergence: a notion of convergence for minimization problems, ensuring minimizers of approximating problems approach minimizers of the limit problem.
- Eulerian vs Lagrangian: Eulerian tracks a density and velocity field at fixed points in space; Lagrangian tracks individual particle paths.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves that, as the random noise in second-order variational mean-field games shrinks to zero, the entropy-minimizing Lagrangian formulation Γ-converges to its deterministic first-order counterpart, and it derives a first-order energy expansion for the original Eulerian problem that selects among deterministic minimizers.
summary.plain: The paper studies large systems of many interacting agents that move under random noise and each try to optimize their own cost. It asks what happens when the noise is made very small, so the system approaches a deterministic model. The authors show that the noisy problem converges, in a precise variational sense, to the deterministic one, and that the noisy version also recovers a known result linking random transport (the Schrödinger problem) to optimal transport.
summary.why: The text indicates the work connects a noisy game-theoretic model with its noiseless limit and gives a new dynamical route to the Schrödinger-to-optimal-transport convergence. It also says a small-noise expansion selects particular minimizers of the deterministic problem; the broader significance beyond these claims is not stated in the text.

title: Small noise limit for Entropic Variational Mean-Field Games

abstract: This paper continues the results published in [G. Marinoschi, Appl. Math. Optimiz. 94:44, 1-29, 2026], by presenting an approximating method of calculating the solution to the $H^{\infty }$-optimal control problem, which solves the robust stabilization of a system by a feedback controller, and to the associated Riccati equation. This method generates a sequence of infinite dimensional systems approximating the original system and the solution to the approximating $H^{\infty }$-optimal control problem is proved to converge to the solution of the original $H^{\infty }$-optimal control problem. An example for calculating the solution to the Riccati equation and the feedback controller is provided at the end.
label: arXiv:2611.27520v1

summary.background:
- Optimal control: choosing inputs over time to make a system behave well at minimal cost.
- Robust stabilization: designing a controller that keeps a system stable despite uncertainty or disturbances.
- H-infinity norm: a measure of how strongly disturbances can affect a system's output in the worst case.
- Riccati equation: a nonlinear matrix equation whose solution gives the optimal feedback gain in many control problems.
- Infinite-dimensional systems: models where the state is a function (e.g., of space), not a finite list of numbers, so they are approximated by finite or simpler systems.
- Convergence: the approximate solutions get closer to the true solution as the approximation is refined.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes an approximation scheme that builds a sequence of infinite-dimensional systems to compute solutions of the H-infinity optimal control problem and its associated Riccati equation, and proves convergence of the approximate solutions to the original one.
summary.plain: The paper is about designing a feedback controller that keeps a system stable even when it is affected by unknown disturbances or modelling errors. Since the exact solution is hard to compute directly, the author builds a series of simpler approximating problems and shows that their solutions approach the true one. A worked example at the end shows how the method computes the controller and the related Riccati equation.
summary.why: Robust control of this kind is used in engineering settings where guarantees against disturbances matter, and a provable approximation method makes such designs more practical to compute. The text does not indicate specific applications or how the method performs beyond the single example, so its practical reach is uncertain. It continues earlier work by the same author cited in the text.

title: Approximating technique for the solution to the ${H}^{\infty}$ -optimal control problem

abstract: We develop a factorization method with finite-sample statistical guarantees for two-dimensional acoustic scattering by impedance obstacles whose boundary is random and whose data are finitely many noisy multistatic measurements. In the two-dimensional far-field normalization, the symmetrization must act on a phase-rotated far-field operator; we prove the optical and range identities for every realization of a compact family of uniformly bi-Lipschitz domains, with jointly measurable regularized indicators. A quadrature-weighted finite-sample analysis separates angular approximation, measurement noise, test-vector error, and regularization, and yields a consistency theorem for empirical means and variances, joint in all data parameters. Bounded indicators admit simultaneous confidence bands, a diagonal threshold recovers the probability that a sampling point lies in the random obstacle, and a nested design yields unbiased variance components. Computations use a combined-field integral equation proved invertible at all frequencies, and the finite-grid guarantees are examined in a coverage study against a high-accuracy Monte Carlo reference.
label: arXiv:2611.26761v1

summary.background:
- Acoustic scattering: waves sent at an object and the echoes or far-field patterns recorded.
- Impedance obstacle: an object whose surface partly absorbs or reflects waves, described by a boundary condition.
- Factorization method: an inverse-scattering technique that tests sampling points to decide whether they lie inside the object.
- Multistatic data: measurements taken from several sending and receiving positions.
- Monte Carlo reference: a brute-force simulation used as a benchmark for accuracy.
- Confidence band and coverage: a range that should contain the true value with a stated probability, and the check of how often that holds.
- Integral equation: a reformulation of the wave problem that can be solved numerically.
summary.one_liner: A factorization method for locating two-dimensional impedance obstacles with random boundaries from finitely many noisy multistatic measurements, with finite-sample confidence guarantees, simultaneous confidence bands, and a combined-field integral equation computed numerically.
summary.plain: The paper looks at how to find an object that sound waves bounce off when the object's edge is not fixed but varies randomly from one trial to the next. Using a limited set of noisy measurements, the authors build an imaging method and attach statistical error bounds to it, so the picture of where the object is comes with stated uncertainty. They check the resulting coverage of those error bounds against a high-accuracy Monte Carlo reference.
summary.why: Imaging hidden objects from scattered waves is used in radar, sonar, and medical or geophysical imaging, and attaching confidence statements to the image is the kind of step those fields need. The text does not discuss applications, so any connection beyond this specialist setting is my inference rather than something the paper states.

title: Pathwise Factorization and Uncertainty Quantification for Impedance Obstacles with Random Boundaries

abstract: We study convex empirical risk minimization (ERM) with non-Gaussian features and nonsmooth penalties through a surrogate driven by a single Gaussian vector. The surrogate preserves the penalty and calibrates its coefficients using the actual joint law of the feature-label model. We prove that this population calibration exists and is unique. We prove a Gaussian approximation for fresh prediction scores when the data satisfy a Poincar\'e inequality. Together with regularity conditions on the losses, this approximation yields agreement between the ERM minimizer and its surrogate in normalized means and prediction variances, as well as formulas for prediction and classification risks. The result covers general uniformly strongly convex penalties and pure Lasso under projection anti-concentration. The core proof relies on a cavity Hamilton-Jacobi argument that compares the main statistics of the two minimizers without differentiating the penalty.
label: arXiv:2611.27754v1

summary.background:
- Empirical risk minimization (ERM): choosing model parameters to minimize average loss on a training sample.
- Convex penalty: an added cost term (such as the Lasso's sum of absolute values) that keeps the problem well behaved and encourages simple solutions.
- Gaussian approximation: replacing a complicated random quantity with a normal (bell-curve) one that has matching mean and variance.
- Poincaré inequality: a condition limiting how much a random function can fluctuate, used to control the non-Gaussian data.
- Anti-concentration: the requirement that random projections are not too likely to fall in a tiny interval.
- Hamilton-Jacobi / cavity method: a technique from statistical physics that compares a system with and without one data point.
summary.one_liner: The paper builds a one-Gaussian-vector surrogate for convex empirical risk minimization with non-Gaussian features and nonsmooth penalties, calibrates it to the true joint law, and proves agreement of minimizers, prediction variances, and risks under a Poincaré inequality and regularity assumptions.
summary.plain: The paper studies a common way of fitting statistical models: pick settings that make the model's error small on training data while penalizing complexity. Real data are rarely Gaussian (bell-curve shaped), which makes exact analysis hard. The authors replace the messy data with a simpler surrogate built from one Gaussian random vector, and they show that, under stated conditions, the fitted solution and its predictions behave similarly to those of the surrogate.
summary.why: It offers a way to predict test error and classification risk for penalized models on non-Gaussian data without relying on the data being Gaussian, which matters for anyone relying on such formulas. The text does not show how widely the conditions apply in practice, so its reach beyond the stated settings is uncertain.

title: An Asymptotic One-Sample Surrogate for Non-Gaussian ERM with General Convex Regularization

abstract: Functional time series have a wide range of practical applications to modeling complex datasets such as Electroencephalogram (EEG) and other biological signals. Often latent states are hidden within the data dictating how a system is behaving and changing over time. The Hidden Markov Model (HMM) is one common and highly applicable latent state space model where the hidden state sequence evolves as a Markov chain. While the HMM has had much success modeling discrete, multivariate, and fully functional time series, it is also restricted by the Markov property which causes hidden states to persist only at geometrically decaying rates. This work investigates the implementation of hidden semi-Markov models for modeling fully functional time series data. This allows for the hidden state sequence to persist in a given state for a data-driven sojourn time, which can be parametrized by a discrete distribution (e.g. negative binomial) or left non-parametric. For efficient fitting of such a model, the hidden semi-Markov chain is embedded into a larger state space Markov chain and classic methods like the Baum-Welch and Viterbi algorithms are applied. We furthermore consider functional time series in the general setting of Gaussian measures in locally convex topological vector spaces. This is applied to a time series of pediatric EEG signals collected via overnight polysomnography.
label: arXiv:2611.26838v1

summary.background:
- Hidden Markov model: a model where an unseen state changes over time, and each state produces the observed data.
- Markov property: the next state depends only on the current one, which makes durations decay geometrically.
- Semi-Markov / sojourn time: a model that lets the time spent in a state follow its own distribution, such as a negative binomial.
- Baum-Welch and Viterbi: standard algorithms for fitting such models and finding the most likely hidden state sequence.
- Functional time series: data where each observation is a whole curve or function, not a single number.
- Gaussian measures on locally convex spaces: a generalization of normal distributions to infinite-dimensional settings, used here to handle curves.
- EEG and polysomnography: recordings of brain electrical activity and other signals during sleep.
summary.one_liner: The paper extends hidden semi-Markov models, with data-driven state durations, to fully functional time series, embedding the hidden chain in a larger Markov chain so Baum-Welch and Viterbi fitting can be used, and applies this to pediatric EEG signals in the Gaussian-measure setting of locally convex spaces.
summary.plain: Many signals, such as brain recordings, switch between hidden modes over time, and a common model for this is the hidden Markov model. That model forces each mode to last for a random time that drops off quickly, which often does not fit real data. This paper replaces it with a version where each hidden mode can last for a more flexible, data-driven length, and applies the approach to overnight sleep-study EEG recordings from children.
summary.why: Modeling how long a hidden state lasts is central to interpreting physiological signals such as sleep stages, so a more realistic duration model may matter for that kind of analysis. The provided text does not report comparative results against standard models, so its practical gain is not established here.

title: Hidden Semi-Markov Models for Fully Functional Time Series

abstract: We introduce a generalized Bayesian approach to multiple changepoint analysis in dynamic network data based on a multinomial log loss function and a prior distribution that imposes low-rank structure and sparsity on the model parameters. The method can detect local and global changes in network structure by incorporating information from both the full adjacency matrices and network summary statistics. Moreover, the proposed method is agnostic to the true data-generating process. From the generalized posterior distribution, we can make simultaneous inferences with meaningful uncertainty quantification about the locations of changepoints as well as deduce the network attributes and summary statistics that characterize them. For posterior simulation, we develop an efficient Gibbs sampler based on P\'olya-Gamma data augmentation with a computational cost that grows linearly with the number of observed edges in the dynamic network. Simulations across several benchmark network models show that the proposed method is often more accurate and flexible than competitors. We demonstrate the practical value of the method through applications to an email communication network and an international conflict network.
label: arXiv:2611.26955v1

summary.background:
- A dynamic network is a sequence of snapshots over time, each recorded as an adjacency matrix (a grid where an entry marks whether two nodes are linked).
- A changepoint is a time at which the underlying process generating the data shifts.
- Bayesian inference combines a prior belief with observed data to get a posterior distribution, which expresses uncertainty about unknown quantities.
- A generalized posterior replaces the usual likelihood with a loss function, so the method does not depend on knowing the exact data-generating process.
- Low-rank structure and sparsity are simplifying assumptions that keep the model parameters compact and mostly zero.
- Gibbs sampling and Pólya-Gamma data augmentation are computational techniques for drawing samples from the posterior.
summary.one_liner: A generalized Bayesian changepoint method for dynamic networks uses a multinomial log loss, a low-rank sparse prior, and a Pólya-Gamma Gibbs sampler to locate local and global structural shifts in time-indexed adjacency matrices.
summary.plain: The paper addresses how to find the moments when a network that changes over time (such as who emails whom, or which countries are in conflict) suddenly shifts its pattern. The authors build a statistical method that looks at both the full set of connections and simple summary measures of the network, and it estimates where the change points are along with how uncertain those estimates are. They report that in simulations it was often more accurate than competing methods, and they illustrate it on an email network and an international conflict network.
summary.why: Detecting when relationships in a network change matters for fields that track communication, social ties, or political conflict over time. The text does not say how broadly the method will transfer beyond the benchmark simulations and the two applications shown.

title: A generalized Bayesian method for identifying local and global changepoints in dynamic network data

abstract: Post-hoc transformer linearization replaces the key-value cache of full attention, which grows linearly with generation length, with a fixed size state. This change reduces memory consumption but often hurts accuracy. In reasoning tasks, which require long generations, this effect is especially pronounced. In this work we introduce Turnout, a method that mitigates accuracy loss as a result of linearization, while maintaining its memory-reduction benefits. We apply post-hoc linearization to a pretrained full-attention model, training a linear path through distillation while leaving the original full-attention path unchanged. During response generation, the resulting hybrid model retains both paths and uses a learned policy to control when each layer switches from full to linear attention. We train the policy with reinforcement learning using a reward that balances answer correctness and memory use. Empirical evaluation of our method shows that the learned adaptive policy achieves a better accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier on reasoning tasks compared to fixed switching and static hybrid baselines.
label: arXiv:2611.27500v1

summary.background:
- Transformer: the neural network architecture behind most modern language models.
- Attention: the mechanism that lets the model look back at earlier tokens when producing the next one.
- Key-value (KV) cache: stored memory of past tokens that grows as the output gets longer; it is the main memory cost during generation.
- Linear attention: an approximation with a fixed-size memory that does not grow with length, but is typically less accurate.
- Linearization / distillation: converting a trained model to use the cheaper mechanism by training the new path to mimic the original.
- Hybrid model: a model that uses both full and linear attention in different layers.
- Reinforcement learning: training a policy by rewarding good outcomes; here the reward combines correctness and memory use.
- Pareto frontier: the set of trade-offs where you cannot improve accuracy without spending more memory, or vice versa.
summary.one_liner: Turnout converts a pretrained full-attention transformer into a hybrid that can switch each layer between full and linear attention at generation time, with the switching policy learned by reinforcement learning under a reward that trades off answer correctness against memory use.
summary.plain: Large language models remember what they have already written using a growing memory store, which gets expensive when they produce long chains of reasoning. This paper takes an existing model and swaps part of that memory for a fixed-size one, which saves memory but usually makes answers less accurate. The authors add a learned controller that decides, layer by layer and during writing, when to use the full memory and when to use the cheaper one, and report that this gives a better balance of accuracy and efficiency than fixed rules on reasoning tasks.
summary.why: Memory cost of long reasoning outputs is a practical limit on how these models are deployed, so a method that keeps accuracy while cutting memory could matter. The text reports only that the learned policy beats fixed-switching and static hybrid baselines on a Pareto frontier; it gives no specific numbers here, so the size of the gain is unclear from this summary alone.

title: Turnout: Adaptive Attention Switching for Efficient Reasoning

abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) in long-horizon and continual interactions requires maintaining reusable memory states for future inference, posing challenges for existing architectures. Standard Transformers accumulate layer-wise, token-level KV caches, incurring linear GPU memory growth and quadratic computational complexity as the context expands. In contrast, linear-time architectures compress history into fixed-size states, but struggle to retain fine-grained details. We introduce MemOnce, a foundation architecture that learns scalable memory states for language models. MemOnce is based on two core designs: (a) Memory encoder-decoder: it caches only a small subset of final-layer hidden states as compact memory representations and dynamically decodes them back into KV caches for attention layers; (b) Memory sparse attention: for each continual input, MemOnce adaptively retrieves relevant memory representations, with the sparse indices computed only once across layers. Coupling these two designs enables efficient on-the-fly memory loading and KV cache decoding, drastically reducing the GPU memory footprint and achieving linear-time complexity. We conduct extensive experiments to show that MemOnce outperforms Transformers and other architectures across varying model sizes, context lengths, and training paradigms (pretraining and post-training adaptation). In particular, adapting Qwen3.5-4B with MemOnce reduces memory state cache by 1313$\times$ and prefill latency by 6.9$\times$ at 1M context, and improves throughput by 3.5$\times$ and overall memory performance by +5.77%. Finally, MemOnce generalizes zero-shot to downstream representation tasks, achieving competitive results against specialized models.
label: arXiv:2611.27973v1

summary.background:
- Transformer language models store a "KV cache": per-token internal values reused for attention, which grows with context length.
- Attention cost grows quadratically with context length in standard Transformers; linear-time models compress history into a fixed-size state instead.
- Hidden states are the internal numerical representations a network produces at each layer.
- Sparse attention means attending to only a selected subset of past items rather than all of them.
- Pretraining trains a model from scratch on broad data; post-training adaptation tunes an existing model further.
- Zero-shot generalization means applying a trained model to new tasks without task-specific training.
summary.one_liner: MemOnce proposes a language model memory architecture that caches a small set of final-layer hidden states, decodes them into attention KV caches on demand, and uses sparse retrieval whose indices are computed once and shared across layers, with reported gains in memory footprint, latency, and throughput at 1M-token contexts.
summary.plain: Chatbots and other language models normally keep a growing scratchpad of everything they have read, and this scratchpad takes up more and more computer memory as conversations get longer. This paper proposes a different way to store that history: it keeps only a compact summary of each part and rebuilds the detailed working memory from those summaries when needed. The authors report that, when they adapt a 4-billion-parameter Qwen3.5 model with this method, the stored memory shrinks about 1,313 times and the time to process a 1-million-token input drops about 6.9 times, though these results come from the authors' own experiments.
summary.why: Memory cost is a practical limit on running language models over long, continuing interactions, so a method that keeps detail while cutting storage could matter for that use. The text does not show how the approach compares under independent testing, so its significance is still open.

title: MemOnce: A Scalable Memory Architecture for Large Language Models

abstract: Neural networks have parameter symmetries: parameter transformations that do not affect the represented function. How do these symmetries affect the functions that neural networks ultimately learn? We study the implicit bias arising from these symmetries by calculating the equilibrium distribution over represented functions under Langevin dynamics with Gaussian regularization. To isolate the effect of symmetries on this distribution, we study the limit in which the strength of the regularization is taken to zero. In certain cases, we show that the zero-regularization and infinite-time limits commute. In the low temperature limit, we recover known effective regularizations. At positive temperature, a renormalization procedure allows us to derive a novel entropy which predicts symmetry-induced preference for certain functions. For linear networks, we obtain explicit entropy terms that favor singular and low-rank functions. For networks with homogeneous activations, we find entropy terms that favor inactive neurons, which can lead to neural "heat death" in which equilibrium mass concentrates on networks with vanishing output. We interpret these results through the neural tangent kernel, as a simplicity bias selecting for functions that vary slowly under variations in the parameters.
label: arXiv:2611.27889v1

summary.background:
- Parameter symmetry: a change to a network's weights that leaves the computed function identical (for example, rescaling connected layers in a ReLU network).
- Langevin dynamics: a noisy gradient-descent process whose long-run behavior settles into an equilibrium distribution over parameters.
- Gaussian regularization: a penalty that pulls weights toward zero, here with a strength that is taken to zero.
- Low-temperature limit: the regime where the noise is small, so the process concentrates near minima of the loss.
- Entropy (in this context): a measure of how much parameter space corresponds to a given function; more volume means more probability.
- Neural tangent kernel: a linearized approximation describing how a function changes as parameters change; the paper uses it to interpret the "simplicity bias".
- Homogeneous activation: an activation such as ReLU where scaling the input scales the output by the same factor.
summary.one_liner: The paper derives the equilibrium distribution over functions learned by neural networks under Langevin dynamics with weak Gaussian regularization, showing how parameter symmetries induce a renormalized entropy that favors singular, low-rank functions in linear networks and inactive neurons in homogeneous-activation networks.
summary.plain: Neural networks can be reparameterized in many ways that leave the function they compute unchanged, and this paper asks whether those redundancies quietly steer which functions training tends to settle on. The authors study a noisy training process in the limit of vanishing regularization and find that, at nonzero noise, a renormalized "entropy" favors certain functions. In their examples, this pushes linear networks toward low-rank functions and pushes networks with homogeneous activations toward switched-off neurons, which can drive the output toward zero.
summary.why: It offers an explicit account of how symmetry alone can bias what a network learns, a question relevant to understanding generalization and implicit regularization. The text does not show how far these results extend beyond the linear and homogeneous-activation cases it treats, so broader impact is uncertain.

title: Renormalized Entropy from Symmetries: Simplicity Bias and Neural Heat Death

abstract: Writing Neural tangent kernel (NTK) theory explains why very wide neural networks trained by gradient methods converge in the lazy-training regime. Its standard proof combines matrix concentration, random Gram matrices, continuous-time dynamics, spectral perturbation, and a bootstrap argument, but has lacked machine-checked verification. We present a Lean\~4 formalisation for two-layer networks, proving an end-to-end theorem: for a smooth bounded activation (instantiated with $\sigma=\tanh$), frozen biases, paired $\pm 1$ initialisation, and explicit width conditions, gradient flow exists uniquely with probability at least $1-\delta$, and $$ \|r(t)\|^2 \leq \|y\|^2 e^{-\lambda_0 t/2}. $$ The sole data assumption is population NTK non-degeneracy, $\lambda_0>0$. Initial coercivity, kernel drift, the movement bootstrap, the residual ODE, and flow existence and uniqueness are formally proved. The formalisation also sharpens the standard analysis in two ways. First, replacing the conventional matrix-Bernstein variance proxy with the classical row-covariance proxy yields estimated concentration-width certificates for $\tanh$ that are $36$--$53\times$ smaller at $(m,d)=(16,8)$ and $94$--$121\times$ smaller at $(32,16)$. Lean certifies the inequality; the ratios are numerical. Second, the network Hessian has operator norm $\Theta(\sqrt{p})$ on the sup-norm parameter ball (a paper calculation), preventing the expected $O(1/\sqrt{p})$ linearisation bound via sup-norm Taylor estimates. An $L^2$ parameter geometry resolves this issue. Required widths remain polynomial but far beyond practical scales, limiting applicability.
label: arXiv:2611.27487v1

summary.background:
- Neural network: a function built from layers of weighted sums and simple nonlinear functions, whose weights are tuned by training.
- Gradient descent / gradient flow: repeatedly nudging weights downhill on an error measure; gradient flow is the continuous-time version.
- Neural tangent kernel (NTK): a fixed similarity measure between inputs that describes how a very wide network changes during training.
- Lazy training: a regime where weights move only slightly from their starting values, so the network acts almost like a fixed linear model.
- Concentration inequalities: bounds stating that random quantities stay close to their average with high probability; the matrix-Bernstein bound is one such tool.
- Operator norm and Hessian: a measure of the largest stretching a matrix or curvature matrix applies; the Hessian describes local curvature of the loss.
- Lean 4: a proof assistant in which mathematical statements and proofs are checked by computer.
- Width: the number of units in a hidden layer.
summary.one_liner: A Lean 4 machine-checked formalisation of the two-layer neural tangent kernel (NTK) convergence theorem for tanh networks, which also tightens the standard concentration-width bounds and flags a Hessian-norm obstacle to the usual linearisation argument.
summary.plain: Very wide neural networks trained by gradient descent are often claimed to behave in a simple, predictable way, and a known theory (neural tangent kernel theory) explains why. This paper rebuilds the main argument for a small two-layer network inside a computer proof assistant, so every step is checked by machine rather than by reading. The authors report that the checked proof holds with explicit width conditions and that the error shrinks exponentially over training time.
summary.why: Checking a standard theory line by line can catch hidden gaps, and the paper reports that its alternative variance bound gives concentration-width certificates 36 to 121 times smaller than the conventional one in the stated settings. The required widths remain far beyond practical sizes, and the text itself says this limits applicability, so the work is best read as a verification and sharpening exercise rather than a practical advance.

title: Verifying and Strengthening Neural Tangent Kernel Theory

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) develop rich internal representations of language, but whether their individual coordinate axes carry meaning, or whether meaning is encoded only in directions in representation space, is still an open question. A common assumption is that individual axes in LLMs are arbitrary. We here challenge this view: across 12 LLMs from six model families, the native axes are reliably more aligned with other models' representations, with human brain responses to language, and with interpretable linguistic features than randomly rotated axes that preserve the same geometry. The native axes nonetheless fall well short of the best achievable alignment, so LLM coordinates are not fully arbitrary but also not fully canonical: they are partially canonical. A theory of how LLMs represent language must explain both the population geometry they learn and why individual units acquire patterns of response profiles that recur across systems.
label: arXiv:2611.26920v1

summary.background:
- Hidden representation: the list of numbers a neural network produces internally for a piece of text.
- Coordinate axis: one of those numbered positions; rotating the whole space changes the axes but not the overall geometry of the points.
- Random rotation baseline: a control in which the same data is spun to a random orientation, to test whether the original axes are special.
- Representational alignment: a measure of how similar two systems' internal geometry is, used here to compare models with each other and with brain recordings.
- Interpretable linguistic features: properties such as part of speech or syntactic role that humans can name.
- Canonical vs. arbitrary axes: canonical means the axes pick out meaningful units; arbitrary means any rotation would work equally well.
summary.one_liner: Across 12 LLMs from six families, the native coordinate axes of hidden representations align better with other models, human brain responses, and interpretable linguistic features than randomly rotated axes with the same geometry, yet fall short of the best achievable alignment, so the axes are "partially canonical."
summary.plain: A common assumption is that the individual numbered slots inside a language model's internal state are arbitrary, and only whole directions carry meaning. This paper tests that by comparing the model's actual slots against versions of the same data rotated to a random orientation. The authors find the real slots match other models, human brain activity during language, and simple linguistic features somewhat better than the rotated versions, but not as well as the best possible alignment.
summary.why: If individual units in language models carry consistent meaning, that matters for interpreting how these systems work and for comparing them with brains. The paper's claim is a middle position rather than a full answer, and the text does not show how large or robust the effects are beyond the summary given.

title: Partially canonical axes in large language model representations

abstract: Personalized long-form generation asks a language model to write new text the way a specific user would. The standard recipe, retrieval-augmented generation, places a few of the user's past texts in the prompt but leaves the model to decide what to take from them. We introduce StylePrism, a taxonomy of 28 stylistic aspects in seven categories, and SP-Refine, an inference-time method that makes style extraction an explicit step: the model first fills StylePrism with the user's patterns, quoted evidence, and habits to avoid, then drafts from the user's samples and revises the draft twice against this profile, guided by its own style scores. On the three long-form tasks of LongLaMP with three LLMs, SP-Refine outperforms LongLaMP's retrieval-augmented baseline in 25 of 27 ROUGE and METEOR comparisons, by 10.2% on average and by up to 35.8%. Annotating users' own texts with the extracted profiles shows that StylePrism captures concrete, checkable habits, from the order of rhetorical moves to a reviewer's sign-off. Ablations show that the profile helps as revision guidance, not as a replacement for the samples: writing from the profile alone is worse in all 27 comparisons, while a single implicit-inference call is a cheaper alternative that comes close. Oracle variants that let the reviser see the reference, together with reference-free controls, show that larger refinement gains require information unavailable at inference time.
label: arXiv:2611.27211v1

summary.background:
- Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): putting relevant examples from a user's past into the model's prompt before it writes.
- Personalized long-form generation: producing multi-paragraph text that matches a specific person's style.
- ROUGE and METEOR: automatic scores that measure word overlap between generated text and a reference text; they are imperfect proxies for quality or style match.
- Inference-time method: a technique applied when the model is run, without retraining it.
- Ablation: a test that removes one component to see how much it contributes.
- Oracle variant: a version that peeks at the answer, used to estimate an upper bound.
summary.one_liner: SP-Refine makes style extraction an explicit inference-time step for personalized long-form generation, using a 28-aspect taxonomy (StylePrism) to build a user style profile that guides draft revision on LongLaMP tasks.
summary.plain: Language models that write in a particular person's voice usually get a few of that person's past texts pasted into the prompt and must work out the style on their own. This paper proposes a method where the model first writes down an explicit profile of the user's writing habits, with quoted examples, then drafts and revises against that profile. Across three long-form writing tasks and three models, the method beat the standard retrieval-based baseline in 25 of 27 ROUGE and METEOR comparisons, by 10.2% on average.
summary.why: Personalizing text generation is a practical goal for writing assistants, and the paper's ablations suggest the explicit profile works mainly as revision guidance rather than a replacement for the user's samples. Whether the gains carry over to real users and to other metrics is not shown in the text; the authors also note that larger gains depend on information unavailable at inference time.

title: Explicit Style Extraction for Personalized Long-Form Text Generation

abstract: Few-step diffusion distillation reduces sampling cost but often weakens adjustable classifier-free guidance (CFG) and runtime negative prompting. We introduce PP-CFG, an architecture that keeps positive and negative text conditions separate and combines their attention responses with opposite signs within a shared visual backbone. Its Scale-Time Polarity Mixer refines each condition using the guidance scale and denoising timestep, allowing prompt influence to vary throughout generation. The student retains a continuous scale input and selectable negative prompts with one visual backbone pass per step. We evaluate PP-CFG on Wan2.1 for video generation with distribution matching distillation (DMD), and on Qwen-Image with both latent consistency model (LCM) distillation and DMD. PP-CFG achieves 81.46 VBench in four steps and lower video teacher-student distances across guidance scales than step-distilled DMD. On NegElement-1K, our benchmark of 1,000 matched image and video prompt cases, it achieves higher target-removal rates than the corresponding teachers. These experiments support the method's generality across attention architectures, generation modalities, and distillation objectives while retaining competitive generation quality.
label: arXiv:2611.27266v1

summary.background:
- Diffusion models generate images or videos by starting from noise and removing it over many denoising steps.
- Distillation trains a faster "student" model with few steps to imitate a slower "teacher" model.
- Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is a dial that controls how strongly the output follows a text prompt.
- Negative prompts tell the model what to leave out of the output.
- Attention is the mechanism through which parts of the model weigh and combine information from the text and image.
- VBench is a standard benchmark suite for scoring video generation quality.
- Distribution matching distillation (DMD) and latent consistency models (LCM) are two specific distillation techniques named in the paper.
summary.one_liner: PP-CFG is a few-step diffusion distillation method that keeps positive and negative text conditions separate, combines their attention responses with opposite signs, and uses a scale-and-timestep mixer to keep adjustable classifier-free guidance and negative prompting for image and video generation.
summary.plain: Modern AI image and video generators often need many small refinement steps to produce output, and speeding them up by distilling them into fewer steps tends to remove the ability to fine-tune how strongly a prompt is followed or to tell the model what to avoid. This paper proposes a way to keep those controls in a four-step student model. The authors report results on video (Wan2.1) and image (Qwen-Image) generators, including a VBench score of 81.46 in four steps and higher target-removal rates on their own 1,000-case negative-prompt benchmark than the teacher models.
summary.why: Making generation both fast and controllable is a practical bottleneck for image and video tools, so a method that preserves guidance and negative prompts in few-step models is worth watching. The text supports claims across two backbones and two distillation methods, but the evaluation is described only at a high level and the benchmark is the authors' own, so the strength of the generality claim is not yet established.

title: PP-CFG: Polarity-Preserving Guidance for Controllable Few-Step Image and Video Generation

abstract: Learning representations of visual images is a challenging task. It requires extracting abstract patterns from high-dimensional data without explicit supervision. This becomes pronounced with 3D MR imaging due to sparse features, higher dimensional inputs, and smaller datasets. Many state-of-the-art representation learning algorithms successfully rely on transformers and diffusion-based architectures. However, these methods struggle with smaller datasets. In effect, solution methods relax the problem by slicing 3D volumes and solving the problem for 2D medical imaging, resulting in a loss of spatial 3D information. We present R2RG, a representation learning method based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) honing the reconstruction task. Our key insights lie in exploiting architectural biases in 3D CNNs, combined with data-efficient auto-encoding GANs and a composite loss function to enhance reconstruction fidelity and stabilize training. Our experiments on three standard datasets and a locally collected dataset show that R2RG not only achieves superior performance but also generalizes to heterogeneous and smaller datasets. Furthermore, representations learned with R2RG outperform those learned with contrastive-based representation learning methods on Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease classification. Our work demonstrates that reconstruction-based representation learning is a promising direction for 3D medical imaging under limited data availability.
label: arXiv:2611.27057v1

summary.background:
