- Representation learning: training a model to turn raw data into compact numerical features that other tasks can use.
- Reconstruction-based learning: learning by trying to rebuild the original input from its compressed form, with no human labels needed.
- Contrastive learning: learning by pulling similar examples together and pushing different ones apart in feature space; a common alternative.
- CNN (convolutional neural network): a common type of image model that detects local patterns; a 3D version works on volumes rather than flat images.
- GAN (generative adversarial network): two networks trained against each other, one generating images and one judging them, often used to make outputs look realistic.
- MRI: magnetic resonance imaging, which produces 3D scans of soft tissue such as the brain.
- Parkinson's and Alzheimer's classification: deciding from scans whether a patient has these diseases, used here as a test of the learned features.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes R2RG, a 3D CNN-based representation learning method that uses an auto-encoding GAN and a composite loss to learn reconstruction-based features from 3D MRI scans with limited data, reporting gains over contrastive methods on Parkinson's and Alzheimer's classification.
summary.plain: Medical scans like MRI are 3D, but many AI methods handle only flat 2D slices, which throws away depth information, and they often need more data than medical datasets provide. This paper presents a method that learns compact summaries of whole 3D brain MRI volumes by training a network to rebuild the scans, with a generative adversarial network (a pair of AI models that compete to make realistic images) helping sharpen the rebuilt results. The authors report that these learned summaries work across several datasets, including small ones, and perform better than certain competing approaches on Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease classification.
summary.why: Many medical AI tasks have little labelled data, so methods that learn useful features without labels could matter in clinical research. The text reports results on a few datasets, but it does not show how well the approach would hold up in routine clinical use, so its wider significance is still to be tested.

title: Learning 3D MRI Representations with Generative Adversarial Networks

abstract: Deep parallel cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (CMARL)} trains multiple agents that all act at every time step to optimize a common objective. Like single-agent RL, CMARL can produce unsafe behaviors that violate implicit safety requirements not captured by the reward, and these behaviors are hard to explain. However, testing CMARL policies for safety has received less attention than the safety testing of single-agent RL policies. In this paper, we propose DisQ, a test case selection method that identifies failure-revealing states in value-based CMARL by exploiting a signal specific to trained Q-learning agents. The signal is the Q-value gap, an explainable metric that flags a state when the agents' estimates of the achievable return diverge by more than a calibrated threshold. DisQ selects such states for execution and skips those without a gap. Our experiments in four CMARL benchmark environments show that, in most of the evaluated configurations, DisQ improves failure detection over single-agent RL testing methods applied to CMARL, namely random testing and search-based testing with genetic algorithms. Our main contributions are the Q-value gap, an indicator of potential miscoordination computable from a single state without executing the system, and DisQ, a test case selection method that adapts existing single-agent testing methods to CMARL.
label: arXiv:2611.27368v1

summary.background:
- Reinforcement learning: an AI learns by trying actions and receiving rewards.
- Multi-agent reinforcement learning: several agents learn at the same time, here aiming at one shared goal.
- Q-value: a learned estimate of the total future reward from taking an action in a given state.
- Coordination failure: agents' individual choices work against each other, so the team does badly.
- Test case selection: choosing which situations to run a system in, to find failures efficiently.
- Random testing and genetic-algorithm search: standard baseline methods for finding failures.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes DisQ, a test-case selection method that uses a "Q-value gap" (disagreement between agents' value estimates in a state) to find failure-revealing states when testing value-based cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning policies.
summary.plain: Teams of AI agents that learn to work together can behave unsafely in ways their reward signal does not capture, and those failures are hard to explain. This paper proposes a way to pick which situations to test by flagging states where the agents' estimates of future reward diverge beyond a set threshold. The authors report that, in most of four benchmark environments tested, this selection finds more failures than random testing or genetic-algorithm search methods borrowed from single-agent testing.
summary.why: Testing multi-agent systems for safety has received less attention than testing single agents, and the authors offer an explainable signal computable from one state without running the system. Its practical value beyond the four benchmarks evaluated is not established in the text.

title: Testing for Coordination Failures in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) from verifiable outcomes gives a language agent one reward per episode: every step is credited alike, and nothing about the task is learned when all rollouts fail. The last mile, step-level credit, usually requires step labels, a learned critic, costly LLM judges or hand-written rules. We introduce DM-PRM, which turns a general-purpose decision model -- one answering yes/no questions with probabilities -- into a general-purpose process reward model (PRM), zero-shot: no step labels, no fine-tuning, no critic. DM-PRM asks one question per step and adds the standardised answers to the advantage. It plugs into any policy-gradient method; one model, with one question text per environment, serves household tasks, web shopping and multiple RL methods. With Qwen2.5-1.5B it lifts GRPO by over twenty points on ALFWorld and over ten on WebShop, overtakes GiGPO on ALFWorld and learns in far fewer iterations; it also improves GiGPO and GraphGPO on both benchmarks and reaches the highest success of our comparison, ahead of critic-based PPO and of state-of-the-art GiGPO, HGPO and GraphGPO. Its scores locate useful steps in failed rollouts, and trained agents drop idle actions and explore instead of circling. DM-PRM shows that step credit need not be learned: it can be asked for.
label: arXiv:2611.27068v1

summary.background:
- Reinforcement learning (RL): training by trial and reward; here an AI language agent learns from task success or failure.
- Policy gradient: a family of RL update rules that make good actions more likely.
- Reward and credit assignment: deciding which steps in a long attempt deserve the credit or blame for the result.
- Process reward model (PRM): a scorer that rates intermediate steps, not just the final outcome.
- Advantage: how much better an action turned out than expected; used to scale the learning update.
- GRPO, PPO, GiGPO, HGPO, GraphGPO: named RL training methods for language agents; PPO uses a learned critic.
- ALFWorld and WebShop: simulated benchmarks for household tasks and online shopping.
- Zero-shot: used without task-specific training.
summary.one_liner: DM-PRM turns a general-purpose yes/no decision model into a zero-shot, step-level process reward that is added to the advantage in policy-gradient RL for language agents, evaluated on ALFWorld and WebShop.
summary.plain: Training AI agents with reinforcement learning usually gives one score at the end of a whole attempt, so the agent cannot tell which individual steps helped. This paper proposes asking a general yes/no question about each step, using a model's probability answer as a step-by-step score, without extra labels or training. The authors report that this improves the GRPO training method on two household and web-shopping task benchmarks, and that it helps other methods too.
summary.why: It offers a way to get per-step credit without hand-made step labels or a separately trained critic, which are costly to build. Whether this holds beyond the two benchmarks and one small model (Qwen2.5-1.5B) is not shown in the text, so its broader value remains to be tested.

title: Decision Models Are General-Purpose Process Reward Models

abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has become an important component in the post-training of diffusion models. In practice, however, standard RL often improves the target reward without reliably preserving holistic generation quality, leading to unstable reward-quality trade-offs that we view as a form of reward hacking. Since Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) is known to improve visual clarity, prompt alignment, and perceptual quality in generation, we investigate whether its underlying structure can serve as a useful prior during RL. We present a unified geometric view that interprets both CFG and RL as correction vectors in a common prediction space, and identify the projection of the RL-induced correction onto the pretrained CFG correction as a useful diagnostic of quality-related structural preservation. Geometric analysis and rotation intervention further show that the pretrained CFG direction carries information useful for generation quality that reward-driven RL updates do not necessarily preserve. Based on this insight, we propose Conditional Contrast Regularization (CCR), which uses the frozen reference model's conditional contrast as a local structural prior during RL. Experiments across multiple reward settings and backbones show that CCR more consistently preserves generation quality while maintaining competitive reward, yielding a better reward-quality trade-off than standard RL and generic regularization methods.
label: arXiv:2611.27288v1

summary.background:
- Diffusion models: image generators that start from noise and refine it step by step.
- Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training: adjusting a trained model to maximize a score (reward) on its outputs.
- Reward hacking: the model improves the score in ways that do not reflect the real goal.
- Classifier-free guidance (CFG): a standard sampling technique that pushes outputs toward the prompt, improving clarity and alignment.
- Correction vectors: the difference between a model's prediction and a baseline, used here to compare CFG and RL updates geometrically.
- Frozen reference model: a copy of the original model whose weights are not updated, used as an anchor.
- Regularization: an extra penalty that keeps training close to a desired behavior.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes Conditional Contrast Regularization (CCR), which uses the frozen pretrained model's classifier-free guidance direction as a structural prior to keep diffusion-model generation quality from degrading during reinforcement-learning fine-tuning for a target reward.
summary.plain: Image-generating AI models are often fine-tuned with reinforcement learning to score higher on a chosen reward, but this can make the images worse overall even as the score rises. The authors treat this as a kind of reward hacking and look at a built-in guidance technique (classifier-free guidance) that already makes images clearer and better aligned with prompts. They use it as a reference point to keep the fine-tuning from drifting away from good-quality behavior.
summary.why: Reward-driven fine-tuning that quietly lowers overall quality is a practical concern for deployed generative models, and this work offers a concrete, cheap regularizer tied to an existing component. Its broader significance beyond the reported experiments is not established by the text, which describes results only across unspecified reward settings and backbones.

title: Preserving Pretrained CFG Structure in RL for Diffusion Models with Conditional Contrast Regularization

abstract: Large language models behave differently across languages, and are noticeably less safe in lower-resource languages. This gap is well established behaviorally, but not mechanistically. Directions in activation space, including the assistant persona direction, are almost always extracted from English and assumed to generalize across languages. We extract the assistant persona direction in 31 languages in Qwen3-32B, and find that the resulting axes differ substantially: their cosine similarity to the English axis ranges from 0.378 to 0.911. Moreover, each language's assistant persona direction and its magnitude are correlated with the language's resource level. We also find that the model's default assistant state is farther from the helpful assistant pole in lower-resource languages. Finally, steering against a language's own axis amplifies persona-based jailbreak more than steering against the English axis. These results indicate that the model does not carry a single assistant representation across languages. More broadly, the assistant persona may need to be an explicit target of multilingual alignment.
label: arXiv:2611.27504v1

summary.background:
- Activation space: the set of internal numerical states a neural network passes through when processing text.
- Direction: a particular axis in that space; a "persona direction" is one linked to a role or personality the model adopts.
- Cosine similarity: a score from -1 to 1 for how closely two directions point the same way; 1 means identical.
- Steering: nudging the model's internal activations along a direction to change its behavior.
- Jailbreak: a prompt crafted to get a model to ignore its safety rules.
- Resource level: how much text data exists for a language; "lower-resource" languages have less.
- Qwen3-32B: a specific open large language model with 32 billion parameters.
summary.one_liner: The paper extracts an "assistant persona" direction in activation space for 31 languages in Qwen3-32B and finds that these directions differ across languages, correlate with resource level, and affect how steering changes jailbreak susceptibility.
summary.plain: Language models are known to be less safe in languages with less training data. This paper looks inside a model to ask whether its internal "helpful assistant" setting is the same across languages. The authors found that the internal direction for this persona differs noticeably from language to language, and that the differences track how much data each language has.
summary.why: It offers a mechanistic, inside-the-model account of a safety gap that has so far mostly been measured from outside through behavior. The text suggests that multilingual alignment may need to target the assistant persona directly, though the findings come from a single model and the text does not show whether this carries over to other models.

title: The Assistant Persona Differs Across Languages in Activation Space

abstract: Causal Abstraction defines a notion of \emph{equivalence} between a neural network and an algorithm, thus serving as a powerful framework for mechanistic interpretability. In this paper, however, we show the existence of a class of \emph{spurious features} which straightforwardly pass such equivalence tests. Suppose there are two directions in a model's representation space where: (i) one discriminates the input based on some feature, and (ii) the other steers the model towards a certain output. Interpretability methods based on Causal Abstraction (e.g., Distributed Alignment Search) can \emph{spuriously} simulate these directions' combined behavior by leveraging pathways passing through them, giving the impression that the model implements this feature. In such cases, we say the method discovered a \defn{parasite feature}. Experimentally, we show that Distributed Alignment Search finds parasite features using linear alignment maps in two tasks: syntactic agreement and two-digit addition. Our paper highlights an important consideration for Causal Abstraction and contributes to the ongoing debate about best practices for mechanistic interpretability.
label: arXiv:2611.26711v1

summary.background:
- Neural network "representation space": the internal numerical state of a model, where concepts can be encoded as directions.
- Mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering what internal parts of a model do.
- Causal abstraction: testing whether a network's internal computation matches a simpler algorithm by intervening on internal states and checking that outputs match.
- Distributed Alignment Search (DAS): a method that learns a linear map to find directions in the network that correspond to an algorithm's variables.
- Spurious feature: something that looks like the real mechanism in a test but is not actually what the model relies on.
summary.one_liner: The paper shows that Distributed Alignment Search, a causal-abstraction interpretability method, can be fooled into crediting a neural network with a feature it does not actually use, via "parasite features" formed by two directions in representation space that together pass equivalence tests.
summary.plain: Researchers study how to check whether a neural network does a task in the same way a human-written algorithm would. They argue that a common checking method can be fooled: two separate directions inside the network, one that sorts inputs by some feature and one that pushes the output toward an answer, can together mimic the intended behavior. The method then appears to show the network uses that feature when it may not. They test this on grammar agreement and two-digit addition.
summary.why: Causal abstraction is a leading tool for explaining what neural networks compute, so a case where it gives false positives matters for how its results should be read. The text does not say how widespread this failure is in practice, and it only reports experiments on two tasks.

title: Parasite Features: Causal Abstraction Through Spurious Pathways

abstract: As the capabilities of large language models keep improving, traditional mechanistic interpretability methods struggle to keep pace. In contrast, trainable introspection methods emerge as a promising alternative; they repurpose the model itself as a self-diagnostic tool, trained to verbalize what it has learned during finetuning in natural language. While training on datasets of finetuned experts achieves encouraging results, it currently lacks robustness and generalization. Building on the data augmentation framework of MiXup, we introduce WaXup, a method that augments the introspection training set through linear interpolation in the weight space. This is motivated by the linear mode connectivity property: weight averaged experts interpolate the behaviors of the initial experts. We evaluate WaXup on three benchmarks: hidden-behavior models, a meta-dataset of real-world NLP tasks and AuditBench, a challenging alignment auditing suite of models adversarially trained to conceal their behaviors. WaXup improves the accuracy of generated descriptions as well as robustness to various distribution shifts. We hope to improve the reliability of trainable introspection methods towards better and safer models.
label: arXiv:2611.27353v1

summary.background:
- Mechanistic interpretability: studying a model's internal parts (weights and activations) to understand what it computes.
- Finetuning: extra training of a general model on a narrow task or behavior, producing a specialized "expert" version.
- Introspection (here): training a model to describe, in natural language, the behavior it acquired during finetuning.
- Weight space and weight averaging: each model is a long list of numbers (weights); blending two such lists gives a model whose behavior is often between the originals.
- Linear mode connectivity: the observation that some finetuned models can be averaged without losing performance, suggesting they lie in a smooth region together.
- Data augmentation: creating extra training examples from existing ones to make learning more robust. MiXup, the framework built on, is a related augmentation method.
- Alignment auditing and AuditBench: checking whether a model has hidden or concealed behaviors; AuditBench is a suite of models adversarially trained to hide theirs.
summary.one_liner: WaXup augments the training data for trainable introspection (models trained to describe their own finetuned behaviors) by linearly interpolating weights of finetuned experts, motivated by linear mode connectivity, and evaluates it on hidden-behavior models, a real-world NLP meta-dataset, and AuditBench.
summary.plain: Researchers are trying to get AI language models to explain, in plain words, what they were taught during extra training, rather than relying on hard-to-read technical inspection of their internals. This paper proposes WaXup, which creates extra training examples by blending the settings of several specialized versions of a model. The authors report that this improves how accurately the model describes its behaviors and how well it holds up when the test situations change.
summary.why: Being able to ask a model what it has learned, and trust the answer, could help people audit models for hidden or concealed behaviors, which matters for safety. The text reports gains in accuracy and robustness but gives limited detail on size or scale of those gains, so its practical impact is not yet clear.

title: WaXup: Weight Averaging of Experts as Data Augmentation for Robust Introspection

abstract: Large language model (LLM) theorem solvers differ in both proving capability and inference cost. Applying an expensive solver to every subgoal wastes computation when cheaper models are sufficient, while always starting from the cheapest solver wastes attempts on subgoals that require stronger models. We present BudgetPV, an agentic budget-aware predict-and-verify system that allocates computation across unresolved subgoals and heterogeneous LLM solvers. BudgetPV uses a cross-solver predictor to guide solver selection for each subgoal and revises the allocation as verification feedback becomes available. The allocation problem changes as proving progresses. Early decisions mainly determine which solver should handle an untried subgoal, while later decisions determine which previously attempted subgoals should receive additional computation. We train the predictor with two objectives for these two stages. Class-weighted cross-entropy improves assignment to less frequent stronger solvers during the initial stage, while plain cross-entropy provides better calibrated probabilities for later allocation among previously attempted subgoals. We evaluate BudgetPV on Lean Workbook, miniF2F, ProofNet, and PutnamBench using three progressively expanded solver settings: a strong but expensive solver alone, adding a medium-cost solver with intermediate solving capability, and further adding a cheap solver with lower solving capability. BudgetPV requires less LLM generation computation than uniform allocation to solve the same number of subgoals across the evaluated settings. The experiments further show the computation savings obtained as medium- and lower-cost solvers are added.
label: arXiv:2611.26906v1

summary.background:
- Theorem proving: a formal proof is checked by a computer; here the proof assistant is Lean.
- Subgoal: a smaller statement that must be proved on the way to the full theorem.
- LLM solver: a language model that tries to write a proof; solvers differ in skill and cost.
- Predict-and-verify: a predictor guesses which solver is likely to succeed, and the proof checker confirms the result.
- Cross-entropy: a standard training loss for classification; class weighting makes rare classes count more.
- Calibrated probabilities: predicted probabilities that match how often the outcomes actually occur.
- Benchmarks named: Lean Workbook, miniF2F, ProofNet, PutnamBench.
summary.one_liner: BudgetPV is an agentic predict-and-verify system that uses a cross-solver predictor, trained with two different loss objectives for early and late allocation stages, to route Lean subgoals across heterogeneous LLM provers under a compute budget.
summary.plain: Automatic theorem provers use AI language models to break math proofs into smaller pieces, but some models are costly and others are cheap. This paper describes a way to decide which model should try each piece, and how to spend more effort on pieces that are still unsolved. The authors report that their method used less model computation than giving every piece the same effort, while solving the same number of pieces on four math benchmarks.
summary.why: Running large models on every step of a formal proof is expensive, so a better way to split effort across models could make automated proving cheaper. The text does not say how large the savings are in absolute terms or how the approach compares with other budget-allocation methods, so its wider significance is uncertain.

title: Budget-Aware Predict-and-Verify Theorem Proving with Heterogeneous LLM Solvers

abstract: High accuracy on mathematical benchmarks does not establish whether reasoning remains reliable as problem complexity increases. We examine how executable symbolic representations change accuracy scaling in large language models compared with natural-language reasoning. To address this limitation, we introduce the GSM Arithmetic Benchmark (GSM-AB), a controlled benchmark that independently varies operand digit length and operation count to probe numerical scale and compositional complexity. We find that executable representations can improve accuracy and slow its decline as complexity increases. Lean reduces average sensitivity to operand digit length at every tested model size. By contrast, slower degradation with increasing operation count emerges at the larger model sizes. A Python program-of-thought (Python-PoT) control shows a similar operation-axis pattern, suggesting that this finding is not specific to Lean. These findings show that reasoning representation shapes arithmetic accuracy scaling and support executable symbolic representations for more reliable reasoning on complex arithmetic tasks.
label: arXiv:2611.27203v1

summary.background:
- LLM: a large language model, an AI system trained on text that generates answers from patterns learned in data.
- Natural-language reasoning: the model writes out its steps in ordinary sentences.
- Executable symbolic representation: the model writes its reasoning as formal code or proof that a computer can run and check.
- Lean: a proof assistant language used to write machine-checkable mathematics.
- Program-of-thought (PoT): a method where the model writes a short program to compute the answer rather than doing the arithmetic in its head.
- Operand digit length: how many digits the numbers in a problem have.
- Operation count: how many calculation steps a problem requires.
- Accuracy scaling: how accuracy changes as problems get harder.
summary.one_liner: The paper introduces GSM-AB, a benchmark that separately varies operand digit length and operation count, and reports that executable symbolic representations (Lean, with a Python program-of-thought control) slow accuracy decline in LLM arithmetic reasoning compared with natural-language reasoning.
summary.plain: Large language models often score well on math tests, but that does not show whether they stay accurate when problems get harder. The authors built a controlled test where they could separately make numbers longer and make problems involve more steps. They report that having models write answers as runnable formal or code-based programs (Lean and Python) kept accuracy higher and made it fall more slowly than plain-language reasoning.
summary.why: Reliability on harder, multi-step calculations is a practical concern for using AI in math and science, so a method that makes accuracy degrade more gently is relevant. The text does not report how large the effects are or how broadly they hold beyond the tested models, so its significance should be treated as provisional.

title: Improved Accuracy Scaling with Problem Complexity in LLM Arithmetic Reasoning Using Executable Symbolic Representations

abstract: Humanoid robots can reduce personnel exposure in electrical switching, but safe control is challenging because the tool must reach a target switch next to similar devices, where an imprecise operator command can contact a non-target switch. This study proposes a runtime safety filter that checks each operator command during virtual-reality teleoperation of a humanoid robot. The filter integrates a scene model estimated from the robot head camera and a target-conditioned control barrier function quadratic program that keeps the tool away from the non-target switch while passing safe commands unchanged. In real-world experiments on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot, with six rounds at each of two standing positions, target operations succeed in all ten rounds with an unchanged target and no non-target actuation. A simulation study achieves 9/9 safe completions, compared with 5/9 for raw teleoperation, demonstrating the feasibility of the method for humanoid switching operations.
label: arXiv:2611.27845v1

summary.background:
- Humanoid robot: a human-shaped robot with arms, legs and a head camera.
- Teleoperation: a person controls the robot remotely, here through virtual reality.
- Scene model: a computer's estimate of where objects are, built from camera images.
- Control barrier function (CBF): a mathematical boundary that keeps a system inside a safe region.
- Quadratic program (QP): an optimisation step that finds the closest safe version of a command.
- Safety filter: a layer that passes safe commands unchanged and corrects unsafe ones.
- Simulation vs. real-world test: simulation is a computer model; real-world tests use the physical robot.
summary.one_liner: A runtime safety filter that screens each operator command during VR teleoperation of a humanoid robot, using a head-camera scene model and a target-conditioned control barrier function quadratic program to keep the tool clear of a non-target electrical switch.
summary.plain: The paper looks at using humanoid robots to flip electrical switches so workers stay out of harm's way. The main risk is that a slightly imprecise remote command could make the robot's tool touch a neighbouring switch that should not be touched. The authors add a software filter that checks each command before it reaches the robot and adjusts only the unsafe ones, and they report it worked in ten real-robot trials on a Unitree G1 and in a simulation study.
summary.why: Electrical switching is a real safety hazard for people, so a way to let robots do it with fewer errors is worth watching. The text reports small-scale tests only, so it shows feasibility rather than readiness for field use.

title: Humanoid robots for safety-critical electrical switching: A perception-informed runtime constraint filter

abstract: As humanoid robots increasingly enter real-world environments, recovering their 3D whole-body pose from monocular imagery is becoming increasingly important for external state perception, motion analysis, and robot learning. However, Humanoid Robot Pose Estimation (HRPE) lies at the intersection of conventional Robot Pose Estimation (RPE) and Human Pose Estimation (HPE), while not being fully addressed by either paradigm: RPE primarily focuses on non-humanoid robots, particularly fixed-base manipulators, whereas HPE is built upon human-specific skeletal topologies, body models, and motion priors. Despite recent progress in humanoid 2D keypoint detection and HPE adaptation, humanoid-native 3D pose recovery remains insufficiently studied, and a dedicated benchmark with suitable training data and evaluation protocols is still lacking. To address this gap, we introduce Humanoids, a benchmark for monocular 3D humanoid robot pose estimation, and propose HumanoidPose, a framework for this task. Humanoids provides synthetic 3D supervision across diverse humanoid embodiments, manually annotated real-world 2D data, and real-world RGB sequences paired with robot states for 3D evaluation on a physical Roban humanoid. HumanoidPose combines human-inspired visual perception with robot articulation modeling and explicit kinematic grounding. Experiments on Humanoids and the DHRP-H1 benchmark demonstrate strong performance in articulation recovery and 3D pose estimation, including zero-shot transfer to real-world 2D and 3D evaluation. Ablation studies further show the contribution of robot-native articulation modeling and explicit kinematic grounding. The dataset and code will be publicly released to support future research in the community.
label: arXiv:2611.27181v1

summary.background:
- Pose estimation: finding the positions and angles of a body's joints from an image.
- 2D vs 3D pose: 2D is joint locations in the picture; 3D adds depth and the true spatial arrangement of the joints.
- Monocular: using a single camera, with no depth sensor or stereo pair.
- Kinematics: the rules describing how connected links and joints move, such as limb lengths and joint angle limits.
- Synthetic data: computer-generated training images with known ground-truth poses.
- Zero-shot transfer: applying a model to new data it was not trained on, without extra tuning.
- Benchmark: a shared dataset and test protocol for fair comparison between methods.
summary.one_liner: HumanoidPose introduces the Humanoids benchmark and a monocular framework for recovering the 3D whole-body pose of humanoid robots from single camera images, using robot articulation modeling and explicit kinematic grounding.
summary.plain: Humanoid robots are becoming more common, and it is useful to know their full body posture from an ordinary camera image. Existing tools were built either for factory-style robot arms or for human bodies, so they fit humanoid robots poorly. This paper provides a benchmark with synthetic and hand-labeled training data, plus a method called HumanoidPose that is designed for humanoid bodies.
summary.why: Estimating a robot's posture from a camera, without extra sensors, could support monitoring, motion analysis, and robot learning. The text reports strong results on its own benchmark and on the DHRP-H1 benchmark, including zero-shot transfer to real-world data, but the abstract gives no comparison numbers, so its practical impact is not yet clear.

title: HumanoidPose: Monocular 3D Pose Estimation for Humanoid Robots

abstract: Migrating brownfield 5G Core networks to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is difficult because deployed network functions, base images, and TLS libraries evolve under different upgrade constraints. This paper evaluates a deployment-controlled migration strategy that enables hybrid post-quantum/traditional key establishment through externally deployed Boundary Cryptographic Execution Entities (BCEEs), without modifying participating network function source code. The approach is evaluated using the Open5GS AMF-NRF Service-Based Interface as a representative 5G Core scenario. Classical and hybrid configurations are compared under an unchanged mediation topology. Packet-level analysis confirms successful negotiation of X25519MLKEM768, and functional validation demonstrates that representative SBI procedures remain operational through the mediated path. In 120 NF-registration transactions, the median AMF-facing registration latency increased from 22.968 ms under the classical state to 26.351 ms under the hybrid state, reflecting a 3.383 ms (14.73 percent) increase, with a whole-block 95 percent confidence interval of [1.193, 7.872] ms. At the mediated TLS boundary, the hybrid configuration shows a 4.599 ms higher median segment-local TLS-establishment time than the classical configuration. These two reported differences reflect system-level runtime effects and do not isolate key-encapsulation cost. Packet evidence verifies rollback from hybrid-mediated operation to classical mediated operation and, separately, restoration of the native direct path. NF-facing compatibility legs remained plaintext and outside the hybrid post-quantum scope. The results demonstrate a packet-verifiable and manually reversible brownfield mechanism for introducing hybrid post-quantum key establishment on a controlled 5G SBI segment.
label: arXiv:2611.27735v1

summary.background:
- 5G Core: the software that runs the central part of a mobile network, split into network functions (such as AMF and NRF) that talk over a Service-Based Interface (SBI).
- Open5GS: an open-source implementation of the 5G Core used for the experiments.
- TLS: the standard protocol that encrypts connections; it begins with a key-establishment handshake.
- Post-quantum cryptography (PQC): encryption designed to resist attacks from future quantum computers.
- Hybrid key establishment: combining a classical method (X25519) with a post-quantum one (ML-KEM-768, named X25519MLKEM768), so security holds if either one is unbroken.
- Brownfield: an existing, already-deployed system that must be changed gradually.
- Rollback: returning a system to its earlier working configuration.
- Median and confidence interval: the middle value of measurements, and a range that expresses the uncertainty in the estimated difference.
summary.one_liner: A deployment-controlled method for adding hybrid post-quantum/classical key establishment to an unmodified Open5GS AMF-NRF 5G Service-Based Interface via external boundary cryptographic entities, with packet-level verification, latency measurements, and rollback tests.
summary.plain: Phone networks use encryption to protect messages between their internal software components, and future quantum computers could eventually break some of the math that current encryption relies on. This paper looks at how an existing (brownfield) 5G core network can be upgraded to newer, quantum-resistant key exchange without changing the software of the network functions themselves, by routing traffic through external mediating units. In a lab test on one representative link, the authors found the new handshake worked and the network kept functioning, with a median registration delay rising from about 23 ms to about 26 ms, and they could switch back to the old setup.
summary.why: Operators running large networks cannot rebuild everything at once, so a way to add quantum-resistant encryption to deployed software without code changes is a practical question for the telecom security field. The results come from a single controlled testbed and one interface, so they say little yet about production networks or about the cost of the key exchange alone.

title: Post-Quantum Migration in Brownfield 5G Core Networks: Verified Hybrid Key Establishment, Performance, and Rollback

abstract: The MoT virtual environment, called the Metaverse of Things (MoT), combines machine learning (ML) and Internet of Things (IoT) to offer significant business opportunities in various sectors such as entertainment, healthcare, and education. In addition to its benefits, the MoT poses risks to privacy and security through unauthorized access, which threatens trustworthiness. While traditional intrusion detection systems (IDS) exist to handle this challenge, they struggle with high-dimensional data and poor interpretability. To address this challenge, the research conducted a thorough analysis of different ML models and proposed the optimal model to secure the MoT environment. The research employed explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to identify the most effective features that contributed to optimal model selection. The research presented an optimal framework combining ML and XAI to safeguard MoT networks from the most recent cyberthreats. The research used three advanced benchmark security datasets: ToN-IoT, CIC-IoT-2023, and BoT-IoT, to examine the XAI-based intrusion detection framework. The XAI-based intrusion detection framework achieved 99.83% accuracy on ToN-IoT and 96.45% on CIC-IoT-2023 using the XGBoost model. On the BoT-IoT dataset, the Random Forest (RF) and Extra Trees (ET) classifiers reached 99.99% accuracy. The Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) techniques used for XAI further enhanced feature relevance and user confidence in the optimal model.
label: arXiv:2611.27199v1

summary.background:
- Intrusion detection system (IDS): software that watches network traffic and flags suspicious or malicious activity.
- Internet of Things (IoT): everyday devices (sensors, cameras, appliances) connected to the internet.
- Metaverse of Things: a concept linking virtual environments with IoT devices.
- Machine learning (ML): algorithms that learn patterns from example data to make predictions, here classifying traffic as normal or attack.
- Classifiers named in the text: XGBoost, Random Forest, and Extra Trees are common types of ML models.
- Explainable AI (XAI): methods that show why a model made a particular decision.
- SHAP and LIME: two popular XAI techniques that estimate how much each input feature contributed to a prediction.
- Accuracy and benchmark datasets: accuracy is the share of correct classifications; benchmark datasets are shared test collections used to compare methods.
summary.one_liner: The paper compares machine learning models for intrusion detection in Internet-of-Things-linked metaverse environments across three benchmark datasets (ToN-IoT, CIC-IoT-2023, BoT-IoT), and uses SHAP and LIME explainability methods to identify influential features and justify the chosen model.
summary.plain: The paper looks at how to spot unauthorized access in the "Metaverse of Things," a setting where virtual worlds are linked to connected physical devices. The authors tested several machine learning models on three public security datasets and chose the best performers, reporting accuracy of 99.83% on ToN-IoT and 96.45% on CIC-IoT-2023 with XGBoost, and 99.99% on BoT-IoT with Random Forest and Extra Trees. They also used explanation tools to show which data features drove those decisions.
summary.why: Intrusion detection systems that are hard to interpret are harder for operators to trust and check, so pairing high accuracy with explanations speaks to a practical concern for connected devices and virtual platforms. The text does not show how these results hold up in real deployments, and the datasets are benchmarks, so real-world performance remains unclear.

title: Enhancing Metaverse Security using Explainable AI-based Intrusion Detection Framework

abstract: We study the time complexity of finding a Tarski fixed point. We provide a subexponential-time reduction from the Unique End of Potential Line (UEOPL) problem to the problem of finding a Tarski fixed point. Using a range of known cryptographic lower bounds for UEOPL, our reduction implies a range of conditional lower bounds on the running time of any algorithm that finds a Tarski fixed point. The strongest of these give quasi-polynomial-time lower bounds for the problem. We also obtain a similar quasi-polynomial-time lower bound for Tarski based instead on a weak exponential-time type hypothesis for UEOPL. These running time lower bounds match the recently discovered quasi-polynomial query lower bounds for the problem.
label: arXiv:2611.27977v1

summary.background:
- Fixed point: an input that the rule maps back to itself.
- Tarski fixed point: the guaranteed fixed point of a monotone map on a lattice (an ordered grid), which exists by Tarski's theorem but may be hard to locate.
- Polynomial time vs. quasi-polynomial time: efficient algorithms grow polynomially with input size; quasi-polynomial time grows slightly faster but still far slower than exponential.
- Reduction: a way of showing one problem is at least as hard as another by converting instances of one into instances of the other.
- UEOPL (Unique End of Potential Line): a search problem in a class believed to be hard, used here as the source of hardness.
- Cryptographic lower bounds: results that rest on widely believed assumptions about the difficulty of breaking cryptographic primitives.
- Query lower bound: a limit on how many times an algorithm must query the input, as opposed to total running time.
summary.one_liner: The paper gives a subexponential-time reduction from UEOPL to Tarski fixed-point finding, yielding conditional quasi-polynomial running-time lower bounds that match known query lower bounds.
summary.plain: The paper studies how fast a computer can find a "Tarski fixed point," a point that stays put when a rule that only ever pushes things in one consistent direction is applied to a grid of options. The authors show that solving this problem could be used to solve a different, known-hard search problem (UEOPL) with only a modest overhead. Their result is that, if certain cryptographic assumptions hold, no algorithm can solve Tarski fixed points in polynomial time.
summary.why: It moves the known query lower bounds for this problem to conditional running-time lower bounds, which is a stronger kind of hardness statement. The connection to cryptographic assumptions means the conclusion holds only if those assumptions are true, so it is a conditional result rather than an unconditional proof.

title: No Polynomial-Time Algorithm For Tarski Fixed Points Unless Cryptographic Assumptions Fail

abstract: A crucial property of bounded-variable fragments of first-order logic is that they can be evaluated in polynomial time. It is therefore a useful preprocessing step to rewrite, if possible, a first-order query to a logically equivalent one with a minimum number of variables. However, it may occur that reducing the number of variables causes an increase in formula size. We investigate this trade-off for the existential-positive fragment of first-order queries, where variable minimisation is decidable in general. In particular, we study the blow-up in the formula size when compiling existential-positive queries to the bounded variable fragment of positive first-order logic. While the increase of the formula size is always at most exponential, we identify situations (based on the signature and the number of variables) where only a polynomial blow-up is needed. In all other cases, we show that an exponential lower bound on the formula size of the compiled formula that matches the general upper bound. This exponential lower bound is unconditional, and is the first unconditional lower bound for formula size with respect to the studied compilation; it is proved via establishing a novel interface with circuit complexity which may be of future interest.
label: arXiv:2611.26869v1

summary.background:
- First-order logic: a formal language for statements about objects, using quantifiers such as "for all" and "there exists".
- Existential-positive queries: queries built only from "there exists", "and", "or" and atomic conditions, with no negation or "for all".
- Variable count: the number of distinct variable names a formula uses; bounded-variable fragments restrict this number.
- Polynomial vs. exponential: polynomial growth is manageable; exponential growth means length can blow up very quickly with input size.
- Formula size: the length or number of symbols in a formula, which the paper treats as the cost of rewriting.
- Circuit complexity: the study of how large Boolean circuits (networks of logic gates) must be to compute functions; used here to prove the lower bound.
- Unconditional lower bound: a proof that does not rely on an unproven assumption such as P not equal to NP.
summary.one_liner: The paper studies the formula-size cost of rewriting existential-positive first-order queries into the bounded-variable fragment of positive first-order logic, giving exponential upper bounds, polynomial bounds in some signature and variable regimes, and an unconditional exponential lower bound proved via circuit complexity.
summary.plain: Database-style queries can often be rewritten using fewer variable names, which makes them faster to evaluate. This paper asks what that rewriting costs: the rewritten query may become much longer. The authors show the growth in length is at most exponential, identify cases where it is only polynomial, and prove that in the remaining cases an exponential increase is unavoidable.
summary.why: The result gives a provable limit on a common preprocessing trade-off: fewer variables help evaluation, but the formula can grow sharply. The lower bound is described as the first unconditional one for this kind of compilation, and the circuit-complexity link is said to be of possible future interest; the text does not show further practical consequences.

title: Compiling Existential-Positive Queries to Bounded-Variable Fragments

abstract: The fundamental changes in software engineering driven by generative AI will have profound effects not only on the number of available software engineering jobs but also on what software engineering itself looks like. As the career evolves, questions arise about what the skillset and interests of the next generation of software engineers will be and whether long-time engineers will continue to be attracted to the career. In this paper, we contribute to answering these questions by studying how software development with AI tools is perceived to differ from traditional development and how the differences are modulated by years of programming experience. We find that, in terms of programming activities, engineers report less talking with peers about technical problems, less decomposition, less searching of documentation, and less using a debugger, while they report more task switching. We also find experiential differences, including less deep focus and less sense of control over code and design. We call these the different craft results, in contrast to core code-production activities such as writing, refactoring, and fixing code, which show only small mean differences. We also find that these differences are amplified by years of programming experience (an experience gradient), with software engineers who started programming before the age of generative AI perceiving greater changes in both activity and developer experience. We discuss our findings and their implications on training of the next generation of engineers and on engineers who may have difficulty transitioning to the AI-infused world of software engineering.
label: arXiv:2611.27947v1

summary.background:
- Generative AI: software that produces text or code in response to prompts, such as coding assistants.
- Software engineering "craft" activities: decomposing problems (breaking them into smaller parts), searching documentation, debugging, and refactoring (reorganizing code without changing what it does).
- Self-reported survey data: the findings are based on what engineers say about their own work, not on direct observation.
- Experience gradient: a pattern where the size of an effect grows with years of experience.
summary.one_liner: A study of how software engineers perceive their activities and experience differ when developing with generative AI tools versus traditional methods, and how those differences vary with years of programming experience.
summary.plain: This paper looks at how programmers feel their daily work has changed now that they use AI tools to write software. Based on what engineers report, they talk less with peers about technical problems, break work down less, search documentation less, and use debuggers less, while switching between tasks more and feeling less deep focus and less control over code and design. Core coding tasks like writing, refactoring, and fixing code show only small differences, and the changes are larger for engineers who started programming before generative AI existed.
summary.why: It matters for how the next generation of engineers is trained and whether experienced engineers will stay in the field and adapt. The text reports perceptions rather than measured performance, so it shows how people feel their work has changed, not whether the changes improve or harm software quality.

title: Perceived Differences in Activity and Experience Between Developing Software With and Without AI

abstract: The correctness of modern effectful programs depends not only on their final results but also on the temporal evolution of observable interactions with their environments. Interaction Trees (ITrees) provide a reusable denotational semantics for such programs by representing effectful computations as potentially infinite trees of observable interactions. However, reusable temporal reasoning over ITrees remains largely unexplored. This paper presents a compositional temporal specification framework for ITrees. We introduce iBuchi, a shallowly embedded temporal specification language based on Choice Trees, which represents finite and infinite interaction traces and supports expressive temporal operators, including sequencing, branching, conjunction, repetition, and Linear Temporal Logic modalities. We define trace- and tree-level satisfaction relations between iBuchi specifications and ITrees, together with compositional reasoning principles for modular verification of effectful programs. We integrate iBuchi into the Dijkstra Monads Forever framework, thereby enabling temporal specifications to compose with conventional Hoare-style specifications and supporting a generator-based encoding of future conditions. We have formally developed and verified our framework in Rocq and demonstrated its expressiveness and compositionality through several non-trivial case studies.
label: arXiv:2611.27553v1

summary.background:
- Formal verification: proving mathematically that a program meets a specification.
- Interaction Trees: a data structure that represents a program's effects as a tree of possible interactions with its environment, possibly infinite.
- Temporal properties: statements about how behaviour unfolds over time, such as "a response always eventually follows a request."
- Linear Temporal Logic (LTL): a notation for such time-based statements, with operators like "always" and "eventually."
- Hoare-style specifications: pre- and post-condition statements about what a program does.
- Rocq (formerly Coq): a proof assistant used to write and machine-check proofs.
- Shallow embedding: encoding a specification language directly within the host language rather than as a separate syntax tree.
summary.one_liner: The paper introduces iBuchi, a shallowly embedded temporal specification language over Choice Trees for reasoning about the ordering of observable interactions in Interaction Trees, with trace- and tree-level satisfaction relations, compositional principles, and integration into the Dijkstra Monads Forever framework, all mechanized in Rocq.
summary.plain: Programs often interact with their surroundings over time, such as reading input, writing output, or making requests, and the order of those interactions matters as much as the final answer. This paper gives a way to write down rules about the timing and order of such interactions and to check that a program follows them. The authors built the framework in the Rocq proof assistant and tested it on several non-trivial examples.
summary.why: Being able to state and verify how a program behaves over time, in modular pieces, matters for software that runs continuously or reacts to its environment. The text does not claim wider impact, so its practical reach beyond the Interaction Trees and Rocq setting is unclear from this summary alone.

title: Compositional Temporal Specifications for Interaction Trees

abstract: While Linux containers benefit from a rich ecosystem of Container Network Interface (CNI) plugins such as Calico and Cilium, FreeBSD Jails lacked native, standardized solutions for advanced networking. As a result, users have relied on manual, error-prone configurations, limiting scalability and integration with modern orchestration platforms. This paper introduces porting Calico, a widely adopted CNI plugin, to the FreeBSD operating system. Our approach replaced Linux-specific components with FreeBSD-native equivalents: iptables with ipfw, netlink sockets with routing sockets, and Linux network namespaces with FreeBSD's vnet. This work aims to bridge the gap between Linux and BSD container networking. By providing scalable, policy-driven capabilities that are compatible with existing Linux-centric infrastructure, FreeBSD can participate more fully in the broader container networking ecosystem.
label: arXiv:2611.27320v1

summary.background:
- Container: a way to run an isolated program with its own view of files and network, sharing the host's operating system.
- FreeBSD Jails: FreeBSD's built-in container-like isolation.
- CNI (Container Network Interface) plugin: a standard add-on that handles networking for containers in orchestration systems such as Kubernetes.
- Calico: a widely used networking plugin that also enforces rules about which containers may communicate.
- iptables / ipfw: packet-filtering rule systems on Linux and FreeBSD respectively.
- Netlink / routing sockets: the interfaces programs use to query and change network settings in the kernel.
- Network namespace / vnet: a way to give each container its own separate network stack.
summary.one_liner: The paper describes porting Calico, a widely used Kubernetes-style container networking plugin, to FreeBSD Jails by swapping Linux networking components for FreeBSD equivalents (ipfw for iptables, routing sockets for netlink, vnet for network namespaces).
summary.plain: Software that runs many isolated programs on one computer, called containers, needs a way to connect them to networks and set rules about who can talk to whom. On Linux, a popular tool called Calico does this, but FreeBSD (an operating system with its own style of containers called Jails) lacked an equivalent, so users set things up by hand. This paper describes adapting Calico to run on FreeBSD by replacing Linux-only pieces with FreeBSD's own built-in tools.
summary.why: It aims to let FreeBSD work with the same container orchestration systems that Linux users rely on, which could matter for anyone running FreeBSD servers at scale. The text is a short abstract only, so it does not report measured results, and how complete or well-tested the port is cannot be judged from it.

title: Bring Cloud-Native Networking to FreeBSD Jails: Porting Calico from Linux

abstract: Concurrent kernel execution is a ubiquitous paradigm in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) across both training and inference. That said, concurrency causes potential slowdown as concurrent kernels contend for limited GPU resources (cores, caches, memory bandwidth), which are shared between these kernels rather than exclusively available to one, as in isolated execution. This raises an important research question: to what extent does concurrency slow down kernel execution and how can it be mitigated. To answer this question, our work presents two studies. First, we characterize concurrent kernel execution extensively for the first time, to our knowledge. We conduct not just performance analysis of concurrent kernels but also memory behavior under concurrency on state-of-the-art AMD Instinct MI300X GPUs designed for datacenter AI, using the AMD-internal millisecond sampler. Based on the observations, we share insights on the slowdown along two dimensions (memory vs. compute bound, large vs. small kernels) to inform future optimizations. Second, we put the derived insights to use, aiming to deliver higher performance via targeted, flexible overlap of ML operators. Frameworks today make the simple decision of early-first for concurrent kernels, which is suboptimal. Noticing the opportunity that ML dataflow has inherent flexibility in which operators can be overlapped and how hardware resources can be allocated, we deduce simple heuristics to tune both overlap anchors and resource allocation for concurrent kernels to improve performance. We evaluate our proposed contention-aware flexible execution (termed CAFEML) across a variety of ML scenarios (inference decode, inference prefill, training) and demonstrate a speedup of up to 13% end-to-end with simple scheduling changes and no kernel rewrites.
label: arXiv:2611.26840v1

summary.background:
- GPU (graphics processing unit): a chip with many parallel cores, widely used to train and run AI models.
- Kernel: a single compute job launched on a GPU, such as one matrix multiplication.
- Concurrent execution: running several kernels at once so the chip is used more fully.
- Contention: competition for shared resources like cache and memory bandwidth, which slows each job.
- Memory-bound vs. compute-bound: whether a job is limited by how fast data moves or by how fast arithmetic can be done.
- Training vs. inference (prefill and decode): training updates a model; inference uses it to generate output, with prefill and decode being its two phases.
- End-to-end speedup: the improvement in total run time for a whole workload, not just one piece.
summary.one_liner: A characterization of how concurrently running GPU kernels slow each other down on AMD MI300X hardware, followed by CAFEML, a contention-aware scheduler that tunes operator overlap and resource allocation for ML training and inference, reporting up to 13% end-to-end speedup without kernel rewrites.
summary.plain: Modern AI software runs many small computing tasks (called kernels) at the same time on a graphics processor, and they compete for shared parts of the chip such as memory and cache, so each can run slower. This paper measures how much that slowdown happens on a current datacenter AI chip, and sorts the results by whether a task is limited by memory or by computation, and whether it is large or small. It then proposes simple scheduling rules for when to start overlapping tasks and how to split chip resources between them.
summary.why: Keeping expensive AI accelerators busy is a practical concern for anyone running large models, and the paper suggests that the default "start whatever is ready first" policy used by frameworks leaves performance on the table. The gain reported (up to 13% end-to-end) comes from scheduling changes alone, which is a modest but practically relevant result; the text does not show how well it generalizes beyond the scenarios tested.

title: Contention-Aware Flexible Execution for Machine Learning Workloads

abstract: AI supporters for mental well-being are becoming more prevalent. When these AI supporters start acting in ways beyond their expected function it leads to relational harm. Standard approaches to evaluating such AI supporters are limited to inspecting their efficacy in narrow task-specific settings, which do not explain these discrepancies in expected and actual behavior. To address this gap, we propose the AROMA (A Role-Oriented Model of Analysis) framework to provide a common role taxonomy for different support contexts. We developed AROMA using a theory-informed annotation of over 7,515 conversations from 13 datasets and propose eight "Role States" based on observed-not prescribed-behavior. We show these Role States vary according to the context of support; depict unique structural and temporal characteristics of AI supporters vis-a-vis Humans; and inform novel AI support prompting strategy for better role alignment. This framework provides a new lens to understand AI support failures.
label: arXiv:2611.26843v1

summary.background:
- Role theory: a social-science idea that people behave according to expected parts in a relationship, such as counselor or friend.
- Relational harm: damage to trust or the relationship when one party behaves in unexpected ways.
- Annotation: human labeling of data (here, conversation turns) to create a coded dataset.
- Role States: the paper's term for eight behavior categories inferred from what speakers actually did, not from what they were told to do.
- Prompting strategy: instructions written to steer a language model's behavior.
- Structural and temporal characteristics: how conversation turns are organized and how roles shift over the course of a conversation.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes AROMA, a role-oriented framework that annotates over 7,515 conversations from 13 datasets to derive eight observed "Role States" for AI mental well-being supporters, and uses them to analyze support contexts, structural and temporal differences from humans, and a prompting strategy for better role alignment.
summary.plain: AI chatbots that offer emotional support sometimes act outside the role they were meant to play, and this can hurt the relationship with the user. Standard tests only check whether such bots work in narrow tasks, so they miss why these mismatches happen. The authors labeled thousands of real conversations from 13 datasets by the roles the speakers actually took, and identified eight recurring role patterns.
summary.why: The work offers a shared vocabulary for describing when and how AI supporters drift from their intended role, which may help explain failures that task-based evaluations overlook. The text does not report how much the proposed prompting strategy improves outcomes, so its practical impact is unclear from the abstract alone.

title: AROMA: Understanding AI Support For Mental Well-being through Role Theory

abstract: India's AI debate often swings between two insufficient options: replicating the compute-intensive, capital-heavy foundation-model programmes of the United States or China, or remaining a downstream adopter of foreign AI with localised interfaces and safeguards. Neither serves a country that must deliver AI to a very large, diverse population across uneven infrastructure and within constrained budgets. This white paper from the Centre for Responsible AI (CeRAI), IIT Madras, proposes a third path: Responsible Frugal AI, which applies principle-based frugal engineering alongside Responsible AI. Responsible Frugal AI is right-sized AI: it fixes the functional requirement first, asks whether AI is needed at all, and then chooses the smallest sufficient model, meeting the requirement with minimal resources while keeping a verified margin, robustness and responsible governance. The framework applies frugality across four dimensions (data, compute, model and operations) through seven levers spanning the AI lifecycle, each with practices and measures. It calls for public AI rails, vernacular-first design, measured resource use, human oversight for high-stakes decisions, and a cap on total resource consumption so that efficiency gains are not cancelled out by rising usage. We argue that India is resource-imbalanced rather than resource-poor, and that frugal principles offer the most viable route to population-scale deployment, fit naturally with India's digital public infrastructure, and make sovereignty operational by preserving India's capacity to specify, deploy, govern, inspect and adapt its AI systems. A seven-point adoption checklist and eleven policy statements translate the framework into practice, positioning AI in India as a responsible, frugal public-value system that maximises social value per rupee and per joule.
label: arXiv:2611.27189v1

summary.background:
- Foundation model: a very large AI model trained on huge datasets, costly in computing power and money.
- Compute: the processing power (and electricity) needed to train or run AI.
- Responsible AI: designing AI to be fair, safe, transparent and accountable.
- Digital public infrastructure: shared government-built digital systems (such as identity or payment platforms) that others can build on.
- Sovereignty: a country's ability to control, inspect and adapt the technology it relies on.
- Vernacular-first: designing for local languages before English.
- Right-sized model: the smallest model that meets a defined requirement with a safety margin.
summary.one_liner: A CeRAI (IIT Madras) white paper proposing "Responsible Frugal AI" as a right-sized, resource-conscious policy and engineering framework for deploying AI at population scale in India, with seven levers, a seven-point checklist and eleven policy statements.
summary.plain: This white paper argues that India should not try to copy the huge, expensive AI models built in the US or China, nor simply use foreign AI with local tweaks. Instead it proposes a third approach: use the smallest AI system that does the job well enough, with careful checks, human oversight for serious decisions, and limits on total resource use. The authors frame this as a policy and design guide rather than a set of experimental results.
summary.why: India must serve a very large and varied population under tight budgets and uneven infrastructure, so a cost-aware approach to AI is a practical question for public services. The text is a position paper with a framework and checklist; it does not report measured outcomes, so its practical effect is untested from this text alone.

title: A Frugal AI Framework for India: Responsible and Right-sized AI

abstract: A codeword spans a fixed number of correlated Gaussian fading blocks. The receiver knows the gains and the transmitter knows only their law. At fixed average signal-to-noise ratio, we require the decoding error probability to decay exponentially with the number of receive antennas. When does outage predict the achievable rate? If block length grows faster than the number of antennas, outage gives the limiting optimal rate. If both grow to infinity at a fixed positive ratio of block length to array size, outage strictly overestimates the limiting rate. We determine the critical ratio above which positive rates are possible. For sufficiently large finite ratios, we find the exact limiting rate over all codes satisfying a total energy constraint on each codeword. The leading rate loss is inversely proportional to the ratio. Its coefficient depends on Gaussian channel dispersion at the most likely fade causing outage and on how quickly the outage rate decreases as the required error exponent increases. In the long-block limit, equal power loses rate on every window of three or more blocks under stationary first-order autoregressive fading with positive lag-one correlation. In a different three-block channel with identical marginal gains, tightening the reliability requirement first makes it optimal to leave the middle block unused and later to use it again.
label: arXiv:2611.27694v1

summary.background:
- Block fading: the channel gain stays fixed within a block and changes between blocks.
- Outage: the event that the channel is too weak to support a chosen rate; outage probability is its chance.
- Error exponent: how fast the chance of decoding error shrinks as a parameter (here, the number of receive antennas) grows.
- Dispersion: a measure of how much the achievable rate fluctuates around the capacity for finite-length codes.
- Power allocation: how a fixed total energy is split across the blocks of a codeword.
- Autoregressive (AR(1)) fading: a model where each block's gain is correlated with the previous one.
summary.one_liner: For a Gaussian block-fading channel with correlated fades, the paper studies when outage probability predicts the achievable rate under an exponential error-exponent requirement with many receive antennas, and it characterizes the optimal power allocation across blocks.
summary.plain: The paper looks at how to send a message reliably over a wireless link where signal strength varies in blocks of time that are correlated with each other. The transmitter knows only the statistical pattern of the fading, not the actual values, and the receiver has many antennas. The authors find when the simple "outage" measure (the chance the link is too weak to support a rate) correctly predicts the best rate, and when it overestimates it.
summary.why: It sharpens when a standard engineering shortcut for wireless links, outage, is accurate, and it gives explicit examples where power should be left off a block and then used again as reliability demands tighten. The text does not indicate links to specific applications beyond wireless communication.

title: Coding Length and Optimal Power Allocation in Correlated Block Fading

abstract: We establish qualitative stability in $L^1$ and Ruzsa distance for Shannon's entropy power inequality in $\mathbb{R}^d$, without any moment assumptions. The proof uses the optimal transport argument by Rioul (2017), majorization bounds of density rearrangements, and the stability of the sharp form of Young's inequality due to Christ (2019). Along the way we also extend recent one-dimensional results on de Bruijn's identity, the continuity of differential entropy, and the equality case of the entropy power inequality to random vectors of any dimension.
label: arXiv:2611.27790v1

summary.background:
- Differential entropy: a measure of spread or uncertainty for a continuous random vector, with a density function.
- Entropy power inequality: a bound saying the entropy power of a sum of independent random vectors is at least the sum of their entropy powers; equality holds for Gaussians.
- Stability: if the inequality is almost an equality, the distributions are close to Gaussian-type extremizers in some measured distance.
- L^1 distance: the total amount by which two probability densities differ, integrated over space.
- Ruzsa distance: a distance between random variables that is used in additive combinatorics and probability.
- Optimal transport: a way of moving one probability distribution into another at minimal cost, used here as a proof tool.
- Young's inequality: a sharp inequality on convolutions of functions; its sharp form has known extremizers (Gaussians).
- Moment assumptions: conditions that random variables have finite averages of powers of their size; the paper removes these.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves qualitative stability of Shannon's entropy power inequality in R^d in L^1 and Ruzsa distance without any moment assumptions, using an optimal transport argument, majorization of density rearrangements, and Christ's stability result for sharp Young's inequality.
summary.plain:
The paper studies a basic inequality from information theory that bounds how the uncertainty (entropy) of a sum of independent random quantities relates to that of the parts. It asks what happens when that inequality is nearly tight, and shows the near-equality stays close in a precise sense, without requiring the random quantities to have finite moments (a technical condition on how spread out they can be). The authors also extend several earlier one-dimensional results to random vectors of any dimension.</plain>
<parameter name="why">Stability results say that near-optimal cases must look close to the extremal ones, which matters for proofs and for understanding when the bound is sharp. The text does not describe applications beyond this mathematical setting, so any wider connections are unclear from the abstract alone.

title: $L^1$ stability of the entropy power inequality in $\mathbb{R}^d$ without moment assumptions

abstract: In this paper, we investigate Type-II quasinormal modes (QNMs) of a magnetically charged dilaton--Euler--Heisenberg black hole in anti-de Sitter (AdS) spacetime. The Type-II includes coupled gravitational, dilaton and electromagnetic perturbations. Its coupled equations are derived for $\ell=0,1,2$ modes and the QNM frequencies are calculated by employing direct integration and Chebyshev pseudospectral methods, giving consistent results. For nondegenerate dipole ($\ell=1$) mode at fixed curvature, the nonlinear correction starts at order $Q^2$ for electromagnetic-led branch and at order $Q^4$ for scalar-led branch. In this case, stronger AdS curvature enhances reduction of the electromagnetic-led real frequency for positive coupling, while gravitational-led quadrupole real frequency changes weakly with charge. As the curvature weakens, the dipole frequencies approach the AdS normal-mode scale and their damping decreases. We find that all modes computed have negative imaginary parts for nonextremal black holes, implying this black hole is stable against Type-II perturbations. Furthermore, we explore the connection between thermodynamic phase transition and QNMs for $\ell=0$ dilaton. For a subcritical isobaric process, the QNM real frequency of $\ell=0$ dilaton decreases with increasing temperature of small black holes, while it increases with increasing temperature of large black holes. At coexistence, the damping rate for large black holes is about 4.28 times that for small black holes.
label: arXiv:2611.27195v1

summary.background:
- A black hole's quasinormal modes are damped oscillations with a real frequency (pitch) and an imaginary part (how fast they fade); negative imaginary part means stability.
- AdS (anti-de Sitter) is a universe with negative curvature that acts like a box confining signals.
- The dilaton is a hypothetical scalar field coupled to electromagnetism, appearing in some string-inspired gravity theories.
- Euler–Heisenberg corrections are nonlinear modifications to electromagnetism at strong fields, from quantum vacuum effects.
- ℓ is the angular-momentum label of a mode: ℓ=0 monopole, ℓ=1 dipole, ℓ=2 quadrupole.
- Chebyshev pseudospectral methods are numerical techniques for solving the governing equations accurately.
- A thermodynamic phase transition is a qualitative change in a system's state (like water boiling); here it is studied in the black hole's isobaric (constant-pressure) process.
summary.one_liner:
Computes Type-II quasinormal modes (coupled gravitational, dilaton and electromagnetic perturbations for ℓ=0,1,2) of a magnetically charged dilaton–Euler–Heisenberg black hole in AdS, using direct integration and Chebyshev pseudospectral methods, and links the ℓ=0 dilaton modes to the black hole's thermodynamic phase transition.</one_liner>
<parameter name="plain">The paper studies how a charged black hole in a curved, AdS-type universe "rings" after being disturbed, the way a struck bell rings at certain tones that fade over time. It looks at several coupled kinds of disturbance (gravity, a scalar "dilaton" field, and electromagnetism) and computes the tones and fading rates numerically. It reports that the black hole appears stable, since all modes it computes decay, and that the fading rate shows a change near the black hole's thermodynamic phase transition.
summary.why: Quasinormal modes are the characteristic signals a black hole emits when perturbed, so they are a theoretical handle on black-hole stability and on how such objects might be probed. The link drawn between these modes and a thermodynamic phase transition is the most unusual part; the text does not say how directly this could be tested, so the broader significance is uncertain.

title: Type-II quasinormal modes of dilaton--Euler--Heisenberg AdS black holes

abstract: We exhibit random matrix statistics in the scaling dimensions of non-BPS primary operators in a family of two-dimensional conformal field theories. Specifically, we consider the sigma model with K3 target space and $\mathcal N=(4,4)$ supersymmetry in a neighborhood of the Kummer orbifold point $\mathbb T^4/\mathbb Z_2$.
