summary.one_liner: Single-cell transcriptomics of the medial septum in a novel four-core-genotype (FCG) rat model, compared with the FCG mouse, tests whether sex chromosome complement (XX vs. XY) or gonads drive sex-biased gene regulation across species.
summary.plain: Men and women differ in many brain-related conditions, but it is hard to tell whether the cause is the sex chromosomes or the sex hormones made by the gonads. The authors used a special rat model that separates these two effects and measured gene activity in individual brain cells from a small brain region called the medial septum. They report that differences in the sex chromosomes had a stronger effect on gene activity than gonads, and that this pattern was similar in mice and rats even though many individual genes differed.
summary.why: The finding argues against the common view that hormones from the gonads are the main source of sex differences in the brain, which matters for how sex differences in brain disease are studied. The authors also link the sex-biased genes to conditions such as anxiety, Alzheimer's disease, epilepsy and schizophrenia, but the text gives only the association, not evidence that these genes cause those conditions.

title: Single-cell study of the FCG rat model and cross-species comparison reveal stronger gene regulation by sex chromosome complement in the medial septum

abstract: Background: Energy excess, and particularly long-chain saturated fatty acid (SFA) overload, are instrumental in promoting obesity and hampering metabolic health. However, SFA contribution to human adipocyte metabolic and endocrine dysfunction remains elusive. Nonetheless, we have already provided evidence that a 48-hour palmitic acid (PA) exposure is not sufficient to hamper Simpson-Golabi Behmel Syndrome (SGBS) adipocytes insulin signalling. Objective: This study aims at evaluating whether a 96-hour exposure to PA is able to disrupt SGBS adipocyte metabolic health and induce the release of a secretome capable of hampering insulin signalling in skeletal muscle cells. Methods: SGBS adipocytes were treated with either 1000 uM PA or bovine serum albumin (BSA) for 96 hours followed by the assessment of the NFkB signalling and the expression of genes associate with inflammation and adipocyte metabolic stress. Furthermore, adipocytes were labelled with BODIPY and lipid droplet as well as cell size semi-quantified using ImageJ. Insulin-induced phosphorylation of Akt and Akt substrate of 160 kDa (AS160) was assessed by Western Blot. The effect of PA on SGBS secretome was assessed by both ELISA as well as MILLIPLEX. Finally, human immortalised myotubes were co-cultured with BSA or PA-treated SGBS adipocytes for 24 hours followed by the assessment of insulin signalling at the Akt level. Results: PA did not activate the NFkB signalling pathway, but induced the expression of MCP-1 while tending to upregulate IL-6 mRNA levels. Despite 96-hour PA exposure leading to an increase in lipid droplet and cell size, this was not coupled with an impairment in insulin signalling. Nevertheless, this SFA promoted an increase in IL-6 and IL-8 secretion while tending to enhance the release of adiponectin by SGBS adipocytes. Finally, the secretome from PA-treated SGBS adipocyte did not impair insulin-induced phosphorylation of Akt relative to controls in myotubes. Conclusions: Thus, in the absence of the stromal vascular fraction, direct exposure of SGBS adipocytes to PA overload is not sufficient to elicit overt dysfunction. The absence of full-blown adipocyte dysfunction is reflected in the secretome of these cells which failed to disrupt skeletal muscle insulin signalling.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767488 v1

summary.background:
- Adipocytes are fat-storing cells; SGBS is a human pre-adipocyte line that matures into fat cells in the lab.
- Palmitic acid (PA) is a long-chain saturated fatty acid common in the diet; BSA (bovine serum albumin) is the carrier protein used for the control condition.
- Insulin signalling works through proteins such as Akt and AS160; if it is impaired, cells take up less sugar, a feature of insulin resistance.
- NF-kB is an inflammation-related signalling pathway; MCP-1, IL-6 and IL-8 are inflammatory messenger molecules; adiponectin is a hormone usually considered protective.
- The secretome is the set of molecules a cell releases into its surroundings; it was tested by transferring it onto muscle cells (myotubes).
- The stromal vascular fraction (immune and support cells found in fat tissue) was absent here, which the authors note limits how far the results apply to real tissue.
summary.one_liner: In cultured SGBS human adipocytes, a 96-hour palmitic acid (PA) exposure raised lipid droplet and cell size and shifted cytokine and adiponectin secretion, but did not impair insulin signalling in adipocytes or in co-cultured myotubes.
summary.plain:
Eating too much saturated fat is thought to help drive obesity and poor metabolic health, but it is unclear how much it damages human fat cells directly. This study grew fat cells from a human cell line (SGBS) in palmitic acid, a common saturated fat, for four days and checked their fat storage, inflammation signals, and the chemicals they released. The fat cells stored more fat and released more of some inflammatory signals, yet they did not become clearly dysfunctional, and their released chemicals did not block insulin action in muscle cells.</plain>
<parameter name="why">It suggests that a saturated fat alone, acting directly on fat cells without other immune or support cells present, may not be enough to produce the full set of problems linked to obesity. This is relevant to how fat tissue contributes to insulin resistance, though the result comes from a single cell model and says little about whole bodies.

title: Palmitic acid overload does not promote full-blown dysfunction in SGBS adipocytes which is reflected in their secretome

abstract: Traumatic optic nerve injury interrupts retinal ganglion cell output and can produce permanent visual disability, yet a therapeutic strategy that couples retinal protection with recovery of visual-pathway activity remains unavailable. Here, we evaluated human retinal organoid transplantation at the site of optic nerve crush in C57 mice. Human retinal organoids derived from embryonic stem cells were used at day 30 and showed retinal-lineage immunoreactivity together with spontaneous microelectrode-array activity. Across post-surgical days 7, 14, and 28, transplantation was associated with preservation of optic-disc appearance and ganglion cell layer thickness. The structural benefit became statistically distinguishable from the crush group at day 28 and remained incomplete relative to the uninjured or sham group. Serial RBPMS and TUJ1 immunostaining further supported attenuation of retinal ganglion cell body and neurite loss, while IBA1 staining indicated an altered microglial response. Full-field electroretinographic b-wave responses showed no detectable between-group differences, arguing against a major outer-retinal effect. In contrast, flash visual evoked potential P2 amplitude was higher in transplanted than in crush-only mice at all measured time points, consistent with improved visual-pathway responsiveness. Transplant recipients also showed enhanced optomotor responses across tested spatial-frequency and contrast conditions. Light-dark behavior shifted toward greater dark-compartment occupancy and activity, although this assay remains non-specific for visual recovery. Together, these findings support a model in which hROs transplantation at an optic nerve injury site promotes multi-level functional preservation after optic nerve crush. Definitive evidence for donor-derived circuit reconstruction will require graft tracing, synaptic validation, and prespecified electrophysiologic analyses.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767615 v1

summary.background:
- Retinal ganglion cells: the eye's output neurons whose long axons form the optic nerve to the brain.
- Optic nerve crush: a standard lab injury model that mechanically damages this nerve.
- Retinal organoids: three-dimensional tissue grown from stem cells that mimics parts of the retina.
- Microelectrode array (MEA): a plate that records electrical activity from cells.
- Electroretinography (ERG) and visual evoked potentials (VEP): recordings of electrical responses from the retina (ERG b-wave) and the visual cortex (VEP P2 peak) to light flashes.
- Optomotor response: a mouse's reflex to turn its head with rotating stripes, used to gauge vision.
- Immunostaining (RBPMS, TUJ1, IBA1): labelling that marks ganglion cells, their axons, and microglia (immune cells of the nervous system).
- Mouse strain C57: a common inbred laboratory mouse line.
summary.one_liner: In C57 mice with optic nerve crush, transplanting day-30 human retinal organoids at the injury site was associated with preserved optic-disc appearance, ganglion cell layer thickness, and flash VEP P2 amplitude, with a b-wave showing no between-group difference, though donor-derived circuit integration was not demonstrated.
summary.plain: Damage to the optic nerve, the cable that carries vision signals from the eye to the brain, can cause lasting vision loss. In this study, researchers placed small lab-grown human "mini-retinas" (retinal organoids) at the site of a crushed optic nerve in mice and tracked the eyes and visual responses for up to 28 days. Transplanted mice kept more of their nerve-cell layer and showed stronger visual-brain signals and better responses to moving stripes than mice with the crush alone, though the authors say the results do not yet prove the graft wired into the visual circuit.
summary.why: Optic nerve injury has few treatments that protect the nerve cells and restore signalling at the same time, so a graft-based approach is of interest. The text is measured about its limits: the benefits were incomplete compared with uninjured mice, and the behavioural light-dark test is non-specific, so the work is an early preclinical signal rather than evidence of a therapy.

title: Extra-sheath transplantation of human retinal organoids (hROs): effects on visual recovery and retinal repair following optic nerve injury

abstract: The liver is one of the most frequent sites for hematogenous metastasis across different types of cancer, but how the liver mounts effective immune responses against arriving tumor cells is not fully understood. Using intravital imaging, we have visualized the initial steps of liver metastasis and delineated three phases in the immune response at the earliest stages of liver metastasis: first, there is continuous surveillance of the liver parenchyma by discrete immune cell subsets in the premetastatic tissue. Second, upon metastatic cell arrival, there is massive neutrophil recruitment and tumor-cell material uptake mediated by resident macrophages. Third, antitumor-specific T-cell activation takes place in situ within intrahepatic leukocyte clusters. We find that tumor-derived material uptake triggers transcriptional programs in liver myeloid cells that upregulate chemoattraction programs in Kupffer cells and cDCs, leading to T-cell activation. Antigen cross-presentation and a functional partnership between cDC1s and local macrophages to recruit and form T-cell activation clusters are required for the elicitation of these intrahepatic T-cell responses. Consequently, prior expansion of cDCs by Flt3L-Ig treatment significantly enhances immunosurveillance, curtailing successful metastasis development. Collectively, our findings identify coordinated immune responses that are essential for anti-metastatic immunity within the liver, uncovering a program to mount defenses against tumor cells arriving in the liver.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.21.768283 v1

summary.background:
- Metastasis: cancer cells leaving a tumor and seeding new growth elsewhere, here in the liver.
- Intravital imaging: filming living cells inside an intact animal organ with microscopes.
- Kupffer cells: macrophages (immune cells that engulf material) resident in the liver.
- Dendritic cells (cDC1): immune cells that capture antigens (molecular pieces of a pathogen or tumor) and present them to T cells; cross-presentation means displaying material from outside the cell.
- T cells: immune cells that can kill targeted cells once activated.
- Flt3L-Ig: a drug used in mice to expand dendritic cell populations.
summary.one_liner: Intravital imaging of early liver metastasis in mice shows that resident Kupffer cells, macrophages and cDC1 dendritic cells cooperate via antigen cross-presentation to recruit T cells into activation clusters that help control arriving tumor cells.
summary.plain: Cancer often spreads to the liver through the bloodstream, and this study asks how the liver's own immune cells respond when the first tumor cells arrive. Using live imaging inside the organ, the authors describe three stages: routine immune patrolling, a rush of neutrophils and macrophage uptake of tumor material, and T-cell activation in small clusters within the liver. Boosting dendritic cell numbers with Flt3L-Ig reduced successful metastasis in their experiments.
summary.why: It maps the earliest immune steps against metastasis in a major target organ, which may matter for designing therapies that prime local immunity. The text does not show whether these mouse findings translate to human patients, so that link remains open.

title: Local macrophage and cDC1 cooperation in the liver drives T-cell immune surveillance against pioneering metastatic cancer cells.

abstract: Viral burden does not necessarily predict the extent or composition of the host immune response, reflecting the complexity of virus - host interactions. Rabies virus (RABV) provides a powerful model to investigate this question because genetically distinct RABVs differ in replication, immune evasion, and neuroimmune activation. Here, we performed integrated temporal proteomic and spatial imaging analyses of recombinant RABV, including pathogenic, attenuated, and a newly generated interferon-sensitive variant with disrupted phosphoprotein antagonistic activity. Following intracerebral infection of mice, viruses established distinct neuroimmune states that diverged over time in antiviral signaling, complement activation, and immune response. Notably, the pathogenic field viruses rDogA and rFox both exhibited substantial viral accumulation, but elicited markedly different central nervous system (CNS) responses, with rDogA inducing limited host immune engagement, whereas rFox triggered early and broad antiviral, complement, and immune recruitment programs. Disruption of phosphoprotein-mediated interferon antagonism in rDogA enhanced interferon-stimulated gene expression and antiviral effectors, restricting viral accumulation without inducing broad neuroimmune remodeling. Conversely, the attenuated glycoprotein-modified rSAD GASGAS elicited strong complement activation and T cell recruitment with little detectable viral levels, revealing a highly immunogenic neuroimmune state. Spatial profiling further identified virus-dependent patterns of myeloid, astrocyte-associated, complement, and lymphocyte responses across brain regions. Together, these findings demonstrate how viral genetic background and its modulation of host antiviral responses shape divergent neuroimmune states in which viral accumulation, antiviral immunity, and CNS immune activation are differentially coordinated.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.768130 v1

summary.background:
- Rabies virus (RABV) spreads through the nervous system and is nearly always fatal once symptoms appear.
- Field strains are viruses taken from wild or domestic animals; attenuated strains are weakened versions, often used as a basis for vaccines.
- Interferons are signalling proteins that alarm cells and trigger antiviral defences; some viruses carry proteins (here, the phosphoprotein) that block this alarm.
- Complement is a group of blood and tissue proteins that help clear pathogens and can also drive inflammation.
- Proteomics measures the proteins present in tissue; spatial imaging shows where in the tissue they are found.
- Recombinant viruses are built in the lab with specific genetic changes to test what each change does.
summary.one_liner: In mice infected intracerebrally with genetically distinct rabies viruses, temporal proteomics and spatial imaging show that viral genetics, through interferon antagonism, shape divergent brain immune states that are not simply proportional to viral load.
summary.plain: Rabies is a virus that attacks the brain, and different strains can cause very different immune reactions even when they reach similar levels in the tissue. The researchers infected mice directly into the brain with several engineered rabies viruses, including disease-causing field strains, a weakened strain, and a new variant that is more sensitive to interferon, an antiviral alarm signal. They then tracked protein changes over time and mapped where immune cells appeared in different brain regions.
summary.why: The text suggests that how much virus is present does not fully predict the strength or type of the host's immune response, which matters for understanding why some infections trigger brain inflammation and others do not. The work is limited to mice and a direct brain-injection model, so any link to human rabies or to vaccine design is an open question the text does not settle.

title: Viral genetic variation programs divergent neuroimmune states during rabies infection

abstract: Metastasis is the spread of cancer cells from primary tumors to distant organs and accounts for the majority of melanoma deaths, with a 5-year survival rate of only 30%. Despite strong evidence that myeloid cells promote metastasis, there are limited clinically effective myeloid-directed therapies. Here, we demonstrate that targeting myeloperoxidase (MPO), a myeloid-lineage restricted enzyme, significantly reduced multi-organ metastatic burden using an immunocompetent mouse model of spontaneous melanoma. Adjuvant MPO inhibition remodeled the metastatic microenvironment by a reduction in Ly6G+Ly6C+ myeloid cells and enrichment of B and T cell populations. Importantly, adjuvant MPO inhibitor-mediated metastatic control was dependent upon B, CD8+ T cells and CD4+ T cells, and rapidly reduced circulating and disseminated tumor cells. MPO inhibition markedly decreased NET release, while NET deficiency and inhibition recapitulated the anti-metastatic effects of targeting MPO, implicating NETs as a potential downstream mediator of MPO-driven metastasis. We further validated these findings in a distinct spontaneous breast cancer model where adjuvant MPO inhibition similarly reduced multi-organ metastatic burden with comparable changes within the metastatic immune microenvironment. Collectively, our studies introduce MPO as a druggable regulator of metastasis where MPO inhibition limits metastatic disease by targeting immunosuppressive myeloid cells.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.768197 v1

summary.background:
- Metastasis: cancer cells leaving a primary tumor and forming new tumors in distant organs.
- Myeloid cells: a family of white blood cells, including neutrophils, that the paper says can suppress immune attacks on tumors.
- Myeloperoxidase (MPO): an enzyme found in myeloid cells; the paper treats it as a drug target.
- Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs): web-like strands of DNA and proteins released by neutrophils; the paper proposes them as a downstream mediator of MPO's effect.
- B and T cells: adaptive immune cells that can attack tumors; the study shows the MPO inhibitor's effect depends on them.
- Adjuvant therapy: treatment given after the main tumor is removed or controlled, aimed at preventing recurrence or spread.
- Spontaneous model: mice that develop tumors on their own rather than from injected cancer cells.
summary.one_liner: In an immunocompetent mouse model of spontaneous melanoma, adjuvant myeloperoxidase (MPO) inhibition reduced multi-organ metastasis in a manner dependent on B, CD8+ and CD4+ T cells and linked to reduced neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) release, with similar effects reported in a spontaneous breast cancer model.
summary.plain: Melanoma is a skin cancer that spreads to distant organs, and that spread causes most deaths from it. This study tested whether blocking an enzyme called myeloperoxidase, which is made by a type of immune cell, could slow that spread in mice with a natural form of melanoma. The authors report fewer spread tumors across several organs, more B and T immune cells in the affected tissue, and fewer tumor cells circulating in the blood.
summary.why: Most current immune-directed cancer treatments do not target the myeloid cells that the authors say help metastasis, so an enzyme that can be blocked by a drug is a potentially new angle. The text does not establish that this approach works in patients, and the mouse results would need clinical testing before any conclusions about treatment.

title: Adjuvant myeloperoxidase inhibition promotes B and T cell mediated control of murine melanoma metastasis

abstract: Modeling cancer initiation, progression, and metastasis has greatly impacted our understanding of fundamental cell and molecular mechanisms driving disease and has led to breakthrough treatments that greatly improve patient outcomes. Understanding the earliest stages of tumor formation is particularly important for uncovering the root causes of oncogenic transformation and tumor evolution. It has been historically difficult to model the cellular dynamics that drive the earliest stages of tumor evolution, largely due to difficulties in culturing and manipulating normal primary cells in 3-dimensional environments, triggering oncogenesis, and observing the resulting effects. Recent advances in 3D organoid culture provide a promising avenue to address these challenges. In this study, we have developed a Kras based organoid model of early tumorigenesis. In our model, oncogenic transformation was triggered by Cre-mediated expression of oncogenic KRASG12D in otherwise healthy murine-derived mammary epithelial organoids. While normal organoids displayed controlled organoid growth and morphogenesis, induction of KRASG12D caused neoplastic organoid growth that occurred with the absence of lumen formation. Gene expression analysis revealed up regulation of several KRAS effectors, and a broad repertoire of genes associated with tumor development and human breast cancer. Induction of oncogenic Kras in our model resulted in heterotypic organoids that possessed KRASG12D + cells growing alongside KRASG12D- cells. In this context, amplification of KRASG12D + cells occurred at the expense of KRASG12D- cells. Finally we observed that neoplastic growth of KRASG12D expressing organoids was associated with a suppression of apoptosis. We believe that our organoid model provides a platform that is suitable to examine the earliest stages of tumor development and can be expanded to study several questions related to cancer biology, prevention studies, therapeutic development, and beyond.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.766834 v1

summary.background:
- Organoids: small 3D clusters of cells grown in a dish that mimic some features of a real organ.
- KRAS: a gene that normally helps control cell growth; the G12D change is a common cancer-linked mutation that keeps it switched on.
- Cre-mediated expression: a genetic switch that turns a gene on in selected cells.
- Lumen: the hollow central cavity that normal mammary ducts and organoids form.
- Heterotypic organoid: an organoid containing a mix of two cell types, here mutant and normal cells.
- Apoptosis: programmed cell death, a normal way cells are removed.
- The study is a model-building paper in mice-derived cells; it does not test treatments in patients.
summary.one_liner: A mouse mammary (breast) epithelial organoid model in which Cre-induced KRASG12D expression produces neoplastic growth without lumen formation, with heterotypic competition between mutant and wild-type cells and suppressed apoptosis.
summary.plain: Researchers wanted a lab system for watching the very first steps of cancer forming in breast tissue. They grew small 3D clusters of healthy mouse mammary cells (organoids) and switched on a cancer-linked mutation, KRASG12D, in some of them. The mutated clusters grew abnormally and failed to form the hollow central space that normal ones develop, and mutant cells gained ground over normal neighbors.

title: A KRASG12D-based organoid model for early oncogenic transformation of the mammary epithelium

abstract: Biodiversity loss generally impairs functions on which nature and societies depend upon. Yet, it is difficult to predict under which conditions losing biodiversity has larger effects on functions such as primary production or carbon retention. We present a theory that demonstrates that biotic interactions mediate the intensity of these effects. In species interaction networks with many or strong trophic links, biodiversity loss has weaker effects on functioning because alternative interaction pathways allow surviving species to compensate for species loss. In contrast, in networks with fewer or weaker links, ecosystem functioning is very sensitive to the extinction of species. Here, we identify interaction erosion as a hidden dimension of the biodiversity crisis that provides a unifying explanation for functional consequences of biodiversity loss across ecological contexts.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.768031 v1

summary.background:
- Ecosystem functioning: the processes an ecosystem performs, such as producing plant biomass (primary production) and storing carbon.
- Trophic link: a feeding relationship, such as a predator eating prey or a herbivore eating a plant.
- Species interaction network: a map of which species interact with which, drawn as nodes (species) joined by links (interactions).
- Interaction strength: how much one species affects another's numbers or activity.
- Compensation: when surviving species take over the role of lost ones, cushioning the effect on the whole system.
- Theory vs. data: this is a model-based argument; the abstract does not report empirical tests.
summary.one_liner: A theoretical model of species interaction networks suggests that the number and strength of trophic links determine how strongly losing species reduces ecosystem functions such as primary production and carbon retention.
summary.plain: Losing species from an ecosystem often weakens things like plant growth and carbon storage, but it is hard to say when the damage will be large. This paper builds a theoretical model showing that the web of who eats or affects whom shapes the answer. In networks with many or strong feeding links, surviving species can make up for lost ones through alternative pathways, so the loss hurts less; in networks with fewer or weaker links, the ecosystem is much more sensitive to extinctions.
summary.why: It offers a single framework for why biodiversity loss matters more in some systems than others, and it proposes that losing interactions, not just species, is a hidden part of the biodiversity crisis. The text is only an abstract, so the strength of the evidence and how well the model fits real ecosystems cannot be judged from it.

title: Biotic interactions buffer the effects of biodiversity loss on ecosystem functioning

abstract: Rapid evolution in one species can restructure ecological communities, but how its effects vary across environmental conditions remains poorly understood. Here we mapped the consequences of antibiotic resistance evolution in Aeromonas caviae across 64 combinations of resource availability and antibiotic stress in three- and 16-species bacterial communities. Resistance evolution changed where community-state boundaries were located, with boundaries lost or gained depending on resource availability. The same evolutionary change increased diversity in some environments but decreased it in others. Species success was partly explained by growth traits at zero or low antibiotic concentrations and by intrinsic resistance at inhibitory concentrations. Resistance evolution reversed dominance between the two dominant species and changed which traits mattered. It also altered other species' responses below inhibitory concentrations, mostly between closely related species. Our findings show that the consequences of evolution depend on environmental context but can be partly explained by species traits.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.768032 v1

summary.background:
- Antibiotic resistance: a heritable ability of bacteria to survive a drug that would normally kill or stop them.
- Community: a set of coexisting species interacting in the same place.
- Community-state boundary: the tipping line between environmental conditions where different sets of species dominate or persist.
- Inhibitory concentration: the drug level high enough to stop a species growing; below it, the drug may still affect growth.
- Intrinsic resistance: a species' inherent tolerance to a drug, as opposed to one acquired by evolution.
- Dominance and diversity: which species take over a community, and how evenly many species coexist.
summary.one_liner: Mapping how antibiotic resistance evolution in one Aeromonas caviae lineage reshapes three- and 16-species bacterial community states, diversity and dominance across a grid of resource and antibiotic conditions.
summary.plain: Evolution can happen fast enough to change a whole community of organisms, not just the species that evolves. This study asked how one bacterial species becoming antibiotic-resistant changed the wider community, and whether those changes depended on food supply and antibiotic level. The authors tested 64 combinations of resources and antibiotic and found that the same resistance change had different effects in different settings.
summary.why: It suggests that the ecological effects of evolution cannot be judged from one environment alone, which matters for predicting how resistance spreads through microbial communities. The text does not indicate applications beyond this experimental system, so the wider significance is uncertain.

title: Resistance evolution in a single species reorganizes community responses across a resource-antibiotic landscape

abstract: High temperatures reprogram gene regulatory responses and are particularly deleterious for crop yield, especially when these events occur at night. This emphasizes that partitioning of heat responses is based on time of day. Coordination between time of day and environmental responses relies on the circadian clock. However, the precise regulatory mechanism of how the clock achieves this partitioning at different levels of gene regulation is poorly understood. Using circadian clock mutants with altered CCA1 and LHY expression, we generated a time-resolved transcriptome, proteome, and metabolome following a short-term heat stress in Arabidopsis. We identified regulatory connections specific to CCA1 and LHY, as well as those shared with other clock components linked to heat stress responses. Additionally, new connections between CCA1 and LHY and non-cycling genes highlight a broader role for the clock in regulating heat responsive gene expression. CCA1 and LHY regulated processes, such as sulfur assimilation and ROS scavenging, may contribute to time-of-day specific thermotolerance. Overall, heat responses were dampened in both the transcriptome and proteome in cca1lhy, suggesting both transcriptional and post-translational circadian-regulated processes are important for heat responses. Lastly, we identified differences in metabolic responses in cca1lhy and suggest a role for circadian regulation of starch degradation in thermotolerance. This study generates and utilizes data across levels of gene regulation to identify heat responses in the transcriptome and proteome regulated by CCA1 and LHY. These findings establish shared and distinct regulatory mechanisms of clock components in response to heat stress and provide new candidates for network integration and a foundation to engineer plants more tolerant to high temperatures depending on time of day.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767892 v1

summary.background:
- Circadian clock: an internal roughly 24-hour timekeeper that controls when many genes are switched on in a plant.
- CCA1 and LHY: two closely related clock genes; the mutant plants have altered levels of them.
- Transcriptome, proteome, metabolome: the full sets of RNA messages, proteins and small molecules in a sample, measured to see how a stress ripples through the cell.
- Heat stress: a short period of high temperature that changes gene activity.
- Thermotolerance: a plant's ability to survive and function under high heat.
- Post-translational regulation: control of protein activity or levels after a protein is made.
- Arabidopsis: a small model plant widely used in laboratory research.
summary.one_liner: A time-resolved transcriptome, proteome and metabolome study of Arabidopsis clock mutants (altered CCA1 and LHY) after short heat stress, mapping shared and distinct clock-linked heat-response regulation across gene expression layers.
summary.plain: Heat is especially harmful to crops when it hits at night, so plants may need to respond differently depending on the time of day. This paper looks at how the plant's internal daily clock, specifically two clock genes called CCA1 and LHY, shapes the plant's response to a short burst of heat. The authors measured genes, proteins and metabolites over time in normal plants and in mutants lacking these clock genes.
summary.why: Crop losses from heat are a practical concern, and the text suggests timing-dependent heat tolerance could guide breeding or engineering. The work is mainly a data resource and set of candidate connections; the text does not show that these findings would translate to crops.

title: Circadian clock components CCA1 and LHY shape heat responses across regulatory layers

abstract: Colourful motifs on the surface of flower petals fulfill important ecological functions, mediating pollination and providing protection against environmental stressors. These patterns form when epidermis cells in different subdomains of the petal acquire contrasting chemical and structural features. While some of the enzymes and transcription factors involved in specifying the production of different pigments, cell shapes and textures have been identified, the signalling events and upstream processes that divide the petal surface in distinct regions are not yet understood. Plant hormones play key roles in orchestrating all aspects of plant development but whether and how they contribute to the establishment of petal patterns remain to be tested. Here, we investigate the roles of auxin during bullseye pattern development in Hibiscus trionum. We found that auxin does not initiate bullseye boundary formation during the pre-patterning phase. Instead, auxin signalling is essential for regulating cell behaviour in the distal region and preserving the bullseye proportions established in young petal primordia. Therefore, auxin could act as a pattern modifier over evolutionary timescales, shifting bullseye dimensions by modulating the relative growth of different petal regions.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767829 v1

summary.background:
- Petal patterns such as bullseyes are made of epidermis cells (the outer skin layer of the petal) that differ in pigment and surface texture across regions.
- Auxin is a plant hormone that controls cell growth and direction of development across many plant organs.
- A petal primordium is the very young, not-yet-open petal tissue, where early pattern layout is set.
- "Pre-patterning" means the early stage when regions of the petal are first marked out before colours appear.
- "Distal region" means the part of the petal farthest from where it attaches to the flower.
- "Proportions" here means the relative sizes of the bullseye's inner and outer zones.
summary.one_liner: In the petals of Hibiscus trionum, auxin signalling is not needed to set up the initial bullseye boundary during pre-patterning, but it is needed in the distal petal region to maintain the bullseye's proportions established in young primordia.
summary.plain: Many flowers have coloured patterns on their petals, such as the dark centre of a bullseye, that guide pollinators. This paper asks whether a plant growth hormone called auxin helps draw the boundaries of these patterns in the hibiscus Hibiscus trionum. The authors report that auxin does not start the boundary, but it is needed to keep the pattern's proportions steady as the petal grows.
summary.why: The study suggests that a general growth hormone could change how big different parts of a pattern are, which may help explain how flower patterns vary between species over evolutionary time. The summary provided is limited to the abstract, so the strength of the evidence and the specific experiments cannot be judged from it.

title: Auxin regulates the proportions, but not the initiation, of Hibiscus trionum bullseyes

abstract: Conventional antibodies targeting the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) primarily inhibit receptor activation rather than efficiently eliminating the receptor from tumor cells. Here, we investigated whether engineering full-length anti-EGFR antibodies with internalizing peptides could promote receptor degradation, enhance their biological activity and enable the development of recombinant receptor-depleting antibodies. Chemical conjugation of cetuximab (CTX) to the polyarginine peptide R12 enhanced intracellular uptake, reduced surface-accessible EGFR and decreased total receptor abundance in vitro. CTX-R12 conjugate also enhanced inhibition of wound repopulation in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cell lines, an effect reproduced using the R12 variant LINC18, and transferred to the independent blocking anti-EGFR antibody LEI. Incorporation of LINC19, a variant of LINC18, into recombinant full-length antibody fusion proteins preserved their activity. The LEI-LINC19 fusion (LEIP), reduced surface-accessible and total EGFR, with bafilomycin A1 reversing receptor loss and supporting an acidification-dependent endolysosomal component of degradation. Functional studies indicated that the antibody-peptide reduced DNA synthesis rate. Furthermore, siRNA-mediated EGFR depletion increased TKI-associated reductions in cellular biomass in PC9 cells and increased gefitinib responsiveness in H1975 cells. Consistently, combining LEIP with either osimertinib or gefitinib produced greater inhibition of H1975 wound repopulation than the corresponding individual treatments. LDH analysis revealed increased membrane-damage-associated LDH release following LEIP-gefitinib treatment but no additional increase with LEIP-osimertinib relative to osimertinib alone. These effects extended to 3D NSCLC models. CTX-R12 inhibited PC9 3D colony development, whereas LEIP restricted expansion of established PC9 colonies and reduced the projected area of H1975 spheroids. In H1975 spheroids initiated with 1,000 or 5,000 cells per well, LEIP-containing combinations with osimertinib or gefitinib produced greater inhibition of the spheroid size than the corresponding TKI-only treatments. Nuclear Green DCS1 staining revealed no detectable baseline core necrosis in untreated H1975 spheroids, whereas LEIP treatment was associated with DNA-positive material within and surrounding the spheroids. Moreover, LEIP-treated H1975 spheroids exhibited markedly reduced EGFR immunofluorescence compared with control and parental LEI-treated spheroids. Together, these findings demonstrate that internalizing-peptide engineering of blocking anti- EGFR antibodies can generate full-length EGFR-depleting fusion proteins with enhanced biological activity. The recombinant LEIP format and its activity in 3D in vitro NSCLC tumor models support further investigation of fusion antibody-mediated EGFR degradation as a complementary strategy to EGFR kinase inhibition.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.768013 v1

summary.background:
- EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor) is a cell-surface protein that drives growth signals; it is overactive in some lung cancers.
- Antibodies such as cetuximab usually block EGFR activity without removing the protein from the cell.
- Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs such as gefitinib and osimertinib) block EGFR's internal signaling switch.
- Cell-penetrating peptides (here polyarginine peptides like R12) help molecules enter cells.
- Endocytosis and lysosomes: cells take in surface proteins in bubbles, which fuse with acidic lysosomes that break them down; bafilomycin A1 blocks this acidification.
- Fusion protein: a single engineered protein combining an antibody with a peptide.
- 2D cell wound-healing assays and 3D spheroids are lab models that mimic tumors more closely than flat cell layers.
- siRNA: a tool that silences a gene to reduce a protein's production.
summary.one_liner: Engineering full-length anti-EGFR antibodies (cetuximab and the blocking antibody LEI) with cell-penetrating arginine-rich peptides yields recombinant fusion proteins that promote EGFR lysosomal degradation and enhance growth inhibition of NSCLC cells in 2D and 3D models, alone and with EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors.
summary.plain: Many cancer drugs that target the EGFR protein only block its signaling, leaving the protein sitting on the cell surface. This study attaches short peptides that help cells take in material to antibodies against EGFR, so the antibody pulls the receptor inside the cell where it is broken down. In lung cancer cell cultures and 3D clumps of cells, the engineered fusion proteins reduced EGFR levels and slowed growth more than the unmodified antibodies, especially when combined with EGFR kinase inhibitors.
summary.why: It offers a possible complementary approach to kinase inhibitors: removing the target protein rather than only blocking it, which may matter for drug resistance in lung cancer. The text reports laboratory and 3D culture results only, so whether this works in animals or patients is unknown.

title: Internalizing-peptide engineering converts blocking anti-EGFR antibodies into EGFR lysosomal targeting degraders

abstract: Integrated single-cell analysis linking time-resolved cellular phenotypic dynamics with gene expression is essential for understanding cellular heterogeneity but remains technically challenging. Here, we report a dual photoresponsive hydrogel that combines a photoactivatable cell-trapping material with a photodegradable hydrogel, enabling light-directed single-cell capture, time-resolved imaging, and the on-demand release of selected cells for downstream gene expression analysis. This approach allows cells to be arrayed at a high density with uniform spacing, facilitating high-throughput monitoring of morphological dynamics. Cells exhibiting phenotypes of interest can be precisely retrieved by localized hydrogel degradation induced by secondary light irradiation and subsequently subjected to single-cell gene expression analysis. Using this workflow in combination with high-throughput real-time image processing technology, we directly link dynamic morphological features to gene expression and demonstrated the ability of the workflow to examine transcriptional alterations associated with invasive cancer cell behavior.
label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767535 v1

summary.background:
- Hydrogel: a water-swollen, soft gel-like material that cells can sit on or be held in.
- Photoactivatable / photodegradable: materials that change behavior or break down when hit with specific light.
- Single-cell gene expression analysis: measuring which genes a single cell is actively using, usually by reading its RNA.
- Morphological dynamics: how a cell's shape and structure change over time, often followed by microscope imaging.
- Heterogeneity: the fact that cells of the same type can behave differently from one another.
- Invasive cancer cells: cancer cells that move into surrounding tissue, a key step in spread.
summary.one_liner: A dual photoresponsive hydrogel surface that uses light to trap single cells in a uniform array, track their shape changes over time, and then photodegrade the gel locally to release chosen cells for single-cell gene expression analysis.
summary.plain: Scientists want to watch individual cells change shape over time and then check which genes those cells are switching on. This paper describes a gel-coated surface that uses two kinds of light: one beam holds cells in place in an evenly spaced grid, and a second beam melts the gel under chosen cells so they can be collected. The authors report using this to link cell shape changes to gene activity, including in invasive cancer cells.
summary.why: Separating what a cell looks like from what it is doing inside is a central problem in studying cell variation, and this workflow tries to connect the two in the same cells. The text does not report how broadly the approach has been tested, so its wider usefulness remains to be seen.

title: Dual photoresponsive hydrogel surfaces enabling integrated single-cell analysis of morphology and gene expression

abstract: Sample-driven cross-reactivity remains a fundamental bottleneck for sensitive and selective biosensing in complex biological environments, particularly in microfluidic systems where high surface-to-volumes ratios amplify non-specific interactions. Here, we address this challenge with a one-step, biomimetic surface functionalization strategy based on engineered lipid-based nanocarriers that self-assemble within minutes into immunoassay-ready, antifouling interfaces that couple pegylated-lipid passivation with biorthogonal, site-specific probe conjugation. This approach enables rapid, tuneable, and reproducible surface functionalization, which suppresses sample-specific cross-reactivity even in undiluted serum, and supports direct, label-free digital biosensing assays directly in native biological environments. When integrated into an optofluidic platform combining digital in-line holography and microfluidics, this approach allows time-resolved quantification of tetraspanin-positive extracellular vesicle secretion dynamics from two-dimensional and three-dimensional lung cancer cell models using 50 {\mu}L of sample within 10 min, without isolation or purification. Because the presented surface functionalization proceeds via self-assembly rather than covalent surface modification, this one-step modular-approach is intrinsically decoupled from device fabrication and applies to both glass and PDMS, coating the entire microfluidic channel, thereby establishing a general route for integrating biomimetic nanostructures into robust, high-performance immunoassays, advancing biosensing beyond end-point measurements, and towards rapid and continuous real-time monitoring.
label: arXiv:2611.27422v1

summary.background:
- Biosensor: a device that detects a specific molecule or particle, often by using a capture probe on a surface.
- Non-specific binding (fouling): unwanted sticking of proteins or other molecules to a surface, which creates false signals.
- Lipid-based self-assembly: fat-like molecules that spontaneously organize into a layer on a surface without chemical reactions.
- PEGylated lipids: fat molecules carrying a polyethylene glycol chain that repels proteins and helps surfaces resist sticking.
- Microfluidics: handling tiny volumes of fluid in channels a fraction of a millimetre wide.
- Digital in-line holography: a lens-free imaging method that records interference patterns to count and size particles.
- Extracellular vesicles: small membrane bubbles that cells release, often studied as messengers or disease markers; tetraspanins are surface proteins used to identify them.
summary.one_liner: A one-step, self-assembling lipid-polymer coating for microfluidic channels that suppresses non-specific binding in undiluted serum and enables label-free digital holographic counting of tetraspanin-positive extracellular vesicles from lung cancer cell models.
summary.plain: Medical sensing devices often give false signals because proteins and other molecules in blood or serum stick to their surfaces. This paper describes a simple coating, built from fat-like molecules that assemble themselves within minutes, that makes the inside of tiny fluid channels resist this sticking and still lets test molecules attach where intended. The authors used it with a microscope-based imaging setup to track tiny cell-released particles (extracellular vesicles) over time from lung cancer cells, using 50 microlitres of sample without first purifying it.
summary.why: Real-time, continuous monitoring of biological samples would be more useful than one-off end-point tests, and this coating is presented as simple and compatible with both glass and PDMS plastic devices. The text does not give comparison benchmarks or independent validation, so its practical reach beyond these experiments is uncertain.

title: One-Step Self-Assembling Lipopolymer Coatings Enable Direct Longitudinal Biosensing in Native Biological Matrices

abstract: Pathological transitions in nervous tissue, including epileptiform discharges and cortical spreading depolarization, depend on the interplay between cellular and interstitial mechanisms. We develop a biophysically detailed two-dimensional model of the neurogliovascular unit (NGVU) integrating neuronal populations in the Hodgkin-Huxley formalism, astrocyte-regulated extracellular potassium dynamics, extracellular neurotransmitter spillover, and noradrenergic neuromodulation. Numerical simulations show that inhibitory interneurons enter depolarization block (DB) at significantly lower extracellular potassium concentrations and stimulation intensities than pyramidal neurons. Early loss of inhibition shifts the local excitation-inhibition balance and triggers network hyperexcitability. In the spatially extended network, exceeding a critical stimulation threshold induces a transition from heterogeneous but spatially uniform firing to network fragmentation into stable active microclusters with self-sustained high-frequency firing. Pyramidal neurons with lower excitatory synaptic input receive less recurrent excitation, which protects them from DB. By continuously releasing potassium ions and glutamate into the extracellular space, pyramidal neurons drive strong depolarization in more densely connected neighbors and push them into deep DB. Simulations of localized astrocytic dysfunction predict a spatial limit for potassium clearance defects. Small damaged cores are fully compensated by diffusion and uptake by surrounding healthy astrocyte units. However, above a critical damage size, activity-dependent potassium buildup and firing positive feedback disrupt homeostasis in surrounding units, promoting persistent depolarized centers with self-sustained, spatially segregated pathological activity.
label: arXiv:2611.27847v1

summary.background:
- Neurons communicate through electrical spikes; "firing" means producing spikes.
- Hodgkin-Huxley model: a standard mathematical description of how neurons generate spikes from ion currents.
- Depolarization block: a state where a neuron is pushed so far from its resting voltage that it can no longer fire.
- Extracellular potassium: excess potassium outside cells raises neuronal excitability; astrocytes normally clear it.
- Excitation vs. inhibition: pyramidal neurons excite the network, interneurons calm it; their balance governs stability.
- Glutamate spillover: neurotransmitter leaking beyond synapses to affect neighboring cells.
- Neuromodulation (noradrenergic): chemical signals from norepinephrine that tune neuron activity.
- Microclusters: small, spatially separated groups of cells firing persistently.
summary.one_liner: A spatial computational model of a neuron–astrocyte–vascular unit shows how inhibitory interneurons lose firing first under high extracellular potassium, how stimulation can fragment a network into self-sustaining active microclusters, and how a damaged astrocyte region can destabilize surrounding healthy tissue once it exceeds a critical size.
summary.plain: This paper studies how brain tissue can slip into harmful patterns such as seizure-like bursts and spreading waves of depolarization, where cells become electrically stuck. Using a detailed computer simulation of a two-dimensional patch of neurons, support cells called astrocytes, and blood-vessel-linked units, the authors found that inhibitory cells switch off before excitatory pyramidal cells, and that strong stimulation breaks the network into small clusters of persistently overactive cells. They also report that a small area of faulty astrocyte potassium clearance is compensated by healthy neighbors, but a larger damaged area can tip surrounding tissue into lasting pathological activity.
summary.why: Epileptiform discharges and spreading depolarization are serious events in conditions such as seizures and stroke, and the model offers a testable account of how local astrocyte damage could spread into wider dysfunction. As a purely simulation study, its predictions depend on the chosen model parameters and would need experimental checking before any clinical relevance can be claimed.

title: Self-organized fractional silencing of pyramidal neurons under global depolarization in a spatial neuron-glial microcircuit model

abstract: Background. Clinical diagnosis often relies on a snapshot: a single measurement interpreted against a population threshold. Repeated (longitudinal) measurements, however, may reveal an individual's typical level and how it changes over time. Extracting this information is challenging when measurements are sparse and biological fluctuations may resemble sustained changes. Using data from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA), we investigated whether individual glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) trajectories improved the prediction of incident diabetes beyond the most recent measurement, whether they were associated with incident diabetes, and how reliably they could be estimated. Methods. In this secondary analysis of a prospective cohort study, we analysed venous HbA1c measured approximately every four years in ELSA, with a longer final interval of about seven years. A linear mixed model estimated each person's usual HbA1c level and rate of change (personal slope) from their measurements before each diabetes-free health visit, with model parameters estimated in other participants (cross-fitting). We derived four longitudinal features: deviation from the person's usual level, personal slope, change since the last measurement, and the forecast probability that the next HbA1c reaches the diagnostic threshold for diabetes. We evaluated the associations of these features with incident diabetes and their incremental predictive value beyond baseline HbA1c and clinical risk factors in internal, cross-fitted validation, compared predictive performance with a self-supervised Transformer, and modelled within-person variation as serially correlated drift (an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process) to assess how reliably personal slopes can be recovered under different measurement schedules. Results. The analysis included 5,828 diabetes-free baseline visits from 3,603 participants, of which 234 were followed by incident diabetes. Neither the engineered longitudinal features nor a Transformer that also used additional clinical variables improved discrimination beyond baseline HbA1c and clinical risk factors (difference in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, {Delta}AUC, -0.002 to +0.010; all 95% confidence intervals [CIs] including zero). The estimated personal slope was nevertheless associated with incident diabetes after adjustment for baseline HbA1c, age and other clinical factors (odds ratio [OR] per standard deviation [SD] 1.18, 95% CI 1.02--1.36, and 1.39, 1.11--1.74, among visits with at least two earlier HbA1c values), whereas deviation from the person's usual level was not (OR 0.99, 95% CI 0.81--1.21). In the drift model, serially correlated fluctuations accounted for 77--81% of residual within-person variance, although the estimated temporal structure was sensitive to the treatment of the first HbA1c values at or above the diagnostic threshold. Under this model, persistent individual trends were difficult to distinguish from slowly varying fluctuations: with the intercept-slope correlation set to zero, estimated and underlying slopes correlated weakly for four-yearly measurements over up to 12 years (r [≤] 0.26), and more frequent measurements improved this little. Conclusions. Estimated personal HbA1c slopes carried adjusted prognostic information beyond baseline HbA1c and clinical factors, but longitudinal features, including those learned by a Transformer, did not clearly improve prediction. The drift model suggests that slowly varying within-person fluctuations may limit the reliable estimation of individual slopes from sparse measurements, and that longer observation histories are more informative than more frequent measurement. Whether personal laboratory histories improve prediction depends not only on their association with disease, but also on how reliably individual change can be recovered from the available measurements.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.26368578 v1

summary.background:
- HbA1c: a blood test reflecting average blood sugar over roughly the previous two to three months; a diagnostic threshold marks diabetes.
- Incident diabetes: diabetes that develops during follow-up, not present at the start.
- Prospective cohort: a group of people followed over time, with measurements taken repeatedly.
- Linear mixed model: a statistical model that estimates each person's typical level and rate of change while borrowing information across people.
- Cross-fitting: fitting model parameters on other participants to avoid overfitting to the person being predicted.
- AUC (area under the ROC curve): a 0 to 1 score of how well a method ranks people who will and will not develop the condition; 0.5 is chance.
- Transformer: a neural network architecture, here trained on the lab sequences, used as a comparison method.
- Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process: a model of random fluctuations that drift back toward an average and are correlated over time, used to mimic biological noise.
- Odds ratio per SD: how much the odds of diabetes change for each standard-deviation increase in a measure.
summary.one_liner: In English older adults (ELSA), individual HbA1c trajectories gave modest adjusted association with incident diabetes but did not improve prediction beyond baseline HbA1c, and a drift model suggests personal slopes are hard to recover from sparse measurements.
summary.plain: This study asks whether tracking a person's blood sugar marker (HbA1c) over several years predicts who will develop diabetes, better than a single test result. Using repeated measurements from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing, the researchers found that a person's personal upward or downward trend was linked to later diabetes after adjustment, but adding these trend features did not clearly improve prediction overall. They also found that slow natural fluctuations make individual trends hard to pin down when tests are spaced years apart.
summary.why: It bears on how doctors might use repeated routine lab results rather than a single snapshot, and on the limits of such data for personal risk estimates. The text is an observational secondary analysis of one cohort, so its findings are measured and not a basis for changing clinical practice.

title: Personal HbA1c trajectories and incident diabetes: association, prediction and observability in the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing

abstract: Importance: Dementia prevention frameworks treat depression as a leading modifiable risk factor, but cohort estimates of the association vary widely; whether this variation reflects how cognitive outcomes are ascertained is unknown. Objective: To examine whether associations between depressive symptom trajectories and incident cognitive impairment vary by outcome ascertainment rigor. Design, Setting, and Participants: This harmonized cohort study included 91,043 adults aged 50 years or older from 4 national longitudinal aging cohorts (CHARLS [China], HRS [US], ELSA [England], and SHARE [16 European countries]); baseline waves spanned 2006 to 2011, with follow-up through 2023. Exposure: Depressive symptom trajectory classes (persistent low, persistent high, incident worsening, remitting) derived using group-based trajectory modeling. Main Outcomes and Measures: Incident cognitive impairment ascertained under a 5-level hierarchy of increasing rigor, from self-report (level 1) to clinical consensus diagnosis (level 5; Harmonized Cognitive Assessment Protocol [HCAP]). Cohort-specific Cox models were pooled by random-effects meta-analysis; meta-regression tested ascertainment rigor as a moderator of heterogeneity. Results: Under nonadjudicated outcomes, the incident-worsening trajectory was associated with incident cognitive impairment in CHARLS (HR, 1.31; 95% CI, 1.06-1.62) and SHARE (HR, 1.99; 95% CI, 1.87-2.13) but not HRS (HR, 1.05; 95% CI, 0.95-1.16) or ELSA (HR, 1.10; 95% CI, 0.95-1.27); the persistent-high trajectory was not significant under any nonadjudicated outcome (HR range, 1.07-1.15). Under clinical consensus diagnosis (n = 3,196), all non-low trajectories were independently associated with mild cognitive impairment or dementia (OR range, 1.66-2.29; dementia-only persistent high: OR, 3.32; 95% CI, 1.85-5.95). Effect sizes increased stepwise with ascertainment rigor (meta-regression slope, 0.314 log HR per level; P < .001; residual I2 = 0%; R2 = 100%; exploratory). Findings were robust to lagged, weighted, and competing-risk analyses; biological aging acceleration did not differ across trajectories. Conclusions and Relevance: The detectability and magnitude of depression-related cognitive risk depend on outcome ascertainment rigor. Prevention trials and burden projections relying on self-reported outcomes may underestimate the benefit of depression treatment.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.26368449 v1

summary.background:
- Cohort study: following a group of people over time and recording who develops an outcome.
- Depressive symptom trajectories: groups of people with similar patterns of depression scores over time (e.g., persistently low, persistently high, worsening, remitting), identified statistically.
- Incident cognitive impairment: new memory or thinking problems that appear during follow-up.
- Ascertainment rigor: how carefully a condition is identified, from self-report up to a clinical expert consensus diagnosis (HCAP is a standardized cognitive assessment protocol).
- Hazard ratio (HR) and odds ratio (OR): measures of how much more likely an outcome is in one group than another; values above 1 mean higher risk.
- Meta-analysis and meta-regression: combining results across studies, and testing whether study features explain differences between them.
- Mild cognitive impairment (MCI): a stage between normal ageing and dementia.
summary.one_liner: In four harmonized national aging cohorts (91,043 adults aged 50+), depressive symptom trajectories were associated with incident cognitive impairment more strongly when outcomes were ascertained with more rigorous, clinically adjudicated methods, with a meta-regression exploring ascertainment rigor as a moderator of heterogeneity.
summary.plain: Researchers asked whether the link between long-term depression symptoms and later memory or thinking decline in older adults depends on how that decline is measured. They pooled data from aging studies in China, the US, England and Europe and found that when cognitive problems were judged by self-report, the link was weak or inconsistent across countries. When judged by a full clinical diagnosis, depression-related risk appeared for every non-low symptom pattern, and the effect grew with each step up in measurement rigor.
summary.why: It suggests that differences in past estimates of depression as a dementia risk factor may partly reflect how outcomes were measured, which matters for prevention trials and burden forecasts. The authors note the meta-regression is exploratory and based on only five levels, so the pattern should be checked in other data before being relied on.

title: Depressive Symptom Trajectories and Incident Cognitive Impairment by Outcome Ascertainment

abstract: Background: Women with acute cerebral ischemia receive intracranial vascular imaging less often than men, but the value of expanding imaging is uncertain. We estimated the treatment rates and functional benefits required for additional imaging to be cost-effective. Methods: We developed a decision tree and state-transition model comparing additional imaging followed by timely endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) for M1 occlusion with current care from Ontario public-payer and US Medicare perspectives. Women-specific 90-day modified Rankin Scale distributions from HERMES were projected over a lifetime. We jointly varied the proportion of additional scans leading to additional timely EVT and the treatment effect relative to HERMES. Cost-effectiveness thresholds were CAD 50,000 and USD 100,000 per quality-adjusted life-year. Program costs represented health-care resources in Ontario and additional payments under Medicare. Results: At variable program costs of CAD 1,000 or USD 1,000 per additional scan, assuming the full HERMES effect and no additional fixed costs or pathway-related harm, expected cost-effectiveness required one additional timely EVT per 48 scans in Ontario and 57 under Medicare (2.07% and 1.74%, respectively). Treatment rates of 3.07% and 2.65% were required for a 90% probability of cost-effectiveness under these assumptions. At three additional thrombectomies per 100 scans and the same costs, treatment effects had to reach 76.9% and 67.3% of the HERMES effect. With the full effect, 1,000 additional scans at this treatment rate yielded approximately 5 additional functionally independent survivors at 90 days. Deterministic analyses restricted to 5 years increased the required treatment rates to 4.44% and 4.22%. Conclusions: Additional vascular imaging in women could be cost-effective when a small proportion of scans leads to timely thrombectomy, provided sufficient functional benefit is retained. Prospective evaluations should assess additional treatment opportunities, functional outcomes and program costs against these conditional thresholds, which depend on projected long-term outcomes.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.26368544 v1

summary.background:
- Acute cerebral ischemia: a stroke where blood flow to part of the brain is cut off, usually by a clot.
- Intracranial vascular imaging: scans (such as CT or MR angiography) that show the blood vessels inside the skull and whether one is blocked.
- M1 occlusion: a blockage in a major artery in the brain (the proximal middle cerebral artery).
- Endovascular thrombectomy (EVT): a catheter procedure that threads into the brain's arteries to physically pull out the clot.
- HERMES: a pooled analysis of randomized trials that measured the benefit of thrombectomy.
- Modified Rankin Scale (mRS): a 0 to 6 scale of how dependent a person is after stroke; scores 0 to 2 are usually treated as functionally independent.
- Decision tree and state-transition model: standard health economic tools that follow patients through possible outcomes and health states over time.
- Cost-effectiveness threshold: the price per quality-adjusted life-year (QALY) a payer is willing to accept; here CAD 50,000 and USD 100,000.
- Sensitivity analysis: rerunning the model with different assumptions to see how robust results are.
summary.one_liner: A decision-tree and lifetime state-transition model estimating how many additional intracranial vascular scans in women with acute cerebral ischemia would need to lead to timely endovascular thrombectomy to be cost-effective under Ontario and US Medicare assumptions.
summary.plain: Women with a sudden stroke caused by a blocked blood vessel in the brain are less likely than men to get a scan that looks at those brain vessels. This paper asks how much extra scanning would need to lead to a clot-removal procedure, and how well that procedure would need to work, before the extra care is worth its cost. The authors used computer models of costs and health over a lifetime, with results reported for Canada (Ontario) and the US Medicare program.
summary.why: The question matters for fairness in stroke care, since a sex gap in access to imaging and treatment is a concrete, actionable problem. The findings are conditional thresholds from modelling rather than measured outcomes, so they indicate what a future prospective program would have to achieve rather than showing that it would pay off.

title: Additional Vascular Imaging in Women With Acute Cerebral Ischemia: Thresholds for Cost-Effectiveness

abstract: Introduction: Lack of access to essential health services has remained a significant public health challenge in sub-Saharan Africa. The conventional health service delivery models often fail to account for the mobility patterns and socio-cultural values of these communities. These communities are frequently affected by recurrent droughts, conflicts, floods, and disease outbreaks. This study assessed the contribution of a mobile health services (MHS) delivery model designed to improve access to and utilisation of maternal, neonatal, and child health services in pastoralist contexts of Ethiopia. Methods: A multi-method embedded implementation research with a non-randomized controlled quasi-experimental study design was employed in four selected Woredas of Ethiopia. Baseline data from July 2022 to June 2023 and endline data from July 2023 to June 2024 were extracted from DHIS2. The MHS delivery model was co-designed with stakeholders, redefined communitycentred outreach sites, and established a multidisciplinary team, that was implemented monthly. The average distance between the health facility and the centre of the targeted community village was 29.6 kilometres. Data were captured from routine health service records, MHS databases, and program reports, and 143 in-depth interviews among service providers and beneficiaries. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistical methods and difference-indifferences using Stata 18, while qualitative data were coded and analysed using ATLAS.ti. Results: During the twelve months, the MHS reached 79,404 people through 190 sessions held and offered an integrated essential health service in 20 hard-to-reach villages. In the study area, ANC use was 64.0% in Chifra and 75.6% in Dasenech. In addition, penta-3 antigen vaccination improved from 66.0% to 69.7% in Chifra and from 91.2% to 102.1% in Dasenech, respectively. In the difference-indifferences analysis, the MHS significantly enhanced access to ANC follow-up and completion of pentavalent and full vaccination coverage. A Woreda-led approach, community engagement, context-tailored and timely communication, and comprehensive service delivery by a multidisciplinary team enhanced the use and acceptability of the MHS in the pastoral setting. The contribution of MHS to ensuring access and use of MNCH services ranged from 13.0% to 19.1% for continuing family planning and antenatal care, respectively. Conclusions: The study highlights that the MHS delivery model is a suitable platform that has substantially contributed to improving access to and use of maternal, newborn, and child health services in pastoral, agropastoral, and scattered settlements. Being a woreda-led, participatory codesign, community-centred approach, and context-tailored health service delivery approach enhanced the acceptability and effectiveness of the MHS in reaching the underserved community. Integration of MHS with the existing PHC system, with an innovative, sustainable financing mechanism, is recommended to ensure access and use of MNCH in hard-to-reach settings.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.26368458 v1

summary.background:
- Pastoralists move herds seasonally, so fixed clinics are often far away; the average facility-to-village distance here was 29.6 km.
- MNCH means maternal, newborn and child health; ANC is antenatal care (check-ups during pregnancy).
- Penta-3 is the third dose of a five-in-one childhood vaccine, used as a common coverage marker.
- DHIS2 is a national routine health information database used for facility records.
- Difference-in-differences is a comparison method: it compares the change over time in the intervention areas with the change in comparison areas, to estimate the program's added effect.
- Quasi-experimental means there was an intervention and comparison group but people or areas were not randomly assigned.
- Implementation research studies how a program is delivered in practice, not only whether it works in principle.
- PHC means primary health care.
summary.one_liner: A multi-method implementation study with a non-randomized quasi-experimental (difference-in-differences) design evaluates a district-led, monthly mobile health service model for maternal, newborn and child health in four pastoralist woredas of Ethiopia, using DHIS2 routine data and 143 interviews.
summary.plain: Many people in remote, mobile pastoralist communities in Ethiopia are far from clinics, so they often miss care during pregnancy and for young children. This study tested a monthly mobile health service, run through the local district, that brought antenatal care, vaccines and other services to 20 hard-to-reach villages. The authors report that over one year the service reached about 79,000 people across 190 sessions, and that it was linked to better antenatal and vaccination coverage compared with comparison areas.
summary.why: It addresses a real gap in reaching mobile and remote populations, where standard clinic-based models struggle, and it gives practical lessons on district leadership and community co-design. The design is non-randomized and the outcomes are from routine records, so the effect estimates are best read as suggestive rather than definitive; the text does not show long-term sustainability or costs.

title: Enhancing Access to and Utilization of Maternal and Child Health Service through Implementation of a District-led Integrated Mobile Health Service Delivery Model in Pastoral Ethiopia: A Multi-Method Implementation Research

abstract: Biological rhythms modulate symptoms of brain disorders, yet brain stimulation therapies largely overlook the temporal organization of pathological brain states. Harnessing these rhythms could improve therapeutic efficacy. Here, we show that circadian coordination of hippocampal network connectivity is a biomarker of therapeutic response to responsive neurostimulation in epilepsy. Using longitudinal electrocorticography from individuals with bitemporal epilepsy, we find that alignment of circadian connectivity rhythms between the left and right hippocampus predicts seizure reduction. The daily distribution of stimulation also predicts how these rhythms evolve over months. We capture these dynamics using a nonlinear Kuramoto oscillator model and demonstrate that optimizing stimulation timing in silico can improve predicted circadian network alignment. Our findings establish a cycle-based, control-theoretic framework for modelling and potentially reshaping brain network rhythms, offering new opportunities for personalized neurostimulation in epilepsy and other neurological and psychiatric disorders.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.26368528 v1

summary.background:
- Epilepsy: a condition with recurring seizures; here the focus is on seizures arising in both temporal lobes (bitemporal).
- Responsive neurostimulation: a device that detects abnormal brain activity and delivers electrical pulses in response.
- Electrocorticography (ECoG): recording brain electrical activity with electrodes placed on the brain surface.
- Circadian rhythm: a roughly 24-hour biological cycle, such as sleep-wake timing.
- Hippocampus: a brain region involved in memory; the study compares its left and right sides.
- Kuramoto oscillator model: a mathematical model of many rhythmic units that synchronize with one another, used here to describe how the two hippocampi's rhythms align.
- In silico: carried out in computer simulation rather than in patients.
summary.one_liner: Longitudinal ECoG study in bitemporal epilepsy reporting that daily alignment of hippocampal connectivity rhythms predicts seizure reduction under responsive neurostimulation, modeled with a nonlinear Kuramoto oscillator and in-silico stimulation-timing optimization.
summary.plain: This paper looks at whether the body's daily (roughly 24-hour) cycles affect how well brain stimulation works for epilepsy. The researchers followed people with seizures starting in both temporal lobes over months, recording brain activity from electrodes on the brain surface. They found that when the rhythms in the left and right hippocampus (a memory-related brain region) lined up in time, patients had more seizure reduction, and the timing of when stimulation was delivered during the day was linked to how these rhythms changed.
summary.why: It suggests that the timing of stimulation within the day, not just its amount, may matter for treatment, which could inform personalized neurostimulation for epilepsy and possibly other brain disorders. The text itself does not show that timing-based stimulation improves outcomes in patients; the timing optimization was only tested in simulation.

title: Cycle-based neurostimulation for control of circadian brain network dynamics in human epilepsy

abstract: Background: Restless legs syndrome (RLS) is a common neurological disorder with established links to atherosclerotic disease and secondary causes such as ischemic stroke. Hypothesizing that internal carotid artery stenosis (CAS) could induce secondary RLS through chronic hypoperfusion or microemboli to dopaminergic subcortical structures, even without overt stroke, we investigated the association between bilateral CAS and RLS. Methods: A retrospective propensity score-matched case-control study was conducted using the TriNetX Global Health Research Network. Cases (n=58,382) had bilateral CAS/occlusion (ICD-10-CM I65.23); controls (n=58,382) had atherosclerosis without CAS. Patients were excluded for prior stroke/TIA, iron deficiency, antipsychotic use, and other secondary RLS causes. Cases and controls were 1:1 matched on age, race/ethnicity, chronic kidney disease, peripheral neuropathy, peripheral artery disease, Parkinson's disease, and SSRI use. The outcome was RLS diagnosis (G25.81), assessed via conditional logistic regression. Results: RLS was diagnosed in 1,154 (1.977%) patients with bilateral CAS/occlusion versus 1,060 (1.816%) controls, yielding an absolute risk difference of 0.161% (95% CI 0.005-0.317%; p=0.0437). The adjusted odds ratio was 1.09 (95% CI 1.002-1.186), indicating a modest but significant association.
