Conclusion: Severe bilateral CAS/occlusion is associated with a small but statistically significant increase in RLS risk, independently of overt cerebrovascular events and known confounders. These findings support a potential vascular contribution to RLS pathogenesis, possibly through subclinical hypoperfusion affecting basal ganglia dopaminergic pathways. Prospective studies are needed to explore causality, dose-dependency, and the impact of carotid revascularization.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.26368361 v1

summary.background:
- Restless legs syndrome (RLS): a common disorder causing uncomfortable leg sensations and a strong urge to move, usually worse at rest or at night.
- Internal carotid artery stenosis (CAS): narrowing of the main arteries on each side of the neck that carry blood to the brain.
- Chronic hypoperfusion: long-term reduced blood flow to brain tissue.
- Dopaminergic pathways: brain circuits using dopamine, a chemical messenger; these are thought to be involved in RLS.
- Retrospective case-control study: looks back at existing records, comparing people with and without an exposure.
- Propensity score matching: pairing patients on many background traits so the groups are comparable.
- Odds ratio (OR): a measure of how much more likely an outcome is in one group; 1.09 means about 9% higher odds, a small effect.
- Confidence interval (CI): the range of values consistent with the data; this one is narrow and just above 1.
- Absolute risk difference: 1.977% vs 1.816%, about 0.16 percentage points.
summary.one_liner: A TriNetX propensity-matched case-control study (58,382 per group) reports a small association between bilateral internal carotid artery stenosis/occlusion (ICD-10 I65.23) and later restless legs syndrome diagnosis (G25.81), with an adjusted OR of 1.09 (95% CI 1.002-1.186).
summary.plain: Restless legs syndrome is a common condition that causes an urge to move the legs, often at night. This study asked whether narrowing or blockage of the large arteries in the neck that supply the brain is linked to getting that condition, even when the person has not had a stroke. Using a large database of electronic health records, the researchers compared patients with severe bilateral neck-artery narrowing to similar patients with hardening of the arteries but no narrowing, and found a small increase in restless legs diagnoses.
summary.why: If a blood-flow problem in the brain contributes to restless legs, that would add a possible vascular cause to a condition usually treated as neurological or iron-related. The effect is small, though, and the study is observational, so it only suggests a link and cannot show that narrowed arteries cause the condition. The authors themselves call for prospective studies.

title: Carotid Artery Stenosis is Associated with Restless Legs Syndrome in the Absence of Stroke

abstract: A diagnosis of mismatch repair deficiency (MMRd) can unlock immunotherapy treatment for a patient. However, existing sequencing-based detection methods require matched normal samples, panel-specific baselines or dedicated microsatellite loci, none of which are available to the tumour-only targeted panels that dominate routine clinical practice. Here we present captureMMRd, an open-source classifier that diagnoses MMRd using mutational signatures computed from the somatic variant calls any panel already produces. Applying a single locked model to 7,514 samples from 16 independent cohorts, spanning whole-exome, whole-genome, targeted panel and plasma cfDNA sequencing, captureMMRd achieved a pooled sensitivity of 94.36% and specificity of 99.02% against orthogonal MMR IHC and MSI-PCR testing, and outperformed microsatellite-based callers on panels with limited microsatellite content. We demonstrate that as few as 3 indels and 44 single-base substitutions are sufficient for reliable diagnosis, defining a minimum panel footprint that most clinically deployed assays already exceed. Our findings extend clinically actionable MMRd detection to the sequencing workflows of routine precision oncology, with the potential to broaden patient access to immunotherapy without new assays, baselines or matched normal samples.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.26368513 v1

summary.background:
- Mismatch repair (MMR) is a cell system that fixes copying errors in DNA; when it fails (MMRd), mutations pile up.
- MMRd tumours can respond to immune checkpoint immunotherapy, so detecting them matters clinically.
- Standard confirmatory tests are immunohistochemistry (IHC, staining for repair proteins) and MSI-PCR (checking microsatellite instability, i.e. length changes in repeated DNA stretches).
- Targeted panels sequence only selected genes; tumour-only means no matched healthy-tissue sample is sequenced for comparison.
- Mutational signatures are characteristic patterns of mutation types that reveal the processes that caused them.
- Sensitivity is the share of true cases detected; specificity is the share of true non-cases correctly cleared.
summary.one_liner: A tumour-only classifier (captureMMRd) that infers mismatch repair deficiency from mutational signatures in somatic variant calls already produced by targeted panels, validated across 7,514 samples from 16 cohorts against IHC and MSI-PCR reference tests.
summary.plain: Some cancers lose a DNA repair system called mismatch repair, and patients whose tumours have this loss may respond to immunotherapy. Current tests for it often need a matched normal sample or special genetic markers that many routine gene panels lack. This paper describes an open-source tool that spots the loss using patterns in the mutations already found in a tumour's sequencing data.
summary.why: If it holds up, it could let hospitals that already run tumour-only gene panels screen for a treatment-relevant condition without adding a new test. The text reports strong agreement with standard lab tests, but these are retrospective results across many cohorts, and real-world performance on individual panels still needs checking.

title: Panel-agnostic tumour-only diagnosis of mismatch repair deficiency

abstract: Background In randomized trials, first-line immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-based therapy has shown excess early mortality versus chemotherapy- or targeted therapy-containing regimens. ICI monotherapy is often chosen for frail patients because it is perceived as less toxic. Whether treatment benefit varies with baseline prognosis is unknown, as poor-prognosis patients are underrepresented in trials. Methods Using the US Flatiron Health electronic health record-derived database, we emulated target trials among 8,688 patients initiating first-line therapy during 2011-2023 across five comparisons: pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy versus pembrolizumab in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC; PD-L1 CPS [≥] 1 or unknown) and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC; PD-L1 TPS [≥] 50%); carboplatin plus gemcitabine versus pembrolizumab in urothelial carcinoma; pembrolizumab versus chemotherapy in dMMR/MSI-H colorectal cancer; and ipilimumab plus nivolumab versus BRAF/MEK inhibition in BRAF-mutant melanoma. Baseline prognosis was estimated with machine learning models predicting 6-month survival. Overlap-weighted pseudo-observation regression evaluated whether differences in 2-year restricted mean survival time (RMST) varied with predicted survival. Results In HNSCC, adding chemotherapy to pembrolizumab did not clearly improve RMST overall (11.5 days; 95% CI, -18.4 to 41.1), but benefit was 102.4 days greater at the 10th versus 90th percentile of predicted survival (95% CI, 40.5 to 164.3; interaction P=.001). Similar gradients favored carboplatin plus gemcitabine over pembrolizumab in urothelial carcinoma (10th-90th percentile difference, 51.4 days; 95% CI, 4.8 to 98.1; P=.03) and, less certainly, adding chemotherapy to pembrolizumab in NSCLC (73.7 days; 95% CI, -3.7 to 151.2; P=.06). Higher-risk patients in these cohorts were more often trial-ineligible. ICI-based therapy improved overall RMST in colorectal cancer (difference, 79.7 days; 95% CI, 49.5 to 107.0) and melanoma (68.3 days; 95% CI, 33.9 to 101.9), without clear variation by predicted survival (interaction P=.32 and P=.91). Conclusions Among patients with poorer prognosis, chemotherapy-containing regimens were associated with greater benefit than ICI monotherapy in HNSCC and urothelial carcinoma, and possibly NSCLC. ICI-based therapy appeared beneficial across prognosis in dMMR/MSI-H colorectal cancer and BRAF-mutant melanoma. Baseline prognosis may complement tumor biomarkers when selecting first-line immunotherapy strategies.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.26368610 v1

summary.background:
- Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are drugs that release the brakes on the immune system; pembrolizumab and nivolumab are examples.
- Chemotherapy and targeted therapy (e.g., BRAF/MEK inhibitors) are the main alternatives compared here.
- Target trial emulation: analyzing observational records as if they were a randomized trial, to reduce bias.
- Flatiron Health: a US electronic health record database of oncology patients.
- PD-L1 CPS/TPS, dMMR/MSI-H: tumor biomarkers used to predict who responds to immunotherapy.
- Restricted mean survival time (RMST): the average survival time over a fixed window (here 2 years), a way to compare groups.
- Overlap weighting and pseudo-observation regression: statistical methods for balancing groups and modeling survival.
- Interaction P value: tests whether the treatment effect differs across levels of a factor such as predicted prognosis.
summary.one_liner: A target trial emulation using US electronic health records (8,688 patients, first-line therapy 2011–2023) tests whether benefit from immunotherapy-based regimens varies with machine-learning-predicted 6-month baseline survival across five advanced solid tumor comparisons.
summary.plain: Doctors must choose first-line treatment for patients with advanced cancer, and some immunotherapy drugs cause early deaths in trials, especially in frail patients who are often given immunotherapy alone because it seems gentler. This study used real-world hospital records from the US to copy the design of trials and asked whether patients with a worse outlook gain more from adding chemotherapy than from immunotherapy alone. In head and neck, urothelial (bladder-lining), and possibly lung cancers, the answer was that patients with poorer predicted survival appeared to benefit more from chemotherapy-containing regimens, while in colorectal cancer and melanoma immunotherapy helped across the range of predicted prognosis.
summary.why: Trials rarely enroll the sickest patients, so this suggests baseline prognosis could guide treatment choice alongside tumor biomarkers. It is observational data, so the gradients are associations that may be affected by unmeasured differences between patients; the lung cancer result was not clearly significant.

title: Baseline Prognosis and Treatment Benefit From First-Line Immunotherapy Strategies: Target Trial Emulations Across Advanced Solid Tumors

abstract: Background. Short-term prediction of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in cirrhosis is complicated by the competing risk of death from liver disease. We aimed to develop an interpretable model on region-wide routine data that predicts HCC while separating competing mortality, and to compare it with established risk scores. Methods. From a region-wide cohort of adults with cirrhosis in the Andalusian Population Health Database, we trained the model on 17,177 patients with a prediction date set 12 months before their outcome, between 2020 and 2023. From one year of electronic health records before that date (demographics, liver and chronic disease codes, and eight routine laboratory tests), an Explainable Boosting Machine without interaction terms classified the following 12 months as HCC, death or liver transplantation without HCC, or event-free. We evaluated it in 20 repeats of 5-fold cross-validation against a binary model, a model with pair interactions and a model using the full health record, all on the same folds. We then applied the cross-validated models, without retraining, at the first routine encounter at which aMAP or the Toronto HCC Risk Index could be computed, and compared them with the scores in patients followed forward under competing risks, with and without a 6-month washout and with each province left out of training in turn. Findings. 771 patients (4.5%) developed HCC within 12 months and 3,314 (19.3%) died or underwent liver transplantation without HCC (3,061 deaths, 253 transplants). In cross-validation, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) for HCC was 0.734 (SD 0.018). A binary formulation, pairwise interactions and the full health record (more than 3,000 features) did not improve it; the full record lowered it by 0.024. At routine encounters the model discriminated 12-month HCC better than aMAP (time-dependent AUC 0.790 vs 0.688; difference +0.102, 95% CI +0.071 to +0.132) and the Toronto HCC Risk Index (0.761 vs 0.703; +0.057, +0.032 to +0.081), and remained better after excluding HCC diagnosed within 6 months (concordance difference +0.055 and +0.040) and when each of the eight provinces was left out of training. At equal group size, its high-risk group held as much HCC as the scores' high-risk categories, with 20-28% fewer competing deaths. Its shape functions separated cancer-specific signal (AFP rising from 2 to 20 g/L, platelets below 150 x10^9/L) from liver failure (bilirubin above 51 mol/L, albumin below 35 g/L); a binary model showed only the first. Interpretation. An interpretable three-class model on routine data outperformed established scores for short-term HCC risk in cirrhosis, while showing whether each abnormal value points to cancer or to competing death.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.26368516 v1

summary.background:
- Cirrhosis: late-stage scarring of the liver, a major risk factor for liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma, HCC).
- Competing risk: when another event (here death from liver disease or liver transplant) prevents the outcome of interest from happening, so it must be modelled alongside it.
- aMAP and Toronto HCC Risk Index: existing clinical scores that estimate liver cancer risk from routine measurements.
- Explainable Boosting Machine: a machine-learning method built from simple per-variable curves, so each input's effect can be inspected.
- AUROC / time-dependent AUC: measures of how well a model ranks patients who will and will not develop the outcome (0.5 is chance, 1.0 is perfect).
- Cross-validation: repeatedly splitting data into training and test parts to estimate performance on unseen patients.
- AFP (alpha-fetoprotein) is a blood marker often raised in liver cancer; bilirubin and albumin reflect liver function.
summary.one_liner: A three-class, interpretable Explainable Boosting Machine trained on one year of routine electronic health records predicts 12-month hepatocellular carcinoma (liver cancer) in cirrhosis while treating death or liver transplant as a competing outcome, and outperformed aMAP and the Toronto HCC Risk Index in a region-wide Andalusian cohort.
summary.plain: The study looks at who with advanced liver scarring (cirrhosis) is likely to develop liver cancer within the next year. Because many of these patients die of liver failure before any cancer appears, the model was built to score cancer risk and death risk separately. Using routine records from a large regional health database, it discriminated cancer risk better than two established scoring tools, and it shows which abnormal lab values point toward cancer and which point toward liver failure.
summary.why: Liver cancer is often found late in people with cirrhosis, so better short-term risk estimates could help decide who gets closer surveillance. The approach of using routine data and showing how each value contributes may be useful for clinical decision support, but the text is a retrospective study with cross-validation and a single region's data, so external validation and effects on patient outcomes remain unknown.

title: Interpretable competing-risk prediction of hepatocellular carcinoma in cirrhosis from region-wide routine health data

abstract: Background: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI), frailty, and fall risk often co-occur in older adults and share motor signs, yet they are screened and modeled separately. A unified model that predicts all 3 conditions from 1 sensor-based assessment could support earlier and more efficient screening, but such a model has rarely been developed or rigorously compared with separate models. Objective: This study aimed to develop a unified machine learning model that predicts MCI, frailty, and fall risk together from sensor-based motor-function data, compare it with separate single-label models, explain its predictions, and test its robustness. Methods: Community-dwelling older adults (n=79) completed a multimodal motor-function assessment with the Mizzou Point-of-Care Assessment System (MPASS), covering gait, sit-to-stand, static balance, step-down, and reaction time, with some tasks repeated under a dual-task condition. With demographic and family-history data, this yielded 59 features. Unified classifier-chain and single-label models were built with 5 algorithms across 6 modeling stages, evaluated with repeated nested cross-validation, and compared using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and paired bootstrap tests. The final model was explained with Shapley additive explanations (SHAP), and its robustness and the sufficiency of the sample size were tested with chain-input, chain-order sensitivity, domain-ablation, learning-curve, and power analyses. Results: With class weighting, the unified model had a higher mean AUC than the single-label models in 17 of 20 configurations and was never significantly worse, and it performed at least as well under nested model selection (0.615 vs 0.605; P=.58). The final extra trees model achieved a mean AUC of 0.645 (95% CI 0.569-0.722); discrimination was best for MCI (AUC 0.779, 95% CI 0.680-0.872) and lower for frailty (0.606) and fall risk (0.551). The model overestimated risk for all 3 outcomes, most for frailty. Most features (43/59, 73%), led by stride length, were shared across the 3 conditions, with consistent SHAP rankings in training and test participants ({rho}=0.99). Predicted frailty was the most important input for fall risk, and the 45 sensor features alone performed as well as the full model. Learning curves suggested that fall-risk prediction would benefit from more participants. Conclusions: A unified model predicted MCI, frailty, and fall risk together from one sensor-based assessment and performed as well as 3 separate models. It identified motor features shared across the conditions and used the link between frailty and fall risk. It performed best for MCI; with improvement for frailty and fall risk, recalibration, and external validation, such a model could support efficient screening of older adults for several conditions at once. KEYWORDS mild cognitive impairment; frailty; fall risk; machine learning; multi-label classification; classifier chain; gait; dual task; explainable artificial intelligence; Shapley additive explanations.
label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.26368462 v1

summary.background:
- Mild cognitive impairment (MCI): early memory or thinking decline that is not yet dementia.
- Frailty: a state of low physical reserve and weakness that raises vulnerability to health problems.
- Fall risk: the likelihood that a person will fall, which is often assessed through movement tests.
- Machine learning classifier: a program that learns patterns from labeled examples to predict a category.
- Multi-label classification: predicting several yes/no conditions for the same person at once, instead of one.
- AUC (area under the ROC curve): a 0.5 score means chance-level discrimination and 1.0 means perfect separation.
- Cross-validation: a way of testing a model on data it was not trained on, to estimate real-world performance.
- SHAP: a method that shows how much each input feature pushed a prediction up or down.
- Dual-task condition: a movement test done while also performing a mental task, which can reveal hidden problems.
summary.one_liner: A small study (n=79 community-dwelling older adults) tests a single multi-label machine learning model that predicts mild cognitive impairment, frailty and fall risk together from sensor-based motor tests, comparing it with separate single-label models and probing its explanations and robustness.
summary.plain: Older adults often have memory decline, physical frailty and a higher risk of falls at the same time, and these are usually screened separately. This paper asks whether one model, built from a single sensor-based movement assessment (walking, standing up from a chair, balance, stepping, and reaction time, some done while doing a second task), can flag all three. The authors report that the combined model performed about as well as three separate models, with its best accuracy for memory impairment and weaker results for frailty and fall risk.
summary.why: Screening several age-related conditions in one short test could make checkups quicker and cheaper if the approach holds up. The text reports only modest accuracy (overall mean AUC 0.645) and a small sample, and the authors themselves say recalibration and external validation are needed before any clinical use.

title: Unified Machine Learning Model for Early Detection of Mild Cognitive Impairment, Frailty, and Fall Risk Using Multimodal Motor-Function Data

abstract: We provide the first economy-wide and cross-AI model evidence on the effects of agentic AI on labor demand. We combine proprietary OpenRouter data covering about two quadrillion tokens of realized AI consumption (2 percent of global AI token consumption) across more than 400 AI models, including 1.1 quadrillion agentic tokens, with the full text of 34.8 million U.S. job postings for public firms from Lightcast. We compute our measure of firm-level exposure to aggregate agentic AI consumption (agentic beta) using the comovement of U.S. public firms' stock returns with realized weekly aggregate agentic AI token consumption. We find that a one-standard-deviation increase in a firm's exposure to agentic AI predicts 2.11 percent lower growth in job postings over the next six months and 3.20 percent over nine months. We then conduct an event study based on the release of Claude Code 2.0, which significantly expanded the capabilities of AI agents, and show that a one-standard-deviation higher pre-release exposure to agentic AI predicts 4.73 percent lower posting growth over six months post the release. Furthermore, we show that the decrease in job postings is concentrated among non-senior jobs and is statistically insignificant for senior jobs. In contrast, we find no statistically significant relation between broad AI realized consumption exposure and subsequent job posting growth once agentic exposure is controlled for. Finally, we validate our market-implied agentic exposure measure using independent evidence from firms' mentions of AI deployment in securities filings and earnings calls.
label: arXiv:2611.27210v1

summary.background:
- Job postings: openings firms advertise; their growth is used as an early signal of hiring demand.
- AI agents: AI systems that plan and take multi-step actions (e.g., writing and running code), as opposed to answering a single prompt.
- Tokens: the chunks of text an AI model reads and writes; total token counts are a proxy for how much AI is being used.
- Stock-return comovement ("beta"): how strongly a firm's share price moves with a market-wide factor; here, with aggregate agentic AI usage.
- Event study: comparing outcomes before and after a specific event (here, the Claude Code 2.0 release) to isolate its effect.
- Standard deviation: a unit of spread; the results are reported per one-standard-deviation difference in exposure.
- Senior vs. non-senior jobs: a split by seniority level used to see which roles are affected.
summary.one_liner: Using OpenRouter token-consumption data and Lightcast job postings, the paper estimates how firm-level exposure to agentic AI (measured via stock-return comovement with aggregate agentic token use) predicts subsequent declines in U.S. public-firm job postings, including an event study around the Claude Code 2.0 release.
summary.plain: The paper asks whether AI agents, software that carries out multi-step tasks on its own, are reducing the number of job openings at companies. The authors track how much AI is actually being used across many models, and how each public company's stock moves with that usage, to rank firms by how exposed they are. They find that more exposed firms post fewer new jobs in the following months, and that the drop is concentrated in non-senior roles.
summary.why: Most earlier work on AI and jobs uses occupation exposure scores or survey data, so a firm-level, usage-based measure tied to agents is a new angle. It bears on the wider debate about whether AI is substituting for entry-level or routine white-collar work, though the text alone does not establish causation beyond the event-study design.

title: The Rise of Agents and the Human Labor Market

abstract: This paper addresses the normative question of whether one should condition on the data when performing robust Bayesian analysis under partial identification. We provide an ex ante representation of the conditional Gamma-minimax criterion and show that it can violate Aumann plausibility, a set-valued generalization of the rational expectations property. Our main characterization result establishes that Aumann plausibility holds if and only if the decision maker's prior set exhibits partially identified ambiguity. The latter condition requires the prior set to equal the Aumann expectation of a random set of distributions supported on the parameter's identified sets. We interpret these results as suggesting that conditional Gamma-minimax should only be used under partially identified ambiguity. The implications for various robust Bayesian methods are discussed.
label: arXiv:2602.07634v3

summary.background:
- Partial identification: data only narrow an unknown parameter to a set of values (an "identified set"), not a single value.
- Prior: a probability distribution expressing beliefs before seeing data; a "prior set" is a collection of such distributions.
- Robust Bayesian analysis: reasoning with a set of priors instead of one, to guard against dependence on a single belief.
- Gamma-minimax: a decision rule that picks the action with the best worst-case expected outcome across the prior set.
- Conditioning on the data: updating each prior in the set using Bayes' rule after observing data.
- Aumann expectation: the set-valued analogue of an average, taken over a random set of distributions.
- Aumann plausibility: a set-valued version of the rational expectations idea that beliefs should be consistent with the true data-generating process.
summary.one_liner: The paper asks whether conditional Gamma-minimax (a robust Bayesian rule that conditions on observed data) satisfies Aumann plausibility under partial identification, and characterizes when it does via "partially identified ambiguity" in the prior set.
summary.plain: When data cannot pin down an unknown quantity exactly, analysts use a set of possible prior beliefs rather than a single one. This paper asks whether it is sensible to update that set of beliefs using the observed data, and finds that a common updating rule can break a natural consistency requirement. The authors say the requirement holds only when the set of priors has a specific structure they call partially identified ambiguity.
summary.why: Robust Bayesian methods are widely used when models are only partly identified, so the question of whether to condition on data affects how such results are reported. The text does not show how widely these methods are adopted or what practical errors follow, so the practical stakes are unclear from this abstract alone.

title: Partially Identified Ambiguity

abstract: Many institutions let incumbents exchange positions while allocating announced vacancies by priority, withdrawing positions released by vacancy recipients. A policy specifies permitted exchanges, vacancy eligibility, and priorities. A strategy-proof, individually rational rule protecting exchange rights and vacancy priorities exists precisely for policies without conflict cycles. Restricting protection to first choices does not enlarge this class. We introduce the propose-and-trade rule, which satisfies these properties and selects the applicant-optimal core allocation under every conflict-free policy. We identify when propose-and-trade is the unique strategy-proof, individually rational rule protecting first choices. These axioms characterize deferred acceptance and top trading cycles in their classic settings. Under a policy with a conflict cycle, propose-and-trade is manipulable but protects exchange rights and first-choice claims. Replacing it with any strategy-proof rule makes some applicant worse off at some profile. We show when priority reform alone can eliminate conflict cycles and when eligibility or exchange permissions must change.
label: arXiv:2611.27684v1

summary.background:
- Strategy-proof rule: a matching procedure where reporting true preferences is always best, so no one gains by lying.
- Individually rational: nobody is assigned something worse than what they already hold.
- Priorities: rankings that decide who gets a vacant position first when several people want it.
- Deferred acceptance and top trading cycles: two classic matching procedures in economic theory, used here as benchmarks.
- Core allocation: an assignment that no group of participants could improve by trading among themselves.
- Conflict cycle: a circular pattern of exchanges and vacancy claims that blocks a consistent rule.
summary.one_liner: The paper studies strategy-proof, individually rational allocation rules for policies that combine permitted position exchanges with priority-based allocation of announced vacancies, showing when such rules exist, introducing the propose-and-trade rule, and characterizing it against classic deferred acceptance and top trading cycles.
summary.plain: The paper looks at institutions, such as school or job placement systems, where people already holding positions can swap them, and where open spots go to whoever has priority. It asks when a fair assignment rule can protect both the right to swap and the priority for open spots, so that nobody gains by misreporting their preferences. The authors find that such a rule exists exactly when the policy has no "conflict cycles," and they propose a rule called propose-and-trade that works in those cases.
summary.why: Allocation systems that mix reassignment with vacancy filling are common, and the paper clarifies exactly which policy designs allow a manipulation-resistant rule. The text does not show practical adoption or empirical impact, so its significance beyond theory is unclear from the summary alone.

title: Exchange rights and vacancy priorities

abstract: Uncoupled learning, in which players know only their own payoff, are a standard model of decentralized learning toward Nash equilibrium. We study their quantum counterpart, where strategies are quantum states and, in each round, a player receives a physical copy of their opponent's current strategy and updates their own state by a quantum channel. This adds to uncoupledness a constraint with no classical analogue: every update must be physically realizable. In fact, this constraint is decisive in conjugation games, in which Bob has a strictly dominant pure strategy and Alice's unique best response is its transpose. In this work, we show some limitations of uncoupled (learning) dynamics in finding the Nash equilibrium for conjugation games. First, we prove that no autonomous, memoryless, uncoupled dynamics converge to Nash equilibrium in a family of four single-qubit conjugation games. Specifically, any memoryless channel that keeps all four equilibria fixed will leave Alice's strategy frozen. This result also extends to $4^n$ games on $n$-qubit registers. Second, we show that this barrier disappears with a small classical memory: for any finite family of $L$ pure targets, a guess-and-test rule with $O(\log L)$ classical bits converges to equilibrium, with an explicit bound on its convergence rate. Finally, we prove that no finite memory, classical or quantum, suffices for the continuum of all pure-qubit targets. Our proof of the impossibility for memoryless channels relies on Stinespring's dilation theorem, while the impossibility for finite-memory channels relies on the optimal universal-NOT (in)fidelity bound by Bu\v{z}ek, Hillery, and Werner.
label: arXiv:2611.27251v1

summary.one_liner: The paper shows that quantum versions of uncoupled learning dynamics, where each player updates a quantum strategy using only their own payoff and a physical copy of the opponent's state, cannot reach Nash equilibrium in certain conjugation games under memoryless or finite-memory rules, while small classical memory can help for finite target families.
summary.plain: The paper studies how two players, each choosing a quantum state, might learn their way to a stable outcome when each only sees their own payoff and gets a physical copy of the other's current state. The authors show that for a specific family of simple two-player games, no memoryless rule that follows the laws of quantum physics can reach the equilibrium. They also show that a small amount of classical memory fixes this for a finite set of target strategies, but not for all possible pure qubit targets.
summary.why:
It sharpens the question of what decentralized learning can achieve when updates must be physically realizable, a constraint with no classical counterpart. The connections it draws to quantum information theory (Stinespring's dilation theorem and the universal-NOT fidelity bound) suggest a useful bridge between game-theoretic learning and quantum physics, though the broader implications are not spelled out in the text.</why>
<parameter name="background">- Nash equilibrium: a set of strategies where no player gains by switching alone.
- Uncoupled learning: each player adjusts using only their own payoff, not others' payoffs or strategies.
- Qubit: the quantum analogue of a bit; a strategy here is a quantum state of one qubit.
- Quantum channel: a physically allowed way to transform a quantum state (it must be realizable by a physical process).
- Conjugation game: a game where one player's best reply is the transpose (a mathematical flip) of the other's pure strategy.
- Stinespring's dilation theorem: a standard result stating every physical quantum operation can be implemented by adding an auxiliary system and acting unitarily.
- Universal-NOT: a quantum operation that tries to flip an unknown state; its best achievable fidelity is a known limit (Buzek, Hillery, Werner).
- Memoryless vs. finite-memory: whether the update rule can use past information beyond the current state.</background>
<parameter name="difficulty">research-level

title: Stinespring's Dilation, Universal-NOT, and Limitations of Quantum Uncoupled Learning

abstract: We study a repeated quadratic incentive design game in which a leader learns a follower's private type from noisy observations of the follower's actions and uses her estimates in an affine incentive rule. The follower knows the leader's learning policy, which incorporates past observations to produce estimates of the follower's type, and can deviate from his myopic best response to influence the leader's future estimates. We ask how the follower's ability to manipulate these observations affects the leader's performance. Under a manipulation budget $C_T$ constraining the expected cumulative squared deviation of the follower's actions from his myopic best response, we establish a minimax regret rate of order $\max\{\log T, \min\{C_T,T\}\}$ for approximately rational followers. Our information-theoretic lower bound applies to a general class of causal estimation and manipulation policies for the leader and the follower. We provide a simple learning policy that achieves the lower bound. Finally, we show that under a fixed learning rule, increasing the manipulation budget of the follower can counterintuitively reduce the leader's regret.
label: arXiv:2611.26736v1

summary.background:
- Incentive design: a leader offers rewards or rules (here an affine rule) to shape a follower's actions.
- Private type: a hidden parameter of the follower that the leader must estimate.
- Regret: the total loss of the leader compared with an optimal player who knew the type from the start; minimax means the best worst-case guarantee over all followers.
- Manipulation budget C_T: a cap on the expected total squared deviation the follower may make from his myopic best response over T rounds.
- Approximately rational follower: one who responds nearly optimally, not perfectly.
- Lower bound: a proof that no policy can do better than a given rate, here information-theoretic, meaning it holds regardless of computing power.
- Log T: a slowly growing term typical of learning problems where the number of rounds is T.
summary.one_liner: A repeated quadratic incentive design game in which a leader learns a follower's private type from noisy actions while the follower may strategically deviate from myopic best responses, giving a minimax regret rate of max{log T, min{C_T, T}} under a manipulation budget C_T, with a matching lower bound and policy.
summary.plain: A leader wants to set incentives for a follower but does not know the follower's private type, so she estimates it from the follower's noisy actions. The follower knows how she learns and may act slightly differently from his best short-term choice to steer her future estimates. The paper measures how much this manipulation, capped by a budget, costs the leader in regret, and finds a matching best-possible rate along with a simple learning method that achieves it.
summary.why: It gives a precise accounting of how strategic behavior that distorts the data a learner sees limits learning performance, which matters for pricing, mechanism design and any setting where the people being learned about can game the learner. The text does not show applications beyond this formal model, so broader relevance is uncertain.

title: Learning under Bounded Manipulation for Quadratic Incentive Design

abstract: This paper develops a Solvency II-based pricing framework for structural longevity risk in incomplete longevity markets. The valuation scheme relies on the Cost-of-Capital principle underlying the Risk Margin and combines it with a continuous-time affine mortality model. Mortality dynamics are specified in calendar time, with age-dependent mortality patterns linked to a latent longevity factor driving long-term mortality improvements. The affine structure preserves closed-form survival probabilities and provides a tractable basis for repeated Best Estimate, Solvency Capital Requirement and Risk Margin calculations. We derive the conditional distribution of one-year discounted Best Estimate variations, obtaining analytical expressions for their asymmetry and Value-at-Risk under the Gaussian affine specification. Within this setting, we introduce a stress-based assessment by applying adverse shocks to the deterministic parameters governing the longevity trend. The trend-based stress is compared with a mortality-level stress and with a Value-at-Risk-based capital assessment. The methodology links stochastic mortality modelling, prudential capital valuation and longevity-linked payoff assessment within a unified actuarial framework. A numerical application based on Belgian mortality data illustrates the implementation and shows that the mortality-level stress produces substantially larger scenario-based capital-cost measures than the trend-based stress. These findings highlight the sensitivity of longevity risk valuation to the specification of adverse mortality scenarios. The approach offers a transparent and operational basis for assessing and pricing structural longevity risk under a Solvency II Cost-of-Capital perspective.
label: arXiv:2611.26670v1

summary.background:
- Longevity risk: the danger that people live longer than an insurer or pension fund has assumed, so payouts last longer than planned.
- Solvency II: the European Union regulatory regime for insurers, which sets how much capital they must hold.
- Best Estimate: the probability-weighted present value of future cash flows, without a safety margin.
- Solvency Capital Requirement (SCR) and Risk Margin: the capital buffer for severe losses, and the extra charge reflecting the cost of holding that capital for others to pay for.
- Cost-of-Capital principle: the Risk Margin is the annual cost of the capital held, discounted over time.
- Affine mortality model: a model where mortality rates depend on a hidden (latent) factor in a way that keeps calculations, such as survival probabilities, in simple closed form.
- Value-at-Risk (VaR): a loss level not expected to be exceeded at a given confidence level.
- Incomplete market: a market where some risks cannot be fully hedged or traded away.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes a Solvency II Cost-of-Capital pricing framework for structural longevity risk, using a continuous-time affine mortality model with a latent longevity factor, and compares a trend-based stress with a mortality-level stress on Belgian data.
summary.plain: The paper looks at how an insurer should price the risk that people live longer than expected, a risk that matters for pension and annuity books. It builds a pricing method that follows the European insurance rules (Solvency II) for holding capital against that risk, using a mathematical model of how mortality changes over time. On Belgian mortality data, the authors find that stressing the mortality level produces much larger capital-cost figures than stressing the long-run trend.
summary.why: Longevity risk is a major concern for insurers and pension funds, and the paper ties together mortality modelling and prudential capital rules. The text shows that the choice of adverse scenario changes the result a lot, which is a useful point for regulators and practitioners; its wider practical impact is not established from the abstract alone.

title: A Solvency II-Based Framework for Pricing Structural Longevity Risk under an Affine Mortality Model

abstract: Risk sharing is usually viewed as beneficial for risk-averse agents facing independent risks with finite means, but this situation can be reversed for infinite-mean losses. In this paper, we explore the effects of risk sharing for positively dependent infinite-mean losses using background risk models. Under both linear and conditional mean risk sharing, we show that risk sharing of infinite-mean losses can increase the risk in the sense of usual stochastic order. Our results cover classical multivariate loss distributions, including the Pareto-Clayton and the Fr\'echet-Gumbel models. For linear risk sharing, we further derive stochastic dominance relations between diversified portfolios, including those with Pareto marginals coupled by convex mixtures of commonly used Archimedean copulas. For conditional mean risk sharing, we additionally discuss peakedness and stochastic order relations for stable distributions. Consequently, under the stated conditions, retaining the original risk or a less diversified portfolio is preferred under every law-invariant monotone risk measure that is well defined for infinite-mean models.
label: arXiv:2611.27485v1

summary.background:
- Risk sharing: splitting a total loss among several agents, e.g., through linear or conditional-mean allocation rules.
- Background risk: an extra independent source of uncertainty that affects every agent's wealth.
- Infinite-mean (heavy-tailed) losses: distributions such as Pareto where the average loss is unbounded, so usual averages and variances do not exist.
- Positive dependence and copulas: a copula is a function describing how variables move together, separate from their individual distributions; Archimedean copulas (e.g., Clayton, Gumbel-type) are common examples.
- Stochastic order: one risk is "larger" than another if it takes bigger values with higher probability across all thresholds.
- Law-invariant monotone risk measure: a rule for scoring risk that depends only on the distribution and gives higher scores to larger losses.
- Stable distributions and peakedness: stable laws generalize the normal and allow heavy tails; peakedness compares how concentrated a distribution is around its center.
summary.one_liner: The paper studies when risk sharing among agents with positively dependent infinite-mean losses, modeled with background risk, can increase total risk in the usual stochastic order, under linear and conditional mean sharing rules.
summary.plain: The paper asks whether pooling and splitting a risk among several people, which normally makes things safer, can backfire when the possible losses are so heavy-tailed that their average size is effectively infinite. The authors show that under the stated conditions, sharing such losses can make the overall risk larger, and they check this for common heavy-tailed multivariate models. In that setting, keeping the original risk or a less diversified split is preferred under any law-invariant monotone risk measure that works for infinite-mean models.
summary.why: Risk sharing is a basic idea in insurance and finance, and the usual argument that diversification helps assumes finite averages. This work points to a specific setting where that assumption fails, which matters for pricing and regulating heavy-tailed risks; the text itself does not go beyond the stated results, so wider practical impact is unclear.

title: Risk sharing for background risk models with infinite mean

abstract: Portfolio risk is not limited to the variance of returns. The moments of portfolio returns depend directly on the covariance matrix and higher-order co-dependences (coskewness, cokurtosis, etc.). In practice, however, these objects are extremely noisy, especially for large portfolios. Here we introduce filtering methods based on tensor decompositions that extend cross-validated covariance cleaning and the Average Oracle methodology to even-order co-moment tensors. Using returns on historical Russell 1000 constituents, we find that the proposed filters improve out-of-sample estimation accuracy relative to sample estimators, both for correlation and cokurtosis tensors, as measured by relative squared Frobenius errors. These improvements translate into lower relative errors on portfolio volatility and kurtosis, and into lower out-of-sample volatility and kurtosis when the portfolio objective penalizes both variance and the fourth moment.
label: arXiv:2611.27274v1

summary.background:
- Portfolio returns have a variance (volatility), which is the second moment, and a kurtosis, which is the fourth moment and reflects how heavy the tails are.
- A covariance matrix records how pairs of assets move together; coskewness and cokurtosis extend this to three- and four-way co-movements, stored in tensors (multi-dimensional arrays).
- "Noisy" estimates come from limited historical data; with many assets, sample estimates can be unreliable.
- Shrinkage or filtering means adjusting raw estimates toward more stable values to reduce estimation error.
- Out-of-sample testing evaluates a method on data not used to build it.
- The Frobenius error is a standard way of measuring the overall size of the gap between an estimated matrix or tensor and the true one.
summary.one_liner: The paper extends covariance cleaning methods (cross-validated filtering and the Average Oracle approach) to even-order co-moment tensors, such as cokurtosis, and tests them on large portfolios of Russell 1000 stocks.
summary.plain: Investors care about more than how much a portfolio's returns vary; they also care about how often extreme gains and losses occur. Estimating these higher-order measures from historical data is very noisy when a portfolio holds many assets. The authors develop filtering methods that reduce this noise and test them on historical returns of Russell 1000 stocks.
summary.why: The text reports that the filtered estimates were more accurate out of sample than plain sample estimates, and that this carried over to portfolio volatility and kurtosis, including when the portfolio objective penalized the fourth moment. Its relevance beyond this dataset and setup is not shown in the text.

title: Nonlinear Shrinkage for Higher Moments Estimation in Large Portfolios

abstract: Portfolio allocation is driven by probabilities of losses, not only by forecasts of the direction (up/down) of the market. A decision model such as Jev returns a probability for a yes/no question and has been reported to be well calibrated on a set of benchmarks. However, the model's calibration against realised market outcomes has not been tested. In this study, every Friday we ask whether the Nasdaq-100 will close lower four weeks later and compare a two-regime Markov-switching model estimated on data from 1990 to 2026, Jev reading weekly headlines and geolocated news features computed with spatial queries in PostGIS, and their combination. A knowledge probe shows that Jev knows events up to late 2024, so we evaluate it on 88 weeks from January 2025 onwards. None of the models predicts the direction better than the historical base rate. A key finding is that raw Jev overestimates the probability of a decline: its mean forecast is 0.48 against an observed frequency of 0.38, and its ECE is 0.10. A prior shift to the historical base rate, which uses no outcomes from the test period, lowers the ECE to 0.015. In contrast, Platt scaling, isotonic regression and the combination with the Markov model all make the forecasts worse. In a half-Kelly allocation, the raw Jev strategy returns 3.1% per year, whereas after the prior shift it returns 14.5%; a simple buy-and-hold strategy in QQQ returns 15.3% per year. The Markov model forecasts large declines (more than 10%) well, with an AUC of 0.81, and its strategy has the highest Sharpe ratio over 1999-2026. Asked about such a large decline (base rate 4%), raw Jev forecasts 16-24% on average, and the same prior shift removes this offset. The practical lesson is that decision-model probabilities must be anchored to the base rate of the market event before they are used to size positions.
label: arXiv:2611.26716v1

summary.background:
- Calibration: whether a stated probability matches how often the event actually happens (a forecast of 40% should come true about 40% of the time).
- Expected calibration error (ECE): a single number summarising the average gap between stated probabilities and observed frequencies; lower is better.
- Base rate: the long-run historical frequency of an event, here how often the index falls over four weeks.
- Markov-switching model: a statistical model that assumes markets move between a small number of hidden regimes, such as calm and turbulent.
- AUC: a score from 0 to 1 for how well a model ranks likely events above unlikely ones; 0.5 is no better than chance.
- Platt scaling and isotonic regression: standard methods that adjust raw probabilities to better match outcomes, here reported as not helping.
- Half-Kelly allocation: a position-sizing rule based on expected edge, scaled down by half to reduce risk.
- Sharpe ratio: return earned per unit of volatility taken.
- PostGIS: a geographic database extension used to tag news by location.
- Knowledge probe: a check of what events a language model was trained on, so that test weeks are after its training cutoff.
summary.one_liner: A test of whether the Jev probability model, a Markov-switching regime model, and geolocated news features are calibrated against realised Nasdaq-100 outcomes over 88 out-of-sample weeks in 2025 onward, with half-Kelly position sizing.
summary.plain: The paper asks whether a tool that gives probabilities for yes/no market questions is accurate about how often the Nasdaq-100 index falls over the next four weeks. Each Friday, the authors compare several forecasting approaches with what the market actually did, and then see what each would have returned if used to size positions. The main finding is that the raw Jev model overstates the chance of a decline, and simply anchoring its forecasts to the long-run historical base rate makes them much better calibrated.
summary.why: It shows a specific, checkable failure mode: a probability model can look well calibrated on benchmarks yet be miscalibrated on real market outcomes, and that matters when probabilities are used to size positions. The authors' lesson, to anchor probabilities to base rates, is a narrow finding from one index and one test period of 88 weeks, so its wider applicability is uncertain.

title: Are Calibrated Decision Models Calibrated on Markets? Geolocated News, Markov Switching and a System One Model for Nasdaq-100 Allocation

abstract: Intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) has been considered a promising technology in optical wireless communication (OWC) networks due to its potential to overcome the line-of-sight (LoS) blockage issue and enhance coverage. In this paper, a dynamic IRS-assisted indoor non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA)-OWC network is modeled, and an optimization problem is formulated to maximize the sum rate subject to the quality-of-service (QoS) requirements of multiple mobile users, by jointly optimizing the power allocation and the IRS mirror orientations, from which the user's decoding order is induced rather than being fixed. Since the problem is non-convex and the channel conditions vary with user mobility, conventional optimization methods may incur considerable computational overhead. Therefore, a two-stage deep neural network-deep reinforcement learning (DNN-DRL) framework is proposed. In the first stage, the DNN estimates the user's positions and orientations in real time, removing the need for perfect knowledge of the user state. In the second stage, a deterministic policy gradient (DPG)-based DRL algorithm uses these estimates to jointly optimize the power allocation and IRS mirror orientations, with the decoding order updated according to the resulting effective channel gains. The results show that the proposed framework approaches the performance upper bounds and outperforms standard DRL algorithms, conventional optimization methods, and deployments without IRS in terms of sum rate and fairness, while achieving faster convergence. Furthermore, online adaptation of the decoding order maintains higher QoS satisfaction than a fixed decoding order, particularly under high user mobility.
label: arXiv:2611.26742v1

summary.background:
- Optoptical wireless communication (OWC): sending data with light, such as LEDs, instead of radio waves.
- Line-of-sight (LoS) blockage: when a person or object cuts the direct light path between transmitter and receiver.
- Intelligent reflecting surface (IRS): a flat array of adjustable reflectors that steers signals toward users.
- Non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA): several users share the same channel at once, with different power levels; the receiver decodes signals in a set order.
- Sum rate and QoS: total data throughput across users, and minimum service guarantees per user.
- Deep neural network (DNN) and deep reinforcement learning (DRL): machine-learning models; DRL learns decisions by trial and reward, and a deterministic policy gradient method is one specific DRL technique.
- Non-convex optimization: a hard class of design problems where standard solvers can get stuck or be slow.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes a two-stage deep neural network plus deterministic-policy deep reinforcement learning framework that jointly sets power allocation and reflector (IRS mirror) orientations in an indoor IRS-assisted NOMA optical wireless network, with the decoding order adapted to channel gains.
summary.plain: The paper looks at how to keep indoor wireless-by-light connections fast and fair when people are moving and the light path can be blocked. A small set of mirrors, called an intelligent reflecting surface, bounces light toward users, and the system must decide how much power to give each user and where to aim the mirrors. The authors use a neural network to estimate where users are and how they are oriented, then a learning method to pick the power and mirror settings.
summary.why: Light-based indoor networks are a possible complement to radio, and the main difficulty is blocked line-of-sight paths for moving users. The reported comparisons (against standard learning methods, conventional optimization, and no-mirror setups) suggest the approach could help, but the text is only an abstract, so the size and realism of the gains cannot be judged from it.

title: DNN-Assisted Deterministic Policy Learning for Adaptive IRS-NOMA-OWC Networks

abstract: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) enables wireless systems to reuse communication signals for environmental sensing, potentially reducing the need for dedicated sensing resources. However, the achievable localization accuracy of communication-centric waveforms under practical hardware constraints remains an important challenge. In this paper, we experimentally investigate near-field target localization using OFDM pilot signals in a distributed communication system. We consider both coherent and noncoherent localization approaches, exploiting multistatic propagation delays and time-difference-of-arrival (TDOA) information extracted from pilot-based channel estimates. A hardware setup comprising two transmitters and four receivers was developed and configured to operate at 3.4 GHz with 198 MHz occupied bandwidth to evaluate localization performance under realistic propagation and synchronization conditions. Experimental results across 16 static target positions demonstrate mean localization errors of 19.8 cm and 18.8 cm for coherent backprojection and noncoherent delay-TDOA fusion, respectively. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of occupied bandwidth on localization accuracy of the two proposed algorithms. These findings provide experimental insights into the capabilities and practical limitations of OFDM pilot-based sensing, supporting resource-efficient localization in future ISAC systems.
label: arXiv:2611.27503v1

summary.background:
- ISAC (integrated sensing and communication): using one wireless system to both transmit data and sense the surroundings.
- OFDM: a common modulation scheme that splits a signal across many narrow frequency slots; pilot signals are known reference tones used to estimate the channel.
- Near-field: the close-range zone around an antenna where wavefronts are curved, which changes how position is computed.
- Multistatic / TDOA: using several separate transmitters and receivers and the small differences in signal arrival times to pin down a location.
- Coherent vs. noncoherent: coherent methods use the full phase of the signal; noncoherent methods use only timing or power information, which is more robust to synchronization errors.
- Backprojection: a method that maps measured signal echoes back onto a grid of candidate positions and picks the best match.
- Occupied bandwidth: the width of the frequency band the signal uses; wider bandwidth generally allows finer timing resolution.
summary.one_liner: An experimental study of near-field target localization using OFDM pilot signals from a distributed multi-transmitter, multi-receiver ISAC testbed, comparing coherent backprojection with noncoherent delay-TDOA fusion at 3.4 GHz.
summary.plain: The paper asks whether wireless signals meant for communication can also be used to find where an object is, with good accuracy. The authors built a hardware setup with two transmitters and four receivers and tested it on 16 fixed target positions. Two localization methods gave average errors of about 19.8 cm and 18.8 cm, and the effect of signal bandwidth on accuracy was also examined.
summary.why: Reusing communication signals for sensing could reduce the need for dedicated radar hardware in future wireless networks, so real measurements of achievable accuracy are useful. The text reports only static targets and one hardware setup, so how well these results carry over to moving targets or other environments is not shown here.

title: From Pilots to Position: Experimental Near-Field Localization for ISAC

abstract: Spoken dialogue synthesis aims to generate multi-turn conversational speech from dialogue scripts while maintaining speaker consistency and contextual appropriateness. However, existing models largely lack fine-grained controllability, which is critical for capturing the dynamic, context-dependent style shifts in natural conversations. While prompt-based TTS has enabled such control for single-speaker speech, existing datasets heavily rely on predefined tags, which fundamentally limits their capacity to capture open-ended styles. To address this gap, we propose a scalable pipeline for extracting conversational speech from multi-narrator audiobooks, featuring an improved two-stage alignment algorithm to preserve dialogue continuity, paired with LLM-based extraction of style descriptions directly from narrative text. We release PromptDialog, a large-scale multi-speaker conversational speech dataset comprising 8,383 hours of Chinese speech and 120 hours of English speech, with open-ended style descriptions for 79% of utterances. We further introduce PromptTTSD, a spoken dialogue synthesis model built via a prompt-aware fine-tuning strategy that integrates style prompts into text-speech interleaved sequences. PromptTTSD is an open-source spoken dialogue synthesis model that supports both zero-shot voice cloning and natural language style control. Experiments demonstrate that PromptTTSD not only maintains strong fundamental synthesis capabilities but also achieves competitive open-ended style control compared with proprietary models, and substantially improves contextual appropriateness in multi-turn dialogues.
label: arXiv:2611.27601v1

summary.background:
- Text-to-speech (TTS): software that turns written text into spoken audio.
- Spoken dialogue synthesis: generating a multi-turn conversation with several voices, not just one reading.
- Zero-shot voice cloning: copying a voice from a short sample without extra training for that voice.
- Prompt-based control: steering the speaking style by giving a text description (e.g., "calm, slightly sad") instead of choosing from preset labels.
- Audiobook alignment: matching audio recordings to their text so that individual spoken lines can be cut out and labeled.
- Large language model (LLM): an AI text model used here to write style descriptions from story passages.
- Proprietary vs. open-source: the comparison models are closed commercial systems; this model's code and weights are publicly released.
summary.one_liner: PromptTTSD is an open-source model for generating multi-speaker conversational speech from dialogue scripts with open-ended natural-language style control, trained on a new dataset (PromptDialog) extracted from multi-narrator audiobooks.
summary.plain: Current systems that turn written dialogue into spoken conversation struggle to make each line sound right for its moment, such as shifting tone as a conversation changes. This paper builds a large set of conversational speech from audiobooks, with style descriptions written in ordinary language and pulled from the story text by a language model. The authors then train a model, PromptTTSD, that accepts both the script and a plain-language style description.
summary.why: The work targets a real gap: most prior datasets only label style with fixed tags, which limits how expressive the output can be. The text reports that the model keeps strong basic speech quality, competes with proprietary systems on style control, and improves how well lines fit the surrounding conversation; the evaluation details are not given in the summary, so the size of these gains is unclear.

title: PromptTTSD: Controllable Text to Spoken Dialogue Synthesis with Open-Ended Text Descriptions

abstract: Voice cloning now needs only seconds of audio, and detectors tuned to one dataset often fail when the generator, channel, or language changes. We introduce ARCAS 290M, Neural Defend's foundation model for detecting AI-generated audio. A single frozen production model, with no benchmark-specific fine-tuning, generalizes across text-to-speech, voice-conversion, and codec-language-model generators, telephone and Bluetooth channels, recording conditions, and languages. We evaluate it on the complete official test sets of ten public benchmarks, scoring every recording exactly as released, and against commercial systems on independent leaderboards. ARCAS 290M ranks first among all systems on the Podonos leaderboard and has the lowest equal error rate among commercial detectors on ASVspoof5. It separates real from AI-generated speech almost perfectly on ASVspoof5, SpeechFake, and ShiftySpeech, and detects nearly all AI-generated speech in Hindi, Tamil, Bengali, and Telugu. On every benchmark with a published zero-shot comparison, including in-the-wild audio, partial fakes, and the conditions hardest for the field, it surpasses the strongest reported detector by a wide margin. These results establish ARCAS 290M as a general-purpose foundation for AI-generated audio detection in fraud prevention, platform safety, and media verification.
label: arXiv:2611.27784v1

summary.background:
- Voice cloning / text-to-speech (TTS): software that generates speech in a chosen voice from text.
- Voice conversion: changing one speaker's voice to sound like another.
- Deepfake audio detection: classifiers that label a recording as real or AI-generated.
- Foundation model: a large general-purpose model trained once and reused for many tasks.
- Zero-shot / fine-tuning: testing on data the model was not specifically tuned for, versus adapting it to a benchmark.
- Equal error rate (EER): a standard score where lower means the detector confuses real and fake less often.
- Benchmarks and leaderboards (e.g., ASVspoof5, SpeechFake): shared test datasets and public rankings used to compare systems.
- Codec language model: a speech generator that works on compressed audio tokens.
- Channel effects: distortion from telephone or Bluetooth transmission that can confuse detectors.
summary.one_liner: A company report presents ARCAS 290M, a frozen foundation model for detecting AI-generated speech that is claimed to generalize across generators, channels, and languages without benchmark-specific fine-tuning, evaluated on ten public benchmarks and commercial leaderboards.
summary.plain: Cheap voice-cloning tools can now copy someone's voice from a few seconds of audio, which makes scam calls and fake recordings harder to spot. This work describes a single detector model, ARCAS 290M, built by a company called Neural Defend, that is meant to tell real speech from AI-generated speech across many kinds of fakes, phone lines, and languages. The authors report strong results on several public test sets and leaderboards, though these are self-reported claims in a summary.
summary.why: Reliable detection of synthetic voices matters for fraud prevention, platform safety, and verifying media. The text, however, is a promotional-style summary without the detailed methods, error rates, or independent verification needed to judge how strong the claims are.

title: Neural Defend ARCAS 290M: A Robust Foundation Model for AI-Generated Audio Detection

abstract: Model predictive control (MPC) of urban traffic signals relies on a model of how queues respond to signal decisions, which is hard to specify and calibrate in heterogeneous networks, particularly when incidents change capacities and turning shares. Measurements add a second limitation: the controlled lanes at the stop line are often short, so queues extending upstream of them fall outside lane-level measurements. We propose GNN-MPC, a receding-horizon controller that plans with action-conditioned network dynamics learned by graph neural networks. Phase sequences are coordinated across intersections by approximate best responses, with an acceptance test that keeps the predicted cost no higher than that of the initial plan. In microscopic simulation under non-recurrent incidents, GNN-MPC reduces travel time and increases completed trips relative to all tested controllers, on a homogeneous grid and a heterogeneous 21-intersection network. Controlled comparisons on the heterogeneous network distinguish the roles of observation and prediction. With nearly as many vehicles entering the network, GNN-MPC reduces travel time by 13% relative to MaxPressure with the same upstream measurement, and GNN-MPC without the upstream representation does not reproduce its performance. Under the same traffic measurements, planner and objective, replacing the learned dynamics with calibrated store-and-forward predictors increases travel time by 31-34%. Observing hidden demand and predicting its response to control are thus complementary requirements of network-level predictive control.
label: arXiv:2611.27435v1

summary.background:
- Model predictive control (MPC): at each time step, the controller simulates several future steps under a model, picks the best action sequence, applies only the first action, then repeats.
- Graph neural network (GNN): a neural network that operates on a graph of nodes (here, intersections and lanes) and passes information between connected nodes.
- Action-conditioned dynamics: a model that predicts how the system will evolve given the control action being considered.
- Store-and-forward model: a simple queueing model where vehicles are held at a link and released downstream, used here as a baseline predictor.
- MaxPressure: a known traffic-signal heuristic that favors phases that relieve the most congested movements.
- Non-recurrent incident: an unexpected, temporary disruption such as a crash or closure.
- Microscopic simulation: software that models each vehicle individually.
summary.one_liner: GNN-MPC is a receding-horizon traffic-signal controller that plans with action-conditioned graph-neural-network dynamics, coordinates phases across intersections via approximate best responses with an acceptance test, and is evaluated in microscopic simulation under non-recurrent incidents on a homogeneous grid and a heterogeneous 21-intersection network.
summary.plain: Cities use traffic lights to manage queues, and a crash or lane closure can make those queues behave in ways that are hard to predict. This paper proposes a controller that uses a learned model of how the whole road network responds to each light decision, rather than a hand-calibrated model. In computer traffic simulations with incidents, it reduced travel time and completed more trips than the controllers it was compared with.
summary.why: Traffic signals that adapt to incidents could reduce delays, and the paper's comparison suggests that both seeing queues that extend beyond short lanes and predicting how queues respond to control matter. The results come from simulation only, so it is unclear how they would transfer to real streets; the text does not address deployment.

title: Learned Network Dynamics for Model Predictive Traffic Signal Control under Incidents

abstract: This paper introduces an event-triggered source seeking control (ET-SSC) strategy for autonomous vehicles modeled as nonholonomic unicycles. The key feature of the proposed design is the separation between the continuous probing motion required for gradient extraction and the event-triggered update of the source-seeking correction. This separation enables aperiodic computation and transmission of the correction while the periodic probing signals remain continuously active. The triggering mechanism acts on a low-pass-filtered gradient estimate, obtained by high-pass (washout) filtering, demodulation, and low-pass filtering of the measured signal, and combines a relative and an absolute threshold. Stability is proved with a time-periodic Lyapunov function constructed along the exponentially stable periodic solution of the filtered closed loop, establishing practical exponential convergence of the vehicle to a neighborhood of the unknown source. The guaranteed minimum dwell time is strictly positive and independent of the probing frequency, which excludes Zeno behavior. Unlike available Lie-bracket analyses of the forward-velocity design, the proposed averaging-based analysis accommodates anisotropic quadratic source fields with distinct spatial curvatures. The resulting ET-SSC framework therefore provides a resource-aware implementation in which the source-seeking correction is updated aperiodically while the information-generating probing motion remains continuous.
label: arXiv:2611.26802v1

summary.background:
- Source seeking: steering a vehicle toward a hidden maximum (or minimum) of an unknown signal, using only measurements.
- Nonholonomic unicycle: a wheeled vehicle that cannot move sideways directly and must steer by turning and moving forward.
- Event-triggered control: updating the control only when a measured error crosses a threshold, instead of at fixed time steps.
- Dither/probing signals: small periodic wiggles that let the vehicle estimate the local slope of the signal.
- Washout, demodulation and low-pass filtering: standard signal-processing steps that extract the slope estimate from the wiggles.
- Lyapunov function: a energy-like certificate used to prove a system settles toward a target.
- Zeno behavior: an unphysical case where triggered updates pile up infinitely fast; the paper proves a positive minimum gap between updates to rule this out.
- Lie-bracket / averaging analysis: mathematical tools that approximate the fast wiggling motion by its average effect.
summary.one_liner: An event-triggered source-seeking controller for nonholonomic unicycle vehicles that separates continuous probing motion from aperiodically updated correction, with practical exponential convergence proved via a time-periodic Lyapunov function and a positive minimum dwell time.
summary.plain: This paper looks at how a robot vehicle can find the strongest point of a signal, such as the peak of a field, without constantly recalculating its steering. The vehicle keeps wiggling in a steady probing pattern to sense which way the signal rises, but it only updates its course correction when a trigger condition is met. The authors show, using mathematical proof, that the vehicle still gets close to the source and that updates never happen so rapidly that they pile up.
summary.why: Reducing how often a vehicle must compute and send control updates can save computing and communication resources, which matters for battery-powered or networked machines. The text does not report experiments or hardware results, so its practical payoff is not yet shown.

title: Nonholonomic Event-Triggered Source Seeking
